Around the house (defensible space) - First 5 ft around the house (🖼 the three zones): nothing that burns. Firewood and lumber 30 ft away (OSFM, p. 13; the ODF Josephine County handout says at least 20 ft). - Within 100 ft: grass mowed to 4 in or less, 10 ft between tree crowns, limbs 10 ft from the chimney, no "ladder fuels" (brush under trees - 🖼 drawing). - Clean roofs and gutters; cover vents with 1/8-inch metal mesh (🖼 how embers get in); clear around propane tanks; keep the driveway clear enough for a fire engine.

🌎 Earthquake (Cascadia) and tsunami - A Cascadia magnitude-9 quake would shake for 4-6 minutes, with aftershocks for months (CREW scenario, p. 10). Drop, Cover, Hold On. - Expect landslides on mountain roads and damage to bridges. Coast-to-inland routes like US-199 are exactly the kind expected to be cut, so the valley may be isolated for a long time. - State estimates for inland western Oregon: power out 1-3 months, water/sewer 1 month to 1 year, main highways 6-12 months to partly reopen, fuel shortages (Oregon's fuel hub is near Portland) (Oregon Resilience Plan, p. 6). - Plan to be on your own for at least 2 weeks - longer in rural areas. - At the coast (Brookings, Gold Beach, Crescent City): if you feel a long quake, walk to high ground immediately. The first waves can arrive in 15-30 minutes; surges continue 12+ hours and the first is not the largest. Details: Earthquake-Tsunami\ (Living on Shaky Ground, 2 Weeks Ready toolkit, Cascadia scenario, tsunami evacuation maps for Brookings-Harbor, Gold Beach, Crescent City, Smith River). ☢ Nuclear fallout - Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Fallout is dust; put mass between you and the roof and outside walls (🖼 drawing). It loses 90% of its strength in 7 hours and 99% in 2 days (FEMA H-20, p. 8). - A one-story wood house with no basement is poor shelter. Know now where you'd go: a basement or masonry building nearby, a shielded crawl space, or a trench shelter. - Potassium iodide (KI) protects only the thyroid, from radioactive iodine - adults 130 mg, children less (FDA, p. 9). - Everything else - shielding, how long to stay in, decontamination, food, water, livestock, homemade fallout meter: Nuclear Fallout Guide and Nuclear-Radiation\. 📚 Go deeper: CDC: Get Inside, Stay Inside, Stay Tuned - where to shelter, on one page; Nuclear War Survival Skills - expedient shelters and fallout meters.

🦌 Hunting and 🎣 Fishing While seasons and tags are still enforced, the 2026 rule booklets are in Hunting\ and Fishing\ (big game, fishing) (the 2027 big game and fishing booklets come out around December 2026 - see Keeping this current). With or without rules, the units, waters and seasons below tell you where game and fish are, and when - and leaving breeding animals and spawning runs alone is what keeps them there next year. Hunting units: US-199 is the line. West of the highway (Illinois River canyon, Kalmiopsis) is Chetco Unit 27 (82% public land). East of it (Lake Selmac, Takilma, Oregon Caves, Williams) is Applegate Unit 28 (57% public land). In Cave Junction, Kerby, Selma and O'Brien, which side of the highway you're on decides the unit. North of the Rogue at Grants Pass is Evans Creek Unit 29. 2026 general seasons, for orientation (check the current booklet): western Oregon buck rifle Oct 3-Nov 6 · archery deer & elk Aug 29-Sep 27 · Unit 28 coast elk rifle Nov 14-17 and Nov 21-27 (Unit 27 is controlled hunts only) · black bear Aug 1-Dec 31 · cougar all year (quotas) - bear and cougar must be checked in at ODFW within 10 days · grouse and quail Sep 1-Jan 31 · fall turkey Sep 1-Jan 31 · spring turkey Apr 15-May 31. and Fishing\How-To (knots, rigs, casting, cleaning and filleting). Game meat safety: - Cook bear and other wild game to 165 °F inside. Freezing, curing, smoking or drying does not reliably kill the trichinella worms in wild game. - Wear gloves when cleaning rabbits and rodents (tularemia). - Shot with lead? Trim generously around the bullet path: fast-expanding lead bullets scatter fragments 5-14 in from the wound, sometimes 18 in (Minnesota DNR X-ray study, p. 6; the older 4-in rule in OSU PNW 517, p. 1 is too small). Give lead-shot meat to adults, not children or pregnant women (rule of thumb). - Don't bring deer or elk brain or spine parts back into Oregon from another state (chronic wasting disease rule). 🪤 Trapping How-to: start with the national Trapper Education Manual and the NY trapper manual (trap types, baits, water and land sets, snares, running a trapline, fur handling), then the species guides (beaver, coyote, raccoon, bobcat, gray fox). For improvised traps with no store-bought gear, see the 1907 Deadfalls and Snares (illustrated) and the snare and deadfall chapters of the Army survival manuals (Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals; FM 21-76, p. 95). Hides and furs: USDA Home Tanning of Leather and Small Fur Skins. - Check traps at least daily - animals spoil, suffer, or get taken by other predators. - Beaver, raccoon, muskrat and rabbits are the most dependable meat from traps here; wear gloves for rabbits and rodents (tularemia), and cook all wild meat thoroughly. - Don't catch your own dogs: the AFWA dog-friendly guides show sets that avoid pets. While Oregon's rules are still enforced (details in the 2026-2028 furbearer booklet in Trapping\): - License: trapping needs an Oregon Furtaker's License - that includes "unprotected" animals like coyote, skunk, opossum and porcupine. A landowner can get a free license for land they own and live on (register the land with ODFW first). - Trapper education (free, online at hunter-ed.com/oregon/trapper) is required if you were born after June 30, 1968 or are trapping in Oregon for the first time - except on your own or family land, or when controlling damage to

if you were born after June 30, 1968 or are trapping in Oregon for the first time - except on your own or family land, or when controlling damage to livestock or crops. - Every trap and snare must carry your ODFW brand number. Check traps at least every 48 hours. - Banned: toothed jaws; oversized footholds and land killing traps (size limits are in the booklet); game meat as bait; visible bait within 15 ft of a foothold set for carnivores. In the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest west of I-5 (that includes the Illinois Valley), no traps or snares hung in trees. On public land, stay 50 ft from trails and 300 ft from trailheads, campgrounds and picnic areas. - 2026-27 seasons: bobcat Dec 1-Feb 28 (needs a record card) · gray fox Oct 15-Feb 28 · raccoon, river otter and beaver Nov 15-Mar 15 · mink and muskrat Nov 15-Mar 31 · marten closed west of I-5 · fisher and ringtail closed all year. - Wolves are federally endangered here. Use coyote traps no bigger than #3 and snares with breakaways. A wolf track is about 5 in long; a coyote's is about 2.5 in (furbearer booklet, p. 16; 🖼 side by side). ⚡ Off-grid power and creek hydro Start with the US Navy NEETS modules (electricity basics, AC, circuit protection, wiring, generators) in Off-Grid-Power\Electrical-Basics, then the solar guides, then the micro-hydro handbooks in Off-Grid-Power\Micro-Hydro. Generators - Never run one indoors, in a garage, crawlspace or shed, even with doors open. Carbon monoxide kills in minutes. Keep it outdoors, away from windows and vents, and use battery-powered CO alarms. - Never plug a generator into a wall outlet ("backfeeding"). It sends power back through the lines and can kill anyone working on them. Wire into the house only through a transfer switch. - Store fuel outside living areas, in proper cans. Let the engine cool before refueling. - Engine won't start, carburetor gummed up, generator makes no power? See the Engines, Motors and Generators guide - it also covers chainsaws, rewinding motors, and turning motors and car alternators into generators. - Fuel: how long gas and diesel keep, rescuing stale or watery fuel, and getting fuel out of station tanks, drums and vehicles with no power: Fuel Guide. - EMP or solar storm: protecting solar gear, inverters and spares, and Faraday containers: EMP Guide. Sizing a solar system (Sandia and IEA guides) - Panel size (kW) ≈ (kWh you use per day ÷ peak sun hours) × 1.2. - Lead-acid batteries: count on only 40% of the rated capacity. At our latitude, plan

Panel size (kW) ≈ (kWh you use per day ÷ peak sun hours) × 1.2. - Lead-acid batteries: count on only 40% of the rated capacity. At our latitude, plan 7-9 days of storage for a solar-only system, and vent battery rooms at the top (hydrogen rises). - System voltage: 12 V under 1 kWh/day, 24 V for 1-4 kWh/day, 48 V above that. Low voltage over long wires needs very heavy wire. Sizing creek hydro (NRCan, NCAT) - Real output (watts) ≈ flow (liters/second) × drop (meters) × 9.8 × 0.5. In US units: kW ≈ flow (cubic ft/min) × drop (ft) ÷ 709 × 0.5. Example: 50 gallons/minute falling 100 ft ≈ 470 W around the clock ≈ 11 kWh a day, more than solar gives most of the year here. - Design for late-summer low flow (the flow you have 95% of the time). Size the pipe so friction eats less than 10% of the drop. Screen the intake and leave water in the creek. - A hydraulic ram pump (Clemson plans) lifts creek water uphill with no fuel or power. Firewood (OSU, heat per cord when dry): Oregon white oak and madrone ≈ 30 million BTU, Douglas-fir ≈ 21, alder ≈ 18, ponderosa pine ≈ 17. Each 1% of extra moisture costs about 1% of the heat: split and stack wood through one dry summer (two is better) and keep it covered through the rains. A good stove is 60-80% efficient; an open fireplace 10-15%. Carbon monoxide kills. Never run a generator, grill, charcoal, camp stove or a wood-gas unit indoors, in a garage or near windows. CO feels like flu without a fever. A battery CO alarm near the bedrooms is cheap insurance. A wood-gas generator keeps making CO-rich gas for ~20 minutes after the engine stops. 🧰 ARK Vault: the Ammo-Can Library Computer The ARK Vault is the whole library packed in one steel ammo can: a small computer (a Raspberry Pi), a battery, a charger, a little printer, a crank radio and an old phone to read it on. Most of the time it sits sealed, lid taped shut, protected from an EMP or solar storm. When you need it, open the lid and flip the red switch on. The phone joins the Vault's own Wi-Fi and opens the library and the AI in its web browser. No internet, screen or keyboard needed. ### The short version - Switch on, switch off. Flipping the switch off is always safe. - Lid shut and taped = protected. Lid open = in use. Never run it with the lid shut. - The phone in the can is the screen. Any other phone nearby can join too. - Hold the little red button to see how much battery is left. - Charge it from the wall with the lid open. Solar is for after an emergency (see Power and charging). - Steel can only. Plastic ammo cans don't block anything. - Practice now. Build it, test it

the lid open. Solar is for after an emergency (see Power and charging). - Steel can only. Plastic ammo cans don't block anything. - Practice now. Build it, test it with the internet off, and check it every few months.

🧰 The idea Inside the can: - the Raspberry Pi stuck under the lid, with the library drive (a small thumb drive) plugged in - the battery - the wall charger, and a solar charge controller stored for later (not wired) - a printed stand (the riser) holding the printer, the power switch and the battery meter - a crank radio and an old phone, about half charged - optional: a mesh radio under the lid beside the Pi, for texting with no cell service, with its antenna, and a pocket mesh radio taped to a second phone, packed beside the battery (see The mesh radio) - a card with the Wi-Fi name and password, and a spare roll of foil tape Outside the can: the solar panel, with nothing plugged into it. Panels survive a pulse fine (Sandia, p. 39); the danger is a pulse running down the wires into whatever they're plugged into (EMP guide). So the charge controller waits inside the can, and you wire it up only after an event. Never connect a panel straight to the battery. | | What you do | | Stored (most of the time) | Lid shut and taped, switch off, panel outside | | In use | Open the lid, flip the switch on, take out the phone. 🧭 How it works - Lid shut and taped: the steel can acts as a shield (a Faraday cage) and keeps an EMP out. Nothing is switched on. - Lid open, switch on: the Pi starts in 2-3 minutes and makes its own Wi-Fi. Phones join it and use the library. An EMP lasts only seconds, and solar storms come with hours of warning, so having it open is fine the rest of the time. - Why not run it sealed? It would overheat, phones couldn't reach it, and any wire or hole through the can ruins the shield (🖼 right and wrong ways through a shield). - The power switch just cuts the power. That's safe because the Pi is set to read-only: it never writes anything that could be left half-done. (The catch: a setting changed on the running Pi is forgotten. See Changing a setting later.) - The meter stays dark. Hold the little red button and it shows the battery's volts (top) and the amps being used (bottom). - The phone is the screen. Several phones can use it at once. The AI answers one person at a time, in about a minute.

📐 The parts to print and etch ⬇ Download the parts (ark-can-parts.zip). It has every measurement and the wiring in one file (READ-ME-FIRST.txt). - printed/: four parts to 3D-print in ABS, no supports, 3 walls (0.4 mm nozzle): - the printer riser: a stand that holds the printer, switch and meter - the wall cleat: a small strip the riser hooks onto - the Pi's base: a thin plate that sticks under the lid - the mesh radio's base (only if you add the mesh radio): a thin plate with two rails and a tab for the antenna's socket. It also sticks under the lid The parts as they print. - laser/: the ARK Vault logo, and bare-metal strips around the lid seam for the foil tape. No laser? Scrape the paint off the same strips by hand. The long sides (both the same). The ends: one band of tape goes right round the can, over the hinge and the latch.
the-parts-to-print-and-etch

1. Get the can ready 1. Bare metal around the seam: etch or scrape the paint off a strip on the lid's edge and one on the body just below it, all the way round (see the pictures above). The foil tape sticks here, metal to metal. 2. Cover every bare wire end and bolt (rubber boots, heat-shrink or tape) so nothing metal touches the can.
1-get-the-can-ready

2. The battery Stand it at the latch end, against the back wall, terminals toward the back. Bolt on the main + and - leads and the wall charger's leads, then push the rubber boots over both terminals.
2-the-battery

3. The chargers In front of the battery: stand the solar controller on its long edge, terminals toward the hinge end (stored, not wired). Lay the wall charger flat on top, with its cord coiled on top of it.
3-the-chargers

4. The printer riser 1. Snap the meter and power switch into their holes in the riser's front strip. Screw the microswitch into its slot, button up (2 × M2). 2. On the inside of the riser's leg: screw the converter to the raised frame, terminals toward the front, with short screws (M3 × 6 mm; longer ones poke through). Stick the fuse holder across the leg below it, about 1 cm up from the bottom. 3. Drop the printer into the top. 4. Stick the wall cleat inside the can's hinge-end wall, thick edge up, its top corners about 29 mm (1⅛ in) below the rim and about 6 mm from the back wall. 5. Wire it (step 6), then lower the riser into the hinge end: its leg stands beside the battery and its other end hooks onto the cleat. It lifts straight out for repairs.
4-the-printer-riser

5. The Pi on the lid 1. Fit the cooler and plug its fan onto pins 4, 6 and 8 (red, black, blue). 2. Screw the Pi to its printed base, and stick the base under the lid at the hinge end, USB ports toward the front, about 13 mm in from the hinge wall and 9 mm in from the back wall. 3. Plug the library drive into a blue USB port and the printer's cable into a black one.
5-the-pi-on-the-lid

6. Wiring The whole wiring. The 3D model shows where each wire runs. - Battery + → 7.5 A fuse → power switch → converter Input + and printer +. - Battery - → meter's thick black wire. Meter's thick red wire → converter Input - and printer -. - Meter's thin wires: black → battery -. Yellow → + after the fuse. Red → the microswitch (COM and NO) → + after the fuse. (Check your meter's own wiring sheet; some are reversed.) - Converter Output + → Pi pin 2. Output - → Pi pin 14. > ⚠ Before plugging this onto the Pi, switch on and check it with a multimeter: it must read > 5.0 to 5.25 V, with + and - the right way round. A mistake here can kill the Pi. - Fan → pins 4 (red), 6 (black), 8 (blue). - Printer's USB cable → a Pi USB port. - Route: run the Pi's power wires and the printer cable together along the front wall to the hinge corner, and up into the lid. Leave a loop of about 6 cm (2½ in) so the lid opens freely. Tie the short wire from battery + to the fuse down, away from sharp edges. All five wires go on the outer row. Pin 2 is the corner pin farthest from the USB ports. Pi

battery + to the fuse down, away from sharp edges. All five wires go on the outer row. Pin 2 is the corner pin farthest from the USB ports. Pi 5: its cooler plugs into its own fan socket instead; the power still goes on pins 2 and 14.

7. The rest - The radio stands on the floor in front of the riser, and the phone stands on its end against the front wall beside it. - If you add them: tape the pocket mesh radio to the back of the second phone, clear of the camera. The pair lies on its long edge in the slot between the solar controller and the battery, screen toward the controller (lift the wall charger to reach it). The mesh radio's antenna, folded at its joint, stands in the corner between the battery and the latch end. These are packed for storage and come out after an event. - Keep loose metal off the can's walls (CISA, p. 45).

8. The mesh radio (optional) ⚠ This part is new and has not been built or tried yet. Check the printed base against your own board before you stick it down. 1. Leave the pin strips off the board. With pins soldered on, it won't slide into its base. 2. Slide the board into the base from its USB end, screen up, until it stops. Put one M2.5 × 8 mm screw in either post at the USB end to shut it in. 3. The antenna's socket: push the screw-on socket of the thin lead through the hole in the tab, and tighten its nut on the outside. Clip the lead's small end onto the board's antenna end. Tuck the spare loop flat. 4. Stick the base under the lid beside the Pi, on the latch side: about 5 mm from the Pi's base, the antenna end about 10 mm in from the front wall, the USB end toward the back. 5. Plug it into the Pi: the short USB cable goes from the board to the blue USB port above the library drive. Run it along the lid between the Pi and the base, and tape the slack flat. 6. Keep the wall charger's coiled cord and plug toward the latch end, so nothing sits under the radio when the lid shuts.

The steps 1. Fill the library drive with the installer kit, like any library drive: ⬇ Download the installer kit (ark-illinois-valley-kit.zip) (see Get the whole library). Storage: the small card. - When it asks about customisation, choose No. - When it's done, take the card out and put it back in. 3. The green light flickers like a heartbeat while it sets itself up (5-10 minutes), then it restarts. A few minutes later its Wi-Fi appears. Changing a setting later The Pi forgets changes made while it runs (that's what makes switching off safe). - To change the Wi-Fi name or password: finish the card again (step 3) with the new ones. - Anything else needs a screen and keyboard: log in (user ark, password = the Wi-Fi password), type bash /mnt/emergency-library/OfflineLibrary/SETUP-Raspberry-Pi.sh --writable, restart, make the change, then run the same line without --writable to lock it again.

Test it 1. Flip the switch on and wait 2-3 minutes. 2. On the phone, join the Pi's Wi-Fi (Emergency-Library unless you changed it). If it says no internet, tap Stay connected. 3. In the browser (Safari on an iPhone), type http://192.168.4.1:8096. Add it to the home screen. 4. Search, open a guide, ask the AI, print something, and hold the meter button. 5. Switch off. Then do it all again with your home internet off.

🆘 Using it 1. Open the lid all the way. Mesh radio fitted? Screw its antenna on now, before the switch. 2. Flip the red switch on. Keep it in the shade. 3. Take out the phone and wait 2-3 minutes. 4. Join the Pi's Wi-Fi and open the address from the card in the lid. 5. When you're done, flip the switch off, close the lid and tape the seam again. If a solar-storm warning comes, switch off and seal it right away (see the EMP guide). Switch off when nobody's using it to save the battery; the AI uses the most power. The map: 🔧 Tools → 🗺 Map shows roads, topo lines and property lines on any phone on the Vault's Wi-Fi. 📍 shows where you are (the phone warns once; the map says what to tap), and 🖨 prints the part on screen in strips. See Offline maps. Family photos: plug a USB drive of photos into a free USB port. They show under 🔧 Tools → 🖼 Family photos & videos. Nothing on that drive can be changed.

📡 The mesh radio (optional) A mesh radio sends short text messages and positions from one radio to another, with no cell service and no internet. Every radio in range passes messages along. It needs no license. The software is Meshtastic, which is free. - One radio stays with the Vault, under the lid. The Vault powers it whenever the switch is on. - The pocket radio (the card) goes with whoever leaves, along with the second phone. - Each radio talks to its own phone by Bluetooth, through the Meshtastic app. You type and read messages in the app. The Vault's library page does not show mesh messages yet. ⚠ Antenna first, every time. Screw the antenna on before you flip the switch. A radio that sends with no antenna can burn itself out. Do these now, while there is internet: 1. Put the Meshtastic app on both phones. 2. Check each radio has Meshtastic on it and set its region to US (the app asks). The pocket card comes with it. The Vault's board may need it put on first, from a computer, at flasher.meshtastic.org. 3. Pair each radio with its phone, give both radios the same channel, and send a test message each way. How far it reaches (rule of thumb): through thick forest or hills, ¼ to 1 mile; around town, 1 to 3 miles; with

🖨 Printing on paper Anyone on the Vault's Wi-Fi can print a guide section, an AI answer or a book page on the little receipt printer. It uses heat-sensitive paper: no ink to run out. - 🖨 Print is at the top of every guide and page, and under each AI answer (🖨 Print this answer). Every book has a 🖨 button too. - Pick a size: Tiny fits the most on the paper; Small or Medium are easier to read; Large for weak eyes. The preview shows how much paper it will take. - Book pages: print the words (re-flowed to fit, least paper) or a picture of the page (for drawings and tables). A picture can be printed bigger, in strips you tape together; each strip is labelled (A1, A2, B1...) so you know where it goes. - Doses and measurements: in Tiny, check every number, or print in Small. Paper: 57 × 30 mm thermal rolls (2¼ in wide). If the paper comes out blank, the roll is in upside down. Prints fade in heat and sun, so copy anything important in pencil. Keep spare rolls cool and dark.

🔋 Power and charging How long it runs: a full battery runs the Pi for about 30-40 hours of use: a long day of use every day for a week (rule of thumb). Checking the battery: hold the meter button. About 13.3 V is full, 13.0 V half, and 12.0 V nearly empty: charge it then (rule of thumb). From the wall: with the lid open, plug the wall charger in (set to lithium). About 10 hours from empty. Unplug it when the Full light comes on. From the sun (after an event): 1. Set the controller up once in the VictronConnect phone app (battery type LiFePO4, charge current about 10 A). The BlueSolar needs a Victron VE.Direct Bluetooth dongle or USB cable to talk to the app. 2. Wire the battery first: BATT+ → battery + through the 20 A fuse, BATT- → battery -. 3. Then the panel: PV+ and PV-. 4. When done, unplug the panel first, then the battery, and store the panel outside with nothing plugged in. A 100 W panel fills it in about a sunny day. More in Off-Grid Power. The phone: charge it from any phone charger, or from the Pi's USB port while it runs. Keep it about half charged in storage. ⚠ Never charge with the lid shut, never run a cable through a hole in the can, and never

📦 Packing and sealing 1. Switch off, unplug the chargers, and put the phone back. Mesh radio fitted? Unscrew its antenna and stand it back in its corner, and put the pocket radio and second phone back. 2. Charge the battery to about half for storage, and top it up every few months. 3. Close and latch the lid, then run one band of foil tape right round the can over the bare strips (about 1 m), over the hinge and the latch, overlapping at the end. Press it down well (🖼 why seams matter). 4. Test the seal: tape a phone inside and call it. If it doesn't ring, the seal is good. (More in the EMP guide.) Store it somewhere cool and dry, not in a hot car or shed.

"Power too weak", or the AI takes minutes The Pi isn't getting a full 5 volts. It can then slow itself down to about a third of its speed, and the AI suffers most: an answer can take 10 minutes instead of one or two. Weak power can also make the Pi or its drive misbehave, so fix it even if the AI seems fine. Quick test: switch off, unplug the Pi's power plugs from pins 2 and 14, and run the Pi from an official Raspberry Pi USB-C power supply instead (never both at once). If the warning goes away, the can's power wiring is the problem. To see what the Pi is doing, open ⚙ Settings → How the Pi is doing on the phone, while the AI is answering. It shows the power, the temperature and how fast the processor is running. 1. Check the battery: hold the meter button. Under about 12.5 V, charge it. 2. Check the converter: ask the AI a question, and while it's working, touch a multimeter to the converter's two output screws. It should read 5.1 to 5.25 V. Lower than that? If the converter has a small adjusting screw, turn it up to about 5.2 V; if not, replace it. 3. Check the wires to the Pi: if the converter reads fine, the power is lost on the way to
power-too-weak-or-the-ai-takes-minutes

it up to about 5.2 V; if not, replace it. 3. Check the wires to the Pi: if the converter reads fine, the power is lost on the way to the Pi. The usual weak spot is the two little plugs on pins 2 and 14: thick wire doesn't crimp well into them. Re-crimp or solder them so they're solid, and keep the wires as short as the route allows. 4. Switch off and on again so the old warning clears, and ask the same question. A healthy Pi should start writing within a minute or two.
power-too-weak-or-the-ai-takes-minutes

Shut it down before unplugging: a Pi 5 has a power button; on a Pi 4, add a push button on pins 5 and 6. A push button on pins 5 and 6 shuts a Pi 4 down safely.

💾 Get the Whole Library on a USB Drive The full library (every book, Wikipedia, offline maps and an offline AI) is too big for a website. You copy it onto a USB drive while you still have internet. 🤖 How to Run the Offline AI The library comes with an AI that runs on the computer itself. It needs no internet, and nothing you type leaves the computer. ### ⭐ Easiest: use the Library Assistant Double-click START-Windows, START-Mac or START-Linux.sh in the OfflineLibrary folder (other devices: see Start on Any Device). Type a question. It searches every book, guide and encyclopedia on the drive, and the AI writes an answer with links to the exact pages. - It picks the right AI size for your computer. To change it, open ⚙ Settings. - Search results show up in a second. The written answer takes 30 seconds to a few minutes. - Keep the black window open while you use it. Most people can stop reading here. The rest is for chatting with the AI on its own, without the library search. ### ⚠ Remember - The AI can be wrong or make things up. Check anything about health or safety in the books. - It can't look anything up online. Its knowledge stops when it was made.

🩹 Injuries & Illness When No Help Is Coming What to do when someone is hurt or sick and no ambulance, hospital or doctor is coming - from the first minutes through weeks of nursing. It follows the newest books on the drive: the US Army's 2026 first-aid manual (ATP 4-02.11), the Joint Trauma System (JTS) guidelines for care when evacuation is delayed, and WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care. Older books are used only where nothing has changed. The books are in Medical\Field-Care\ (Trauma-Bleeding, Wounds-Burns-Fractures, Nursing-Care, Dental, Childbirth-Newborn), Medical\Manuals-PDF, Medical\Where There Is No Doctor and Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals. Medicines and doses are in the companion guide, Medical - READ ME FIRST. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Make sure whatever hurt them can't hurt you - fire, a falling tree, a downed power line, traffic. Then check the person in order, bleeding first (ATP 4-02.11, p. 52). - Life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg: tourniquet FIRST. Heavy bleeding can kill in about 3 minutes (ATP, p. 62). Older books call a tourniquet a "last resort" - that is outdated. - Never cut, suck, ice or tie off a snakebite (JTS snakebite guideline, p. 27; no ice: ATP, p. 179). - Never close a dirty or old wound. When in doubt, leave it open (JTS wound guideline, p. 10). - Heat stroke: cool them first, right now (Emergency War Surgery,

- Never close a dirty or old wound. When in doubt, leave it open (JTS wound guideline, p. 10). - Heat stroke: cool them first, right now (Emergency War Surgery, p. 428). - Keep every injured person warm and off the ground, even in summer - cold blood doesn't clot well (ATP, p. 103).

🚨 The first look: check in this order Fix each problem before moving on. The Army calls it MARCH; WHO uses the same idea as ABCDE (ATP, p. 53; WHO-ICRC, p. 49). | Letter | Check | Do | | M - Massive bleeding | Spurting or pooling blood | Tourniquet or packing (next section) | | A - Airway | Noisy, gurgling, unconscious | Clear the mouth; recovery position or jaw thrust (🖼 ATP, p. 78) | | R - Respiration | Breathing? Hole in the chest? | Tape plastic over a chest wound; lift it if breathing gets worse (ATP, p. 94; 🖼 chest seals, p. 88; Occlusive dressing) | | C - Circulation | Pale, confused, weak wrist pulse (🖼 feeling it, WTND ch. 3, p. 4) | Treat for shock (🖼 shock position, ATP p. 99) | | H - Hypothermia, Head | Cold, wet, knocked out | Insulate; watch the head | Then pain, antibiotics, wounds and splints ("MARCH-PAWS"). Recovery position (unconscious but breathing, no injury suspected): roll them onto the left side, bend the top leg forward, and rest the head on the straight lower arm with the mouth pointing down so vomit drains out (WHO-ICRC, p. 190). If the neck might be hurt, push the jaw forward ("jaw thrust") instead of tilting the head back (p. 49; 🖼 ATP drawing, p. 78; Jaw

out (WHO-ICRC, p. 190). If the neck might be hurt, push the jaw forward ("jaw thrust") instead of tilting the head back (p. 49; 🖼 ATP drawing, p. 78; Jaw thrust), and turn the body as one unit - a "log-roll" (ICRC First Aid, p. 163; 🖼 WHO-ICRC, p. 188). Recovery position; 🖼 ATP drawing, p. 79. On the side, top leg bent forward, head on the straight lower arm so the mouth drains; only when no injury is suspected (WHO-ICRC, p. 190). CPR: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, at least 2 inches deep, 100-120 a minute, letting it come all the way back up - 30 pushes, then 2 breaths (ATP, p. 95; CPR). Know its limits: - When an injured person's heart stops, assume blood loss - CPR can't pump blood that isn't there (ICRC First Aid, p. 119). - The ICRC advises 5 minutes of CPR when the cause is not an injury, and none for an injured person with obvious signs of death (p. 167). - With no defibrillator, the best chances are drowning, lightning and very cold people (general practice). Feel a cold person's pulse for a full 60 seconds first (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 221). 📚 Go deeper: ATP 4-02.11 - the whole MARCH-PAWS sequence with drawings; WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care - the ABCDE check for any sick or

🩸 Stopping life-threatening bleeding, then shock Tourniquet - arm or leg, blood spurting or pooling (ATP, p. 62): 1. Put it 2-3 inches above the wound, directly on the skin. 2. Tighten until the bleeding stops and there's no pulse below it. It will hurt badly - that means it's tight enough. 3. Still bleeding? Add a second tourniquet just above the first (often needed on the thigh). 4. Write down the time it went on (p. 63). No tourniquet? A band at least 2 inches wide twisted tight with a stick - never wire or a shoelace (FM 4-25.11, p. 48; this tip still holds; 🖼 stick-and-knot steps, pp. 49-50). Tourniquet; Combat Application Tourniquet. "Above the wound" means between the wound and the body (a diagram drawn for this guide). Where a tourniquet can't go (groin, armpit, neck - 🖼 ATP, p. 69): pack the wound. Stuff gauze or clean cloth tightly in, right down to where the blood comes from, press hard at least 3 minutes - sometimes up to 10 - then wrap a pressure bandage over it (ATP, p. 64; JTS wound guideline, p. 5; 🖼 direct pressure, WHO-ICRC p. 169; 🖼 pressure dressing, FM 4-25.11 p. 45; Hemostatic agent). The hand or foot beyond should stay warm and pink (ATP, p. 65). - Never pack a chest or belly wound (p. 64). - Leave stuck

p. 45; Hemostatic agent). The hand or foot beyond should stay warm and pink (ATP, p. 65). - Never pack a chest or belly wound (p. 64). - Leave stuck objects in. Pad bulky cloth around the stick or shard and bandage it so it can't move (p. 65). Tourniquet timing when no surgeon is coming (JTS Prolonged Casualty Care, p. 18): - Under 2 hours is the safe window; after about 6 hours the limb is probably lost. - If packing plus a pressure bandage can hold the bleeding, loosen ("convert") the tourniquet before 2 hours and watch for bleeding. Leave it in place, loose, ready to re-tighten (rule of thumb). - Never remove a tourniquet that has been on more than 6 hours. - (ATP says only medics remove them - but it assumes a hospital is coming.) Shock. An injured person who is confused (no head injury) with a weak or missing wrist pulse has lost a lot of blood and will die without fast action (ATP, p. 98). Stop the bleeding, lay them flat with feet raised (after any broken leg is splinted), loosen tight clothing, and insulate them above and below (p. 100; 🖼 shock position, p. 99; Shock)). Drinks: standard first aid says nothing by mouth (same page), because surgery may come soon. With no help coming, that changes: if they're awake and can

With no help coming, that changes: if they're awake and can swallow, give sips of electrolyte (rehydration) drink, not plain water, which can drop the body's salt dangerously (JTS, p. 18). 🔥 Burns First aid (ATP, pp. 131-132): - Stop the burning. Put out flames. Cut clothing away around the burn, leaving cloth that is stuck to the skin. - Small burn: clean cool water right away, not ice, for no more than 20 minutes. Never put ice, grease, fat, herbs or dung on a burn (WTND, p. 96). - Chemical: brush off powder, then flush with lots of running water. Not in a tub - it chills them and spreads the chemical. - Electrical: shut off the power, or drag them clear with dry rope, cloth or wood. - Big burns: don't soak them. Keep them warm and off the ground - they chill fast in any weather. How big? Their own palm is about 1%. Rule of nines: head 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, front of trunk 18%, back 18%. Don't count red skin without blisters (ATP, p. 130; adult chart in WHO-ICRC, p. 197, child chart on p. 198). Rule of nines; 🖼 adult and child charts, JTS p. 53; 🖼 photos of 1st-, 2nd- and 3rd-degree burns, JTS burn guideline p. 5; Burn. Add front and back: head 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, front of the trunk 18%, back 18% (ATP, p. 130). Fluids without an IV (JTS burn guideline, pp. 6-8): - Burns over 20% cause shock in the first 1-2 days.

front of the trunk 18%, back 18% (ATP, p. 130). Fluids without an IV (JTS burn guideline, pp. 6-8): - Burns over 20% cause shock in the first 1-2 days. With "coached" drinking on a schedule, burns up to about 30% can be treated by mouth. - Rehydration drink, not plain water: 1 liter clean water + 6 level teaspoons sugar + ½ level teaspoon salt. - Adult rate: burn % × 10 = ml an hour (30% burn ≈ 300 ml an hour). - Enough? An adult passes more than 180 ml of urine every 6 hours (30-50 ml an hour). - Can't keep it down? Last resort: the same drink as an enema, up to 500 ml an hour (p. 7). Dressings (p. 9): leave unbroken blisters alone; cover with clean, dry gauze (wet dressings chill). For longer care, once a day wash gently with mild soap and clean water, remove loose dead skin, apply silver sulfadiazine cream (not on babies under 2 months, eyelids or lips) or a thin layer of honey (WTND, p. 96), re-cover (🖼 washing and covering a burn, ICRC First Aid p. 217). Give pain medicine first. 📚 Go deeper: JTS Burn Wound Management - sizing, drinking schedules, urine targets, daily care; WHO Surgical Care at the District Hospital - burns in a small hospital.

🧼 Wounds and infection when there's no hospital Wash it out with lots of water (JTS wound guideline, pp. 4-5): - Cleanest water you have. Not safe to drink? Boil 3 minutes, cool to body temperature. - 1-3 liters for a small cut, 4-8 for a medium or dirty wound, 9 or more for a large dirty one. A syringe, or a bottle with holes poked in the cap, gives the right pressure (🖼 washing a dirty wound, ICRC War Surgery p. 218). - Washing the whole person lowers infection too. Iodine, alcohol or antibiotic in the water does not help. Close it or leave it open? (p. 10) - Only close a cut that is clean, under 12 hours old (24 on the face or scalp) and closes without pulling. - Leave everything else open under a clean dressing. If it stays clean, close it 3-7 days later, or let it heal from the bottom up. Red Cross surgeons do the same (ICRC War Surgery, p. 219). - A closed wound that turns red, hot and full of pus: reopen it and let the pus out (p. 11). Bites (dog, cat, human): scrub at once with soap and water, let them heal open, think about rabies; most need antibiotics (p. 12). Tetanus: check vaccination with every wound (p. 10) - and get boosters now (general practice). When infection spreads:

let them heal open, think about rabies; most need antibiotics (p. 12). Tetanus: check vaccination with every wound (p. 10) - and get boosters now (general practice). When infection spreads: - In the wound: worsening pain, spreading redness, pus (p. 11; Cellulitis; Abscess). Draw a pen line around the red edge; if it spreads past the line on antibiotics, the treatment is failing (drug choices: MSF, p. 145). - Whole body (sepsis): fever or unusually low temperature, pulse over 90, breathing over 20 a minute, confusion, less urine. Low blood pressure comes late - don't wait for it (JTS sepsis guideline, p. 5). 🦴 Broken bones, sprains, spine and head Splinting (WHO-ICRC, p. 191; arm slings: 🖼 ATP pp. 141-143, Sling)): 1. Take off rings and jewelry. 2. Before and after, check beyond the injury: pulse, color, feeling, movement. 3. Pad the splint and bony points; reach past the joint above and the joint below (🖼 board and improvised splints, ATP pp. 146-148; 🖼 the good leg as a splint, p. 149). 4. Deformed, no pulse (cold, pale): gently straighten it. Deformed with a good pulse: don't force it. The boards reach past the joint above (knee) and the joint below (ankle), with ties above and below the break (ATP, p. 147). Cast too tight from swelling: split it and rewrap with an elastic bandage (Hospital Corpsman, p. 96; 🖼 cutting a cast, WHO Surgical Care p. 393). Splint). Sprains - treat like a break (WTND, p. 102): keep it still, wrap firmly from the toes up (loosen briefly every hour or two), keep it raised. Cold wet cloths 20-30 minutes every hour for a day or two, then warm soaks. Never rub or massage it. A bad sprain takes 3-4 weeks. Dislocated shoulder - the longer you wait, the harder it gets (WTND, p. 101): lay them face down on a table, arm hanging over the edge. Pull steadily down 15-20 minutes, or hang 5-10 kg from the arm (start with 5).

🐍 Rattlesnakes, spiders and stings Rattlesnakes (the Northern Pacific rattlesnake; 🖼 how to tell a pit viper, ATP p. 176), yellow jackets, ticks (western black-legged tick) and poison oak are normal hazards along the Rogue (BLM, p. 4). Rattlesnake bite - DO (JTS snakebite guideline, p. 16; ATP, p. 179): - Keep them calm and still. Take off rings, watches and tight clothing. - Loosely splint the limb, a little below heart level. Wash the bite gently. - Get them to antivenom as fast as possible, even if they have to walk - it's the only real treatment. DON'T cut, suck, shock, burn, use chemicals, ice, or tie on a band or tourniquet, or use "venom extractor" kits - "outdated interventions that should not be performed" (p. 27; ice: ATP, p. 179). If a band is already on, don't rip it off: people can collapse when it comes off. Remove it with them lying down, ready to treat shock (p. 16). Without antivenom, expect permanent damage or death, and weeks of nursing (p. 27). Black widow (Western black widow; 🖼 venomous spiders and other biters, ATP p. 180): shiny black or brown, usually a red or yellow mark. Lives in woodpiles and sheds; bites often happen in bed in fall and early winter. Painful cramps spread from the bite within 15-60 minutes; the belly can go board-hard. Death or lasting

🦷 Teeth: pain and emergencies WHO's protocols for non-dentists (WHO Oral Health, p. 56): - Knocked-out adult tooth: rinse it and push it back in within 1 hour, without touching the root. Where There Is No Dentist allows up to 12 hours, but sooner is far better. Wash with saline, milk or clean water; don't scrape the root; don't replace a baby tooth (p. 107; 🖼 pushing it back and waxing it in place, p. 108; Dental avulsion). - Loosened tooth: gently push it back into place. - Broken tooth: temporary filling - zinc oxide mixed with oil of cloves (p. 156; 🖼 the instruments, p. 155; Zinc oxide eugenol). - Infection: antibiotics, pain relief, and drain any abscess. - Don't put medicines directly on the tooth or gum. Abscess signs: constant pain (even at night), the tooth feels "long" or loose, a gum boil, a swollen gum or face. Swelling pressing on the throat, or fever, is an emergency (p. 103; penicillin doses p. 104). Bring swelling down before pulling a tooth - the numbing shot won't work in a swollen jaw. Dental abscess. 📚 Go deeper: Where There Is No Dentist - abscesses, pulling teeth, fillings; WHO AFRO protocols - urgent-care flowcharts (images only).

🛏 Nursing a bedridden person for days and weeks From the JTS nursing guideline (CPG 70): - Turn them at least every 2 hours (hourly on a hard surface). Pad heels, elbows, tailbone and the back of the head; pillows between knees and ankles (p. 10). Pressure sores. - Head up about 30° if unconscious - it lowers pneumonia risk (same page). - A red patch that doesn't fade when pressed is a sore starting: circle it, keep weight off it (p. 11; 🖼 where sores form, WTND ch. 15, p. 22). - Mouth care: brush every 12 hours; unconscious, wipe with moist gauze every 4 hours (same page). - Washing and toileting: bed bath daily; check every 2 hours for soiling; dry skin folds (p. 12). - Food and fluids: 5-6 small high-protein meals a day. Judge fluids by urine - little or dark means more to drink (p. 9). - Moving: sit up, then the bed edge, a chair, short walks with help; move every joint at least every 8 hours - this also helps prevent leg clots (pp. 13-14). Diarrhea (WHO Treatment of Diarrhoea; signs of dehydration: 🖼 the skin-pinch test, WTND ch. 13, p. 1): - After each loose stool: under 2 years 50-100 ml; ages 2-10, 100-200 ml; older, as much as they want (p. 14). Dehydrated: about 75 ml per kg over 4 hours

⚖ Knowing when someone can't be saved Some people will die whatever you do. Seeing it early lets you save those who can, and comfort the dying instead of putting them through useless treatment. - Many hurt at once: the Red Cross sorts people into urgent (simple care now saves them), serious (can wait a little), minor, and not to be treated or moved - injuries care can't help, and the dying (ICRC First Aid, p. 125; Triage). - No CPR on an injured person with obvious signs of death (p. 167). - A newborn with no heartbeat after 10 minutes of good breaths has died (WHO, p. 152). - Snakebite without antivenom, very large burns, sepsis that keeps worsening, a limb under a tourniquet past 6 hours - expect to lose some lives and limbs; do what you can, but not at the cost of those who can live (rule of thumb). Caring for the dying (Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 17, p. 28): keep them comfortable and free of pain, have family sit with them, let them make their own decisions and talk about death if they want - pretending they aren't dying doesn't help. Then look after the carers (Community guide). 📚 Go deeper: ICRC First Aid in Armed Conflicts - triage; ICRC War Surgery - sorting casualties with few resources.

🧰 The kit to build now The Army's first-aid kit (ATP, p. 231) - one per adult (rule of thumb): 2 tourniquets, 2 clotting (hemostatic) gauzes, 2 compressed gauzes, 2 gauze rolls, a triangular bandage, a vented chest seal (🖼 ATP, p. 88), 2 eye shields, 2 pairs of gloves, a safety cutter, tape and a marker. First aid kit. For the household (rule of thumb unless a page is given): - An irrigation syringe; a pressure cooker with a rack kept for instruments (JTS, p. 18) - Tweezers, scissors, a thermometer, elastic bandages, splints, clean cloth - Salt, sugar and level measuring spoons for rehydration drink - Silver sulfadiazine cream (JTS, p. 9); zinc oxide and oil of cloves (WTNDentist, p. 156) - Medicines from the WTND kit list - doses and storage in the Medical guide - A notebook for times, pulses, urine and doses Now, while you can: practice a one-handed tourniquet on yourself (🖼 ATP, p. 62), update everyone's tetanus shots, and take a first-aid or CERT class (general practice). 📚 Go deeper: ATP 4-02.11, Appendix A - kit lists; WTND - the medicine kit - home and village kits.

🦵 Recovering From Injuries: Rehab Without a Clinic How to get a hurt, sick or bed-bound person moving, strong and working again with no physical therapist, X-ray or surgeon: when to start, how much and how often, exercises joint by joint, strength and balance, common injuries, long bed rest, burns, head injuries, home-made crutches, and the road back to firewood and water hauling. This guide is not a clinician. It names the danger signs, where a clinic would normally be essential, and the safest course without one. First aid is in the Field Care guide; medicines and doses in the Medical READ-ME-FIRST. The rehab books are in Medical\Rehab-Physical-Therapy, with Hesperian's Disabled Village Children chapters ("DVC") in its Disabled-Village-Children folder; the WHO 1989 family packages there are scanned pictures that search can't read. WHO Surgical Care at the District Hospital and ICRC War Surgery are in Medical\Field-Care\Wounds-Burns-Fractures, the JTS nursing guideline and Navy Hospital Corpsman in Medical\Field-Care\Nursing-Care. Page numbers are PDF pages. ### The short version - Know the red flags (table below) and stop when you see one: spreading redness or fever, numbness or weakness getting worse, a joint that keeps giving way, night pain, back pain with fever, and one calf swollen, hot and painful: a clot. Never rub or massage it (A Book for Midwives, p. 6). - Protect, then move early. Move every joint that isn't hurt

one calf swollen, hot and painful: a clot. Never rub or massage it (A Book for Midwives, p. 6). - Protect, then move early. Move every joint that isn't hurt from day 1: "Immobilized extremities quickly lose their functional abilities" (WHO Surgical Care, p. 398). - Pain is the guide. Stretching "should not be very painful" (DVC ch. 42, p. 8); pain that is worse and still there the next day means too much (VA/DoD, p. 4). - Add no more than about 10% a week; it takes "as long to get back ... as you were out" (Ship's Medicine Chest, pp. 139-140). - Never force a stiff joint. Hold a slow stretch while you count to 25, then a little more (DVC ch. 42, p. 6). - In bed: every joint 5-10 times at least every 8 hours, deep breaths every hour, up and walking as soon as it's safe (JTS CPG 70, pp. 13-14). - Back pain: stay active. "Bed rest is a consequence of having pain, not a form of treatment" (VA/DoD, p. 4). - Head injury: no work that day, then light activity that doesn't worsen symptoms; no ladders, roofs or machinery until recovered (CDC 2024, p. 2).

🩹 How healing goes, and when to start moving Protect, then move. A limb kept still loses strength and bone; moving early "helps to prevent venous thrombosis and pressure sores" (WHO, p. 398). With no therapist the family takes over, and "it is the motivation of the patient that will determine the outcome"; "Begin motion and strengthening of uninjured extremities as soon as possible" (p. 399). When to move the hurt part, the books differ: the Air Force manual waits 4-6 weeks for a severe joint injury (AFH 10-644, p. 64), DVC "usually 4 to 6 weeks" for broken bones (DVC ch. 42, p. 8), and WHO gives a schedule for each injury. Swelling: raise it, cool it, wrap it, then warm it - Raise it 24-48 hours and "wiggle your fingers or toes frequently" (WHO, p. 392); a hurt hand stays raised the first week (p. 413). Wrap from the toes or fingers upward and loosen it every hour or two (WTND, p. 28). - Cold: the books range from 10 to 30 minutes for one to three days (WTND; AFH, p. 63; 105-Page Manual, p. 48). This guide: wrapped cold 15-20 minutes every 1-2 hours while awake, for about 2 days; off when the skin goes numb (AFH), never nonstop (105-Page). A rag in cold creek water works (AFH, p. 58). - Heat once the swelling stops growing, 24 hours after the last cold pack (Hospital Corpsman, p. 196); "cold works better on hot, inflamed joints and heat on sore, stiff joints". Hot compress: a thick cloth wrung out of water you can "hold your hand in ... comfortably", covered with thin plastic and a towel (DVC ch. 15, p. 4). Hot water bottles "must never exceed 125°F (51°C)" (Hospital Corpsman, p. 99).

📏 Pain and progress rules - OK: "no more than minimal discomfort" (AFH, p. 65). Stop: "DO NOT PUSH THROUGH SEVERE PAIN" (Ship's, p. 67). Next day: discomfort that "increases and remains the following day" means cut back (VA/DoD, p. 4). - An activity brings more pain: stop it a few days, then try again; if it still hurts more, stop it. Some swelling after activity is OK unless it keeps growing (WHO 1989, package 15, p. 176). A sore joint: "use less weight and repeat fewer times" (DVC ch. 16, p. 8). - Step up slowly: about 10% a week (Ship's, p. 139); too fast "may aggravate the injury", too slow "risks general deconditioning"; keep a written log (FM 7-22, p. 96). The VA plan: 10-20 minutes every other day; after a week with no more pain, add 5 minutes every other day, toward 30 minutes three times a week (VA/DoD, p. 6). - The ladder for any joint: a helper moves it → you move it with help → alone → against a weight → in daily work (DVC ch. 08, p. 7). Before running or heavy work on a leg, walk 30 minutes without symptoms getting worse (FM 7-22, p. 158).

🔄 Range-of-motion exercises Range of motion (ROM) means moving a joint as far as it normally goes in every direction. It prevents contractures, joints that no longer straighten because muscle and skin have shortened (DVC ch. 08, p. 1). Passive: a helper moves it. Assisted: the person moves it as far as they can and the helper does the rest. 💪 Getting strong again Start with exercises without motion (isometric: tightening a muscle without moving the joint), "useful across injured joints" (WHO, p. 400). Then climb the best ladder in the library, for the thigh and knee (DVC ch. 16, pp. 6-8): | Step | Exercise | Dose | Move up when | | 1 | Lying down, tighten the thigh without moving the knee | Count 25, 10 times, 3-4 times a day | After a few days; then do it sitting | | 2 | Straight-leg raise: tighten, lift the straight leg, count 5-10, lower slowly | Until the leg shakes | The knee doesn't bend at all | | 3 | The same with a sandbag on the ankle | ½ kg, then 1, then 1½ kg | No bend at each weight | | 4 | The same raise sitting up | Building to 5 kg (11 lb) | Not with a sore or tight hip | | 5 | Lying, a rolled blanket under the knee, lift the foot | 10-30 times, building to 5 kg | Steady and painless | | 6 | Chair rise; step-ups, "Start with low steps"; hills | Below | Ready for work | Steps 1-5 of the ladder: move up only when the knee stays straight (a diagram drawn for this guide). Weights: DVC's are for children. An adult

Ready for work | Steps 1-5 of the ladder: move up only when the knee stays straight (a diagram drawn for this guide). Weights: DVC's are for children. An adult starts at what they can lift 10 times cleanly, about 1-2 kg (2-5 lb), adding ½-1 kg a week (rule of thumb). For healthy adults Ship's starts women at 2-3 lb and men at 5-10 lb, "two sets of 8-12 repetitions" twice a week (Ship's, p. 138); the Army uses "1-3 sets of 10 repetitions" (FM 7-22, p. 98). Use a "cloth bag filled with sand", or bands cut from an old inner tube: "The wider the band, the more resistance" (DVC ch. 42, p. 7). Weigh a sandbag by balancing it on a stick against a measured liter of water (1 kg, 2.2 lb) (arithmetic). For the hand: a strip of tire between two sticks to squeeze; milking goats, wringing laundry and punching leather all count (DVC ch. 42, p. 26). Chair rise (CDC STEADI, p. 1): at the front of a sturdy chair, feet flat, hands resting lightly on the seat, lean forward, breathe out and "slowly stand up, using your hands as little as possible"; pause; sit down slowly, "Do not let yourself collapse". 10-15 times, rest a minute, 10-15 more; start with fewer if needed. The goal is no hands. Lean forward and stand, using your

down slowly, "Do not let yourself collapse". 10-15 times, rest a minute, 10-15 more; start with fewer if needed. The goal is no hands. Lean forward and stand, using your hands as little as possible; sit back down slowly, without collapsing (CDC STEADI, p. 1). Other building blocks: - Side of the hip (a limp that leans to one side): lie on your side, lift the leg and hold it until it drops; 3 times, 3 times a day (DVC ch. 42, p. 24). The Army lifts the foot 6-8 inches, "no more than 10 repetitions" (FM 7-22, p. 104). - Arms for crutches: sitting, push yourself up off the seat, 3 or 4 times a day, building to 50 times (DVC ch. 42, p. 22); modified push-ups, hips and legs on the mat (TM 8-292, p. 116). - Strengthen the weak side, not the strong one, or the joint is pulled into a contracture (DVC ch. 42, p. 10). Hold stretches 20-30 seconds; "Don't bounce" (Ship's, p. 139; FM 7-22, p. 97).

⚖ Balance and walking again The 4-stage balance ladder (CDC STEADI 4-Stage, pp. 1-2): with a helper or a counter beside you, hold each for 10 seconds without moving your feet: 1 feet side by side; 2 the instep of one foot against the big toe of the other; 3 heel to toe in a line; 4 one foot. An older adult who can't hold stage 3 for 10 seconds "is at increased risk of falling"; CDC names Tai Chi for fall prevention. To train, practice the hardest stage you can hold a few times a day, up to 30 seconds, then with eyes closed, then on a folded blanket (rule of thumb). Lift one leg, then the other; later walk "on a log or narrow board" (DVC ch. 42, p. 3). In bars: walk sideways and backward, stand on one leg holding on with the opposite hand, then use one bar (🖼 WHO 1989, package 13, p. 122). The four stages, each harder than the last: hold each for 10 seconds without moving your feet (CDC STEADI 4-Stage, p. 2). After an ankle or knee injury (rule of thumb; the library has no ankle plan): one-leg stands on the hurt side, 30 seconds, 3-5 times a day; then eyes closed; then on a blanket; then small hops in place and side to side, before running or rough trail. 🦴 Common injuries First aid is in Field Care, "Broken bones, sprains, spine and head". Thin spots are marked (rule of thumb).
common-injuries

Ankle sprain 1. Days 1-2: raise, cool, wrap; "Use crutches to give a sprained foot as much rest as possible" (WTND, p. 28). Trace circles and the alphabet with the toes (JTS, p. 13; written for clots, a classic early ankle exercise (rule of thumb)). 2. No better after 48 hours, or "very loose or floppy": more than a sprain; "Surgery may be needed" (WTND). A broken outer ankle bone gets a splint, then a walking cast after 7-10 days (WHO, p. 424). 3. Week 1 on, then weeks 2-3 (rule-of-thumb timing): walk with as much weight as is comfortable, stretch the calf leaning on a wall (🖼 DVC ch. 08, p. 7), heel raises; then the balance steps above, with an elastic wrap or ankle brace while it's weak (DVC ch. 15, p. 3). 4. Last: jumping and running "with the most caution", shorter, shallower lunges (FM 7-22, p. 159). A loose ankle can stay weak "for months or years" (DVC ch. 15): lace boots firmly on rough trail (rule of thumb).
ankle-sprain

Knee - Strength: the ladder above. Stiff knee: stretch sheet 2, count 25, several times, 3 times a day; never by pulling on the foot (DVC ch. 42, p. 18). Overuse pain follows "an abrupt increase" in miles or hills: strengthen thigh, hamstrings and trunk, stretch the calf (ATP 3-21.18, p. 132). - Kneecap slipped out: straighten the knee and push the kneecap toward the middle. Can't straighten the leg after a blow: a torn tendon or broken kneecap needing surgery (WHO, p. 420). A kneecap crack that hasn't moved: splint or cast 4-6 weeks, full weight allowed. Top of the shin broken: motion at 1-2 weeks, no weight 6 weeks, then crutches or a stick 6 more (p. 421). - Back to work: lunges and squats "with a reduced range of motion and fewer repetitions" first (FM 7-22, p. 158).
knee

Low back This guide follows the VA/DoD (2022), not the older "rest flat on your back for a few days" (WTND, p. 24). "Remaining active is key"; most people improve "within the first month" (VA/DoD, p. 3); "If possible, continue to work and make simple changes in how you do your job" (p. 2). Rest a day or two only "if rest is necessary". Moist heat 15-20 minutes, two or three times a day, not if you hurt it in a fall; no bouncing or jerking (p. 4). | Exercise (VA/DoD, pp. 5-6) | How | Dose | | Pelvic rock | On your back, knees bent; tighten belly and buttocks, press the low back down, then arch | Hold 5 s each way, 5 times | | Cat/camel | On hands and knees, round the back up, then let it sag | Hold each for a count of 15; 30 s-2 min | | Backward stretch | Stand, hands on the low back, lean back gently | Hold 5; 3 or 4 times | | Knee to chest | On your back, pull one knee to the chest | Hold 10; 10 times each leg | Cat/camel: round the back up and hold for a count of 15, then let it sag and hold (VA/DoD, p. 5). - WWHND adds the knee hug, the twist and the pelvic tilt

back up and hold for a count of 15, then let it sag and hold (VA/DoD, p. 5). - WWHND adds the knee hug, the twist and the pelvic tilt every day; "Stop if any of these exercises cause pain" (WWHND ch. 26, pp. 8-9). Walk on the VA plan (Pain and progress rules). - Daily life: roll onto your side and push up with your arms to get out of bed; sleep with a pillow under or between the knees (VA/DoD, p. 7); sit with knees at 90° and a rolled towel at the low back (p. 9), not one way for long (🖼 WHO 1989, p. 177). - Back to work: lunges and squats are "generally well tolerated, because the trunk remains straight" (FM 7-22, p. 161). Sudden pain lifting or twisting with pain or numbness down one leg may be "a slipped disc" (WTND, p. 23); other red flags are in the table at the top.
low-back

Neck - The person moves it, slowly, many times, without force: turn, tilt, nod. Forcing a stiff neck can make the bones slip and cause "total paralysis or even death", above all with arthritis, Down syndrome or a neck injury (DVC ch. 42, p. 10). Shoulders: up and down, roll forward and back, pull the blades together, 2 or 3 times whenever stiff (WWHND ch. 26, p. 13). - Loads: no head straps (p. 8); numb arms under a pack mean a hip belt and frame (ATP 3-21.18, p. 133). Whiplash or a strained neck: the library has no plan; keep it moving gently within comfort, use heat, and treat new arm numbness or weakness as a red flag (rule of thumb).
neck

Shoulder - Hanging-arm exercise (WHO's "motion with gravity"): lean forward and let the arm hang, moving it gently with the joint unweighted; it "works well for shoulder injuries" (WHO, p. 400; 🖼 p. 402). Collarbone: sling until pain-free (4-6 weeks adults, 3-4 children), hanging-arm exercise within days (p. 402). Separated shoulder: off the sling daily to straighten the elbow, strengthening "by the second week" (p. 403). - After a dislocation, the books differ: bind it a week to a month, no lifting for a month (WTND, in Field Care); splints off at 7-14 days (FM 3-05.70, p. 51); strengthening "at 6 weeks, with an emphasis on internal rotation" (WHO, p. 404). This guide: sling 1-3 weeks with hanging-arm exercise from the first days, no lifting or overhead work for 6 weeks, then strengthen (rule of thumb where it goes past the books). It comes out again easily, "especially in younger patients" (p. 403). - Upper arm break: hanging-arm exercise as soon as tolerated, weights once healed at 6-8 weeks (p. 405); "The major complication is shoulder stiffness" (p. 404). A dropped wrist after it usually recovers: splint it bent back and begin "passive extension exercise" (p. 405). - Strength: lying face down, raise both straight arms 3-6 inches in the shapes I, T, Y, L and W, 5 slow repetitions each (FM 7-22, pp. 113-115); push-ups "may start from the
shoulder

face down, raise both straight arms 3-6 inches in the shapes I, T, Y, L and W, 5 slow repetitions each (FM 7-22, pp. 113-115); push-ups "may start from the knees" (p. 162). - Stiff or "frozen" shoulder: a rope over a branch, a handle at each end; the good arm pulls the stiff arm straight up, 10 times (🖼 WHO 1989, package 16, p. 193). That is all the library has. It usually stiffens over months and loosens over a year or more; keep up the rope, hanging-arm exercise and walking the fingers up a wall daily, to mild discomfort (rule of thumb). Pain raising the arm out or forward can be impingement (WHO, p. 449).
shoulder

Elbow, wrist, hand and fingers - Elbow put back in: move it after 10 days, splint off at 4-6 weeks (WHO, p. 409). Forearm break: the risk is losing the turn of the palm; out of the cast at 6-8 weeks (p. 410). A "sprained" wrist tender in the hollow at the base of the thumb (snuffbox) is a broken scaphoid until proved otherwise: "often overlooked", 6-20 weeks in a thumb splint (pp. 411-412). - Hand: splint with the wrist back about 20°, knuckles bent to a right angle, finger joints straight; raise it the first week; "Begin active exercises as soon as possible" (🖼 p. 413). Fingers: tape a hurt finger to its neighbor; fingers that cross in a fist mean a twisted hand bone; a drooping fingertip (mallet finger) is splinted straight continuously 6-8 weeks (🖼 p. 414). - The hand program, 10-20 times each, at least twice a day, once bones have healed: close and spread the fingers; fist and open; "O"s with the thumb and each finger, large then small; wrist forward and backward ("especially important"); thumb out and in; wrist side to side; palm up and down (DVC ch. 42, p. 25).
elbow-wrist-hand-and-fingers

After a splint or cast comes off 1. Plaster: soak it "in water, or water with vinegar added, for 10-15 minutes and then remove it like a bandage" (WHO, p. 393). 2. Expect stiffness and thin muscles. Warm it, then move it with the other hand through a range "which can be tolerated without pain", then on its own, then against weight (AFH, p. 65). 3. An arm: no force for another month (WTND, p. 24). A leg goes back to weight in steps (WHO, p. 400): non-weight bearing (held off the ground) → touch down (the limb's own weight only) → partial (some weight, the rest on crutches) → full (the aid only "for balance and in case of emergency"). Foot stress fractures: limit time on your feet (p. 426).
after-a-splint-or-cast-comes-off

Hip - An old person, a simple fall, a leg short and turned out: a broken hip. Without surgery: if it hasn't moved, light traction and gentle motion until healed, 8-12 weeks; if it has, traction a few weeks, "then begin sitting and walking with crutches"; sitting up prevents "pressure sores and pneumonia" (WHO, p. 417). Hip put back in: crutches, "weight bearing after 12 weeks" (p. 418). - Exercises: the side-hip lift; time lying face down (DVC ch. 08, p. 5); stretch sheet 3 (DVC ch. 42, p. 19). A tight hip hides because the back arches (DVC ch. 08, p. 3). Pain lying on that side: bursitis (WHO, p. 449).
hip

Tendons: tennis elbow, Achilles and overuse - Where: "the lateral elbow, radial side of the wrist, knee, Achilles tendon" and heel; tennis elbow hurts "with use of the hand for gripping" (WHO, pp. 449-450). - First weeks: rest; a soft splint (cloth around "a thin piece of wood") at work and rest; hot, moist cloths; switch hands; move the joint fully every hour. A red, hot joint "might be infected"; not better in 6 months, get help (WWHND ch. 26, p. 14). - Then load it slowly (rule of thumb; no book on the drive gives a plan). Tennis elbow: forearm on a table, palm down, a 1-2 lb can in hand; lift the wrist with the other hand's help, lower it alone over 3-5 seconds; 15 times, 3 sets a day. Achilles: on a step edge, rise on both feet, lower slowly on the sore one; 15 times, 3 sets, twice a day, about 12 weeks. A mild ache is fine; sharp pain is not. - A sudden "kick" at the back of the calf and no push-off is a torn Achilles (Ship's, p. 321 lists it). Without surgery: crutches and the foot held pointed down for weeks, then slow stretching (rule of thumb).
tendons-tennis-elbow-achilles-and-overuse

🛏 After long bed rest Turning, padding, skin and food are in Field Care, "Nursing a bedridden person for days and weeks"; this adds the exercise. Lying still wastes muscle fast and brings clots and bed sores; unhurt parts "may be exercised" (TM 8-292, p. 11), and a bed patient can do "more exercise than ordinarily is thought possible": about 45 minutes a day, in sessions of 25 and 20 (p. 49).
after-long-bed-rest

Getting up in stages Minimum: sit on the edge of the bed 2-3 times a day. Better: sit in a chair through the day. Best: sit in a chair and "walk 2-3 times a day with assistance" (JTS, p. 13). Dizziness on standing (blood pressure dropping) comes with "Prolonged bed rest" and "Dehydration" (CDC STEADI, p. 2): 1. Before getting up, pump the feet and clench and unclench the hands. Sit up; sit on the side of the bed; stand holding something solid; march in place. Drink 6-8 glasses a day unless told otherwise; avoid very hot baths (CDC). 2. "Do not walk if you feel dizzy." Lie down and try again more slowly (🖼 WHO 1989, package 12, pp. 75-76, with two helpers standing a weak person up); lying down and fluids usually clear it (Ship's, p. 43). Fainting: lie them down, or head between the knees (Hospital Corpsman, p. 206).
getting-up-in-stages

Breathing exercises - Every hour awake: in slowly through the nose, hold 3-5 seconds, out through pursed lips, 10 times; cough if there is phlegm; "as effective as using an incentive spirometer" (JTS, p. 14). Broken ribs: don't bind the chest; 4-5 deep breaths in a row every 2 hours (WTND, p. 25). - Thick phlegm in someone old or weak: plenty of water, breathe steam, then pound the back lightly with a cupped hand (🖼 WTND ch. 13, p. 19, "postural drainage"). Weak chest muscles (spine injury): push in on the chest as they cough (DVC ch. 23, p. 8).
breathing-exercises

Stiff joints and bed sores Lie straight with "a pillow between legs", never twisted or bent; feet at right angles against a padded board or hanging over the end of the bed; some time face down; knees as straight as possible (🖼 DVC ch. 08, p. 5). Don't "SPEND ALL DAY SITTING DOWN"; anyone sitting long pushes up on their arms and counts to 25 every 15-20 minutes (DVC ch. 42, p. 20). Every joint 5-10 times at least every 8 hours; turning and skin checks are in Field Care.
stiff-joints-and-bed-sores

Blood clots: prevent them, spot them, never rub them - Prevent: foot pumps, ankle circles, leg raises, hamstring stretches, shoulder rolls. JTS says 10 of each "every hour" in one place and "every 2 hours" in another; do about 10 of each every hour or two while awake, but not on a broken or badly hurt leg; elastic wraps from the toes up, toes showing (JTS, p. 13). Walk early; don't sit with legs crossed (WWHND ch. 26, p. 13). - Spot: swelling, pain, cramping or warmth, red skin in one leg (JTS); pain when the calf is squeezed, a hard lump (🖼 Midwives, p. 6). - Two kinds of leg massage: JTS rubs the legs upward to prevent clots in someone unconscious, with no deep pressure behind the knee (p. 14). A leg that has clot signs is never rubbed or massaged; the clot "can go into her lung" (Midwives).
blood-clots-prevent-them-spot-them-never-rub-them

🔥 Burns: keeping scars from locking joints Lupito lay with his burned arm and knee bent because it "hurt less"; once healed he "could not lift or straighten his arm or straighten his leg" (DVC ch. 28, p. 1). First aid is in Field Care. Positions: splint against the pull of the scar; a joint burned on both sides is splinted straight; for the armpit, hold the arm out ("Airplane-strut type splints") (ICRC War Surgery, p. 296). Keep the head "tilted up", elbows and knees straight (tied if needed so they don't bend in sleep), and fingers and toes apart with Vaseline gauze (🖼 DVC ch. 28, p. 2). The hand, the books differ (WTND "slightly bent", DVC straight); this guide follows the ICRC "safe position": wrist back 30°, knuckles bent close to 90°, finger joints straight, fingers apart; "A hand should never be immobilized longer than ten days" (🖼 ICRC, p. 295). Raise burned hands 48 hours, then start hand exercises (WHO, p. 92). Stretching: 1. Gentle ROM at once, 2 or 3 times a day, best at the dressing change (DVC ch. 28, p. 2). Straighten fingers, arms and legs "completely several times a day ... This is painful but helps prevent stiff scars" (WTND, p. 23). Pain relief first (MSF, p. 342). 2. Splint at night, stretch by day; once healed, tight elastic bandages and scar massage
burns-keeping-scars-from-locking-joints

painful but helps prevent stiff scars" (WTND, p. 23). Pain relief first (MSF, p. 342). 2. Splint at night, stretch by day; once healed, tight elastic bandages and scar massage (ICRC, p. 296), with oil rubbed into the healed burn ("not a fresh burn") before stretching (DVC). 3. Keep at it until the skin "no longer tightens and shrinks" (DVC): 6-12 months (ICRC), longer in children, whose scars can't keep up with growth. "Eggs and peanut oil are good, locally available supplements" (WHO, p. 93). An old scar contracture can be straightened with a series of casts, cut and wedged a little straighter every few days; check daily for sores, a bad smell and cold or blue toes, and stop if 3 changes gain nothing (DVC ch. 59, pp. 2-3).

🧠 Head injury and concussion Watch the whole way through for: a headache that gets worse, vomiting over 30 minutes, odd behavior or slurred speech, drowsiness or can't be woken, weakness or numbness, seizures, double vision. Most people recover "within a few days or weeks" (CDC 2024, p. 1). Rest, then light activity. The Army book says "Physical and cognitive rest" (ATP 4-02.11, p. 122); this guide follows the newer CDC (2024) sheet (p. 2): 1. The day of the injury: no work, driving, sports or physical activity. 2. Then: good sleep and "light activity such as short walks. If an activity makes symptoms worse, be sure to stop and rest." Less bright light and noise if they bother you. As you feel better: "aerobic exercise for 20-30 minutes". 3. Back to work in steps, with breaks. More time off for work "from heights ... ladder or a roof" or with machinery: here, felling, chainsaws, roofs and riding (rule of thumb). A second blow before healing "may slow your recovery". A practical ladder: short walks → longer walks and light chores → 20-30 minutes' brisk work → normal work on the ground → full work; at least a day at each step without symptoms, and back a step if they return (rule of thumb built on CDC).
head-injury-and-concussion

♿ Stroke and spine injuries: the basics Stroke: many "get better with time"; help them "walk with a cane and to use her good hand to care for herself" (WTND ch. 22, p. 5). - Daily ROM of the weak side (WWHND ch. 9, p. 6), very slowly: "Fast movements increase spasticity" (stiff, jerky muscles) (DVC ch. 42, p. 10). The cane goes in the hand opposite the weak leg (DVC ch. 43, p. 2). - Bed to chair: feet on the floor, lean forward, head down and weight over the knees, push up and swing across (🖼 DVC ch. 43, pp. 2-3); a smooth board about 23 × 65 cm (10 in × 2 ft) with rounded ends bridges the gap (🖼 p. 4). - WHO 1989 picture lessons: turning and sitting (🖼 p. 53), moving about (🖼 p. 88), washing, dressing and eating (🖼 p. 149). Spinal cord injury (DVC ch. 23, pp. 8-9): gentle ROM from the day after. Until the spine heals (6 weeks or more) keep it "very gentle and limited", don't move the back or neck, and start with "feet, ankles, hands, wrists, and elbows": about 10 minutes per arm and leg, twice a day. Turn every 2-3 hours; lying on the belly is best against sores. Stretch paralyzed fingers only with the wrist bent down, so they still close when the wrist bends
stroke-and-spine-injuries-the-basics

day. Turn every 2-3 hours; lying on the belly is best against sores. Stretch paralyzed fingers only with the wrist bent down, so they still close when the wrist bends back. Recovery can't be judged "during the first several days" (WHO, p. 427); most comes in the first months, and what remains after a year is "almost certainly there to stay" (DVC ch. 23, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: DVC ch. 23 - skin, bladder and bowel, transfers and self-care after a spinal injury; WHO 1989, package 14 - picture lessons in washing, dressing and eating.

🩼 Crutches, canes and walkers Which aid: usually bars → walker → crutches → elbow crutches → wide-based cane → cane → nothing (DVC ch. 63, p. 1). "A cane makes him use his leg. A crutch lets him avoid using his leg" (p. 9). Teach each person before they walk alone, and light the way at night (Hospital Corpsman, p. 98). | Aid | Fit | Source | | Underarm crutch | Top 2-3 fingers' width below the armpit (ch. 43 says 2-3, ch. 63 says 3). Weight on the hands, never the armpits: hanging on the tops "can cause paralysis of the hands" | DVC ch. 43, p. 1; ch. 63, p. 6 | | Crutch handgrip | Elbow bent a little; grip about ⅓ of the way down | DVC ch. 63, p. 6 | | Walker | Grips at elbow height, arms "half-bent" | DVC ch. 63, p. 4 | | Cane | Top at the wrist crease with the arm hanging; elbow slightly bent holding it | (rule of thumb) | Walking patterns: - One bad leg, crutches: both crutches and the bad leg forward together, then step through with the good leg, with only as much weight on the bad leg as its stage allows ("After a splint or cast comes off") (rule of thumb). - Both legs weak: right crutch with left leg,

as much weight on the bad leg as its stage allows ("After a splint or cast comes off") (rule of thumb). - Both legs weak: right crutch with left leg, then left crutch with right leg; or "swing to" ("slow but sure"), or "swing through" (🖼 DVC ch. 43, p. 1). - Cane: "on the side opposite the weaker leg"; the cane and the weaker leg go down together (🖼 p. 2). - Walker or bars: move the frame (or one hand, then the other), then the weak leg, then the other leg (🖼 WHO 1989, pp. 121, 128). No wheels is "very stable but harder to move"; 3-4 wheels "can easily roll out from under" (DVC ch. 63, p. 4). Stairs (rule of thumb; no book on the drive covers them): "Up with the good, down with the bad." Going up, the good leg steps up first, then the crutches or cane and the bad leg; going down, the crutches and bad leg first, then the good leg. Use a rail if there is one (rail in one hand, crutches or cane in the other), one step at a time, with a helper below the person both ways; the same for porch steps, banks and logs. Our ground: wet porches, mud and leaves are slick all winter, and damp cold can "lead to accidents" (WWHND ch. 8, p. 12);

same for porch steps, banks and logs. Our ground: wet porches, mud and leaves are slick all winter, and damp cold can "lead to accidents" (WWHND ch. 8, p. 12); keep rubber tips sound and make them extra wide for soft ground (DVC ch. 63, p. 9). Fit the crutch so the weight is on the hands, move the hurt leg together with its support, then step with the good leg (a diagram drawn for this guide). 🪵 Making walking aids Expensive equipment isn't needed; most can be "made by a carpenter from available supplies" (WHO, p. 399). - Sapling crutch: "pick out a sapling with limbs growing opposite ... cut out the central stem, trim, and shave down" (🖼 Kephart Vol. 1, p. 223). A single forked branch is weaker than a two-sided crutch; pad the top (🖼 DVC ch. 63, p. 6). - Wooden crutch: two side poles, a padded top and a handgrip dowel 2½ cm (hardwood) or 3 cm (softwood) thick about ⅓ of the way down; bolts and wing nuts through a row of holes make it adjustable. A metal one is ¼-⅝ in steel rod or re-bar, welded (🖼 DVC ch. 63, p. 7; Blacksmithing guide). Pad with sponge rubber, leather or soft cloth (pp. 7-8). Tips: a plug cut from a car tire, forced into the end and screwed. Canes from forest plants: split the top for a grip, bind it so it splits no further (🖼 p. 9). - Walkers: boards about 2 × 4 cm or thin trees, nailed with diagonal braces; wooden wheels roll when pushed but brake under full weight (🖼 p. 3); joints tied with inner-tube strips (p. 4); rubber on the feet so it "will not slip" (🖼 WHO 1989, pp. 127-128). - Parallel bars: "Fix 2 poles for support" (🖼 WTND ch. 21,

🪓 Lifting, carrying and getting back to work Lifting: "Use leg muscles-not back muscles"; kneel or squat; keep back, shoulders and neck straight; "Get someone to help you lift heavy objects ... later on you may lose time because of a back injury" (🖼 WWHND ch. 26, p. 7). Straight legs with a twisted trunk raise the risk (ATP 3-21.18, p. 97; 🖼 p. 98). Carrying: close to the body, on the back rather than one side, switch sides, split the load, no head straps (🖼 WWHND, p. 8); high and close costs less, and the cost climbs above 30% of body weight (ATP, p. 99).
