👵 Children and older people Children: - Bones mend fast (WTND, p. 24). Growth straightens some shortening and angle but not a twist; a break through the growth plate can change growth, so make only "two attempts" at setting it (WHO, p. 430). After an elbow break in a small child, check the pulse (p. 431). - Make it a game, "satisfying and fun" (DVC ch. 42, p. 1): ball games stretch stiff joints (p. 11); bikes and hills build thighs (p. 23). Poles taller than the child, so a fall can't poke the eyes; sitting walkers only as "an early and temporary step" (DVC ch. 63, pp. 5, 9). - Joint pain with no injury may be rheumatic fever (after a sore throat) or TB (DVC ch. 15, p. 1; WTND, p. 23); see the Childbirth & Children guide. "It is never too late to start being physically active": strength 2 days a week plus balance (Dietary Guidelines, p. 143). Walk 20-30 minutes daily, avoiding slippery wet ground, with handrails and a cane (WWHND ch. 8, p. 12). - Heat and cold burn more easily, and some with joint pain "lose their sense of feeling in the skin" (WWHND, p. 12; Hospital Corpsman, p. 99). 🚑 The first few minutes When someone is hurt, check in this order and act on the first problem you find (FM 4-25.11, p. 18-19; the newer Army order is MARCH - ATP 4-02.11, p. 53): 1. Protect yourself - gloves or a clean plastic bag on your hands if there's blood. 2. Responsive? Tap and ask "Are you OK?" 3. Breathing? If not, open the airway and give rescue breaths (🖼 head-tilt, ATP p. 77; 🖼 mouth-to-mouth, WTND p. 80). 4. Bleeding? For heavy, life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg, put a tourniquet on first - 2-3 inches above the wound, on bare skin, tight until the bleeding stops (it will hurt; that means it's tight enough), and write the time on the person (ATP 4-02.11 (2026), p. 62). For other bleeding, press hard on the wound with a thick, clean cloth (🖼 WHO-ICRC, p. 169), or pack the wound tightly where a tourniquet can't go (groin, armpit, neck - 🖼 ATP, p. 69). The library's older FM 4-25.11 calls the tourniquet a "last resort" - that advice is out of date. Full steps: Injuries & Illness guide. 5. Shock)? Weak, fast pulse, pale cold sweat, confusion. Lay them down with feet a little raised (🖼 ATP, p. 99), keep warm; unconscious = on the side (🖼 ATP, p. 79; Recovery position) and nothing by mouth; awake and

💊 Using found or expired medicines 1. Identify it. US pills must carry an imprint code. Open Pill-Identifier\PILL-IDENTIFIER.html, type the code, then check that the color, shape and size also match - the same code can be two different drugs (e.g. "I2" is ibuprofen 200 mg or amitriptyline 25 mg depending on size; "N 4" is nitroglycerin or a diet pill). No code at all = a supplement, a foreign or compounded product, or an illegal pill. 2. Never trust street pills. Pills that didn't come from a pharmacy can be counterfeits pressed with fentanyl - fake blue "M30" oxycodone, Xanax and Adderall are common, and many contain a deadly dose. 3. Look it up before giving it. In the WHO Model Formulary or MSF Essential Drugs (Medicines\), read what it treats, the dose, who must not take it, and interactions. For children, use the WHO Formulary for Children - children's doses go by weight. Give the right dose, no more and no less; finish every antibiotic course; antibiotics do nothing for colds (WTND, p. 56). 4. Expired medicines. Most tablets and capsules kept sealed, cool and dry lose potency slowly - military testing extended most stockpiled lots by years (88% of 3,005 lots, on average by 66 months), and some drugs kept 90% strength decades past their date (Zilker 2019, p. 54-55). That was warehouse storage, and inhalers and
using-found-or-expired-medicines

(88% of 3,005 lots, on average by 66 months), and some drugs kept 90% strength decades past their date (Zilker 2019, p. 54-55). That was warehouse storage, and inhalers and epinephrine often failed. But: - Don't rely on expired or badly stored: insulin (lasts only ~28 days unrefrigerated; never use if it froze), nitroglycerin) tablets (lose strength once opened - keep in the original glass bottle; WHO: discard 8 weeks after opening, p. 276), epinephrine pens (photo; weaker when expired - but an expired pen with clear liquid is better than none in anaphylaxis), and mixed liquid antibiotics (amoxicillin suspension: 14 days in the fridge). - Throw out anything discolored, crumbling, sticky or smelling odd - especially tetracycline-family antibiotics, which can damage the kidneys when degraded. Also caked, brownish rehydration salts, and melted creams or suppositories (MSF, p. 648). - Don't raise the dose to make up for age - MSF warns of overdose. Heart and seizure medicines need exact doses, so respect their dates (p. 649). - Store medicines cool and dry (not the bathroom, kitchen or a car - a vehicle can reach 50-60 °C, MSF, p. 647), in their original containers, out of children's reach. 5. The biggest dangers - Allergy - face or throat swelling, trouble breathing or widespread hives after a medicine is anaphylaxis: give epinephrine if you have it. After any reaction, never use
using-found-or-expired-medicines

biggest dangers - Allergy - face or throat swelling, trouble breathing or widespread hives after a medicine is anaphylaxis: give epinephrine if you have it. After any reaction, never use that medicine again (WTND, p. 70). - Acetaminophen (Tylenol) - no more than 4,000 mg a day for adults, counting every product; it's hidden in Norco, Vicodin, Percocet and many cold medicines. Too much causes liver failure (MSF, p. 244) - and an overdose needs urgent care even if the person feels fine (WHO, p. 68). - Opioids - a dose that's normal for someone used to them can stop the breathing of someone who isn't, or of a child. Never combine with benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium, Klonopin), alcohol or other sedatives. Naloxone (Narcan) reverses opioid overdose - keep some. - Children - no cough/cold medicines under age 4 (US labels; never under 2), no aspirin for children or teens (Reye syndrome - WHO, p. 226). - Interactions - check the formulary when someone already takes blood thinners, heart medicines or antidepressants. - Poisoning: Oregon Poison Center 1-800-222-1222 (24/7, while phones work). 6. Measure it right (WTND ch. 8): 1 g = 1,000 mg · 1 mg = 1,000 mcg · 1 grain = 65 mg · 1 teaspoon = 5 ml · 1 tablespoon = 15 ml. Kitchen spoons vary - mark one at 5 ml measured with a syringe

1 grain = 65 mg · 1 teaspoon = 5 ml · 1 tablespoon = 15 ml. Kitchen spoons vary - mark one at 5 ml measured with a syringe (🖼 WTND p. 61; cutting tablets: 🖼 p. 60). Check the mg on the label: strengths differ. Never give medicine by mouth to someone asleep, unconscious or having a seizure (p. 62). 7. Getting rid of medicines - mix with coffee grounds or cat litter and seal; flush only what the FDA lists, like fentanyl patches - deadly to children even after use (FDA; 🖼 FDA decision flowchart). Stock up now: ask your doctor about extra supplies of the medicines your household depends on, and keep an emergency kit (wound care, pain/fever medicine, antihistamines, oral rehydration salts, naloxone). 📚 Go deeper: WTND Green Pages - uses, doses and warnings for each medicine; MSF Essential Drugs, p. 646 - storage, spoilage and expiry; Zilker 2019 - what testing shows about old medicines.

💧 Diarrhea and dehydration: the homemade drink Most children who die of diarrhea die of dehydration. Signs: thirst, little or dark urine, dry mouth, sunken tearless eyes, skin that stays up when pinched (🖼 the pinch test, WTND p. 151). Start the drink at the first watery stools (WTND, p. 151-152). Rehydration Drink (🖼 drawn step by step, Hesperian Ch 5, p. 53; Oral rehydration): in 1 liter of clean water, stir ½ level teaspoon of salt and 8 level teaspoons of sugar. Taste before adding the sugar: it must be less salty than tears. - Give sips every 5 minutes until they urinate normally - 3 liters or more a day for a large person, at least 1 liter for a small child. - Keep giving it even if they vomit. Keep feeding, and keep breastfeeding babies. - No repeat doses of medicines that can build up until they urinate normally (WTND, p. 54). - Getting worse, or other danger signs? Get medical help. 📚 Go deeper: WTND, p. 152 - the sugar and cereal recipes, with pictures; MSF Clinical Guidelines - severe diarrhea and cholera.

🌿 Medicinal plants - go carefully 📷 Not sure what it is? Photograph it with the plant and mushroom identifier (🔧 Tools tab). It suggests names and flags poisonous groups, but it's often wrong: confirm every feature here before you eat or use anything. Signs a home remedy probably doesn't work: many different "cures" for one illness, disgusting remedies, and anything using animal or human waste - that causes infections (WTND, p. 10-11). Deadly look-alike: foxglove leaves have been mistaken for comfrey (🖼 foxglove photos, WSU p. 28), with fatal "comfrey tea" poisonings - and comfrey itself can harm the liver (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 243). If in doubt, don't - and call the Poison Center. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Monographs Vol 1 - evidence plant by plant (Vols 1-4); WSU Poisonous Plants of the PNW, p. 28 - foxglove and other local poisons.

👶 Childbirth, Newborns & Young Children When No Help Is Coming Getting a mother and baby through pregnancy, birth and the first weeks, and keeping young children alive and learning, with no hospital, pharmacy or phone. Current WHO guidance comes first. Hesperian's A Book for Midwives (2026) and Where There Is No Doctor (2025) add detail; where they differ from WHO, this guide gives the WHO answer. The books are in Medical\Childbirth-Children (Birth, Newborn, Mothers, Child-Health), Medical\A Book for Midwives, Medical\Field-Care\Childbirth-Newborn, Medical\Where There Is No Doctor and Southern-Oregon\Children-Learning. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Bleeding after birth kills fastest. Every mother gets a bleeding medicine within 1 minute of the last baby (WHO 2025, p. 19), and someone feels her womb every 15 minutes for the first hour (p. 29). - Never push on the belly, pull the cord, put anything in the vagina, or give drugs to speed labor (PCPNC, p. 170). - A baby not breathing by 1 minute needs breaths now, 40 a minute. Stop only after 10 minutes with no heartbeat (PCPNC, p. 152). - Put nothing on the cord stump. Keep it clean and dry. - Count a sick child's breaths for a full minute. Fast breathing means pneumonia. - Never make a child vomit, and never give salt water.

📋 Plan now, while doctors and pharmacies still exist Cheap medicines bought ahead save mothers and children. Most need a US prescription, so talk to a doctor now: | Medicine | For | Notes | | Misoprostol | Preventing and treating bleeding after birth | No fridge needed; keep dry (WHO, p. 19). A child who fell behind resumes without repeating doses (Table 3). Adults: tetanus boosters, MMR if never vaccinated, and Tdap in every pregnancy (general practice). Clean birth kit (PCPNC, p. 169;

🤰 Pregnancy: checkups and danger signs - Due date: add 9 months and 7 days to the first day of the last monthly bleeding (BfM, p. 88). - Checkups: monthly, then weekly in the last month (general practice): blood pressure, urine and the womb's height. The top of the womb rises about 2 finger-widths a month: just above the pubic bone at 3 months, the navel at about 5, nearly the ribs by 8½-9. Much faster or slower is a warning sign (BfM, p. 130; Fundal height). - Pre-eclampsia causes fits and death before, during or after birth. Surest signs: blood pressure 140/90 or higher plus protein in the urine. Also: strong headache, spots or blurred vision, steady pain high in the belly, puffy face or hands on waking (BfM, p. 125). - Urine protein test: boil the top of a tube of urine. If cloudy, add a few drops of vinegar. Still cloudy means protein. Low-dose aspirin (81 mg a day) may prevent pre-eclampsia; ask a doctor now (BfM, p. 127). - Breech? If the hard, round head is at the top of the belly late in pregnancy (MCPC, p. 234; 🖼 listening for the heartbeat above the navel, WTND p. 252), WHO wants the birth in a hospital (p. 239). Go before labor. Go for help at once, day or night, for bleeding from the vagina, fits, severe

WTND p. 252), WHO wants the birth in a hospital (p. 239). Go before labor. Go for help at once, day or night, for bleeding from the vagina, fits, severe headache with blurred vision, fever with weakness, severe belly pain, or fast or difficult breathing (PCPNC, p. 162). She eats more, rests and drinks no alcohol (same page). Smoke harms pregnant women more: in fire season keep her in a "cleaner air room" with a box-fan filter (EPA). 📚 Go deeper: A Book for Midwives, ch. 8 - every prenatal check; PCPNC counselling sheets - birth plans.

🛏 Labor and birth: what helpers do Labor has started with painful contractions every 20 minutes or less, waters breaking, or a bloody sticky discharge (PCPNC, p. 162). During labor (WTND, p. 259): - The first stage can last over 20 hours with a first baby. Don't hurry it. - She doesn't push until she feels she must. - She urinates and drinks often, eats lightly, walks, and doesn't lie flat on her back for long (🖼 positions for labor, MCPC p. 111; 🖼 for the birth, p. 123; 🖼 WTND p. 260). - Helpers scrub hands, keep nails short and wear gloves. Never: drugs to speed labor (they can kill mother and child - WTND, p. 266), anything in the vagina, pushing on the belly (it can tear the womb - BfM, p. 205), pulling on the cord. Leave for Grants Pass now if waters broke with no labor after 6 hours, contractions last over 12 hours, she soaks over 2-3 pads in 15 minutes, or the placenta isn't out 1 hour after the baby (PCPNC, p. 170). Right after the baby is born (🖼 a head-first birth, WTND p. 261; Childbirth): 1. Dry the baby, lay it skin-to-skin on the mother's belly, and cover it, head too (BfM, p. 240). 2. Feel her belly for a second baby, then give the bleeding medicine within 1 minute - misoprostol
labor-and-birth-what-helpers-do

on the mother's belly, and cover it, head too (BfM, p. 240). 2. Feel her belly for a second baby, then give the bleeding medicine within 1 minute - misoprostol 400-600 µg by mouth, or oxytocin 10 units in the thigh. (The 800 µg dose is for treating bleeding, below.) Never before the last baby is out (WHO, p. 19). 3. Cut the cord after 1-3 minutes (same page), once it is white and stops pulsing; waiting gives the baby iron. Tie it tightly 2 finger-widths from the belly, tie a second string farther out, and cut between with a new or sterilized blade (BfM, pp. 214-215; 🖼 tying and cutting, WTND p. 262; Umbilical cord). A baby needing breathing help gets it cut at once. 4. Let the placenta come by itself, and check it is whole (PCPNC, p. 169; Placenta). 5. First breastfeed within the hour. No bath the first day. Don't leave the mother alone for 24 hours (same page). Wait 1-3 minutes, tie twice, cut between the ties (a diagram drawn for this guide). Cord care: clean and dry, nothing on it. Dirt and dung cause tetanus (WTND, p. 263; Neonatal tetanus). WHO's one exception is 7.1% chlorhexidine daily for a week, where a health authority recommends it (PCPNC, p. 169). Fold the diaper below the stump; it usually falls off within 1-3 weeks (sometimes in

7.1% chlorhexidine daily for a week, where a health authority recommends it (PCPNC, p. 169). Fold the diaper below the stump; it usually falls off within 1-3 weeks (sometimes in 5-7 days). 📚 Go deeper: A Book for Midwives, ch. 12 - the birth in drawings; PCPNC home delivery.

🩸 Heavy bleeding after birth: the #1 killer Bleeding after birth kills more mothers than anything else (general knowledge), and delay is a common reason they die (WHO, p. 59). A soft womb causes about 70% of it (p. 9). Feel the womb every 15 minutes for the first hour. Hard like your forehead is good. Soft like the tip of your nose needs rubbing (🖼 how to rub it, BfM p. 224). The top should be at or below the navel (WHO, p. 29). Teach the family to check and rub (BfM, p. 236). Dangerous bleeding: measure, don't guess (WHO, p. 43; p. 15): - 500 mL or more (about 2 cups), or - 300 mL or more plus a warning sign: pulse over 100, top blood-pressure number under 100, bottom under 60, or pulse higher than the top number. - No cuff? Soaking 2-3 pads in 15 minutes, or faint, pale, sweaty or confused (BfM, p. 239). A slow steady trickle is as dangerous as a gush (p. 226). - Mark 250 and 500 mL lines on the basin that will catch blood (rule of thumb). Then do ALL of these within 15 minutes, in any order (WHO "MOTIVE", p. 47): | Step | What to do | | Massage | Cupped hand on top of the womb; rub in circles until hard. Alone? Massage first | |

🔄 Stuck shoulders and breech Stuck shoulders: the head is born, pulls back like a turtle, and the shoulders won't come. The baby has about 5 minutes before brain damage (BfM, p. 210). Call every helper. WHO's order (MCPC, pp. 243-244): 1. Knees to chest: two helpers push her bent knees firmly up to her chest (🖼 MCPC p. 244). 2. Press hard just above the pubic bone, not on the belly, while you draw the head steadily downward. Cup the head; don't grip the neck; never jerk. 3. Hand inside along the baby's back: push a shoulder toward the baby's chest to turn it. 4. Bring the back arm out, swept across the chest. Hesperian tries hands-and-knees first (BfM, p. 211); use it if WHO's steps fail. Never push on top of the womb: it can burst. Be ready to help the baby breathe. Breech (bottom first) with no hospital (BfM, pp. 215-217): feet first is the most dangerous kind. No pushing until the cervix is fully open. Hands off: the bottom, belly and legs come on their own, and you never pull on the baby. Wrap the body so it doesn't chill and gasp inside her. A helper presses above the pubic bone to keep the head tucked. Hold the baby by the hips, never the belly (p. 217; 🖼 "hold the baby at the hips, but do

presses above the pubic bone to keep the head tucked. Hold the baby by the hips, never the belly (p. 217; 🖼 "hold the baby at the hips, but do not pull," MCPC p. 378). Hold the baby at the hips, never the belly, and don't pull (MCPC, p. 378). 📚 Go deeper: A Book for Midwives, ch. 12 - each move drawn; WHO Managing Complications - hard births.

🫁 A baby who isn't breathing Most babies breathe within 1-2 minutes, and drying is often enough. Never hold a baby upside down or slap it (BfM, p. 241). WHO's steps (PCPNC, p. 152; Neonatal resuscitation): 1. Dry and rub the back. Not breathing, or only gasping? Start within 1 minute of birth. Cut the cord; move the baby to a warm, dry, flat place. 2. Open the airway: head slightly tipped back, a folded towel no thicker than ¾ in (2 cm) under the shoulders (🖼 MCPC p. 311). Suction only if the mouth or nose is full. 3. Breathe for the baby: mask over chin, mouth and nose (🖼 fitting the mask, MCPC p. 313). Give 5 squeezes and watch the chest rise; if it doesn't, fix the head and seal. Then 40 breaths a minute (one every 1½ seconds). 4. No bag? Your mouth over the baby's mouth and nose: small puffs from your cheeks only (BfM, p. 242). 5. After 1 minute, check the heart with a stethoscope or 2 fingers on the chest. Count 6 seconds, times 10 (BfM, p. 243). 6. Stop when the baby breathes over 30 times a minute without deep chest sucking-in. Skin-to-skin, check every 15 minutes. 7. No heartbeat (or under 60) after 10 minutes of good breaths: the baby has died. Stop and care for the family. Head only
a-baby-who-isn-t-breathing

sucking-in. Skin-to-skin, check every 15 minutes. 7. No heartbeat (or under 60) after 10 minutes of good breaths: the baby has died. Stop and care for the family. Head only slightly tipped back: a newborn's neck is bent back less than an adult's (MCPC, p. 311). The mask covers the chin, mouth and nose, but not the eyes (MCPC, p. 313). Alone with a bleeding mother? Baby first, then her medicine and womb check as soon as you can (WHO, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: PCPNC resuscitation chart; A Book for Midwives, p. 242 - rescue breathing drawn.

🌡 Warmth, small babies and newborn danger signs Warmth: skin-to-skin, head covered, out of drafts. A baby needs only one more layer than an adult (BfM, p. 240). Watch for overheating in valley summers over 100 °F, and chilling November-March (general knowledge). Kangaroo care for babies under 2,500 g (5½ lb) or born 3+ weeks early (WHO KMC, p. 10): - Skin-to-skin as close to 24 hours a day as possible, at least 8, an hour or more at a time, breastfeeding every 2-3 hours (p. 20). - Baby upright between the breasts, head to one side, hips spread; a cloth wrap tied high across the chest, its top just below the baby's ear (p. 32; 🖼 IYCF p. 84). - Room at 77-82 °F (25-28 °C) (PCPNC, p. 140). Continue to about 2,500 g, or until the baby wriggles out (KMC, p. 40). Upright, skin to skin between the breasts, head to one side, hips spread; then wrap the cloth high across her chest (WHO KMC guide, p. 31). Newborn danger signs: treat as an emergency (Caring for the Newborn at Home, p. 71): - not feeding, or stopped feeding well; fits - 60 or more breaths a minute (count twice, baby calm); chest sucking in - 99.5 °F (37.5 °C) or more, or 95.7 °F (35.4 °C) or less (digital thermometer in the armpit - p. 78) -

(count twice, baby calm); chest sucking in - 99.5 °F (37.5 °C) or more, or 95.7 °F (35.4 °C) or less (digital thermometer in the armpit - p. 78) - yellow soles; moves only when touched, or not at all - red or pus-draining navel (Omphalitis), boils, or pus from the eyes (Neonatal conjunctivitis) Newborn antibiotic doses: BfM, p. 279. Jaundice (IMCI, p. 46): - Yellow on the first day, or yellow palms and soles at any age, is severe. It needs hospital light treatment; there is no home cure. Press the soles with your thumbs and look in daylight (Caring for the Newborn, p. 81). - Yellow after day 1 with palms and soles clear: breastfeed often, check daily. Yellow past 14 days needs a check. - No direct sun. WTND's bright window light is harmless if the baby doesn't chill or overheat, but don't count on it (WTND, p. 274). 📚 Go deeper: WHO Caring for the Newborn at Home - checking each sign; WHO KMC guide - pictures.

🤱 Breastfeeding and the mother's recovery Breast milk only for 6 months. Unmodified animal milk is not suitable under 6 months; it can damage the kidneys (WHO IYCF, p. 18). A baby who can't suckle is fed by cup, not bottle (p. 81; 🖼 cup feeding, p. 86). No breast milk? See the Food Security guide for wet-nurses, relactation and formula. Enough milk? After day 5: 8-12 feeds a day with visible swallowing, pale urine at least 6 times a day, yellow stools 3+ times a day until 6 weeks, birth weight back by 2 weeks, then 5-7 oz (150-200 g) a week. Few wet diapers or dark urine is a reliable warning (IYCF, pp. 135-136). Breast problems (🖼 good and poor attachment, IYCF p. 42): - Overfull, hard breasts (Breast engorgement): get the milk out by feeding or hand-expressing (🖼 IYCF p. 155; 🖼 WTND p. 277); warmth before, cool cloths after (IYCF, p. 140). - Mastitis (fever, red painful breast): keep breastfeeding, good side first. She rests; the family does her work. Antibiotics only if not better after 24 hours of good draining (p. 142; doses BfM, p. 289). Well attached: mouth wide open, lower lip turned out, chin touching the breast, more of the dark skin showing above the mouth than below (IYCF, p. 42). Womb infection (fever 100.4 °F / 38 °C or more, bad-smelling discharge,

chin touching the breast, more of the dark skin showing above the mouth than below (IYCF, p. 42). Womb infection (fever 100.4 °F / 38 °C or more, bad-smelling discharge, chills, belly pain, fast pulse) can kill quickly. Antibiotic plan: BfM, p. 271. Check mother and baby within 24 hours, on day 3, on days 7-14 and at 6 weeks (PCPNC, p. 170). Depression after birth hits 1 in 10 to 1 in 5 mothers, and her baby grows worse too (Thinking Healthy, p. 11): - Sadness or worry that is very strong, or lasts over 2 weeks, is depression. The family takes over chores, lets her sleep, sees she eats and moves a little each day (BfM, p. 274). - Thinking Healthy lets a trusted neighbor run home sessions in 3 steps: spot unhelpful thoughts, swap in healthier ones, practice healthy actions (p. 15). - Ask her directly about suicide and whether she has a plan. Asking doesn't make it more likely. A woman with a plan needs help now and must not be left alone (Where Women Have No Doctor, p. 431). 📚 Go deeper: WHO Infant Feeding (2025) - breastfeeding problems; Thinking Healthy - the sessions.

🤒 Sick children under 5: fever, breathing, diarrhea, measles, worms Danger signs: act now - can't drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, has had fits, very sleepy or can't be woken (IMCI, p. 5), or fever with a stiff neck (p. 8). Fever is a sign: look for the cause. Give plenty to drink, boiled water for babies (WTND, p. 76). Paracetamol (acetaminophen) every 6 hours for high fever: one 100 mg tablet at 2 months-3 years, 1½ at 3-5 years - with 500 mg tablets, ¼ and ½ (IMCI, p. 17). No aspirin for children. Pneumonia: count breaths for a full minute, child calm (IMCI, pp. 6, 45): | Age | Fast breathing | | Under 2 months | 60 or more | | 2-12 months | 50 or more | | 1-5 years | 40 or more | Fast breathing or chest sucking in means pneumonia: amoxicillin 250 mg twice a day for 5 days - 1 tablet at 2-12 months, 2 at 1-3 years, 3 at 3-5 years (syrup 250 mg/5 ml: 5, 10 or 15 ml) (p. 16). Diarrhea. Severe dehydration is two or more of: very sleepy or unconscious, sunken eyes, drinks poorly or not at all, a pinch of belly skin taking over 2 seconds to flatten (IMCI, p. 7; 🖼 the pinch, WTND p. 151; Dehydration). - Keep breastfeeding and feeding, plus zinc 10-20
sick-children-under-5-fever-breathing-diarrhea-measles-worms

all, a pinch of belly skin taking over 2 seconds to flatten (IMCI, p. 7; 🖼 the pinch, WTND p. 151; Dehydration). - Keep breastfeeding and feeding, plus zinc 10-20 mg a day for 10-14 days (WHO, p. 14). - After each loose stool, by spoon: under 2 years, 50-100 mL (¼-½ cup); ages 2-10, 100-200 mL (same page). - ORS packets are best. Home mix: 1 liter clean water, ½ level teaspoon salt, 6 level teaspoons sugar (JTS, p. 7), no saltier than tears (Oral rehydration). - Blood in the stool needs an antibiotic (IMCI, p. 7). Measles starts like a cold with red eyes; days later a rash spreads from behind the ears downward (WTND, p. 311). Give vitamin A: 100,000 IU at 6-12 months, 200,000 IU from 1 year (IMCI, p. 20). Clouded eyes or deep mouth sores mean severe measles (p. 8). Worms: pinworm itches at night. Cut nails short, wash hands and bottoms every morning, treat the whole family (WTND, p. 141). Hookworm enters bare feet (🖼 how it spreads, WTND p. 142): latrines and shoes (p. 142). Mebendazole 500 mg once, from age 1, at most every 6 months (IMCI, p. 20). Untreated creek water brings giardia and weeks of diarrhea (general knowledge). 📚 Go deeper: WHO IMCI charts - every decision and dose; WHO Treatment of Diarrhoea - plans A, B, C.

📏 Growth, malnutrition and toddler food Weigh monthly and plot it on the WHO-standard charts in pounds and inches (boys; girls; Growth chart). A homemade beam scale works (WTND, p. 297; Steelyard balance). A baby whose weight drops across 2 lines is not growing well (IYCF, p. 136). Arm measurement (MUAC), 6 months-5 years, around the middle of the upper arm (IMCI, p. 10; MUAC): under 11.5 cm, or swelling of both feet (Kwashiorkor), is severe malnutrition; 11.5-12.5 cm is moderate; 12.5 cm or more is OK. Mark a paper strip at 11.5 and 12.5 cm (rule of thumb). Refeeding a severely malnourished child needs care: WHO 1999 and the Food Security guide. Toddler food and water (WHO, p. 38; p. 46; 🖼 "five keys to safer food," IYCF p. 56): - Boil water, and boil milk that isn't pasteurized (goat milk too). - Eat cooked food within 2 hours, or reheat it until it is all boiling hot. - Feed by cup or spoon, never a bottle. Wash hands with soap. Keep animals out of the house. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Complementary Feeding - first foods; WTND, ch. 21 - growth charts.

🛡 Accidents: drowning, burns, poisoning 📷 A child ate a plant, berry or mushroom? Keep a piece (and any vomit) and photograph the plant: the plant and mushroom identifier may name it for whoever is helping. Don't wait for it to act. Drowning: a small child can drown in a few centimeters of water in a bucket (WHO, p. 78). Empty buckets and tubs; cover wells, cisterns and barrels (p. 86). Here that means rain barrels (Rain barrel), stock tanks, ditches, and the cold, deep pools of the Illinois and Rogue rivers (general knowledge). Burns: keep babies away from fires and wood stoves; turn pan handles inward. Cool a burn in clean cool water (not ice) up to 20 minutes. Never grease, fat, herbs or dung (WTND, p. 96). Canning kettles and soap-making lye are local hazards; see the Field Care guide. Poisons: lock up lye, kerosene and lamp oil, rat poison and medicines (iron pills especially), and never store them in drink bottles (WTND, p. 103). Teach children to leave alone western water hemlock by creeks and ditches, "the most poisonous plant in North America" (PNW 109; Cicuta douglasii), and the death cap mushroom (BCCDC; Death cap). If a child swallows poison (WHO, p. 155): 1. Get them away from it; strip soaked clothes; flush skin and eyes with lots of water. 2. Airway and breathing first. Unconscious: on

child swallows poison (WHO, p. 155): 1. Get them away from it; strip soaked clothes; flush skin and eyes with lots of water. 2. Airway and breathing first. Unconscious: on their side (🖼 ATP p. 79). 3. Activated charcoal within 1 hour helps for many poisons, not fuels, lye, alcohol or iron. 4. Do not make the child vomit. 🧼 Sanitation, Hygiene & Stopping Disease When sewers, pumps and power fail, cholera, dysentery, typhoid and hepatitis follow, and they all travel from human waste to someone's mouth. This guide covers toilets for every season in our clay soils, septic systems with no power, greywater, handwashing, keeping clean with little water, lice and scabies, stopping an outbreak, flies and mice, garbage with no pickup (sorting, pits, compost, bears, burning, hazardous waste), sickroom waste, dead animals, and caring for the dead. The books are in Sanitation-Hygiene\ (Latrines-Toilets, Septic-Greywater, Hygiene-Washing, Disease-Outbreaks, Pests-Vectors, Waste-Burial, which holds Oregon's burning and livestock-mortality guides) and Homestead-Skills\Sanitation-Water; the compost bulletins are in Gardening-Food, the bear and vet books under Animals\. The twin-bucket toilet, soap and cleaners are in the Make-Do Household guide; nursing the sick is in the Field Care guide. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Keep every latrine, garbage pit and grave at least 100 ft (30 m) from wells, springs and creeks, and downhill of them, with the pit bottom 5 ft (1.5 m) above groundwater (Sphere, p. 140). Some books say 65 ft (20 m). Use 100. - Wash hands with soap or ash after the toilet and before food. It cuts diarrhea by 42-47% (Tippy-Tap, p. 1). - Diarrhea kills by drying people out. Start the rehydration drink at the first watery stool (WTND ch. 13, p. 2). -

It cuts diarrhea by 42-47% (Tippy-Tap, p. 1). - Diarrhea kills by drying people out. Start the rehydration drink at the first watery stool (WTND ch. 13, p. 2). - Never climb down into a septic tank, pit or vault. The gases can kill in minutes (rule of thumb). - Never mix bleach with urine, ammonia or vinegar. It makes poison gas (Make-Do guide). - Never sweep or vacuum mouse droppings (hantavirus). - Never burn plastic, rubber, tires, oil, wet garbage or dead animals: Oregon bans it anywhere, any time (DEQ, p. 1). No open burning June-October (rule of thumb). - No food scraps in the garbage pit: bears dig up buried garbage (ODFW, p. 2). Never cut open an animal that died suddenly with dark blood at the nose or mouth (anthrax; WTNAD, p. 215).

🗺 Choosing and siting a toilet in our soils Siting: 100 ft (30 m) from any well, spring or creek, downhill of it, with the pit bottom 5 ft (1.5 m) above the water table; more in cracked rock (Sphere, p. 140). Keep latrines downwind and well away from the kitchen (FM 21-10, p. 77). On gravelly Illinois River terraces sewage travels fast toward shallow wells, so add distance (rule of thumb). Our clay is waterlogged in winter. Valley-floor soils such as Brockman clay loam have a perched winter water table only 24-36 in down and very slow drainage; septic drainfields "function poorly" on them (Soil Survey, p. 33). A pit dug there in winter fills with water. So: - Dig pits in the dry season, on higher, well-drained ground. - November to April, on the valley floor, use a bucket toilet or a compost toilet built on top of the ground. The Army switches to a pail latrine whenever the water table is too high (FM 21-10, p. 134; 🖼 pail latrine, p. 135). 100 ft away, downhill, 5 ft above groundwater; on valley clay in winter, don't dig a pit at all (a diagram drawn for this guide). | Situation | Use | | One use, away from home | Cat hole (🖼 FM 21-10, p. 131) | | First 1-3 days, a few people | Straddle trench

⛏ Latrines step by step - Cat hole: 6-12 in deep, used once and covered at once (🖼 FM 21-10, p. 131). - Straddle trench: 1 ft wide, 2½ ft deep, 4 ft long, parallel trenches at least 2 ft apart. Cover each use with the dug earth (Special Forces Handbook, p. 162; 🖼 FM 21-10, p. 133), and cover well: a thin layer of soil can increase fly breeding (Rozendaal, p. 321). - Simple pit: a bit under 3 ft (1 m) across and 3-6½ ft (1-2 m) deep, under a slab whose hole has a lid that stays on (WTND ch. 12, p. 9). Hesperian says at least 6½ ft deep, with the top lined so the edge can't collapse (Ch 7, p. 19). - VIP latrine (pit latrine): add a vent pipe that rises at least 20 in (50 cm) above the roof, with fly screen on top (Hesperian Ch 7, p. 22), and keep the shelter dark, door shut. Smells go up the pipe; flies head for the light at its top and die there (Practical Action VIP Latrine, p. 1; 🖼 how the air flows, Rozendaal p. 163; 🖼 Hesperian Ch 7, p. 22). - Neighborhood trench latrine: about 3 ft wide, 5-10 ft deep, no more than 20 ft long, one stall per 3 ft (🖼 WHO/WEDC, p. 57). Line the top 20 in

Neighborhood trench latrine: about 3 ft wide, 5-10 ft deep, no more than 20 ft long, one stall per 3 ft (🖼 WHO/WEDC, p. 57). Line the top 20 in so the edges don't cave in. Solids build up at 3-5 litres (about a gallon) per person per month (Compendium, p. 44): a family of 5 fills about a cubic yard every 3 years (arithmetic). - Closing a full pit: when the waste is 1 ft below the surface, fill the rest in packed 3-in layers and mound at least 1 ft of earth on top so fly pupae can't dig out (Special Forces Handbook, p. 162). Or let it settle, top up, and plant a tree on it (Hesperian Ch 7, p. 19; 🖼 a toilet for tree planting, p. 26; Arborloo). Straddle trenches: cover each use with the dug earth (FM 21-10, p. 133). Air goes down the hole and up the vent, carrying the smell; flies head for the light at the top of the pipe and die at the netting (Rozendaal, p. 163). Indoor vented bucket: a lidded 5-gallon can lined with a heavy bag, with a hose taped into a hole near the top and run outdoors to 6 in above the ground. A full bag lifts out tied (Kearny, p. 108). Bury or compost the bags; piled outside, they breed flies. 📚 Go deeper:

♻ Composting toilets, humanure and urine After every use, cover the deposit with 1-2 cups (200-500 mL) of wood ash or lime. It dries it, raises the pH to kill germs over time, and cuts flies and smell (SEI EcoSanRes, p. 39; Humanure). Lime burns skin and eyes: wear gloves and goggles. How long to store it before it touches a garden (SEI, pp. 39-40), with nothing fresh added: | Treatment | Store at least | | Average temperature 36-68 °F (2-20 °C) - our climate | 1½-2 years | | Average temperature 68-95 °F (20-35 °C) | More than 1 year | | Kept alkaline, pH above 9 (plenty of ash or lime) | More than 6 months | | Hot compost: all of it above 122 °F (50 °C) for a week | Hard to do at home | Then wait 1 month between spreading and harvest (p. 40). Our mean annual air temperature is 48-54 °F (Soil Survey, p. 32), so use the 2-year rule: in home composting toilets, temperatures "typically never become high enough to rapidly destroy pathogens" (EPA, p. 4). Build two chambers on top of the ground, not in it, so they work in waterlogged soil, and use them in turn (Practical Action, p. 2; 🖼 a 2-chamber dry toilet, Hesperian Ch 7, p. 28; 🖼 double-vault toilet, Compendium p. 60). Make each big
composting-toilets-humanure-and-urine

waterlogged soil, and use them in turn (Practical Action, p. 2; 🖼 a 2-chamber dry toilet, Hesperian Ch 7, p. 28; 🖼 double-vault toilet, Compendium p. 60). Make each big enough to take a year or more to fill (rule of thumb). Two chambers on top of the ground: one is used while the other is closed and resting; ash goes in after each use (Practical Action, p. 3). Urine carries few germs (Kearny, p. 108), and keeping it apart (urine-diverting toilet; 🖼 urine-separating seats, SEI p. 35) stops the smell (OSU, p. 3). On your own garden, dilute it with water and pour it on, but stop on food crops a month before harvest. For crops others will eat, store it sealed 1 month, or 6 months to be safe (SEI, pp. 21, 39). Using the finished product: worm eggs survive in soil for years (SEI, p. 23). Use aged humanure around fruit trees, berries, and crops whose edible parts don't touch soil, never on greens or root crops (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: SEI Safe Use of Urine and Faeces - the storage tables; Practical Action Compost Toilets - building a two-chamber toilet.

🏠 Septic systems with no power, and greywater Find out now which kind of septic system you have (🖼 tank cross-section, Compendium p. 68; Drain field). - Gravity (pipes slope down to the tank and drainfield) keeps working with no power (Texas AgriLife, p. 2). Flush with a bucket of used wash water (rule of thumb). - Pump tanks, sand filters, aerobic units, pressure or drip lines stop. The reserve may be only 80 gallons for a 3-bedroom house. Use water only to flush and wash hands, stop if drains slow, and stop all use in a long outage (Texas AgriLife, p. 3); switch to a bucket toilet. Many Josephine County homes on clay or serpentine have these (rule of thumb). With no pump trucks: a tank needs pumping when scum is within 6 in of the outlet or sludge within 12 in, normally every 3-5 years. Additives do nothing. Never pour grease, oil, solvents or paint down a drain (EPA SepticSmart, pp. 3, 4, 7); keep food scraps and wipes out too (rule of thumb). After a flood: don't use it until water has left every part, and don't pump a tank empty while the ground is soaked: it can float out of the ground (Texas, p. 4). Greywater, following Oregon's rules (DEQ, pp. 3-4): - Store it no more than 24 hours. - Release it at least 2
septic-systems-with-no-power-and-greywater

can float out of the ground (Texas, p. 4). Greywater, following Oregon's rules (DEQ, pp. 3-4): - Store it no more than 24 hours. - Release it at least 2 in under soil or mulch, 4 ft above groundwater, 100 ft from wells, and never onto edible parts of crops or root vegetables (🖼 a simple system, DEQ p. 15). - A soak pit (🖼 FM 21-10, p. 130) is 5-13 ft deep, filled with rocks, 6½ ft above the highest groundwater. Clay won't take it (Compendium, p. 150). On valley clay in winter, carry greywater to higher ground or use it to flush (rule of thumb). - Kitchen water: a barrel grease trap (gravel, then ashes or sand, burlap on top), cleaned every 2 days (Special Forces Handbook, p. 164; 🖼 FM 21-10, p. 131; Grease trap). 📚 Go deeper: Texas AgriLife Septic Systems in Outages and Floods - which systems stop; EPA Homeowner's Guide to Septic Systems; Oregon DEQ Reusing Graywater.

🧼 Handwashing and water for hygiene Build a tippy tap (USAID, pp. 1-2): 1. Take a 1½-gallon (5 L) plastic jug with a handle. Warm the base of the handle over a candle, pinch it shut with pliers, and let it cool watertight. 2. With a candle-heated nail, make a small hole in the handle just above the seal, and two bigger holes in the back, halfway up, for the hanging string. 3. Hang it from a stick so the full jug tilts at 45°. Hang soap on a string under an upside-down tin can. Pull a string tied to the cap to tip water onto your hands. 4. Scrub the outside daily; clean the inside weekly. Pull the cap string and water runs out of the small hole in the handle (a diagram drawn for this guide). Put one within 16 ft (5 m) of every toilet and wherever food is made. No water? Rub hands with ash or alcohol hand rub (Compendium, p. 40). Sanitizer needs 60%+ alcohol and fails on visibly dirty hands (OSU, p. 4). See hand washing (🖼 the steps, WHO/WEDC p. 40; 🖼 WHO handwashing steps, MCPC pp. 51-53; 🖼 field handwashing devices, FM 21-10 p. 139) and hand sanitizer. Wash hands before cooking, eating or feeding anyone, and after the toilet, caring for someone with diarrhea, cleaning a child's bottom, cleaning up feces
handwashing-and-water-for-hygiene

21-10 p. 139) and hand sanitizer. Wash hands before cooking, eating or feeding anyone, and after the toilet, caring for someone with diarrhea, cleaning a child's bottom, cleaning up feces or vomit, or touching a body (MSF Cholera, p. 46). How much water (WHO/WEDC, pp. 36-37): | Use | Per person per day | | Drinking | 2.5-3 L (about ¾ gal) | | Hygiene | 2-6 L | | Cooking | 3-6 L | | Bare survival, total | 7.5-15 L (2-4 gal) | | Minimum for real hygiene | 20 L (5 gal) | | A cholera patient | 60 L, plus 15 L for the carer | Enough water matters as much as safe water (Hesperian Ch 5, p. 3). 📚 Go deeper: Tippy-Tap - the picture guide; WHO/WEDC, p. 36 - water quantities; Army FM 21-10 - field hygiene for a group.

🧺 Dishes, laundry and periods Dishes: scrape scraps into a bucket for the chickens. Wash in hot soapy water (120-140 °F) and rinse. Then dip in boiling water for 10 seconds, or in 1 Tbsp unscented bleach per gallon, and air-dry (FM 21-10, p. 114; OSU EM9273, p. 3). Laundry: soap and cold water don't get rid of lice. Wash clothes and bedding above 140 °F (60 °C), then iron or dry in full sun (Rozendaal, p. 274). No hot water? Seal them in a plastic bag for 72 hours for scabies, or 2 weeks for head-lice items (MSF Clinical Guidelines, pp. 133, 136). Never wash a sick person's clothes in a creek or any drinking source (MSF Cholera, p. 46). Periods: a year's supply per woman is 6 reusable pads (or 4 m² of absorbent cotton), 6 pairs of underwear, and an extra 250 g (½ lb) of soap a month (Sphere, p. 129). Change cloth pads (🖼 pattern, WASHplus) several times a day, wash with soap and dry in the sun. Change a tampon at least 3 times a day, or it can cause serious infection (WWHND ch. 5, p. 4). Plan a private place to wash and dry pads by the latrine (Compendium, p. 44). 📚 Go deeper: WASHplus pad pattern - sew your own; FM 21-10, p. 114 - dishwashing setup; Make-Do guide - laundry soap

dry pads by the latrine (Compendium, p. 44). 📚 Go deeper: WASHplus pad pattern - sew your own; FM 21-10, p. 114 - dishwashing setup; Make-Do guide - laundry soap and hand washing.

🦠 How germs spread, and stopping an outbreak The "F-diagram" (fecal-oral route): germs from feces reach the mouth by fingers, flies, fields, fluids (water) and food. Every barrier counts: latrines, handwashing, safe water, covered food, animals kept out of the house (Hesperian Ch 5, p. 6; WTND ch. 12, p. 3; 🖼 the barriers drawn, WHO/WEDC p. 39; 🖼 SEI p. 12). An outbreak is starting when you see bloody diarrhea, watery diarrhea in anyone over 5, suspected cholera, or yellow eyes or skin in several people. Start isolation and hygiene measures neighborhood-wide (WHO, p. 115). "Enteric isolation" (cholera, shigella dysentery, typhoid, E. coli, hepatitis A) means handwashing, the sick person's own dishes, and safe disposal of their feces and soiled things (WHO, p. 133). - Typhoid: a separate room; stools buried deep. People who recover can carry it for a long time and must not cook for others (WTND ch. 14, p. 12). - Hepatitis A and E: antibiotics don't help, and acetaminophen (Tylenol) further damages the liver (WTND ch. 13, p. 22). Isolate kindly (WHO, p. 132): let one family member care for each sick person, with gloves and an apron and a lesson in using them. Explain isolation to everyone. Shame and fear make people hide sick relatives, and hidden cases spread the outbreak. Rehydration drink (WTND ch. 13, p. 2; oral rehydration; 🖼 drawn, Hesperian Ch
how-germs-spread-and-stopping-an-outbreak

isolation to everyone. Shame and fear make people hide sick relatives, and hidden cases spread the outbreak. Rehydration drink (WTND ch. 13, p. 2; oral rehydration; 🖼 drawn, Hesperian Ch 5, p. 10): 1 litre (about 1 quart) of clean water and ½ level teaspoon salt. Taste it: it must be less salty than tears. Then add 8 level teaspoons sugar. Keep giving food and breast milk. Cholera or bloody diarrhea in the house (MSF Cholera, pp. 46-48): 1. Wipe up vomit or feces first, put it in the latrine or bury it, then wash the spot with soap. 2. Wash the sick person's clothes and bedding with soap and dry them in the sun. Sun the mattress too: the cholera germ dies when dried. 3. Don't spray whole houses with chlorine. No study shows it helps, and it makes families hide cases. A kit of bucket, soap, detergent and cloths does more. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Communicable Disease Control in Emergencies - isolation and disease pages; MSF Management of a Cholera Epidemic - household rules.

🧪 Chlorine strengths from household bleach These are for cleaning - never for drinking. Even the weakest (0.05%) is far too strong to drink. To make drinking water safe, use 8 drops of 6% bleach (6 drops of 8.25%) per gallon and wait 30 minutes (Water Purification guide; EPA, p. 2). | Strength | Use it for (Compendium, p. 174) | From 6% bleach | From 8.25% bleach | | 0.05% | Skin and hands (if no soap), laundry, latrines, kitchen | About 2 Tbsp per gallon | About 1½ Tbsp per gallon | | 0.2% | Floors, beds, clothes, objects | About ½ cup per gallon | About 6 Tbsp per gallon | | 2% | Feces, vomit, washing bodies | 1 part bleach + 2 parts water | 1 part bleach + 3 parts water | The rule is parts of water = (bleach % ÷ % wanted) - 1 (MSF Cholera, p. 226); the amounts above are that arithmetic. - Read the strength on the label; use plain, unscented bleach. - Mix fresh every day, and clean first: bleach doesn't work through dirt. - Never pour it into a urine bucket or mix it with ammonia or vinegar. - Drinking water needs a far weaker dose: see the Water Purification guide. 📚 Go deeper: MSF Cholera, p. 226 - dilution tables; Compendium, p. 174 - cholera disinfection.

🪰 Flies, mosquitoes, lice and scabies Flies (housefly) go from egg to adult in 6-42 days, faster in heat (Rozendaal, p. 314; 🖼 the fly and its life cycle, p. 315). In hot weather empty and bury garbage at least twice a week: maggots leave closed bins after 3-4 days. Cover a garbage pit with fresh soil at least weekly; fit latrines with tight lids or screened vents (p. 321; 🖼 tight-lidded bins, p. 321; 🖼 a fly- and mosquito-proof latrine lid, p. 160). June-September is peak fly season here (rule of thumb). Mosquitoes take about 7-13 days from egg to adult, so empty and scrub small water containers weekly, and cover barrels with tight lids or netting (Rozendaal, pp. 23, 156; 🖼 mosquito life cycle, p. 22; 🖼 lids and netting, p. 156; Mosquito). Ditches, stock tanks, old tires and open rain barrels breed them here, and West Nile virus has been found in southern Oregon (rule of thumb) (West Nile virus; Culex tarsalis). Body lice (body louse) live and lay eggs in clothing seams, and spread typhus, relapsing fever and trench fever. Hot washing and ironing fix it; in an outbreak, dust 0.5% permethrin powder inside clothes (Rozendaal, p. 274; 🖼 how to dust clothing, p. 275; MSF Clinical, p. 136). Head lice (🖼 the three kinds of lice, Rozendaal p. 266; 🖼 checking hair and combing, pp.
flies-mosquitoes-lice-and-scabies

p. 274; 🖼 how to dust clothing, p. 275; MSF Clinical, p. 136). Head lice (🖼 the three kinds of lice, Rozendaal p. 266; 🖼 checking hair and combing, pp. 268-271): dimeticone (from age 6 months) or 1% permethrin (from 2 months) lotion, repeated after 7 days; treat only contacts with live lice or nits (same page). Scabies (🖼 the mite and an infested wrist, Rozendaal pp. 291-292; Sarcoptes scabiei): itching worse at night, with fine wavy burrows between the fingers and on the wrists. Treat everyone in close contact at the same time, even if they don't itch: permethrin 5% cream (age 2 months and up) left on 8 hours, repeated after 7 days. Wash bedding hot or bag it 72 hours (MSF Clinical, pp. 133-134). A first-time rash can take 4-6 weeks to show, so one case means others are probably infested already (Rozendaal, p. 292). Stock permethrin and dimeticone now (rule of thumb). Ticks (western black-legged tick) are in the Make-Do guide. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Vector Control (Rozendaal) - flies, mosquitoes, lice, fleas and mites; MSF Clinical Guidelines, p. 133 - scabies and lice treatment.

🐭 Mice, hantavirus, fleas and plague Hantavirus: in the West the deer mouse carries it, and people usually catch it by breathing dust from droppings. Illness starts 1-8 weeks later with fever, aches and vomiting; 4-10 days after that comes shortness of breath. There is no specific treatment (NPS, p. 1). Woodsheds, cabins, root cellars and barns here all hold deer mice (rule of thumb). Keep them out: seal every gap wider than ¼ in (🖼 gaps around pipes, USDA p. 18), keep food and trash sealed, and keep plants 18 in from walls (NPS, p. 1). Use snap traps (Mousetrap) or cats, not poison, which kills pets and children (WTND ch. 14, p. 12). Cleaning up droppings (NPS, p. 2): 1. Open the windows and leave for 30 minutes. Never sweep or vacuum. 2. With gloves on, soak droppings, nests and dead mice with 1:10 bleach (about 1½ cups per gallon of water), mixed fresh that day. Spray 2 ft around, and wait at least 10 minutes. 3. Wipe up with paper towels. Pick up dead mice with a bag turned inside out over your gloved hand. Double-bag everything. 4. Spray the gloves before taking them off, then wash your hands with soap. Fleas and plague): flea cocoons can wait up to a year in an empty house and hatch all at once when people move in (Rozendaal, p.
mice-hantavirus-fleas-and-plague

your hands with soap. Fleas and plague): flea cocoons can wait up to a year in an empty house and hatch all at once when people move in (Rozendaal, p. 256; 🖼 rat, human and cat fleas, p. 255; Oriental rat flea). Don't handle dead rats or squirrels: their fleas jump to people. Drown dead rats, then burn them (WTND ch. 14, p. 12), or bury them deep in fire season. Plague lives in wild ground squirrels (California ground squirrel), chipmunks and their fleas in parts of Oregon. Keep cats from hunting, and treat a cat with a swollen neck or fever as dangerous (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: NPS Hantavirus Fact Sheet - cleanup steps; USDA Rat Proofing Buildings, p. 27 - keeping rodents out.

🗑 Garbage when no truck comes Open trash piles breed rats, flies and mosquitoes, and their chemicals seep into soil and water (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 5); heaps catch fire, and rain washes them into water supplies (WHO/WEDC, p. 27). So make less, and sort it in the kitchen into two or three bins (🖼 Hesperian Ch 18, p. 13). Sorting later, at a dump, is dangerous and works worse (p. 14). | Kind of waste | Where it goes | | Vegetable scraps, peelings, coffee grounds | Chickens, pigs, a worm bin or compost. Never the garbage pit: bears dig it up (see "Garbage, bears and pests") | | Meat, bones, fat, fish | Cook scraps before pigs get them: raw garbage gives pigs trichinosis (Zoonoses, p. 121). Render fat into soap; burn bones in a hot stove (rule of thumb) | | Paper, cardboard, sawdust | Shredded into compost, sawdust into dry toilets (Hesperian Ch 18, pp. 18-19), or burned in the cooking or heating fire (p. 24) | | Jars, bottles, tin cans, buckets | Wash and keep: bottles reuse as they are, cans make lamps and planters (Hesperian Ch 18, pp. 19-20). Food-safe ones: "Containers and storage" in the Make-Do guide | | Batteries, oil, paint, pesticides, medicines, bulbs | A separate toxics store (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 13): see "Hazardous waste" below | | Broken

storage" in the Make-Do guide | | Batteries, oil, paint, pesticides, medicines, bulbs | A separate toxics store (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 13): see "Hazardous waste" below | | Broken glass, plastic, rubber, scrap | Rinse off any food, then the garbage pit. Never burn it |

A household garbage pit or trench - Where: 100 ft (30 m) from wells, springs and creeks, downhill of them, the bottom 5 ft above groundwater (Sphere, p. 140), 100 ft from the kitchen (FM 21-10, p. 129), and on higher ground, dug in the dry season, as for latrines. - A pit is 4 ft square and 4 ft deep, filled to 1 ft below ground and mounded over with earth (Special Forces Handbook, p. 164; 🖼 FM 21-10, p. 129). Cover each layer with 4 in of soil or ash, and a full pit with 20 in (WHO/WEDC, p. 29). - A trench lasts longer: 2 ft wide, 3-4 ft deep, filled to within 1 ft of the top and dug onward, the new dirt covering the last load (Special Forces Handbook, p. 164). - In the wet months, dig a small new hole each week or month and roof it against rain (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 29). Fence it, and keep it deep enough that animals can't dig in (WWHND ch. 10, p. 4).
a-household-garbage-pit-or-trench

A shared neighborhood dump Country garbage usually goes into family or shared neighborhood pits (WHO/WEDC, p. 28). A shared one needs: 1. A site 820 ft (250 m) from streams and ponds and 1,640 ft (500 m) from homes and wells, out of any flood zone, its bottom 6½ ft (2 m) above the highest groundwater (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 27). 2. A fence with a locking gate, sand or soil kept there for fires (🖼 p. 28), and no open flames (WHO/WEDC, p. 28). 3. Each load pressed down and covered with soil, or soil, ash and sand, under a roof (Hesperian p. 29). 4. One person or team in charge, with gloves, boots, masks, overalls and tetanus shots (WHO/WEDC p. 28). 5. When full, a cap of 3 ft (90 cm) of soil, planted with grass, never food plants, and no grazing until it's grown over (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 29). Circles of dead grass mean landfill gas: keep 33 ft (10 m) away (p. 30). 📚 Go deeper: Hesperian Ch 18 Solid Waste - reducing, sorting, reusing, landfills; WHO/WEDC Technical Note 7, p. 27 - solid waste in emergencies.

🌱 Composting food, yard waste and manure A hot pile reaches 130-150 °F, which kills most weed seeds and germs; a slow pile kills far fewer (WSU EB1784E, p. 2, written for the Northwest; Compost). Building a hot pile (WSU, pp. 3-6): 1. Collect at least 1 cubic yard at once: a heap 5 ft wide and 3 ft high, or a bin 3 × 3 × 3 ft of pallets, lumber, wire mesh or blocks (pp. 4-5). Small piles stay cold. 2. Mix 1 part "greens" to 2 parts "browns" by volume (p. 3). Greens are wet and rich in nitrogen (p. 2): food scraps, fresh manure (Hesperian Ch 18, pp. 17-18). Browns are dry: straw, brown leaves, husks, shredded paper (p. 18), wood chips (WSU p. 3). 3. Squeeze a handful: barely a drop should come out. Too dry, add water; too wet, add browns (p. 5). 4. Turn it weekly for 4-6 weeks, and cover it in rainy weather, or in a wet winter it may never heat (pp. 4-5). 5. After several hot weeks it cures 2-3 months. It's ready when turning no longer heats it and it looks dark and crumbly (p. 6). Rotting instead of heating? Add browns. Smells? Turn it for air. Flies? Cover it better with soil (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 18). Slow pile: heap yard waste for a year, tucking scraps
composting-food-yard-waste-and-manure

of heating? Add browns. Smells? Turn it for air. Flies? Cover it better with soil (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 18). Slow pile: heap yard waste for a year, tucking scraps into the middle, then turn it and leave it a second year (WSU, pp. 4-5; 🖼 two-pile system, p. 5). It won't kill weed seeds or germs, so pull weeds before they seed (p. 5). Worm bin (vermicompost): 1 cubic foot of bin, no more than 1 ft deep, per pound of scraps a week (a 14-gallon tote suits 2-3 people); outdoors, on the north side of a building, safe from rats and raccoons (OSU EM 9034, pp. 2-3; 🖼 p. 4). Keep out: meat, bones, fish, grease and dairy, which draw pests and bears (WSU, p. 6; ODFW, p. 2). Bury fruit and vegetable scraps fully inside the pile, or use a pest-proof bin (🖼 WSU, p. 5). Also keep out dog and cat feces (WSU p. 7), plastic, metal, glass and poisonous plants (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 18). Human waste: see "Composting toilets, humanure and urine". Manure can carry Salmonella and E. coli O157:H7: give manure compost a year or more before it goes on root crops, lettuce or strawberries. Bought hay or straw may carry clopyralid or aminopyralid weed killers that pass into manure and harm tomatoes, potatoes and beans: ask the grower (WSU, p. 7). Cover
composting-food-yard-waste-and-manure

or strawberries. Bought hay or straw may carry clopyralid or aminopyralid weed killers that pass into manure and harm tomatoes, potatoes and beans: ask the grower (WSU, p. 7). Cover dung heaps with plastic so the heat kills fly maggots (🖼 Rozendaal, p. 320). Each animal's manure: "Manure for the garden" in the Rabbits guide, "Manure, litter and feathers" in the Chickens guide, "Teeth and worms" in the Horse guide. Use 1-3 in mixed into a new bed, then ½-1 in a year. Moist, backyard-size piles don't catch fire (WSU pp. 6-7). 📚 Go deeper: WSU Backyard Composting - hot and slow piles, bins; OSU Composting with Worms - worm bins; OSU EC 1561, p. 7 - leaf and yard compost; Hesperian Ch 18, pp. 16-17 - pit compost and a fast layered pile.
composting-food-yard-waste-and-manure

🐻 Garbage, bears and pests Oregon has 25,000-30,000 black bears; one that gets human food or garbage loses its fear of people and often has to be killed (ODFW Living with Black Bears, p. 1; American black bear). "Do not bury garbage or fish refuse; bears will dig it up" (p. 2). A homestead still needs a pit, so keep every food smell out of it, cover each layer, and fence it, with electric wire whenever bears are about (rule of thumb). Around the house (ODFW, p. 2): keep garbage cans in a shed or behind chain-link or electric fence, scrubbed with bleach. ODFW also suggests mothballs: don't, they poison children and pets (rule of thumb). Electric-fence compost, gardens, orchards, berries and hives; pick up fallen fruit; feed pets indoors; lock up livestock feed, since plastic tubs won't stop a bear (BearWise, p. 1); and ask the neighbors to do the same. Electric fence for bears (BearWise, p. 2; Electric fence): - At least 3 wires (5 or 6 is better), 8-10 in apart: lowest 7-9 in up (a little lower stops skunks and raccoons too), top 36-42 in. - An energizer of at least 6,000 volts and 0.5 joules; plants kept off the wires; voltage tested often. - Step-by-step photos: "Bears and fire season" in the Bees guide (🖼 UF, pp. 3-5). Cougars: leave no food or garbage outside;
garbage-bears-and-pests

plants kept off the wires; voltage tested often. - Step-by-step photos: "Bears and fire season" in the Bees guide (🖼 UF, pp. 3-5). Cougars: leave no food or garbage outside; anything that draws other wildlife can draw a cougar, and so can animal kills (ODFW, p. 2). Raccoons that learn the garbage cans go after the poultry next (Kentucky ID-245, p. 2). Rats: "Neatness is of prime importance": covered cans, a deep covered pit for tin cans, lumber on racks 18 in high, woodpiles and manure piles away from food (USDA Rat Proofing, p. 6). Deer mice: see "Mice, hantavirus, fleas and plague". Flies breed mostly in garbage, then rotting grass clippings and compost (Rozendaal, pp. 316-317), and spread dysentery, typhoid and cholera (p. 319). Empty and clean bins twice a week in hot weather, weekly in cool, scraping out the bottom (p. 321); more in "Flies, mosquitoes, lice and scabies". 📚 Go deeper: ODFW Living with Black Bears, p. 2 - the homeowner's checklist; BearWise, p. 2 - electric fence facts.
garbage-bears-and-pests

🔥 Burning trash and brush, and ash Oregon bans burning these in the open, anywhere, any time, and a burn barrel counts as open burning (DEQ Southern Oregon Outdoor Burning Guide, p. 1): plastic, rubber, tires (even to start a fire), wet garbage and food waste, dead animals, oil and anything petroleum-treated, asphalt, auto parts, asbestos, and anything making dense smoke or foul odors. Plastic smoke carries dioxins, furans and PCBs (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 24). Never burn treated wood, even in a stove: its smoke and ash carry poisons (Wood Handbook, p. 329) such as arsenic (ATSDR, p. 1); nor old paint (lead: Shelter guide), batteries, bulbs or chemicals (Hesperian Ch 18, p. 25). Every 3 bags burned still leave about 1 bag of toxic ash (Hesperian Ch 19, p. 6). With nobody to ask: no open burning June-October (rule of thumb), and otherwise only on wet, calm days, in daylight (OSU EC 1574, p. 4). 🐄 Dead animals and gut piles Move a dead animal at once: carcasses draw predators (Kentucky ID-245, p. 6), and botulism poison builds up in maggots on dead birds, which chickens eat (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 70). Oregon law, while enforced: a carcass within ½ mile of a home or ¼ mile of a running stream must be dealt with within 15 hours of death or discovery, and may not be burned in the open (ODA Livestock Mortality, pp. 1, 3). Could it be anthrax? If an animal died suddenly with dark blood from the nose, mouth or anus, don't cut it open: the spores foul the soil for good (Where There Is No Animal Doctor, p. 215). People catch it too. Keep dogs and scavengers off, and bury it unopened, where it lies, deep, under quicklime (Zoonoses, pp. 69-70; Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 108). Zoonoses would rather burn it in a pit, with old tires for heat (p. 69): never burn tires, and Oregon bans burning carcasses (DEQ, p. 1). Burying a carcass (Oregon's recommendations, ODA, pp. 1-2): - A dry hole bottom: never soggy, flooded or floodplain ground, and groundwater 25 ft below it. Valley clay is wet 2-3 ft down in winter (Soil Survey, p. 33), so bury on higher ground. - 500 ft from creeks, ponds and wells where you can, never under 100 ft; 300

2-3 ft down in winter (Soil Survey, p. 33), so bury on higher ground. - 500 ft from creeks, ponds and wells where you can, never under 100 ft; 300 ft from a neighbor's house and 50 ft from a property line, on nearly flat ground. - Lime under the carcass and dusted on top (it cuts smell and seepage), sod and manure around it, and 3-4 ft of soil over it, mounded for settling and topped up as it sinks. More than 3 ft (1 m) keeps dogs from digging it up (WTNAD, p. 229). Lime is for animals; for people, see "Caring for the dead". - No more than 1,000 lb per hole, except one bigger animal; over 4,200 lb needs an ODA plan or DEQ permit. Put down by a vet, or shot with lead: the usual euthanasia drug, pentobarbital, poisons eagles, hawks, ravens, bears, coyotes, cougars and dogs that eat the remains, and lead harms scavengers too (AVMA, p. 17). Bury these deep at once (if the ground is frozen, cover them securely until you can), and never leave one out for scavengers (ODA, p. 2), nor gut piles from lead-shot game (rule of thumb). ⚰ Caring for the dead Bodies don't cause epidemics when people died of injury, fire, cold or hunger. The exceptions are deaths from cholera, Ebola-type fevers and similar infections (PAHO, p. 17). Handlers need waterproof gloves, an apron and boots, and must wash with soap before eating; masks aren't essential (p. 18; 🖼 photo of the gear, p. 18). Burial (PAHO, p. 38; WHO/WEDC, p. 33): - An individual, marked grave 5-10 ft (1.5-3 m) deep, no lime or chemicals on the body (🖼 wrapping a body for burial, WHO/WEDC p. 32). - At least 100 ft (30 m) from springs or streams and 650 ft (200 m) from any well. - At least 4 ft between the grave bottom and the water table (5 ft in sand). With our valley clay wet 2-3 ft down in winter, choose higher, well-drained ground, and choose it now (rule of thumb). - Record who is buried where, on a map and with a durable marker. After a cholera death (MSF Cholera, pp. 47-48): bury within 24 hours, near the place of death, more than 165 ft (50 m) from water, under at least 3 ft of soil. Wash hands after touching the body. Funeral meals cooked by people who handled the body spread cholera. Let families keep their customs with these hygiene rules; banning funerals makes people hide deaths (p. 48). While

⚠ Old advice in the library to ignore - The "burn-out latrine", burned daily with 1 qt gasoline to 5 qt diesel (Special Forces Handbook, p. 162). It wastes fuel and risks burns and wildfire; the same page admits burning and lime don't stop flies or smell. Use a lidded pit, VIP or bucket toilet, with ash. - Spraying latrine pits with insecticide twice a week (same page). Use tight lids, screened vents and ash. - DDT and lindane for lice, scabies and spraying (Rozendaal, pp. 274, 293). Obsolete and toxic. Use permethrin or dimeticone. - Tossing each day's waste bag outside (Kearny, p. 108). Fine for two weeks in a fallout shelter; for long-term living, bury or compost the bags. - Boiling laundry "with soap and kerosene" (Household Discoveries, p. 191). Fire and fume hazard. 🚰 Water Purification - With What You Have How to make creek, spring, rain or well water safe to drink when there's no store and no power: settling and straining, homemade sand, biosand and clay-pot filters, charcoal (what it does and doesn't do), boiling, bleach and pool shock, sunlight, solar stills, simple tests, and safe storage. The manuals are in Water-Purification\ (Filters-Sand-Charcoal-Ceramic, Disinfection, Settling-Coagulation, Overviews-Testing), Water\ and Homestead-Skills\Sanitation-Water. Getting the water out of the ground is in the Wells & Pumps guide. ### The four rules of safe water 1. Clear it, then kill the germs. Settle or filter muddy water first; then boil or disinfect. 2. Charcoal and sand filters alone do NOT make water safe. They clear water and improve taste; charcoal beds even grow bacteria and shield them from chlorine. Charcoal goes last, after disinfection (WHO, pp. 51-52; Wilderness Medical Society, p. 6). 3. Boiling kills germs but removes no chemicals - not fuel, metals, salt or fire-retardant runoff. 4. Keep treated water clean: covered container with a spout, never dip a cup into it.

🫙 Step 1 - Clear the water - Let it settle. Three-pot method: fill pot 1 from the source; each day pour pot 1 gently into pot 2, and pot 2 into pot 3 (your drinking pot) - water sits at least 2 days and much of the dirt and some germs settle out. Still disinfect it (CAWST, p. 4). - Strain through cloth: old, soft cotton folded 7-8 times catches particles bigger than about 20 microns - silt, worms, the plankton cholera rides on - but not bacteria or viruses. Wash the cloth after each use (CAWST, pp. 14-15; 🖼 photo of a folded-cloth filter, p. 14). - Make the mud drop (coagulants): - Alum (pickling alum): about ⅛ tsp per gallon; stir fast 1 minute, slowly 5 minutes, settle at least 30 minutes, pour off through cloth (WMS, p. 7; how the mud clumps). - Wood ash, lime, crushed beans also work as rough coagulants (same source). - Moringa seed: about 1 crushed kernel per liter of muddy water - shake the paste in a cup of water, strain it in, stir 1 minute fast and 5-10 minutes slow, settle 1-2 hours (ECHO note; WEDC, p. 3). Moringa won't grow here (frost) - stockpile seed if you want it. - Coagulants clear water; they don't make it safe. Always disinfect afterward. - Is it clear enough? Look down

won't grow here (frost) - stockpile seed if you want it. - Coagulants clear water; they don't make it safe. Always disinfect afterward. - Is it clear enough? Look down through a clear 2-liter bottle of the water at large print - if you can read it, it's under about 50 NTU, clear enough for filters. For chlorine, clearer is better: if the water is still cloudy, use double the bleach dose (CAWST Testing, p. 81). Biosand filter (best household filter you can build) A concrete or plastic box of sand with a living layer on top (the "schmutzdecke") that eats germs (CAWST Biosand Construction Manual; 🖼 labeled cut-away, p. 17): - Layers, bottom to top: 2 in of drainage gravel (¼-½ in), 2 in of small gravel, then fine washed sand (0.7 mm or finer) filled with water already in the box so no air gets trapped (pp. 59, 92; 🖼 filling it, step by step, p. 92). - About 2 in of water must stand above the sand when it stops flowing - more starves the living layer of air; letting it dry out kills it. A diffuser plate keeps poured water from digging up the top (pp. 18-19; 🖼 the standing-water level drawn, p. 24). - Use it every day, one bucket (12-18 L) at a time, 6-12 hours apart. The living layer takes up to 30 days to grow - disinfect the output until then and always for babies and the sick. When flow gets slow, stir the top inch and scoop off the dirty water ("swirl and dump") (CAWST Fact Sheets, pp. 18-19; 🖼 swirl-and-dump drawings). - Results once mature: bacteria about 88-98% removed in the field, Giardia-type parasites over 99.9%, viruses less reliable (p. 19). - Cold winter water slows the living layer - filter slower and disinfect (EPA slow

about 88-98% removed in the field, Giardia-type parasites over 99.9%, viruses less reliable (p. 19). - Cold winter water slows the living layer - filter slower and disinfect (EPA slow sand, p. 9). The outlet tube's height keeps about 2 in of water standing over the sand, so the living layer never dries out (CAWST Biosand Manual, p. 17). "Swirl and dump" when the flow gets slow: repeat steps 2-4 a few times, then put the diffuser back and wash your hands (CAWST Biosand Manual, p. 104).

Slow sand filter (for a group or homestead) The same idea, bigger: water trickles down through about 3 ft of fine sand at 0.1-0.2 m per hour; build two beds so one can be cleaned (scrape off the top inch). A mature filter removes 95-100% of fecal bacteria and nearly all viruses and cysts. Takes about 3 weeks to "ripen" when new (IRC Slow Sand Filtration, pp. 38, 48; 🖼 parts of a slow sand filter, p. 32).

The bucket "layer filter" - gravel, sand, charcoal A bucket of gravel, sand and charcoal clears and improves water but is not a germ barrier. The right way to use charcoal is the three-stage system: gravel roughing filter → slow sand biofilter (germs) → crushed charcoal (chemicals and taste) → covered storage; replace the charcoal yearly (Aqueous Solutions Biochar Water Filter, pp. 2-9; 🖼 the three-drum layout, p. 2; 🖼 what goes in each drum, p. 9).

Clay pot (ceramic) filter Clay mixed with sawdust or rice husk (about 50:50 by volume to start) is pressed into a pot and fired to about 900 °C (1,650 °F) - the sawdust burns out and leaves tiny pores (CMWG Ceramic Pot Filters, p. 62; RDIC handbook). It sits in a covered bucket with a tap (🖼 drawing; 🖼 Potters for Peace filter) and gives 1-3 liters an hour. Test local clay first (clay testing); flow-test each pot (at least 1 liter in the first hour, not too fast - too fast means cracks) (CMWG, p. 114). They work best with a colloidal silver coating, which you can't make from raw materials - without it, still disinfect. Replace every 1-2 years or when cracked. Kiln plans: Mani kiln (🖼 cut-away drawing, p. 3). 📚 Go deeper: CAWST Biosand Filter Construction Manual; IRC Slow Sand Filtration; CMWG ceramic filter manual; Wikipedia: biosand filter · slow sand filter · ceramic water filter.

⚫ Charcoal: making it and using it right - What it does: soaks up taste, odor and many organic chemicals (pesticides, some fuel residues). What it doesn't: reliably remove germs - WHO doesn't recommend it for germs, and bacteria grow in the bed (WHO, pp. 51-52). - Plain vs. activated: ordinary charcoal has its pores clogged with tar, so it adsorbs poorly. Factories "activate" it by heating to about 800 °C in steam, which opens the pores (FAO Industrial Charcoal Making, p. 28). - Homemade water-treatment charcoal (Aqueous Solutions Char Drum Oven): 1. Pack dry wood pieces (1-2 in thick) tightly in a steel drum, set a chimney drum on top, and light it from the top (🖼 the stacked drums). It burns about 2 hours down to faint blue flames (🖼 flame colors). 2. Quench with plenty of water (🖼 photo) - the steam partly opens the pores (crude activation, not true activated carbon). 3. Crush and sieve to 1-5 mm pieces; wash out the dust. - Use it as the LAST step after the water is filtered and disinfected, or in a column after a sand filter; replace it yearly. Hardwood (oak, madrone) makes good charcoal. Chemical activation (acids, zinc chloride) isn't a safe home method (rule of thumb). - Charcoal-making in bulk: Practical Action brief (🖼 a portable metal kiln, p. 3) and the Peace Corps charcoal

(acids, zinc chloride) isn't a safe home method (rule of thumb). - Charcoal-making in bulk: Practical Action brief (🖼 a portable metal kiln, p. 3) and the Peace Corps charcoal manual. 📚 Go deeper: FAO - what activated charcoal is, p. 28; Aqueous Solutions - charcoal oven; Wikipedia: activated carbon.

🔥 Step 3 - Kill the germs Boiling - the surest method. A rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 ft - we're far below that) kills bacteria, viruses and parasites even in cloudy water. Let it cool covered; don't add ice (WHO Boil Water, p. 1; OSU, p. 5). Fuel cost: about 0.2 kg (½ lb) of wood per liter - a family's 4 gallons a day is about 7 lb of wood a day (WHO Bulletin, p. 4) - see the Firewood guide. Bleach (plain unscented, 6-8.25% sodium hypochlorite) - EPA, p. 1: | Water | 6% bleach | 8.25% bleach | | 1 quart, clear | 2 drops | 2 drops | | 1 gallon, clear | 8 drops | 6 drops | | 1 gallon, cloudy or very cold | 16 drops | 12 drops | Stir, wait 30 minutes. It should smell faintly of chlorine; if not, dose again and wait 15 more minutes. Cold water needs longer: 1 hour at 50-65 °F, 2+ hours below 50 °F - winter creek water (CAWST, p. 59). Bleach loses strength - use it within a year. Chlorine is weak against Cryptosporidium: settle or filter first. Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) - stores for years as dry granules. Dissolve 1 heaping teaspoon in 2 gallons of water to make a stock solution; then use 1 part stock

Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) - stores for years as dry granules. Dissolve 1 heaping teaspoon in 2 gallons of water to make a stock solution; then use 1 part stock to 100 parts water (1 pint per 12½ gallons), wait 30 minutes (EPA, p. 2). Use plain granules (no algaecide or stabilizer), mix outdoors with eye protection, and make stock in small batches - it lasts about a month in heat, longer cool and dark (CDC Safe Water Systems, p. 62). Iodine: 5 drops of 2% tincture per quart (10 if cloudy), wait 30 minutes (EPA, p. 2) - fine short-term (a month at most), never for pregnant women or anyone with thyroid disease or an iodine allergy (WMS, p. 14). Sunlight (SODIS): clear plastic (PET) bottles of clear water, lying flat in full sun 6 hours (2 days if more than half cloudy). Works well here March-September, poorly in the winter rains (EAWAG SODIS manual, p. 23; 🖼 how-to drawings, p. 26; 🖼 the home poster, p. 76). Clear bottles, clear water, lying flat in full sun for 6 hours (a diagram drawn for this guide). Solar pasteurizing: water held at 65 °C (150 °F) is pasteurized - a solar box cooker can do several gallons on a summer day (Ciochetti & Metcalf). A lump of beeswax in a sealed tube melts at about 62 °C - just under the target, so melted wax means "nearly there": keep it hot a while longer, or boil it, to be sure (CAWST, p. 75). 📚 Go deeper: EPA Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water; CDC Safe Water Systems handbook - making and storing chlorine; Wilderness Medical Society guidelines; Wikipedia: SODIS.

☀ Salty or chemical water: the solar still A shallow black basin under sloped glass or clear plastic: the sun evaporates the water, it condenses on the cover and runs into a gutter (🖼 photos of stills, CAWST p. 71) - leaving salt, metals and germs behind. Expect about 1 gallon a day per 10-12 sq ft of glass (CAWST, p. 71; Aprovecho, p. 43). Some fuel-type chemicals can carry over (rule of thumb). Salt, metals and germs stay in the basin; only the water that condenses on the glass reaches the jar (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: CAWST - solar distillation; Wikipedia: solar still.

🔬 Simple tests - Turbidity tube: a clear tube with a black-and-white disk at the bottom - pour water in until the disk disappears; the depth tells cloudiness (disk gone at 18 cm ≈ 50 NTU; at 85 cm ≈ 5 NTU) (Myre & Shaw, pp. 11-16; 🖼 the parts, p. 7; 🖼 finished tubes, p. 10; Secchi disk - the same idea in a lake). - H₂S bacteria test: a paper strip with a special medium in a bottle of water turns black in 1-2 days if fecal bacteria are present - keep it warm (above 77 °F). Agreed with lab tests about 90% of the time; sulfur well water can give false alarms (WHO, pp. 16, 33; 🖼 a test vial, CAWST; coliform bacteria). The test bottles must be bought ahead. - Chlorine check: a faint chlorine smell 30 minutes after dosing means enough was added (🖼 checking it with a color comparator). - Sanitary check: look at the source - animals, outhouses, runoff upstream? Fix the source first (CAWST Testing; 🖼 how springs and wells get polluted). 📚 Go deeper: CAWST Introduction to Drinking Water Quality Testing; Turbidity tube.
simple-tests

🪣 Storing water safely - Covered container with a tap or narrow spout, opaque, easy to clean; never put untreated water in it; clean it with soap or chlorine; keep it off the ground in shade; pour, don't dip (CAWST, pp. 83-84; 🖼 safe storage containers; 🖼 a tap fitted to a bucket; jerrycan). - Don't reuse milk jugs - they can't be cleaned well (OSU, p. 2). - Chlorinated water keeps best; boiled water can be recontaminated - drink it within a day or two. 📚 Go deeper: CAWST - safe storage and handling, p. 83; CDC Safe Water Systems - choosing a storage vessel, p. 69; CAWST Biosand Manual - cleaning a storage container, p. 106.
storing-water-safely

🔥 After a wildfire Burned slopes send ash, metals, nitrate and organic chemicals into creeks after storms - levels jumped 10 to 10,000 times after a Colorado fire (USGS, p. 1). Boiling, chlorine, sunlight and sand or clay filters do not remove these. Fire-damaged plastic pipes can leach benzene, and boiling doesn't remove it (WQA). After a fire, prefer springs or wells outside the burn, or rainwater; distilling and charcoal are the only partial chemical barriers here. 📚 Go deeper: USGS Wildfire Effects on Source-Water Quality; OWRD - your well after wildfire.
