💧 Water Wells, Pumps, Springs & Cisterns How to keep water coming when the power is out for good: understanding your well, running the well pump from a generator or solar, getting water up by hand, moving creek water uphill with no fuel (ram pumps), developing a spring, catching rain in a cistern, and keeping it all clean. The manuals are in Water-Wells-Pumps\ (Wells, Pumps-No-Grid, Hand-Ram-Rope-Pumps, Springs-Cisterns, Water-Quality, Oregon) and Water\. Making water safe to drink is in the Water Purification guide. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst problems - Never pour outside water into a well and never leave a well open - one bucket of creek water or a drowned animal can contaminate it (OWRD Wells and Drought). - Well pumps run on 240 volts. Shut off the breaker before touching the pressure switch or wiring, and connect a generator only through a transfer switch - never backfeed. - Don't run a flooded pump until it's dry and checked (EPA). - Test the water - clear, cold water can still carry bacteria or arsenic.

🕳 Know your well Three kinds of wells (USGS Ground Water and the Rural Homeowner, pp. 16-17; 🖼 all three drawn side by side, p. 15): - Dug wells: wide and shallow, often lined with rock or concrete rings. Easy to contaminate and the first to go dry in drought - but you can lower a bucket into them (🖼 a lined dug well). - Driven wells (sand points): a pipe with a screened tip driven into shallow sand or gravel. Cheap, shallow, easily contaminated (🖼 a well point; 🖼 driving one by hand). - Drilled wells: a steel or plastic casing (usually 6 in) sealed into the ground, often hundreds of feet deep, with an electric submersible pump at the bottom (🖼 OWRD drawing of a drilled well's parts; borehole). Most valley homes have this kind. About 5 gallons a minute is a normal household supply. Dug wells are wide and shallow, driven wells narrow and shallow, drilled wells narrow and deep (USGS, p. 15). Find your well's records. Oregon has driller's reports for most wells drilled since 1955 - Josephine County well IDs start with "JOSE". The report gives the depth, where water was found, the static water level and the tested yield - all things you need to plan a hand pump or generator (OWRD Water Well Owner's Handbook, pp. 27, 30; 🖼 a filled-in sample report,
know-your-well

level and the tested yield - all things you need to plan a hand pump or generator (OWRD Water Well Owner's Handbook, pp. 27, 30; 🖼 a filled-in sample report, p. 28). Print it and keep it with this drive. Look it up on OWRD's Well Log Query (by owner, location or well ID) while the internet works (rule of thumb). What the ground here gives (Grants Pass area, the nearest USGS study; 🖼 how aquifers hold water; aquifer): river gravels 5-50 gpm but easily polluted when shallow; weathered granite up to 50 gpm, solid granite under 5; serpentine rock - common around the Illinois Valley - gives few if any good wells, and high-magnesium water (USGS HA-480 Plate 1; Plate 2). In summer a household uses several times its winter water. Measure your water level (water table; 🖼 how pumping draws it down; cone of depression) twice a year (spring and fall), from the same point on the casing, after the pump has rested several hours, and keep a log. A ¾-in slotted PVC measuring tube taped to the pump pipe lets a tape get past the wires (OWRD Handbook, pp. 15-16; 🖼 measuring-tube diagram). A chalked weighted tape shows the wet line (rule of thumb). Rules worth knowing: household use up to 15,000 gallons a day, livestock water and up to ½ acre of garden need no water
know-your-well

shows the wet line (rule of thumb). Rules worth knowing: household use up to 15,000 gallons a day, livestock water and up to ½ acre of garden need no water right (OWRD Exempt Uses). Wells must be at least 50 ft from septic tanks and 100 ft from drain fields, with the top at least 12 in above ground (OWRD Handbook, pp. 23-24; 🖼 setback diagram, p. 24). 📚 Go deeper: OWRD Water Well Owner's Handbook - Oregon's complete owner guide; USGS Ground Water and the Rural Homeowner; Wikipedia: water well.

🔌 Running the well pump without the grid From a generator (Franklin Electric AIM Manual, pp. 8-9; generator photos) - a well pump needs far more power to start than to run: | Pump size | Minimum generator - 2-wire pump | 3-wire pump (has a control box) | | ½ hp | 3 kW | 2 kW | | ¾ hp | 4.5 kW | 3 kW | | 1 hp | 6 kW | 4 kW | | 1½ hp | 7.5 kW | 5 kW | - Example: a ½ hp pump runs on about 670 watts but draws over 6 times that for a moment when it starts (AIM, p. 41). The pump's size is on the control box or the well report. - Start the generator first, then the pump; switch the pump off before stopping the generator. Never let the generator run out of fuel with the pump on (AIM, p. 8). - Pump into storage - run the generator an hour or two and fill tanks, instead of running it all day. From solar: a DC solar well pump with its own panels pumps whenever the sun shines (🖼 NRCS system drawing, p. 9; 🖼 set up on a well, p. 35; photos). Store water, not electricity - a tank holding about 3 days' water beats batteries for cost and upkeep (NRCS Solar-Powered

Choose a brushless pump; brushed ones need new brushes about every 2 years (Practical Action, p. 4). Pressure tank and switch (UNL G2152, pp. 2-3; 🖼 well-to-house layout, p. 1; 🖼 inside a bladder tank, p. 3; pressure switch): the switch starts the pump at a low pressure (often 30 or 40 psi) and stops it at a high one (50 or 60). ✋ Getting water up by hand The suction limit: a pump at the top of a well doesn't "lift" water - air pressure pushes it up. In practice a pitcher pump or any suction pump stops working at about 20-22 ft of lift, a little less at our elevation (USDA FB 1448, p. 27; Peace Corps Wells Construction, p. 262; 🖼 how a piston pump works). Deeper than that, the pumping part must be down in the water - there's no limit on pushing water up from below. A pump on top can lift water only about 20-22 ft; below that, put the pumping part in the water (a diagram drawn for this guide). | Water level | Options | | Under ~20 ft | Pitcher pump (🖼 drawing); rope pump; bucket and windlass on a dug well (🖼 drawing) | | 20-150 ft | Rope pump (to about 115 ft); deep-well lift handpumps (Afridev, India Mark II up to about 160 ft) | | Deeper | Generator or solar on the existing submersible; well bucket (below) | - Rope pump: an endless rope with small pistons every meter runs up a pipe over a hand wheel. About 35 liters a minute at 33 ft, 10 at 115 ft; fits a 3-in borehole; can be built from local materials (Practica Rope Pump Handbook, pp. 8-9; 🖼 assembly drawing, p. 48;
getting-water-up-by-hand

a minute at 33 ft, 10 at 115 ft; fits a 3-in borehole; can be built from local materials (Practica Rope Pump Handbook, pp. 8-9; 🖼 assembly drawing, p. 48; 🖼 older bucket and chain pumps). - Deep-well handpumps: a cylinder set below the water on rods. Set the cylinder below the lowest water level you've measured while pumping (Afridev manual, p. 26; India Mark II manual; 🖼 a deep-well pump on a borehole; 🖼 suction, force and deep-well pump parts). Commercial deep-well hand pumps can be fitted beside the electric pump in a 6-in casing (rule of thumb). - Well bucket (bailer): a narrow tube about 3 in wide with a flap valve in the bottom fits down a 4-6 in casing beside the pump pipe and brings up 1-2 gallons a trip on a rope and pulley. You must open the well cap and keep everything clean - sanitize the bucket and rope, and close the well between uses (rule of thumb; no manual found). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Human-Powered Handpumps, p. 5 - which pump for which depth; Practica Rope Pump Handbook - building one; Peace Corps Wells Construction - digging and lining a well by hand; Wikipedia: rope pump.

🔁 Ram pumps: creek water uphill with no fuel A hydraulic ram uses the force of falling water in a long pipe (water hammer) to push part of that water much higher - day and night, with no fuel (Practical Action Hydraulic Ram Pumps; 🖼 how it works, p. 2; 🖼 step-by-step drawings). - Rule of thumb: water delivered ≈ water going in × fall ÷ lift × about 0.5, with both measured from the ram. Example: 10 gallons a minute falling 20 ft into the ram can push about 0.8 gpm - roughly 1,200 gallons a day - to a tank 100 ft above the source (120 ft above the ram) (Peace Corps Hydrams, p. 66). Another: 3 gpm with a 12-ft fall lifts about 780 gallons a day to 48 ft (USDA FB 1448, pp. 24-25). - The drive pipe from the source to the ram must be straight, rigid (steel is best) and long - about 3-7 times the fall, and at least 100 times its own width (Practical Action, p. 3; 🖼 layout of a ram installation). - You need: a reliable flow and a few feet of fall - a creek with a small dam or a spring above the ram. The water that doesn't get pumped flows back out the waste valve. - Tune the waste valve's stroke for the best output; build one

or a spring above the ram. The water that doesn't get pumped flows back out the waste valve. - Tune the waste valve's stroke for the best output; build one from pipe fittings with the Peace Corps manual (🖼 a homemade ram from plumbing parts). - Oregon water law and fish screens apply to diverting creek water - see the Engines guide creek-power section. Measure the fall and the lift from the ram; it sends only part of the water up (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: Peace Corps Hydrams workshop manual - build and repair one; USDA FB 1448 - rams and windmills; Wikipedia: hydraulic ram.

🌬 Windmills Wind power rises with the cube of wind speed (twice the wind = 8 times the power); a water-pumping windmill (🖼 photo; photos) pays off where the average wind is above about 7 mph, and needs a storage tank for calm days (Practical Action Wind Pumping, p. 2). Sheltered valley floors here may be too calm - ridges and open ground are better (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Wind Pumping; USDA FB 1448 - windmills; Wikipedia: windpump.
windmills

⛲ Springs A spring box collects spring water before animals and surface runoff can foul it (Virginia Tech Spring Development, p. 5; 🖼 spring box drawings, p. 5; springs)): - Dig back to where the water comes out of the ground and lay a gravel-packed collection pipe or trench (🖼 cross-section, p. 3; 🖼 a seep spring, p. 4). - A concrete box at least 4 ft deep, sticking up 1 ft above ground, with a tight overlapping lid, an outlet pipe, a screened overflow (so animals and insects can't crawl in) and a drain for cleaning. - Dig a ditch upslope to steer surface runoff away, and fence livestock out of the area above the spring; keep outhouses and corrals at least 100 ft away (🖼 a protected spring, 1933). - Measure flow with a bucket and a watch; test the water and shock-chlorinate a new box (Virginia Tech Shock Chlorination). - Spring water runs by gravity to the house or garden - no pump at all if the spring is uphill. The ditch and fence uphill keep runoff and animals off the spring; the lid overlaps the box and locks (EPA Manual of Individual Water Supply Systems, p. 70). 📚 Go deeper: Virginia Tech Spring Development and Protection; EPA Manual of Individual Water Supply Systems - springs, wells and cisterns.
springs

🛢 Cisterns and rainwater Our winters are wet: every square foot of roof catches about 0.6 gallons per inch of rain (Texas Rainwater Harvesting, p. 34; 🖼 a whole system, p. 10; rainwater harvesting). A 1,500 sq ft roof in a 10-inch rain month could fill a 9,000-gallon tank (rule of thumb arithmetic). - First-flush diverter: dump the first dirty water off the roof - about 13-49 gallons per 1,000 sq ft (Texas, p. 13; 🖼 standpipe diverter, p. 14; 🖼 its parts, OSU). A standpipe of 4-in pipe holds about 1 gallon per 18 in. - Size the tank for summer: almost no rain falls June-September, so store enough to carry you through (🖼 ferrocement tank; 🖼 1933 cistern and filter plans; cistern; rain tanks). - Opaque, covered, screened tanks; clean gutters; treat roof water before drinking (Water Purification guide). Oregon rules for rain tanks: OSU EM 9448 (🖼 system diagram, p. 4). The capped pipe catches the dirtiest first water; empty it after each rain (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: Texas Manual on Rainwater Harvesting; OSU Harvesting Rainwater for the Garden.
cisterns-and-rainwater

🧪 Keeping well water clean - Test yearly for coliform bacteria and nitrate, and at least once for arsenic (treat at 10 ppb or more) (OWRD Handbook, p. 34). Without a lab, a home H₂S bacteria test helps - see the Water Purification guide. - Shock chlorination after repairs, floods or a bad test: for 5.25% bleach, about 2½ quarts for a 4-in well with 100 ft of water, 4 quarts for a 6-in well with 100 ft, 1½ gallons for 6-in with 200 ft. Run every tap until you smell chlorine, leave it 12-24 hours, flush it away from the septic system, and retest in 1-2 weeks. Today's bleach is often stronger (6-8.25%): the same amounts just make it stronger. Oregon's OHA bulletin uses 1 cup of 8.25% bleach per 100 gallons of water standing in the well, left at least 8 hours (Virginia Tech Shock Chlorination, p. 3; OHA bulletin; 🖼 pouring and circulating the chlorine). - After a flood: wells under 50 ft deep or over 10 years old are probably contaminated (EPA, p. 1; 🖼 cleaning out a flooded dug well). - After a wildfire: check the wellhead, wiring and pipes, and test before drinking (OWRD after wildfire). - "Dry" well? Often the water only dropped below the pump - lower the pump (not to the very bottom) and fit a pump-saver switch (OWRD Wells and

after wildfire). - "Dry" well? Often the water only dropped below the pump - lower the pump (not to the very bottom) and fit a pump-saver switch (OWRD Wells and Drought; 🖼 how a well "goes dry"). - Protect the wellhead: tight sanitary cap, ground sloping away, no fuel, manure or chemicals nearby (OSU Twelve Simple Things; 🖼 two wellhead types, p. 4; 🖼 how wells and springs get polluted; 🖼 sealing the top of a dug well). 📚 Go deeper: OWRD Handbook - testing schedule, p. 34; Virginia Tech Shock Chlorination; OSU Twelve Simple Things to Protect Your Well Water.

🥫 Food When It's Scarce: Storage, Rationing & Nutrition How to keep a household fed for a year or more with no stores: how much food people need, what to store and how to keep it good for decades, how to share it out fairly, how to prevent the hunger diseases, how to refeed someone who is starving, how to keep babies alive, and what wild food the Illinois Valley gives month by month. The books are in Food-Security\ (Storage-Rationing, Nutrition-Deficiency, Foraging). Growing, milling and cooking staples are in Food-From-Scratch\, and cellars and drying in Food-Storage\. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Grain alone is not enough. Stored wheat, rice and beans have almost no vitamin C. Store vitamin C tablets and learn to sprout seeds. Under 10 mg a day can cause life-threatening scurvy within months (BYU, p. 1). - Never oxygen-pack or vacuum-seal moist food. It can grow botulism. Dry food under 10% moisture only (USU, p. 97). - Feed a starving person slowly. Big meals all at once can kill them. - Babies: breast milk first. Never give plain animal milk under 6 months (WHO 2004, p. 40). - Never cut the share of children, pregnant or nursing women, or the sick first. - Eat no wild plant you have not identified for certain. Death camas and water hemlock grow right here and kill.

🍽 How much food people need Daily needs (US official tables; "active" there only means walking over 3 miles a day - wood, water and hand-digging are heavier, so plan from the top of each range) (Dietary Guidelines, pp. 153-154; protein p. 146, p. 148): | Person | Calories a day | Protein a day | | Man, 19+ | 2,200-2,600 inactive; 2,800-3,000 active | 56 g | | Woman, 19+ | 1,600-2,000 inactive; 2,000-2,400 active | 46 g | | Teen boy | up to 3,200 | 52 g | | Child 9-13 | - | 34 g | | Child 2-8 | 1,000-2,000 | 13-19 g | | Pregnant | +340 (2nd trimester), +452 (3rd) | 71 g | | Nursing | +330 (first 6 months), +400 after | 71 g | Plan on 2,100 kcal per person per day, averaged over all ages, with at least 10-12% from protein and 17% from fat (WHO 2002, p. 6; Sphere, p. 228) - at least 53 g protein and 40 g fat (Sphere, p. 260). Adjust it (WHO 2002, pp. 11-13): - Cold: add 100 kcal for every 9 °F (5 °C) the average temperature is below 68 °F. Valley winter days average about 40 °F, so a poorly heated house should plan about +300 kcal per person, November-March (rule of thumb from that formula). - Sick or already
how-much-food-people-need

Valley winter days average about 40 °F, so a poorly heated house should plan about +300 kcal per person, November-March (rule of thumb from that formula). - Sick or already thin: add 100-200 kcal. Heavy work: more. What 2,100 kcal looks like: 400 g cereal (about 2 cups dry), 60 g beans, 25 g oil (2 Tbsp), 50 g fortified flour, 15 g sugar, 5 g iodized salt = 2,113 kcal, 58 g protein (WHO 2002, p. 14). For a year: about 322 lb grain, 48 lb beans, 20 lb oil, 12 lb sugar, 4 lb salt per person (our arithmetic). Handy number: 790 g (1.74 lb) of dry wheat gives 2,600 kcal and 103 g protein - so 1 lb of dry grain ≈ 1,500 kcal (Kearny, p. 90). 📚 Go deeper: Food and Nutrition Needs in Emergencies, p. 11 - adjusting for cold, sickness and work; Dietary Guidelines, p. 153 - calories by age and activity.

📦 Storing it for years Heat is the main enemy. Keep food at 40-70 °F. In BYU research, wheat stayed good 25 years in a cool basement but only 5 in a hot garage or attic. Keep containers off bare concrete (USU, p. 31). Our summers pass 100 °F and sheds get hotter - use the coolest inside room or a cellar (Root Cellar guide). Keep grain dry. Above 12% moisture it starts to break down, above 15% it molds, at 20% bacteria grow. Freezing does not harm it (USU, p. 66). Seal it in the dry season (July-September), not in wet winter air (rule of thumb). Packing with oxygen absorbers (USU, p. 98): 1. Use oxygen-tight containers only: #10 cans or Mylar/foil bags. Plastic buckets slowly let oxygen in - put a Mylar bag inside the bucket; the bucket keeps rats out. 2. Absorber size: 100 cc per quart jar, 300 cc per gallon bag or #10 can, 2,000 cc per 5-gallon bucket. (Some charts say 500 cc, but a full bucket of grain holds about 1,500 cc of oxygen (arithmetic); extra absorber does no harm.) 3. Work fast: an opened pack starts in 20 minutes and is spent in about 5 hours. Reseal spare packets in a small jar. Label every bag with contents and date. - Absorbers are not edible; hand warmers are not a substitute. -
storing-it-for-years

in about 5 hours. Reseal spare packets in a small jar. Label every bag with contents and date. - Absorbers are not edible; hand warmers are not a substitute. - Dry food under 10% moisture only. Never moist food, home-canned butter or oil-coated raw eggs at room temperature - botulism (USU, p. 32). The Mylar bag keeps oxygen out and the bucket keeps rats out; the absorber goes in just before you seal (a diagram drawn for this guide). Bugs (USU, p. 95): oxygen held under 1% for 12 days kills every stage, so Mylar with absorbers kills weevils (🖼 the common grain pests, FAO p. 78). Dry ice: 3-4 inches of grain in a bucket, 2-3 oz crushed dry ice, fill, lid loose 30 minutes, then seal (p. 66). Freeze 2-3 days, warm a day, freeze again. ⚖ Setting and running a fair ration Work out the ration (rule of thumb): 1. Weigh everything, item by item. 2. Count the days to the next harvest and add about 3 months of reserve. 3. Daily ration per person = stock ÷ (people × days), for each food. 4. Turn it into calories (1 lb dry grain ≈ 1,500 kcal) and compare with 2,100. The gap is what the garden, hunting, fishing, foraging and animals must make up. Example (our arithmetic): 3 adult-equivalents, 13 months (395 days). 900 lb of grain ÷ (3 × 395) ≈ 0.76 lb per person per day ≈ 1,100 kcal - half the need. Start the garden and the rabbits and chickens now. Keep it fair (rule of thumb, except where cited): - One standard scoop per food, marked with its weight. A written daily log: date, what went out, to whom, what is left. - Two people present whenever stores are opened. Keep stores locked and out of sight. - Make sure children, the sick, older people and pregnant and nursing women really get their share - give them smaller, more frequent portions (Sphere, p. 235). - Fuel, pots and water matter as much as food - lacking any one hurts as much as a short ration (WHO Management of Nutrition, p. 74). Store salt and spices: people eat more of a dull
setting-and-running-a-fair-ration

much as food - lacking any one hurts as much as a short ration (WHO Management of Nutrition, p. 74). Store salt and spices: people eat more of a dull diet when it tastes good (p. 75). - Grind just before eating (🖼 Kearny's pipe-and-can grinder). Milling loses about 10% of wheat or corn (WHO, p. 75), and ground whole corn keeps only 6-8 weeks (Sphere, p. 232). If this goes wrong: one person losing weight faster → check they really eat their share (children and old people often give theirs away). Stores shrinking faster than the log → reweigh, check for rats and spoilage before suspecting people. 📚 Go deeper: Sphere, p. 235 - fair distribution; WHO Management of Nutrition, p. 74 - rations, fuel, milling (scanned, not searchable); Kearny, p. 84 - a homemade grain grinder.

🔥 Cooking with little fuel A fuel shortage is a nutrition problem: one refugee pellagra outbreak happened partly because people had no fuel to cook the beans they were given (WHO Pellagra, p. 29). 1. Soak beans first (USU Dry Beans, p. 2). 2. Crack or grind grain - meal cooks much faster than whole kernels. 3. Boil briefly, let insulation finish it. Cook meal with at least 4 parts water to 1, boil briefly, then finish in a fireless cooker for 4-5 hours (Kearny, p. 89). 4. Build a haybox: a box packed with hay, wool or blankets around a lidded pot (🖼 the parts; 🖼 cut-away drawing). Beans and meat boil 20-25 minutes before going in (Practical Action, p. 5); old beans longer (USDA FB 771, p. 16). A haybox: insulation packed all around the pot, a tray under it and a thick cushion on top, so no heat escapes (Practical Action, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: USDA Homemade Fireless Cookers, p. 4 - building one; Firewood guide - making the wood count.

Rose hips and many berries have over 300 mg per 100 g; cooking destroys it; breast milk covers a nursing baby (p. 33). Sprouting for vitamin C (WHO Scurvy, pp. 35, 50; 🖼 Kearny's sprouting drawing; photos): 1. Soak whole

100 g; cooking destroys it; breast milk covers a nursing baby (p. 33). Sprouting for vitamin C (WHO Scurvy, pp. 35, 50; 🖼 Kearny's sprouting drawing; photos): 1. Soak whole (unsplit) beans, peas, lentils or wheat 12-21 hours. 2. Drain and spread between damp cloths; keep them damp. 3. Eat when shoots are ½-1 inch (30-48 hours) - the shoot holds the vitamin. Raw, or cooked under 30 minutes. Babies nursed by deficient mothers can die within hours, usually at 1-3 months old (p. 22). Don't over-wash rice or pour off its water. Strong tea, raw fermented fish and molds in damp food block thiamine (p. 17). Pellagra comes from corn-heavy diets with untreated corn (WHO Pellagra, p. 13); one outbreak began 4 months after peanuts were dropped from a ration. If corn is a staple, nixtamalize it (FAO, p. 19; Food from Scratch) and eat beans or meat with it. Rickets and our winter sun: 10-15 minutes of sun on

If corn is a staple, nixtamalize it (FAO, p. 19; Food from Scratch) and eat beans or meat with it. Rickets and our winter sun: 10-15 minutes of sun on a child's bare skin daily prevents it. Treatment: 5,000 IU vitamin D daily for 4-6 weeks, then 1,000 IU daily for 6 months, usually from fish-liver oil (WHO Management of Nutrition, p. 46). Rule of thumb: at 42° N the November-February sun is too weak to make vitamin D, and the valley is often cloudy - store cod-liver oil or vitamin D, and get children into the summer sun. Iodine: adults need about 150 µg a day (WHO, pp. 36-37), and 250 µg when pregnant or nursing (WHO 2007). About ½ teaspoon of US iodized salt gives roughly 150 µg - you don't need more salt than that. The Pacific Northwest was historically part of the US "goitre belt" (rule of thumb) - store iodized salt sealed, dry and dark, and use fish and kelp from the coast. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Scurvy, p. 35 - the famine sprouting method; WHO Thiamine, p. 19 - forms of beriberi; WHO Pellagra, p. 8 - the rash and outbreaks; Where There Is No Doctor, p. 24 - goitre.

🦴 Starvation and refeeding slowly Recognize it (WHO Management of Nutrition, pp. 25-26; malnutrition; 🖼 signs in children, mild to severe): - Marasmus - "skin and bones", an old man's face, loose "baggy pants" skin on the buttocks (🖼 drawing). - Kwashiorkor - swollen feet and legs, peeling "flaky-paint" skin, thin loose hair, misery, no appetite (🖼 drawing). - Adults - wasting and weakness, sometimes swelling. - For every severe case there may be about 10 moderate ones. Refeed low and slow: 1. Sudden big meals can cause fatal refeeding syndrome (rule of thumb). 2. Starter formula (WHO F-75) for a severely malnourished child, used for the first days until appetite returns: 25 g dried skim milk + 70 g sugar + 35 g cereal flour + 27 g oil + water to 1 litre, boiled 5-7 minutes. Or 300 mL fresh cow's milk + 70 g sugar + 35 g flour + 17 g oil + water to 1 litre (WHO Severe Malnutrition, p. 21). After it cools, WHO adds 20 mL of mineral mix per litre (potassium and magnesium - "it must be added") and 140 mg vitamin mix or a multivitamin; recipes on p. 61. 3. Small feeds every 2-3 hours, day and night (p. 22). No iron in the first week (p. 9). 4. Adults: WHO aims for about 40 kcal per kg of body weight
starvation-and-refeeding-slowly

feeds every 2-3 hours, day and night (p. 22). No iron in the first week (p. 9). 4. Adults: WHO aims for about 40 kcal per kg of body weight a day; once appetite returns, give ordinary food with added oil (WHO, p. 111). But if they've eaten almost nothing for a week or more, start lower - about 10-20 kcal per kg a day, building up over 4-7 days (UK NICE guidance). Feeding too much too fast can stop the heart (refeeding syndrome). 5. Dehydrated and starving: don't give full-strength rehydration salts. One ORS packet in 2 litres plus 50 g sugar and 40 mL mineral mix (ReSoMal) (WHO Severe Malnutrition, p. 18). Note: these manuals are from 1999-2000; WHO updated its guidance in 2013, including some drug doses. F-75 and ReSoMal are still used - leave the drugs to someone trained. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Severe Malnutrition, p. 21 - F-75 and F-100 recipes and charts; Where There Is No Doctor, p. 6 - recognizing malnutrition; WTND ch. 21, p. 12 - malnourished children.

🍼 Babies and toddlers in a shortage Breastfeeding first (WHO 2004, pp. 21-23): - Only extreme hunger lowers a mother's milk - feed the mother well. Keep nursing when mother or baby is sick, and nurse more often. - Weak or premature babies: express milk and feed it from an open cup (🖼 removing milk by hand; 🖼 cup feeding). - Substitutes only for babies with no breast milk, by cup, not bottle (p. 27). If a baby is due or small, store real infant formula as a backup: about 110 g a day, 3.3 kg (7¼ lb) a month (same page). If the milk has stopped or the mother is gone: - Relactation: a woman who stopped breastfeeding can make milk again, for her own or an adopted baby, without another pregnancy; even a woman never pregnant (a grandmother) can sometimes make some (WHO Relactation, p. 7; scanned). Frequent suckling brings the milk. - A healthy wet-nurse is next best (WHO 2004, p. 23). - Homemade dry-milk formulas in two old books are a last resort - see the last section. Babies 6-24 months: - Porridge thick enough to stay on the spoon, not thin gruel, enriched with mashed beans, oil, egg or greens. Flour from sprouted grain cooks thinner, so more food fits a small stomach (WHO Complementary Feeding, pp. 17-18). - Non-breastfed babies under one need 5

beans, oil, egg or greens. Flour from sprouted grain cooks thinner, so more food fits a small stomach (WHO Complementary Feeding, pp. 17-18). - Non-breastfed babies under one need 5 meals a day, not 3 (p. 37). - Non-breastfed toddlers: 200-400 mL milk a day if they eat other animal foods, otherwise 300-500 mL. Goat, cow or sheep milk - boil raw milk (WHO 2005, pp. 14-16). 📚 Go deeper: WHO Infant Feeding in Emergencies, p. 21 - keeping breastfeeding going; A Book for Midwives, p. 7 - cup feeding removed milk; Where There Is No Doctor, p. 14 - the first 6 months.

🌿 Wild food around the valley 📷 Not sure what it is? Photograph it with the plant and mushroom identifier (🔧 Tools tab). It suggests names and flags poisonous groups, but it's often wrong: confirm every feature here before you eat or use anything. What the Takelma ate here. The Takelma people lived along the middle Rogue and south toward the Illinois River (Sapir 1907, p. 3). Their staple was the "black acorn" (Sapir, p. 8; California black oak; 🖼 photo), pounded, sifted, leached with hot water on clean sand and boiled as mush (Sapir, p. 9). Camas (🖼 photo) was pit-roasted on alder over hot stones, sometimes for days, then mashed into cakes for winter. Manzanita berries (🖼 flowers and berries) were pounded to flour with sugar-pine nuts; tarweed and sunflower-type seeds were parched and ground. They also ate madrone berries, pine nuts, salmon, steelhead, trout, crawfish and freshwater mussels. ☠ Foraging safety rules 📷 Not sure what it is? Photograph it with the plant and mushroom identifier (🔧 Tools tab). It suggests names and flags poisonous groups, but it's often wrong: confirm every feature here before you eat or use anything. 1. Eat nothing not 100% identified - ideally confirmed by two people with a book. 2. Skip the whole wild-carrot family (white umbrella-shaped flower heads - 🖼 poison and water hemlock photos; wild carrot, poison hemlock). Western water hemlock grows along valley creeks and kills fast, by seizures (PNW 109, p. 5; 🖼 chambered root and stem, p. 1; 🖼 look-alikes side by side, pp. 3-4). 3. Camas: dig only from a patch you watched bloom and marked plant by plant, only blue-flowered plants. Skip every white or cream-flowered plant - death camas is creamy-white and every part is poisonous (PNW 104, p. 2; 🖼 WSU photos; 🖼 Army drawing). 4. Always leach acorns. Always cook elderberries; never eat their stems, leaves or green berries (OSU, p. 4; 🖼 elderberry drawing). 5. Never eat bracken fern - it holds a cancer-causing compound and an enzyme that destroys thiamine (WSU, p. 11; 🖼 drawing). 6. Cook anything from ponds (wapato, cattail, watercress) - parasites (rule of thumb). 7. Throw out moldy, damp or discolored grain, and grass seed heads with black ergot spurs (USU, p. 66; rule of thumb;
foraging-safety-rules

(wapato, cattail, watercress) - parasites (rule of thumb). 7. Throw out moldy, damp or discolored grain, and grass seed heads with black ergot spurs (USU, p. 66; rule of thumb; 🖼 ergot photo). 8. Lean meat alone starves you. Living on rabbit or lean venison without fat causes "rabbit starvation" - keep fat in the diet (render lard; rule of thumb). 9. Try a new wild food in a small amount first, and take no more than a third of a patch (rule of thumb). Western water hemlock: the thick rootstalk is hollow, with cross-walls making chambers full of poisonous juice (AIB 415, p. 110). Water hemlock flowers: white umbrellas like the rest of the carrot family; leaf side veins run to the notches, not the tips (AIB 415, p. 109). Death camas in bloom: yellowish-white flower clusters above grass-like leaves; skip every white or cream-flowered plant (AIB 415, p. 35). If someone may be poisoned: death camas causes drooling, mouth numbness, vomiting, weakness, confusion and an irregular heartbeat 1-8 hours after eating (PNW 104, p. 2). Keep them warm, on their side if drowsy, watch their breathing, and keep a piece of the plant (rule of thumb). See the Field Care guide. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 109 Western Waterhemlock, p. 5 - look-alikes side by side; USDA Plants Poisonous to Livestock, p. 23 - bracken; PNW 104, p. 2

⚠ Old advice in the library to ignore - "Two pounds of cooked grain per day" as an adequate diet (FEMA HS-4, p. 111). It should be about 1½-2 lb of DRY grain; 2 lb cooked is only about 800-1,200 kcal. The same page says "adults do not get rickets" - they do (it is called osteomalacia). Instead: plan from 2,100 kcal and the tables above. - Grain puree for babies under 6 months, and scarce cow's milk saved for them (FEMA HS-4, p. 114) - outdated and dangerous. Instead: breast milk, relactation or a wet-nurse; no animal milk or solids before 6 months. - Homemade skim-milk + oil + sugar infant formula (FEMA HS-4, p. 114; Kearny, p. 96) - a last resort only, when no breast milk, wet-nurse or real formula exists. It is not a complete infant food, and emergencies make all artificial feeding riskier (WHO 2004, p. 27). If you must: boiled water, a cup not a bottle, made fresh. Kearny himself says mother's milk is best. - "Ferns on toast" - Saunders 1920, pp. 146-147 recommends bracken. Don't (cancer, thiamine loss). - Camas with no death-camas warning - Saunders, pp. 43-45. Instead: follow rule 3 above. - Drug doses in the WHO 1999-2000 malnutrition manuals predate WHO's 2013 update. Use the feeding methods; leave the drugs to trained hands. 📚 Go deeper: WHO 2004, p.

above. - Drug doses in the WHO 1999-2000 malnutrition manuals predate WHO's 2013 update. Use the feeding methods; leave the drugs to trained hands. 📚 Go deeper: WHO 2004, p. 40 - why no animal milk before 6 months; WHO Severe Malnutrition, p. 21 - the feeding methods that still hold.

🌾 Food From Scratch How to make staple ingredients - flour, masa, leavening, salt, sweetener, fat - from what grows or can be raised around the Illinois Valley, and how to turn them into bread, tortillas, pasta, crackers and other everyday food. Details and more recipes are in Food-From-Scratch\ (grain, wild and local staples, breads and staples) and Gardening-Food\. The links open each book on the drive at the right page. ⚠ Two foods here can kill if you get them wrong: camas has a deadly look-alike (death camas), and acorns and lye/ash-cooked corn must be processed properly. Follow the steps exactly, and never eat a wild plant you can't identify with certainty.

🌾 Flour from grain - Grow hulless varieties of oats and barley if you can - hulled types need dehulling. Wheat and corn are the easiest staples to grow and grind. Winter grains are sown in fall and cut the next summer: ¼-½ inch deep, about 1 foot apart each way (SARE, p. 2). - Harvest when the heads are fully tan and nodding and the kernels are too hard to dent with a fingernail. Cut about 10 inches below the heads. - Thresh by stomping the heads in a clean bin or on a tarp (🖼 a threshing box); winnow by pouring the grain slowly in front of a fan (or in a breeze) so the chaff blows away. Repeat. (SARE handout, p. 1) - Dry to 12-13% moisture before storing - wetter grain heats, molds and draws insects. Field test: a dry kernel resists your thumbnail and cracks sharply between your teeth. (Peace Corps Small Farm Grain Storage, p. 55) If you dry it with heat, keep eating grain below 140 °F and seed grain below 113 °F (p. 53). - Store whole grain, grind as needed. Whole grain keeps for years; flour goes rancid within months once milled. A hand grain mill (🖼 drawing; 🖼 a homemade pipe grinder) is worth owning; otherwise grind between two stones (a quern: a turning top stone on a fixed bottom
flour-from-grain

milled. A hand grain mill (🖼 drawing; 🖼 a homemade pipe grinder) is worth owning; otherwise grind between two stones (a quern: a turning top stone on a fixed bottom one) and sift out the bran (Shifts and Expedients, p. 519). - Kill pests in stored grain: freeze small bags 2-3 days, or heat a ½-inch layer at 140-150 °F for 30 minutes (may weaken bread rise). Store airtight, and only when dry. (USU Food Storage in the Home, p. 14; 🖼 the common grain pests, FAO p. 78; rice weevil) - A sealed, full container kills bugs on its own - they use up the oxygen. Keep the grain you dip into daily in a separate small container (Peace Corps, p. 279). Winnowing after threshing: the breeze carries off the light chaff and the grain drops into the tub; pour it through again until it's clean (a diagram drawn for this guide). Best-quality rotation times (sealed, about 70 °F; a 90 °F shed roughly halves them - USU, pp. 11, 17-19): whole wheat kernels 25 years · white flour 1 year · cornmeal 1 year · dry beans 1 year · whole-wheat flour only 2 weeks. USU says these are for rotating stock, not how long food stays usable; dry beans and rice packed with oxygen absorbers keep for decades (Food Security guide). | If this goes wrong |

🌰 Acorn flour 📷 Not sure what it is? Photograph it with the plant and mushroom identifier (🔧 Tools tab). It suggests names and flags poisonous groups, but it's often wrong: confirm every feature here before you eat or use anything. Our oaks - tanoak (the traditional favorite), California black oak, Oregon white oak and canyon live oak (🖼 tanoak photo; 🖼 oak and acorn drawing) - all make good flour, but every acorn must be leached to remove bitter tannins. A tanoak can drop over 200 pounds in a good year and bears some crop every year (NRCS Tanoak, p. 1). 1. Gather the second fall (late September-October); the first acorns down are mostly wormy. Dry them 2-5 days in the sun or 20 minutes in a 175 °F oven, door ajar. Whole, dry acorns keep several years - in sacks or jars, not plastic. (UCCE, p. 2) 2. Crack and shell them, and remove any moldy or wormy ones. Grind the nutmeats to a coarse meal or flour. 3. Leach - any one of these: - Hot: soak in hot water for an hour, drain, repeat several times (fastest). - Running water: a cloth bag of meal in cold running water for several hours. - Daily change: 3 parts water to 1 part meal in jars, kept cool; pour off the dark water and refill every day for
acorn-flour

cold running water for several hours. - Daily change: 3 parts water to 1 part meal in jars, kept cool; pour off the dark water and refill every day for about a week. - Traditional: pour nearly scalding water over fine flour in a hollow scooped in clean sand (Hupa, p. 38). 4. It's done when it tastes sweet, not bitter or puckery. Cold leaching keeps more of the starch's binding power (better for bread); hot is faster. 5. Use it wet as mush/porridge, pat it into flatbread on a hot stone or pan, or dry it and replace ¼ to ½ of the wheat flour in bread (acorn flour has no gluten on its own). 6. Ground meal goes rancid in a warm room - grind only a few weeks' worth and keep it cold (UCCE, p. 2). Other local nuts need no leaching: hazelnuts (June-July, dry and eat raw; 🖼 photo) and sugar pine nuts (October; pound the cones to free the seeds) - Hupa, pp. 39-40. Bay nuts (Oregon myrtle; 🖼 peeled bay fruit) must be roasted at 350 °F for 30-45 minutes until dark-chocolate brown; they taste of coffee and contain a caffeine-like stimulant (UCCE, pp. 2-3). 📚 Go deeper: UCCE Foods from the Tanoak Forest, p. 2 - modern acorn and bay-nut processing step by step; Goddard, Life and Culture of the Hupa, p. 37

🌿 Camas, cattail and other local starches - Camas bulbs (Camassia quamash - meadows, blue flowers in spring; 🖼 photo) were a major food here. They must be pit-roasted or slow-baked 24-36 hours - long cooking turns the indigestible starch sweet. Dry cooked bulbs or cakes for storage. ⚠ Death camas grows in the same meadows and its bulbs look the same. Flower color is not a safe test. Only harvest from a bed you have watched bloom and learned plant by plant; if there's any doubt, leave it. (USDA Great Camas guide, pp. 1-2; Wild-Plants\ death camas guide; 🖼 death camas flowers and leaves) - Dig after flowering, take only the big bulbs, replant the small ones, and rest each patch a few years. 🌽 Corn: masa, tortillas and hominy Always cook dried corn with lime or wood ash ("nixtamal") before making it a staple - it unlocks the corn's niacin. People living mostly on untreated cornmeal get pellagra (FAO Maize, p. 13). - Masa with lime (food-grade slaked lime, cal): use lime 1% of the dry corn's weight (5 g of lime per 500 g of corn - weigh it if you can) and water 1½ times the corn's volume. Heat to just below a simmer (200-210 °F) until the skins slip off but the center is still firm (often under 30 minutes). Rest 8-12 hours in the liquid, then rub and rinse off the skins. Grind while cold (a metate or stone mill, with a little cold water; 🖼 metate and hand mill); use the masa within a day. (Smithsonian method, pp. 1-3) Fresh corn needs less lime and cooking; old, hard corn more (FAO, p. 66). - With wood ash instead: boil shelled corn 15-30 minutes in weak lye water made from hardwood ashes until the hulls loosen, then rinse very thoroughly in running water until no lye remains. Lye is caustic - gloves and eye protection; never taste it. - Lye hominy with store lye (USDA) - use pure lye (100% sodium hydroxide, sold for soap-making), never a drain cleaner with other chemicals: 5 oz lye in 6 quarts cold

🍞 Leavening without store yeast or baking powder - Wild sourdough starter: mix equal weights of flour (whole-grain or rye starts fastest) and unchlorinated water in a jar. Every day, discard all but a little and feed it equal weights of flour and water (twice a day from day 4). Keep it at 70-82 °F. Usable around day 7, strong in 2-4 weeks - it's ready when it doubles within 4-6 hours of feeding and smells yeasty and pleasant. Throw it out if mold appears. (Illinois Sourdough 101, pp. 1-3) - Keep it going: save ½ cup each time you bake; the night before, feed it equal parts flour and water and leave it warm 6-8 hours. Store in glass, not metal, with the lid loose. (Alaska's guide warns against all metal; Illinois allows stainless steel but never copper, iron or galvanized.) (UAF Sourdough, p. 2) - Back-up: spread some starter thin, dry it until brittle, and store it airtight. Revive by crumbling into warm water overnight, then feeding. - Sourdough pancakes and muffins get ½ tsp baking soda dissolved in 1 Tbsp water, stirred in last. Never put soda in the starter itself - it can kill the yeast (UAF, pp. 2-3). - Potato yeast and "saving a piece of dough" for next time: USDA Bread and Bread Making (FB 807, p. 10) - liquid yeast keeps about two

🧂 Salt, 🍯 sweeteners and 🥓 fat - Salt from seawater (sea salt): seawater is about 3.5% salt - roughly 4-5 gallons per pound of salt in practice. Collect it away from harbors and outfalls, filter through cloth, boil down to a slush, then finish drying slowly; pour off the last bitter liquid for better taste. - Bigleaf maple syrup (OSU 2025 guide): tap after leaf drop and a hard freeze, through winter freeze-thaw days, until buds break. 5/16-inch spile in a 2-inch hole (🖼 tapping, step by step); collect sap daily and boil it within 24 hours. Bigleaf sap is thin - about 80 gallons of sap per gallon of syrup (20 gallons ≈ 1 quart after ~8 hours of boiling). Syrup is done at 7 °F above the boiling point of water where you are - about 216 °F around Cave Junction's elevation (219 °F at sea level). (OSU EM 9163, pp. 2-8) Keep buckets lidded - "ropey" (stringy) sap is spoiled (🖼 photos). Let syrup settle and pour it off the gritty "sugar sand"; to keep it on a shelf, bottle it at 180-190 °F into just-boiled jars (pp. 6, 8-9). - Honey: strain through progressively finer cloth, keep it sealed (wet honey ferments); render the wax for candles and salves (Practical Action brief, p. 1). Never heat honey to dry it - blow air over a

cloth, keep it sealed (wet honey ferments); render the wax for candles and salves (Practical Action brief, p. 1). Never heat honey to dry it - blow air over a pan instead. 🥩 Jerky - Heat the meat to 160 °F (poultry 165 °F) before or right after drying - drying alone doesn't kill E. coli, Salmonella or trichinosis. Ten people caught trichinosis from cougar jerky in 1995 (PNW 632, p. 8); cougar and bear are hunted in our units (ODFW, pp. 67-68). Either dip strips 1½-2 minutes in simmering brine before drying, or heat the dried strips 10 minutes in a 275 °F oven (pp. 9, 17; 🖼 oven-heated jerky, p. 14). - Dry at 145-155 °F (check with a thermometer; an oven with the door propped open works). Sun drying isn't recommended. Done when a cooled strip cracks but doesn't snap (pp. 9, 18; photos). 🥖 Staples - No oven thermometer? Put a scrap of white paper or ½ tsp flour on a tin plate in the oven; if it turns light golden brown in 5 minutes, it's right to start bread (FB 807, p. 15). Over a fire, cook on coals, not flames (OSU EM 9331, p. 4). - Danger zone: cooked food left between 40 °F and 140 °F for over 2 hours can make you sick (OSU EM 9331, p. 5). Basic yeast bread - per loaf (USDA FB 807, pp. 13-17): 1 cup lukewarm liquid, about 3 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 1 Tbsp sugar or honey, up to 1 Tbsp fat, and yeast (or ½ cup active sourdough starter in place of yeast and part of the liquid). Knead until smooth and springy, let it double, shape, let it rise again, and bake at about 400 °F for 40-50 minutes, until it sounds hollow when tapped. Stop adding flour once the dough doesn't stick to unfloured hands - too much flour makes heavy bread. Rise it covered, at about 80 °F; it's ready for the oven when a light touch leaves a slight dent. Simple sourdough loaf: 1 cup active starter + 1 cup water + about 3 cups flour + 1½ tsp salt. Knead, let rise 4-8 hours (longer when cool), shape, rise 2-4 hours more, bake at about

Cellar storage is in the Root Cellar guide; how much to put up is in the Food Security guide. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent botulism and poisoning - You can't see, smell or taste botulism. Meat, fish, poultry, milk, beans and every vegetable except most tomatoes are low-acid. They go in jars only in a pressure canner. There is no tested way to can them without one, so dry, ferment, salt or cellar them instead. - Use a tested recipe, set for our elevation (about 1,300 ft): the 15-lb weight or 11 lb on a dial for pressure canning; water-bath times plus 5 minutes. - Boil home-canned meat and vegetables 11 minutes before anyone tastes them. - Never taste a suspect jar. Bulging lid, leaks, spurting, bad smell or mold: detoxify it and throw it out. Low-acid jars can be deadly with no signs at all. -

Never taste a suspect jar. Bulging lid, leaks, spurting, bad smell or mold: detoxify it and throw it out. Low-acid jars can be deadly with no signs at all. - Weigh curing nitrite exactly. Too much is poison. - Smoke and drying don't cook food. Cold-smoked fish is raw. Jerky must reach 160 °F.

☠ Botulism: why low-acid food needs a pressure canner Clostridium botulinum spores are on most fresh food. Sealed in a jar of moist, low-acid food at 40-120 °F with no air, they can make a deadly toxin in 3-4 days (USDA Guide 1, p. 6). The food can look, smell and taste normal (PNW 361, p. 2). | Acid foods (pH 4.6 or lower) | Low-acid foods | | Fruit, jam, pickles, sauerkraut, tomatoes with acid added | Meat, fish, poultry, milk, beans, every fresh vegetable, most soups and stews | | Boiling-water or steam canner | Pressure canner only | The spores die only at 240-250 °F, which takes a pressure canner (🖼 what one looks like). A boiling-water canner would need 7-11 hours, and no such times have been tested (USDA Guide 1, p. 8). Signs of botulism, usually 18-36 hours after eating: double or blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, dry mouth and weakness, then paralysis spreading down to the breathing muscles (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 110). Bad cases need weeks on a breathing machine, so prevention is everything. No honey for babies under 12 months (p. 111). Boil before eating: 10 minutes plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft above 1,000 ft, so 11 minutes here, timed from a full boil. This destroys the toxin, not the spores (PNW 361, p. 2). No pressure

Keep beans, corn and grain dry and roots in the cellar; ferment or salt vegetables; jerk, cure or salt meat; salt, dry, or smoke-and-can fish; and keep animals alive until you need them (general practice). Canned fruit, tomatoes, vegetables and meat need no sugar or salt for safety, only flavor (USDA Guide 1, p. 31). ♨ Running a pressure canner off-grid Choose a weighted-gauge canner. It never needs testing. A dial gauge must be tested yearly; one reading high gives unsafe food (PNW 421, p. 5). The canner must hold at least 4 quart jars. Every batch (USDA Guide 1, pp. 20-22; PNW 421, p. 9; 🖼 step-by-step drawing): 1. 2-3 inches of hot water, or 4-5 inches for fish and other long processes. Jars on the rack (🖼 photo). 2. Lock the lid, weight off. Heat until steam pours out, then vent a full 10 minutes. Put the weight on. 3. Start timing when the weight jiggles. If pressure ever drops below the target, bring it back up and start the whole time over. 4. Turn off the heat and let it cool by itself. Never cool it with water. At zero pressure, take off the weight, wait 10 minutes, and open the lid away from your face. Every batch, in order; if the pressure drops, the timing starts over (a diagram drawn for this guide). On a wood stove, campfire or outdoor burner there is no tested method. Canner makers forbid outdoor LP burners and any burner over 12,000 BTU. In Utah State tests, canners boiled dry within minutes and warped, and cold outdoor air breaks jars and spoils seals (WSU flyer, p. 1). Never "can" in any oven (PNW 361, p. 2).

Use 4-5 inches of water. Control heat by sliding the canner between hotter and cooler parts of the stovetop, not by adding wood. Restart the timer every time pressure dips. Replace a gasket that's worn, stretched or hardened. Small steam leaks are fine if pressure holds; add extra water. Clean the vent with a string. 🥫 Jars, lids, storage and spoilage - Mason jars last for years; only the flat lid must be new (🖼 jar, lid, sealing compound and band). Throw out chipped jars (PNW 361, p. 3). Mayonnaise-type jars are for acid foods in a water bath only, never a pressure canner (USDA Guide 1, p. 13). - One-time metal lids shouldn't be reused. Opening warps them and the sealing compound is spent. Unused lids keep about 5 years, so stockpile them. Buy from the maker; many other sellers' lids were poor in 2021 (FN2028, p. 1). - Reusable plastic lids with rubber rings (the Tattler type) sealed safely in tests reported by NDSU Extension. Follow the maker's directions exactly, which may include tightening the band as soon as the jar comes out (FN2028, p. 1). - If you must reuse a one-time lid (general practice, not tested): only on high-acid jars (jam, fruit, pickles, kraut), where failure shows as mold or fizzing, not hidden toxin. Never on low-acid food. Test seals after 12-24 hours, bands off. Press the middle: if it springs back, it's not sealed. Tap with a teaspoon: a ringing note means sealed; a dull one means not (USDA Guide 1, p. 25; 🖼 photo). Store cool, dark and dry, 50-70 °F, never above 95 °F; best quality within a year, though sealed jars stored this way stay safe longer

🍑 Water-bath and steam canning; jam without pectin Water bath (USDA Guide 1, p. 18; 🖼 illustrated steps): keep 1-2 inches of water over the jars. Start timing at a hard boil; if the boil stops, start over. At the end, take the lid off, wait 5 minutes, lift the jars out, and leave them alone 12-24 hours. Steam canner (saves fuel and water): approved for acid foods only, using a tested boiling-water recipe. The total time must be 45 minutes or less. Vent until a full column of steam shows, and never open it to add water (K-State MF3241, p. 2). Jam and jelly without bought pectin: - Apples, crab apples, gooseberries, some plums and grapes have their own pectin; strawberries, cherries and blueberries don't. For jelly, use ¾ ripe and ¼ under-ripe fruit (USDA Guide 1, p. 29). - Berry jam: 4 cups crushed berries and 4 cups sugar makes 3-4 half-pints. ☀ Drying in our dry summers Trays and solar dryers are in the Root Cellar guide. - Sun drying needs about 90 °F, low humidity and clean air. A solar dryer (🖼 USDA solar drier; 🖼 brick-and-plastic dryer plan) is dependable with 3-5 days in a row near 95 °F, which is an ordinary July to September here (PNW 651, p. 16). - Not in wildfire smoke. Bring trays in when smoke settles in the valley (general practice). - Dries well (photos): apples, pears, plums, cherries, peaches, grapes, huckleberries. Not blackberries. - No sulfite dips for anyone with asthma (p. 18). - Fruit leather from windfalls: heat the purée to 160 °F first (p. 20). - Done? Pack it loosely in covered jars 2-4 days, shaking daily. Moisture on the lid means dry it more (p. 18). - Kill insect eggs before storing: 160 °F for 30 minutes (general practice). 🥩 Jerky and pemmican Safe jerky (PNW 632): 1. Slice lean meat into strips. 2. Bring it to 160 °F (poultry 165 °F): dip strips 1½-2 minutes in simmering brine before drying (p. 17), or heat dried strips 10 minutes at 275 °F (p. 9; 🖼 photo). 3. Dry at 145-155 °F, checked with a thermometer (🖼 which kind), until a cooled strip cracks but doesn't snap (p. 18; 🖼 photo). 4. Keep it sealed; it's best within 1-2 months (p. 21). Don't sun-dry meat (USU, p. 59). Bear and cougar carry trichinosis; ten people caught it from cougar jerky (PNW 632, p. 8). Pemmican: lean meat dried by sun, wind or smoke (not salt-cured), pounded, and mixed with hot rendered fat. About 6 lb of meat makes 1 lb, and it keeps for years, depending on the fat (Special Forces handbook, p. 174). There's no modern tested recipe, so (general practice): do the 160 °F step, then dry the meat brittle; render the fat until it stops bubbling; use about equal weights of meat and fat; firm tallow (deer, elk, beef) keeps better than lard; fully dry any berries. Store it cool, dark and airtight; throw it out if rancid or sour. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 632 Making Jerky at Home Safely - tested methods and the hot-brine dip; Food From Scratch - jerky basics.

🥚 Lard, confit, eggs and vinegar - Lard: render slowly at 235-245 °F and don't let it scorch. The fuller the rendering, the less water and the better it keeps (Minnesota, p. 3). Steps are in Food From Scratch. - ⚠ Confit and potted meat (meat sealed under lard) are airless and low-acid, exactly what botulism needs. No method is tested. Use them only short-term in a cold winter cellar, and boil before eating (general practice). - Eggs: fresh, clean, uncracked spring eggs, wiped not washed, in 1 quart water glass (sodium silicate) to 9 quarts boiled, cooled water, 2 inches over them, or in clear limewater (2 lb lime in 5 gallons boiled water). Prick the shell before boiling (USDA 1935, pp. 3-4). USDA says 6-9 months, FAO only 1-6 (FAO, p. 83); plan on the shorter. - Vinegar: yeast turns fruit juice to alcohol in 4-6 days. Then add 1 part unpasteurized vinegar to 4 parts juice, leave it open under cheesecloth at 70 °F or warmer, and don't disturb the "mother." It takes 3-6 months (USDA FB 1424, pp. 9-12; 🖼 barrel "converter"). Only a titration test proves its strength (p. 30), so use it for cooking, never for canned pickles. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Home Methods of Preserving Eggs - water glass and lime; USDA FB 1424 Making Vinegar.

Instead: the MSU amounts or a premix label. - Hot-smoking fish in 130-150 °F air for 2-3 hours (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 14). 🥔 Root Cellars & Food Storage Without Power How to keep a year's harvest with no refrigerator: root cellars, storage rooms, pits and buried barrels, cooling with water and evaporation, sun and solar drying, curing and smoking meat, fermenting, and keeping eggs. The manuals are in Food-Storage\ (Root-Cellars-Pits, Cooling-Without-Power, Drying, Curing-Smoking, Fermenting-Eggs-Vinegar); canning and freezing are in Gardening-Food\. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent food poisoning and losses - Low-acid food in sealed jars needs pressure canning - never "water bath" or "oven can" vegetables, meat or beans, and never can wild mushrooms. Follow the USDA canning guide exactly. - Cured meat needs exact amounts. Weigh salt and any curing salt (nitrite/saltpeter) - too little lets meat spoil, too much nitrite is poisonous. Follow one tested recipe; don't mix them. - Cold-smoked fish is not cooked. Hot-smoke fish to 150-160 °F inside for 30 minutes (PNW 238) unless it's heavily salted and dried. - Green potatoes are toxic (why) - store potatoes in the dark and cut away green parts. - Check stored food weekly. One rotting apple or potato spreads; remove it at once.

🌡 The Illinois Valley problem: warm ground Old root-cellar books assume cold ground. Deep soil stays near the average yearly air temperature, and across most of the U.S. that's 49-58 °F; at 6 ft down clay still swings about ±11 °F through the year (MSU Earth Tempering, p. 2; 🖼 ground-temperature map and chart). Here the yearly average is roughly 54 °F (rule of thumb, from Cave Junction's average highs and lows). So: - A cellar here idles around 50-58 °F. That's perfect for winter squash, pumpkins, sweet potatoes, and fine for a few weeks of most other crops. - To get it down to the 32-40 °F that potatoes, carrots, cabbage and apples want, you must cool it with cold night air in winter: open the vents on cold nights, close them on warm days (USDA FB 1939 (1960), p. 5; Agriculture Canada Pub. 1478, p. 12; 🖼 where the cold air comes in). November-February nights here regularly fall into the 20s and 30s. - In a 50-60 °F space, root crops keep only 3-4 weeks; packing them in damp (not wet) sand or soil cuts the shriveling, and a partitioned-off room or outdoor cellar let in to outside air about doubles the time (USDA FB 1939 (1943), pp. 29-30). - Mild winters are also an advantage: many crops can simply stay in the garden all winter (see below),

air about doubles the time (USDA FB 1939 (1943), pp. 29-30). - Mild winters are also an advantage: many crops can simply stay in the garden all winter (see below), so you need less cellar than people in cold country. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1939 (1943) - storage in a 50-60 °F space, p. 29; MSU Earth Tempering - ground temperature map, p. 2; PNW 548 - winter vegetables west of the Cascades.

🏗 Building a root cellar The essentials (Canada A Practical Farm Root Cellar, pp. 2-6; Novia Handbook for Building a Root Cellar; 🖼 plan of a 10×14 ft farm cellar): 1. Drainage first. Pick a slope or high ground. On the wet valley floor, build at or above ground level and heap earth over it rather than digging into a winter water table; lay a drain pipe along the footings (Novia, pp. 8-9; 🖼 plan and section drawings). 2. Earth cover: at least 3½ ft of soil and straw over the roof (layers of ~6 in straw and 8-12 in soil), carried well past the sides. Add soil as the straw rots. 3. Two vents at opposite ends, about 12 in square for a 10×14 ft cellar (🖼 how the air flows through; 🖼 vents in a cellar cross-section): - Intake: brings outside air down to about 1½ ft above the floor. - Outlet: starts at the ceiling and rises well above the roof (warm air leaves high). - Both adjustable, and screened against rodents and insects. 4. Double doors about 4 ft apart act as an air lock. Face the door north and keep it shaded so summer sun doesn't heat it (Novia, pp. 13-14). 5. Floor of earth or gravel - it holds moisture. Shelves of slats 4 in off the floor and walls so air moves around

doesn't heat it (Novia, pp. 13-14). 5. Floor of earth or gravel - it holds moisture. Shelves of slats 4 in off the floor and walls so air moves around everything. 6. A thermometer and a humidity gauge inside (or a wet rag test: if things shrivel, it's too dry - sprinkle the floor). Night venting: open both vents on cold nights so cold air pours in low and warm air leaves high; close them on warm days (a diagram drawn for this guide). The same idea in a USDA plan: air comes in under the slat floor and leaves through the ventilator at the top (USDA FB 1939 (1943), p. 14). Simpler options: - Basement-corner storage room: about 10×10 ft with an outside window. Insulate the two inside walls and the ceiling (vapor barrier on the warm side), and run an intake duct from the window down to about 18 in above the floor (Pub. 1478, pp. 8-12; 🖼 perspective view; 🖼 cross-section). - Above-ground and part-underground cellars: plans in USDA FB 1939 (1960) (🖼 partly underground cellar; 🖼 outdoor cellar, side view). - Unheated outbuilding, porch or garage: works for squash, onions and dry goods - not for the cold & moist group. 📚 Go deeper: Canada A Practical Farm Root Cellar - full plan, p. 2; Novia Handbook for Building a Root Cellar - photo step by

🕳 Pits, clamps, buried barrels - and the garden itself - Cone pit (USDA FB 1939 (1943), p. 16; 🖼 cross-section): on well-drained ground, dig 6-8 in deep, line with straw or leaves, pile the vegetables in a cone, cover with straw, then 2-3 in of earth, thickened as winter comes. Leave a tuft of straw sticking out the top as a vent and cap it with a board. Open a pit all at once and use a new spot each year (FB 1939 (1960), p. 9). - Clamp (long mound) for potatoes: a straw bed, a vent duct along the bottom, about 8 in of packed straw and up to 12 in of soil; in mild climates use more straw and less soil (FAO Prevention of Post-Harvest Losses; 🖼 clamp drawing). - Buried barrel or trash can: a clean food-safe barrel laid in the ground on a slant so water runs out, mouth facing the path, covered with straw and earth (USDA FB 1939 (1943), p. 18; 🖼 barrel pit; 🖼 buried trash can). Line or wrap it with ¼-inch hardware cloth against gophers and voles (rule of thumb). - Leave it in the ground (🖼 in-garden and mound storage): parsnips, carrots, beets, leeks, kale, collards and rutabagas can stay in the garden through most Illinois Valley winters - in raised or ridged beds so roots don't rot in

❄ Cooling without power - Springhouse: water from a spring or deep well sits near ground temperature - about 52-55 °F here (rule of thumb). Run it through an insulated tank or a shaded stone trough and stand crocks, milk cans and butter in it (USDA FB 976; 🖼 insulated cooling tank). See springhouse. - Evaporative cooler - made for our dry summers: a screened cabinet covered in flannel or burlap, kept wet by wicks from a pan of water on top, in shade and breeze. In hot, dry weather it can hold about 50 °F inside; it works poorly in humid weather (USDA The Iceless Refrigerator). Bigger versions use a wall of wet charcoal, or a double brick wall with wet sand between (about 400 bricks keeps 220 lb of produce), wetted twice a day (Practical Action Evaporative Cooling, p. 2; 🖼 charcoal cooler; 🖼 brick cool chamber). The clay-pot zeer is the small version (Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools; 🖼 how it works; 🖼 pot sizes). - Ice house): ice packed in at least 15 in of sawdust on all sides, on a drained floor, keeps through summer (USDA FB 475, pp. 6, 12-13; 🖼 insulation diagram). Valley ponds rarely freeze thick, but the bulletin shows freezing ice in metal cans on cold nights. Realistically a small ice store is a winter-only luxury here. ☀ Drying food Our hot, dry late summer is ideal drying weather. Sun drying needs about 90 °F, low humidity and clean air; dependable drying needs several days in a row near 95 °F (PNW 651, p. 16). - Trays: wooden frames with food-safe screen (not galvanized); cover with cheesecloth or netting against insects; bring trays in at night so dew doesn't re-wet the food (USDA FB 984, pp. 13-14; 🖼 screened solar drier). - Solar dryer: a dark box with a clear top, vents low and high, and screened trays - a 3×6 ft dryer serves a household of 4-6 (Practical Action A Simple Solar Dryer; 🖼 layout); more designs in the Peace Corps solar food technologies manual and Practical Action Solar Drying (🖼 cabinet and tent dryers). - Is it dry? Fruit is leathery with no moist center (photos); vegetables are brittle. Squeeze a handful of fruit: it should spring apart "like rubber bands." Then condition it at least 2-4 days in a covered jar, shaking daily - if moisture beads up, dry it more (USDA FB 984, p. 47; PNW 651, pp. 17-19). - Don't dry outdoors in wildfire smoke - ash settles on the food (rule of thumb). - Jerky: PNW 632 (🖼 dry enough: cracks, doesn't snap). 🥓 Curing and smoking meat Dry-cured country ham and bacon keep without refrigeration once cured, smoked and aged. - Cure in the cold season: meat must stay 36-40 °F for the whole cure - warmer risks spoilage, colder stops the salt from soaking in (USDA Curing Pork Country Style, p. 5). Here that means December-February, in a cellar or shed vented on cold nights. Carver's bulletin covers curing where winters are too warm (Carver 1912). - The cure: about 8 lb salt + 2 lb sugar per 100 lb of meat, rubbed in, repeated after about a week; 1½-2 days per pound of ham (🖼 parts of a ham; 🖼 rubbing in the cure; Virginia Tech 458-223, p. 3; Kentucky ASC-213). Curing salt (nitrite) must be weighed exactly - use a commercial premix by its label. - Smoke with hardwood (never pine) at 100-120 °F for cured pork (Leaflet 273, p. 8). A barrel smoker at the top of a sloping covered trench, fire at the bottom, is the simplest smokehouse (USDA AWI-68; 🖼 firebox plan). - Store: wrap cooled hams, bag in muslin or paper (🖼 wrapped and bagged), and hang in a dark, dry, airy, rat-proof place; skipper flies don't breed below 45 °F (Leaflet 273, p. 8; 🖼 ham pests). - Fish: dry-salting keeps longer than brining in warm weather (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 5); hot-smoke fish

🥬 Fermenting, salting, eggs and vinegar - Sauerkraut: 2½% salt - 1 lb salt to 40 lb cabbage (about 3 Tbsp per 5 lb); pack in a crock) (🖼 crocks and jars), weight it so brine covers the cabbage, skim scum. Ferment 3-4 weeks at 70-75 °F or 5-6 weeks at 60-65 °F; below 60 °F it may not ferment, above 75 °F it goes soft (USDA FB 1438, p. 14; USDA canning Guide 6). Old bulletins say 86 °F and paraffin seals - don't. - Salted vegetables (beans, greens, corn) in crocks: recipes in the 1918 Food Administration bulletin. - Eggs for months (USDA says 6-9, FAO only 1-6; plan on the shorter - see the Preserving guide): fresh, clean, uncracked spring eggs in a crock of 1 quart water glass (sodium silicate) to 9 quarts boiled, cooled water, with 2 in of liquid over them; or clear lime water. Prick the shell before boiling (USDA Home Methods of Preserving Eggs). - Vinegar: fruit juice → alcohol (yeast) → vinegar (air-loving bacteria). Leave the container open to air under cheesecloth and keep it at least 70 °F (USDA FB 1424; 🖼 barrel "converter"). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1438 Fermented Pickles and Sauerkraut; USDA canning Guide 6 - fermented foods; Wikipedia: sauerkraut.

🐀 Keeping rats, mice and bugs out - Mice get through ¼-inch gaps. Use ¼-inch hardware cloth on vents and storage bins (rule of thumb); line corncribs and grain bins with galvanized hardware cloth (USDA Rat Proofing Buildings, p. 10; 🖼 rat-proof grain bin and walls). - Foundations: concrete curtain walls 2 ft below ground, and metal or stucco on lath 2 ft up the walls, stop burrowing rats (Rat Proofing, p. 8; 🖼 concrete curtain wall). - Grain, beans and dried food in metal or glass with tight lids. Freeze dry beans and grain 2-3 days, warm them a day, then freeze again (freezing alone misses some eggs), or heat them, to kill weevils - not the old chemical fumigants (USU, p. 95). - Cats, traps and tidiness - no open feed, no clutter for nesting. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Rat Proofing Buildings and Premises; Food From Scratch - storing grain.

🧀 Milk, Butter & Cheese Without a Fridge How to milk cleanly, keep milk safe and cool with no power, and turn it into butter, buttermilk, ghee, yogurt, kefir and cheese that keep for weeks or months, from goats, cows or sheep. The animal itself (breeds, feed, kidding, udder health) is in the Goats guide. The books are in Animals\Dairy-Cheese, with the old USDA butter and cheese bulletins in Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools, milk cooling in Food-Storage\Cooling-Without-Power, milk-borne disease in Animals\Veterinary, and the family cow in Animals\Cattle-Horses-Pigs. Where this guide works out a number it says (arithmetic); check it with the Unit Converter or the Practical Math guide. ### The short version - Raw milk can carry brucellosis, tuberculosis and Listeria. Pasteurize: 145 °F for 30 minutes or 161 °F for 15 seconds (UMN, p. 1). No thermometer? Bring it just to a boil. Children, pregnant women, the old and the sick never get raw milk or soft raw-milk cheese (Zoonoses, pp. 91-92). - Cool milk below 50 °F within an hour. Above that, bacteria multiply very fast (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 13). Spring water is often 65 °F (USDA FB 976, p. 15). Milk you can't cool becomes yogurt, cheese or ghee the same day (rule of thumb). - Scald every pail, cloth and churn. Clean milk kept sweet two to three times as long as ordinary milk in the USDA's tests

the same day (rule of thumb). - Scald every pail, cloth and churn. Clean milk kept sweet two to three times as long as ordinary milk in the USDA's tests (FB 976, p. 5). - Pasteurized milk won't sour cleanly by itself. Add a spoonful of last batch's yogurt, clabber or buttermilk as a starter (ILCA, p. 34; USDA FB 1451, p. 7). - What keeps: ghee over 12 months (Practical Action, p. 4); butter salted to 3% up to 4 months cool and dark (ILCA, p. 49); hard cheese and feta in brine for months. - Make hard cheese in the cool months; age it at 40-60 °F, turn it daily, and put cheesecloth over cellar windows against the skipper fly (USDA FB 1191, p. 15). - Rennet comes from the stomach of a kid, lamb or calf that has had only milk. Never curdle milk with milkweed sap: milkweed poisons livestock (AIB 415, p. 71).

🧼 Clean milking 1. Clean, dry bedding. A goat lying on wet straw lets bacteria in through the teat opening. Clip the udder hair so dirt doesn't fall in (Lincoln, pp. 1-2). 2. No dust at milking time. Feed, brush and sweep after milking, or long enough before for the dust to settle; sprinkle the floor (Book of Cheese, p. 48). 3. Wipe the udder and flank with a damp cloth, a separate cloth for each animal, so mastitis germs don't travel (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 82; Book of Cheese, p. 47). Never wash teats in the milk pail (Keeping One Cow, p. 17). 4. Strip the first squirts into a strip cup and look for clots every milking. Clots mean mastitis: discard that milk and milk her last (Lincoln, p. 2). 5. Dip the teats in iodine, wipe them dry, and milk with dry hands, never wet with milk (Book of Cheese, p. 48). Don't wring the teats; dip again after. 6. Milk into a small-top pail; less dirt falls in than into an open one (Book of Cheese, p. 49; 🖼 pails). 7. Strain at once through several layers of cheesecloth, or sterilized cotton between two cloths (FB 920, p. 29), then cool it. Lincoln's target is 38 °F within an hour; kept that cold, raw milk stays fresh 12-14 days (Lincoln, p. 2). 8. Wash the gear

920, p. 29), then cool it. Lincoln's target is 38 °F within an hour; kept that cold, raw milk stays fresh 12-14 days (Lincoln, p. 2). 8. Wash the gear right away: rinse in cold water, scrub in hot water with washing soda (soap leaves a film), then boil 5 minutes or scald, and let it dry by itself; no dish towel (USDA FB 876, p. 6). With no sanitizer, scald with water at 176 °F or hotter; three small rinses beat one big one (ILCA, p. 74). Milk to keep out of the house: the first 4-5 days after kidding (colostrum, for the kid) (FB 920, p. 28); clotted or bloody milk; and milk from an animal on antibiotics until the label's withdrawal time is over (see the Goats guide).

☣ Raw milk dangers: brucellosis, TB and Listeria | Disease | How it reaches people | Signs in people | Signs in the herd | | Brucellosis ("undulant fever") | Raw milk and soft raw-milk cheese; birth fluids | Fever that goes away and comes back, sweats, weakness; can cripple for life (Zoonoses, p. 30) | Abortions. Goats are the classic carrier (p. 29); a cow sheds it in milk up to 2 years (Cattle, p. 117) | | Bovine TB (M. bovis) | Raw milk; children were the main victims (Zoonoses, p. 23) | Swollen, draining neck glands; belly, bone and spine TB | Slow weight loss, long cough, hard lumps in the udder (Cattle, p. 113) | | Listeria | Raw milk, soft cheese | Worst for pregnant women (miscarriage), newborns, the old and the sick (Zoonoses, p. 91) | Circling, drooping ear and face in goats and cattle (p. 92) | - "Raw unpasteurized milk from any species should never be consumed" (Zoonoses, p. 92). Clean farms reduce germs but don't guarantee milk free of them; pasteurizing does (UMN, p. 2). - Hard, aged cheese is safer than soft, but not safe: TB germs lived about 5 months in a Cheddar (Book of Cheese, p. 393). Pasteurize milk for every cheese you can. If you must make raw-milk cheese, make it hard and age it at least

months in a Cheddar (Book of Cheese, p. 393). Pasteurize milk for every cheese you can. If you must make raw-milk cheese, make it hard and age it at least 60 days (rule of thumb). - Young children: no raw milk. Yogurt resists contamination better and can be spoon-fed (WHO, p. 16). Animal milk is no food for babies under 6 months: see the Childbirth & Children guide. - Plant poisons pass into milk. Lupine poison in milk can cause birth defects in a pregnant woman's baby (WSU, p. 15). - Never feed raw milk or whey to pigs; it is a main way TB spreads (Zoonoses, p. 27). Brucellosis in people needs weeks of doxycycline (p. 31; Medical).

After fallout 5-10% of the radioactive iodine a cow eats goes into her milk; it halves every 8 days. Keep milking animals in the barn on hay stored before the fallout. Don't dump contaminated milk: make it into butter or cheese and store it 1-2 months to let the iodine decay. Save clean or canned milk for babies (USDA AH 234, p. 22). See the Nuclear Fallout guide.

🔥 Pasteurizing, with or without a thermometer With a thermometer (UMN, p. 1): 1. Use a double boiler, or a pot set in a pan of water; milk heated straight over the fire scorches. 2. Heat to 145 °F and hold 30 minutes, stirring, or to 161 °F for 15 seconds. If it drops below 145 °F, start the 30 minutes again (rule of thumb). UMN's own home method has a margin: stir until an accurate thermometer reads 165 °F, then cool at once. Cream needs 150 °F for 30 minutes or 166 °F for 15 seconds. 3. Cool it at once in cold running water. Kept refrigerator-cold it lasts 7-10 days; ILCA gives pasteurized milk only 2-3 days, after which it rots instead of souring (ILCA, p. 34). With no thermometer: - Bring it just to a boil, the moment the foam climbs the pot, stirring, then take it off and cool it (rule of thumb). Boiling milk has long been the home protection against milk-borne TB and brucellosis (Zoonoses, p. 27; Cattle, p. 118). - Don't trust the first steam or bubbles. In water, steam shows at about 122 °F and the first good bubbles at about 131 °F, both below pasteurizing heat (Ciochetti & Metcalf, p. 5). - A beeswax check: pure beeswax melts at about 144-147 °F. A pea of it in a small capped jar
pasteurizing-with-or-without-a-thermometer

°F, both below pasteurizing heat (Ciochetti & Metcalf, p. 5). - A beeswax check: pure beeswax melts at about 144-147 °F. A pea of it in a small capped jar standing in the milk turns fully liquid when the milk is near 145 °F; from then on hold the heat 30 minutes (rule of thumb). - Solar box cooker: on clear days from mid-March to mid-September, gallon jugs of water in an insulated solar box reached 149 °F and stayed above milk-pasteurizing heat for at least an hour (Ciochetti & Metcalf, p. 1). Milk heats the same way (rule of thumb). See "Solar pasteurizing" in the Water Purification guide. - Check a thermometer in boiling water: at our 1,300 ft it should read about 210 °F (rule of thumb). Pasteurizing costs only a little vitamin C and thiamine (UMN, p. 2).

❄ Cooling milk with no power Why hurry: milk leaves the udder a little above 90 °F. Ordinary milk soured in 12 hours at 100 °F and clean milk in 36; at 40 °F they kept about 7 and 16 days (FB 976, p. 5; 🖼 chart). In shade at 61 °F milk is still 82 °F after 3 hours; in running water it reaches 61 °F in 1 hour (ILCA, p. 33). Keep it below 50 °F (FB 976, p. 16). Springhouse or spring tank (FB 976, pp. 9-15): 1. Pipe the spring several feet underground to a covered tank in the shade; surface-run spring water has warmed 20 °F on the way. Ours runs about 52-55 °F (Root Cellar guide, "Cooling without power"). 2. Water in at the bottom, out near the top, as high on the can as the milk inside; cans on cleats (FB 876, pp. 7-8; 🖼 tank). 3. Cover and insulate it (6 in of dry sawdust, FB 876, p. 8): a covered, insulated tank in a shed lost 7.6 lb of ice in a test; an open metal tank in the sun, 168 lb (FB 976, p. 12). 4. No running water or ice: 6-10 gallons of water per gallon of milk, changed often (FB 976, p. 14). Stir the milk. Even ice water needs volume: a can of 85 °F milk in
cooling-milk-with-no-power

ice: 6-10 gallons of water per gallon of milk, changed often (FB 976, p. 14). Stir the milk. Even ice water needs volume: a can of 85 °F milk in 3 times its volume of 37 °F water only gets to about 50 °F (p. 6). Even three times the milk's volume of ice water only brings 85 °F milk down to about 50 °F: use plenty of water, and cover and insulate the tank (FB 976, p. 7). A creek: a lidded can tied in a cold stream works (🖼 Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 13). Our creeks and the Illinois River run warm by midsummer, so measure first, use a shaded side-channel or deep pool, and weight and lash the lid against raccoons and bears (rule of thumb). Evaporative cooler ("iceless refrigerator") for butter, cheese and cooled milk (USDA 1917, p. 3): a 42 × 16 × 14-inch screened frame, covered in canton flannel or burlap, with cloth wicks from a pan of water on top; stand it in shade and a breeze. In warm dry air it gets down to about 50 °F; in damp weather it barely works. Our dry summer afternoons suit it (rule of thumb). Brick and charcoal versions are in the Root Cellar guide. Brick and charcoal versions are in the Root Cellar guide. Water wicks from the top pan into the cloth cover, and the breeze dries it and cools the inside (a diagram drawn for this guide). Hold the cold: chill milk first, then shut it in a hay-box: it "may make many hours difference"; with a little cracked ice a quart holds 24 hours in hot weather (USDA FB 771, p. 17). Ice and cold-water numbers: the Storing Energy guide, "Cold: storing winter for summer". Summer plan (rule of thumb): milk at dawn and dusk, cool at once, drink the morning's milk that day, and turn the rest into yogurt, cheese, butter or ghee before the afternoon heat.

🥛 Separating cream by hand | Method | How | Fat left in the skim milk | | Shallow pan | Fresh milk in a pan 16-24 in across and 4 in deep, in a cool place; skim with a ladle after 36 hours | 0.5-0.6%, or more: up to a third of the butterfat lost | | Deep-setting | Fresh milk in a tall narrow "shotgun" can (about 8½ × 20 in) in ice water 12 hours or cold water 24 hours; draw the skim milk off a bottom tap | 0.2-0.5% | | Hand-cranked separator | Milk at 90 °F or warmer, crank at the stated speed, flush with skim milk at the end | a trace | Sources: ILCA, p. 38 (🖼 pan and can); FB 876, pp. 4-6; can size p. 21. - Cool fast for more cream: quick chilling makes cream rise faster and more completely (FB 876, p. 5). Don't jostle the pans; rough handling breaks up the rising fat (ILCA, p. 38). - Goat milk: the cream barely rises (FB 920, p. 7), so skim what you get and churn soured whole milk (below), or use a separator. - A separator is the one dairy machine worth trading for (ILCA, p. 37). Set it for cream of about 30-35% (FB 976, p. 17): a gallon of 30% cream makes about 3 lb of
