one dairy machine worth trading for (ILCA, p. 37). Set it for cream of about 30-35% (FB 976, p. 17): a gallon of 30% cream makes about 3 lb of butter (FB 876, p. 3). Take it apart and wash it after every use; rinsing it and washing it once a day is "a filthy practice" (p. 6; 🖼 cutaway). - Cool the cream at once and never pour warm cream into cold; it sours the lot (FB 976, p. 17).

🧈 Butter and buttermilk Butter from cream (FB 876, pp. 8-15, 23-24): 1. Ripen: warm the saved cream to 65-75 °F and hold it until it thickens, looks glossy and is mildly sour, about 12 hours. Overripe (too sour) cream makes poor butter. 2. Cool it to churning heat and hold 2 hours: 52-60 °F in summer, 58-66 °F in winter, set so the butter comes in 30-40 minutes (p. 10). Warm or cool it by standing the can in water (🖼 p. 7); never pour hot water or ice into cream. 3. Churn in a scalded, cold-rinsed churn filled only a third full (p. 12). No churn: a jar or a closed can, shaken, rolled on a mat or swung from a tripod (ILCA, p. 60; 🖼 small churns). Let the gas out a few times early on. 4. Stop when the grains are the size of wheat and drain the buttermilk through a strainer (🖼 p. 13). Churning on into a lump traps buttermilk. 5. Wash, don't work, the buttermilk out: twice, with clean water at the buttermilk's temperature, twice its volume in all; three times in hot weather (pp. 14-15; ILCA, p. 46). Use drinking-quality water. 6. Salt and work: about ½ oz salt per pound (3%) for keeping butter; FB 876 uses ¾ oz. Press and fold with a wooden paddle, never your warm hands (Keeping
butter-and-buttermilk

Salt and work: about ½ oz salt per pound (3%) for keeping butter; FB 876 uses ¾ oz. Press and fold with a wooden paddle, never your warm hands (Keeping One Cow, p. 18), just until the salt is even and the butter breaks "like broken steel" (p. 16; 🖼 working it). Stop when the grains are the size of wheat, before they gather into a lump (a diagram drawn for this guide). Butter from soured whole milk (goat milk, or no separator) (ILCA, pp. 60-62): collect milk over 2-3 days until it is pleasantly sour; fresh milk churns slowly and loses fat. Churn at 63-66 °F (17-19 °C), the jar a third to half full. Warmer than 68 °F churns fast but loses fat: at 79 °F as little as 60% comes out as butter. Colder can take 5 hours (🖼 products chart). Keeping butter without a fridge: - Salted to 3% in a sealed crock, cool and dark: up to 4 months; more salt adds nothing (ILCA, p. 49). Pack it firmly from one churning, in a well-glazed crock (FB 876, p. 16; ILCA, p. 47). - Under brine: rolls of butter wholly submerged in 1 lb salt to 4 lb water; or a crock topped with a wax seal (FB 876, p. 20). - Butter for storing keeps best made from pasteurized sweet cream: 145-150 °F for
butter-and-buttermilk

to 4 lb water; or a crock topped with a wax seal (FB 876, p. 20). - Butter for storing keeps best made from pasteurized sweet cream: 145-150 °F for 25-30 minutes, cooled below 50 °F and held 3 hours before churning (p. 19). - Unsalted butter in warm weather turns rancid within days (Practical Action, p. 5); make surplus into ghee. Cultured buttermilk: skim milk heated to 203 °F, cooled to 68-77 °F, seeded with 1-2% starter, 16-20 hours (Practical Action, p. 1). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 876 Making Butter on the Farm - every step and every fault; ILCA Rural Dairy Technology - churning, overrun and keeping butter.
butter-and-buttermilk

🫕 Ghee and clarified butter for storage Ghee is butterfat with the water and milk solids cooked out, so germs have nothing to grow in. It keeps more than 12 months at room temperature (Practical Action, p. 4). 1. Melt butter (or, the traditional way, boil cream) in a heavy pot and boil gently and steadily, skimming the scum. Don't scorch it (ILCA, p. 49). 2. It is done when the water stops spitting and the milk solids on the bottom turn golden brown; color is the only test (Practical Action, p. 4). 3. Let it settle; pour off through boiled cheesecloth until it runs clear. 4. Store airtight, dark and cool, in glazed crocks or glass, not iron or copper, which speed rancidity. Fill jars full; a clean, dry spoon every time (rule of thumb). Clarified butter with less fuel: melt butter in water at about 176 °F, let the fat set on top as in a deep-setting can, drain the water off, then heat the fat just long enough to drive off the last moisture. It kept well through a 5-month test (ILCA, p. 49). A pound of butter (80% fat) gives about ¾ lb of ghee (ILCA, p. 45; arithmetic). In fire season do the long boil on the stove indoors or before dawn, never over an open fire outside (rule of thumb).
ghee-and-clarified-butter-for-storage

🦠 Cultured milk, yogurt and kefir Soured milk keeps where fresh milk won't: the acid stops most germs, though not mold (ILCA, p. 34). Yogurt (Practical Action, pp. 1-4): 1. Heat milk to 176-185 °F and hold 15-20 minutes, stirring. Cool fast to 104-113 °F, standing the pot in cold water. 2. Stir in 20-50 g of live yogurt per liter (about 1½-3 tablespoons per quart (arithmetic)). 3. Keep it at 104-113 °F for 4-6 hours: a thermos, an insulated box (p. 4), a hay-box, or a cooler with jars of hot water (rule of thumb). Then cool it. 4. It keeps up to 10 days cold (p. 1); in a springhouse plan on less (rule of thumb). Clabber and soured milk: milk soured naturally in a warm room for 1-2 days keeps 3-8 days (p. 1). The ILCA way keeps longer: a vessel smoked hot with burning embers (they used olive and acacia; a clean hardwood such as oak (rule of thumb)), the milk fermented slowly at 61-64 °F for 2-4 days, keeps 15-20 days; warmer, it wheys off and gets gassy (ILCA, p. 59). Pouring off the whey and topping up with fresh milk for up to a week concentrates it and keeps it longer still (p. 60). Pasteurized milk must be seeded; it won't sour cleanly alone (p. 34). Kefir needs no warm box (ILCA, p. 59):
cultured-milk-yogurt-and-kefir

week concentrates it and keeps it longer still (p. 60). Pasteurized milk must be seeded; it won't sour cleanly alone (p. 34). Kefir needs no warm box (ILCA, p. 59): heat milk to 185 °F for 30 minutes, cool it, add kefir grains (lumps in which the bacteria and yeasts live), and leave about 12 hours at 72 °F. Lift the grains out with a clean spoon into the next jar of milk. They multiply; give spares away or feed them to hens (rule of thumb). Keeping cultures alive for years: - Mother culture: keep a small jar going from clean, freshly heated milk, use 1-3% of it to seed each day's batch, and start a new mother from the last of it. It runs for months until stray germs spoil it (Practical Action, p. 3). Seeding from yesterday's yogurt works but spoils sooner (same page); after a collapse it may be all you have. - Homemade starter from nothing: fill several boiled pint jars with fresh milk from different animals, keep them at 75 °F, and keep the one that curdles in 24-30 hours into a firm, smooth, marble-like curd with no gas holes and a clean, sharp sour taste. Carry it on daily: a teaspoon into a quart of skim milk that was heated to 175 °F for 30 minutes and cooled to 75 °F (FB 1451, p.
cultured-milk-yogurt-and-kefir

taste. Carry it on daily: a teaspoon into a quart of skim milk that was heated to 175 °F for 30 minutes and cooled to 75 °F (FB 1451, p. 7; 🖼 starter jars; FB 876, pp. 9-10). - Throw out any starter that tastes off. Natural starters often pick up bad flavors that are hard to notice at first (Book of Cheese, p. 67). - Keep two of each culture in two places, and share with neighbors: their jar is your backup (rule of thumb).

🧀 Soft cheeses: paneer, queso fresco, chèvre, cottage cheese Soft cheeses are quick and need little gear, but they keep only days: about 3 days cold, 5 in brine (Practical Action, p. 1). Make them from pasteurized milk. Paneer or queso blanco (lemon or vinegar cheese, no rennet) (ILCA, pp. 50-52; Practical Action, p. 2): 1. Heat milk to 180 °F, or to a simmer for 5 minutes. This pasteurizes it too. 2. Stir in lemon or lime juice: Practical Action uses 1-1.5% of the milk's weight, ILCA about 3 mL per 100 mL diluted with equal water (2 tablespoons per quart (arithmetic)). Add it in three parts, stopping when the curds clump and the whey runs clear and yellow-green. Vinegar works the same way (rule of thumb). 3. Settle 15 minutes; drain in a cloth, stirring so it doesn't mat. 4. Salt (3.5-5% of the curd) and press overnight (🖼 step chart). A liter makes about 250 g of moist paneer; a firm pressed queso blanco about 1 lb per gallon. Queso fresco is the same fresh cheese set with rennet instead of acid: make the one-gallon rennet cheese (hard-cheese section) up to bagging the curd, salt the curd, press it lightly a few hours, and eat it within a few days (rule of thumb). Chèvre-style goat cheese (soft, spreadable, a little rennet): FB 920 calls French goat cheese
soft-cheeses-paneer-queso-fresco-ch-vre-cottage-cheese

press it lightly a few hours, and eat it within a few days (rule of thumb). Chèvre-style goat cheese (soft, spreadable, a little rennet): FB 920 calls French goat cheese "Chevret" (p. 7); this is the USDA rennet cottage-cheese method (FB 1451, pp. 9-11): 1. Pasteurize the milk, cool it to 75 °F, and stir in starter: about ½ cup per gallon (a pint per 3½ gallons). 2. Add rennet: about 3 drops of liquid rennet per gallon, first stirred into a half-cup of cold water; or one junket tablet dissolved in a pint of cold water, using a third of it for 3½ gallons. 3. Cover and leave at 75 °F 12-15 hours (overnight), until clear whey lies on the curd. Don't cut or heat it. 4. Ladle into fine cotton cloth; drain 20-30 minutes, then tie it up and hang it, or press lightly under about 25 lb until it is like thick cream cheese (🖼 boards and weight). 5. Salt about 1 teaspoon per pound; herbs if you like. Cottage cheese with no bought culture (FB 1451, pp. 6-7): let skim milk clabber at about 75 °F (about 30 hours) until clean and pleasantly sour; cut it in 2-inch pieces; set the pan in hot water to bring it to 100 °F and hold 30 minutes, stirring gently (hotter makes it tough); drain in a cloth bag,
soft-cheeses-paneer-queso-fresco-ch-vre-cottage-cheese

in 2-inch pieces; set the pan in hot water to bring it to 100 °F and hold 30 minutes, stirring gently (hotter makes it tough); drain in a cloth bag, rinse cold, salt. A gallon makes about 1½ lb. Keep it in glass or earthenware and eat it soon: 36 hours at room temperature puts it off flavor (p. 10).
soft-cheeses-paneer-queso-fresco-ch-vre-cottage-cheese

🐮 Rennet from a kid or calf stomach, and from plants Rennet is an enzyme from the true (fourth) stomach, the abomasum, of a suckling calf. After weaning, the calf makes pepsin instead (ILCA, pp. 49-50), so stomachs that have digested anything but milk make weak rennet. Cheesemakers hold that kid or lamb rennet suits goat or sheep milk (Book of Cheese, p. 55). Making rennet (Book of Cheese, pp. 55-56): 1. Take the fourth stomach of a kid, lamb or calf that has had nothing but milk, butchered soon after a full feed. Empty it, clean it, blow it up and dry it in airy shade. Dried "rennets" keep until needed. 2. Cut it open and soak it in 3-5% salt water (about 4-7 oz salt per gallon (arithmetic)), stirring and pounding it, 5-7 days. Wring it out and soak it again in fresh brine, 4-6 weeks in all. 3. Filter through straw, charcoal and sand (or several cloths), add more salt, and keep it cool and dark in a stone jug or brown glass. Light destroys it, and heat kills it. 4. Good rennet is clear, with a clean salty taste. Cloudy, muddy or bad-smelling rennet taints cheese: throw it out. 5. Quick way: a small piece of dried stomach left in a little water overnight curdles milk (Henley's, p. 176). Test every batch: homemade rennet varies in
rennet-from-a-kid-or-calf-stomach-and-from-plants

throw it out. 5. Quick way: a small piece of dried stomach left in a little water overnight curdles milk (Henley's, p. 176). Test every batch: homemade rennet varies in strength and spoils (p. 55). It works slowly below 70 °F and best at 84-94 °F; dilute it in about 40 times its volume of cold water before stirring it in (pp. 95-96). Warm a quart of milk to 86 °F, stir in a measured half-teaspoon of diluted rennet, and time it: aim for a curd that splits cleanly in 25-40 minutes, then scale up (rule of thumb). Bought liquid rennet runs about 2 teaspoons per 100 lb of milk (FB 1191, p. 6). Plant rennets (Practical Action, p. 1): papaya sap, fig bark, and the stems or leaves of two tropical plants also curdle milk. Fig trees grow in valley yards; a few drops of the milky sap from a green fig stem per quart of warm milk is the old way. The sap burns skin, so wear gloves (rule of thumb). Thistle flowers (cardoon) and nettle are traditional too (rule of thumb). - Use plant rennets for fresh cheese. Many plant and other enzymes turn aged cheese bitter (ILCA, p. 50). - Never use milkweed. Named for its "milky, sticky juice", it poisons livestock (AIB 415, pp. 71, 73). - No rennet at all? Make acid cheese (paneer)
rennet-from-a-kid-or-calf-stomach-and-from-plants

(ILCA, p. 50). - Never use milkweed. Named for its "milky, sticky juice", it poisons livestock (AIB 415, pp. 71, 73). - No rennet at all? Make acid cheese (paneer) or lactic cheese (cottage cheese, chèvre without the rennet).
rennet-from-a-kid-or-calf-stomach-and-from-plants

🏋 Hard cheese step by step, with a home-made press The USDA's simple farm Cheddar ("granular" process) from whole milk: 5-6 hours, then minutes a day (FB 1191, pp. 4-17). Cool nights make the best cheese; hot weather breeds gas germs (p. 4). Use milk under 12 hours old, kept at 60 °F or below (p. 5). Pasteurize it if you can, then add ¼-½ cup of clean buttermilk or clabber per gallon as starter (rule of thumb). For 4 gallons (about 34 lb) of milk, making about 3½ lb of cheese (arithmetic from p. 5): 1. Warm the milk to 86 °F in a big pot set in a tub of warm water; keep it there until the curd is cut. 2. Rennet: about ⅔ teaspoon of liquid rennet (FB 1191 uses ⅓ oz, 2 teaspoons, per 100 lb (arithmetic)), stirred into a cup of cool water, then stirred through the milk 3 minutes (p. 6). Cover; don't let it move for 30-35 minutes. 3. Test the set: slide a finger in at a slant, lift, and split the curd with your thumb. When it splits cleanly with nothing left on the finger, cut it (p. 7; 🖼 trying the curd). 4. Cut into ⅜-inch cubes with a long knife: lengthwise, crosswise, then give the curd a quarter turn and cut lengthwise again. Cut, don't crush (p. 8; 🖼
hard-cheese-step-by-step-with-a-home-made-press

the curd). 4. Cut into ⅜-inch cubes with a long knife: lengthwise, crosswise, then give the curd a quarter turn and cut lengthwise again. Cut, don't crush (p. 8; 🖼 curd knives). 5. Stir gently 15-20 minutes, then heat slowly, about 2 °F every 5 minutes, to 100 °F, still stirring. 6. Hold at 100 °F until firm and acid: a squeezed handful falls apart when you open your hand (🖼 firmness), and a pinch of curd pressed on a clean hot iron draws out fine threads ¼-½ inch long (pp. 9-10; 🖼 hot-iron test). 7. Drain: dip off the whey; spread the curd on a cloth over a slatted rack, keep it covered and near 100 °F, and stir it every 5-10 minutes so the pieces stay hickory-nut size (pp. 10-11; 🖼 draining box). 8. Salt when the hot-iron threads reach ¾-1 inch: about 3 oz salt per 10 lb of curd. Let it dissolve and the curd cool to 85 °F (p. 13). 9. Press: into a cloth-lined hoop; light weight 30 minutes, more for an hour; take it out, dip it in warm water, smooth the cloth ("dressing"), and press at full weight 24 hours (p. 14). 10. Cure at 50-60 °F, turned daily for 2 weeks, then twice a week; coat it at 2 weeks; eat it from 6 weeks (mild), or keep it many months
hard-cheese-step-by-step-with-a-home-made-press

10. Cure at 50-60 °F, turned daily for 2 weeks, then twice a week; coat it at 2 weeks; eat it from 6 weeks (mild), or keep it many months for sharp (pp. 15-16). Steps 3 and 4: test the set with a finger, then cut the curd into ⅜-inch cubes (a diagram drawn for this guide). Smaller batch (1 gallon, goat or cow) (FB 920, p. 8): a junket tablet dissolved in a little cold water into a gallon of milk at 88 °F; cut after 30 minutes into 1-inch cubes; warm the pot in 100 °F water so the curd reaches 98 °F in an hour; bag it 2-3 hours; press between two plates in a can under a weight 24 hours; rub with salt two days running, then daily for a week. Ready at 10 days.
hard-cheese-step-by-step-with-a-home-made-press

A home-made cheese press - Hoop (mold): a tube with drain holes and a loose wooden follower (disk) on top: 4-inch plastic drainpipe cut 4-10 in long on a wooden base (Practical Action, p. 7), or FB 1191's hoop, 7-8 in across and 10 in tall, for a 5-10-lb cheese (🖼 p. 13). Use wood, food-grade plastic or stainless, not galvanized metal, which acid curd eats (rule of thumb). - Lever press (FB 1191, pp. 14-15; 🖼 press): a long pole (the bulletin's is about 12 ft) hinged to the wall, the hoop under it about 3 ft out, and a pail of stones (35-40 lb) that slides along the pole: halfway out for light pressing, at the end for full pressure. - Weight press: boards above and below and a pail of stones or water on top, about 25 lb for soft cheese (FB 1451, p. 10), more for hard. Or a screw press (🖼 Practical Action, p. 5). The hoop stands about 3 ft from the wall; sliding the pail of stones outward along the pole presses harder (FB 1191, p. 15).
a-home-made-cheese-press

🧂 Feta and halloumi: cheese that keeps in brine Feta needs no press and keeps for months under brine with the air kept out. Cow, sheep or goat milk all work (ILCA, pp. 52-56; 🖼 steps): 1. Warm the milk to 90 °F and let it stand 1 hour (with a little starter if it was pasteurized (rule of thumb)). 2. Rennet at 25 mL per 100 liters, about ¾ teaspoon for 4 gallons (arithmetic). Firm in 40-50 minutes. 3. Cut into 1-inch cubes; let the whey separate 15 minutes, stirring now and then; settle; dip off the whey. 4. Ladle curd into cloth-lined molds with lids; turn them every half hour for the first few hours; drain overnight. 5. Cut into blocks, sprinkle with salt, and put them in 15% brine (about 1¼-1½ lb salt per gallon of boiled water (arithmetic)). The cheese ends near 6-8% salt. 6. Keep the air out (a full crock with a weighted plate, or a full sealed jar): mold grows where air reaches the brine. Eat after a few days or keep it for months; it softens and crumbles as it ripens. Yield about 1 lb per gallon (1 kg from 9 kg of milk) (arithmetic). Halloumi, cooked in its own whey and kept in whey brine (ILCA, pp. 52-53; 🖼 steps): set whole milk with rennet at 90-95 °F; cut the curd;
feta-and-halloumi-cheese-that-keeps-in-brine

of milk) (arithmetic). Halloumi, cooked in its own whey and kept in whey brine (ILCA, pp. 52-53; 🖼 steps): set whole milk with rennet at 90-95 °F; cut the curd; warm it to 104 °F stirring 20 minutes; drain and press 2 hours. Meanwhile heat the whey to 176-194 °F: the whey cheese that rises is skimmed off. Cut the pressed curd into 4 × 4 × 1¼-inch slabs and simmer them in the hot whey until they float and turn soft and stretchy; fold them, rub with dry salt and dried mint, cool, and store in cool, boiled whey brine (15% salt). Ripen about 30 days; it keeps several months below 54 °F.
feta-and-halloumi-cheese-that-keeps-in-brine

🕯 Salting, waxing and aging without a fridge Salt is the main preservative: it pulls out water and slows the germs that remain (Practical Action, p. 1): in the curd for hard cheese, brine for fresh. Where to age it: - Cool: FB 1191 calls 50-60 °F most favorable (p. 15); older books want about 45 °F, never over 50-52 °F, and no sudden swings (Henley's, p. 177). Cheddar cured at 40 °F scored best, at 60 °F worst; never let it freeze (Book of Cheese, p. 282). At 70-80 °F it cures fast and goes bad more often (FB 1191, p. 16). Our cellars sit near 55 °F by midsummer (Root Cellar guide): good enough. - Damp: above 85% humidity (Practical Action, p. 4). If the room dries out, wet the floor; open it to cool night air and close it by day (Book of Cheese, p. 286). Care: turn every cheese daily so it dries evenly and doesn't stick or mold to the shelf; if the cloth loosens and the rind cracks, rub it with butter. Cracks let in flies and mold (Book of Cheese, p. 284). Wipe mold off with a dry cloth; if it molds badly, scrub it with strong brine and move it somewhere drier (FB 1191, p. 15). Cover cellar windows with cheesecloth: the cheese-skipper fly gets through window screen (same page; Cheese fly).
salting-waxing-and-aging-without-a-fridge

scrub it with strong brine and move it somewhere drier (FB 1191, p. 15). Cover cellar windows with cheesecloth: the cheese-skipper fly gets through window screen (same page; Cheese fly). Coating cuts drying and mold. Coat once the rind is dry, 4-6 days to 2 weeks after pressing (Book of Cheese, p. 286): - Beeswax (from the Bees guide) is the no-store wax: melt it in a can set in a pot of water, never over a bare flame, and dip or brush thin coats (rule of thumb). The cheese must be dry or the wax blisters and peels (p. 287). - Cloth and fat: leave the pressing cloth on and rub it with butter or lard as it dries (rule of thumb, from p. 284). - Brine instead of a rind (feta, halloumi). Waxing and brining both cut weight loss (ILCA, p. 56). Cut cheese: wrap it in a cloth wrung almost dry, then paper, and keep it cool; don't shut it fully airtight, which makes it mold faster (Book of Cheese, p. 396). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1191 - farm Cheddar with home-made gear; The Book of Cheese, pp. 281-293 - curing rooms and defects (old book: raw-milk methods); ILCA - queso blanco, halloumi, feta, yields.
salting-waxing-and-aging-without-a-fridge

♻ Whey and buttermilk: using everything A hard cheese leaves 8-9 lb of whey for every pound of cheese (arithmetic). Whey can be a drink, become whey cheese, or feed animals (Practical Action, p. 2). - Ricotta (whey cheese): heat sweet whey to about 200 °F; the albumin rises and is skimmed off; a little acid speeds it (Book of Cheese, p. 319). Albumin is only about 0.7% of the milk, so expect a small amount (same page). - Brown whey cheese (mysost): boil the rest down, stirring as it thickens, until it is a brown, sweet paste; stir the skimmed albumin back in and cool it in molds. Whey is nearly 5% milk sugar (same page). It takes a lot of fuel; use a solar cooker or the back of a stove running anyway (rule of thumb). - Hens: skim milk and buttermilk make a wet mash with ground grain, and can be their only drink: about 4-5 gallons a day per 100 hens (USDA FB 1841, p. 24). Whey does the same job (rule of thumb); see the Chickens guide. - Pigs: only boiled or pasteurized whey and milk (Zoonoses, p. 27). Old factories spread disease by sending whey home in the milk cans (Book of Cheese, p. 49). - Buttermilk and sour milk: drink it; bake with it (a cup plus ½ teaspoon of soda replaces sweet
whey-and-buttermilk-using-everything

whey home in the milk cans (Book of Cheese, p. 49). - Buttermilk and sour milk: drink it; bake with it (a cup plus ½ teaspoon of soda replaces sweet milk and baking powder: "Leavening" in the Food From Scratch guide); seed the next batch. Ayib curd: heat sour buttermilk or skim milk to about 122 °F (104-158 °F all work) until curd forms, cool slowly, strain: at least 1 kg from 8 liters (ILCA, p. 62). - Waste: don't tip whey into creeks, and keep it out of compost, which draws bears; bury it or feed it out (rule of thumb; Sanitation guide).

🌱 Your Seed Bank: Grow, Harvest and Save Seed How to keep a heirloom seed bank alive for good in the Illinois Valley: store it so it lasts, test it, plant each variety at the right time here, keep varieties from crossing, and save your own seed every year - including seed from the fruits (tomatoes, cucumbers, melons, squash, peppers). It ends with the calorie crops the kit is missing and how to propagate fruit trees and berries, whose seeds don't grow true. The manuals are in Gardening-Food\Seed-Saving, Gardening-Food\Fruit-Propagation and the rest of Gardening-Food\. Written for the Heaven's Harvest "10 Year" seed bank. The company's list has 39 varieties (they note some may be swapped when seed is short), so check your own packets - the rules below are by crop, so they still apply. ### The five rules of a seed bank 1. Don't plant it all. Plant part of each packet; keep the rest sealed as a backup. 2. Start saving seed in year one - the short-lived ones first: onions, leeks, sweet corn, peppers and okra keep only 1-2 years. 3. Test germination every winter so you know what still sprouts before you need it. 4. Know which varieties cross. Several in this kit cross with each other; save seed from only one of each group per year (or hand-pollinate). 5. Vegetables aren't enough calories. Add potatoes,

which varieties cross. Several in this kit cross with each other; save seed from only one of each group per year (or hand-pollinate). 5. Vegetables aren't enough calories. Add potatoes, dry beans, a flour corn and grains. Every variety in this kit is open-pollinated (heirloom): seed you save grows the same plant as long as it didn't cross with a relative. Hybrids ("F1" on a packet) don't come true - don't save from those. (OSA Seed Saving Guide, p. 5)

🗄 Keeping the seed bank alive Seed dies from heat and damp. Two rules from seed-storage research (Seed Processing and Storage, p. 9): - Every 10 °F cooler roughly doubles seed life. - Every 1% less moisture in the seed roughly doubles it too (🖼 chart: moisture, humidity and storage life). - Quick test for a storage spot: temperature (°F) + relative humidity (%) should add up to less than 100. (OSA, p. 17) Where to keep it here: - Not in a shed, garage, attic or vehicle - Illinois Valley summers top 100 °F. - Best: the coolest, driest room of the house, a closet on a north wall, or a dry root cellar. - Fridge or freezer only for very dry seed in an airtight jar. Let the jar warm to room temperature before opening, or moisture condenses on the cold seed. Very dry seed (about 5% moisture) held below 20 °F still sprouted well after 20 years. (Seed Processing and Storage, p. 9) - Once you open a Mylar packet, reseal it, or move the seed into a glass jar with a desiccant packet (silica gel; 🖼 chart: how the container affects sprouting). Label every jar with the variety and year. How long seed stays good in ordinary cool, dry storage (Univ. of Illinois seed life table, p. 2; McCormack, p. 17): | Years of good sprouting

🧪 Germination test ("rag doll") Do this every winter, and before planting any packet more than a year old (what germination looks like). (OSA, p. 18; Univ. of Illinois, p. 1) 1. Dampen a paper towel - damp, not dripping. 2. Lay out 10 seeds (more is more accurate) spaced apart, roll the towel up, and put it in a plastic bag with a little air. Label it. 3. Keep it warm: about 70 °F for most crops; 75-80 °F for peppers, eggplant, melons. Lettuce and celery sprout better with some light. 4. Check from day 3; remove sprouted and moldy seeds and count them. Slow crops (peppers, parsley-type seeds) can take up to 3 weeks. 5. Read the result: 10 of 10 - plant normally. 7-9 - sow thicker. 6 or fewer - this packet is failing: plant it now and save fresh seed this year. Ten seeds make the count easy to read as a share (a diagram drawn for this guide). Fresh spinach, lettuce and pepper seed can be dormant for a few months - retest before giving up on it. 📚 Go deeper: OSA germination test, p. 18; McCormack - germination testing, p. 20.

🏡 Growing it here - Raised beds with good soil (🖼 how they drain wet ground). Many valley soils are serpentine (high magnesium, low calcium) or slow-draining clay. Build raised beds, get a soil test before adding amendments, and add lots of compost. (OSU Soil Test Guide; Improving Garden Soils) - Water is the summer limit. Only 5-7 in of rain falls April-September. Rogue Valley gardens can lose ½ inch of water a day in hot wind (Growing Your Own, p. 21). Apply 1-1.5 in per watering (EC 871, p. 9), use drip lines, and mulch thickly. - Frost pockets: cold air drains to low ground. Plant warm crops on the warmest, sunniest ground you have, and keep row cover or old sheets ready for late-May frosts (🖼 row cover on hoops). - Heat: lettuce, spinach and cabbage-family crops bolt or go bitter in July heat. Grow them in spring and fall, or under shade cloth on the north side of taller crops. - Deer and gophers: a 7-8 ft fence for deer; hardware-cloth bottoms on raised beds or wire baskets around roots for gophers (rule of thumb). - Bugs: encourage beneficial insects rather than spraying (PNW 550). 📚 Go deeper: Growing Your Own - Rogue Valley section, p. 21; Drip Irrigation in the Food Garden; Food Gardening with Less Water; Josephine County soil survey.

❌ Which of your seeds cross - and what to do Plants that are pollinated by insects or wind cross with relatives of the same species flowering nearby (🖼 a bumblebee working a tomato flower). The seed looks fine; the next generation is a mix. Self-pollinating crops rarely cross. ✋ Hand-pollinating and caging Squash, pumpkin and cucumber - save pure seed even when relatives grow nearby (Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 12; 🖼 male and female squash flowers; hand pollination): 1. In the evening, find male and female flowers that will open tomorrow (yellow showing at the tips; the female has a tiny fruit behind the flower). Tape or tie them shut (🖼 taped flowers). 2. Next morning, once the dew is off, pick a male flower, peel back its petals, and rub its pollen onto the center of the opened female - use 2-3 males. 3. Tape the female shut again and tie a tag or yarn on its stem. Save seed only from tagged fruit. Corn: cover young ear shoots with paper bags before silks appear; when silks show, bag a tassel that's shedding pollen, shake the pollen into the bag the next morning, pour it onto the silks and re-bag (OSA sweet corn guide, p. 6; 🖼 bags and tools). Cabbage family, carrots, peppers: cover them with a cage of row cover on hoops (🖼 row cover on hoops). Cabbage-family plants need insects to set seed (they can't pollinate themselves), so put flies or bees in the cage - or alternate-day caging: uncover only one variety each day and cover them all at night (Isolation Distances, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: Cucurbit Seed Production, pp. 12-17; OSA

cage - or alternate-day caging: uncover only one variety each day and cover them all at night (Isolation Distances, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: Cucurbit Seed Production, pp. 12-17; OSA sweet corn hand pollination, pp. 5-8; Isolation Distances - caging, p. 17.

🍅 Saving seed from the fruits Fruit crops have wet seed (seed saving): let the fruit get riper than you'd eat it, scoop out the seeds, clean them, and dry them. (OSA, pp. 15-16, 21-24) Tomatoes - ferment them: 1. Pick fully ripe fruit from several healthy plants of the variety. 2. Squeeze the seeds and juice into a jar; add a little water if thick. Label it. 3. Leave it at about 70-80 °F for 2-3 days, stirring 2-3 times a day. A thin white mold on top is normal (keep stirring so it doesn't take over) - it eats the gel coat that keeps seed from sprouting. Stop before any seed sprouts, and keep it out of high heat (liquid in the high 80s °F can kill half the seed). (Tomato Seed Production, p. 11) 4. Add water and stir: good seed sinks; pour off the mold, pulp and floaters. Rinse in a strainer. 5. Spread thin on a plate or screen to dry (paper towels stick). Ferment, add water, keep what sinks, dry on a plate (a diagram drawn for this guide). Cucumbers: leave the fruit on the vine 4-5 weeks past eating stage, until it's big, yellow to orange-brown and slightly soft. Scrape the seeds and pulp into a jar and ferment about 3 days at 70-75 °F like tomatoes; good seed sinks. (Cucurbit Seed Production,
saving-seed-from-the-fruits

yellow to orange-brown and slightly soft. Scrape the seeds and pulp into a jar and ferment about 3 days at 70-75 °F like tomatoes; good seed sinks. (Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 18) Melons and watermelon: seed is ripe when the fruit is ripe to eat. Scoop the seeds, rinse them in a strainer (watermelon can ferment 2-3 days), and dry. (OSA, pp. 22, 24) Squash and pumpkins: leave on the vine until hard - a thumbnail won't dent it - and the stem dries. Summer squash for seed gets "about the size of your leg." Then store winter squash and pumpkins about 2 months (summer squash a few weeks) before cutting them open: the seed keeps filling out. Scoop, rinse, dry. Ferment no more than a day, if at all. (OSA, p. 24; Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 15) Peppers: pick at full color (red for both kit peppers), hold them 7-10 days at room temperature, then cut them open and scrape out the seeds. Good seed is ivory, not brown. Seed from green peppers often won't sprout. Wear gloves for jalapeños. (OSA, p. 23; Pepper Seed Production, p. 9; 🖼 ways to get the seed out) Eggplant: leave the fruit until it turns dull brown and hard, 2-3 weeks past eating. Grate or blend the seedy end with water; good seed sinks. (OSA, p. 21) Drying all of them: a

🫘 Saving seed from dry crops These dry on the plant; harvest, thresh (beat or stomp the seed out), and winnow (pour in a breeze to blow off chaff). (OSA, pp. 19-24; 🖼 threshing box; 🖼 winnowing in front of a fan) - Beans and peas: let pods dry on the plant; pull plants when 70-80% of pods have turned color and finish drying under cover. Freeze shelled seed 3 days to kill bean weevils. (zine, p. 6) - Lettuce: let a few of the best plants bolt) (don't save from the first to bolt). When heads look fluffy ("feathered"), shake them into a paper bag; repeat a week or two later. In our hot summers, lettuce must flower by May or early June or seed set suffers. (OSA, p. 21; Climatic Considerations - Rogue Valley, p. 21) - Radish: dig the best roots, replant them, and let them flower; harvest when 60-70% of pods are brown and papery. (OSA, p. 23) - Spinach: sow early (it bolts as days lengthen); harvest when most seed is brown. (OSA, p. 23) - Onions and leeks: cut the seed head (umbel) when about a half-dollar-sized patch of black seeds shows; dry 10-14 days on paper. (OSA, p. 22) - Sweet corn: let ears dry on the stalk, rub the kernels off, finish drying below 95 °F. Grow it in a block of

days on paper. (OSA, p. 22) - Sweet corn: let ears dry on the stalk, rub the kernels off, finish drying below 95 °F. Grow it in a block of 100+ plants and save from as many as you can (200 is OSA's minimum, table above) - corn weakens fast when inbred. (zine, p. 9) - Okra: let a few pods dry on the plant until they rattle. - Asparagus: female plants make red berries in fall; mash, rinse and dry the black seeds. 📚 Go deeper: OSA crop-by-crop tips, pp. 19-24; OSA Bean Seed Production; OSA Lettuce Seed Production; OSA Spinach Seed Production.

🥕 Biennials: seed in the second year Carrots, beets, onions, leeks, celery, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, collards, kale, turnips and rutabagas flower only after a winter (biennials; vernalization) - they need 8-12 weeks below 50 °F. (OSA, p. 4) - Leave them in the ground where winters rarely drop below about 14 °F - true for most of the valley, but use well-drained raised beds so roots don't rot, and watch for voles. December-January cold snaps of 5-10 °F still happen some years and kill most biennials: hill soil over them or cover them with row cover (Climatic Considerations, p. 21). - Or dig and store the best roots ("stecklings") at 35-38 °F and high humidity - in moist sand in a root cellar - and replant them in early spring. This lets you choose the best-looking roots. (OSA, p. 4; OSA Carrot Seed Production, p. 7; 🖼 carrot stecklings trimmed for storage) - Carrots for seed: sow in June, not April, so roots are small going into winter (small roots survive cold better). (zine, p. 15) - Cabbage: overwinter a loose, full-size head; in spring cut an X in the top so the flower stalk can get out. Kale and collards: sow June 20-July 15 and overwinter them in place. (OSA, pp. 20-21) - Beets: small roots (1-1.5 in) overwinter best. (OSA Beet Seed Production; 🖼 trimming beet tops)

and collards: sow June 20-July 15 and overwinter them in place. (OSA, pp. 20-21) - Beets: small roots (1-1.5 in) overwinter best. (OSA Beet Seed Production; 🖼 trimming beet tops) Biennials need a winter between the root and the seed: leave them in the bed, or dig the best and replant in spring (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: OSA Carrot Seed Production; OSA Beet Seed Production; Climatic Considerations - Rogue Valley, pp. 20-21.

🌾 Filling the calorie gap This kit is mostly vegetables - vitamins and variety, but not many calories. To live from a garden you also need: - Potatoes - the most food per square foot in this climate. Save your own "seed potatoes": keep healthy, egg-sized tubers cool and dark over winter (rule of thumb). - Dry beans - protein that stores for years. Your Provider and Blue Lake beans can be left to dry and eaten as dry beans. (OSU Preserving Dry Beans) - Winter squash - your butternut and pumpkin store for months. - Flour or flint corn - Golden Bantam is a sweet corn; it dries for parched corn but makes poor meal. - Grains (wheat, oats, barley) and garlic - see the Food From Scratch guide for growing, threshing and milling. 📚 Go deeper: OSU Survival Basics - Food; Growing Your Own - amounts for a family of four, p. 9.

🍎 Fruit trees and berries: seeds don't come true An apple seed grows a new, different apple tree - usually a poor one. Fruit trees are kept true by grafting a twig ("scion") of the variety you want onto a rootstock (🖼 whip-and-tongue graft, step by step). (Univ. of Minnesota Grafting and Budding; Univ. of Kentucky, p. 1) - Grow rootstocks from seed: apple and pear seeds need 70-90 days cold and moist) (in damp sand or a damp paper towel in a sealed bag in the fridge); peach 90-120 days. Then plant them; graft when the seedling is about pencil-thick. (Mississippi State Basic Grafting, p. 3) - Collect scionwood while trees are dormant (here, January-February, before buds swell): last year's growth, pencil-thick, a foot or more long. Wrap in damp (not wet) paper towel or sawdust in a sealed bag, label it, and keep it at 34-38 °F. Never store scions with apples or pears - the gas they give off ruins them. (Mississippi State, p. 3; Kentucky, p. 4; 🖼 scion wood ready for storage) - When to graft: whip-and-tongue Feb-early March while dormant; cleft graft late Feb-March (🖼 cleft graft); bark graft in spring once the bark slips (🖼 bark graft). Budding (a single bud under the bark) in July-September. (Mississippi State, pp. 3-4; USDA FB 1567, p. 43; 🖼 T-budding) - Peaches and apricots from seed
fruit-trees-and-berries-seeds-don-t-come-true

slips (🖼 bark graft). Budding (a single bud under the bark) in July-September. (Mississippi State, pp. 3-4; USDA FB 1567, p. 43; 🖼 T-budding) - Peaches and apricots from seed often give usable fruit, but not the same as the parent (rule of thumb). - Berries and grapes are easier: - Raspberries and blackberries: bury a cane tip in late summer - it roots ("tip layering") - or dig suckers. (Virginia Tech, p. 4; 🖼 tip layering; Layering) - Strawberries: root the runners. (Virginia Tech, p. 5) - Grapes: dormant hardwood cuttings. (USDA Grape Propagation; 🖼 heeling in cuttings) - Currants, gooseberries, apple rootstocks: mound or stool layering. (Virginia Tech, p. 5; 🖼 mound layering) Whip-and-tongue graft: cut both pieces alike, lock the tongues together with the inner bark lined up on at least one side, then wrap (USDA FB 1567, p. 35). Budding (July-September): slip one bud from the variety under a T-cut in the rootstock's bark and tie it in (USDA FB 1567, p. 44). Grape cuttings tied in bundles and buried in a trench until spring planting (USDA FB 471, p. 5). 📚 Go deeper: Mississippi State Basic Grafting Techniques - illustrated step by step; Univ. of Kentucky Budding and Grafting; USDA Propagation of Trees and Shrubs; OSU Growing Tree Fruits and Nuts; PNW Training and Pruning.

Seasons, hunting units, local waters and trapping rules are on Illinois Valley - Start Here. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Be sure of your target and what is beyond it. Bullets pass through game and keep killing. Never shoot at a sound, a color or movement. - Cook all wild meat through. Bear, cougar, raccoon and beaver can carry trichinella worms that survive freezing, smoking and drying. - Wear gloves to skin rabbits, rodents, beaver and anything with fleas (tularemia, plague). Never shoot a deer or elk that looks sick, and never eat its brain, spine, eyes or lymph nodes. - Check every trap every day at first light. 🌱 Take the surplus, never the seed Every year a wild population has two parts. The breeding stock is what the land can carry through the hard season. The surplus is the animals that will die anyway before next year's young are born. Take the surplus and the land feeds you again next year. Take the breeding stock and it doesn't (NY trapper manual, p. 13). Game laws were written to do exactly this, after the last time it went wrong. While ODFW and the state police still work, follow the rules. If enforcement stops, the reasons don't: - Elk nearly vanished from our forest. In 1910 the Forest Service called elk "very scarce" on the Siskiyou National Forest, and in 1932 it counted about 40. Elk mate in October, calve in June, and have one calf, so a shot-out herd takes decades to recover (Bailey 1936, p. 114; p. 115). - Deer: "unrestricted hunting soon cleans out the deer." Keep no more than about 5 does per buck. If does aren't each raising their usual two fawns, there are too few bucks or too many predators (Bailey, p. 120; written for mule deer, but it holds for blacktails). - Spare the hens. "Adult hens are the backbone of Oregon's forest grouse flocks." They are most exposed early in the season while tending chicks. Spring turkey is one bearded bird

Spare the hens. "Adult hens are the backbone of Oregon's forest grouse flocks." They are most exposed early in the season while tending chicks. Spring turkey is one bearded bird only, because hens are nesting (ODFW bird regs, p. 32; p. 24). - Let small fish go. Fit traps with escape gaps (🖼 drawing). A gill net's mesh should be about 0.4 × the girth of the fish you want; smaller mesh kills young fish before they spawn (FAO, p. 24; Twinework, p. 64). - Lost gear keeps killing for days or months, and nylon nets never rot. Mark and anchor gear, and tie one panel with cotton or plant twine that rots away (FAO, p. 59; Twinework, p. 41). - The Hupa weir. On the Trinity River, about 70 miles south, Hupa families built a salmon weir in late summer, fished it at night, and kept family fishing spots that were "always respected." The first high water swept it away (Goddard 1903, p. 34; p. 36). A weir left across a whole river all season would take the whole run. Leave gaps, and fish only part of each night and part of the run (general practice). Illinois River coho are federally threatened. 📚 Go deeper: NY trapper manual, p. 13 - surplus and carrying capacity; Bailey, p. 120 - how deer herds were shot out; Goddard, p. 34 -

🎯 Safe shooting, shot placement and tracking The four rules (Hunter ed, p. 40): 1. Point the muzzle in a safe direction. 2. Treat every gun as loaded. 3. Be sure of your target and what is in front of it and beyond it. 4. Finger off the trigger until you are ready to shoot. Shot placement (Hunter ed, p. 61; CT DEEP, p. 3; 🖼 where the organs lie in deer, elk, bear and small game): - Big game: heart and lungs, just behind the front shoulder, broadside. With a bow, a third of the way up the chest when the near leg is forward. - Never take head-on, rear-end, running or straight-away shots. A wounded, stressed animal suffers, and its meat tastes stronger. - Turkey (🖼 gobbler and hen): head and neck. Rabbits and squirrels: head or chest (Ohio DNR, p. 2). Oregon's legal minimums are also humane-kill minimums: no .22 rimfire on deer, elk or bear; broadheads unbarbed and at least 7/8 in wide; bows at least 40 lb draw (ODFW big game regs, p. 22). Not a law, but keep bow shots to 40 yards or less (Hunter ed, p. 70). After the shot (Hunter ed, pp. 62-63): 1. Watch every move the animal makes after the shot. Wait 30-60 minutes unless it is down in sight. 2. Follow blood, hair, kicked leaves and broken twigs.
safe-shooting-shot-placement-and-tracking

pp. 62-63): 1. Watch every move the animal makes after the shot. Wait 30-60 minutes unless it is down in sight. 2. Follow blood, hair, kicked leaves and broken twigs. Wounded animals often head downhill toward water. Flag the trail; if you lose it, search in a circle or grid. 3. Approach from above and behind the head. If the open eye doesn't blink when touched with a stick, it is dead. 📚 Go deeper: Hunter ed manual, p. 61 - shot angles with drawings; Big Game Recovery - reading blood sign; CT DEEP - vital zones.

🔪 Field dressing and the gutless method Field dressing (PNW 517, pp. 7-8; Hunter ed, p. 64; 🖼 step drawings; 🖼 step photos): 1. Prop the animal on its back with its head slightly downhill. 2. Cut the hide from the inside out, so hair stays off the meat. Open the belly without cutting the stomach (rumen). 3. Cut the diaphragm and the windpipe. Tie off the colon before you pull it through. 4. Don't touch the dark-haired glands inside the hind legs, just below the hock. They taint the meat. 5. Drain the blood. If you must drag it, sew the cavity shut. Gutless method) - best on steep ground, alone, or in hot weather (Kentucky, p. 1; PNW 517, pp. 9-10; 🖼 illustrated steps): 1. Skin the top side. Take off the front shoulder (no joint holds it on) and the hindquarter. 2. Take the backstrap and neck meat. Ease the tenderloins out last, without nicking the gut. 3. Flip the animal and repeat. You never open the body or saw the spine, which also avoids the spinal cord (chronic wasting disease). Drag the gut pile at least 25 ft from where you hang the meat (PNW 517, p. 11). 📚 Go deeper: OSU PNW 517 Big Game from Hunt to Home - dressing and quartering with photos; Kentucky gutless method; Kentucky elk quartering.

🌡 Cooling meat in our heat Heat is the enemy. Cave Junction's summer average is 67 °F and Grants Pass has hit 108 °F (Josephine soil survey, p. 5), and archery deer season falls in late August and September. - Get the meat below 40 °F within 24 hours (PNW 517, p. 6). - Hang it in a shady thicket at night. By day, wrap it in cold canvas and lay sleeping bags over it to hold the night's chill. Skin the carcass unless the night will freeze (Montana State, p. 2). - Don't wrap warm meat. Game bags, canvas and paper hold heat in. Keep it in moving air until it is below 40 °F (PNW 517, p. 11). - Meat from a warm day, or from an animal that ran hard or was wounded, should not be aged. Cut it up and preserve it as soon as it is chilled. - Scrape off blowfly egg clusters. Black pepper on moist spots and flapping cloth strips keep flies and ravens off (p. 12). - Birds: keep them at 40 °F or below (NDSU game birds, p. 2). - With no refrigerator, cut and preserve meat the same day: can it, cure it in winter, or make safe jerky (see the Preserving Food guide). 📚 Go deeper: PNW 517, p. 11 - cooling, game bags and flies; Montana State Field

🥩 Butchering, using the whole animal, and hides Bone it out (Wyoming B-884R, p. 2; p. 4): - Take the shoulder off along its natural seam, then the loin. Follow the hind leg's muscle seams into the sirloin tip, top, bottom and eye of round (🖼 photos of each cut). - Grind the tough heel and trimmings, and preserve trimmings the day you cut them. - A 349-lb field-dressed cow elk gave 148 lb of boneless meat, about 42%. Use the whole animal: - Heart, liver, tongue and kidneys are good. Wash the heart and liver in cold water at once (PNW 517, p. 12). A healthy liver is smooth, wet and deep red-purple. Throw out a spotted or odd-colored liver; the muscle meat may still be fine (general practice). - Beaver, muskrat and raccoon are good eating: the quarters and back. The rib cage is usually discarded (Trapper Education Manual, p. 106; FM 3-05.70, p. 153). - Save the fat. People living on lean meat alone get sick ("rabbit starvation," (rule of thumb); see the Rabbits guide). Brain-tanned buckskin), no chemicals (Farnham 1916, pp. 73-74; brain tanning)): 1. Soak the hide in water, or water and wood ashes, until the hair slips. Flesh it, then scrape off the hair and grain (🖼 unhairing). 2. Boil the brains about an hour in a gallon of water. Cool until you can

the hair slips. Flesh it, then scrape off the hair and grain (🖼 unhairing). 2. Boil the brains about an hour in a gallon of water. Cool until you can hold your hand in it. 3. Work the hide in it, and stretch it while it dries. Repeat until soft (🖼 softening over a stake). 4. Smoke it over smoldering punky wood, never flame (p. 145). Use brains only from healthy animals, and wear gloves (chronic wasting disease). Bark tanning one heavy cowhide takes well over 100 lb of finely ground oak or hemlock bark, added 30-40 lb at a time over about 4 months (USDA FB 1334, p. 14); our tanoak was the old "tanbark" (general practice). 🪤 Trapping, snaring and deadfalls Where you set matters more than the trap (FM 3-05.70, pp. 127-128): - Set on a run (small, used by one species) or at feeding, watering and bedding spots. A trail is used by many species. - Funnel the run with sticks down to just wider than the animal (🖼 drawing). Don't use freshly cut green wood, which smells of sap. Hide your scent with mud or smoke. - A squirrel pole carries several wire nooses 2-2¼ in across, set 1 in off the pole (p. 132; 🖼 drawing). Check current ODFW rules first: western gray and Douglas squirrels are protected game in Oregon. Traps with no store-bought gear: the figure-4 and Paiute deadfalls need only sticks and cord (FM 3-05.70, p. 137; 🖼 Paiute deadfall). Harding's 1907 Deadfalls and Snares shows many more (🖼 spring-pole snare, 🖼 trail snares). A box trap keeps rabbits unhurt ("the best for eating") and lets you release a cat, dog or hen unharmed (p. 146; 🖼 drawing). Figure-4 deadfall: where the notches go on the upright, release and bait sticks, and the set trap holding up a log (FM 3-05.70, p. 137). Paiute deadfall: a cord and a 2-inch catch stick hold the diagonal stick; when the animal moves the bait stick, the weight falls (circles: close-ups of the catch) (FM 3-05.70, p. 138). Check every trap every

2-inch catch stick hold the diagonal stick; when the animal moves the bait stick, the weight falls (circles: close-ups of the catch) (FM 3-05.70, p. 138). Check every trap every day, at first light. Most furbearers move at night. Early checks mean less suffering, fewer escapes and less theft by other animals. Don't set more traps than you can check, and stay away from places where pets roam (Trapper Education Manual, p. 99; NY manual, p. 3). Keeping pets out (AFWA body-grip guide, pp. 9, 15-16): - For raccoon, use sweet baits (marshmallow, molasses, corn syrup, corn) that dogs and cats ignore, not meat or fish. - Raise body-grip cubbies 4-6 ft up a tree (🖼 cubby on a tree). - Set trail traps 5-6 ft in front of a fence crossing, not under it, so big dogs pass by (🖼 trail-set drawings). Beaver: #330 body-grip traps or cable devices at slides, scent mounds and channels. Bait with fresh poplar, willow or cottonwood sticks. Use sliding-lock sets in water so the beaver drowns quickly (Trapper Education Manual, p. 138). 📚 Go deeper: Trapper Education Manual - sets, baits and running a trapline; Harding Deadfalls and Snares - illustrated improvised traps; AFWA dog-friendly sets - keeping pets safe.

🎣 Fishing, nets, fish traps and fish care While the rules are enforced (ODFW fishing regs, p. 19): one rod per person, lines closely attended (so no unattended set lines), and no snagging. Local waters and seasons are on Start Here. Nets and stream traps (AFH 10-644, pp. 311, 314): - Set a gill net at a slight angle to the current so debris washes off (🖼 drawing). Check it at least twice a day. - In small streams, a brush or stake fence that funnels fish into a pen works. Leave a way through for most of the run (general practice) (🖼 fish-trap layouts; 🖼 maze traps). - Nets are knotted with the sheet bend, using a netting needle (🖼 drawing) and mesh gauge (🖼 drawing) (Twinework, p. 46). A fyke net (a netting hoop trap with wings) is the river version of a fish trap (p. 137). A gill net seen from above, set at a slant to the current (arrow) so drifting debris slides off (FM 3-05.70, p. 145). A basket trap and a stake pen whose funnel mouth faces the current; the stone tidal-flat trap is for the coast (FM 3-05.70, p. 146). Fish care (NDSU, p. 2; NYSDEC, p. 4): 1. Bleed the fish by cutting the throat. Pull the gills and guts (🖼 filleting drawing). 2. Scrape out the dark kidney along the backbone.

p. 2; NYSDEC, p. 4): 1. Bleed the fish by cutting the throat. Pull the gills and guts (🖼 filleting drawing). 2. Scrape out the dark kidney along the backbone. Wipe it and keep it cold. 3. Don't let cleaned fish sit warm more than 2 hours. 4. Contaminants collect in fat: skin the fish and trim the fat (🖼 where to trim). Smoke alone does not preserve fish. Hot-smoked fish must reach 150 °F inside (160 °F better) for 30 minutes, and still keeps only in a refrigerator (PNW 238, pp. 1-2). Without one, can it or salt it (see the Preserving Food guide). Mercury: Oregon has a statewide mercury advisory on bass, and Applegate Lake has one for resident fish. Sea-run salmon and steelhead carry fewer local contaminants. Children under 6 and pregnant or nursing women should eat the fewest resident fish (ODFW fishing regs, p. 24). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Twinework - making and mending nets by hand; FAO Fishing with Traps and Pots - funnels, doors and escape gaps; NYSDEC Care of Your Catch - cleaning and filleting.

🦞 Crawfish, mussels and lamprey - Crawfish (signal crayfish) come out at night. By day, look under stream stones. They grab offal tied on a string; pull them in before they let go. Cook all freshwater shellfish and fish (FM 3-05.70, p. 118). While the rules stand: open all year, no license, by hand, line with no hook, net, ring or trap, 100 a day (ODFW fishing regs, p. 22). - Freshwater mussels are famine food only. Some, like the western pearlshell (🖼 shells), live over 100 years. About 1 in 100,000,000 larvae becomes a young mussel, and the larvae must ride on salmon or trout to survive (🖼 life-cycle drawing). A bed stripped bare does not come back in a lifetime (Xerces, p. 12; p. 18). Taking them is illegal while the rules stand. - Pacific lamprey: leave it to the tribes (🖼 photo on the ODFW Rogue fishes poster). The Hupa netted lamprey on warm spring nights and dried them over the fire (Goddard, p. 35). Tribes still prize it as food and medicine, but it is in steep decline (PLCI fact sheet, p. 1), and Oregon allows it only by tribal or Willamette Falls permit (ODFW, p. 22). 📚 Go deeper: Xerces Freshwater Mussels of the PNW - ID and why beds don't recover; PLCI fact sheet - lamprey and the tribes.

☣ Disease and safety Trichinella in bear, cougar, raccoon and beaver: wild strains survive freezing (larvae lived 5 years in frozen bear meat), and curing, smoking and drying don't reliably kill them. Cook it through (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 142; NY manual, p. 26). Jerky is safe only if the meat reaches 160 °F (PNW 632, p. 8). Tularemia (rabbit fever) comes from rabbits, hares, beaver and muskrat, and from ticks and deer flies. An infected liver and spleen have white spots. As few as 10 bacteria breathed in can infect you, so don't make dust or spray while skinning. Wear gloves and cook thoroughly (Trapper Education Manual, p. 92; Bad Bug Book, p. 64). It needs antibiotics for 10-21 days, depending on the drug (doxycycline 14-21) (CDC, p. 34). Chronic wasting disease isn't in Oregon yet but is in California, Idaho and Washington. Never shoot or eat a deer or elk that looks sick. Never eat the brain, eyes, spinal cord, spleen or lymph nodes. Bone out the meat, and soak tools in half bleach, half water for an hour (ODFW big game regs, p. 48; Hunter ed, p. 65; Kentucky elk guide, p. 2). Ticks: the western blacklegged tick (Lyme disease) lives here (🖼 tick photos and sizes). Soft ticks in rodent nests in rustic cabins spread relapsing fever, in the hills above about 1,500 ft. Pull

blacklegged tick (Lyme disease) lives here (🖼 tick photos and sizes). Soft ticks in rodent nests in rustic cabins spread relapsing fever, in the hills above about 1,500 ft. Pull a tick with fine tweezers close to the skin, straight up, no twisting, no heat or petroleum jelly (🖼 removal photos). Treat clothing with permethrin (CDC, p. 50; ODFW fishing regs, p. 15). Grip the tick right at the skin with fine tweezers and pull straight up, with no twisting, heat or petroleum jelly (a diagram drawn for this guide). Plague): southern Oregon is one of the two US plague regions. Its main flea lives on the California ground squirrel, and a trapper caught plague from a cut while skinning a bobcat. Bag any flea-covered catch at once, spray insecticide in the bag and tie it shut (Plague in Washington, p. 4; Trapper Education Manual, p. 102). Hantavirus comes from deer mice. Never sweep or vacuum droppings. Soak them in 1 part bleach to 9 parts water for 5 minutes, then wipe up with gloves (🖼 cleanup steps). Use snap traps, not live or glue traps (CDC 2021, pp. 11-12). Lead: fast-expanding lead bullets threw fragments 5-14 in from the exit hole, and lead turned up 18 in away. Rinsing didn't help. A solid copper bullet left few fragments, mostly within about 4 in. Trim wide, throw out bloodshot or

exit hole, and lead turned up 18 in away. Rinsing didn't help. A solid copper bullet left few fragments, mostly within about 4 in. Trim wide, throw out bloodshot or bone-flecked meat, and grind one animal at a time (Minnesota DNR, p. 6; PNW 517, p. 1). Give lead-shot meat to adults, not children or pregnant women (general practice). Coastal clams and mussels: paralytic shellfish toxin and domoic acid aren't destroyed by cooking or freezing, and there's no antidote. Numb lips or tingling hands within hours means get help. With no state testing, leave coastal shellfish alone (ODA, p. 1; OHA, p. 1). Cold rivers: the Illinois and Rogue stay dangerously cold even in summer. Sudden cold water causes gasping (cold shock) and drowning, and water drains body heat 25 times faster than air. Strainers (logjams, overhanging branches) pin people under (OSMB handbook, p. 17; p. 14). 📚 Go deeper: CDC Tickborne Diseases - tick ID, symptoms and treatment; Minnesota Bullet Fragmentation - the X-rays; OHA PSP sheet - symptoms that mean get help now; Field Care guide - treating illness with no doctor.

⚠ Old advice in the library to ignore - "You can eat these raw" for sea fish caught far offshore, and "there are no poisonous freshwater fish" (FM 3-05.70, p. 121). Ocean fish commonly carry worms, and mercury advisories apply here. Instead: cook all fish. - Poisoning fish with rotenone plants, lime or walnut husks (FM 3-05.70, pp. 148-150; AFH 10-644, p. 315). It kills every fish, the young salmon and the insects they eat, and ruins a stream for years. Never do it. - Bow traps and pig-spear traps (FM 3-05.70, pp. 138-140), which the manual itself calls deadly to people. Instead: snares, deadfalls and box traps, never near homes, trails or where children walk. - Smoked meat eaten "without further cooking," eating the brain (FM 3-05.70, p. 154), and sun-dried raw strips (p. 156). Smoked or dried bear still carries trichinella, and deer and elk brain carries chronic wasting disease risk. Instead: cook it through; jerky reaches 160 °F. - Ixodes dammini as the Lyme tick (Trapper Education Manual, p. 92), an old eastern name. Ours is the western blacklegged tick, Ixodes pacificus (CDC, p. 4). - A "minimum" 4-inch trim around the bullet path (PNW 517, p. 1; also repeated on the Start Here page). Instead: trim much wider; fragments went 5-14 in (Minnesota DNR, p. 6). - Aging birds at 40-45 °F (Wyoming waterfowl sheet, p.

1; also repeated on the Start Here page). Instead: trim much wider; fragments went 5-14 in (Minnesota DNR, p. 6). - Aging birds at 40-45 °F (Wyoming waterfowl sheet, p. 1). That is above the danger line. Instead: 40 °F or below (NDSU, p. 2). - Arsenic sprayed on hides (Farnham, p. 64), plus the book's chrome (bichromate) and sulfuric acid tanning. These are poisons. 🍄 Mushroom Guide How to identify, use, preserve and grow mushrooms in the Illinois Valley - and how not to die doing it. The field guides, poisoning reports and growing manuals are in Mushrooms\ (Identification, Poisoning-Safety, Uses-Growing-Preserving). Wild-Plants\ also has the Forest Service Wild Edible Mushrooms of the Pacific Northwest and death cap ID sheets. ### ⚠ The rules that keep foragers alive 1. Only eat a mushroom you have identified with complete certainty - every feature, including the spore print and the base of the stem. "Pretty sure" is how people die. 2. No folk test works. Silver turning dark, a peeling cap, animals or insects eating it, soaking in salt water, cooking - none of these tell you anything. Cooking, drying, freezing and canning do not destroy the deadly toxins. (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 218) 3. The deadliest ones taste fine and make you sick late - 6 to 24 hours or more after eating. By then the toxin is already in your liver or kidneys. 4. Dig up the whole mushroom - the cup or bulb at the base is what tells you it's a deadly Amanita. Never eat unopened "buttons" of gilled mushrooms; nobody can tell a deadly button from a safe one. (USDA FB 796, pp. 3, 6) 5. Cook every wild mushroom thoroughly. Try a small amount of any new kind, eat in

tell a deadly button from a safe one. (USDA FB 796, pp. 3, 6) 5. Cook every wild mushroom thoroughly. Try a small amount of any new kind, eat in moderation, and keep one uncooked specimen in the fridge in case someone gets sick. (PNW/BC White Paper, p. 10)

🔎 How to identify a mushroom 📷 Have a photo? The plant and mushroom identifier (🔧 Tools tab) suggests names and flags deadly groups. Never eat a mushroom on its word: confirm every feature below, with a spore print. Check all of these, every time: - Underside: gills (thin blades), pores (a sponge of tubes - boletes), teeth or spines (hedgehogs), or blunt ridges (chanterelles). (See gills); 🖼 labeled drawing of the parts; 🖼 gills, pores, ring and cup.) - Stem base: dig it up. A cup (volva) or bulb at the base, plus a ring on the stem and white gills, means Amanita - leave all of them alone. (FB 796) (See volva) and ring); 🖼 a death cap dug up, showing both; 🖼 the "egg" the cup comes from.) - Spore print: cut off the stem of a mature cap, lay the cap gills-down on half white, half dark paper, cover with a glass, and wait a few hours. The color (white, pink, brown, rusty, purple-black) places the mushroom in its family. Without a hospital, expect the worst. When did the symptoms start? 🚑 If someone may have eaten a bad mushroom - Get medical help immediately, even if they feel fine - the dangerous ones are delayed. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222. - Bring the mushroom - leftovers, the uncooked ones, even scraps from the trash - in a paper bag (they rot in plastic). A photo is far less useful than a sample. (White Paper, p. 6; Michigan sheet, p. 2) - The main hospital treatment for amatoxin is aggressive IV fluids - NAMA calls it "by far the best single intervention" (NAMA 2018-20, p. 4; CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3). Liver drugs such as silibinin (from milk thistle) are tried, but proof is thin. Sources disagree on activated charcoal: FDA lists it as part of prompt treatment (Bad Bug Book, p. 229), CDC says it has no proven benefit for amatoxin, and NAMA says it's useless more than about 1 hour after eating. With no hospital: replace fluids constantly (oral rehydration solution - see the Medical guides), give activated charcoal only if they ate the mushroom within the last hour or so, and rest. Survival odds are much worse without a hospital - which is why rule 1 matters so much. - Don't be fooled by the false recovery. 🫙 Cooking, drying and storing - Cook all wild mushrooms - never raw, and morels especially well done. Don't mix alcohol with morels the first time (some people react). - Eat a few mouthfuls, not a plateful, of any wild mushroom, and not several days running - big servings cause reactions even with "safe" kinds like morels (White Paper, pp. 10-11). In 1991, 77 of 483 guests at a Vancouver banquet got sick from morels served raw (p. 10). - Fresh storage: in the refrigerator (40 °F or colder) in a paper bag - CDC's advice for morels (CDC 2024, p. 5). Don't freeze them raw - bacteria keep growing (NAMA 2018-20, p. 2). - Dry slices about ½ inch thick at about 120 °F with good airflow (dehydrator) until crisp; morels lose about 90% of their weight. Store airtight. Rehydrate in hot water. Ventilate while drying - spores can trigger asthma. (OSU SP 50-919, p. 2; USFS PNW-GTR-710, pp. 66-67) - No dehydrator? In warm, dry weather, dry on screens, threaded on fishing line, or in a single layer on a tarp, turning them; or use the warm air near a wood stove with a fan. Moving dry air matters more than heat - don't go over 120 °F (GTR-710, pp. 66-67). Shiitake dried in sunlight gain vitamin D; 7 lb fresh makes about 1 lb dried (Agroforestry Note

matters more than heat - don't go over 120 °F (GTR-710, pp. 66-67). Shiitake dried in sunlight gain vitamin D; 7 lb fresh makes about 1 lb dried (Agroforestry Note 13, p. 4). - Freeze after sautéing (best) or steam-blanching. To steam: soak 5 minutes in 1 teaspoon lemon juice per pint of water, then steam whole 5 minutes, quarters 3½, slices 3, cool in ice water, pack and freeze (OSU SP 50-919, p. 2). - Never can wild mushrooms - only store-type button mushrooms have tested canning times (OSU SP 50-919, p. 1). Improperly canned chanterelles gave diners botulism in Vancouver in 1987 (White Paper, p. 10). - Recipes from the old books - fine for cooking ideas once the mushroom is safely identified: McIlvaine's 15-page recipe chapter (p. 813), Mrs. Rorer's recipes in Atkinson (p. 379), Gibson (p. 321) and Thomas (p. 381). 🪵 Growing your own - Shiitake on logs: fresh hardwood logs (oak is among the best) 4-6 inches across, cut in the dormant season while the bark is tight. Drill holes 7/16 inch wide, 1¼ inches deep, 3 inches apart in a diamond pattern, plug with spawn, seal with wax (🖼 drill, plug, wax). Keep shaded and moist. Mushrooms start in 6-18 months; after that, soak a log 24 hours and it fruits about a week later. Rest logs 8-12 weeks between soaks. (UVM/Cornell, p. 20; USDA Agroforestry Note 13, p. 3) - Oysters on straw: chop straw 4-5 inches, soak overnight, pasteurize at 165 °F for 1-2 hours, mix in 5-10% spawn, pack into bags with holes, keep warm and humid. Fruits in weeks. (UF IFAS SS662, p. 2; 🖼 step-by-step photos) - Keep your strain going: a piece of a fruiting log or colonized straw can start the next batch, so you don't need to buy spawn again. Shiitake details: - Logs: 3-8 inches across and 2-4 feet long. A 4-foot, 8-inch log can weigh 80 lb. Cut from live trees roughly Thanksgiving to St. Patrick's Day, and inoculate within two weeks (Agroforestry Note 13, pp. 2-3). - Hole spacing: the sources differ - Cornell says 3 inches apart with as many rows as the log has inches of diameter (p. 20); the USDA note says 6 inches

Hole spacing: the sources differ - Cornell says 3 inches apart with as many rows as the log has inches of diameter (p. 20); the USDA note says 6 inches apart with one row fewer (p. 3). Either way, stagger the rows in a diamond pattern. - Spawn: one 5-lb bag of sawdust spawn does about 20-25 logs 4-6 inches by 3 feet (Cornell-UVM, p. 21). - Laying yard (🖼 ways to stack logs): 75-100% shade all year - under conifers is best; the north side of a house or shed works for a few logs. Keep logs above 30% moisture; in a dry spell soak them a few hours or sprinkle them (Cornell-UVM, p. 23). - Harvest when caps are 60-75% open, edge still slightly curled under (Agroforestry Note 13, p. 4; Cornell-UVM, p. 39). Logs keep producing for up to 6 years; about 10 logs feed a family. - Check every brown mushroom on your logs. Deadly Galerina can pop up on shiitake logs. Make a spore print: shiitake is white, Galerina brown; shiitake never has a ring (Cornell-UVM, p. 41; 🖼 Galerina photo; Galerina vs. shiitake photos). Cornell's spacing: holes 7/16 in wide and 1¼ in deep, 3 in apart, rows staggered into diamonds, one row per inch of log width; the USDA note spaces them 6 in (a diagram drawn for this guide). 🌿 Medicinal mushrooms Turkey tail, reishi, lion's mane and shiitake have real research behind them as add-ons to treatment - turkey-tail extract (PSK) is a prescribed cancer add-on in Japan - but most evidence is from lab and animal studies. They are not cures. Turkey tail and reishi are traditionally simmered for hours as tea. (VA Mycomedicinals, pp. 1-3) - Making the tea: simmering or boiling in water for 20 minutes to 2 hours breaks down the tough cell walls and releases the active compounds (VA, p. 1). - Who should be careful: people with leukemia or lymphoma, after a bone-marrow transplant, or on drugs that suppress the immune system - these mushrooms act on the immune system (VA, p. 3). - No panacea: in one mouse study a reishi extract made tumors grow faster (GTR-309, p. 31). 📚 Go deeper: VA Mycomedicinals - what the research shows for turkey tail, reishi, lion's mane and shiitake; Agroforestry Note 13 - growing lion's mane on logs.The old mushroom books here (1895-1928) are great for pictures, descriptions and recipes, but some of their safety advice is wrong and has killed people: Marshall's Mushroom Book lists false morels as edible, Thomas says the parasol has no poisonous look-alike, and USDA FB 796 recommends raw mushrooms and old first aid. 🌰 Skills of the Valley's First Peoples How the peoples of this corner of Oregon and California lived well here for thousands of years, as how-to for a household with no stores: food through the year and how to keep it, fibers and baskets, houses and fire, tools, tending the land with fire, and the community ways that kept people fed and at peace. The skills come from the Takelma, whose country reached "perhaps as far west as Illinois river" (Sapir, p. 3); the Athabaskan-speaking peoples of Galice Creek and the Applegate (Sapir, p. 4); the Shasta of the upper Rogue (Kroeber, p. 344); and the Karuk, Hupa, Yurok and Tolowa to the south. No book here names the people of the upper Illinois Valley itself. These are living nations: after the wars of the 1850s the Takelma were moved to the Siletz reservation (Sapir, p. 7), and the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians, Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde, Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians, Karuk Tribe and Tolowa Dee-niʼ Nation still gather, weave and burn today (NRCS Beargrass, p. 4; KBO, p. 8). This guide covers everyday skills, not ceremonies. Dig only plants you marked while they bloomed blue. - Leach every acorn until sweet; tannin is "deleterious to health" (Chesnut, p. 349). Cook every elderberry (OSU, p. 4). - Never eat raw buckeye (Chesnut, p. 384), yew or dogbane (AIB 415, pp. 50, 113), fresh iris roots (NRCS Douglas Iris, p. 1) or carrot-family roots: water hemlock kills (PNW 109, p. 1). - Poison oak's oil is in every part, even in winter, and its smoke has put people in intensive care (OSU PNW 108, pp. 2, 4). Learn it before you gather, weave or burn. - Most old ways of taking salmon and deer are illegal today: weirs, nets, spears, snares, dogs, fire drives (ODFW, p. 21; ODFW Big Game, p. 21). They are here so the knowledge survives. - No burning in fire season. The Karuk burned "in the fall before it starts in to rain" (Harrington, p. 116); now burn only outside fire season, on burn days (DEQ, p. 1), small, with experienced people and a fire line (KBO, pp. 43-44). - Never dig old village sites or graves, or carry off mortars, points or bones. with experienced people and a fire line (KBO, pp. 43-44). - Never dig old village sites or graves, or carry off mortars, points or bones. Graves and sacred objects are protected on any land, and artifacts on public land (ODFW Today's Hunter, p. 33). - Take what you need and leave the plant alive: "You never over-take anything from any of the plants and trees" (NRCS Beargrass, p. 5).

🗓 The year's round People moved with the food: a winter house in the valley, summer camps in the hills, and stores for the cold months.
