🌰 Acorns: from tree to mush The modern short method is "Acorn flour" in Food from Scratch; here is the local way. Which oaks: tanoak was "most esteemed" (Goddard, p. 37) and bears some crop every year, over 200 lb on one tree (NRCS tanoak, p. 1). Black oak was the Shasta's first choice, then Oregon white oak (Dixon, p. 51), whose mush is "more slimy" (p. 54) and which ripens in one year, August-November (NRCS Oregon Oak, p. 1). Canyon live oak is "poisonous when raw" and needs "more washing" (Chesnut, p. 355). How many: "some 400 or 500 pounds" was a family's "year's supply" (Chesnut, p. 348); the NRCS says 500 to 2,000 lb (tanoak, p. 1). A 150-year-old black oak gives about 100 lb in a medium crop (PSW-GTR-185, p. 16), so 500 lb is five big black oaks (arithmetic). Acorns lack protein (Chesnut, p. 347): add salmon or meat. 1. Gather soon after they fall; the first drops are often "unsound because of insects, immaturity" (PSW-GTR-185, p. 16). 2. Dry them in the sun ("The roof of the house is often used", Goddard, p. 37); store them "in the shell, in large baskets" under an upturned basket (Kroeber, p. 126), safe from mold and "robbing squirrels" (NRCS tanoak, p. 1). 3. Shell them on a rock, tapping with a stone, and dry the meats again (Goddard,
acorns-from-tree-to-mush

basket (Kroeber, p. 126), safe from mold and "robbing squirrels" (NRCS tanoak, p. 1). 3. Shell them on a rock, tapping with a stone, and dry the meats again (Goddard, p. 37); rub off the thin inner skin by hand, a step "often overlooked" (Kroeber, p. 351). 4. Pound on a flat stone set in the floor, inside a bottomless basket hopper "wider at the top and entirely open at the bottom" (Sapir, p. 9), held down by your legs over its rim; lift the pestle with the wrist turned and let it fall straight (Kroeber, p. 125). Grind to powder: oily meal won't leach otherwise (Chesnut, p. 349). 5. Sift on a tilted, shallow basket; pound the coarse bits again (Goddard, p. 38). Pounding acorns: the seated woman's legs hold the basket hopper down over its rim (Kroeber, p. 690).
acorns-from-tree-to-mush

Leaching in a sand basin 1. Scoop a saucer in clean sand and build up the rim (Goddard, p. 38). The Shasta raised theirs 6-12 in off the ground on sticks and pine needles (Dixon, p. 53). 2. Spread the meal about 2 in thick (same page); lay a cedar sprig or small tule mat on top so pouring doesn't scour it (Chesnut, p. 350). 3. Pour on water "nearly scalding hot", gently: "As fast as it soaks away more water is added until the material loses its bitter taste" (Goddard, p. 38); "A couple of hours are usually required" (Chesnut, p. 349). Use clean, safe water (KBO, p. 9). Taste it: done is sweet, with no bitterness or pucker. 4. Slap your palm onto the drained dough, lift it, and wash the sand off its underside in warm water (Dixon, pp. 53-54). Dried, the dough stores and was traded to "the Rogue River people" (p. 54). Leaching in sand: the meal is the pale patch in the basin; stones from the fire heat the basket of water poured over it (Kroeber, p. 117).
leaching-in-a-sand-basin

Stone-boiling mush and baking bread 1. Pick stones that "did not splinter or disintegrate when heated and suddenly cooled" (Dixon, p. 54). Never heat wet or porous river rocks; they can burst (rule of thumb). Rinse off the ash; lift them with green-wood tongs (Chesnut, p. 350). 2. Dough and "a little water" in a tight basket or pot, hot stones in, then more water and stones, "vigorously stirred" (Goddard, p. 39) so they can't burn through (Kroeber, p. 125; Stone boiling). With salt "it is quite agreeable" (Goddard, p. 39). 3. Bread: small cakes on a flat rock tilted toward the fire, eaten with salt (Dixon, p. 54); a loaf on leaves in an earth oven about 12 hours turns sweet (Chesnut, p. 351).
stone-boiling-mush-and-baking-bread

Telling camas from death camas - Fruit and stem: death camas has a "less rigid stem" and smaller capsules of "three nearly distinct valves"; camas has one "ellipsoidal capsule". The bulbs "are very nearly identical", and late summer, "when the stems are often broken off", is when poisonings happen; two of three cases Chesnut knew were fatal (Chesnut, p. 333). - Death camas: bulb with "blackish scales"; V-shaped leaves "edged with stiff hairs"; stem 6-18 in; flowers "greenish to yellowish-white" in April-May (PNW 104, pp. 1-2). - Not colour alone: great camas can be "creamy-white to deep blue-violet" (NRCS camas, p. 2), so skip every white or cream flower. Not smell: death camas bulbs "do not give off an onion-like odor", which tells them from wild onion (PNW 104, p. 2); no book here says camas smells of onion, so smell can't separate the two. - The safe way: mark blue plants in bloom, dig them after seed set, and pull every death camas out of your beds, as the traditional camas tenders did (NRCS camas, p. 4). Camas in bloom: open, six-petaled flowers spaced up a tall stalk above long, narrow leaves (Saunders, p. 44). The flowers are blue (this old drawing has no color): mark the blue ones while they bloom, and dig only those. Death camas: small yellowish-white flowers in a crowded cluster atop the stalk, grass-like
telling-camas-from-death-camas

(this old drawing has no color): mark the blue ones while they bloom, and dig only those. Death camas: small yellowish-white flowers in a crowded cluster atop the stalk, grass-like leaves; left, meadow death camas (AIB 415, p. 35).
telling-camas-from-death-camas

Tending a camas bed and pit-roasting Lift the turf in small sections, take only the larger bulbs, break up and replant the rest, put the turf back, and dig each patch "only every few years" (NRCS camas, p. 1). Replant bulblets ½-1 in deep and big bulbs 4-6 in (p. 3). A family of five needed about 2.7 ha (6.7 acres) (p. 2). The Takelma dug with a sharpened hardwood stick with a deer-horn handle (Sapir, p. 9). Raw camas is gluey and tasteless, cooked very sweet (Chesnut, p. 340), because "lengthy cooking" turns its starch to sugar (NRCS, p. 2): 1. Dig a pit, fill it with alder brush with stones on top (Sapir) or line it with stones (Chesnut), and burn it until the stones are hot (Sapir, p. 9; Chesnut, p. 340; Earth oven). 2. Lay alder bark or pine needles on the hot stones, then the bulbs, more needles, then earth; Chesnut's cooks kept a small fire on top overnight (same pages). Oak bark "burns slowly without flame" (Chesnut, p. 354). 3. "The succeeding day, if the roots were not yet well cooked, a fire was again built" (Sapir, p. 9). Camas takes 24-36 hours (NRCS, p. 2), until soft and sweet all through (rule of thumb). 4. Mash into cakes and dry them for winter (Sapir, p. 9); soak dried bulbs overnight before eating (NRCS,
tending-a-camas-bed-and-pit-roasting

p. 2), until soft and sweet all through (rule of thumb). 4. Mash into cakes and dry them for winter (Sapir, p. 9); soak dried bulbs overnight before eating (NRCS, p. 2). The layers from the bottom up, as Sapir and Chesnut give them; the books give no size for the pit (a diagram drawn for this guide).
tending-a-camas-bed-and-pit-roasting

Other bulbs and roots - Brodiaeas and mariposa lilies were "roasted in the ashes or boiled in baskets" (Goddard, pp. 40-41; Dixon, p. 52). Same death-camas rules. - Soaproot, famine food only: raw, it holds "the poisonous substance sapotoxin" (Chesnut, p. 331). The Hupa pit-cooked it "for about two days" (Goddard, p. 40); baked overnight it was "a significant food to the Karuk" (NRCS Soaproot, p. 1), but Chesnut found no clear sign it was eaten in Mendocino (p. 331). Try a little first (rule of thumb). Death camas is also called "soap plant" (PNW 104, p. 1): learn the plant, not the name. - Yampah roots taste nutty (Saunders, p. 31), but it is in the water-hemlock family: leave it to an expert. Tule rootstocks were "pounded into a kind of flour" (NRCS Tule, p. 1).
other-bulbs-and-roots

🫐 Seeds, nuts and berries 📷 Not sure what it is? Photograph it with the plant and mushroom identifier (🔧 Tools tab). It suggests names and flags poisonous groups, but it's often wrong: confirm every feature here before you eat or use anything. Sugar-pine nuts (Sugar pine): in October families went "men and women together, to the tops of the ridges" and camped; cones were "pounded until the seeds loosen" (Goddard, p. 40). Gather fallen cones (rule of thumb). To keep them, the Shasta steamed the nuts in leaves in a covered pit of hot stones and water "for several hours", dried them, and later pounded them into cakes or mixed them with powdered salmon (Dixon, pp. 54-55). Hazelnuts: gather "as soon as ripe, for the bears are very fond of them": June-July by Goddard (p. 39), early autumn by the NRCS, so summer into early fall. Eat them raw or roasted, pound them into cakes "with berries, meat, or animal fat", or boil them for oil (NRCS hazelnut, p. 1). Pinole (parched seed meal): beat the seeds into a basket with a wicker beater, winnow and pick them clean, toss them with live tanoak coals in a basket tray, "constantly shaken and tossed to prevent the burning of the seeds and the basket", and grind (Goddard, p. 41). One kind at a time, with salt (Chesnut, p. 321; Pinole).
seeds-nuts-and-berries

"constantly shaken and tossed to prevent the burning of the seeds and the basket", and grind (Goddard, p. 41). One kind at a time, with salt (Chesnut, p. 321; Pinole). For tarweed, "gathered in the fall" (Chesnut, p. 413), the Takelma first burned the stalks "to remove the pitchy substance", and ate the meal dry (Sapir, p. 10). Manzanita: the Hupa took berries "dry and powdery" in midsummer and later, dried them on sand, pounded them in the hopper and separated the flour from the seeds (Goddard, p. 41); the Takelma mixed the flour with sugar-pine nuts and stored it (Sapir, p. 10). Cider: scald ripe, sound berries "until the seeds are soft", crush, add an equal amount of water, pour at once over dry pine needles or straw in a sieve basket and let it drain (Chesnut, p. 394); drink it within four days (NRCS manzanita, p. 2). ⚠ Too much whole fruit can kill: "The bowels become stopped with great masses of seeds and pulp" (Chesnut, p. 394). Huckleberries: evergreen huckleberries ripen "around October or November", "even tastier after freezing"; dry them in sun or smoke, mash, press into cakes and wrap in leaves or bark (NRCS Evergreen Huckleberry, p. 1). Elderberries: the NRCS says Native Americans ate them "raw, cook, or dry" (NRCS Blue Elderberry, p. 1); this guide follows OSU: cook every berry, never eat stems,
seeds-nuts-and-berries

Huckleberry, p. 1). Elderberries: the NRCS says Native Americans ate them "raw, cook, or dry" (NRCS Blue Elderberry, p. 1); this guide follows OSU: cook every berry, never eat stems, leaves or green berries (OSU, p. 4). Others: thimbleberries, blackcaps, blackberries, currants, gooseberries (Goddard, p. 42); serviceberries dried for winter (Dixon, p. 55); salal, leaving some fruit on each plant (GTR-513, p. 76); drying: Preserving Food.

🐟 Salmon, lamprey and other fish The Takelma took trout, steelhead, coho and Chinook, crawfish and mussels (Sapir, p. 10). On the Klamath "there is scarcely a month in the year when some variety of salmon can not be taken" (Kroeber, p. 123). How it was done (illegal today): - Dip net at an eddy: from a platform over a backwater, a triangle of poles held a bag net with a fan of strings across its mouth, gathered to a cord in the fisherman's hand; when a salmon shook them he lifted the net (Dixon, pp. 56-58). "A single night's vigil sometimes produced a hundred salmon [...] a winter's supply" (Kroeber, p. 123). - Weir: "in a shallow, gravelly spot", stakes slanting downstream, a pole lashed at water level and guyed to shore with grapevines, weighted brush upstream, and "long willow fish-traps" in the gaps (Dixon, p. 56; Fishing weir). The Hupa built theirs in alternate years (Goddard, p. 34). - Also two-pronged harpoons (Kroeber, p. 124) and bone hooks baited with crawfish (Sapir, p. 10). Never poison: "No poisons [...] were used" (Goddard, p. 36). Drying and storing the catch: 1. Skin, take off head and tail, gut, and split at the backbone (Sapir, p. 11); wipe the blood with ferns and leaves (Goddard, p. 36). 2. Cut it "into three or more layers", held open with sticks (Goddard,
salmon-lamprey-and-other-fish

split at the backbone (Sapir, p. 11); wipe the blood with ferns and leaves (Goddard, p. 36). 2. Cut it "into three or more layers", held open with sticks (Goddard, p. 36), or roast it on split-hazel spits (Sapir, p. 11). Smoke and dry it over the fire; the Takelma "never salted" it. 3. Store slabs in baskets (Kroeber, p. 123), or bone it, rub it "to powder between the hands" and pack it in leaf-lined baskets (Dixon, p. 55) or tule sacks (Kroeber, p. 352). 4. Use it all: heads crushed into cakes for winter hunting trips, bones pounded for soup (Dixon, pp. 53, 55), dried eggs, "no form of food more concentrated" (Goddard, p. 36). Dried salmon "is very hard and nearly tasteless, but rather satisfying" (Kroeber, p. 123). Dry it until brittle (rule of thumb): smoke alone doesn't keep moist fish (PNW 238, p. 1), and lightly field-smoked fish keeps "2 weeks to a month" (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 17). Safe methods: "Fish: smoking, canning and salting" in Preserving Food. Lamprey, slit "many times to the skin" and dried over the fire (Goddard, p. 36), are now in steep decline and tribal-permit only (PLCI, p. 1): leave them to the tribes. The law today: game fish by angling, "using a hook and line" (ODFW, p. 16); no snagging, spearing, netting, trapping or clubbing them, and salmon, steelhead
salmon-lamprey-and-other-fish

them to the tribes. The law today: game fish by angling, "using a hook and line" (ODFW, p. 16); no snagging, spearing, netting, trapping or clubbing them, and salmon, steelhead and trout by day only (p. 21). Suckers and other nongame fish may be taken by hand, bow or spear; lamprey and mussels may not (p. 22). Legal gear: Hunting, Trapping & Fishing.

🦌 Deer, elk and small game How it was done (mostly illegal today): - Takelma deer fence: small gaps, each with a "finely spun" grass-rope snare; before daybreak men and dogs drove the deer while shoulder blades rattled over the gaps; near creeks or salt licks, with up to "one hundred and fifty" snares (Sapir, p. 11). Shasta and Takelma also made beargrass snares, used with fire (NRCS Beargrass, p. 3). - Shasta drives: in autumn, fences with nooses in the openings; after the oak leaves fell, fire set in broken circles, with women rattling deer bones at the gap and hunters hidden in the brush (Dixon, p. 59). - Stalking: the Shasta hunter wore a whole deerskin with head and antlers (Dixon, p. 59); the Hupa hunter hid his scent by "bathing and smoking with green fir boughs" (Goddard, p. 32). - Trail snares "where there is but one road to the feeding ground, salt-lick, or watering place" (Goddard, p. 32); deer "seem to have been snared more often than shot" (Kroeber, p. 124). Robins were snared with twine "baited with acorns" (Goddard, p. 33). The law today: no dogs, artificial lights, traps, snares or poison for game mammals (ODFW Big Game, p. 21); bows for deer and elk pull at least 40 lb, with unbarbed broadheads at least 7/8 in wide (p. 22). Scent control and patient stalking
deer-elk-and-small-game

(ODFW Big Game, p. 21); bows for deer and elk pull at least 40 lb, with unbarbed broadheads at least 7/8 in wide (p. 22). Scent control and patient stalking are still yours. More: Hunting, Trapping & Fishing. Use the whole animal. "None of the animal was wasted": marrow bones saved, sinews kept for bowstrings, the brain dried for "dressing the hide", spare meat cut in strips and cured over a fire (Goddard, pp. 32-33); elk antler made spoons and wedges. Deer fat went into "hard dough-like cakes" for winter (Sapir, p. 11); bones were pounded for winter soup, and bear meat boiled before drying (Dixon, p. 55; trichinella: "Disease and safety" in the Hunting guide). Hides were worked soft with "deer brains and water", or the hair loosened for leather by burying the hide "in wet sand for several days" (Goddard, p. 46); full steps: "Tanning hides" in Clothing & Leather. Sinew: take the back sinew or hind-leg tendons (the finer shank tendons make bowstrings) (Pope, pp. 11-12); dry them, pound them into fibres, wet them and twist or lay them on: "the moistened sinew is sticky and it hardens when dry" (FM 21-76, p. 151; Tendon).
deer-elk-and-small-game

🧵 Fibers, cordage and nets Iris cord, the local net and snare fibre: 1. Gather leaves "in the fall when fully mature"; plants "under oaks" beat those "under pines" (Goddard, p. 45). 2. Take only the two fibres near the leaf edges, drawing the leaf past your thumb against a mussel-shell "thumbnail" (Goddard, p. 45), and scrape them "clean of all tissues" (NRCS Douglas Iris, p. 1). 3. Roll them between palm and thigh into two-ply cord (Goddard, p. 45; 🖼 twisting fibres). 4. Expect slow work: "it takes nearly six weeks to make a rope twelve feet long" (NRCS, p. 1). An iris deer rope was "near 20 feet long" and "about half an inch in diameter" (same page). ⚠ "Fresh iris roots may be toxic" (same page). Dogbane: "The stems are cut in the fall; they are then split open and the long, silky fibers removed", then twisted into string (NRCS Indian Hemp, p. 1); Shasta string was "either of iris or Apocynum fibers" (Kroeber, p. 349). The leaves are poisonous "even when they are dry" (AIB 415, p. 50). Others: willow inner bark, "collected in spring", for rope (Chesnut, p. 344); fishing line of grass "rolled together by hand" (Sapir, p. 10). No book here covers nettle fibre; see "Linen, nettle and native fibers" in Clothing & Leather. Test a new fibre: tie "an overhand knot [...]
fibers-cordage-and-nets

by hand" (Sapir, p. 10). No book here covers nettle fibre; see "Linen, nettle and native fibers" in Clothing & Leather. Test a new fibre: tie "an overhand knot [...] If the knot does not break, the material is usable" (FM 3-05.70, p. 201); finger-spun cord 1/32 in thick can hold "20 to 30 pounds or more" (AFH 10-644, p. 275). Nets were knotted on a mesh stick from a shuttle (Goddard, p. 46), both often elk antler, with grooved stones for weights (Kroeber, p. 124).

🧺 Baskets The local style is twining: "Substantially the only technique is simple twining", patterns laid on top, and "Three-strand twining is customary for starts and strengthening courses", reaching north to "the Athabascan tribes on the Umpqua River" (Kroeber, p. 128; Basket weaving). The upright sticks (warps) are hazel or willow; the strands woven round them (wefts) are split root or grass (Sapir, p. 12). | Material | Used for | When | How to prepare | | Hazel shoots | Warps | Spring, "as soon as the sap is well started", from a patch burned 1-3 summers before | Peel while fresh; dry in the sun (Goddard, p. 48; Harrington, p. 161). Willow works, but insects attack it (Goddard, p. 49) | | Pine roots | Wefts; water-tight baskets | Not given | Bury them where a fire was built; if after a night they don't split "into thin flat pieces", fire again; soak, scrape, split (Goddard, p. 49) | | Beargrass | White pattern | Late summer, "when the tips begin to show white" (Goddard, p. 49); the summer after a burn (Harrington, p. 116) | Pull single leaves, never cut; leave flowering plants (NRCS Beargrass, pp. 3, 5); dry, braid in bundles, remove the midrib (p. 2); edges cut bare hands (p. 4) | | Ferns | Black and red pattern | Not given | Pound maidenhair
baskets

5); dry, braid in bundles, remove the midrib (p. 2); edges cut bare hands (p. 4) | | Ferns | Black and red pattern | Not given | Pound maidenhair stems till the black outside shreds off; redden chain-fern strands with chewed alder bark (Goddard, p. 50) | Harrington says hazel is cut "the second year after burning", Goddard "the second or third year": take shoots the first to third summer after a light burn (rule of thumb). A simple twined basket, from a Karuk weaver's own account, "from the time the warp sticks were first held together" (Harrington, p. 165): 1. Soak the root strands, with a bowl of water by you to wet them often (p. 167); keep the sticks wet "by letting them slip through the wet hand"; no fine work on a windy day, as "the material dries too rapidly" (Goddard, pp. 52-53). 2. Start: two hazel sticks together, tips opposite; two more the same way; hold the four in your left hand and lay four more crosswise on top (Harrington, pp. 165-166). 3. Lash the cross: from a corner, run a root strand diagonally across, then under; turn the bundle over and repeat until both groups lie flat and tight (pp. 167-177). 4. Two-strand twining, one round, four sticks at a time: one strand passes inside, one outside, crossing between groups (pp. 177-178; 🖼 Mason's
baskets

groups lie flat and tight (pp. 167-177). 4. Two-strand twining, one round, four sticks at a time: one strand passes inside, one outside, crossing between groups (pp. 177-178; 🖼 Mason's drawing). To join a strand, twist old and new together once "so it will not come loose again" (p. 177). 5. Three-strand twining: "I take the hindmost one all the time [...] it goes over two sticks and passes under one. Every once in a while I pull it tight" (p. 180). 6. Add sticks as the bottom widens, "whenever there seems to be a gap"; chew the butt end soft so it won't back out; add most on the bottom, few once the sides start up (p. 180). 7. Hold it inside-down on your thigh for the bottom, then against your knee; press each twist down with your left thumb (p. 181). Pattern: lay beargrass on the outside of the root strand and twine them as one (p. 182). 8. Finish: add three-strand rounds wherever it needs strength (Kroeber, p. 128); trim the stick ends only when all weaving is done, or bend them down and wrap them with willow, as some Hupa did (Mason, p. 99). Two-strand twining: the pair of strands gives a half twist between each upright, so one passes in front of the stick and one behind (White, p. 216). Start easy with an open-twined

🏠 Houses and sweathouses The winter house was dug in, with a plank roof: - Takelma: split sugar-pine boards; a floor "a foot and a half to two feet below the surface", stamped smooth; corner posts and cross-beams lashed with hazel fibre; a door raised about 3 ft with an earth ramp and notched-pole ladder; a central fire and smoke-hole (Sapir, p. 13). Poorer families used pine bark (p. 14). - Shasta: a pit about 16 by 20-23 ft, no more than 3 ft deep; the dug earth heaped as walls and lined with cedar-bark slabs; sugar-pine roof boards "split out with wedges", with eaves that "protected the earthen walls" (Dixon, pp. 44-45; metres converted, arithmetic). Copy the porch: its door "always at the extreme corner", so "all direct draught into the house was stopped"; it held firewood, nets and spears (p. 45). - Hupa: about 20 ft square over a pit 12 ft square and 5 ft deep, cedar planks on end, a round door "closed by a plank slid from within" (Goddard, p. 23); roof planks laid double "with a good projection to carry the rain away from the walls", and poles over the fire for smoking fish and venison (p. 24). Planks without a saw: split logs with elk-horn wedges "driven home with stone mauls" into planks "two or more feet wide and two and a half
houses-and-sweathouses

and venison (p. 24). Planks without a saw: split logs with elk-horn wedges "driven home with stone mauls" into planks "two or more feet wide and two and a half to three inches thick" (Goddard, p. 25); the wedge's edge was "produced by rubbing on stone" (Kroeber, p. 136). With steel: "Splitting and laying your own shingles and shakes" in Shelter Building. Before digging a pit house, read "Quake rules for earth walls" in Natural Building, and ditch it so winter rain runs away (rule of thumb). Summer: a brush shelter round a fire (Sapir, p. 13). Firewood: big logs that burn all night, fed small pieces (Harrington, p. 260); mix fast-burning manzanita with slow wood (Chesnut, p. 393; Firewood guide).
houses-and-sweathouses

The sweathouse: for cleanliness and warmth The Takelma sweathouse was partly underground and earth-covered; hot stones went in through a side hole and water was poured on them; women used "a small temporary stick structure covered over with blankets" (Sapir, p. 14). The Shasta sweat lodge was "a small hemisphere of pine bark and skins thrown over a few bent willows" (Kroeber, p. 348). To build one: bend willow poles into a dome about 5 ft high and across, cover it with blankets, put a pit of stones heated almost red-hot inside, and pour water on them. Drink "plenty of water"; "Half an hour of this is enough for most persons" (Seton, pp. 340-341; Sweat lodge). ⚠ Keep it short, cool down slowly rather than plunging into a cold river, keep out anyone sick, pregnant or with heart trouble, and never leave a child alone in one (rule of thumb).

🔥 Making, keeping and carrying fire Hand drill (Fire making): 1. Wood: the Hupa used cottonwood root "well seasoned by hanging in the sweathouse" (Goddard, p. 48); buckeye wood also made drills (Chesnut, p. 384). 2. Hearth: "about a foot long one inch wide and three fourths of an inch thick", with "Several small shallow holes" near one edge and a groove from each hole to the edge. Drill: "about fifteen inches long and one-half inch in diameter" (Goddard, p. 48). Tinder: "finely shredded cedar bast" at the groove; the Takelma carried hearth, drill and tinder in the quiver (Sapir, p. 12). 3. Spin the drill between flat palms "with downward pressure" (Pope, p. 16); when your hands reach the bottom, bring them back to the top fast (rule of thumb). "Soon little glowing dust runs down the notches and ignites the prepared tinder" (Goddard, p. 48). The bow drill is easier to learn: "Fire and light without stores" in Make-Do Household (rule of thumb). The hand drill in use: kneel over the hearth on the ground and spin the drill between flat palms, pressing down (Harrington, p. 261). Keep fire rather than make it. The Karuk drilled fire "Only once in a long time"; they kept big logs burning and carried fire: "They pack fire along in a bowl basket" with earth in it, to warm themselves where they
making-keeping-and-carrying-fire

once in a long time"; they kept big logs burning and carried fire: "They pack fire along in a bowl basket" with earth in it, to warm themselves where they cut wood (Harrington, p. 260). A fire bundle of "dry punk or fibrous barks (cedar) encased in a bark" carries coals, with "just enough" air to keep them burning slowly (AFH 10-644, pp. 228-229). ⚠ Carried coals start wildfires: carry none in the dry months (rule of thumb).

🏹 Tools: bows, arrows, points, wedges and soaproot The local bow was yew, "so thin that only the sinew backing kept it from breaking" (Kroeber, p. 127), with sinew laid "in several layers [...] over a glue consisting of steel-head salmon skin" (Sapir, p. 23). The Hupa laid it on "while the wood is green", bound it until dry, and seasoned the bow in the sweathouse (Goddard, p. 42); it was "effective for game up to fifty or seventy-five yards" (p. 43). Ishi's way, step by step. Ishi was Yahi, from Mill Creek far south in California, not local, but Pope's account is the fullest in the library: 1. Length: the stave across your chest from right hip to left hand, arm out at 45°; limbs three or four fingers wide. Season the split stave flat in a warm, sheltered place; scrape it to shape, finish with sandstone (Pope, p. 10). 2. Back it: soak strips of back or hind-leg tendon in warm water for hours; glue the back (boiled salmon skin) and let it dry; chew the wet sinew "soft and pulpy" and lay it in overlapping parallel lines; bind with bark for one night; when "thoroughly dry and hard", days later, scrape it smooth (p. 11). 3. Season again "for days or weeks". String: shank tendons chewed into fine threads and rolled into "a very tight, simple twist
tools-bows-arrows-points-wedges-and-soaproot

hard", days later, scrape it smooth (p. 11). 3. Season again "for days or weeks". String: shank tendons chewed into fine threads and rolled into "a very tight, simple twist one-eighth of an inch thick", dried taut (p. 12). His bows of 44 and about 54 in pulled 40 and 45 lb; yew "produced the best weapon", and tanoak, red cedar and juniper also served (p. 10). ⚠ Yew is "probably one of the most toxic of all poisonous plants", and children are poisoned by "the scarlet fruit" (AIB 415, p. 113). The Army's quick bow uses "Dead, dry wood" (FM 3-05.70, p. 141): a different, unbacked bow. Arrows: Hupa shafts of syringa with a serviceberry foreshaft and three hawk feathers bound with sinew, 30-36 in long (Goddard, p. 44); Ishi used straight hazel shoots "about a yard long", peeled and seasoned in a bundle (Pope, p. 15). Straighten each bend by warming it over embers or a hot stone and pressing with the thumbs ("To burn or discolor the wood was evidence of bad technique"), smooth it between two sandstones (pp. 15-16), and set the point in heated pine resin bound with sinew (p. 22). Points: press off flakes with "a piece of antler lashed to a stick of wood about fifteen inches in length", the stone on a buckskin pad in your palm (Goddard, p. 44; Knapping). A
tools-bows-arrows-points-wedges-and-soaproot

with "a piece of antler lashed to a stick of wood about fifteen inches in length", the stone on a buckskin pad in your palm (Goddard, p. 44; Knapping). A deer point took Ishi about half an hour, and his people guarded their eyes from the flakes (Pope, p. 21): wear eye protection (rule of thumb). Use stone found loose in a creek, never from an old site. Small stone points don't meet the 7/8-in broadhead rule for deer. Soaproot (Chlorogalum) grows "up into southwestern Oregon". The bulb was soap "for washing the body, hair, baskets, and utensils"; its fibre coat makes brush bristles, and the cooked, mashed bulb glues them to a handle and glues feathers to arrows (NRCS Soaproot, p. 1; Chesnut, pp. 331-332). Dig it after it seeds, drop the seeds back in the hole and leave some bulb (NRCS Soaproot, p. 2). Other glues: boiled salmon skin (Pope, p. 11), sturgeon glands (Goddard, p. 43), pine resin (pitch glue: Make-Do guide). Needles were bone or hardwood with an eye, threaded with sinew (Sapir, p. 12).

🌲 Tending the land with fire "All that they used to do was to burn the brush at various places, so that some good things will grow up," says the Karuk text Harrington took down. "They do not set the fire for nothing" (Harrington, pp. 115-116; Cultural burning). Why they burned: - Acorns: easier gathering, fewer "diseases and [...] acorn pests", straight shoots, fewer "major conflagrations that would destroy the oaks", more seed plants (NRCS black oak, p. 2). A March burn gave "a bumper crop of sound" acorns beside unburned trees bearing unsound ones (PSW-GTR-185, p. 16). The Karuk burned under tanoaks "lest it be brushy where they pick up acorns", but not "too hard" (Harrington, p. 116). - Basket plants: hazel burned "in summer" was cut "the second summer afterwards" (p. 115); beargrass was picked "the next summer, in July" (p. 116), its new leaves "stronger, thinner, and more pliable" (NRCS Beargrass, p. 6). - Food, game, safety: huckleberries "grow up good" (Harrington, p. 115); oak savannas stay open, with better wildlife habitat (KBO, p. 7); and seasonal fire "can also reduce the occurrence of the larger, more destructive wildfires" (KBO, p. 7; Lake & Long, p. 7). What fire harms: manzanita "does not come up"; tanoak "is not good when it is burned off, the tree dies"; "they are careful lest the trees burn" (Harrington, p. 117).
tending-the-land-with-fire

What fire harms: manzanita "does not come up"; tanoak "is not good when it is burned off, the tree dies"; "they are careful lest the trees burn" (Harrington, p. 117). Black and white oaks survive light fire (KBO, p. 45); hot fire kills beargrass roots (GTR-513, p. 133). | What you tend | How often | Source | | Oak woodland underburn | Every 3-5 years | KBO, p. 42 | | Beargrass patch | About every 3 years; at least every 20 | NRCS Beargrass, p. 6; Lake & Long, p. 5 | | Hazel for basket sticks | Burn, then cut the second summer | Harrington, p. 115 | | Camas prairie | Yearly, after digging | NRCS camas, pp. 1, 4 | | Death camas in a camas bed | Mid-spring, three years running | PNW 104, p. 2 | When: then and now. The Karuk burned "in summer [...] when everything is dry [...] in the fall before it starts in to rain" (Harrington, p. 116); others "in the fall or early winter" (NRCS black oak, p. 2). That timing is inside today's fire season. Open burning is legal "outside of fire season [...] on burn days only"; Josephine County's burn line is 541-476-9663, and fines run "up to $12,000 per day" (DEQ, p. 1). Oak burners now go "prior to leaf out in the spring
tending-the-land-with-fire

days only"; Josephine County's burn line is 541-476-9663, and fines run "up to $12,000 per day" (DEQ, p. 1). Oak burners now go "prior to leaf out in the spring or after leaf fall in the autumn" (KBO, p. 45), and this library's rule is no open burning June-October, until real rain ("Burning on purpose: wet season only" in the Wildfire guide). So: after the fall rains or before spring green-up, on a burn day. How to burn safely (KBO, pp. 43-44): 1. Plan, get the permits, tell the neighbours; it takes "experienced personnel". 2. Thin and pile the brush first, to bring fuel "to safe levels"; rake to bare soil for 2 ft around oaks, snags and logs you want to keep. 3. Clear a fire line "approximately 12 to 24 inches in width" to bare mineral soil all the way round. 4. Burn when "neither too dry nor too wet", never "too windy, or during an inversion"; "Start by igniting small test patches". Keep a crew with water and hand tools on the line (rule of thumb). 5. Patrol "until the fire is dead out", check old stumps and duff for heat, and come back "in the hours and days following". 6. Never burn poison oak: its smoke harms even people "otherwise considered immune" (OSU PNW 108, p. 4). You owe for what your fire burns: under Yurok

and days following". 6. Never burn poison oak: its smoke harms even people "otherwise considered immune" (OSU PNW 108, p. 4). You owe for what your fire burns: under Yurok law a man whose hillside burn destroyed another man's hidden valuables was held liable for them (Kroeber, p. 59). The library has no numbers for a burn prescription (humidity, wind, fuel moisture). The tribes still do this work: the Karuk Tribe with the Klamath and Six Rivers National Forests (Lake & Long, p. 9), a Grand Ronde crew in oak woodland (KBO, pp. 7-8). 📚 Go deeper: Harrington, pp. 115-117 - Karuk burning in Karuk words; KBO, pp. 42-45 - prescribed fire in local oaks; NRCS Beargrass, pp. 5-6 - burning for weavers.

🤝 Community ways that worked Share the catch. Each Shasta fish dam belonged to one family, but its owners "were obliged to give to any one who asked for them as many fish as he could carry" (Dixon, p. 56). "The single hunter always shared his game with others on his return: the chief, however, had no greater share than others"; the hunter kept the hide and legs (Dixon, p. 60). A Hupa village followed its headman "because from him they received food in time of scarcity" (Goddard, p. 68). Clear rules and limits. Shared fishing spots went in 24-hour turns, changing "about the middle of the afternoon" (Kroeber, p. 59); no new fishing place could open below an old one, which "must have very closely restricted the total number" (p. 60); the Hupa weir went in alternate years (Goddard, p. 34). Take big camas only and rest the patch; leave some soaproot "for wildlife and future production" (NRCS Soaproot, p. 2); pull beargrass a few leaves at a time. Take no more than a third of a patch (rule of thumb). Pay instead of fight. A Takelma man who was struck would often "keep cool" and ask for payment instead of hitting back. In serious quarrels a go-between, whose "person was deemed inviolate", carried each side's exact words until the offender paid; the injured side then gave back "a
community-ways-that-worked

instead of hitting back. In serious quarrels a go-between, whose "person was deemed inviolate", carried each side's exact words until the offender paid; the injured side then gave back "a nominal present" "to cement the new friendship" (Sapir, p. 21). Among the Hupa, a respected man proposed the settlement, witnesses were called if facts were disputed, and "After the settlement is accomplished the parties must be friends" (Goddard, p. 69). Yurok law put it plainly: revenge "causes two liabilities to lie where one lay before", and once payment is accepted the claim "is irrevocably and totally extinguished. Even the harboring of a sentiment of injury is thereafter improper" (Kroeber, p. 44). Putting this to work: "Settling disputes and dealing with theft" in Community & Barter. Trade skills and teach the children. A man could "make use of his neighbor's skill" in bow-making (Goddard, p. 42). "Children are seldom punished or handled roughly when small"; they learned from "the father and grandfather at night, and by the grandmother, the great source of wisdom, by day", and "The girl soon begins to weave little baskets" (Goddard, p. 62).

💊 Medicine plants: go carefully 📷 Not sure what it is? Photograph it with the plant and mushroom identifier (🔧 Tools tab). It suggests names and flags poisonous groups, but it's often wrong: confirm every feature here before you eat or use anything. The old books are full of plant remedies; almost none are tested, and some use the most poisonous plants here (death camas, iris root, dogbane, yew). This guide repeats none: read "Medicinal plants - go carefully" in Medical READ-ME-FIRST and use the Field Care guide. Bathing, soaproot soap and short sweats here are for cleanliness only.
medicine-plants-go-carefully

⚖ Respect and the law - Public land: the Forest Service and BLM keep permit lists for forest products (GTR-513, p. 17), and digging wild camas "is rarely appropriate or legal except under salvage situations" (NRCS camas, p. 3). Plant your own camas and soaproot beds (NRCS Soaproot, pp. 1-2). - Tribal and private land: tribes already lack "access to ancestral lands" (KBO, p. 8). Ask before gathering, and don't strip a known weaving or camas site (rule of thumb). - Village sites and graves: "Oregon law protects American Indian graves and certain sacred American Indian objects on both public and private lands. It is illegal to remove, injure, or destroy these" (ODFW Today's Hunter, p. 33). "Do not disturb" a find; report it to the Forest Service or BLM on federal land, or the State Police; for human remains call OSP at once, 800-452-7888 (p. 34; ARPA; NAGPRA). The old stone mortars found in Shasta country "are never used by the Shasta" (Kroeber, p. 349). Leave mortars, pestles and points where they lie. - Fish, game and fire: see the law notes in the salmon, deer and burning sections. Sudden oak death rides "on tools, tires or shoes" (NRCS tanoak, p. 3): clean your gear between tanoak groves (rule of thumb).

🐔 Chickens: Eggs and Meat Year After Year How to keep a flock of chickens that feeds a household and renews itself with no feed store, vet, hatchery or electricity: breeds that still go broody, the coop, local predators, feeding on range, bugs, scraps and home-grown grain, eggs through the seasons, hatching under hens, raising chicks with no heat lamp, roosters, health with no vet, culling, slaughter, manure, and how many birds a family needs. The books are in Small-Livestock\Chickens and Small-Livestock\Slaughter-Processing, and in Animals\Poultry, Animals\Veterinary and Animals\Planning-Predators-Toxic-Plants (all under Southern-Oregon\; the download list is local/library-files.txt). Where this guide works a number out itself it says (arithmetic); check it with the Calculator. ### The short version - Lock birds in every night behind hardware cloth, not chicken wire, buried at least 12 inches. A weasel fits through a ¼-inch gap (Kentucky ID-245, pp. 3, 6). Only an electric fence stops a black bear (ODFW, p. 2). - Keep breeds that go broody (Plymouth Rock, Rhode Island Red, Wyandotte, Orpington, Australorp). Hybrid layers and Cornish-cross broilers rarely sit and won't rebuild a flock (FAO, p. 10). - A broody hen is your incubator and brooder. Set 10-15 eggs; chicks hatch on day 21; she keeps them warm with no fuel at all (USDA FB 1363, p. 3). - On little bought feed expect about 100 eggs a hen a year, few

day 21; she keeps them warm with no fuel at all (USDA FB 1363, p. 3). - On little bought feed expect about 100 eggs a hen a year, few in winter and during the molt (FAO, p. 9). 6-12 hens keep a family in eggs most of the year (FB 1508, p. 8). - Calcium, grit and clean water every day. Never feed moldy grain, spoiled meat or maggots bred on carcasses (botulism), and keep foxglove and Scotch broom out of pens. - One rooster per 10-12 dual-purpose hens; eat spare cockerels before 12-18 weeks, when they start fighting and chasing hens (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 84). - Marek's, bird flu and the chronic coughs have no cure. Cull, burn or bury deeply, wear gloves, and never eat or trade a bird that died of disease (FB 1508, p. 30). - The old bulletins' lice and mite remedies are poisons (sodium fluoride, nicotine sulfate, DDT, carbolic acid). See "Old advice in the library to ignore".

🐔 Choosing breeds that renew themselves Every bird must be able to come from your own flock. Hatchery hybrids can't: they have "very low mothering ability and broodiness" and need bought chicks, brooders and balanced feed, and crossbreds bred among themselves drop back in production the very next generation (FAO, pp. 10, 62). High egg numbers and broodiness pull against each other in the same bird (p. 63), so a self-renewing flock lays a little less and raises its own replacements. | Breed | Good for | As mothers | Notes | | Plymouth Rock, Rhode Island Red, Wyandotte, Orpington, Australorp | Eggs and meat | Most make good mothers | The core of a self-renewing flock (FB 1508, p. 6; 🖼 Buff Orpington) | | Leghorn, Ancona, Minorca | Eggs | "Fickle mothers" | Light birds that fly over fences (🖼 Leghorn flock) | | Brahma, Jersey Giant, Cochin | Meat | Sit well but clumsy on eggs | Big, slow-growing table birds (FB 1363, p. 8; FB 1508, p. 10) | | Hybrid layers, Cornish-cross | Short-term only | Rarely go broody | Use up while feed lasts; don't plan a future on them | - First eggs: Leghorns at about 6 months; Rocks, Reds and similar at about 7 months (USDA FB 1727, p. 21). - Meat birds: Cornish-cross are ready in 6-8 weeks (Kansas State EP71,
choosing-breeds-that-renew-themselves

Leghorns at about 6 months; Rocks, Reds and similar at about 7 months (USDA FB 1727, p. 21). - Meat birds: Cornish-cross are ready in 6-8 weeks (Kansas State EP71, p. 1); a hybrid broiler reaches 4.4 lb in 7 weeks on under 8.8 lb of feed (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 13). They need about 22% protein starter (PNW 477, p. 2), and the fastest growers die of heart failure, "water belly" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 88). After collapse, your meat is the surplus cockerels and old hens of a dual-purpose flock. - Colored birds last longer on range: hawks spot solid colors, especially white, more easily (FAO, p. 10). - Bantams eat much less but lay fewer, smaller eggs (FB 1508, p. 17); a few broody bantam hens make handy spare incubators (rule of thumb). - Starting stock: healthy, vigorous birds from a reliable breeder; yearling hens breed better than pullets (FB 1508, pp. 8-9). Healthy-looking newcomers often carry disease in (UF PS044, p. 3): keep new birds apart for a month (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1508, p. 6 - back-yard breeds; FAO, pp. 61-63 - breeding for family flocks; Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 13 - dual-purpose, layer and meat types.

🏠 The coop: space, roosts, nests, air and litter Where: dry, drained ground out of the prevailing wind, facing south with part of the south side open and curtained in cold weather (FB 1508, p. 19); near where people walk, raised at least 1 ft against rats, skunks and raccoons (OSU EC 1644, p. 1); away from overhanging trees and brush that hide predators (ODFW, p. 1). | Space per bird | Floor | Source | | Chicks to 8 weeks | ½ sq ft | FB 1538, p. 23 | | Grown birds with a run / with no run | 3 sq ft / 8-10 sq ft | OSU EC 1644, p. 1 | | "Safe working rule" for a laying house | 4 sq ft | FB 1508, p. 20 | | Night-only shelter for birds that range all day | 1 sq ft | Practical Poultry Raising, p. 185 | A shed-roof house 10 ft long, 12 ft deep, 7 ft high in front and 5 ft at the back (FB 1508, p. 20) holds about 30 hens at 4 sq ft (arithmetic). Crowding breeds feather picking, cannibalism and egg eating (FB 1841, p. 13). - Roosts: 1-2 inch square lumber, edges rounded, 2 ft off the floor, 10 inches apart, 5-10 inches per bird (OSU EC 1644, p. 2; 🖼 roost layouts) - about 8

Roosts: 1-2 inch square lumber, edges rounded, 2 ft off the floor, 10 inches apart, 5-10 inches per bird (OSU EC 1644, p. 2; 🖼 roost layouts) - about 8 for Leghorns, 10 for Rocks and Brahmas, over a droppings board cleaned twice a week (FB 1508, p. 22). Roosts hung on wire are harder for mites and ticks to reach (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 133). - Nests: one per 4 hens, about 12 × 12 × 12 inches, never lower than the roosts, with a 45° roof so no one sleeps on top; a 5-gallon bucket on its side works (OSU EC 1644, p. 3). Put them in the darkest corner - dark nests entered from the back discourage egg eating (FB 1508, p. 22) - and close them at night (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 34). - Air without drafts: chickens need more fresh air for their weight than any other livestock (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 17) and breathe out up to ¾ pint of water a bird a day (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 96). Vents in gables or eaves carry off ammonia and damp; no insulation needed, just no drafts on roosting birds (OSU EC 1644, pp. 1-2). In our wet winters an ammonia smell or damp litter means more vent, not less (rule of thumb). - Water and minerals: hang the water pan about 18 inches up

In our wet winters an ammonia smell or damp litter means more vent, not less (rule of thumb). - Water and minerals: hang the water pan about 18 inches up so litter stays out (FB 1508, p. 24); grit and shell in their own hoppers (p. 23). - Run: 1 × 2-inch mesh, top covered, fence buried 6-12 inches (OSU EC 1644, p. 1; Kentucky says 12+). Better, two yards, one growing grass or a crop while birds use the other (FB 1508, p. 25). A movable pen (a chicken tractor) puts birds on fresh grass and breaks the parasite cycle. Roosts at the back over a droppings board, nests in the dark, and fresh air moving high above the birds (a diagram drawn for this guide). Deep litter, the easiest floor for a home flock: 1. Start with 2-4 inches of chopped straw, wood chips, dry leaves or shavings; sawdust only after 4 weeks of age; replace wet litter at once (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 31). Never moldy or wet bedding: it causes aspergillosis, a fungal pneumonia (UF PS044, pp. 6-7). 2. Add fresh litter on top to keep it dry (FB 1538, p. 17); turn it often in damp weather. Hens dust-bathe in it against lice and lay well on it, but worms and coccidiosis build up if it stays wet (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 91). 3. Clean

🦝 Predators of the Illinois Valley Who did it? (Kentucky ID-245, pp. 2-5) - all of these live here: | What you find | Likely predator | | Whole bird eaten or gone; leftovers covered with leaves and grass | Bobcat (coyotes and foxes don't do this; here a cougar also covers its kills, usually bigger ones like goats or deer (general practice)) | | Head, crop and breast eaten; heads pulled through the wire; eggs carried 50+ yards | Raccoon | | Bird gone; a few drops of blood and feathers | Fox | | Adult birds missing, no other sign | Dog, coyote, fox, bobcat, hawk or owl | | Birds bitten all over, wounded but not dead | Dog | | Feeding started at the vent, one bird a visit | Opossum | | Several birds killed, bloody, little eaten | Weasel or mink (a least weasel fits a ¼-inch hole) | | Eggs opened at one end and licked out | Skunk | | Eggs or small chicks vanish with no trace | Snake or rats | | Breast eaten, feathers plucked cleanly; day or night | Hawk (day) or great horned owl (night) | Keeping them out (ID-245, pp. 5-6; 🖼 photos): 1. Hardware cloth, buried at least 12 inches. Chicken wire keeps chickens in, not raccoons out. Gaps of ¼ inch or less stop
predators-of-the-illinois-valley

them out (ID-245, pp. 5-6; 🖼 photos): 1. Hardware cloth, buried at least 12 inches. Chicken wire keeps chickens in, not raccoons out. Gaps of ¼ inch or less stop snakes too (p. 4). 2. Lock birds in every night. Feed or water them inside at dusk and they learn to go in on their own. Leave no feed in the run overnight and remove sick and dead birds at once (p. 6). 3. Cover the run against hawks and owls (orange netting shows up best to them) and remove perches within 100 yards. Hawks and owls are federally protected - don't shoot them (p. 5). 4. A guardian dog (such as a Great Pyrenees) that stays with the flock works day and night (p. 6; raising one). 5. Trap only the animal that gets in. A dead predator is soon replaced by another (p. 6). 6. Don't count on lights or noise: animals get used to them, and steady light near the coop upsets laying (p. 6; ODFW, p. 1). Black bears break through coops and chicken wire; three chickens are about 4,500 calories to a bear and chicken feed about 1,500 a pound. Store feed in a locked building or bear-proof container, never in the coop (ODFW, p. 1). A properly installed electric fence, on day and night, is the most reliable protection (p. 2): at least 3
predators-of-the-illinois-valley

building or bear-proof container, never in the coop (ODFW, p. 1). A properly installed electric fence, on day and night, is the most reliable protection (p. 2): at least 3 wires (5-6 better), lowest 7-9 inches up (lower for skunks and raccoons), top 36-42 inches, wires 8-10 inches apart, an energizer of at least 6,000 volts and 0.5 joules, hardware cloth inside so hens can't touch the wires, and weeds kept off (🖼 building a bear fence, step by step (beehive version)). After the grid that means a solar fence charger - see the Off-Grid Power guide. Buried hardware cloth stops diggers, a covered top stops hawks and owls, and only the hot wires outside stop a bear (a diagram drawn for this guide). Cougars: fence and shelter stock and shut them in at night; Oregon law lets a landowner kill a cougar that is damaging livestock (ODFW, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: Kentucky ID-245, p. 5 - the "which predator" table and fixes; ODFW Raising Chickens in Bear Country - electric fence setup; FAO, pp. 28-29 - strings and nets against hawks, rats and snakes; USDA Livestock Guarding Dogs, p. 13 - raising a guardian pup.

🌾 Feeding without a feed store What a hen needs: 6-7 lb of feed a month, laying or not (FB 1727, p. 5), or 70-95 lb of grain a year (FB 1508, p. 25); about 16% protein and 3-4% calcium for layers, 18-20% protein for chicks (PNW 477, p. 2); and 2-3 times as much water as feed by weight (p. 3). Grain alone is short of protein, so they need "meat food": bugs, worms, milk, scraps (FB 1508, p. 27).
feeding-without-a-feed-store

Range, bugs and worms - A household flock of 10-20 may need nothing but table scraps, greens and insects from the garden; bigger flocks do better with a few handfuls of grain (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 39). - Foragers eat insects, worms, snails, seeds, grass and leaves: village hens' crops held 72% household waste, 13% grass, 8% worms, snails, ants and flies; they ranged 120-190 yards, and cattle and goat pens were favorite spots (FAO, pp. 17-18). Range is worth most in spring and summer, little in late fall and winter (PNW 477, p. 4). - Maggots: soak plant stalks or husks with some droppings, let flies lay, and take the larvae at 5-7 days, before they fly; shade the tank in the heat (FAO, p. 24). Black soldier fly larvae are a common choice (rule of thumb). Never feed maggots from carcasses or spoiled meat: they carry botulism ("limberneck") (FB 1652, p. 43). - Earthworm beds: 25 m² (270 sq ft) made 2.2 lb of worms a day, extra protein for 50 chickens - but worms and snails can carry poultry tapeworms (FAO, p. 24).
range-bugs-and-worms

Scraps, milk, sprouts and greens - Mix each day's table scraps into a moist grain mash; nothing sloppy or heavily salted (FB 1508, p. 26). No onion tops, geranium leaves or strong-flavored scraps - they taint eggs (p. 27). Scratch grain, scraps and greens: only what they clean up in about 20 minutes; too many lower laying (PNW 477, pp. 3-4). - With a dairy goat or cow: layers can live on skim milk or buttermilk to drink, all the grain they want and oyster shell - about 4-5 gallons of milk a day per 100 hens (FB 1841, pp. 23-24). Milk draws flies that spread tapeworm: move the pans daily (p. 24). See the Milk, Butter & Cheese guide. - Sprouted oats for winter greens (FB 1508, p. 27): in pails with small holes in the bottom, soak a day's oats 24 hours, then move them to a second pail, moistened, then a third, one pail a day; after 5 days they are ready. Start a pail every day for a steady supply. - Greens all the time (clippings, cabbage, kale, clover) supply vitamin A; sunshine supplies vitamin D (FB 1841, p. 8). Chicks with no sun or greens get leg weakness (FB 1508, p. 16).
scraps-milk-sprouts-and-greens

Calcium, grit and salt - Calcium always: oyster or clam shell, limestone, or eggshells boiled, dried and crushed small so hens don't learn the taste. The flock's own shells aren't enough; old hens and hot weather need more; short hens start eating their eggs (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 117). - Grit: rough gravel the size of small peas; ranging birds find their own, penned birds must be given it (p. 116; FB 1508, p. 28). River gravel is best (FB 1841, p. 7); oyster shell is too soft to be grit (PNW 477, p. 4). - Salt about ½-1% of a mash; bone meal for phosphorus when there's little meat or fish in the feed (FB 1841, p. 7). Not more: chickens poison easily on salt (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 47).
calcium-grit-and-salt

Storing feed and the dry season - Store grain dry. Mold grows above 11% moisture and leaves a poison (aflatoxin) even after the mold is gone (FAO, p. 48). Never feed musty or rancid feed (FB 1841, p. 13). - Our dry season: scavenged feed dries up (FAO, p. 36) - here roughly July-October when the grass browns. Store grain, squash and roots for summer as well as winter, or cut the flock to what the feed supports before then (rule of thumb).
storing-feed-and-the-dry-season

Plants that poison chickens 📷 Not sure what's growing in the pasture? Photograph it with the plant identifier (🔧 Tools tab): it suggests a name and flags poisonous groups. Then check that name against this list. The ones that grow here (WSNWCB, pp. 54-55): foxglove, Scotch broom, poison oak, bracken fern, death camas, poison and water hemlock, lupines, St. John's wort, horsetail, creeping buttercup, rhododendron, nightshades, jimsonweed, tansy, false hellebore, black locust, snowberry and clematis. Penned birds are at more risk - they eat what they're given, while ranging birds mostly avoid these (p. 54). Signs: trouble breathing, seizures, weakness, stumbling, diarrhea, sores on bare skin (p. 55). (The list also names alfalfa and yarrow, which the USDA bulletins feed routinely; feed them in a mix, not alone.) Also never feed avocado, raw dried beans, green or sprouted potatoes, or rhubarb leaves (rule of thumb).
plants-that-poison-chickens

Water every day Chickens drink every 15-20 minutes and must never be without clean, cool water (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 18; 🖼 homemade waterers). A layer may drink more than a quart a day in hot weather (p. 17); FAO allows 50 liters per 100 layers in hot, dry weather, half in mild (FAO, p. 33). A day without water can kill in the heat, and even part of a day drops egg production (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 47; FB 1727, p. 6). 📚 Go deeper: FAO, pp. 16-25 - scavenging, insects, worms and home-grown feeds; USDA FB 1841, p. 23 - home-grown grain and milk rations; Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 38-55 - nutrition and sample rations; Seed Bank guide - growing feed grain and greens.

🥚 Eggs: age, daylight, molt and storing | How the hens live (FAO, p. 9) | Eggs per hen per year | | Scavenging only | 20-30 | | Scavenging + shelter and disease control | 40-60 | | Some feed | about 100 | | Fully fed | 160-220 | - Collect daily. A hen left to sit on her eggs may lay only 30 a year; collected daily, 120; with 15 hours of light, 250 (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 33). Most eggs come between sunrise and mid-morning; don't move nests in the laying months (FAO, p. 36). - By age: best in the first year, about 20% less in the second (FB 1727, p. 5), falling off considerably after the third (FB 1508, p. 6). - Daylight: hens need about 14 hours of light to lay at their best (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 84); lengthening days push laying up, shortening days down (FAO, p. 27). December days here are only about 9 hours (rule of thumb), so expect few eggs November-February. Old farms lit the house from November to late March, early mornings, for 12-13 hours of "working time" (FB 1508, p. 29); that burns lamp fuel daily, so most households will do better storing spring eggs. If you do light, never stop suddenly - the flock may quit and molt (FB 1727, p. 6) - and never

so most households will do better storing spring eggs. If you do light, never stop suddenly - the flock may quit and molt (FB 1727, p. 6) - and never exceed about 17 hours (FAO, p. 28). - The molt: at the end of each laying year, in summer or fall, hens regrow their feathers and stop laying; a feather takes about 6 weeks. Poor layers molt early (June-July) and slowly and may rest 4-6 months; good layers molt late and fast and rest 2-3 months. Keep molting hens in good flesh (FB 1727, p. 12). Afterward they lay a bit less, bigger eggs with thinner shells (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 79). Telling layers from loafers (Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 35-37; 🖼 layer vs. non-layer): | | Laying hen | Not laying | | Comb) and wattles | Large, bright red, waxy | Shrunken, pale, dull, dry (FB 1727, p. 8) | | Vent | Large, oval, moist, pale | Small, puckered, dry, yellow | | Pubic bones | 3 fingers apart | 1 finger; only two fingers from the keel (p. 9) | | Beak and shanks (yellow-skinned breeds) | Bleached white | Yellow returning (p. 10) | Good layers sometimes pause 2-3 weeks between clutches, so check twice before you cull (same pages). A laying hen's comb and wattles are big and full (A); out of lay they

layers sometimes pause 2-3 weeks between clutches, so check twice before you cull (same pages). A laying hen's comb and wattles are big and full (A); out of lay they shrink and dry up (B) (FB 1727, p. 8). Feel for the two pubic bones beside the vent and count fingers laid flat between them (a diagram drawn for this guide). Storing eggs: - Collect at least once a day, several times in hot weather. Eggs at 99 °F go downhill in 3 days; at 37 °F they keep about 100 days; 50 °F is fine for shorter storage (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 34). - Wash only dirty eggs, in water 20 °F warmer than the egg; cold water pulls germs in through the shell (OSU EM 9350, p. 5). Clean, unwashed eggs keep 2-3 weeks at cool room temperature, longer in a cold cellar (rule of thumb). - Spring surplus: water glass or limewater crocks keep eggs 6-9 months (USDA 1935, p. 3; FB 1508, p. 32): 1. Use eggs laid April to early June: fresh, clean, dry, uncracked and preferably infertile (pen the rooster away from the layers those weeks (rule of thumb)). 2. Water glass: 1 quart to 9 quarts of boiled, cooled water in a scalded crock; keep 2 inches of liquid over the eggs; cover, and don't move the crock. 3. Limewater: scald 2 lb

to 9 quarts of boiled, cooled water in a scalded crock; keep 2 inches of liquid over the eggs; cover, and don't move the crock. 3. Limewater: scald 2 lb lime, stir into 5 gallons of boiled water, let settle, use the clear liquid, no salt (USDA 1935, p. 4); never in galvanized cans (FB 1508, p. 32). 4. Rinse eggs before use; prick the big end with a pin before boiling (USDA 1935, p. 4). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1727 - layers vs. loafers and the molt, with pictures; Practical Poultry Raising, pp. 76-80 - daylight and molt; Root Cellar guide - storing eggs cool.

🐣 Broody hens and hatching without power Setting a broody hen - the dependable way without power: 1. A broody hen stops laying, stays on the nest, ruffles up, clucks and pecks your hand (FAO, p. 40). Choose a big, healthy hen with a good record; pullets under a year often make poorer mothers (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 55). 2. After she has sat 2-3 days, move her at night to a quiet, darkish nest with dummy eggs; check her for lice and the box for mites first. Keep her in until the second afternoon; if she returns to the nest after feeding, give her the real eggs (FB 1363, p. 9). 3. Nest: about 18 inches square, on the floor so she doesn't jump down onto the eggs, with 3-4 inches of damp earth under hay or straw shaped slightly hollow (FB 1363, p. 8; FB 1508, p. 11; 🖼 setting a hen). 4. Set 10-13 eggs in cold weather, 13-15 in warm (FB 1363, p. 3). Too few is better than too many, which get chilled (FB 1508, p. 11); hatching often drops above 10 (FAO, p. 40). 5. Set several hens the same day; after candling, combine the good eggs under fewer hens and reset the others (FB 1363, p. 10). No broody when you need one? Leave three or four eggs in a nest in a
broody-hens-and-hatching-without-power

the good eggs under fewer hens and reset the others (FB 1363, p. 10). No broody when you need one? Leave three or four eggs in a nest in a small, quiet pen and put a fat, healthy hen on it at dusk each evening until she sits (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 55). Too many? A broody coop with a slatted floor and wire front breaks a hen in a few days so she lays again (FB 1508, p. 23; 🖼 broody coop). Hatching eggs: from hens 1-2 years old (8-18 months is ideal) and your best layers, of normal size and shape with sound shells (FB 1363, p. 5; Practical Poultry Raising, p. 56). Eggs turn fertile about 4 days after the rooster joins the hens (FAO, p. 40). Keep them at 50-60 °F and set within a week (FB 1508, p. 11): quality drops after 5 days, 3-week-old eggs rarely hatch, and eggs held over 5 days should be turned daily. Wipe dirty ones with a damp cloth; collect 2-3 times a day in frost (FB 1363, p. 5). The sitting hen, day by day: - Corn or wheat, water and a dust bath close to the nest; little green feed or meat, which makes her quit (FB 1508, pp. 11-12; FAO, p. 40). - She should come off once a day; if she isn't back in half
broody-hens-and-hatching-without-power

little green feed or meat, which makes her quit (FB 1508, pp. 11-12; FAO, p. 40). - She should come off once a day; if she isn't back in half an hour, put her back (FB 1363, p. 9). Clear out broken eggs at once - they bring mites and lice and she may desert (p. 10). In very dry spells sprinkle the litter under the eggs, never the eggs (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 55). - Candle on day 7 and day 14 - hold each egg to a bright light in the dark - and remove clear ones (FB 1363, p. 18; 🖼 the air cell on days 7, 14 and 18; 🖼 candling). A flashlight or a beam of sun in a dark room works; brown eggs show 2-3 days later than white, and clear eggs are still good to eat (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 27). - Chicks start pipping the evening of day 19 and are out by day 21 (FB 1538, p. 11). Don't help them out - those that can't hatch alone rarely thrive (p. 15). - Expect about 80% of eggs to hatch under hens (FAO, p. 40) - 7 or 8 chicks from 10-15 eggs, half cockerels (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 55). A hen that has sat a few days will often take day-old chicks slipped under her; then give her a fresh
broody-hens-and-hatching-without-power

10-15 eggs, half cockerels (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 55). A hen that has sat a few days will often take day-old chicks slipped under her; then give her a fresh set of eggs (FAO, p. 40). Take out the clear eggs (good to eat) and the dead ones (throw away); keep the ones with spreading veins (a diagram drawn for this guide). Incubating without electricity: - Oil-lamp incubators need kerosene and tending every day; still-air machines run about 102 °F at egg height; turn eggs at least twice a day from day 2 to day 18 (FB 1363, p. 3; FB 1538, p. 16). - The heated-grain (rice-husk) method of China and Bangladesh warms eggs in the sun, then layers bundles of 25-30 chicken eggs between cloth pillows of grain heated to 140 °F in an insulated basket, rewarming the grain 2-3 times a day and turning the eggs; after about day 13 the older eggs warm the newer ones. It hatches 65-75%, but takes skill and a steady stream of eggs (FAO, pp. 41-43). Practice with a few eggs while you still have broodies (rule of thumb). - With steady power only: fan incubators 99.5-100 °F, about 57% humidity, eggs turned 5-6 times a day (FB 1538, p. 16); a foam cooler (🖼 photos) with a 40-watt bulb and thermostat at 99-100 °F, or a double cardboard box with
broody-hens-and-hatching-without-power

eggs turned 5-6 times a day (FB 1538, p. 16); a foam cooler (🖼 photos) with a 40-watt bulb and thermostat at 99-100 °F, or a double cardboard box with the bulb in a chimney touching nothing (fire risk) - plan on hatching no more than half the eggs. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1363 - setting hens and choosing eggs; FAO, pp. 40-43 - natural incubation and the rice-husk method; 🖼 21 days of chick development; Wikipedia: egg incubation.

🐤 Raising chicks with no heat lamp With the hen - the easy way: 1. Leave hen and chicks on the nest at least 24 hours after the hatch (FB 1538, p. 17); chicks need no food or water the first day, living on the yolk (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 45). 2. A hen broods 10-15 chicks early in the season, 15-20 in warm weather; add more at night, the same age and color as hers (FB 1538, pp. 17-18). 3. Shut hen and chicks in a ventilated brood coop (about 20 × 30 inches, 18-26 inches high) at night against rats, cats and weasels (FB 1538, p. 18; 🖼 drawing). Move it weekly to fresh short grass, on ground old birds haven't used for a year (p. 17). 4. Feed chicks in a creep feeder (gaps only chicks fit through): it saves chicks, and hens not feeding chicks lay again sooner (FAO, pp. 32-33). Without a hen: - Hatch in warm weather. Early in the season chicks need heat 8-12 weeks; later in spring only 4-6 weeks (FB 1538, p. 22). - Heat with no electricity: brooders were once heated with wood, charcoal, straw, kerosene or the sun (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 27), or kept in a box near the kitchen fire (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 45). A low insulated box with cloth-wrapped jugs of hot water, refilled every
raising-chicks-with-no-heat-lamp

Healthy Poultry, p. 27), or kept in a box near the kitchen fire (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 45). A low insulated box with cloth-wrapped jugs of hot water, refilled every few hours, carries a small batch (rule of thumb). - Fire heat has two dangers: carbon monoxide builds up in poorly vented brooders and kills chicks fast on cold nights (FB 1652, p. 41), and fire - keep paper and bedding away from flame (FB 1538, p. 22). - About 95 °F at chick height the first week, then 5 °F less each week to 70 °F (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 27). Watch the chicks: crowding to the heat = cold; spread far off and panting with open mouths = hot; spread evenly = right (p. 29; 🖼 what each looks like; FB 1538, p. 22). Wire across corners stops piling and smothering (same page). - Home-made chick feed: finely cracked grain or rolled oats with chopped hard-boiled eggs (infertile ones from candling) the first few days, milk if you have it, greens and sun; four feeds a day for 2-3 weeks; by 8 weeks they eat whole wheat and cracked corn (FB 1508, pp. 15-16). Water in a dish they can't drown in (PPR, p. 45). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1538, pp. 17-25 - brooding with hens and brooders; Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 27-31 - brooder heat and

they can't drown in (PPR, p. 45). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1538, pp. 17-25 - brooding with hens and brooders; Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 27-31 - brooder heat and chick behavior.

🌡 Heat, smoke and fire season - Chickens can't sweat; they pant. Severe stress above 104 °F (40 °C); 115 °F (46 °C) kills most. They eat less, drink more and lay smaller eggs (FAO, p. 27); above 100 °F some die of heat stroke (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 84). - Do: shade, every vent open, cool water refilled often; white paint reflects up to 70% of the sun's heat on a roof. Heat-stressed birds peck each other (FAO, p. 27). Collect eggs several times a day (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 34); don't catch or move birds in the heat of the day (rule of thumb). - Wildfire smoke (PNW 783, p. 10): watch for coughing, open-mouth breathing, watery eyes, weakness. Keep water clean and fresh, cool them, mist down dust, and put off stressful jobs. - Fire plan: clear brush and dry grass well back from the coop, and keep crates or boxes for the whole flock - chickens are easy to move at night (rule of thumb). See the Wildfire guide and the Illinois Valley page. 📚 Go deeper: FAO, p. 27 - heat, light and housing; PNW 783, p. 8 - evacuating or sheltering stock.

🩺 Health with no vet Prevention is the only medicine you can count on (Where There Is No Animal Doctor, p. 312): keep a closed flock (no contact with other chickens, no visitors in the coop); kill weak and sick birds early and bury the dead at once; dry litter, clean water, fresh ground for chicks, no crowding. Do chores for healthy birds first, sick ones last (FB 1508, p. 30). Coughs, sneezes and swollen faces look alike without a lab (UF PS044, pp. 2-6): - Infectious bronchitis: watery eyes and nose, rattling breath worse at night, eggs crash; birds recover in 5-6 weeks but lay less, with rough shells. Newcastle disease: gasping, twisted neck, paralysis, green diarrhea, sudden deaths (p. 2). None of the viruses can be cured; antibiotics, if you have any, only fight the germs that follow (p. 2). Bird flu (avian influenza) (UF PS044, p. 3): - Mild form: dull, off feed, breathing trouble, diarrhea, a sudden drop in eggs. 🪓 Culling: which birds go, and when Every bird you keep through winter eats 6-7 lb of feed a month (FB 1727, p. 5); culling raised a laying flock's profit by up to 10% (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 80). - Eat: hens not laying and early, slow molters, from June on (FB 1727, pp. 5, 20); runty, slow-growing and late-maturing pullets (FB 1727 suggests about 1 in 10 of the late ones, p. 5); spare cockerels by 12-18 weeks; hens past their third laying year unless they're your best mothers; chronic coughers, Marek's cases, scaly legs that won't clear, egg eaters, repeat prolapses; and roosters that attack people (rule of thumb). - Keep: hens still laying in August-September (persistent layers) for a second year and for breeding (FB 1727, p. 5), and your best broody mothers even if they lay a little less. Recently molted hens may come back into lay (Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 34-35). Mark keepers with colored leg bands (FB 1508, p. 29).

🔪 Humane slaughter and butchering Before: no feed for 8-12 hours, water available; butcher only healthy birds; brush off mud (OSU EM 9273, p. 4). Set a "dirty" area (kill, scald, pluck) apart from a clean area (gut, chill), and allow 1-2 gallons of water per bird (p. 2). 1 tablespoon of plain bleach per gallon of water sanitizes knives and tables while bleach lasts (p. 3). Pinfeathery birds: wait a week or two (UMN EB 385, p. 1). Killing - practice on a dead bird first; the AVMA calls neck dislocation humane only when done by trained people (AVMA, p. 44): - Killing cone: hang the bird head-down in a cone (or by the feet from a line); hold the head, stretch gently and cut the jugular vein on one or both sides of the neck; hold it until bleeding and flapping stop (UMN EB 385, p. 2; Kansas State EP71, p. 1). - Hatchet and block: one clean cut with a sharp blade is acceptable (AVMA, p. 77). - Neck dislocation: hold the shanks; pull the head to stretch the neck while bending the head sharply back until you feel a sudden give, then feel that the bones parted. Crushing the neck is not acceptable (same page). Dressing: 1. Scald young birds at 125-130 °F for 30-75 seconds, older birds near 140 °F; dunk up and down; keep
humane-slaughter-and-butchering

parted. Crushing the neck is not acceptable (same page). Dressing: 1. Scald young birds at 125-130 °F for 30-75 seconds, older birds near 140 °F; dunk up and down; keep boiling water handy to hold the heat (UMN EB 385, p. 2). EP71 uses 140 °F for 30-40 seconds with a little detergent (p. 1). It's right when tail and wing feathers pull out easily. 2. Pluck at once, big tail and wing feathers first, then rub off the rest; scrape pinfeathers with a dull knife; singe hairs over a flame (UMN EB 385, p. 3). 3. Gut (🖼 step by step): head off; slit the neck skin and pull out crop and windpipe; feet off at the hock; cut out the oil gland above the tail; open the belly and draw the insides out toward you; scrape out the lungs; clean the gizzard, heart and liver (EP71, p. 2). Don't cut the gut - a speck of droppings spreads salmonella, which healthy-looking birds carry (OSU EM 9273, p. 4). 4. Chill in ice water to 40 °F (UMN, p. 6); keep unfrozen under 4 days (EP71, p. 2). With no ice, use the coldest spring or creek water and cook or can the bird the same day (rule of thumb). 🌱 Manure, litter and feathers - Compost chicken manure at least 120 days before use (🖼 compost bins), and never put it raw on seedlings or growing plants. Spread raw litter in fall, after harvest, so winter rains leach out the salts (Idaho CIS 1194, pp. 2, 6) - our wet winters suit this. - Mix 20-40% manure to 60-80% bedding; a strong ammonia smell means add more straw or leaves. Lay 2-3 inches of fresh bedding after each clean-out. It's done when it has no bad smell and no straw shows (p. 3). - How much: ½ inch of rich compost (1½ if bedding-heavy) for carrots, peas and beans; 1½-3 inches for corn, cabbage, onions and squash, dug 6-10 inches in (pp. 5-6). - What a flock makes: the litter from 100 layers' year fertilizes about 1 acre of grain or ½ acre of vegetables (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 91). 👪 How many birds for a family - Eggs: 6-12 hens give an average family plenty of eggs for most of the year (FB 1508, p. 8). At about 100 eggs a hen on part-feed, two eggs a day (730 a year) takes 7-8 hens, or 25+ pure scavengers (arithmetic). Each broody stops laying 6-8 weeks (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 45), so about 12 hens and a rooster makes a good self-renewing family flock (rule of thumb). - Feed: 12 hens at 6-7 lb a month eat 860-1,000 lb a year if fully fed (arithmetic, from FB 1727, p. 5); good range in spring and summer cuts that a lot, and 10-20 birds can live on scraps, greens and bugs around a garden household, with fewer eggs (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 39). Grain fed to hens is grain people don't eat: size the flock to your scraps and range. - Meat: each broody hatch gives about 7-8 chicks, half cockerels (PPR, p. 55); four hatches ≈ 15 young roosters a year to eat at 12-20 weeks, plus the cull hens (arithmetic). - FAO's village flock: 15 hens laying 30 eggs each = 450 eggs; 120 set under broodies, 100 hatch, 30 survive (village losses of 70%): 15 pullets replace old hens and 15 cockerels go to the pot (FAO, p. 36). 🧬 Keeping the flock going for years - Eggs for replacements: a traditional flock sets 8-10 eggs per hen a year just to stay the same size (FAO, p. 36). A hen hatching and raising her own chicks can do it 4-5 times a year, about 74 days a round (FAO, pp. 62-63). - Replace about a third of the hens each year with your best pullets; keep good layers 2-3 years and the best mothers longer (rule of thumb, from FB 1727, p. 5, where farms kept about 30% of yearling hens). - Choose breeders that matured early, laid steadily and were still laying in August-September (FB 1727, p. 20) - but, unlike the bulletin, keep good broodies: without them there are no chicks. - Records: a card in the coop with dates of hatches, deaths, feed, daily eggs and any disease (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 37); leg bands for families and keepers (FB 1508, p. 29). - Avoid inbreeding: an unrelated rooster every 2-3 years (trade with neighbors), or 2-3 banded hen families with roosters rotated between them (rule of thumb). Quarantine any newcomer a month. - Never hatch from birds that had mycoplasma or pullorum - they pass it through the egg (WTINAD, pp. 314, 316; UF PS044, pp. 5-6) - or from coryza and ILT survivors, which stay carriers (pp. 3-4). - Rotate ground: chicks on

🦆 Ducks: Eggs, Meat and Slug Control How to keep ducks that feed a household and renew themselves with no feed store, vet, hatchery or electricity: choosing breeds, turning ducks loose on the slugs of our wet winters without losing the garden, a dry house, feeding on forage and home-grown grain, niacin, eggs, hatching under hens or Muscovies, brooding with no power, predators, sickness, plucking with a beeswax dip, down, and how many ducks a family needs. Where duck-keeping is the same as chicken-keeping, this guide sends you to the Chickens guide instead of repeating it. The duck books are in Animals\Poultry (USDA Duck Raising, Raising Healthy Poultry, Practical Poultry Raising), with more in Small-Livestock\Chickens, Small-Livestock\Slaughter-Processing, Animals\Planning-Predators-Toxic-Plants and Gardening-Food (all under Southern-Oregon\; the download list is local/library-files.txt). Great horned owls take ducks (Kentucky ID-245, p. 4), and ducks lay early, so the eggs end up in the house, not the pond (FB 697, p. 19). - Ducks clean slugs out of a garden that isn't growing. not the pond (FB 697, p. 19). - Ducks clean slugs out of a garden that isn't growing. They "keep a mature garden free of snails and slugs. Don't let them in a growing garden - they will devour it" (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 192). Their big months are September-October, before slugs lay their eggs (OSU EM 9027, p. 15). - Water outside, bedding dry. The Runner holds "the same relative position in the duck family that the Leghorn does among the breeds of chickens": active, a good forager, hardy, with a white egg "considerably larger than a chicken egg" (FB 697, p. 11). It stands upright like a penguin (p. 10) and needs only a basin deep enough to dip its beak to the nostrils; the Khaki Campbell was bred from Mallard, Rouen and Runner (FAO, p. 13). Both "produce well for three or four years, and the record the second year is often as high as the first" (FB 697, p. 11). - Meat ducks. A well-fed Pekin reaches about 90% of adult weight, up to 7 lb, at 7 weeks (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 96). It is timid, docile and "easily confined by low fences" (FB 697, p. 6). Rouen and Cayuga mature more slowly and have dark pinfeathers that leave a less clean-looking carcass (pp. 8-9). - Muscovies are "a wide forager", need
