fences" (FB 697, p. 6). Rouen and Cayuga mature more slowly and have dark pinfeathers that leave a less clean-looking carcass (pp. 8-9). - Muscovies are "a wide forager", need "very little care" and are quieter than Pekins, but "can readily fly over ordinary poultry fences" (FB 697, p. 7). They graze grass like geese, need no swimming water (FAO, p. 14), take heat much better than common ducks, and the drake, 30-50% heavier than the duck, carries a big breast (Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 95, 97). A Muscovy duck is the best incubator you can own, and an "excellent brooding mother" for ducks, chickens and guinea fowl too (FAO, p. 14). - Muscovy × common duck = "mule" ducks: good lean meat, but sterile (Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 96-97; FAO, p. 14). - Handling: catch ducks by the wings or neck, never by the legs, which "break easily" (FB 697, p. 19; Practical Poultry Raising, p. 192). 🐌 Why ducks suit our wet winters: slugs, snails and the garden Slugs are our worst garden pest. "Slugs thrive west of the Cascades." They feed when it is warmer than 50 °F, "love mild winters, wet springs, moist summers and irrigation", and many go dormant in hot, dry summers. They lay their eggs in the fall after the rains start, typically in late September and early October, and "if you reduce the population before they lay eggs, you have won half the battle" (OSU EM 9027, p. 15). Ducks eat slugs. Foraging ducks eat "insects, insect larvae, earthworms, snails ... mollusks" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 111), and outside they "do well on grasses and insects, and will keep a mature garden free of snails and slugs" (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 192). They stand the wet better than chickens too: they resist coccidiosis (p. 191), and once fully feathered they hold their body heat "even when the outside temperature is low" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 101). The catch: the same ducks "will devour" a growing garden (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 192): seedlings, lettuce and greens, and they trample soft beds. Timing is everything: 1. September-November, the main duck season: turn the ducks onto each bed as it is harvested. Each slug eaten before it lays is a clutch that never hatches (OSU, p. 15). 2. December-February: bare beds, paths and

the ducks onto each bed as it is harvested. Each slug eaten before it lays is a clutch that never hatches (OSU, p. 15). 2. December-February: bare beds, paths and the orchard on mild, damp days; fence off winter greens you mean to eat (rule of thumb). 3. Two to three weeks before you plant a bed in spring, give it a last going-over, then shut the ducks out (rule of thumb). 4. Spring and summer: pasture, orchard and field edges, not the garden, while plants are small. Big, tough plants (tall corn, squash) can take short, watched visits later; in July-August the slugs are quiet anyway (OSU, p. 15) (rule of thumb). Help them find slugs: slugs shelter under flat trap boards laid between rows by day (OSU, p. 15); flip the boards in the morning with the ducks behind you, and feed them the slugs you hand-pick about two hours after sunset (rule of thumb, using OSU's methods). Earthworms and snails can carry poultry tapeworms (FAO, p. 24), so keep moving the flock to fresh ground. No slug bait, rat poison or insect spray where ducks forage (rule of thumb): some sprays are "highly toxic to ducks", and warfarin rat bait makes them bleed to death (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 118). 🏠 Housing, water and keeping bedding dry Ducks need shelter from predators and weather, and "a clean dry sheltered area where they can retreat, rest, clean and preen their feathers" to keep their plumage waterproof (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 98). A simple shed, cheap fencing, a wooden trough and a waterer are enough for a small flock (p. 99). Ducks don't roost; they sleep on the floor (rule of thumb) and lay "at ground level" (p. 107), so the floor must stay dry - and ducks "drink and excrete more water than chickens", with droppings over 90% water (p. 103). In our rainy season plan for it: 1. Site: high, well-drained ground so rain runs away; sandy soil is best (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 99), on a gentle south slope (FB 697, p. 14). 2. Raise the floor: dirt 4-6 inches above the ground, or boards raised 6-8 inches under 4 inches of sand or dry earth (FB 697, p. 16). 3. Bed it with straw or shavings and add fresh bedding on top whenever it gets wet; clean it out when soaked (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 103). Litter may build up for warmth in cold weather, but then ventilation is "absolutely necessary" (FB 697, p. 16). Never moldy straw (aspergillosis, under health). 4. Water outside, as far from the house as possible, once ducklings are about 3 weeks old;
housing-water-and-keeping-bedding-dry

is "absolutely necessary" (FB 697, p. 16). Never moldy straw (aspergillosis, under health). 4. Water outside, as far from the house as possible, once ducklings are about 3 weeks old; indoors only when it freezes, and then on a wire-mesh screen so spills drain away from the litter (Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 103-104). A screen over a gravel-filled pit does the job of the book's cement drain (rule of thumb). 5. No feed or water in the house at night for ducks over 3 weeks: it keeps litter dry and "is not harmful", if they get water 8-12 hours a day (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 115). 6. Air: "the comfort and health of the ducks depend on an abundant supply of pure, dry air"; open up wide on mild days to dry the bedding (FB 697, p. 16). Window openings and a ridge vent are enough for a small shed (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 105). 7. Yards: gently sloping; scrape off the fouled top few inches and replace with clean soil or sand (p. 103). 🌾 Feeding with no feed store What forage can do. Fewer than about 15 ducks with room to forage can live on that plus "unused garden vegetables, table scraps (bones must be ground), and other food leftovers", but "will likely grow very slowly and produce a small number of eggs"; above 10-15 ducks, feed at least some grain (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 111). "A few handfuls of grain scattered or placed in a trough in the evening will keep them nearer the house" (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 192) and brings them in to be shut up.

Home-grown rations The old duck farms fed a wet mash of ground grain and mill feeds, a little meat or fish meal, and plenty of chopped greens (FB 697, p. 21). Moldy grain and other poisons - Aflatoxin from moldy grain is the big one. Ducks are "highly susceptible", tiny amounts kill, and "wet harvest conditions encourage the growth of this mold" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 118). Store grain at no more than 10-12% moisture; never feed rancid fat or bran or putrid fish (p. 115). After a wet harvest, dry grain hard before storing it (rule of thumb). - Peanut meal often carries aflatoxin and rapeseed meal is "very harmful to ducks" (p. 114); rape greens are the old green feed above, the pressed seed meal is not. - Botulism (limp neck, death in 1-2 days) comes from stagnant ponds and carcasses; castor beans, many insect sprays and rat baits also poison ducks (p. 118). Never feed maggots from carcasses (Chickens guide). - Poisonous plants: the same as for chickens (foxglove, Scotch broom and the rest; Chickens guide). Dry season: forage dries up about July-October, so store feed for summer as well as winter (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 110-122 - duck nutrition, nutrient tables and sample rations; USDA FB 697, pp. 21-23 - mashes and green feed through the year.

💊 Niacin and leg trouble in ducklings Niacin is a B vitamin. In poultry, too little shows as a slipped tendon (perosis), swollen hocks and poor feathering, and its feed sources are wheat middlings, corn gluten meal and alfalfa (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 44). The book's duck starter has about 44-50 mg of niacin per kg of feed for the first two weeks (p. 119). - The library does not say outright that ducklings need more niacin than chicks. Duck keepers widely say so and add brewer's yeast or niacin to chick feed for ducklings (rule of thumb). The book itself accepts chicken rations for ducks (p. 111), so treat it as cheap insurance, not an emergency. - Without a store: B vitamins come in yeasts, fermented feeds and fresh cut greens (p. 44), and brewer's yeast is on the book's list of duck feeds (p. 111). Give ducklings greens, middlings, skim milk or whey, hard-boiled egg and any spent brewing yeast from the first days, and get them onto grass and bugs early (rule of thumb). - A duckling going lame or bow-legged: check the floor first (rough wire and stony ground injure duck legs, p. 102), then add yeast, greens and middlings (rule of thumb). The library gives no niacin dose, so neither does this guide.

🥚 Duck eggs: when and how many - Ducks lay early: mostly before 7 a.m. (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 108), within 3 hours after sunrise (FAO, p. 13). Keep them in until about 9:30 a.m., or they may lay in the pond and the eggs are lost (FB 697, p. 19). Collect about 7 and again about 10, and dig down in the nest bedding: ducks bury their eggs (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 108). - Season: with no lamp, laying follows day length (p. 105): most eggs from late winter to early summer, few in late fall and early winter (rule of thumb, as for chickens). Lighting to 14 hours gives 7-12 months of laying (p. 105) but burns lamp fuel every day; most households will do better storing spring eggs. - How many: egg breeds lay 230-300+ fully fed (p. 97); a Khaki Campbell lays about 90 eggs per 100 duck-days, about 73 g each (FAO, p. 13). On forage and scraps alone, "a small number of eggs" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 111). - By age: egg breeds lay well 3-4 years, the second year often as well as the first (FB 697, p. 11) - longer than hens. - The molt: after 7-12 months of laying, numbers fall and the duck molts; it takes 8-12 weeks to start again (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 108). Let it come on

- The molt: after 7-12 months of laying, numbers fall and the duck molts; it takes 8-12 weeks to start again (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 108). Let it come on its own ("Old advice"). - Size and taste: about one-fourth larger than hens' eggs (FB 697, p. 25), with a stronger taste (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 191); in baking, 4 duck eggs ≈ 5 hens' eggs (arithmetic). - They spoil faster: "in about a week" (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 191), faster in hot weather (FB 697, p. 25). Yard or mud eggs: don't set them; eat them soon, thoroughly cooked (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 108). The water-glass crocks for the spring surplus (Chickens guide; Preserving Food guide) were written for hens' eggs: use only clean, fresh, uncracked duck eggs and check them often (rule of thumb).

🐣 Hatching under hens, Muscovies or ducks Who will sit? Pekin and Runner ducks "rarely sit", so their eggs usually go under hens (FB 697, p. 19). Muscovy ducks are very good setters, "capable of hatching 12-15 duck eggs"; any broody duck needs a clean, dry nest box with feed and water close by (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 110). Setting a broody chicken hen is in the Chickens guide ("Broody hens and hatching without power"). Hatching eggs: - Clean nest eggs only. Most hatching trouble comes from eggs "soiled with duck manure under wet conditions", which lets germs in and makes sick ducklings (Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 107-108). Don't set cracked, misshapen, very big or very small eggs (p. 109). - Fresh: set within 1-3 days if you can; hatching drops about 3% after a week's storage and 10% after two. Store them small end down at about 55 °F, in a cellar (pp. 109-110). - Timing: 28 days; 33-35 days for Muscovies (FB 697, p. 19). Don't set eggs with different hatching times under one bird (FB 767, p. 18). - Under a chicken hen: a big hen covers about 7-10 duck eggs (rule of thumb: chicken hens cover 7-10 of the similar-sized turkey eggs, FB 1409, p. 33). Slip them under her at dusk, 1-4 days after she starts sitting (FAO, p. 40). Through the sitting: 1. A

7-10 of the similar-sized turkey eggs, FB 1409, p. 33). Slip them under her at dusk, 1-4 days after she starts sitting (FAO, p. 40). Through the sitting: 1. A hen sits a week longer than for her own eggs, so she "must be well cared for" (FB 697, p. 19): feed and water by the nest, and treat her for lice before she starts (FB 767, p. 18; FAO, p. 40). 2. Candle about day 5-7 and again about day 24. A living embryo shows a dark spot with veins; a dead one leaves a blood ring, and dead duck eggs rot fast and smell (FB 697, p. 20; Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 109). Hard-boil the clear ones for the ducklings (FB 697, p. 20). At day 25 the air cell fills about one-third of the egg (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 110). 3. Moisture: duck eggs "need more moisture at hatching time than do chicken eggs": sprinkle them with warm water just before they pip (FB 697, p. 19). A nest on slightly damp earth helps (FAO, p. 40). 4. The hatch is slow: 24-48 hours from pipping to out. When the first ones pip, let the hen off to eat and drink, then keep her on the nest until the hatch is over (FB 697, p. 19). First feed comes 24-36 hours after hatching (p. 21). Duck eggs

🐥 Raising ducklings with no power With a mother there is nothing to heat. A Muscovy broods and leads her own ducklings; shut her and the brood in a dry, predator-proof coop at night (rule of thumb). With a chicken hen, "confine the hens and allow the ducklings free range, as the hens are apt to wander too far with their broods" (FB 697, p. 21), and keep water near her (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 192). Warm and dry: "During their first four weeks, ducklings should be kept warm and dry" (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 192). 🦉 Predators: lock them in every night Ducks are slow on land and sleep on the ground, so a duck left out at night is easy prey (rule of thumb). Every predator in the Chickens guide's "Predators of the Illinois Valley" takes ducks; that section has the who-did-it table, hardware cloth and the electric fence. For ducks: - Owls and hawks: the great horned owl hunts at night, even in forest, and eats "chickens, ducks and other poultry"; hawks carry off small birds by day. All birds of prey are federally protected - don't shoot them (Kentucky ID-245, p. 4). Raise ducklings in a covered pen. - Mink and raccoons hunt along creeks and ponds (rule of thumb); the weasel family, mink included, "often kill just for sport" (Kentucky ID-245, p. 3). A pond is not a safe bed: ducks on water at night are still within reach (rule of thumb). - Shut them in every night. Ducks are "easy to herd" (FAO, p. 13): put the evening grain inside and walk them in slowly behind a long stick (rule of thumb). A 2-ft fence holds ducks in, not predators out. - Bears: feed in a bear-resistant container or locked building, and an electric fence powered day and night (ODFW, pp. 1-2). Cougars: "Move them to sheds or barns at night"; Oregon law lets a landowner kill one damaging livestock

🩺 Duck health with no vet Ducks are "less subject to disease than chickens" (FB 697, p. 13) and shrug off most chicken diseases, but they carry Newcastle disease and cholera to chickens and fall easily to their own diseases (FAO, p. 51; Practical Poultry Raising, p. 191). The books' duck vaccines won't exist after the collapse, so prevention is everything: - Keep wild ducks and geese away from your flock, its water and its feed. 🔥 Heat, smoke and fire season - Ducks shed heat through their bills and feet in water cooler than their 107 °F body; 50-70 °F water is ideal (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 115). In July-August give shade (FB 697, p. 15) and a shallow tub of cool water, refilled daily. Muscovies handle heat best (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 95). - Smoke: watch for coughing, open-mouth breathing and watery eyes; keep water clean and fresh and put off stressful jobs (PNW 783, p. 10). Keep crates for the whole flock to walk them into at dusk if you must leave (rule of thumb); see the Wildfire guide.

🔪 Butchering and plucking When: young ducks are best at 8-11 weeks, once the long wing feathers are full length; held longer, "the market quality of their flesh depreciates, their weight decreases", and it takes several weeks to bring them back (FB 697, pp. 5, 24) while the next feathers grow in, full of pinfeathers (rule of thumb). Well grown, they weigh about 5½ lb at 11 weeks (p. 24). A Muscovy drake reaches about 9½ lb at 12 weeks on full feed (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 99) (arithmetic, from 4,300 g). Old layers and spare drakes are stew. Before and killing: no feed for 8-12 hours, water available, a clean area for gutting (Chickens guide, "Humane slaughter and butchering"). Hang the duck by its feet or head-down in a cone and cut the jugular vein and carotid artery on one side of the neck, next to the jaw (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 116); FB 697 first stuns it with a hard blow on the head (p. 24).

Waxing with beeswax The farms dipped ducks in melted wax (paraffin), let it set and peeled it off, "bringing with it hard to remove pinfeathers" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 116). Beeswax does the same job. It is precious, so dip only after dry-plucking and save every scrap to melt down again (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 194). Rendering and storing beeswax are in the Bees guide ("Beeswax: rendering and uses"). 1. The pot: big enough to dunk the whole bird; enamel or stainless (aluminum, copper, brass, zinc, tin and iron stain the wax); soft rainwater (hard water turns wax soapy). Put the beeswax in the water and heat it; it melts and floats on top (FAO Forest, p. 111). 2. Heat: beeswax melts at 62-64 °C (144-147 °F), darkens above 85 °C (185 °F), and boiling ruins it. "Beeswax must never be heated with a direct flame: always heat it in a container of water" (same page). Keep the water just hot enough that all the wax stays liquid. 3. Fire: if wax catches, take it off the heat and smother it with a metal lid or damp cloth; never throw water on burning wax (Practical Action, p. 3). Work outdoors, never on a red-flag day (rule of thumb). 4. Dip: pluck the big feathers, chill the bird, then dip it through the wax 5-10 seconds (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat,

never on a red-flag day (rule of thumb). 4. Dip: pluck the big feathers, chill the bird, then dip it through the wax 5-10 seconds (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 84), holding it by the feet and head as the goose bulletin does for scalding (FB 767, p. 28). A second dip builds a thicker coat (rule of thumb). 5. Set: plunge it in cold water to harden the wax (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 116), or hang it 2 minutes (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 84). 6. Peel the wax off in sheets; the down and pinfeathers come with it. Wash the bird in cool water to finish chilling it (same page). 7. Reclaim the wax: melt the peelings in water, strain through cotton cloth stretched over a can with both ends cut out, and let it cool slowly; the clean wax sets in a cake on top and you scrape the dirt off its underside (FAO Forest, p. 111). Keep this wax for plucking, not candles or salves (rule of thumb). Dry-pick, dip, set, peel, and melt the wax down again (a diagram drawn for this guide). Gutting: as for a chicken, cutting out the oil gland above the tail (Chickens guide); then chill in cold water (FB 697, p. 25). Render duck fat slowly like lard (Food from Scratch) (rule of thumb), and pressure-can the meat

above the tail (Chickens guide); then chill in cold water (FB 697, p. 25). Render duck fat slowly like lard (Food from Scratch) (rule of thumb), and pressure-can the meat as for chicken (Preserving Food guide). 📚 Go deeper: Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 84 - dry-picking and waxing ducks and geese; UMN EB 385, p. 2 - tools, killing and scalding waterfowl; USDA FB 697, pp. 24-25 - killing, picking and cooling.

🪶 Down and feathers Ducks give down for "bedding and warm jackets" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 95): "pillows, comforters and down-filled jackets" (p. 116). - How much: about 2½ ounces of usable feathers a duck (FB 697, p. 25), so a pound of feathers and down takes 6-7 ducks (arithmetic). - Sort as you pluck: big wing and tail feathers apart from body feathers and down, and duck feathers apart from chicken feathers (FB 767, p. 28). Dry-picked down is the cleanest (UMN EB 385, p. 2). Don't pluck live birds: farmers "consider it harmful to the birds" (FB 767, p. 28). - Wash in water with detergent or soap, or borax and washing soda (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 194); rinse well and squeeze out in a cloth bag (rule of thumb). - Dry thoroughly: in thin layers in a loft, turned several times (FB 697, p. 25), or in burlap sacks hung in a loft, or spread in a dry, airy room and stirred now and then (FB 767, p. 28). Damp feathers mold and stink; our dry summer is the time to do a year's worth (rule of thumb). - Sew down into closely woven cloth so quill tips don't poke through, in small stitched pockets so it can't all slide to one end (rule of thumb). Wet down loses its warmth (Clothing & Leather guide). - Manure:

🧬 Keeping the flock going - Breed from your best: for meat, "large, vigorous breeding ducks that have broad, deep bodies" (FB 697, p. 18); for eggs, the ducks still laying well in their second and third years (rule of thumb, since egg breeds lay well 3-4 years, p. 11); for mothers, Muscovies that sit tight. - Drakes a month older than the ducks give fertile eggs sooner; too many drakes injure ducks: 1 to 5-7 (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 107; FB 697 used about 1 to 6-7, p. 19). - Drake or duck? A common drake is coarser and has a curl in his tail feathers (FB 697, p. 19); a Muscovy drake is far bigger than the duck (p. 7). Ducks quack loudly; drakes have a hoarse, quiet voice (rule of thumb). - Don't let breeders get fat: growing breeders kept a little hungry start laying later but lay more, bigger and more fertile eggs; feel the belly for fat (Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 106, 114). On forage and scraps this mostly takes care of itself (rule of thumb). - Keep Muscovy blood separate if you breed both kinds, since the crosses are sterile (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 96): pen the Muscovy drake away from the layers in the hatching months, and eat any mule ducklings (rule of thumb). - Fresh blood: trade drakes with neighbors every few

Never hatch from yard eggs or dirty eggs (Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 107-108), or from a flock that has had a die-off (rule of thumb). 🪿 Geese: Grazing, Guarding, Meat and Down How to keep a few geese that live mostly on grass and give meat, fat, feathers and down with no feed store, vet or power: breeds, weeding with geese, what they can and can't do as alarm "guards", housing and water, pairs, hatching under geese or hens, goslings, feeding, predators, health, butchering and plucking, down, goose fat, the year in the valley, and how many a family needs. The goose books are thin: the main one is USDA Goose Raising (Farmers' Bulletin 767, 1954) in Animals\Poultry, with Raising Healthy Poultry, Practical Poultry Raising and Common Poultry Diseases; butchering is in Small-Livestock\Slaughter-Processing and Animals\Cattle-Horses-Pigs, feather care in Household Discoveries (Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do), all under Southern-Oregon\ (download list: local/library-files.txt). Where the work is the same as for chickens, this guide points to the Chickens guide. Numbers this guide works out itself say (arithmetic); check them with the Calculator. ### The short version - Geese live mostly on grass. 15-25 geese an acre of good pasture in summer and fall, with a little grain (FB 767, p. 24). Our summers are dry: plan irrigated pasture or cut green feed, and grain and hay all winter (p. 25). - Shut them in every night, goslings above all (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124). Geese raise the alarm; they don't beat coyotes, cougars or bears. A working electric fence is the

Shut them in every night, goslings above all (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124). Geese raise the alarm; they don't beat coyotes, cougars or bears. A working electric fence is the surest stop for bears (ODFW, p. 2). - Start with pairs or trios: 1 gander to 1-2 geese while he is young. Matings last for years, and geese are slow to accept a new mate (FB 767, p. 16). - Hatch under a goose (10-15 eggs) or a hen (4-6). Goose eggs take 28-31 days. Under a hen, sprinkle them with lukewarm water every day for the last 10-14 days (pp. 17-18). - Goslings: dry, warm and locked up. No rain the first month, and no swimming until they are partly feathered (p. 22). - Water always, but heads only. No stagnant ponds (botulism), and keep wild ducks and geese away from your flock (bird flu) (UF PS044, p. 11; Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 78). - Kill in late fall, after 3-5 weeks of grain in cool weather and when they are free of pinfeathers. Dry-pick to save the down. Never pluck live geese (FB 767, pp. 26, 28). - Down is one of the warmest natural fills, but only clean and dry; wet, it goes lumpy and loses its warmth (AFH 10-644, p. 177).

🪿 Choosing breeds Geese are "large, hardy, aggressive, noisy birds that need little attention when mature" and may live 30 years (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124). Farms kept them for meat and feathers; the eggs were a side crop (FB 767, p. 5). Standard weights are for a grown gander and goose; farm geese usually weigh less (same page). | Breed | Gander / goose | Eggs a year | Notes | | Emden (white) | 26 / 20 lb | 35-40 or more | The usual meat goose: white pinfeathers, grows fast, matures early, sits better than the Toulouse (FB 767, pp. 5-6) | | Toulouse (gray) | 26 / 20 lb | 25-40 or more; 35-50 in Practical Poultry Raising, p. 193 | Docile, loose-feathered, grows fast; big "dewlap" strains are show birds (p. 5) | | African (gray-brown, black knob) | 20 / 18 lb | Good layer | Grows fast, matures early; dark bill and pinfeathers (pp. 7-8) | | Chinese (brown or white, knob) | 12 / 10 lb | 40-65 or more | Best layers, start earlier in the year; small enough for one family meal (p. 9) | | Pilgrim | 14 / 13 lb | - | Ganders white, geese gray, even at a day old (p. 11) | | Buff | 18 / 16 lb | - | A fair market

Sebastopol and Egyptian geese are for show (p. 12). - Canada geese are a wild species. Kept, they need close confinement, pair only, mature late and lay very few eggs; crossed with tame geese they give a usually sterile hybrid (FB 767, pp. 10-11). Wild geese are game birds with seasons and limits (ODFW, p. 19). - Medium-sized, vigorous birds breed best; extra-large ones don't (FB 767, p. 14). Smaller geese (about 9 lb) are easier for a family flock to manage (FAO, p. 14). - For the valley (rule of thumb): an Emden, a Chinese or a cross of the two. Emdens sit well, big Toulouse breeders want bathing water that our dry summers don't give (FB 767, pp. 6, 14), and the Chinese and African "do best in the tropics" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124), so they should stand our heat. 🌱 Geese as grazers and weeders Geese are "the closest grazers known": grown geese and half-grown goslings "can get most of their living from a good green pasture". Don't overstock; too many geese kill the grass (FB 767, p. 13). They are choosy: they won't eat tough, dry grass and some other plants (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 193). - How many: 15-25 geese an acre of good pasture in summer and fall, with some grain. With other stock and in orchards they "keep down the coarse grasses and weeds" (FB 767, p. 24). - Our dry season: valley farm ground is used "mainly for irrigated hay and pasture" (Josephine County soil survey, p. 7). When the grass browns, cut them alfalfa, oats, clover, rape, rye, barley, beets, cabbages or green corn stalks (FB 767, p. 24). - Serpentine ground grows poor, low-calcium forage and is poor for stock ponds (soil survey, p. 49); graze geese on better ground and keep oyster shell out (rule of thumb). Weeding a crop with geese: 1. Use them where the crop is tough and the weeds are tender. Geese eat "any tender green feed": keep them out of corn until it is "fairly large and tough" (FB 767, p. 24), and out of lettuce, cabbage, beets and other greens they are fed on (rule of thumb). Orchards, vineyards, strawberries and corn with tough stalks
geese-as-grazers-and-weeders

and tough" (FB 767, p. 24), and out of lettuce, cabbage, beets and other greens they are fed on (rule of thumb). Orchards, vineyards, strawberries and corn with tough stalks all suit (Practical Poultry Raising, pp. 193-194). 2. Start young. Put in 6-week-old goslings (or older geese) in spring while the weeds are small, with shade, water and a little grain in the evening (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 194; FB 767, p. 24). 3. Strawberries: 5-7 geese an acre, with grain at about 1 lb a day for five geese (FB 767, pp. 24-25). 4. Move the feed, water and shade every few days. Geese kept in one place too long "destroy older plants". A low shade of posts and wire roofed with straw can be moved around the field (pp. 24-25). 5. Take them out before the fruit. FB 767 keeps them in "until the berries are nearly ready to ripen" and puts them back after picking until late summer or fall (pp. 24-25); the Peace Corps book takes them out at blossom time (p. 194). If you can't watch them daily, use blossom time. 6. Fence 3-4 ft high, or clip the flight feathers of one wing (FB 767, p. 25). Movable electric net rates "highly effective" against dogs, coyotes, foxes and bobcats (UC ANR 8598, p. 5). 7. Expect to hoe too: some weeds geese won't eat

767, p. 25). Movable electric net rates "highly effective" against dogs, coyotes, foxes and bobcats (UC ANR 8598, p. 5). 7. Expect to hoe too: some weeds geese won't eat (FB 767, p. 25). 📣 Geese as alarm "guards": what they can and can't do What they can do. Geese are kept for their "ability to ... act as watch dogs" and are "aggressive, noisy birds" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124). They are "easily disturbed" (FB 767, p. 16), so something new in the yard sets them off. A gander stays by the nest to guard his goose while she lays (p. 15). A watch dog warns of people as well as animals: see the "Early warning with no grid" section of the Home Defense guide. What they can't do: - Fight off a real predator. Goslings must be locked up at night (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124), and a grown goose is a meal for a coyote, bobcat, cougar, bear or loose dog (rule of thumb). - Scare predators off for long. Predators get used to noises (Kentucky ID-245, p. 6). - Replace a guardian dog. A guardian dog that stays with the flock works day and night (same page). Night pens and guardian dogs rate "highly effective" against coyotes, cougars and bears (UC ANR 8598, p. 5); geese aren't on that list at all. See the Dogs guide. - Tell friend from foe. They honk at deer, dogs and the neighbors too, so learn their calls. Nesting ganders go for children (rule of thumb). Using them as an alarm (rule of thumb):
geese-as-alarm-guards-what-they-can-and-can-t-do

foe. They honk at deer, dogs and the neighbors too, so learn their calls. Nesting ganders go for children (rule of thumb). Using them as an alarm (rule of thumb): put the night pen where you can hear it from the bedroom, near the house and the gate. A goose shut in a shed still honks at something prowling the pen. Count them each evening as they go in.

🏠 Housing, fences and water - Shelter: grown geese "seldom use a house" except in extreme cold or deep snow; keep houses clean (FB 767, p. 14). Here the house is for safety at night: shut stock in sheds at night against cougars (ODFW, p. 2); night pens work against coyotes, cougars and bears (UC ANR 8598, p. 5). A light feed "late in the afternoon helps to bring the goslings back to their coops" (FB 767, p. 24). - Goslings: about 1 sq ft each by 2 weeks old on deep litter; no house needed after 6 weeks (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 193), or 6-8 weeks (FB 767, p. 24). Here, still lock them up. - Nests (FB 767, pp. 14, 17): outside nest boxes at least 24 in square; a packing box turned open side down with a hole in one end works. Indoors, nests about 18 in square, divided by bricks or thick boards. Straw in all of them, one nest for every three geese, spaced apart; let the geese choose. FB 767's laying coop is 3 ft deep, 6 ft long, 3 ft high in front and 2 ft at the back (p. 14). - Fences: 3-4 ft keeps geese in a big field (p. 25); 3 ft in the Peace Corps book (p. 193). Clip one wing if they fly out. Water: - To drink,
housing-fences-and-water

3-4 ft keeps geese in a big field (p. 25); 3 ft in the Peace Corps book (p. 193). Clip one wing if they fly out. Water: - To drink, always, in tubs or buckets outside the fence so geese reach through and can't get their feet in. Hog fountains suit a bigger flock (FB 767, pp. 24, 26). - Goslings: containers "deep enough that the goslings can clean their bills" but letting in only their heads (p. 23). - To swim? Not needed. Geese "do not need water to breed" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124). Emdens breed well without it, though big Toulouse breeders like a bathing place (FB 767, pp. 13-14). - Ponds have dangers: botulism grows in stagnant water with rotting plants or carcasses (UF PS044, p. 11), and wild waterfowl bring bird flu (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 78). A tub you empty and scrub is safer (rule of thumb). Grown geese drink from a tub outside the fence; goslings get water deep enough for the bill but room for the head only (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: FB 767, pp. 13-17 - water, houses and nests, with photos; Chickens guide - "The coop: space, roosts, nests, air and litter".

💑 Mating and pairs Geese "mate selectively and for life" (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 193). - How many geese per gander (FB 767, p. 16): 1-5, but pairs and trios are commonest and usually best. A young gander gets 1 or 2 geese; small-breed ganders can take more. Emdens did as well at 4 geese to a gander as at 2 or 3. The Peace Corps book asks for at least one gander for every two geese (p. 193). - Mated groups keep to themselves, each near its own nest, so pairs can share one flock (FB 767, pp. 14, 16). Make matings by December; they usually stay the same for years. Geese are slow to take a new mate: when you change them, keep the old partners as far apart as you can (same pages). - Ages (p. 16): Toulouse and Emden breed well in their first laying year; very large birds not before the second. Both sexes breed best at 2-5 years; put older ganders with young geese. Geese lay to 10 or more, ganders keep 5+ years, but younger flocks pay better. Eat late-hatched goslings and those from a goose's first-year eggs; keep breeders from older geese. - Telling sexes apart (p. 16): the gander is bigger and coarser, with a longer neck, bigger head and a high-pitched voice; the goose's cry is lower and deeper. To

- Telling sexes apart (p. 16): the gander is bigger and coarser, with a longer neck, bigger head and a high-pitched voice; the goose's cry is lower and deeper. To be sure, press gently around the vent: a goose shows a folded, wrinkled muscle; a gander's organ comes out. Pilgrims show their sex by color (p. 11). - New blood: trade a gander with a neighbor every few years, and pair him up in the fall (rule of thumb).

🥚 Eggs and hatching: under geese or hens Laying: geese start in February, March or April and lay until late June, mostly in the morning; Chinese start earlier (FB 767, p. 16). Young geese laid about 30 eggs their first year and older geese 40-50; the older geese's eggs hatched 20% better and weighed 7¼-7½ oz against about 5½ (p. 17). Take eggs daily and a goose lays longer; to stop one sitting, shut her 4-7 days in a slat-bottomed crate near the gander (p. 17). Hatching eggs (FB 767, p. 17): collect twice a day in cold weather, then daily; keep them cool, turn them daily if held over a couple of days, and set them within a week. Wipe dirty eggs with a damp cloth. Under a goose: she covers 10-15 eggs, depending on her size and the season (p. 17). Give her a place to bathe and she needs no extra moisture (p. 18). Geese "make the best mothers" (p. 22). Under a hen (so the geese keep laying) (FB 767, pp. 17-18): 1. 4-6 eggs per hen, by her size. Turkeys and Muscovy ducks are bigger and better sitters than hens. 2. Dust the hen for lice first (see the Chickens guide): she sits a week longer than for her own eggs. 3. Nest on the ground or on grass turf. Sprinkle the eggs with lukewarm
eggs-and-hatching-under-geese-or-hens

lice first (see the Chickens guide): she sits a week longer than for her own eggs. 3. Nest on the ground or on grass turf. Sprinkle the eggs with lukewarm water every day for the last 10-14 days. 4. Mark the eggs and turn them by hand each day: they are too big for a hen to turn, and keep them moist (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 193). Some breeders think turning unnecessary (FB 767, p. 18). 5. Candle between day 10 and day 14 and take out clear eggs and dead embryos (FB 767, p. 18). Timing: 28-31 days, the big breeds slowest; Emdens 29-31 (p. 18). Goslings hatch slowly: leave the hen or goose alone, unless some hatch far ahead of the rest; then take the first ones in and keep them warm until the hatch is over (p. 21). Fertility runs about 90% (p. 18). Machines hatch only 40-60% of goose eggs; a still-air one runs about 102 °F, then 103 °F after day 10, eggs flat, turned right over twice a day and sprayed (FB 767, p. 18). Without power, the goose and the hen are your incubators.

🐣 Raising goslings With a goose or hen (FB 767, pp. 21-22): 1. When geese and hens hatch on the same day, give all the goslings to the geese. One hen raises about five goslings (p. 22); up to six in the Peace Corps book (p. 193). 2. Keep the hen shut in the coop about 2 weeks; the goslings go in and out. In mild weather they need her heat only 10 days to 2 weeks. Dry, clean litter. 3. Keep goslings out of the rain for the first month, and shut them in each morning until the grass is dry, for 2-3 weeks. No swimming until they are partly feathered. A gosling chilled in a cold rain can sometimes be saved by drying it in flannel near the fire (p. 22). 4. Grazing from 3-4 days old. Move the coop often onto fresh grass (p. 22). On range, watch for holes they get stuck in and for soaking; give shade in hot weather and keep them apart from older geese (p. 23). 5. Lock them in every night against predators (p. 21). 6. Mark them with a small V cut in the web of the foot to record age and family (p. 22). The brood coop: 2 by 3 ft holds 25 young goslings: wooden floor with straw, a sliding screen to close the front at night, and
raising-goslings

age and family (p. 22). The brood coop: 2 by 3 ft holds 25 young goslings: wooden floor with straw, a sliding screen to close the front at night, and a portable wire runway moved every day or two onto fresh ground (FB 767, p. 21; 🖼 photo). Goslings brooded by a hen need "good-sized, waterproof coops with board floors" (p. 22). A brood coop for 25 goslings: shut the screen at night and move coop and run onto fresh grass every day or two (a diagram drawn for this guide). Without a hen or goose: goslings need heat only a short time: a brooder starts at about 90 °F, cut gradually over 10 days to 3 weeks by the weather (FB 767, p. 21). Keep them warm and dry the first few weeks (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124). The fire-free ways to heat a brooder are in the "Raising chicks with no heat lamp" section of the Chickens guide.

🌾 Feeding with no feed store Grass first. Grown geese "pick up most of their living" except in winter and early in the breeding season (FB 767, p. 25). With plenty of pasture they need no more than 2 lb of extra feed per bird a week (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124); the Peace Corps book gives 1-2 lb a week, and only until 12 weeks old (p. 193). Goslings (FB 767, pp. 23-24): - Feed them as soon as they hatch. FB 767 asks for about 18% protein; the other books 20-22% (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124). Its plain starter is corn meal and rolled oats with an equal weight of chick mash, fed slightly moist with water or skim milk. - With no store mash: corn meal and rolled oats wet with skim milk, a little chopped hard-boiled egg for protein, and plenty of chopped tender grass, lettuce or cabbage (rule of thumb, from the bulletin's own feeds). - 3-4 feeds a day the first week, 2-3 a day to 4 weeks, only what they clean up in 15 minutes. Fine sharp sand or grit always. - After 2-3 weeks on tender grass, cut the grain way down. Many farm flocks lived on grass alone from then on, but growth slowed: 186 goslings on 5 acres needed mash after 8 weeks, and 42 on 1 acre slowed at
feeding-with-no-feed-store

Many farm flocks lived on grass alone from then on, but growth slowed: 186 goslings on 5 acres needed mash after 8 weeks, and 42 on 1 acre slowed at 7-10 weeks (p. 24). Keep a little grain going. Breeders through the winter (FB 767, p. 25): - Grain plus roughage once the grass stops: oats mixed with corn, wheat or barley, and chopped vegetables, clover or alfalfa hay, chopped corn stalks or mold-free silage. Lots of corn makes breeders too fat. - Before laying, about 4 oz of mash and 4 oz of grain a bird a day. A home mash: 2 parts each ground wheat, corn and oats; 1 part each ground barley and bran; 1 part fish or meat meal (same page). Feed it from late winter so goslings hatch when there is green grass (p. 17). - Oyster shell and grit always (p. 26); boiled, dried and crushed eggshells will do for shell (Chickens guide). Feed safety: - No moldy straw or feed. Mold causes aspergillosis, and mold poisons (aflatoxins) kill ducks in very small amounts (Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 117-118); treat geese the same (rule of thumb). - Store grain where bears can't reach: a bear-resistant container or a locked building, not the pen (ODFW, p. 1). - Poison plants that grow here include bracken fern, death camas, poison and water hemlock, lupines, horsetail, St.

Penned birds are at more risk than ranging ones, so never throw hedge or weed clippings into the pen (p. 54). The same list names alfalfa, which FB 767 calls excellent goose range (p. 24); feed it in a mix. 📚 Go deeper: FB 767, pp. 23-25 - gosling, growing and breeder rations; Seed Bank guide - growing grain, kale, beets and clover.

🦝 Predators Who takes geese: the stock-predator table in UC ANR 8598, p. 5 lists dogs, coyotes, cougars, black bears, foxes and bobcats, all of them here. Great horned owls take "chickens, ducks and other poultry" at night, and hawks carry off small birds by day; hawks and owls are protected by law (Kentucky ID-245, p. 4). For eggs and goslings, the "who did it" table in the Chickens guide fits geese too. 1. Shut them in a secure place every night and close every door; leave no feed in the run overnight; remove dead birds at once (Kentucky ID-245, p. 6). 2. Goslings especially: "confined at night and protected against predatory animals" (FB 767, p. 21). 3. Hardware cloth buried at least 12 inches around the night pen stops diggers (Kentucky ID-245, p. 6). 4. Bears: an electric fence of at least 3 wires (5-6 better), lowest 7-9 in, top 36-42 in, 8-10 in apart, energizer at least 6,000 volts and 0.5 joules, hardware cloth inside, weeds kept off (ODFW, p. 2). Without the grid that means a solar charger (Off-Grid Power guide). 5. Cougars: "Fence and shelter livestock. Move them to sheds or barns at night." Oregon law lets a landowner kill a cougar that is damaging livestock; call ODFW (ODFW, p. 2). 6. A guardian dog that stays with the flock is the day-and-night answer (Kentucky ID-245,

lets a landowner kill a cougar that is damaging livestock; call ODFW (ODFW, p. 2). 6. A guardian dog that stays with the flock is the day-and-night answer (Kentucky ID-245, p. 6). A night pen: shed, buried hardware cloth, and hot wires outside to the bear-fence numbers above (a diagram drawn for this guide).

That means dry litter, clean water, fresh ground for goslings, young birds apart from old ones (p. 23), and a closed flock: no new birds without a month apart (rule of thumb). 🔪 Butchering and plucking When: fatten 3-5 weeks first, best in cool weather (FB 767, p. 26). Young geese can go at 10-13 weeks as "green geese" of 10-12 lb; after that they are thinner and full of pinfeathers "for several weeks". Farm geese were killed at 5-6 months, 11-15 lb, in late fall (pp. 26-27), when they are "free from the small pinfeathers" and carry the most fat (p. 28). Keep the breeders lean (p. 26). Before: no feed for about 12 hours, water left in (FB 767, p. 27). Handle them gently: goose flesh "bruises very easily" (same page). Catch a goose by the neck close to the head, then gather the wings against its body and carry it under your arm (rule of thumb). Killing - practice first, and see the Chickens guide for the setup: 1. Stun: a goose is too big for an easy neck pull. One hard blow to the top of the head is acceptable for big birds; a clean chop with a sharp blade is too (AVMA, p. 77). FB 767 used a sharp blow to the back of the skull "with a heavy stick" (p. 27). 2. Bleed: hang it by the feet (a rope on a clothesline works), hold the head, and cut the neck vein on one or both sides with a sharp knife; hold on until bleeding and

the feet (a rope on a clothesline works), hold the head, and cut the neck vein on one or both sides with a sharp knife; hold on until bleeding and flapping stop (UMN EB 385, p. 2). Plucking - "much more difficult" than chickens (FB 767, p. 27). 🪶 Down and feathers for warmth What down is: "the soft plumage found between the skin and the contour feathers", and geese are a good source. It is "one of the warmest natural materials available when kept clean and dry", but it soaks up rain and sweat, and wet down goes lumpy and loses its insulation (AFH 10-644, p. 177; FM 21-76, p. 177). Goose feathers were worth more than any other poultry feathers, and white more than colored (FB 767, p. 29): worth saving and trading. Saving it: 1. Sort as you pluck: wing and tail quills, body feathers, down, each in its own sack; goose apart from chicken and duck (FB 767, p. 28). Big quills make pens (Paper & Ink guide). 2. Dry: hang dry-picked feathers in burlap sacks in a loft, or spread them in a dry, airy room and stir now and then (p. 28). 3. Clean (Household Discoveries, p. 257): new feathers "quickly become foul as the grease contained in the quills decays". Beat them between wet burlap to loosen dirt. Soak 3-4 days in clear limewater, or in 1 teaspoon of cooking soda per quart of water. Pour through cheesecloth and rinse in cold water. Then boil them in water with a cupful of borax, drain and squeeze. Hang them in the cheesecloth on a line, shaking now and then, for several days.
down-and-feathers-for-warmth

cold water. Then boil them in water with a cupful of borax, drain and squeeze. Hang them in the cheesecloth on a line, shaking now and then, for several days. Don't use soap. Lime burns skin and eyes: gloves and goggles (rule of thumb). 4. Store them dry in a cloth bag in a dry place until you have enough (p. 39). Using it: - Pillows and feather beds take the body feathers. To move feathers from one tick to another, open a little of the seam, baste the new tick's opening over it, and shake them across (Household Discoveries, p. 54). - Quilts: make blocks 2-3 ft square, each sewn into a bag on three sides, filled, tied at intervals and sewn together; no quilting frame is needed (p. 55, written for cotton batting). For down, use smaller pockets so it can't all slide to one end, and tightly woven cloth so it can't work through (rule of thumb). A flattened quilt fluffs up again if shaken, brushed and sunned for a few hours (p. 257). - Our winters are wet: use down for bedding and dry cold, keep it under a shell, and wear wool in the rain (rule of thumb). See the "Dressing for our cold-wet winters" section of the Clothing & Leather guide. - Never pluck live geese: it was "almost entirely discontinued" because "most goose

🫙 Goose fat Where it comes from: "When the weather gets cold in the fall, geese put on considerable fat" (FB 767, p. 28). Geese raised on grass without grain "are likely to be thin"; they fatten best in cool weather on grain fed freely for 3-5 weeks (p. 26). Fattening (FB 767, p. 27): three feeds a day, or two of mash and one of whole corn, oats or barley, at regular times; little exercise in a small yard; some hay or pulped vegetables; and water they can get only their heads into. The bulletin's mash is mostly corn meal (45%) and ground oats, barley or wheat (35%). Force-feeding gives a fatty, swollen liver and isn't worth the labor (same page). In the kitchen: goose meat is "thoroughly infiltrated with fat" (Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, p. 250). Families "draw off much of the fat as grease" while it cooks (FB 767, p. 28). Roast on a rack so the bird sits clear of its own fat, at 325 °F; goose is done at 180-185 °F inside the thick of the breast (Wyoming, p. 2). Pour the fat off into a jar as it gathers (rule of thumb). Rendering the raw fat (pull the fat pads from inside the body when you gut it (rule of thumb)); the method is the one for lard (Minnesota, pp. 2-3): 1. Chill the
goose-fat

raw fat (pull the fat pads from inside the body when you gut it (rule of thumb)); the method is the one for lard (Minnesota, pp. 2-3): 1. Chill the fat at once and render within about 5-7 days. 2. Cut it small. Put a little water in a clean kettle (no copper), start on low heat, stir often, and keep it at 235-245 °F. 3. Stop when the bubbling stops and the cracklings float, a medium chestnut brown. 4. Strain through double cheesecloth into scalded jars, filled to the top; cool fast; store cool and dark. Uses: cooking and baking fat, a winter source of calories (Food Security guide), and soap. For soap, boil scraps with a little salt water, let the fat set into a cake, and dry it well or it won't keep sweet (Household Discoveries, p. 179). More on rendering and rescuing rancid fat is in Food from Scratch.

👪 How many geese for a family - Start: one gander and two geese (a trio), or two pairs: "pair or trio matings are most common and usually give the best results" (FB 767, p. 16). - Eggs: about 30 a goose the first year and 40-50 after (p. 17): two older geese lay 80-100 big eggs (arithmetic). - Goslings: each goose can sit on 10-15 and each broody hen on 4-6 (p. 17). If about half the eggs you set grow into geese, a trio gives 15-20 goslings a year (rule of thumb). - Meat: at 5-6 months a goose weighs 11-15 lb alive (p. 27) and loses 25-30% drawn (p. 28), so about 8-11 lb of dressed bird, plus fat and down. Fifteen geese ≈ 120-165 lb (arithmetic). - Grass: at 15-25 geese an acre (p. 24), a trio and their goslings need about an acre of good pasture through summer and fall, more if it isn't watered (arithmetic). - Grain: at 4 oz of mash and 4 oz of grain a day (p. 25), three breeders eat about 180 lb in a 120-day winter (arithmetic), plus 3-5 weeks of free grain for each goose you fatten. A flock fed grain freely on thin range ate 100 lb a bird from January to July (pp. 25-26). Good grass cuts all of this. - Keeping it going: keep a

flock fed grain freely on thin range ate 100 lb a bird from January to July (pp. 25-26). Good grass cuts all of this. - Keeping it going: keep a young goose or two coming on: younger flocks pay better, and old geese hatch better eggs (pp. 16-17). Trade ganders with neighbors.

🦃 Turkeys: Meat for a Household How to keep a small flock of turkeys that breeds itself and puts big birds on the table with no feed store, hatchery, vet or electricity: breeds that still mate on their own, shelter and range, the protein poults need, hatching and brooding under hens, blackhead (why turkeys and chickens must not share ground), predators, health, butchering, and a year's plan for the Illinois Valley. Turkeys are harder than chickens: poults are fragile for 8-12 weeks, and one disease can wipe them out. The main book is USDA Turkey Raising (Farmers' Bulletin 1409, 1952) in Animals\Poultry; disease books are in Small-Livestock\Chickens and Animals\Veterinary (all under Southern-Oregon\; the download list is local/library-files.txt). Where the work is the same as for chickens, this guide sends you to the Chickens guide. (arithmetic) marks numbers worked out here (Calculator). ### The short version - Keep heritage (standard) turkeys: Bourbon Red, Narragansett, Black, Slate, standard Bronze, White Holland, Royal Palm. Broad-Breasted store turkeys are often too heavy to mate and need artificial insemination - a dead end after collapse (Practical Poultry Raising, pp. 195-196). - Never let turkeys onto ground that chickens use, or onto chicken manure. Chickens carry blackhead without looking sick, the germ lasts in the soil for years inside worm eggs, it kills poults at 6-18 weeks, and there is no cure (FB 1409, p. 68;

blackhead without looking sick, the germ lasts in the soil for years inside worm eggs, it kills poults at 6-18 weeks, and there is no cure (FB 1409, p. 68; FB 1652, p. 51). - Move the flock to clean ground every week or two and use any patch only 1 year in 3; feed and water where droppings can't get in (FB 1409, pp. 66-67). - A broody turkey hen is your incubator and brooder: she covers 15-18 eggs, hatches them on day 28 and broods up to 20 poults with no fuel (FB 1409, pp. 33, 37). - Poults need 24-28% protein - grain alone starves them - and must be taught to eat. They drown in deep water and smother in corners (FB 1409, p. 45; Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 124-125). - Shut them in every night and until well after dawn. Dogs, coyotes and foxes take turkeys, owls take birds roosting in the open, and only an electric fence stops a bear (FB 1409, pp. 56-57; ODFW, p. 2). - Butcher at 26-30 weeks, in cold weather. A 19-lb tom is hard to keep without refrigeration: kill one at a time and pressure-can the rest (FB 1409, p. 75; Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 125). - The 1952 bulletin's lice, mite and crop cures are poisons (sodium fluoride, nicotine, DDT, crankcase oil, bluestone). 🦃 Choosing turkeys that breed on their own Every future turkey has to hatch from your own flock, so the birds must mate, lay and sit by themselves. In 1952 the standard varieties were Bronze, White Holland, Bourbon Red, Narragansett, Black and Slate, with Royal Palm, Jersey Buff and Beltsville Small White as newer ones (FB 1409, p. 7); today such old varieties are sold as heritage turkeys (rule of thumb). The Broad Breasted Bronze, new to the U.S. about 1935, has more breast meat but "in reproductive ability... is inferior to most other varieties": fewer eggs, less fertile, less hatchable (p. 15). Its modern descendants, sold as "Bronze" and "White", "have difficulty in reproducing because of the heavy weight of the males and their poor fertility" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124); very large turkeys "must be inseminated artificially", while birds "closer to the wild cousin" have less breast "and thus, can breed more easily" (Practical Poultry Raising, pp. 195-196). | Type | Size at butchering age | Notes | | Standard Bronze | Heaviest standard variety; a tom of 21½ lb at 6½ months (p. 7) | Dark pinfeathers show on the skin; dark birds get "blueback" (p. 71) | | Narragansett, Black, Slate, Bourbon Red, White Holland | Medium: toms about 19-20 lb, hens about 12 lb at 28 weeks (pp. 10-11, 18) | The core of a

🏡 Housing, range and roosts After about 12 weeks, turkeys "can be raised with very little protection, even in cold climates" (FB 1409, p. 37). What they need is clean, drained ground, shade, a roof over the roosts and a night shelter predators can't enter. - Ground: sloping and drained, no stagnant water; an orchard makes a good yard (p. 20). Poorly drained ground "should be avoided at all costs" (p. 51) - here, the low, soggy winter spots. - Breeding yard: 100-150 sq ft of range per bird, best as two yards used a week each in turn; a flock of 30 needs a 12 × 16 ft shed (p. 20), so 6 breeders need about 600-900 sq ft a yard (arithmetic). Toms in neighboring pens fight through the wire: keep pens 10 ft apart or board the shared fence 3½ ft up (same page). - Shelter: face it south, boards on the storm sides, wire-covered openings 2-2½ ft wide at roost height (pp. 57-58); "in moderate climates... the roof being sufficient" (p. 62). Here: a good roof over roosts and feed, boards on the side the winter rains come from (rule of thumb). Built-up straw or shaving litter, cleaned out once a season (p. 22). - Roosts: poles about 2½ in across, 19-24 in apart, all at one height, 6-12 in up on skids (p. 28; p. 21
housing-range-and-roosts

cleaned out once a season (p. 22). - Roosts: poles about 2½ in across, 19-24 in apart, all at one height, 6-12 in up on skids (p. 28; p. 21 says 14 in); 12-15 in of pole per bird; for heavy broad-breasted birds, tops only 4-6 in up (p. 63). Wire over or under the poles gives better footing and keeps birds out of the droppings (p. 28). Narrow strips and wide flat boards dent the breastbone (pp. 70-71); heavy birds that jump down more than about 1 ft onto hard ground get bumblefoot and breast blisters (pp. 71-72). High roosts save them at night "but not in the early morning hours" (p. 57), so use a low rack inside a closed shelter (rule of thumb). A low roost rack on skids that can be dragged to clean ground (a diagram drawn for this guide). - Nests: about 16 × 20 in and 20 in high, entrance about 8 × 9 in, one for every 4 hens (pp. 28-29); a barrel on its side works (p. 33). Hens hunt for hidden places to lay: keep the yard short-grassed and free of bushes and find hidden nests (p. 32). - Fences and flying: 5-ft fence for young medium and small turkeys, 6-ft for breeders (p. 58), tight and close to the ground (p. 20). Hens and the lighter toms fly well:

and flying: 5-ft fence for young medium and small turkeys, 6-ft for breeders (p. 58), tight and close to the ground (p. 20). Hens and the lighter toms fly well: clip the flight feathers of one wing - but never a breeding tom's before the season; it throws him off balance for mating (p. 66). - Range: ½-2 acres per 100 turkeys of good green range, "possibly doubled or trebled" on dry range (p. 55) - which is what our summer hills become. With feed and water in one spot they stay within a few hundred yards (p. 52). Good range: alfalfa, clovers, orchard grass, ryegrass, kale, rape, vetch; rows of sunflowers, corn or Sudan grass give feed and shade (p. 56). Shade is a necessity in hot, sunny weather (p. 51). Turkeys flock tightly and "can be driven about... in much the same manner as sheep" (p. 56). - Water: clean, pans washed daily; creek or pond water "may carry disease germs or parasites" (p. 30). 📚 Go deeper: FB 1409, pp. 20-29 - breeding yards, roosts and nests; pp. 51-58 - range, shelters and fences.

🌾 Feeding with no feed store The 1952 bulletin feeds bought mashes of soybean meal, meat scrap, fish meal and vitamin oils. After collapse those become milk, eggs, insects, meat and fish scraps, fresh greens and sunshine, and protein is the hard part. Feed goes in hoppers or troughs, never on the ground (FB 1409, p. 49), covered from rain (p. 59). For calcium, grit, storing grain, maggot and worm beds, sprouted oats and poisonous plants, see the Chickens guide, "Feeding without a feed store".
feeding-with-no-feed-store

Protein for poults - How much: a starter of 24-26% protein (FB 1409, p. 45); three books give 28% (p. 46; Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 125; Practical Poultry Raising, p. 196). Then about 20% for growing birds and 15-16% from about 16 weeks (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 125; FB 1409, p. 46). Chicks get by on 18-20% (Chickens guide), so poults need far more "meat food" than chicks. - First feed within 24 hours. Poults live 24-72 hours on the yolk, but kept from feed much longer than a day they learn to eat "with difficulty". Heap feed on boards or pie plates with oatmeal or finely chopped greens scattered on top (p. 44). Tap a finger on the board like a pecking bird; red draws them to feed and water; otherwise they "may starve" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124). - A home-made starter (rule of thumb: the bulletin's ingredients in farm form) - rolled or finely ground grain, plus all of these you can spare: - Milk: sweet or slightly sour skim milk or buttermilk to drink, never in galvanized pans, one pan of water to three or four of milk, pans cleaned daily (FB 1409, pp. 41, 47); curds of soured milk are the same protein, solid. - Eggs: chopped hard-boiled eggs, such as clear ones taken out at candling. Bugs: insects, worms, maggots grown on plant waste

curds of soured milk are the same protein, solid. - Eggs: chopped hard-boiled eggs, such as clear ones taken out at candling. Bugs: insects, worms, maggots grown on plant waste - never maggots from carcasses (botulism; Chickens guide). - Meat and fish scraps, cooked and minced. No fish in the last 10 weeks before butchering, or the meat tastes fishy (FB 1409, pp. 49-50). - Greens chopped very fine (alfalfa, clover, onion tops, young grass, sprouted grain), fresh once or twice a day; never leave wilted greens (p. 45). Long clippings pack the crop (p. 73). - Grit: coarse sand or fine gravel, not needed on sand litter (p. 45). - Short of protein? Rough feathers and a white bar across the wing of dark poults (p. 74).
protein-for-poults

Growing turkeys on range - From 8 weeks, mash and grain are kept in front of them (p. 47). Where range feed is plentiful, from 8-10 weeks feed once a day all they will eat, and skip the grain while they glean stubble (p. 50). On range they eat insects, "great quantities of succulent green feed", waste grain and weed seeds (p. 5). - Grain: corn, wheat, barley, oats, spelt, emmer, proso millet or sorghum - all worth about the same, best two to four kinds in separate hoppers; crack corn until about 18 weeks; rye and buckwheat only a little (pp. 47-49). Oats fatten well (p. 47), and oats as about half the grain helps prevent feather picking (p. 74). Turkeys harvest proso and grain sorghum standing in the field (p. 50). - Milk: after 8 weeks, birds on good range with whole grain and all the skim milk they want need no water (p. 49), but no liquid milk in hot weather - it brings on pendulous crop (p. 73). - Finishing: full feed to the end; cool fall weather speeds it (p. 75). No long moves or sharp feed changes in the last 6 weeks (p. 49).
growing-turkeys-on-range

Feeding the breeders - Fall and winter: grain and a simple mash with sunshine and fresh greens; a third of the grain corn or barley (FB 1409, p. 25). Laying season: a 21-24% mash fed with equal grain, about 15-17% overall, grit and oyster shell always out (pp. 25-26); hay can't replace fresh greens for hatching eggs (p. 27). Standard varieties eat about 0.45 lb a day, 10% more without range (p. 28). Summer: about ¼ lb of grain per hen a day on good range, toms twice that (p. 24). - Store feed where bears can't get it (ODFW, p. 1). - Selenium: "crazy chick" disease (wobbling, falling over backward) hits poults under 2 months short of vitamin E or selenium (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 70). Selenium-shortage disease was first found in Oregon, yet selenium is toxic in excess and must be labeled in Oregon feeds (OSU EM 9094, p. 1): use only a labeled poultry mineral, exactly as the label says (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: FB 1409, pp. 44-50 - starting and growing feeds, grains and milk; Raising Healthy Poultry, pp. 38-55 - poultry nutrition; Seed Bank guide - growing grain, sunflowers and kale.

🥚 Eggs, broody hens and hatching Young hens lay their first egg at about 34-36 weeks old (FB 1409, p. 17), 2-3 weeks after mating; the natural season runs from late winter or early spring to about June 1. Without lamps, young hens averaged about 40 eggs - when broodiness was broken each time (pp. 30, 32); a hen left to sit lays far fewer (rule of thumb). Turkey eggs eat like chicken eggs, two for every three (p. 32). Hatching eggs: collect at least daily, store on their sides or small end down at 45-65 °F (best about 55 °F), and set within a week - two weeks if turned daily (p. 33). Setting a turkey hen (FB 1409, p. 33): 1. Wait until she has sat steadily for 4-5 days, then give her 15-18 eggs. 2. Nest: a box about 2 ft square or a barrel on its side, flat and shallow (deep nests crush eggs and poults), on damp sod with a little straw, out of the rain and safe from rats and crows. 3. Rid her of lice first - the ash-and-sulfur dust in the Chickens guide, not the bulletin's sodium fluoride. 4. Every day let her off to eat, drink and stretch (or give her a small run), with water, grain and fresh greens; see that each hen goes back to her own nest. 5.
eggs-broody-hens-and-hatching

her off to eat, drink and stretch (or give her a small run), with water, grain and fresh greens; see that each hen goes back to her own nest. 5. Keep the tom away: gobblers "often try to break the eggs" (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 196). 6. Candle at about day 7-9 and near day 24: clear eggs are infertile; a red spider-web of veins is a live one (FB 1409, p. 35). 7. The hatch is done by the morning of day 28 (p. 36); Practical Poultry Raising says 26-28 days. A chicken hen can hatch 7-10 turkey eggs (FB 1409, p. 33), but the eggs "must be hand turned" (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 196), and poults raised by hens, "especially chicken hens, are likely to contract disease" (FB 1409, p. 33). If you must, set her in a clean pen away from the chickens and move the poults to turkey ground at hatching (see "Blackhead"). Without any hen, incubator heat is the same as for chicken eggs, for 28 days, turning eggs at least three times a day until day 23-24 (pp. 34-35); "Hatching and brooding turkeys artificially is a difficult business" (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 196). Plan on hens. Too many broody hens? Four days in a slat-floored broody coop sets one laying again (FB 1409, p. 32).

🐣 Raising poults with no power Hen brooding is "a never-failing source of heat"; its faults are disease and parasites from the hen, and poults that wander off and die in storms or to predators (FB 1409, p. 36). Both can be managed. With the hen (FB 1409, pp. 36-37): 1. When the hatch is done, move hen and brood to a coop about 5 ft long, 3 ft wide and 3 ft high with a raised, rat-proof floor and screened openings rain can't beat into - one per hen, set apart on short grass, best with a wire-floored porch. 2. For the first day or so keep the poults in with her, with plenty of light, so they learn to eat and drink. 3. Then open the porch or a small yard. Keep poults out of long wet grass and heavy rain; shut them in every night. 4. With no wire floor, move the coop to fresh ground every few days and clean it weekly; clean sand is the best litter. 5. After about a week the hen may go out with them; make sure every bird comes back at evening. 6. Feed and water always in front of the poults; after 2-3 days put their feed where the hen can't reach, and give her grain and greens. 7. A turkey hen broods up to 20 poults, 25 in

the poults; after 2-3 days put their feed where the hen can't reach, and give her grain and greens. 7. A turkey hen broods up to 20 poults, 25 in warm weather. Move the poults at 8 weeks to clean rearing ground with a shelter. A coop for a turkey hen and her poults, sized from FB 1409, pp. 36-37 (a diagram drawn for this guide). What kills poults: - Cold and damp until about 12 weeks old (FB 1409, p. 37). - Panic: they run into fences and break their necks, pile up and suffocate, drown in a low dish or jump into a bucket (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124). Round off inside corners; start them on small jar-and-saucer waterers (FB 1409, p. 41). - Lice from the hen cause "high mortality" (p. 69): treat her before she sits. - Bad litter they eat: hay, oat or bearded-barley straw, sawdust, splintery shavings (p. 39). - Not a sickness: red fleshy growths on head and neck at 5-7 weeks ("shooting the red") are normal (p. 64). Without a hen the bulletin keeps 95-105 °F under the hover and 70-75 °F on the floor around it for 8 weeks (FB 1409, pp. 37, 40) - a great deal of heat to make without power, and lamp brooders with no stovepipe "do not give best results" (p. 43). For fuel-heated brooders and their carbon-monoxide and fire dangers, see the Chickens guide, "Raising chicks with no heat lamp"; brood only in warm weather (rule of thumb). 🐓 Toms, mating and keeping the line going Hens per tom - the books differ: 4-5 (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 125); 10 (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 196); for young toms, 13-20 depending on size, but only 9-10 for Broad-Breasted (FB 1409, p. 22). A household flock is small anyway: one young tom for up to about 10 heritage hens, plus a spare young tom - the bulletin keeps extra toms "as a safety precaution" (same page) (rule of thumb). - Raise a new tom every year (rule of thumb): toms past their first season show "a rather high percentage of sterility". Hens also do less well after their first year, but a proven good hen is worth a second or third (FB 1409, p. 22). - Put the tom in well before laying; cold weather makes toms inactive (pp. 22-23). Heavy hens mated to heavy toms need canvas saddles over the back; small and standard-weight birds don't. Clip toms' toenails short (not into the quick) and blunt sharp spurs (p. 23). - Pick breeders in October-November from your best birds near butchering age (p. 19): straight keel, broad back, full breast, upright carriage and a free, easy walk with no waddle or limp; straight legs not too short to mate; bright eyes. Skip families with pendulous crop, twisted legs or crooked backs (pp. 19, 71-72). Unlike the bulletin, also keep
toms-mating-and-keeping-the-line-going

waddle or limp; straight legs not too short to mate; bright eyes. Skip families with pendulous crop, twisted legs or crooked backs (pp. 19, 71-72). Unlike the bulletin, also keep the hens that sat and raised poults well (rule of thumb). - Telling sexes apart: toms strut, even as poults; the beard shows at 3-4 months; toms have broader hocks and a bigger snood (the fleshy finger over the beak); at about 12 weeks Bronze and Narragansett toms show all-black breast feathers and hens white-edged ones (p. 64). - Avoid inbreeding. The bulletin's "systematic intercrossing" keeps three or more pens: daughters stay in their mother's pen and sons move on one pen each year, so no outside blood is needed (pp. 23-24). With one small flock, trade toms with an unrelated neighbor's flock every year or two, quarantined first (rule of thumb). Mark families with leg bands or punched toe webs (pp. 65-66).

🦠 Blackhead: why turkeys and chickens don't mix Blackhead is caused by a one-celled parasite, Histomonas meleagridis, that attacks the two blind guts (ceca) and the liver (FB 1409, p. 68). - Signs: droopiness, no appetite, weight loss, sometimes sulfur-yellow droppings; death is often sudden, and the dark head is not always there (FB 1652, p. 51). Worst in poults of 6-18 weeks (FB 1409, p. 68). - Inside a dead bird: ceca swollen with a yellow cheesy core; a liver spotted with round, sunken dark-red, gray or yellow patches (FB 1652, p. 51). - Treatment: none that works (FB 1409, p. 68; FB 1652, p. 51). A blackhead liver: round, sunken spots (FB 1652, p. 52). How it spreads. Chickens catch it mildly and stay carriers, passing "vast numbers" in their droppings; grouse and quail get it too (FB 1652, p. 50). On its own the parasite seldom lives a day outside a bird, but inside the eggs of the cecal worm it survives in soil from one year to the next unless exposed to 0 °F weather (p. 51) - cold that valley winters seldom reach (rule of thumb). Flies, blowing dust and soil on the keeper's boots carry it as well (FB 1409, p. 68). How blackhead travels, and the three ways to stop it (a diagram drawn for this guide). 🦝 Predators "Dogs, foxes, and coyotes cause heavy losses among turkeys"; great horned owls and big hawks take turkeys roosting in the open (FB 1409, pp. 56-57). Bears, cougars, bobcats and raccoons live here too. The "who did it" table, hardware cloth for young birds and the bear fence are in the Chickens guide, "Predators of the Illinois Valley". 1. Shut them in all night and through the early morning, and feed and water them inside then (FB 1409, pp. 56-57). A high roost saves them at night "but not in the early morning hours when turkeys are off the roosts" (p. 57). 2. Build to stop dogs: 16-18 gauge wire, tightly nailed; 1½-in mesh of 16 gauge over openings near the ground (p. 56). Well-fenced yards "seldom are entered", but a determined dog, coyote or fox must be trapped or watched for (p. 57). 3. Dogs and night pens: a watchdog tied near the roost gives good protection (p. 57); for small operations a night pen is rated effective against coyotes, lions, bears, foxes and bobcats (UC ANR 8598, p. 5). Guardian dogs are covered in the Dogs guide. 4. Hawks and owls are federally protected - don't shoot or trap them, whatever the 1952 bulletin says (Kentucky ID-245, p. 5). Shut birds in; cover small runs. 5. Bears break coops and chicken wire; an electric fence powered day

or trap them, whatever the 1952 bulletin says (Kentucky ID-245, p. 5). Shut birds in; cover small runs. 5. Bears break coops and chicken wire; an electric fence powered day and night stops them; keep feed locked up (ODFW, pp. 1-2). 6. Cougars: "Fence and shelter livestock. Move them to sheds or barns at night." Oregon law lets a landowner kill a cougar that is damaging livestock (ODFW, p. 2). 7. A hen sitting out in the brush is easy prey: move her to a sheltered nest box (rule of thumb).

🔪 Butchering and plucking When: standard turkeys are best at 26-30 weeks, about 28; hens may be ready at 24 and toms at 26; small types at 22-26. Birds killed early are thin and full of short pinfeathers; cool weather speeds finishing (FB 1409, p. 75). Is it ready? Hang a bird by the legs: many short pinfeathers on shoulders, breast and drumsticks mean it won't pick clean - wait. Pull a few breast feathers and roll the skin: thick as blotting paper and white or yellowish is well fattened; paper-thin and see-through is not (pp. 75-76). Before: take feed away at dusk the day before, no grain within about 18 hours, never more than 24 hours without feed (or they eat litter and droppings), water to the end; catch them gently in a small pen so they don't pile and bruise (p. 76). Killing: 1. Hang the bird by its feet from a shackle, or a cord through a hole in a 2-in block of wood (FB 1409, p. 76), or head-down in a killing funnel about 22 in long, 12 in across the top and 5 in at the bottom for birds up to 17 lb live, 30 × 15 × 6 in for bigger ones (p. 77). 2. Stun it: one strong blow to the top of the head knocked out turkeys of up to 35 lb;

Bleed at once: holding the head by its sides, cut the jugular veins far back in the throat just below the skull through the open mouth with a narrow 4-in blade - or simply cut the throat, as most plants did. Let the wings flop; gripping them breaks wing bones (FB 1409, pp. 76-77). The bulletin's extra "stick" into the brain loosens feathers but takes practice; scalding does the same job (rule of thumb). Plucking: - Dry picking: start right after bleeding - tail and big wing feathers first, then legs, back and body, then breast, wings and neck. Pull briskly, a few at a time; don't rub, it tears the skin (FB 1409, p. 77). - Semi-scald: when flapping stops, dunk and swish the bird 30-40 seconds at 126-128 °F, or 1-1½ minutes at 124 °F, then pick; these limits "must be observed carefully" (same page). - The books differ on heat: CVM says turkeys need "hotter water than chickens" and dry picking "may also be desirable" (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 84); Minnesota scalds old chickens near 140 °F and warns that

turkeys need "hotter water than chickens" and dry picking "may also be desirable" (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 84); Minnesota scalds old chickens near 140 °F and warns that hotter water strips the outer skin and tears it (UMN EB 385, p. 2). Start at 124-128 °F with a thermometer; if tail and wing feathers still won't pull, as on an old tom, dip again briefly a few degrees hotter (rule of thumb). - Pinfeathers: pull what you can grip; digging out short ones does more harm. White, Buff, Royal Palm, Slate and Bourbon Red pinfeathers hardly show (FB 1409, p. 78). Dressing: squeeze droppings from the vent; take the crop out through a slit at the back of the neck, cut well above and below so nothing spills (FB 1409, p. 78). Then gut it like a chicken, only bigger - see the Chickens guide, "Humane slaughter and butchering" (🖼 step by step, UMN p. 5) - and wash it in cool water (CVM, p. 84). Cooling and keeping: hang the bird by its legs 12 hours or more at 30-36 °F (up to 45 °F for meat eaten soon); "in mild weather, it is not possible to cool the carcasses properly without the use of refrigeration or ice water". The size "has limited carcass storage without refrigeration" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 125), so butcher on cold days, one bird at a time, cut it into legs, wings and breast (CVM, p. 84), and pressure-can what you can't eat in a few days by the USDA chicken procedure, chilling the bird 6-12 hours first (USDA canning guide 5, p. 5; Preserving Food guide). What a bird yields (FB 1409, p. 78): fasting, killing, picking and chilling take off about 14½% of a medium or small turkey's live weight (13% for standard Bronze); drawing (head, feet and guts out, giblets and neck kept) takes 15% more. The picked carcass is about 10% bone and 46% raw lean meat. So a 19-lb Narragansett tom gives about 16 lb picked, 14 lb ready to cook and 7½ lb of lean meat; a 12½-lb Black hen about 10½, 9 and 5 lb (arithmetic). Using the whole bird: cook legs and thighs slowly; wing bones make turkey calls (Ohio DNR, p. 2); big wing feathers make quill pens (Paper & Ink guide); neck, back and giblets make broth (rule of thumb). 👪 How many turkeys for a family - Breeding flock: one young tom, 4-8 hens and a spare young tom (rule of thumb, from the ratios above). A turkey hen sits on 15-18 eggs and broods up to 20 poults (FB 1409, pp. 33, 37); with incubators the bulletin expected 25 grown young per hen a season (p. 33), but under hens plan on one clutch per hen (rule of thumb). - Feed is the limit. On range, standard Bronze ate 86.6 lb of feed each to reach 18½ lb at 28 weeks; Small Whites ate 52.6 lb to reach 12 lb at 24 weeks (FB 1409, p. 51). Plan on 60-90 lb of feed per bird - 12 birds eat about 720-1,080 lb - and 6 breeders eating 0.45 lb a day (p. 28) eat about 320 lb over a 120-day laying season (arithmetic). Range, milk, scraps and stubble stretch it, but grain fed to turkeys is grain people don't eat: size the flock to the grain you can grow. - Range: ½-2 acres per 100 birds (p. 55) is ⅛-½ acre for 25 birds (arithmetic); double or triple it for our dry summer, and keep three such patches so each rests 2 years (rule of thumb, from the 1-year-in-3 rule). - Meat: 12 medium heritage birds, half toms and half hens, give about 75 lb of lean meat

so each rests 2 years (rule of thumb, from the 1-year-in-3 rule). - Meat: 12 medium heritage birds, half toms and half hens, give about 75 lb of lean meat plus fat, broth and giblets; one bird a week from mid-November through February is about 15 birds (arithmetic). - A workable plan (rule of thumb): 1 tom and 5 hens; two hens each hatch a clutch; raise about 20 poults; butcher about 15 from November to February; keep 4 young hens and a young tom for next year and eat the old tom.
