🐇 Rabbits: Meat and Fur on Little Feed How to keep meat rabbits with no feed store, vet or electricity: breeds for meat and fur, hutches and colony pens, predators and fire season, feeding on hay, grain, roots and wild greens (and which local plants poison them), making hay, water, the breeding calendar and records, kindling, nest boxes, fostering and weaning, growing out to butcher weight, health with no vet, humane slaughter, pelts and Angora wool, manure, how many does feed a family, and keeping the line going for years. The books are in Small-Livestock\Rabbits (USDA Farmers Bulletin 1730 and AIB 358, the Oregon State "Raising Rabbits for Meat" sheets, Peace Corps R-41, Value and Use of Rabbit Manure), Animals\Rabbits-Other (USDA Handbook 309, Raising Healthy Rabbits), Animals\Veterinary (Peace Corps Livestock Manual Vol 4, AVMA euthanasia guidelines) and Wild-Plants (toxic plants). Hens and meat birds are in the Chickens guide. ### The short version - Heat kills rabbits. Plan litters for spring, fall and winter, not July-August, and have shade, airflow and water ready before 100 °F days (USDA FB 1730, p. 31). - Every breeding rabbit gets its own hutch, and the doe always goes to the buck's hutch to mate (FB 1730, p. 24). - Feed leafy hay, whole grain, roots, greens, salt and clean water - and change feed slowly. A sudden feed of lush greens can kill

mate (FB 1730, p. 24). - Feed leafy hay, whole grain, roots, greens, salt and clean water - and change feed slowly. A sudden feed of lush greens can kill (R-41, p. 38). - Never feed heated, moldy or sprayed greens, or plants from where dogs and cats go. Poison hemlock, Scotch broom and foxglove grow everywhere here (WSNWCB, pp. 34, 55). - Clean daily and cull the sick. The common killers come mostly from dirty hutches (R-41, p. 52); snuffles spreads, so cull it. - About 4 does and a buck give four people rabbit twice a week; keep 6 does and 2 bucks (arithmetic, below). Rabbit alone is not a diet - it is very lean. Eat it with fat and starch. - Wear gloves to butcher and throw out spotted livers: sick rabbits can carry tularemia (Trapper Manual, p. 92). The old bulletins' lindane, acids, gasoline and mothballs are poisons (last section).

Shelter for wet winters and hot summers - A rain-proof roof is a must - rabbits can't stand a soaked coat (FB 1730, p. 35); out of drafts, adults suffer little from cold (p. 32). Give each hutch) shade and a choice of sun (AIB 358, p. 8). - Face the shed south or east, with curtains or panels for storms (Handbook 309, p. 12). Drafts cause pneumonia: solid side panels outdoors, or a box with its opening away from the wind (EC 1654, p. 1); cold, damp and drafts together spread respiratory disease (Handbook 309, p. 47). - Summer shade: a lath roof, laths ¾ inch apart running north-south so the sun never sits on one spot (FB 1730, p. 47), or trees.

Colony or ground pens Colonies save wire and work, but the books keep breeding does and bucks in single hutches: - Does kept together ride each other and go falsely pregnant for 17 days - separate them 18 days before mating (FB 1730, p. 20); a mixed colony lowers conception (R-41, p. 41). A doe left with a buck for hours gets into fights, and you lose track of matings (R-41, pp. 15-16). - Extra bucks fight - castrate or remove them (R-41, p. 67); castrated bucks can share a pen (Handbook 309, p. 44). Rabbits on the ground pick up more worms and coccidia than on wire (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 339). - Colonies suit weaned fryers, castrated bucks and Angora "woolers" (FB 1730, p. 49). A movable grow-out pen for 8 fryers needs 8 × 4 lb × ¾ = 24 sq ft (arithmetic) - a 4×8-ft frame. They dig and hawks swoop: wire the bottom or lay a 2-ft wire apron, cover the top, and move it daily (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: AIB 358, p. 10 - scrap-lumber hutch; FB 1730, p. 41 - materials list for a two-unit hutch; OSU EC 1654, p. 1 - cages, drafts and bedding.

🦝 Predators, smoke and fire season - Hawks swoop into open pens; dogs and raccoons bend wire and open simple latches; rats climb through wide mesh (OSU EC 1654, p. 1). Use clips a paw can't work (rule of thumb). - A predator close enough to smell can make a doe kindle early on the wire, or stamp her kits in the nest (FB 1730, p. 27). Close the rabbitry at night. - Ground pens: hardware cloth buried 12 inches; a weasel fits a ¼-inch gap (Kentucky ID-245, pp. 3, 6). - Cougars: shelter stock at night; Oregon law lets a landowner kill a cougar damaging livestock (ODFW, p. 2). Black bears: an electric fence of at least 3 wires, lowest 7-9 inches up, top 36-42 inches, is the most reliable protection for a coop (ODFW, p. 2) - the same suits a rabbitry (rule of thumb). - A guardian dog (USDA AIB 588, p. 13) - but never feed dogs raw rabbit: it passes on tapeworm (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 340). Wildfire smoke (PNW 783, p. 10): watch for coughing, open-mouth breathing, watery eyes and weakness. Keep water fresh, cool them, mist down dust, and put off weaning and moving. A ration from home-grown feed The old bulletins were written before pellets (USDA AIB 358, p. 12; FB 1730, pp. 8-11): - Leafy legume hay (alfalfa, clover, vetch) + whole grain (oats, wheat, barley, rye, sorghum, buckwheat, soft corn - any can replace another) + salt. A typical ration: 4 parts grain to 1 part protein feed, all the legume hay they will eat, a little greens and salt; double the protein for pregnant and nursing does (FB 1730, p. 14). - Protein without soybean meal: legume hay; sunflower seeds, eaten readily (Handbook 309, p. 28); whole soybeans (about 1 lb per 10 lb of grain); goat's or cow's milk, and dry bread soaked in milk for does with litters. Table scraps are fine except meat, greasy and sour food (FB 1730, p. 9). - Roots all year, especially winter: carrots, turnips, beets, mangels, sweet potatoes, Jerusalem artichokes (FB 1730, p. 11). They are 90% water and low in protein: the Peace Corps manual limits them to about 1½% of body weight a day for resting rabbits (Vol 4, p. 300) - roughly 2½ oz for a 10-lb rabbit (arithmetic). - Salt: a small block, or 2% salt in the grain when hay is half the ration (FB 1730, p. 12); salt blocks rust wire (Handbook 309, p. 30). Give twigs to chew (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 300). How

Feed per pound of gain runs 3:1 on good feed, 8:1 on poor (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 300). - Too little roughage gives soft droppings and fur-chewing; too much slows the young (Handbook 309, p. 28). Greens and forage: what's safe Feeding greens (FB 1730, p. 12; R-41, pp. 37-38): 1. Fresh, once a day, only what they eat in 4-5 minutes, in a manger, never on the floor. 2. Dew-wet greens are fine. Greens that sat in a pile and heated are dangerous. 3. Never gather where dogs or cats defecate (tapeworm, coccidiosis), on swampy ground, or anything sprayed - nor where pigs or cattle graze (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 299). 4. Change the diet slowly. 🌿 Making and storing hay Cut grass before it blooms, while stems are fine and leafy - it has more protein then (FB 1730, p. 9; Handbook 309, p. 28). Legume hay should be fine-stemmed, leafy, green and free of mold (FB 1730, p. 9). Here most grass heads out in May-June (rule of thumb). 1. Walk the field first and pull tansy ragwort, hemlock and bracken - they stay poisonous in hay (WSNWCB, pp. 24, 34, 36). 2. Cut in a dry spell after the dew is off (rule of thumb), before the grass goes to seed; let it cure in the field and turn it so the underside sees the sun, or it molds (Animal Traction, p. 186). 3. It is cured when a twisted handful snaps without giving up juice - 1-3 days in the tropics (same page), 2-4 in our June sun (rule of thumb). Rake it into cocks if rain threatens (rule of thumb). 4. Store it in a dark, dry shed out of light and wind (same page), away from the hutches. 5. Check new hay for hot spots. Hay stored damp heats, chars inside, and can catch fire by itself (4-H Horse Project, p. 61; War Office, p. 127). Good hay is green, slightly brittle and sweet-smelling, with no dirt or woody stems (Animal Traction, p. 186). Gray or dusty hay is moldy

p. 61; War Office, p. 127). Good hay is green, slightly brittle and sweet-smelling, with no dirt or woody stems (Animal Traction, p. 186). Gray or dusty hay is moldy (WSNWCB, p. 56); visible mold is "unfit for fodder" (War Office, p. 127). If late rains spoil the curing, make silage instead (Animal Traction, p. 186). To feed, cut coarse hay into 3-4-inch lengths on a bench with a saw slot (FB 1730, pp. 9-10; 🖼 bench), and use a manger. How much to put up: see "How many does feed a family".

💧 Water - Fresh water at all times. In summer a 10-12-lb doe and her 8-week litter of seven drink about a gallon a day (FB 1730, p. 12); legume hay raises the need (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 299). - Bottles or nipple valves, not open crocks, which get fouled (OSU EC 1654, p. 2) and keep the chin fold wet until it turns green and sore - if you must use a crock, set it on a brick (AIB 358, p. 23). - Gravity line, no power: a barrel at least 1 ft above the highest hutch feeds a pipe or rubber hose along the backs, with a drinking valve 9 inches above the floor for medium and heavy breeds (7 for small). A half-barrel traps sediment; valves unused for days can stick (Handbook 309, p. 22). - Freezing nights: water that isn't ice-cold at least once a day before feeding, then empty the crocks; coffee cans let you knock the ice out (FB 1730, p. 13). - Wash drinkers in hot soapy water and dry them in the sun - never one rag for every hutch (FB 1730, p. 34). Don't let water pool; it breeds mosquitoes (EC 1654, p. 1), which carry myxomatosis. Clean water: Water Purification guide.

5-6 (p. 15). All agree size and maturity matter more than age - on home feed, use the later ages. Making a mating (FB 1730, pp. 22-26; R-41, pp. 15-16): 1. A ready doe is restless, rubs her chin on things and has a red, swollen vulva (deep red: about 75% conceive). Take her to the buck in the cool early morning or late afternoon. Mating is done when he falls over on his side; take her home. 2. If she refuses, try again that afternoon or next morning, or another buck; or hold her for him (🖼 how). Use a good buck about 3 times a week at most to keep him long. 3. Palpate at 12-14 days (AIB 358, p. 16; Handbook 309, p. 39): hold ears and shoulder skin in one hand; slip the other under the belly in front of the pelvis, thumb one side, fingers the other, and move gently back and forth. The young feel like marbles. Light pressure only - squeezing can cause abortion. Unsure? Feel again a week later (🖼 how to hold her). Lift a small rabbit by the loin, a bigger one by the shoulder skin with a hand under the rump; never by the ears or legs (AIB 358, pp. 23-24).

A year's calendar for the valley Early spring is the natural breeding season; conception drops in late summer and fall (FB 1730, p. 19), when twice as many does need holding (p. 26), and rabbits go temporarily sterile at about 86-90 °F (R-41, p. 42). Records A card on every hutch and one for every buck - date bred, buck, date kindled, born alive and dead, kept, weaned and their weight - tell you which does to cull and which to breed from (FB 1730, pp. 30-31; 🖼 a hutch card). Replace a doe that raises fewer than 5 healthy young two litters running (R-41, p. 16). Mark breeders by ear tattoo - tags tear out (AIB 358, p. 18). No tattoo pliers? Pencil the number inside the ear, wipe with alcohol, and prick it in with a taped sewing needle dipped in India ink, avoiding the veins (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 321). Keep cards dry in a tin (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: FB 1730, p. 18 - gestation, schedule, false pregnancy; R-41, p. 15 - signs of heat and breeding rules; Handbook 309, p. 39 - palpating, with a picture of growing young.

Nest boxes - Put the box in on day 27 with clean straw (AIB 358, p. 16); kits born on the wire can die (EC 1655, p. 2). An apple box with part of one end cut away, or a nail keg with a board across a third to half of the opening and 1-inch air holes (AIB 358, pp. 10-11): 13 inches across for does over 12 lb, 11½ for 8-12 lb, 10 under 8 lb (FB 1730, p. 43). A few ¼-inch drain holes; a box sunk below the floor feels like a burrow and lets strays crawl back in (Handbook 309, p. 23). - Winter box: set it inside a bigger box with 3 inches of straw packed around, cardboard on the floor and under the lid, two or three small vent holes, and fill it with straw so the doe burrows in. With her fur, kits survive 15-20 °F below zero; replace damp cardboard (FB 1730, p. 44). - Hot weather: a shallow nest; take out some fur and shade the box (EC 1655, p. 2). On hot days put newborns in a cooling basket of hardware cloth (15 × 6 × 6 inches) hung high in the hutch, back in the nest to nurse evening and morning (FB 1730, pp. 31-32). - Take the box out at 2-3 weeks (EC 1655, p. 2); scrub it

in the hutch, back in the nest to nurse evening and morning (FB 1730, pp. 31-32). - Take the box out at 2-3 weeks (EC 1655, p. 2); scrub it and sun-dry it before the next litter (FB 1730, p. 34). A box-type nest with the top of one end open for the doe; its top and bottom come off for cleaning (FB 1730, pp. 42-43).

Kindling 1. A day or two before, the doe pulls fur to line the nest and eats less - normal; tempt her with a little green feed (AIB 358, pp. 16-17; 🖼 litter in a fur-lined nest). 2. Most litters come at night. Keep strangers, dogs and noise away (R-41, p. 46). 3. Next day, while the doe is eating, check the nest quietly and remove dead or deformed kits (FB 1730, p. 27); then leave them a few days - too much handling can make a doe abandon them (EC 1655, p. 2). 4. Litters average 7-8; leave 6-8 on a doe, 9 on a heavy milker (FB 1730, p. 27). She nurses once a day, at night or early morning, for a few minutes (R-41, p. 40). If this goes wrong: - Kits cold on the wire: warm them even if they look dead - dip briefly in lukewarm water, dry with a cloth, put them back (R-41, p. 45; Handbook 309, p. 41). Keep a bag of clean spare fur to cover bare litters. Born outside the box: move kits and fur in (rule of thumb). - Litter split between nest and floor: she nurses one group and never carries kits back - you must (AIB 358, p. 18). No milk: kits starve in 2-3 days - foster them. Doe eats her litter: usually poor feed or

and never carries kits back - you must (AIB 358, p. 18). No milk: kits starve in 2-3 days - foster them. Doe eats her litter: usually poor feed or a scare; give a good doe one more chance (FB 1730, p. 28).

Fostering Breed several does the same day so litters can be evened out (FB 1730, p. 27). Move kits only to a litter within 3-4 days of the same age, aiming for 7-9 per doe (AIB 358, p. 18), and mark the movers. Your scent won't make her reject them (FB 1730, p. 27); rubbing your hand over the foster doe's fur first can't hurt (R-41, p. 46). Never move kits from a doe with mastitis (Handbook 309, p. 50).
fostering

Eyes, leaving the nest and weaning - Eyes open at 10-11 days; kits leave the nest and start eating at 19-20 days - earlier means too little milk or a nest too hot (FB 1730, p. 27). Eyes stuck shut: soften with warm water and gently part the lids (AIB 358, p. 18). - Wean at 8 weeks (AIB 358, p. 18); litters under five can go earlier. Don't wean abruptly - milk left in the glands causes caked breasts (Handbook 309, pp. 43, 50). - Separate the sexes at weaning: pressed gently, a buck's opening shows a round tip, a doe's a slit (FB 1730, p. 28). Pressed gently, a buck shows a round tip and a doe a slit (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: OSU EC 1655, p. 2 - palpating, nest boxes, newborn kits; FB 1730, p. 26 - kindling, fostering and losses; Handbook 309, p. 22 - nest box plans.

⚖ Growing out to butcher weight | Class | Age | Live weight | Carcass | Source | | Fryer | 8 weeks | 4-4½ lb | 50-59% of live weight; 78-80% of that edible | FB 1730, p. 47 | | Heavy fryer | 9-10 weeks | 4½-5½ lb | - | Handbook 309, p. 43 | | Roaster | Usually 8 months + | over 4 lb dressed | 55-65%; 87-90% edible | Handbook 309, p. 59 | | Stewer | Over 6 months | - | Meat toughens with age | EC 1651, p. 1 | - On home feed it is slower: R-41, feeding forage and less grain, counts on butcher size at 14-16 weeks (p. 47). - Each extra pound costs more feed: about 5½ lb of feed to go from 4 to 5 lb live, 7 from 7 to 8, over 10 from 9 to 10 (FB 1730, p. 48) - butcher at fryer size unless you want the pelt. - Leave fryers on the doe until butchering; weaned young held a few days stop gaining (same page). 🩺 Health with no vet - Quarantine new rabbits a month, downwind, chores last (OSU EC 1654, p. 1) - FB 1730 says at least 2 weeks; take the month. - Clean daily: manure, wet bedding and spoiled feed out; drinkers and feeders washed and sun-dried (FB 1730, p. 34). The common killers - coccidiosis, pneumonia and enteritis - come mostly from poor sanitation (R-41, p. 52). Look over every rabbit at feeding: appetite, droppings, nose, eyes, ears, front paws, hocks (rule of thumb). - Cull: few rabbit diseases can be treated; it is "simpler and safer to destroy a few sickly animals," especially with snuffles. Burn or bury the dead (FB 1730, p. 35). The books' drugs won't be available.
health-with-no-vet

Heat stress Newborn litters and does late in pregnancy suffer most. Signs: fast breathing, wet mouth, slight bleeding from the nostrils, restless young (FB 1730, p. 31); at worst lying flat with blood-tinged fluid from nose and mouth (Handbook 309, p. 50). Do: move it somewhere quiet and airy, onto a feed sack soaked in cold water, and put jugs of ice or cold water in the hutches (AIB 358, p. 22). On hot, dry days, wetting hutch tops and floors cools the hutch 6-10 °F - it suits our dry summers; in humid heat move air instead (Handbook 309, p. 45).
heat-stress

Snuffles and pneumonia - Snuffles: sneezing, nose-rubbing, runny nose, matted fur inside the front paws (Handbook 309, p. 50; 🖼 photo). The same germ causes pneumonia, abscesses, head tilt and womb infection (Peace Corps Vol 4, pp. 329-330) - the most serious rabbit disease (Handbook 309, p. 48). - Cull it - it spreads (R-41, p. 56) - and save breeders only from clean animals (Handbook 309, p. 52). A buck with an infected testicle spreads womb infection to every doe he serves (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 329). - Pneumonia, "the single greatest cause of death in mature rabbits," comes often at the start of the wet season; prevent it with airflow without drafts and dry bedding (same page) - here, October-November (rule of thumb). Dusty dry mash can set it off (R-41, p. 55).
snuffles-and-pneumonia

Ear mites (ear canker) Signs: head-shaking, ear-scratching, brown, scaly crusts inside the ear (R-41, p. 53) - the commonest parasite after coccidia (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 340). Treat (same page): 1. Swab the whole inner ear with vegetable or mineral oil, letting a little run down the canal. 2. Soak heavy crusts in oil until soft, lift them out with tweezers, oil again. Burn the swabs and crusts. 3. Treat every rabbit in the herd, mildest first; repeat weekly until clean (R-41, p. 53). Untreated canker reaches the inner ear and causes wry neck (head twisted, rolling) - cull those (R-41, p. 59).
ear-mites-ear-canker

Coccidiosis - Gut form: mild cases show nothing; worse, diarrhea and no gain; bad cases a pot belly and mucus in the droppings (Handbook 309, p. 50). Liver form: no signs in life; at butchering, white spots on an enlarged liver - throw that liver away (R-41, p. 56). - Prevention is the cure: the eggs need moisture and warmth, so keep floors dry, feeders rabbits can't sit or dung in, drinkers clean, and droppings cleared often. Recovered rabbits often carry it (Peace Corps Vol 4, pp. 337-338). If you stocked a sulfa drug, follow its label.
coccidiosis

Sore hocks Bruised, scabbed or abscessed pads on the hind feet, weight shifted forward - from wet floors, rough wire, heavy rabbits, nervous stamping. Give a resting board or lath platform, or put it on the ground; cull advanced cases (Handbook 309, p. 49; R-41, p. 26). Check feet often (EC 1654, p. 2); sore hocks also stop does conceiving (FB 1730, p. 19).

Rabbit hemorrhagic disease (RHDV2) A fatal virus that "affects both domestic and wild rabbits"; it has spread across the western states since 2020. "Many times, the only signs of the disease are sudden death and blood stained noses"; some get a fever, stop eating, or show breathing or nerve signs (USDA APHIS, p. 1). It "is very resistant to extreme temperatures" and spreads "from carcasses, food, water, and any contaminated materials", and on people's "clothing and shoes" (same page). No vaccine will be available, so keep it out: - Keep wild rabbits away from your rabbits (p. 1), and keep them off your hay and greens (rule of thumb). - New rabbits apart for at least 30 days, with their own feeders and tools; clean cages and gear with 10% bleach (1 part bleach to 9 parts water) before they go back (p. 2). - Don't touch dead wild rabbits; wash hands before and after the rabbits; don't share equipment with other keepers (same page). - A rabbit that dies suddenly: "A carcass could be a means of spread" (same page) - burn it or bury it deep, away from the rabbitry (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Handbook 309, pp. 48-52 - table of ailments; R-41, p. 53 - disease, cause and treatment; Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 337 - parasite life cycles; Raising Healthy Rabbits - illustrated care;

🔪 Humane slaughter and butchering Killing - practice the grip on a dead rabbit first. AVMA accepts neck dislocation only when done with a high degree of skill; it is harder on heavy rabbits, and devices that hold the head while you pull down on the hips work well (AVMA, pp. 44, 63): - Neck dislocation: hind legs in one hand; thumb just behind the ears, fingers under the chin in the other; stretch and raise the head sharply (FB 1730, p. 52; 🖼 how to hold it). Big old bucks: pin the neck under a broomstick on the ground, stand on both ends, pull the hind legs up sharply (rule of thumb - a homemade head-holding device). - A heavy blow at the base of the skull (FB 1730, p. 52) is less reliable - AVMA keeps it for emergencies (p. 64). Check death: no breath, no heartbeat, wide fixed pupils (p. 63). Butchering (FB 1730, pp. 52-56; AIB 358, p. 25): 1. No feed the day before (R-41, p. 77). Work in the cool morning, in gloves (rule of thumb). 2. Hang it by a hook through the hock tendon of one hind leg; cut off the head at once to bleed. 3. Remove tail, free hind foot and front feet; slit the skin inside each hind leg to the tail and peel it off like a sock,
humane-slaughter-and-butchering

at once to bleed. 3. Remove tail, free hind foot and front feet; slit the skin inside each hind leg to the tail and peel it off like a sock, leaving the fat on the carcass - fat left on the skin burns the pelt (🖼 steps). 4. Slit the belly; remove guts and gall bladder, keeping liver and kidneys; don't spill the bladder on the meat (R-41, p. 79). Heart, kidneys and liver are good food. 5. Rinse in cold water no more than 15 minutes; cool overnight before cutting up. Cut with a knife, not a cleaver - rabbit bones splinter; a fryer makes 7 pieces (🖼 cuts). - Yield: a 4-4½ lb fryer dresses to 50-59%, 78-80% of that edible (p. 47) - about 1¾ lb of meat (arithmetic). Skinning and gutting, step by step from right to left, each rabbit hung by one hind leg (FB 1730, p. 54). Check liver and spleen: white spots on the liver = coccidiosis; discard the liver (R-41, p. 56). Liver and spleen both enlarged and spotted can be tularemia, which people catch from skinning and undercooked meat (Trapper Manual, p. 92) - if the rabbit was sick, bury it whole, scrub up, and always cook rabbit well. Domestic rabbits kept free of ticks and fleas don't get it (Handbook 309, p. 48). Keeping the meat: pressure-can it, soaking dressed
humane-slaughter-and-butchering

whole, scrub up, and always cook rabbit well. Domestic rabbits kept free of ticks and fleas don't get it (Handbook 309, p. 48). Keeping the meat: pressure-can it, soaking dressed rabbit 1 hour in water with 1 tablespoon salt per quart first (USDA canning guide 5, p. 5), or dry thin strips (CVM, p. 90) - 16 oz raw makes about 4 oz jerky (PNW 632, p. 7). In summer, butcher only what you'll cook or can that day (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: FB 1730, p. 52 - slaughter and skinning drawings; R-41, p. 77 - skinning with photos; UF Humane Euthanasia - putting down a sick animal; Preserving Food guide - canning and drying meat.

🧥 Pelts and Angora wool Prime or not: stroke a live rabbit tail to head. A prime coat feels dense and flies back evenly; long and short hairs lying unevenly mean a molt. Skins from rabbits under 4 months are rough, thin and weak; the best pelts come from mature rabbits in the colder months (FB 1730, pp. 57-58; 🖼 prime and unprime). Butcher culled breeders in November-February for fur and use fryer skins for linings and mittens (rule of thumb). Skins make fur garments, glove linings and hat felt (FB 1730, p. 5). Drying a skin (FB 1730, pp. 58-59; Handbook 309, pp. 67-68): 1. While warm, pull it flesh side out onto a shaper of 5 ft of No. 9 wire, all four legs on one side to spare the back fur. Smooth out wrinkles; don't stretch it hard (🖼 pelt on a stretcher). 2. Next day check that edges dry flat, straighten the front legs, scrape off fat. 3. Dry in shade with moving air, never in sun or by a fire. Don't salt rabbit skins for drying. Store them hung in loose bundles, cool and dry, away from rats and mice. Skin flesh side out on the wire shaper, all the legs on one side so the back fur stays whole (FB 1730, p. 55). Conflict: R-41 salts skins before tanning (p. 80). Air-dry skins you
pelts-and-angora-wool

the wire shaper, all the legs on one side so the back fur stays whole (FB 1730, p. 55). Conflict: R-41 salts skins before tanning (p. 80). Air-dry skins you will store; skins going straight into the tan can be salted. Tanning: salt-alum - see the Clothing & Leather guide (FB 1334, p. 27; FB 1730, p. 61). First soak the dry skin soft in several changes of cool water and scrape off all flesh and fat - but don't leave it wet longer than needed or the hair slips (p. 60). Work the skin while it dries, not after, or it dries stiff (p. 61). Angora wool (FB 1730, pp. 49-51; Handbook 309, pp. 59-61): grows about 1 inch a month; shear or pluck every 10-12 weeks from 8 weeks old, for 14-15 oz a year. Scissors flat against the body, starting at the rump; never shear a pregnant doe's belly. In winter leave ½ inch, and shelter newly shorn rabbits at 30-40 °F. Shear on time, or swallowed wool forms a wool block that starves them (FB 1730, p. 33). Spin it on a wheel (p. 51).

🌱 Manure for the garden - Rabbit manure has about 2% nitrogen - more than most farm manures - and won't burn plants: dig it straight in (USDA Rabbit Manure, pp. 4-5), even on the crops you grow for the rabbits (Handbook 309, p. 53). - A doe and her litters make about 6 cubic feet a year (9 with bedding); a buck about 3 (5 with bedding). A cubic foot weighs about 28 lb fresh, 16 lb dry (FB 1730, p. 34). - Raise earthworms under the hutches (vermicomposting): bins the size of the hutch and 1 ft deep on bare ground, kept moist, cut odor and flies, and need emptying only every 5-6 months (Handbook 309, p. 53; Rabbit Manure, p. 5). - Compost: alternate 3-12-inch layers of garden waste (nothing diseased) and manure, tramp, wet just enough, cap with 3-4 inches of soil to hold the nitrogen, and cover against rain; fork over a smoking pile and wet it (Rabbit Manure, p. 6). Manure left in rain-soaked piles loses its value (FB 1730, p. 34). More: Sanitation guide.

🍽 How many does feed a family (Our arithmetic from the sources.) - A doe at full production raises about 28 fryers a year - roughly 60 lb of carcass, 48 lb of meat (FB 1730, pp. 19, 47). - Rabbit twice a week for four people ≈ 100 fryers ≈ 4 does + 1 buck. On home feed expect more like three litters of about 6 (rule of thumb), so keep 6 does and 2 bucks to cover losses and smaller litters. - Feed: each pound of fryer takes 3½-4½ lb of total ration, counting the doe's feed (FB 1730, p. 47). 100 fryers of 4¼ lb ≈ 1,500-1,900 lb a year, plus the bucks - call it a ton of hay, grain and roots, and up to twice that on poor feed (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 300). Plan on roughly half hay and greens, half grain and roots (rule of thumb). - Manure: 6 does × 9 + 2 bucks × 5 ≈ 64 cubic feet a year (FB 1730, p. 34). Work: about 10 hours a year per doe in a commercial rabbitry (p. 47) - much more when you cut greens and hay by hand. Don't live on rabbit. It is high in protein but low in fat (EC 1651, p. 1). People who live mainly on lean meat get "rabbit starvation" within 1-2 weeks

Don't live on rabbit. It is high in protein but low in fat (EC 1651, p. 1). People who live mainly on lean meat get "rabbit starvation" within 1-2 weeks - nausea, diarrhea, weakness and a craving for fat that more lean meat won't fix. Keep protein under about a third of calories and pair rabbit with fat (egg yolks, chicken fat, lard, nuts) and starch (rule of thumb). See the Food Security guide.

🧬 Keeping the line going for years Inbreeding doesn't create defects - it uncovers hidden ones, quickly (FB 1730, p. 20; Handbook 309, p. 10). Beginners inbreed just to avoid getting a new buck - get the buck (FB 1730, p. 21). - Keep at least two unrelated bucks and trade bucks with neighbors every few generations (rule of thumb); buy in a good buck now and then (R-41, p. 17). - With no new blood, keep three doe families (A, B, C): A bucks serve B does, B bucks serve C, C bucks serve A; each daughter stays in her mother's line (rule of thumb). - Recessive defects - splay leg (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 336), bad teeth (R-41, p. 56), a woolly coat (FB 1730, p. 22): when one shows up, don't breed either parent again. Picking replacements: - Save about one young doe and one young buck a month for every 12 working does; good does last 2-3 years, bucks 1 to 5½ (R-41, p. 17). - Pick from does that kindle regularly in every season (FB 1730, p. 19), raise litters well on home feed, and have never had snuffles (Handbook 309, p. 52). Look for calm, stocky rabbits that eat well (R-41, p. 67); disease resistance and long life are inherited too (p. 59). - Good care alone doesn't improve a line - selection

for calm, stocky rabbits that eat well (R-41, p. 67); disease resistance and long life are inherited too (p. 59). - Good care alone doesn't improve a line - selection does (FB 1730, p. 21). Over generations, picking the ones that thrive on home feed breeds a herd that does well on it (rule of thumb). - Keep records of matings and litter sizes (🖼 a hutch card); breed from the best mothers. 📚 Go deeper: FB 1730, p. 20 - inbreeding, line breeding, heredity; Handbook 309, p. 8 - selection and breeding systems; Seed Bank guide - the same idea for seed lines.

Sheep books are used where goats and sheep share a problem, and the guide says so. ### The short version - Shut goats in a shed or barn every night - cougars (ODFW, p. 2). No barbed wire; plain field fence traps horned heads (OSU EC1646, p. 1). - Never feed hedge or garden trimmings. Yew kills before any sign shows; goats like the leaves of rhododendron, azalea and laurel, which poison them (WSU, p. 2; p. 15). - Oregon is short of selenium. Keep a covered selenium goat mineral out all year, and never let sheep eat goat mineral - its copper poisons them

Keep a covered selenium goat mineral out all year, and never let sheep eat goat mineral - its copper poisons them (OSU EM 9094, p. 2; UF VM271, p. 2). - Change feed slowly, over 7-10 days. Bloat, grain overload and enterotoxemia kill in hours (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 95). - Colostrum within 30-60 minutes, at least 10% of body weight; a kid colder than 99 °F must be warmed before it is fed (KSU MF3689, p. 11). - Deworm only the goats that need it (pale eyelids; FAMACHA check every 2-4 weeks). Dewormers will run out, and overusing them breeds worms they can't kill (UF VM271, p. 2). - Some goat diseases infect people: CL pus, sore-mouth scabs, aborted kids and afterbirth. Wear gloves; pregnant women stay away from abortions and hard births (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 114; KSU, p. 4). - A fair doe gives about 1½ quarts a day for 10 months. A family of four needs about 3 does, a shared buck and 1-2 tons of hay a year (see "How many goats feed a family").

🐐 Choosing goats: milk, meat or brush A goat "will supply sufficient milk for the average family and can be kept where it would be impossible to keep a cow"; 6 to 8 goats eat what 1 cow eats (USDA FB 920, p. 3; p. 25). 🏠 Fences, shelter and predators Fences (OSU EC1646, p. 1; FB 920, p. 35): woven or welded wire about 48 inches high, stock panels, high-tensile or electric. No barbed wire - it "can cause severe injury." Field fence traps horned heads; netting entangles goats, so use it only where you watch them. Electric works once goats are trained: two hot wires held mature does but not kids, and "the goats will soon know it" when the charger is off. Wrap young trees in wire (FB 920, p. 25). Tethering: a chain with a swivel at each end, away from trees, shade and water in reach - but a tethered goat can't run from a predator (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 416). Shelter (EC1646, p. 2; FB 920, p. 9): a three-sided shed with clean bedding, room for all, and fresh air without drafts - damp air and ammonia cause pneumonia. "Goats must be kept dry and out of cold winds" (FB 920, p. 26). Plan about 15-20 sq ft of shed floor per adult, plus a separate buck pen (rule of thumb). Add something safe to climb (🖼 climbing structure), a stand or chute to hold one goat, and kidding pens made from hurdles. Store hay in a separate building from the goats (PNW783, p. 8). Predators: dogs, bears and coyotes kill adult sheep and goats; foxes and hawks take

Shut the herd in a predator-proof pen near the house at night (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 132-133). Cougars: "Fence and shelter livestock. Move them to sheds or barns at night" (ODFW, p. 2). Guardian dogs, donkeys and llamas protect a herd (EC1646, p. 1; 🖼 guard dog, llama). 🌿 Feeding with no feed store: browse, pasture and hay Goats browse: they prefer "leaves, twigs, and weeds to grass" (FB 920, p. 25), pick the best part of each plant, and walk twice as far in a day as sheep or cattle (Peace Corps Vol 4, pp. 392-393). But "a doe cannot be expected to produce milk at her maximum level" on browse alone: she needs legume hay or pasture plus grain (FB 920, p. 26). How much (FB 920, pp. 25-26): - Milking doe in winter: all the hay she will eat (about 2 lb of alfalfa or clover), 1½ lb of roots, 1-2 lb of grain; about 1 lb of grain for every 3-4 lb of milk. Young does need no grain spring to fall if browse is plentiful. - One doe for a year: about 500 lb of hay and 450 lb of grain with 6 months of pasture; with none, twice the hay and 20% more grain. 1 acre of good pasture carries 2-3 goats for a 5-6-month season. - Roots keep milk up in winter (mangels, carrots, rutabagas, parsnips, turnips), and with 1 or 2 goats kitchen scraps help - but no green potato peels or sprouts (WSU, p. 21). - Water: a milking doe needs 1-4 gallons a day; running water beats standing pools, and goats refuse water that tastes salty to you

peels or sprouts (WSU, p. 21). - Water: a milking doe needs 1-4 gallons a day; running water beats standing pools, and goats refuse water that tastes salty to you (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 394). Salt: trace-mineral salt free choice (FB 920, p. 26). Here in the valley (rule of thumb): pasture browns from June to the October rains and winter is mud, so plan hay for both. Browse: blackberry, poison oak, willow, maple and oak leaves - "goats will browse woody vegetation like blackberry and poison oak" (OSU EM 9184, p. 14). Oak: goats are "less susceptible than cattle," and leaves lose their poison as they mature (AIB 415, p. 79); young leaves, buds and green acorns are the risky part (WSU, p. 27), so make oak part of the diet, not all of it (rule of thumb). Raked leaves are poor winter feed, only for a shortage (FB 920, p. 26). Poison oak rides on goats: the oil on their coats reaches whoever handles them, so wash goats and clothes with soap and water, and never burn poison oak - the smoke can put people in the hospital (OSU PNW 108, p. 4). Feeding safely: change any feed over 7-10 days; keep hay out when they graze fresh alfalfa or clover so hungry goats don't gorge; keep grain locked up (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 95-96). Let them

🧂 Minerals: selenium, copper and salt Selenium (OSU EM 9094, pp. 1-6): - Most Oregon forage is low in selenium (🖼 map) and most Oregon livestock test below normal (p. 3). White muscle disease was first described here, at OSU in 1958. - It strikes kids 3-8 weeks old: stiffness, trembling, weak hind legs, can't stand or suckle, heart failure (p. 2). Low selenium also causes abortion, stillbirth, and more mastitis in dairy goats (p. 3). - Free-choice selenium mineral salt is simplest. Keep the feeder covered - rain leaches selenium out (pp. 5-6). Injections (such as Bo-Se) need a vet, last under a month, and an overdose kills (p. 5). Alfalfa takes up selenium better than red clover (p. 2). Stock a year or more of selenium goat mineral now (rule of thumb). Copper: goats need it; sheep are poisoned by it. Copper oxide wire particles help control barber pole worm in goats, but "there is a concern for copper toxicity in sheep" (UF VM271, p. 2); pig feed can hold enough copper to poison sheep (No Animal Doctor, p. 74). Never feed goat mineral to sheep, and don't feed goats a low-copper sheep mineral (rule of thumb). The drive has no map of copper in Oregon soils; a goat with a faded, rough coat may be short of it (rule of thumb). Iodine: kids born dead or weak
minerals-selenium-copper-and-salt

drive has no map of copper in Oregon soils; a goat with a faded, rough coat may be short of it (rule of thumb). Iodine: kids born dead or weak with a swollen neck (goiter) mean iodine shortage. Give pregnant does iodized or trace-mineral salt; if you have none, mix 2.2 g of potassium iodide into 10 kg of salt (No Animal Doctor, p. 282; p. 329). Calcium and phosphorus: grain is high in phosphorus, legume hay in calcium; keep the diet near 2-3 parts calcium to 1 of phosphorus against urinary stones in bucks and wethers (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 94). On lush spring grass, offer hay too, against grass tetany (p. 92). 📚 Go deeper: OSU EM 9094 - normal blood selenium for goats (170-300 ng/mL); salt vs injections vs selenium-fertilized pasture.

The last 6 weeks carry 75% of the kid's growth, and twin-bearing mothers need almost twice the energy, but never let does get fat (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 45-46). A few days ahead, give the doe a clean, dry, draft-free pen of at least 5 × 5 ft (KSU MF3689, p. 8; FB 920, p. 29). Signs within a day: she leaves the herd, paws a nest, the udder fills, the vulva swells. 70-80% of kid deaths happen in the first two weeks; check due does every 2-3 hours (Langston, p. 4). When to help (KSU, pp. 4-5): most does need none. A kid should come within 30-45 minutes of the yellowish water bag. Help if there is no progress 30 minutes after it, she strains with no water bag, she is exhausted, or a leg or tail shows wrong. Wash, glove, lube, and feel which legs belong to which kid (🖼 positions). Backward kids: don't turn them - pull straight back, quickly (p. 7). Never pull the front legs unless the head is coming too (FB 920, p. 30); pull only with your hands, as she strains (Peace

pull straight back, quickly (p. 7). Never pull the front legs unless the head is coming too (FB 920, p. 30); pull only with your hands, as she strains (Peace Corps, p. 421). Stuck after 15 minutes of trying? Get the most experienced person you can (KSU, p. 8). Normal (1) is front feet first with the nose between them (KSU, p. 6); rump first (2), a foreleg back (3) or upside down (4) need help (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 422). The first hours (KSU, pp. 10-13): 1. Clear mucus from nose and mouth; if the kid struggles to breathe, pat its side firmly. No mouth-to-mouth - diseases pass (Peace Corps, p. 421). 2. "Clip, dip, strip, sip": cut the navel cord under 2 inches and dip it in iodine; strip the wax plugs from the doe's teats; make sure the kid nurses. 3. Colostrum within 30-60 minutes, at least 10% of body weight: a 10-lb kid needs about 7 oz in the first hour and 16 oz over 24 hours, in 2-4-oz feeds (🖼 tube-feeding photos). It protects only in the first 24 hours; replacer is no substitute; another doe's colostrum is the best stand-in. 4. Kid under 99 °F? Warm it first - a chilled kid can't absorb colostrum. Normal is 102-103 °F. 5. Never pull on the afterbirth; it comes in 4-6 hours. Burn or bury

99 °F? Warm it first - a chilled kid can't absorb colostrum. Normal is 102-103 °F. 5. Never pull on the afterbirth; it comes in 4-6 hours. Burn or bury it, and see that both halves of the udder are emptied (FB 920, p. 30). Retained afterbirth or fever over 3 days needs skilled help (KSU, p. 8). Raising kids (FB 920, pp. 28, 31-32): on the doe is little work - a doe giving 3-4 lb of milk a day raises two kids, and meat-goat keepers wean later (Peace Corps, p. 424). By hand you get the milk and a record of it, and avoid lopsided udders: warm (90-98 °F) milk, as much as they drink readily - at least 1½-2 pints a day, often 2-3 - in 3 feeds until 6 weeks; after 10 weeks hay and grain replace most of it; wean at 3-4 months. Offer hay and a little grain early (1 part cracked corn, 1 oats, ½ bran; up to ½ lb a day). Use the doe's milk for people only from the 4th-5th day. Separate buck kids from doelings at about 4 months - doelings can get pregnant at 4-5 months (p. 32). 📚 Go deeper: KSU MF3689 - when to help, each wrong position, tube feeding; Langston - the stages of birth with photos.

✂ Castration, disbudding and marking Castration: buck kids not kept for breeding are castrated at 10 days to 3 weeks - "the older they are, the more severe the operation" (FB 920, p. 32). Wethers (castrated males) are calmer, grow better and taste less "gamy" (Peace Corps, p. 410; No Animal Doctor, p. 187). Castrating very young raises the risk of urinary stones later (same page), so a wether you will keep for years as a brush goat can wait a few months (our reading). Pick a cool, dry day and give dry bedding. 1. Knife: wash the scrotum, cut off its lower third, press each testicle out and pull it away with its cord; iodine on the wound (Peace Corps, p. 410). Over 4 months, scrape the cords through instead of pulling (FB 920, p. 32); over 6 months, tie each cord first (No Animal Doctor, p. 189). 2. Burdizzo (crushing clamp): no open wound. Crush each cord separately at a different height - never both at one level, or the scrotum dies (pp. 187-188). 3. Rubber ring (elastrator): feel both testicles below the ring before letting go (KSU, p. 14); "less preferable" where tetanus is a risk (No Animal Doctor, p. 189). 4. Give tetanus antitoxin (150-200 units) if you have it; check the wound for 2-3 days; fly ointment or heavy grease keeps maggots off (Peace Corps,
castration-disbudding-and-marking

Animal Doctor, p. 189). 4. Give tetanus antitoxin (150-200 units) if you have it; check the wound for 2-3 days; fly ointment or heavy grease keeps maggots off (Peace Corps, p. 410). Disbudding (FB 920, pp. 33-34): 1. In the first days of life, always before 3 weeks. Clip the hair: on a naturally hornless kid the skin slides over the spot; a horned kid has shiny buds with the skin stuck to the skull. 2. Heat a disbudding iron (or a ¾-inch steel pipe on a handle) cherry-red (🖼 where to burn); ⅞-inch for doelings, 1-inch for bucks. Hold it on each bud 5-10 seconds, rotating, until a copper-colored ring shows. Keep it as short as you can: newer studies found brain injury in kids even at 5 seconds, so have someone experienced show you first (rule of thumb). A second ring behind each bud "de-scents" buck kids (Peace Corps, pp. 412, 415). 3. Give tetanus antitoxin. Meloxicam (prescription) eases the pain (KSU, p. 15). Burn a ring around each horn bud; on a buck kid, a second ring just behind it takes out the scent glands (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 415). Grown goats' horns can be sawn off close to the head with a wire saw in cool, fly-free weather, with pine tar on the stumps (FB 920, p. 33). Marking: notch ears soon after birth, tattoo
castration-disbudding-and-marking

off close to the head with a wire saw in cool, fly-free weather, with pine tar on the stumps (FB 920, p. 33). Marking: notch ears soon after birth, tattoo at 3-6 months (same page; 🖼 ear marks). 📚 Go deeper: Where There Is No Animal Doctor, pp. 187-189 - castration step by step with drawings; Livestock dehorning.

🥛 Milking the goat: daily routine and yield How much: a doe giving about 1,000 lb (about 500 quarts) in a 10-month lactation is a fair milker; 1,200 lb is good, 1,600 lb or more excellent. Good does milk 8-10 months a year and give 8-15 times their own weight (USDA FB 920, p. 5). That is about 1½ quarts a day (our arithmetic). Lactations run 3 to 10 months; regular, thorough milking makes them longer (p. 27). Milk peaks 3-4 weeks after birth (ewes: Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 46). Two does bred a few months apart keep milk coming all year (rule of thumb). Every milking (FB 920, pp. 27-29; Lincoln Univ, pp. 1-2): 1. Doe on a milking stand with a head catch (🖼 stand); a little grain teaches young does to jump up. Milk in a clean place away from the goat pen and the buck. 2. Clip the udder hair. Strip the first squirts into a strip cup and look for clots every milking. Dip the teats; wipe each goat with her own towel. 3. Squeeze the teat in your hand as for a cow; strip small teats between finger and thumb. Don't wring the teats for the last drop. Dip again after. Twice a day, 12 hours apart (a heavy milker 3 times for a while), same milker, gentle and regular. Weigh each doe's milk
milking-the-goat-daily-routine-and-yield

for the last drop. Dip again after. Twice a day, 12 hours apart (a heavy milker 3 times for a while), same milker, gentle and regular. Weigh each doe's milk now and then and write it down (p. 28). 4. Strain it and cool it fast; cooling, pasteurizing and keeping milk without a fridge are in the Milk, Butter & Cheese guide. A milking stand: the doe walks up the ramp and puts her head through the catch, and the milker sits on the stand beside her (FB 920, p. 28). "Goaty" milk comes from a buck near the does, dirty pails, slow cooling, strong weeds like wild garlic eaten close to milking, a sick doe, or a very long lactation (FB 920, p. 29). A monthly California Mastitis Test finds hidden mastitis early (Lincoln, p. 1). Drying off: stop milking about 2 months before kidding so the udder rests (rule of thumb); most does dry up by the tenth month anyway (Peace Corps, p. 424). Cut grain and water back for 2-3 days while she dries, and watch the udder (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 113).

🦶 Hooves and hoof rot Rocky ground wears hooves down; in soft pens and wet pasture they overgrow, and goats "will not thrive or gain weight if their feet are neglected" (Peace Corps, p. 410). Look at every foot monthly (FB 920, p. 35); trim every 4-6 weeks in a wet winter (MSU M2487, p. 1). 1. Hold the goat, or set it on its rump (🖼 trimming), and clean the hoof with a pick. 2. With hoof shears, pruning shears or a sharp knife, trim the wall level with the sole so the foot sits square, following the angle of the hairline (🖼 hoof parts). Stop when the sole turns pinkish instead of white (Peace Corps, p. 410). Bring a badly overgrown hoof back a little at each trimming (FB 920, p. 35). Disinfect the trimmers between goats (MSU, p. 1). Trim the overgrown wall back to the dashed lines, level with the sole, so the foot sits square (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 411). Hoof rot (foot rot) comes with wet winters: lame goats, rotten-smelling tissue between the toes, hoof wall coming loose; it is contagious (🖼 photo; MSU, p. 1). Separate lame goats and trim away all rotten horn. Stand them in zinc sulfate for an hour - 10% = 1 kg in 10 liters of hot water (about 2¼ lb in 2⅔ gallons (our conversion)) with
hooves-and-hoof-rot

rotten horn. Stand them in zinc sulfate for an hour - 10% = 1 kg in 10 liters of hot water (about 2¼ lb in 2⅔ gallons (our conversion)) with a little detergent - weekly for 3 weeks; then put them on ground with no sheep or goats for 2 weeks, and cull goats that don't heal - they carry it (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 116). MSU recommends a 15-18% bath. Water the goats first so they don't drink it (rule of thumb). Dry pens and clean bedding prevent it (MSU, p. 1).

🪱 Worms with few or no dewormers The barber pole worm sucks blood and "can cause sudden death" (UF VM271, p. 1). Dewormers will run out after a collapse and worms already resist them, so use them only on the goats that need them (pp. 2-3): 1. Every 2-4 weeks (every 1-2 weeks in warm, wet weather), score the inner eyelid against the FAMACHA card (1 = red, 5 = white), and check back (body condition), rear (scours), jaw (bottle jaw) and nose (🖼 pale eyelid and bottle jaw, in sheep). 2. Deworm only pale, thin or scouring goats. 20% of goats carry 80% of the worms; FAMACHA usually leaves at least half the herd untreated, which keeps the drug working (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 124). 3. Dose by the heaviest goat's weight - underdosing breeds resistance (p. 76). No scale? Use a heart-girth tape (see "How many goats feed a family"). 4. Cull goats that always need treatment; keep the ones that stay red-eyed and fat (UF VM271, p. 3). Grazing against worms: 80% of larvae live in the bottom 2 inches of forage, so don't graze short. Rest pastures at least 30 days; it helps, but barber pole larvae live 3-6 months on pasture, so resting alone won't clear them. Tannin-rich clovers and birdsfoot trefoil help (UF VM271, p. 3). Hot, dry weather kills larvae; warm, moist ground
worms-with-few-or-no-dewormers

larvae live 3-6 months on pasture, so resting alone won't clear them. Tannin-rich clovers and birdsfoot trefoil help (UF VM271, p. 3). Hot, dry weather kills larvae; warm, moist ground keeps them alive up to a year (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 118) - our dry summers help and wet springs are the danger (rule of thumb). Wide, dry hillside range prevents worms; small, wet, low pastures spread them (FB 920, p. 40). Goats browsing brush at head height pick up far fewer worms (rule of thumb), and cattle grazing behind goats clean up their larvae (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 123). Coccidia cause scours, sometimes bloody, in kids in damp, shady pens fed on the ground; feeders and waterers that manure can't reach, and sunlight, prevent it (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 121-122). Lice: clip long-haired goats; treat the whole herd at once (FB 920, p. 40). 📚 Go deeper: UF VM271 - FAMACHA, the Five Point Check, fecal egg counts; Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 118-126 - worm life cycles and a salt-float egg test (needs a microscope).

🩺 Goat health with no vet Know normal first. No Animal Doctor lists 104 °F for a mature goat, "varies with weather," and 103 °F for young goats (p. 66); newborn kids run 102-103 °F (KSU, p. 11). Pulse about 75 (110 in young goats), felt inside the lower jaw; about 15 breaths a minute (20 in young) (No Animal Doctor, p. 67). A healthy goat eats, chews its cud and drops firm pellets; a goat that stops eating is sick (rule of thumb). 🔥 Brush, fire breaks and fire season Goats are "a mobile pruning machine": they clear undergrowth and "will actually kill some trees up to 6 inches in diameter" (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 392). Cattle keep grass down; goats eat the leaves and green stems of brush, but need temporary fencing, water and predator control (OSU EM 9184, p. 14). How to graze brush down: 1. Hit it hard, then rest it long. Crowd goats on a small paddock briefly, then take them off for a long recovery. It works only on plants goats like, and they eat the good plants too, so don't overstock (Peace Corps, p. 392). 2. Move them when about half is gone. Grazing 40-50% of the forage in the growing season breaks up fuel; ungrazed bunchgrass was 200% more likely to burn than grass grazed in spring (PNW783, p. 3). Come back every year: goats keep poison oak down but won't kill it unless grazing goes on "intensively for several years" (OSU PNW 108, p. 5). 3. Fuel breaks: on flat ground, about 2-3 times as wide as the tallest plants are high, along roads and driveways where most fires start (PNW783, p. 4). Keep the 5 ft around buildings bare and out to 100 ft light on fuel (p. 5); the Wildfire guide shows which zones to clear and when. 4. Wethers and dry
brush-fire-breaks-and-fire-season

the 5 ft around buildings bare and out to 100 ft light on fuel (p. 5); the Wildfire guide shows which zones to clear and when. 4. Wethers and dry does make the best brush crew; keep milking does and kids on better feed (rule of thumb). Walk strange brush for poisonous plants before turning goats in. When fire comes: decide ahead which goats leave and which stay, and where they go; move animals early, calmly, in daylight (PNW783, p. 7). Goats that stay belong in a heavily grazed pasture, gates open, with feed and water for 7-10 days (p. 8). In smoke: less exercise, plenty of water, shade, dampen dusty pens and feed, and put off weaning and other stress (p. 10). After a fire, check burned goats daily - damage can show days later - and give smoke-hurt lungs weeks to heal (ODA, p. 1); badly burned animals may have to be killed (PNW783, p. 9).

🔪 Humane slaughter and butchering When: kids at 8-12 weeks, tasting like lamb; goats "do not fatten" like sheep (FB 920, p. 35). Wethers raised on summer browse can wait for cold fall weather, when meat keeps hanging (rule of thumb). Kill only healthy goats - never one found dead, feverish, very thin or wobbling - and let a doe due to kid give birth first (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, pp. 27-29); wait out any drug's meat withdrawal time (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 76). No feed for up to 24 hours beforehand, but give water; lead the goat by jaw and tail, not legs or hair (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 69). Killing (UF VM114, pp. 5-12): 1. A .22 long rifle is enough for young animals (hollow points may not get through an adult's skull), held a few inches from the head, never pressed against it (p. 5). Hornless goat: top of the head or just behind the poll. Horned goat: behind the poll, aimed toward the muzzle. Not between the eyes (pp. 7-8; 🖼 AVMA placement). Watch for ricochet. 2. Bleed at once: a rigid, pointed knife at least 6 inches long, in behind the point of the jaw and drawn forward through the big neck vessels (p. 11). Hang the goat by the hind legs; stay clear - an unconscious animal kicks hard. Dead means
humane-slaughter-and-butchering

of the jaw and drawn forward through the big neck vessels (p. 11). Hang the goat by the hind legs; stay clear - an unconscious animal kicks hard. Dead means no heartbeat, no breathing, and no blink when you touch the eyeball (p. 12). Skinning and gutting (like sheep, but skinned with a knife: Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, pp. 70-77): 1. Cut off the feet at the joint; slit the skin up the inside of each leg and down the belly; work it off with fist and knife, keeping hair off the meat (🖼 steps). Tie off the food pipe and the rear gut (bung) with string. Open the belly with two fingers inside guarding the knife point; take out the bladder, then let guts and rumen roll out without puncturing them. Cut the gall bladder off the liver; take out heart and lungs; wash the carcass inside and out (pp. 72-74). 2. Look at the liver, lungs and guts. Offal with worms or cysts is not food: boil it and bury it. Don't let dogs eat raw offal or dead goats - it spreads hydatid tapeworm to dogs and people (pp. 74-75; Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 120-121). Trim out CL abscesses (p. 109). Keeping the meat without a fridge (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, pp. 89-92): hung whole in a cool, airy place it keeps no more than
humane-slaughter-and-butchering

out CL abscesses (p. 109). Keeping the meat without a fridge (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, pp. 89-92): hung whole in a cool, airy place it keeps no more than 3 days. Dry it in thin strips, or salt it: 1 part salt to 3 parts meat, strips under 1 inch thick, layered in salt and kept under the brine for at least 28 days; throw the batch out if the brine turns sour, thick or ropy. Canning and jerky are in the Preserving Food guide.

♻ Using everything: hides, manure and more - Hides: short-haired goatskins make shoes, gloves, book bindings and bags (FB 920, p. 35). Let the skin cool overnight, then tan it, or salt it with about 1 lb of salt per lb of skin; salted, it keeps 3-5 months. Never let it freeze or heat (USDA FB 1334, p. 8). Store skins dry, away from the meat (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 75). Give shots in the neck, not the hind leg or loin - injection abscesses spoil hide and the best meat (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 75-76). Tanning is in the Clothing, Leather & Shoes guide. - Manure: pellets and bedding go to the compost pile. Compost it before it touches food crops - fresh manure can carry E. coli; sawdust or shavings bedding robs soil of nitrogen for a long time (OSU EC 1561, p. 6). Use manure compost in small amounts in place of fertilizer (p. 8). Mucking out often also cuts worms and coccidia (FB 920, p. 40). See "Composting food, yard waste and manure" in the Sanitation guide. - Brush and scraps: goats turn brush, prunings (never yew, oleander or rhododendron) and garden waste into milk and meat (rule of thumb). Extra skim milk and whey feed hens (rule of thumb) - see the Milk, Butter & Cheese guide. - Dead goats and gut piles:
using-everything-hides-manure-and-more

milk and meat (rule of thumb). Extra skim milk and whey feed hens (rule of thumb) - see the Milk, Butter & Cheese guide. - Dead goats and gut piles: bury or burn them so dogs and wild carnivores can't spread worms (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 123); see "Dead animals and gut piles" in the Sanitation guide. Work: goats can pull carts and carry loads (EC1646, p. 1).

🧬 Keeping the herd going for years - Records: a big calendar and a notebook - breeding, kidding, weaning and slaughter dates, every medicine, milk per doe, kid survival, FAMACHA scores. "Don't trust your memory" (Peace Corps, p. 425; EC1646, p. 2). - Keep doelings from does that milk long, kid easily, raise twins and stay red-eyed without dewormer; cull the rest, and castrate poor buck kids before they can breed (No Animal Doctor, p. 186). - Start from good grade does bred to the best bucks you can find; keeping their best daughters builds a herd that "will out-produce purebreds of the quality most breeders are willing to sell" (FB 920, p. 22). - Inbreeding (sire × daughter, brother × sister) brings out hidden defects; cull hard if you do it (same page). Better: swap bucks between neighborhoods every few years, keep at least two males around, and don't let goats run loose (No Animal Doctor, pp. 184, 186). - Share a buck: with a few does it is "cheaper and more convenient to send them away to be bred" (FB 920, p. 21).

Sheep and goats share many problems; the Goats guide says more on some of them. ### The short version - Pick sheep for wet winters. Fine-wool breeds "do not, however, do well under wet conditions"; hair sheep and medium-wool sheep do (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 16). Keep them outdoors with an open shed: shut indoors they get pneumonia (p. 130). - Shut the flock in a pen near the house every night. Coyotes, dogs, bears and cougars all kill adult sheep (pp. 132-133). No barbed wire (OSU EC1646, p. 1). -

Shut the flock in a pen near the house every night. Coyotes, dogs, bears and cougars all kill adult sheep (pp. 132-133). No barbed wire (OSU EC1646, p. 1). - Copper kills sheep. Never feed them goat mineral, cattle mineral or pig feed (No Animal Doctor, p. 74). But Oregon forage is short of selenium: keep a covered selenium sheep mineral out all year (OSU EM 9094, pp. 1-5). - Hungry sheep eat poison. Death camas is one of the first green plants in spring, and sheep are the animal most likely to eat lupine (WSU, p. 3; p. 15). - Lambing: if feet show and no lamb comes in about 10 minutes, help her. Every lamb needs colostrum (first milk) in its first hour or two (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 65; pp. 110-111). - Deworm only the sheep that need it (pale eyelids, thin, scouring). Dewormers will run out, and worms already resist them (p. 124; UF VM271, p. 2). - Some sheep diseases infect people: sore-mouth scabs, abscess pus, aborted lambs. 🐑 Choosing sheep: meat, wool, milk or hair "Sheep produce two crops a year-lambs and wool-as well as meat for the family," with little labor and cheap housing (USDA FB 2222, p. 4); they do well on poor forage (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 34). | Type | Good for | Fit for the valley | | Hair sheep (Katahdin, St. Croix, Dorper) | Meat; "very poor quality fiber" | Best for wet ground: they "do well in areas with high rainfall, humidity and heat" (p. 16; 🖼 Katahdin, p. 19). No shearing: they shed (rule of thumb) | | Fine wool (Rambouillet, Merino) | Fine garment wool and meat | Poor: they thrive dry and "do not ... do well under wet conditions" (p. 16) | | Medium and long wool, dual purpose (Texel, Romney, Corriedale, Suffolk) | Meat lambs, milk, wool for outer garments, blankets and carpets | Good family sheep (p. 16; 🖼 Texel, p. 20). Long wools stand wet pasture (rule of thumb) | | Milk sheep (Awassi, East Friesian) | Milk for cheese and yogurt; lambs weaned at 30-45 days | Little wool (pp. 16-17; 🖼 Awassi, p. 21) | | Year-round breeders (Dorset) | Lambs in any season | Breed "even in temperate zones" (p. 52) | Very prolific and big breeds need more and better feed (p. 17); ask local keepers which breeds have

Buying (FB 2222, pp. 4-5; Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 28-29): fall is cheapest, and yearling or 2-year-old ewes have the most years ahead. Don't buy bred ewes (you won't know when they lamb), lame ewes (foot rot), ewes with lumpy udders or past mastitis, or worn or missing teeth. Look for a bright, alert sheep with a clean rear, free walk, clear eyes, teeth that meet the pad, normal hooves, joints not swollen, a soft udder with two good teats, and in a ram large, even, firm testicles. Feel under the wool: a fleece hides a thin sheep (p. 36). Age by the teeth: one pair of big front teeth at 1 year, two at 2, three at 3, all four at 4; then "spreaders," "broken mouths" or "gummers" (pp. 29-30; 🖼 photos). Keep new sheep apart for 30 days (p. 103) and deworm them before they join the flock (p. 123).

🏠 Fences, shelter and pens Shelter (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 130-131; FB 2222, pp. 5-7; OSU EC1646, p. 2): - A shed open to the south ("Sheep like lots of sun, light, and air"), dirt floor, fresh air but no drafts (damp and ammonia cause pneumonia), and a windbreak against freezing rain. Nothing sharp: nails, broken boards, loose wire. - One lambing pen for every five ewes: a hinged panel across an inside corner, each half 3-4 ft high and 4-5 ft long, gaps no wider than 3-4 inches (FB 2222, p. 7). - A lamb creep (a corner only lambs can enter): openings about 8 inches wide and 18 inches high, near where the ewes eat (p. 6; 🖼 p. 8). - Hay racks with openings 9-12 inches wide: a five-sided rack with 2-ft sides feeds 10 sheep, an 8-12-ft rack feeds 20 (🖼 p. 6). A catch pen or chute to hold one sheep. A lambing pen from one hinged panel across a corner: each half 3-4 ft high and 4-5 ft long, gaps no more than 3-4 inches (USDA FB 2222, p. 7). Fences (EC1646, p. 1): high-tensile, welded or woven wire, stock panels, electric. No barbed wire. Netting tangles sheep; use it only where you watch. Wool insulates sheep from an electric fence: shear, or use a stronger charge. Electric works if sheep are "carefully trained

wire. Netting tangles sheep; use it only where you watch. Wool insulates sheep from an electric fence: shear, or use a stronger charge. Electric works if sheep are "carefully trained with it" (FB 2222, p. 7) and "can be run off of solar charged batteries" (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 131). Walk the fence often: fallen limbs, grass on the wire and a dead charger let predators in. Posts last longest cut from heartwood (FB 2222, p. 8). Handling: lead a sheep with one hand under the jaw and one behind the tail, never by the wool or legs (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 69). To set a sheep on its rump: hand under the chin, other hand on the rump, sheep against your legs; turn its head away from you and press the rump down until it sits (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 78).

🌿 Feeding with no feed store: pasture, hay and water Pasture is the cheapest feed. Sheep like short, fine grass; bluegrass with clover, fescue and orchardgrass is excellent. Start grazing when spring growth is 3-6 inches. 1 acre of good pasture carries 5-6 ewes; unimproved, 2-3 (FB 2222, pp. 8-9); rape and kale give summer grazing (p. 9). Here, valley soils are "used mainly for irrigated hay and pasture" (NRCS soil survey, pp. 7-9), so unwatered pasture browns from about June to the October rains: plan hay for summer as well as winter (rule of thumb). Serpentine ground grows thin forage, "very high in ... magnesium and very low in calcium" (p. 49): feed sheep there hay grown elsewhere (rule of thumb). Stubble, crop tops and root crops are good sheep feed (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 41-42). Hay and grain (FB 2222, pp. 9-10): 3-4 lb of hay a day per ewe, from when they leave fall pasture until they are back on grass after lambing, about 5 months: about 500 lb per ewe. Legume hay is best; with grass hay add protein (oil meal, peas or beans: Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 37). Grain only about 100 days a year: ½-¾ lb a day from 30 days before lambing until spring grass, about 75 lb per ewe. Keep grain under half the diet (p. 40) and change any feed over

½-¾ lb a day from 30 days before lambing until spring grass, about 75 lb per ewe. Keep grain under half the diet (p. 40) and change any feed over 7-10 days (p. 95). Feed by the season (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 45-47): - Breeding: "flushing" (about ½ lb extra grain, or better pasture) 2 weeks before and 2 weeks after the ram goes in gives more twins. Mid-pregnancy: check condition every 2-3 weeks. - Last 6 weeks: 75% of the lamb's growth. A 130-lb ewe needs about 3⅓ lb of good hay and 1 lb of grain a day (our conversion of 1.5 kg and 0.5 kg); twins almost twice the energy. Straw alone is not enough. - Milking: the hungriest time: about 4½ lb of hay and 2 lb of grain (our conversion), or lush spring grass. Milk peaks 3-4 weeks after lambing. Lambs nibble grain and leafy hay from 10-14 days in a creep. Body condition: put your hands on the backbone, ribs and hips. Too thin: sharp bones, wasted muscle; too fat: rolls over rump and brisket. Both breed badly, lamb badly and get pregnancy disease (pp. 47-49; 🖼 p. 49). Water (p. 35): about 1 gallon a day for a ewe on dry feed, 1½ nursing lambs, ½ for a growing lamb; they drink more if it is warmed in winter (FB 2222, p. 9).

🧂 Minerals: selenium, copper and salt Selenium (OSU EM 9094): white muscle disease ("stiff lamb disease") was first found in Oregon in 1958 (p. 1), and blood selenium in most Oregon livestock is below normal (p. 3). - Signs, mostly in lambs 3-8 weeks old: stiff muscles, trembling, weak hind legs, can't suckle, heart failure (p. 2). In ewes: fewer twins, weak lambs, poor gains, more sickness; selenium also helps sheep resist foot rot (p. 3). Selenium works with vitamin E, which green feed supplies (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 38-39). - Use a sheep mineral salt with selenium, free choice, in a covered box: rain leaches it out (EM 9094, pp. 5-6). Too much selenium kills: the law caps it in sheep mineral and injections need a vet (pp. 3-5). Never mix your own; stock a year or two of sheep mineral now (rule of thumb). Alfalfa takes up selenium better than red clover (p. 2). Copper: sheep "do not tolerate excess copper"; it bursts the red blood cells and kills (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 39). Pig feed can hold enough to poison sheep (No Animal Doctor, p. 74), and copper wormer boluses made for goats are risky in sheep (UF VM271, p. 2). Keeping goats too? Feed each its own mineral where the other can't reach it (rule of thumb). Salt and the rest (FB 2222, p. 9): iodized
minerals-selenium-copper-and-salt

(UF VM271, p. 2). Keeping goats too? Feed each its own mineral where the other can't reach it (rule of thumb). Salt and the rest (FB 2222, p. 9): iodized or trace-mineral salt all year, in a box out of the rain, near water, in shade; ground limestone or bonemeal can be mixed in equal parts. Lambs born with a "big neck" (goiter) mean iodine shortage (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 39). Keep calcium 2-3 times phosphorus (legume hay is high in calcium, grain in phosphorus) against urinary stones (p. 94). Give hay with lush spring grass, against grass tetany (p. 92).

🍼 Lambing and helping a ewe Get ready (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 62-64; FB 2222, p. 11): with shelter, shear ewes 4-6 weeks before lambing; without it, clip the wool from udder and hindquarters ("crutching") 2-4 weeks before. A clean, dry, familiar place, away from dogs; iodine, bottle, feeding tube, soap, gloves. 70-80% of lamb deaths happen in the first two weeks: check due ewes every 2-3 hours. Lambing is near when she leaves the flock, paws a nest, gets up and down, and the udder fills (Langston, p. 4). Normal birth: labor usually starts within an hour of the water bag breaking; front feet come first, head lying on them; once feet show, a lamb takes a few minutes (longer for a first-timer). A twin usually follows within 30 minutes; to feel for one, push your fist into the right flank. "Do not interfere unless there is some deviation" (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 64-65). Wait, check or help: the times from Raising Healthy Sheep pp. 64-65 and Langston pp. 5, 9 (a diagram drawn for this guide). The books differ: FB 2222 gets help after 30 minutes' hard straining (p. 11); Langston allows 45-60 minutes after the water bag breaks and says "never rush to pull" (p. 9). Our reading: give her time before anything shows, but act once a lamb is stuck in the canal. Helping (Raising Healthy

breaks and says "never rush to pull" (p. 9). Our reading: give her time before anything shows, but act once a lamb is stuck in the canal. Helping (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 66-67; Langston, pp. 7-9): 1. Someone holds the ewe. Short nails; wash her rear and your hands and arms with soap and warm water; glove and lubricate (soap will do); enter with fingers together. 2. Is the cervix open? If not, wait and gently stretch it; never pull a lamb through a half-open cervix. If it won't open ("ring womb"), she needs a surgeon (Langston, p. 8). 3. Find out what you have. Front feet: soles down, nose above. Back feet: soles up, and you can feel the hock. Follow each leg back to its body: twins get mixed. 4. Fix the position, then pull only while she strains, gently, out and down. A lamb can live 8-10 hours after hard labor starts, so take the time to get it right (Langston, p. 6). Soles down means front feet; soles up and a hock mean a backward lamb (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 66; a diagram drawn for this guide). | Position | What to do (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 66-67; 🖼 drawings, p. 68) | | Backward (hind feet first) | Pull gently, working the vulva over the hips; once the hips are out, deliver at once: the

🍼 Orphan, weak and chilled lambs Tube feeding a lamb that can't suck (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 71-72; 🖼 photos): lay the tube along the lamb from mouth to last rib and mark it. With the lamb on your lap, pass the tube down the throat and watch it go down the left side of the neck. If you can't see it and the lamb coughs, it is in the windpipe: start again. Pinch the tube as you pull it out. A chilled lamb below 99 °F can't use colostrum: warm it first (as for goat kids, KSU, p. 11), in warm water to the neck, then dry it hard (rule of thumb). Colostrum, best first (KSU, p. 10): another ewe in your flock; your own frozen colostrum from last year; a ewe from another flock; a cow. Milk replacer and "homemade colostrum" are no substitute. Outside colostrum can carry OPP, a slow lung disease (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 104). Milk out and freeze spare colostrum every lambing (rule of thumb). Fostering (rule of thumb; the library has no source): a ewe that lost her lamb will often take an orphan if you skin her dead lamb and tie the skin over the orphan for a day or two, or rub the orphan in her birth fluids at once. Pen them tight together and hold her for the first sucks.
orphan-weak-and-chilled-lambs

skin over the orphan for a day or two, or rub the orphan in her birth fluids at once. Pen them tight together and hold her for the first sucks. Bottle lambs: ewe milk is far richer than cow or goat milk (about 6% fat and 5% protein, Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 31), so feed whole milk, warm, little and often, 4-6 feeds a day the first week, then 3, with clean bottles every time (rule of thumb). Offer creep feed and leafy hay from 10-14 days; lambs eating well can be weaned at 8-12 weeks (p. 47), and milk-sheep lambs at 30-45 days (pp. 16-17). Orphans make ideal pen-mates for a guardian puppy (USDA AIB 588, p. 13).

✂ Docking and castration Dock long-tailed lambs and castrate ram lambs you won't keep, by 14 days old (FB 2222, p. 12; Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 72-74): young lambs suffer least. Docking keeps the rear clean and prevents fly strike (maggots); fat-tailed and short-tailed sheep are not docked. Hold the lamb by both hind legs above the hocks, with the front legs in the same hand, back against your chest, or lay it in a lamb trough (🖼 p. 73). Docking: tail on a board, cut with a sharp knife or a beveled hot iron (the iron sears the artery under the tail), or put on a rubber ring: the tail falls off in 10-14 days (🖼 p. 74). Never cut shorter than where the skin fold meets the tail (2-3 cm, about 1 inch) (p. 74). Cut or ring where the skin fold meets the tail, never shorter (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 73-74; a diagram drawn for this guide). Castration (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 73; No Animal Doctor, pp. 187-189): 1. Knife: wash the scrotum; cut off its bottom half; squeeze each testicle out and pull it away while pressing on the base of the scrotum with your other hand, which prevents a rupture. Anti-fly ointment on the wound. 2. Burdizzo (crushing clamp): no wound. Crush each cord separately at a different height, never across the middle, or the

Crush each cord separately at a different height, never across the middle, or the whole scrotum dies. 3. Rubber ring at about one week: easiest, but "less preferable" where tetanus is a risk. Very early castration means more urinary stones later (No Animal Doctor, p. 187). Uncastrated ram lambs leave the ewes by 4 months; if the ewes had no tetanus shot before lambing, give lambs one at docking (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 73-74).

🧶 Shearing by hand When: once a year as spring warms, after the cold rains (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 80-81); here, late April-May (rule of thumb); all fleeces off before summer (FB 2222, p. 12). If cold, wet weather follows, keep shorn sheep in for 10-14 days, or leave some wool on (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 81). A sheep gives 2-15 kg (4-33 lb) of wool a year by breed (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 80); the US average fleece was about 8 lb (FB 2222, p. 12). Before (FB 2222, p. 12; USDA Preparing Wool for Market, pp. 5-7): no feed for 10 hours; shear only dry sheep, on a swept floor or canvas; clip off dung locks and burrs first and bag them apart. Order (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 81-82, 110): white sheep first, colored after; youngest to oldest; sick sheep and any with lumps last. Disinfect the shears between sheep: CL abscesses spread on blades. With hand shears (blades that work like big scissors, p. 80): 1. Set the sheep on its rump. Shear belly and brisket first and keep that wool apart, with the short leg and face wool (Preparing Wool, p. 8). 2. Then (rule of thumb): crutch and inner legs, neck and one shoulder, down that side in long strokes, then roll the sheep and do the other side. Blades flat to the skin, points
shearing-by-hand

thumb): crutch and inner legs, neck and one shoulder, down that side in long strokes, then roll the sheep and do the other side. Blades flat to the skin, points away from it; stretch wrinkles flat with your free hand. 3. Cut close, once. "Second cuts" leave short bits that spoil the yarn; a good shearer takes the fleece off in one piece (Preparing Wool, pp. 8-9). 4. Treat every cut with antiseptic (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 81). Learn from a neighbor if you can, and keep the blades sharp on a fine stone (rule of thumb). Lice, keds and mites: right after shearing, a pyrethrin-type pour-on down the back, all sheep at once; again in 2 weeks if heavy (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 128). Skirt, roll and store each fleece as in the picture (FB 2222, p. 12; Preparing Wool, pp. 10-14); keep black wool apart. Store dry, off the ground, and don't close plastic bags: they trap moisture (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 83). Good wool "is, above all, clean wool": never throw hay over sheep's backs (p. 82). Skirt, fold, roll tail to neck, tie with paper twine (USDA Preparing Wool for Market, pp. 10-11; a diagram drawn for this guide).

🧼 Washing and preparing wool at home Raw wool is greasy (lanolin) and dirty; you can spin it in the grease, or wash a few ounces at a time in warm, mild suds without stirring (CSU 4-H Spinning, p. 17). Scouring (washing) works if you have plenty of soft water (rain water) and time; work small lots. Washed and carded wool weighs about 65% of the raw fleece (USDA, How to Prepare Raw Wool at Home, p. 3). Scouring (pp. 3-4): 1. Pick the fleece apart and shake out dirt; remove tags and dung locks. Stained wool won't wash white. 2. Stock soap: heat 1 lb of washing soda (sal soda) slowly with a mild, neutral soap (not strong laundry soap) in 2 gallons of soft water; fill up to 5 gallons. 3. Three suds tubs. First: 1-2 quarts of stock in 13 gallons of water at about 120 °F ("uncomfortable but bearable to the hand"); second and third a little cooler, 110-120 °F, with less soap. About 6 gallons of suds per pound of raw wool; never crowd the tub. 4. Push the wool under with a paddle and let it stand 10 minutes. Don't stir or squeeze: that mats (felts) it; no washing machine. Lift, drain, run it through a clothes wringer, and into the next tub. 5. Rinse at least 3 times in soft water the same
washing-and-preparing-wool-at-home

mats (felts) it; no washing machine. Lift, drain, run it through a clothes wringer, and into the next tub. 5. Rinse at least 3 times in soft water the same temperature as the last suds, with 1-2 pints of vinegar in the last. Soda cuts grease but harms wool once the grease is gone: for clean wool, use it in the first tub only. 6. Dry spread thin on boards set 2-3 inches apart on sawhorses, under a clean white sheet, in the sun. Carding and batts (How to Prepare Raw Wool, pp. 3-4): hand cards straighten the wool and pull out chaff. For a comforter (about 3 lb of clean wool), lay carded wool 1-2 inches thick on paper 18 inches wide, four layers with paper between, under a board weighted with 200 lb or more for 2-3 days. A mattress takes 20-50 lb. Protect wool from moths. Spinning, dyeing, knitting and weaving: "Wool: from sheep to yarn" and the sections after it in the Clothing, Leather & Shoes guide.
