🦶 Hooves and foot rot Sheep on rough ground rarely need trimming; on wet pasture or in pens, once or twice a year (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 77). Look at feet every 4-6 weeks in a wet winter (MSU M2487, p. 1). Set the sheep on its rump (🖼 p. 78), pick each hoof clean, and with hoof shears, pruning shears, tin snips or a sharp knife cut away wall that curls under and loose horn. Trim the foot flat, at the angle of the hairline (🖼 MSU, p. 1); stop when the sole turns pink (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 410). Disinfect the trimmers between sheep. Foot rot - two germs together, one in soil and one carried in sheep's feet; spread on wet, muddy ground and at shared waterholes (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 115-117; 🖼 photo): very lame, may lie down to eat, a moist, rotten-smelling sore between the toes near the heel, the sole coming loose. (Foot scald is a milder, non-contagious redness between the toes: MSU, p. 1.) 1. Separate lame sheep. Trim away all rotten horn (🖼 p. 116); burn the trimmings (rule of thumb). 2. Stand them in 10% zinc sulfate for one hour: 1 kg in 10 liters of hot water (about 2¼ lb in 2⅔ gallons, our conversion) with a little detergent, weekly for 3 weeks. Water them first so they don't
hooves-and-foot-rot

1 kg in 10 liters of hot water (about 2¼ lb in 2⅔ gallons, our conversion) with a little detergent, weekly for 3 weeks. Water them first so they don't drink it (rule of thumb). MSU uses 15-18%. 3. Then onto ground no sheep have used for 2 weeks. Cull any sheep that doesn't heal: it carries the germ (p. 116). Antibiotic shots help bad cases (No Animal Doctor, p. 249). Prevent it: don't buy lame sheep (FB 2222, p. 5), keep pens dry and bedded (MSU, p. 1), and keep selenium up (EM 9094, p. 3).

🪱 Worms with few or no dewormers Stomach worms, worst the barber pole worm, suck blood: pale gums and eyelids, weakness, bottle jaw (a soft swelling under the jaw) and death, lambs worst (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 118-119; 🖼 pale eyelid, bottle jaw). Worms already resist many dewormers, and after a collapse there will be no more (UF VM271, pp. 1-2). Treat only the sheep that need it (UF VM271, pp. 2-3; Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 124): 1. Every 2-4 weeks check each sheep: eye (the FAMACHA eyelid card: 1 red, 5 white), back (condition), rear (scours), jaw (bottle jaw), nose (discharge, nose bots). 2. Deworm only the pale, thin or scouring ones. 20% of the sheep carry 80% of the worms; FAMACHA usually leaves half the flock untreated, which keeps the drug working. Some leave the best 10% untreated every time. 3. Dose for the heaviest sheep in a group of like size (underdosing breeds resistance) and drench slowly so it doesn't choke (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 76). 4. Cull sheep that always need treatment; keep the ones that stay red-eyed and fat (UF VM271, p. 3). Grazing against worms: larvae live up to a year on warm, moist pasture, but hot, dry weather kills them; a dewormed sheep put back on dirty pasture is reinfected in 3 weeks (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 118). Our dry summers help; wet
worms-with-few-or-no-dewormers

pasture, but hot, dry weather kills them; a dewormed sheep put back on dirty pasture is reinfected in 3 weeks (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 118). Our dry summers help; wet springs and irrigated pasture are the danger (rule of thumb). 80% of larvae live in the bottom 2 inches of grass: don't graze short; rest pastures at least 30 days (barber pole larvae live 90-180 days); tannin-rich clovers and birdsfoot trefoil help (UF VM271, p. 3). Safe pasture is a new crop on tilled ground, regrowth after a hay cut, or ground with no sheep or goats for a year; cattle grazing behind sheep "vacuum" up their worm larvae; wean lambs onto clean ground (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 123). Feed hay in racks and grain in troughs, off the ground (UF VM271, p. 2). Other worms (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 120-122): - Liver flukes need snails: ditch banks, slow creeks, ponds, swamps. Fence sheep off wet ground (rule of thumb); most dewormers don't kill flukes. - Hydatid tapeworm passes from dogs to sheep and back, and infects people: never let dogs eat raw sheep offal or dead sheep; deworm dogs for tapeworm; burn or bury dead sheep. - Coccidia: scours, sometimes bloody, in lambs in damp, shady pens fed on the ground: sunlight, and feeders manure can't reach. 📚 Go deeper: UF VM271 - FAMACHA and the Five Point Check;

🩺 Sheep health with no vet Know normal: temperature about 103 °F (39.2-39.6 °C); pulse 70-90, felt on the artery inside the lower jaw; 10-30 breaths a minute (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 31; No Animal Doctor, pp. 66-67). A sheep that stops eating or stands apart is sick (rule of thumb). A whole flock panting on a hot day is normal; one sheep panting is not (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 88). Rabies can look like bloat or choke: think before you put a hand in a sick sheep's mouth (p. 96). 🐕 Predators, guardian dogs and fire season Predators killed 45% of the lambs that died in California in 2014; nationally, dogs caused 21% of predator losses of adult sheep (UC ANR 8598, pp. 2-3). Use several tools together, before the first kill (p. 3). Every night, bring the flock into a predator-proof pen near the house (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 133): night pens rate "highly effective" against coyotes, cougars and bears (UC ANR, p. 5), and lamb in a shed (AIB 588, p. 29). Coyotes and dogs (UC ANR, p. 8): a coyote squeezes through a 4 × 6 inch hole and climbs or jumps fences under 66 inches, so woven wire needs electric top and trip wires. Electric netting, run on batteries and solar, cut coyote entries from 47% to 6%. Coyotes are an unprotected mammal in Oregon (ODFW, p. 74), and a landowner needs no license to take predatory animals on their own land (p. 26). Woven wire with hot wires on top and a hot trip wire outside (UC ANR 8598, p. 8; a diagram drawn for this guide). Cougars: "Fence and shelter livestock. Move them to sheds or barns at night." "Oregon law allows landowners to kill a cougar that is damaging livestock or property"; call your local ODFW office (ODFW, p. 2). Fences are untested against cougars (UC ANR, p. 8), so the night shed
predators-guardian-dogs-and-fire-season

kill a cougar that is damaging livestock or property"; call your local ODFW office (ODFW, p. 2). Fences are untested against cougars (UC ANR, p. 8), so the night shed needs a roof and a door (rule of thumb). Black bears: electric fence to the BearWise spec, at least 3 hot wires (5-6 better), lowest 7-9 in, highest 36-42 in, 8-10 in apart, an energizer of at least 6,000 volts and 0.5 joules, weeds kept off the wires (ODFW bear bulletin, p. 2). Store feed in a secure place (ODFW Living with Black Bears, p. 2). Guardian dogs are the best all-round protection against the predators here (UC ANR, pp. 5-6). Great Pyrenees, Anatolian, Akbash and Maremma are the usual breeds; with bears and cougars, plan 1-2 dogs per 50 ewes; two dogs beat one (Texas A&M, pp. 5-6). A pup raised in a pen with lambs bonds to sheep (AIB 588, p. 13). Black bears usually retreat from a barking dog, but "cougars are known predators of dogs" (pp. 28-29). Choosing, raising and keeping a guardian dog are in the Dogs guide. Llamas and donkeys deter dogs and coyotes but not cougars or bears, and a donkey should be taken out at lambing (UC ANR, pp. 5-7). Remove dead sheep, afterbirths and gut piles at once: they draw predators (UC ANR, p. 9). Fire season: grazing 40-50% of the
predators-guardian-dogs-and-fire-season

taken out at lambing (UC ANR, pp. 5-7). Remove dead sheep, afterbirths and gut piles at once: they draw predators (UC ANR, p. 9). Fire season: grazing 40-50% of the grass in the growing season breaks up fuel; ungrazed bunchgrass was 200% more likely to burn (PNW783, p. 3). Decide ahead which sheep leave and where; move them early, in daylight (p. 7). Sheep that stay go in a heavily grazed pasture, gates open, with water and feed for 7-10 days; store hay apart from the shed (p. 8). In smoke: less activity, clean water always, shade, damp down dust, and put off weaning, vaccinating and moving (p. 10). See the Wildfire guide.

🔪 Slaughter and butchering When: any time after a lamb reaches 100 lb, at 110-140 days: about a 50-lb carcass and 35 lb of meat. "A lamb more than 1 year old does not put on enough weight to pay for its feed" (FB 2222, p. 13). With no fridge, kill in cool weather, early in the day (rule of thumb). Only healthy sheep, past any drug withdrawal time (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 76). Water but no feed for 24 hours before: skinning is easier (FB 2222, p. 13; Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 69). Killing (UF VM114, pp. 5-12): 1. A .22 long rifle is enough for a lamb (hollow points may not get through an adult skull), held a few inches from the head, never against it; watch for ricochet (p. 5). 2. Hornless sheep: top of the head, or just behind the poll. Horned sheep and rams: behind the poll, aimed toward the muzzle (the skull on top is too thick). Not between the eyes (pp. 7-8; 🖼 drawing). 3. Bleed at once (after a captive-bolt stun, within 10 seconds, or the sheep may wake: p. 7): a rigid, pointed knife at least 6 inches long goes in behind the jaw, edge outward, and is drawn out through the big neck vessels (p. 11; Slaughter, p. 70). Stand clear of kicking. Dead: no heartbeat, no breathing,
slaughter-and-butchering

goes in behind the jaw, edge outward, and is drawn out through the big neck vessels (p. 11; Slaughter, p. 70). Stand clear of kicking. Dead: no heartbeat, no breathing, no blink when you touch the eye (p. 12). Pelting and gutting (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, pp. 70-74; 🖼 photos): 1. Clean hands and knives; keep wool off the meat. Leave the fell (the thin skin over the meat) on: it keeps the carcass from drying. 2. Lamb on its back on a rack: open the pelt down the front of each foreleg to the breast and skin out the forelegs; take off the feet at the joint; open the hind legs from hoof to tail. 3. "Fist" the pelt off: push a fist between pelt and carcass from flank and breast, pulling the pelt up with the other hand. Tie off the food pipe. Hang by the hind tendons and fist the pelt down the back and off. 4. Tie off the bung (rear gut). Open the belly with two fingers inside guarding the knife point; let the guts roll out unbroken; cut the gall bladder off the liver; take heart and lungs; wash the carcass. 5. Check liver and lungs. Offal with worms or cysts is not food: boil it and bury it; never feed raw offal to dogs (pp. 74-75; Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 121). Trim
slaughter-and-butchering

liver and lungs. Offal with worms or cysts is not food: boil it and bury it; never feed raw offal to dogs (pp. 74-75; Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 121). Trim out any CL abscesses (p. 109). Cutting up (Slaughter, pp. 151-154; 🖼 cuts): take off breast, flank and foreshank first; cut the shoulder off between the 4th and 5th ribs; split the back down the spine (or leave a small one whole); separate rib from loin at the last (12th) rib, cutting the ribs 3 inches from the backbone; split the legs. Chops 1 inch thick, or bone out roasts. Keeping it without a fridge: hung whole in a cool, airy place, no more than 3 days; then dry it in thin strips, or salt it 1 part salt to 3 parts meat for at least 28 days under brine (Slaughter, pp. 89-92). Canning, jerky and smoking are in the Preserving Food guide.

♻ Sheepskins, tallow and manure Sheepskins make "light and fancy leathers"; skin without cutting the hide and scrape off all fat and flesh (USDA FB 1334, p. 7). Let it cool overnight, then tan it, or salt it with about 1 lb of salt per lb of skin: it keeps 3-5 months. Never let it freeze or heat (p. 8). Store skins dry, away from the meat (Slaughter, p. 75). A wool-on sheepskin is tanned like a fur (rule of thumb): salt-alum paste on the flesh side only, 2-3 coats a day apart, then rinse, oil, and work it over a stake as it dries (FB 1334, p. 27); wash the wool first as above (rule of thumb). Tanning step by step: Clothing, Leather & Shoes guide. Tallow: mutton fat makes candles and soap; render it within a week (Food From Scratch; Light Without the Grid). Manure: an adult drops 2.5-8.5 kg (6-19 lb) a day (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 31); compost it with the bedding before it goes on food crops ("Composting food, yard waste and manure" in the Sanitation guide). Dead sheep: burn or bury deep so dogs and coyotes can't eat them (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 123; "Dead animals and gut piles" in the same guide).
sheepskins-tallow-and-manure

🥛 Sheep milk Ewe milk is rich: about 6.2% fat and 5.4% protein (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 31; the Milk guide's source gives about 7.9% fat), so it makes more cheese and yogurt per gallon than cow or goat milk (rule of thumb). Milk breeds give "large quantities of milk from which cheese and yogurt are made," and their lambs are weaned at 30-45 days (pp. 16-17). The library has no yield figures; a dairy ewe gives perhaps a third to half what a good dairy goat does, over a shorter season (rule of thumb). 1. Milk peaks 3-4 weeks after lambing (p. 46). Share with the lambs (shut them apart at night, milk in the morning), or wean early and milk twice a day (rule of thumb). 2. A stand with a head catch; ewes have small teats, so strip between finger and thumb (rule of thumb). Wash and dry wet or muddy teats and your hands first (p. 113); strip the first squirts and look for clots every time ("Clean milking" in the Milk guide). 3. Drying off: reduce feed and water for 48-72 hours at weaning, and watch the udder (p. 113). 4. Pasteurize (brucellosis; Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 115). Don't milk ewes grazing lupine: its poison passes into milk and can cause birth defects in people (WSU, p. 15). Lamb or kid rennet suits sheep-milk cheese

🧬 Keeping the flock going for years - Records: breeding, lambing and weaning dates, twins, weights, fleece weights, every medicine, FAMACHA scores, culls. "Do not depend on your memory!" (No Animal Doctor, p. 184; Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 52). - Keep the best ewe lambs, from ewes that twin, mother and milk well, stay sound and stay red-eyed without dewormer, and you can double the flock in a few years (FB 2222, p. 4). Cull ewes with ruined udders, foot rot that won't heal, worm-prone ones and broken mouths, and castrate poor ram lambs before they can breed (No Animal Doctor, p. 186). Don't keep lambs from OPP ewes (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 104). - The ram makes most of the change in a flock: choose him hardest (p. 55). Range ewes given good care can lamb well to 8-10 years old (FB 2222, p. 5). - Inbreeding gives weaker, less productive lambs: swap rams with other neighborhoods every few years, keep two males in case one is infertile, and don't let sheep run loose (No Animal Doctor, pp. 184, 186).

Curing and smoking are in the Preserving Food guide. The pig books are in Animals\Cattle-Horses-Pigs (USDA Pasture and Grain Crops for Hogs in the Pacific Northwest, Swine Production and Pork Slaughtering, OSU Care of New Feeder Pigs, Slaughter and Preservation of Meat), with Pork on the Farm in Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools, lard in Food-From-Scratch\Wild-and-Local-Staples, smokehouse and hoist plans in Food-Storage\Curing-Smoking, no-vet medicine and the diseases people catch from pigs in Animals\Veterinary, and poisonous plants in Wild-Plants. The main CVM book, Raising Healthy Pigs, has photos but no text the search tool can read, so this guide does not quote it. ### The short version - Pigs die of heat. Shade and clean water all day: ½-1½ gallons per 100 lb of pig a day, more for nursing sows. Salty slop with too little water kills (No Animal Doctor, p. 47; Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 210; p. 332). - Boil every scrap that has touched meat, and boil milk and whey, before pigs get them: raw meat scraps give pigs trichinosis, raw milk and garbage spread TB (USDA FB 1437, p. 5; Zoonoses, p. 27). - Cook pork until it is gray all through (about 170 °F). Never taste raw sausage; curing and smoking don't make pork safe (Zoonoses, p. 121; USDA FB 1186, p. 41). - Sows crush piglets. Farrow in a pen about 7 × 7 ft with a guard rail 10 in off the floor and 4-6 in from the wall; over half of newborn deaths come in the first 24 hours (FB 1437, pp. 24, 26). - Piglets on a floor need iron: put fresh sod or clean soil in the pen (FB 1437, p. 32). - Butcher in cold weather: carcass down to 34-40 °F within 24 hours; fresh pork eaten or preserved within 3-5 days (FB 1186, p. 3; USDA FB 2138, p. 24). - Never let a pig loose, and never let pigs reach a latrine (pork tapeworm) (Zoonoses, p. 112). 🐖 Choosing pigs: lard, bacon and pasture breeds The hog is "the most valuable farm animal in utilizing farm wastes" (FB 1437, p. 4): scraps, whey, gleanings, acorns and culls become meat and fat. With no store oil, lard is the household's cooking fat, so choose for fat as well as meat. | Type | Built like | Best fed on | Breeds named in the books | | Lard | Short-legged, thick, compact; small litters | Corn and other fattening grain | Poland China: black with six white points, 600-1,000 lb grown, fast-gaining, good survival (Peace Corps, pp. 280-281; p. 284) | | Bacon | Long, lean, muscled | Peas, wheat, barley, oats, rye, dairy by-products and roots: what our valley grows | Landrace: long, prolific, efficient. Yorkshire: good mothers, large litters, forage well, but do poorly with little care (pp. 281, 284) | | Meat (in between) | Large, fast-growing, hungry | Grain plus protein | Duroc: red, litters survive well, sows "fierce in the defense of their young." Hampshire: white belt, sows raise a high share of their pigs; smaller, slower (p. 284) | Pasture pigs: a breed "selected genetically for production" needs "high quality feed, a disease-free environment, good housing" (Peace Corps, p. 280). On pasture and leftovers pick hardy crossbreds or old grazing breeds that mother well, such as Berkshire, Tamworth, Large Black or the
choosing-pigs-lard-bacon-and-pasture-breeds

disease-free environment, good housing" (Peace Corps, p. 280). On pasture and leftovers pick hardy crossbreds or old grazing breeds that mother well, such as Berkshire, Tamworth, Large Black or the small Kunekune, over modern indoor lines (rule of thumb). Crosses give bigger litters, more pigs living and faster growth (p. 282). Sunburn is a trait to select against (p. 281): under our July sun, dark-skinned pigs fare better (rule of thumb). Buying: "start with only a few sows," of one breed and herd, ideally already bred. A good sow lets you into her pen any time, has legs long enough to keep her udder off the ground and at least six teats in each row; keep no pigs from a cross or nervous sow (FB 1437, pp. 5-7). Buy only from herds you know are healthy. Feeder pigs (weaned pigs raised for meat) need a clean, dry, draft-free pen ready; ask what they ate and change feed slowly (OSU EM 9271, pp. 1, 3).

🏠 Pens, fences and rooting Room per pig under cover: sows, gilts and boars 15-20 sq ft; sow and litter 50-65; weaners to 75 lb 5-6; 75-125 lb 6-7; 125-200 lb 8-10; build near the house and the feed, proof against predators (Peace Corps, p. 288). A 50-lb pig is comfortable at 70-82 °F, a 215-lb one at 50-75 °F, and Oregon nights chill young pigs "through the month of May": bed deep with straw (OSU EM 9271, pp. 1-2) and never let pigs sleep on damp bedding (FB 1437, p. 34). A roof on posts with straw-bale walls is a winter house; take the bales out and it is a summer shade (🖼 FB 1437, p. 38). Feed in a V-shaped trough with slats across the top, 1-2 ft per pig (pigs fed on the ground get more worms), and water in a heavy concrete bowl they can't tip (Peace Corps, pp. 290-291). Dig or plow pig lots twice a year and sow them to pasture (FB 1437, p. 37): worm eggs live years in damp soil but die in weeks of sun (No Animal Doctor, p. 347).
pens-fences-and-rooting

Fences that hold pigs Fence "hog tight" with woven wire: about 26 in high on a big field with one barbed strand at the bottom, just above the ground, and 32-36 in around a small pen, where pigs push harder. "Probably 90 percent" of a woven-wire fence's strength is in well-braced corner posts (FB 1437, p. 21). Pigs root under woven wire, so run "one or two electric fence wires near the bottom" (OSU EM 9271, p. 5) on the pig side, where a snout meets them first: about 6-8 in and 12-16 in up (rule of thumb). Woven wire with low hot wires on the pig side; in a dry summer the lower wire becomes the ground wire (FB 1437, p. 21; OSU EM 9271, p. 5) (a diagram drawn for this guide).
fences-that-hold-pigs

Electric wire with no power from the grid - Sun and a battery: "Electric fences can be run off of solar charged batteries" (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 131). Face the panel south (UF bear fences, p. 5); buy a solar charger and a spare battery now (rule of thumb). - Dry summer soil can't carry the shock back to the ground rod: make the bottom wire a ground wire and keep the upper one hot (OSU EM 9271, p. 5). A pig touching both gets the shock. - Train pigs to the wire in a small pen with a solid fence behind it while you still have a charger. Pigs that have been shocked often respect a dead wire for a while, but they test fences: never trust a cold wire alone; with no charger, the woven wire, barbed strand, hog panels, boards or stone are the fence (rule of thumb). - Against bears, an electric pen needs at least 3 strands (5-6 better), the lowest 7-9 in up, the top 36-42 in, wires 8-10 in apart, and at least 6,000 volts and 0.5 joule (ODFW bear-country chickens, p. 2).
electric-wire-with-no-power-from-the-grid

Rooting: the problem and the plow Pigs root hardest in wet ground (FB 599, p. 3), and west of the Cascades winter tramping "puddles" (packs and ruins) wet soil: take them off pasture in heavy rain, except on sandy soil or tight sod (p. 12). English ryegrass sod "stands tramping well" (p. 15), and straw spread first protects heavy soil (p. 17). Keep the winter lot on your best-drained, gravelly ground (rule of thumb). Ringed hogs (rings in the top of the snout) can't dig tubers (same page); buy rings and a ringer now (rule of thumb). Rooting is also free plowing: hogs work stalks into the soil and spread their droppings evenly (p. 7). Turn pigs onto a finished garden in early fall, then move them before the mud (rule of thumb).
rooting-the-problem-and-the-plow

Predators, and pigs as a danger "Store livestock food in a secure place" (ODFW, p. 2), and shelter animals at night against cougars (ODFW, p. 2): a night pen near the house and carrying off carcasses are rated effective against lions, bears and coyotes (UC ANR 8598, p. 5). Bears raid pig pens and take piglets (rule of thumb). Sows with piglets and boars "may attack and bite" (No Animal Doctor, p. 47): carry a board to hold between you, never turn your back on a boar, keep children out of the pen, and keep pigs from chickens, which they kill (rule of thumb).
predators-and-pigs-as-a-danger

🌾 Feeding with no feed store Pasture alone is not enough for growing pigs: they get "big bellied, and thin in flesh or stunted," though dry sows can hold condition on good pasture (FB 599, p. 4). On pasture feed grain at about 2-3% of live weight a day, or 1% for a light ration, then fatten on all they clean up three times a day (p. 5); a growing pig on abundant pasture gets 1-2 lb of grain a day (FB 1437, p. 15). Change feed slowly, a quarter at a time over at least a week (p. 10).

(p. 3); legume pasture means less grain (p. 6). Never plan "just enough": an acre carries 5-15 hogs of 100 lb (FB 1437, p. 19). Here grass and clover quit in July unless watered, so plan summer around grain to hog off (rule of thumb); serpentine ground grows poor, low-calcium pasture (NRCS, p. 49).

Hogging down grain, peas and corn "Hogging off" means turning hogs into a ripe field to harvest it themselves: no threshing or hauling, and the hogs need only "water, shade, and salt" (FB 599, pp. 6-7). In western Oregon: beardless barley July 1-20, soft club winter wheat July 10-August 10, field peas July 25-October 1, corn (planted April 20-May 10) from mid-September, earlier in the Rogue Valley (pp. 15-16). Bearded barley and hard wheat hurt pigs' mouths (pp. 8-9). Fence off only what the herd cleans up in 15-20 days, or rain sprouts the peas and molds the corn; to size it, count how many days a fenced trial acre lasts (pp. 9, 11).
hogging-down-grain-peas-and-corn

Winter feed: kale, roots, squash and artichokes Thousand-headed kale (sown March-April, transplanted in June) stands in the field and feeds October-April, best from a rack; squash planted about May 25 and stored dark under straw feeds November-January (FB 599, p. 16), and squash and pumpkins are "favorite foods" (OSU EM 9271, p. 5). Mangels, beets, carrots and rutabagas go whole from the field (FB 599, pp. 17, 22), though good alfalfa does more (FB 1437, p. 10). Pigs dig Jerusalem artichokes on sandy creek land all winter (FB 599, p. 17). Cooked potatoes: 4½ lb equal 1 lb of corn, no more than 4 lb of potato to 1 of grain (FB 1437, p. 9). Chopped, soaked alfalfa hay can be half the ration of pigs you aren't hurrying (FB 599, p. 22), and unthreshed bundle grain carries dry sows through winter (p. 24).
winter-feed-kale-roots-squash-and-artichokes

Acorns and other mast "Mast" is the nuts that fall in autumn. An English feeder reckoned a peck of acorns a day with a little bran put on about a pound a day for two months; California hogs ate raw acorns "with impunity," though in England they were "occasionally condemned as fatal" (Chesnut 1902, p. 353). OSU replaced 15-30% of a finishing ration with ground cull hazelnuts for the last 42 days, as Spain and Italy finish ham pigs on acorns (OSU EM 9271, p. 7). The oak poison is in young leaves, buds and green acorns (WSU, p. 27). Gather the ripe brown acorns of Oregon white oak, black oak and tanoak in September-November, feed them with other feed, never alone, and dry some for winter (rule of thumb). Bears work the same groves, so bring the acorns to the pigs, never the pigs to the woods (rule of thumb). Windfall fruit feeds pigs too, and picking it up keeps bears away (ODFW, p. 2).
acorns-and-other-mast

Garbage, skim milk and whey: cook it first - Kitchen garbage "containing raw meat scraps or bones" spreads trichinae (FB 1437, p. 5), and cooking garbage stops TB, in many areas "almost as frequent" in pigs as in cattle (Zoonoses, p. 27). Boil all garbage that has touched meat at least 30 minutes, longer with bones (p. 113); see "Garbage when no truck comes" in the Sanitation guide. - Skim milk is "a valuable protein supplement for grain," not a whole ration: about 4-5 lb per lb of grain for weaned pigs, 2-3 lb at 50-100 lb, 1-2 lb for big hogs. Whey is worth half as much, best with barley and peas (FB 1437, pp. 10-11). Boil milk and whey unless the animals are tested free of TB (p. 11): with no testing, always. See "Whey and buttermilk" in the Milk, Butter & Cheese guide. - Meat scraps and offal from healthy animals are good protein, as the old packing-house "tankage" was (FB 1437, p. 10), but only boiled (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 68), and not pork (rule of thumb).
garbage-skim-milk-and-whey-cook-it-first

Grain, protein and minerals - Grains against corn: wheat about 5% better, barley 90-95%, rye 95-100% but less liked, oats 60-70% (good for sows and growing pigs); grind them coarsely (FB 1437, pp. 8-9), and don't cook grain: it is "more harmful than beneficial" (p. 13). - Protein: 24% of the diet at 10-20 lb, falling to 13% over 150 lb (OSU EM 9271, p. 3); 15% for a pregnant sow (FB 1437, p. 14). Without bought meal: milk, whey, peas, clover, alfalfa and cooked scraps (rule of thumb). - Home mineral mix: equal weights of steamed bone meal, ground limestone (or air-slaked lime) and salt, plus wood ashes up to a third of it, iodized salt where goiter occurs, kept dry in a covered box (FB 1437, pp. 11-12). Even 1 part salt to 4 parts wood ash beats none; sows on grain alone run short of calcium and "dog sit" (No Animal Doctor, p. 327). - Selenium: Oregon is short of it and swine suffer for it, but it is also a poison (OSU EM 9094, p. 1). Stock a swine trace-mineral salt with selenium now and never give more than the label says (rule of thumb).
grain-protein-and-minerals

💧 Water, shade and heat: pigs die of heat "Pigs of all ages can overheat if they struggle, and can even die from heat stress. If boars overheat, they can be sterile for several months. Sows easily overheat when giving birth." Handle pigs only in the cool of early morning or evening (No Animal Doctor, p. 47). "Hogs suffer greatly from heat and must have shade" (FB 1437, p. 37), and sunburn is the other summer hazard (OSU EM 9271, p. 5). 1. Water all day: ½-1½ gallons per 100 lb of pig, the high end for young pigs and nursing sows, more in heat (Peace Corps, p. 210): about 4½ gallons for a 300-lb nursing sow (arithmetic). Clean water whenever they want it, not twice a day in a foul trough (FB 1437, p. 12). Don't share a water source with pigs (Peace Corps, p. 210). 2. Shade that breathes: trees in a clump, or a frame about 4 ft high roofed with hay, straw or weeds at least 2 ft deep, wetted on hot days so it drips, cooling the air and laying the dust. Low farrowing houses and A-frame huts are not shade: pigs crowd into them "even though they suffocate"; shut them in hot weather (FB 1437, p. 37). 3. A wallow: FB 1437 wants 4-6 in of water in a shaded concrete wallow, changed often,
water-shade-and-heat-pigs-die-of-heat

"even though they suffocate"; shut them in hot weather (FB 1437, p. 37). 3. A wallow: FB 1437 wants 4-6 in of water in a shaded concrete wallow, changed often, and calls a mud wallow "a nuisance" because pigs drink the foul water (p. 37); the Peace Corps manual counts a mud wallow as heat protection (p. 286). In a valley August any wallow beats none: keep it shaded and refill it with clean water (rule of thumb). 4. No work in the heat: no moving, weaning or hauling in the hot of the day; breeding above 86 °F (30 °C) "greatly" cuts fertility, so breed morning or evening (Peace Corps, p. 230). 5. Smoke days: clean water, extra shade or sprinkling, and put off weaning, regrouping and hauling until the air clears (PNW783, p. 10). Open straw shade, wetted on hot days; low huts trap heat and must be shut in summer (FB 1437, p. 37) (a diagram drawn for this guide). A pig down in the heat (panting, open mouth, wobbling, lying flat): stop, get it into shade, pour cool water over it, especially the head, let it rest, then offer water; an overheated animal may not drink until it cools (No Animal Doctor, p. 124). A pig that went without water and acts blind or convulses has salt poisoning: small drinks often, not all it wants at

until it cools (No Animal Doctor, p. 124). A pig that went without water and acts blind or convulses has salt poisoning: small drinks often, not all it wants at once (p. 332).

Getting ready to farrow Farrow in spring when the nights have warmed: newborn pigs want about 95 °F for three days, then 85 °F over three weeks, and "demand the most heat of any young domestic livestock" (OSU EM 9271, p. 8); with no heat lamps you have timing, straw and the sow's own heat (rule of thumb). Not in August either: sows overheat giving birth (No Animal Doctor, p. 47). 1. Pen her 3 days before she is due, in a dry, airy pen about 7 × 7 ft with a guard rail of 2-by-4s (or pipe, which can't be chewed) around the inside, about 10 in off the floor and 4-6 in from the walls (FB 1437, p. 24), so a piglet lies safe in the gap when she lies down against the wall (Peace Corps, p. 288). 2. Clean it with scalding water and lye, rinse and dry (FB 1437, p. 25), and if you can leave it empty in the sun for a few weeks (No Animal Doctor, p. 347). Bed it with dry wheat or rye straw or chopped hay, not oat straw, which stays wet; wash the mud off her sides and udder before she goes in (FB 1437, p. 25). 3. Feed her outside in a yard 6-8 ft long off the pen: a sow fed among her piglets cripples or kills them

she goes in (FB 1437, p. 25). 3. Feed her outside in a yard 6-8 ft long off the pen: a sow fed among her piglets cripples or kills them (p. 26). 4. A warm corner she can't enter: a boxed-in "hover" holds the piglets' own heat and stops drafts (OSU EM 9271, p. 8). A farrowing crate (4½-5 ft by 8 ft, the sow unable to turn) stays 20-25 °F warmer than the barn from her heat alone (FB 1437, p. 29; Peace Corps, p. 288). The guard rail keeps the sow from pinning a piglet against the wall (FB 1437, pp. 24-26) (a diagram drawn for this guide). Signs she is close: the udder fills 7-10 days ahead; colostrum (first milk) can be squeezed out within 24 hours; she grows restless, makes a nest, and may turn aggressive (Peace Corps, p. 231). Halve her feed the day before; none for 24 hours after, but plenty of lukewarm water (FB 1437, p. 15).
getting-ready-to-farrow

Farrowing night Someone should be there, checking every hour with a light ready (FB 1437, p. 25; Peace Corps, p. 231). 1. Each piglet: clear the membranes off the nose; if it isn't breathing, a few gentle slaps on the side or a brisk rub. Dry it, tie the cord with thread 1-2 in from the belly, cut beyond the knot, dip in iodine. Keep the litter in a box lined with sacks around warm bricks or a jug of hot water wrapped in cloth, and let them nurse if farrowing drags past 2-3 hours (FB 1437, p. 25; Peace Corps, p. 233). 2. How long: 3-4 hours, about 15 minutes between pigs. Wait up to 4 hours, or a stillborn pig, before reaching in or giving oxytocin, both "last resort measures" for the experienced (Peace Corps, p. 233). 3. The afterbirth ends it; a retained piece infects her, and a cloudy, smelly one may mean brucellosis (same page). Wear gloves (rule of thumb). 4. Colostrum the first day or the piglet dies. A sow raises only as many as she has working teats: foster extras onto another sow, masking everyone's smell. A piglet under 1 lb has "no chance" (pp. 229, 233). A sow with no milk: undiluted cow's milk every 2 hours, ½ in deep in a clean shallow pan (FB 1437, p. 14).
farrowing-night

Piglets: crushing, cold, teeth and iron - "Over 50 percent of the losses of newborn pigs during the first 10 days of life happen in the first 24 hours"; they chill easily (FB 1437, p. 26), and crushing is worst the first week (p. 29). - Needle teeth: snip the top third off all 8 with sharp side-cutting pliers so they don't tear the teats and each other; don't break or pull them (FB 1437, p. 26; Peace Corps, p. 234). Tails need no docking where pigs have room. - Iron: sow's milk lacks it, so piglets kept off soil turn pale, sluggish and rough-coated, then weak, with scours or "thumps" (gasping) (FB 1437, p. 32). Put clean, fresh soil or a sod in the pen (same page), dug where no pigs have been, since soil carries worm eggs (rule of thumb; Peace Corps, p. 234). Injectable iron goes in the ham in the first three days (same page); follow its label (Medical guide). - Creep feed at 3 weeks (a corner with grain only piglets can reach), protein at 5-6 weeks (FB 1437, p. 32).

Castration Castrate boar pigs you won't breed: no stray litters or inbreeding, calmer pigs, and no boar taint (the foul smell of mature boar meat) (No Animal Doctor, p. 192; OSU EM 9271, p. 6). Do it at about 2 weeks, while they suckle, so they heal before weaning (FB 1437, p. 32; Peace Corps, p. 235). 1. A helper holds the pig by the hind legs, or on its back in the lap, rump up. Feel for a hernia (gut in the scrotum): if there is one, don't castrate (No Animal Doctor, p. 192). 2. Wash scrotum and hands. Press a testicle against the skin and cut low, ½-1 in long, so it drains; press it out and pull gently until the cord tears off near the body, which bleeds less than cutting; repeat on the other side (Peace Corps, pp. 235-236). 3. Wash off the blood (it draws flies), dab on iodine, keep the pig on clean, dry bedding for 24 hours, and check it daily for 3 days (Peace Corps, p. 236). Grown boars bleed more and need a skilled hand (No Animal Doctor, p. 193).
castration

Weaning and the next litter Wean at 8 weeks or later: a good sow milks to 10-12 weeks, and a pig stunted by early weaning never catches up. Cut the sow's feed 4-5 days before, then take her away and leave the pigs in their pen (FB 1437, pp. 32-33). She comes back in heat 3-5 days later (Peace Corps, p. 229). Three litters in two years is a good average; fall pigs need extra care, and none should come after October 15 (FB 1437, pp. 33-34). 📚 Go deeper: 🖼 FB 1437, pp. 25-30 - bedded pen, cutting teeth, hover, crate; 🖼 Peace Corps, p. 289 - farrowing stalls; 🖼 No Animal Doctor, p. 192 - castration.

🩺 Pig health with no vet Know normal: about 102.2 °F for a grown pig, 103.6 °F for a young one (No Animal Doctor, p. 66); OSU uses 102.5 °F ± 1 (EM 9271, p. 4). Pulse and breathing are in Illinois Valley - Start Here. Watch daily for coughing, fever, going off feed, dullness and hard or fast breathing, and act at the first sign. Give shots in the neck just behind and below the ear, never the ham or loin, and wait out every withdrawal time before slaughter (EM 9271, p. 4). To hold a big pig, slip the loop of a finger-thick rope at least 10 ft long into its mouth behind the big canine teeth and tie it low to a post (🖼 No Animal Doctor, p. 47). Medicines in general: the Medical guide; this guide gives no doses. Prevention does most of the work. The old USDA sanitation system controls most worms: a clean farrowing pen, the sow washed before farrowing, a clean trip to clean pasture, and clean pasture for the pigs until 4 months old (FB 1437, p. 41). Disinfect with soap and water, then chlorine or iodine, then 48 hours of sun (Peace Corps, p. 288). Change bedding before it is wet and foul (FB 1437, p. 37). Keep new pigs apart 30-60 days (rule of thumb; FB 1437 holds new breeding

Planning a hog-killing day - Wait for cold: the carcass must reach 34-40 °F within 24 hours, 48 at most (FB 1186, p. 3): here, late November to February, in a dry spell with nights near freezing (rule of thumb); in a hard freeze, hang it in a shed or wrap it in a sheet (p. 16). Kill a healthy hog of about 200-225 lb (FB 2138, pp. 5-6), never one found dead, feverish or down (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, pp. 27-28). - Tools: a curved 6-inch skinning knife (it sticks too), a narrow boning knife, steel and oilstone, a 24-28-inch meat saw, bell scrapers, a hook, a thermometer to 212 °F, tubs for edible and inedible insides, plenty of hot and cold water, and a 50-gallon barrel with 25-30 gallons of water, which scalds a hog up to 250 lb, tilted at the end of a scraping table 4½ ft wide, 2½ ft high, 4-8 ft long (FB 2138, pp. 4-5, 9). Hang the carcass from a singletree gambrel on a beam, a limb or a "hobbyhorse" hoist (AWI-68, p. 7). - People: two to scrape, one at each end of the table (FB 2138, p. 5), and a third for the fire and water (rule of thumb). Shut the dogs away: raw pork scraps give them trichinosis (Zoonoses, p. 113). - The day before: pen the hog

a third for the fire and water (rule of thumb). Shut the dogs away: raw pork scraps give them trichinosis (Zoonoses, p. 113). - The day before: pen the hog alone, 24 hours without feed but with water, and never chase or wrestle it: a heated hog bleeds poorly and its "fiery" meat spoils (FB 2138, p. 6). Neighbors who kill several hogs a year can share a scalding vat over a firebox, a scraping platform and a hanging rail (AWI-68, p. 7).

Killing and sticking Shoot or stun first, and make the first shot count (FB 2138, p. 7). The brain is small and behind thick sinuses: aim on the center line of the forehead, slightly above a line between the eyes, not between the eyes (UF VM114, p. 9), toward the spinal canal (AVMA, p. 119). A .22 long rifle does for young animals, but hollow points may not get through an adult skull: use a heavier bullet on old sows and boars. Hold the muzzle a few inches off the head (VM114, p. 5); bullets "glance from a hog's skull," so keep people and stock out of line (FB 2138, p. 7). Aim slightly above the eye line, on the center line, toward the tail (UF VM114, p. 9; AVMA, p. 119) (a diagram drawn for this guide). Stick at once, with the hog hoisted by a hind leg or on its back, a helper astride holding the front feet (FB 2138, pp. 7-8): open the skin about 3 in in front of the breastbone; push the knife in edge down, straight toward the breastbone; follow the bone down until the knife slips under it and push about 1 in more; cut toward the backbone, then thrust forward toward the head to cut the artery. Stay on the center line or you stick a shoulder; don't stick the heart; let

Keep the hole no wider than the blade, so scald water can't get in (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 62). The knife (a) into the fat, (b) above the artery, (c) after the cut; the heart is not the target (USDA FB 2138, p. 8).

Scalding or skinning Scalding keeps the skin for cracklings, salt pork and hams that store well, but takes much hot water and fuel. The books differ, and all work: 143 °F ± 2 for 4-4½ minutes (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 63); 140-145 °F in a barrel, as hotter water may "set" the bristles (AWI-68, p. 7); or on a farm 155-165 °F to start, the hog kept moving and pulled out often (FB 2138, p. 9). Test, don't guess: when the hair on ham, flank, belly and head slips out, take the hog out (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 63). Scrape fast, before the skin sets: twist the hair off the legs, pull dewclaws and toes with the hook while hot, scrape with the bell scraper on edge, put sacks and hot water on stubborn patches, then rinse, singe and shave (FB 2138, pp. 9-11). Skinning suits hogs over about 250 lb: prop it on its back with bricks and skin it like a beef, slowly, since the skin is thin (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, pp. 62-63); it needs no barrel or fire, but you lose the rind (rule of thumb).
scalding-or-skinning

Gutting, chilling and cutting 1. Slip the gambrel under both big hind-leg tendons and hoist (FB 2138, p. 11). Split the breastbone; cut down between the hams, missing the bladder; open the belly with the knife handle inside and the point out (pp. 11-13). 2. Tie off the bung (rear gut) (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 65), free the liver, cut the diaphragm, and lift out guts, heart and lungs without rupturing the guts. Save liver (gall bladder off), heart, tongue, and caul and ruffle fat for lard (FB 2138, pp. 13-15). 3. Look before you eat: white spots on the liver mean roundworm (No Animal Doctor, p. 346); small shiny bladders, ½-1 cm, under the tongue or in jaw, heart, diaphragm or shoulder muscle are pork tapeworm cysts (Zoonoses, p. 111). Boil such offal and bury it under lime (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 67); bury a carcass full of cysts (rule of thumb). 4. Wash out the cavity, saw down the backbone, pull the leaf fat while warm, and hang the halves apart, or hams and bellies spoil overnight (FB 2138, pp. 14, 16): dress in the afternoon, cut next morning (FB 1186, p. 16). If it turns warm, cut up the sides and hang the pieces to air, but nothing is as safe as cold (FB 2138, p. 19). 5. Cut the cold carcass (pp.

it turns warm, cut up the sides and hang the pieces to air, but nothing is as safe as cold (FB 2138, p. 19). 5. Cut the cold carcass (pp. 18-23; 🖼 cuts, p. 19): head off behind the ears; shoulder off between the 2nd and 3rd ribs, split into picnic (cure it with the hams), butt and fat plate (lard or salt pork); ham behind the rise of the pelvic bone; loin sawn off the bacon; spareribs lifted off the bacon; jowls cured like bacon. Eat, cure or can fresh pork within 3-5 days: it spoils faster than other meat (FB 2138, p. 24), and can it only in a pressure canner (pp. 39-40). Curing, smoking and storing hams and bacon: "Curing pork and venison" in the Preserving Food guide; smoke with hardwood, never pine, at 100-120 °F, in a smokehouse at least 50 ft from other buildings (FB 2138, pp. 32-34). - Fresh sausage: ⅓ fat, ⅔ lean; test batch 4 lb trimmings, 5 tsp salt, 4 tsp sage, 2 tsp pepper, 1 tsp sugar (FB 2138, p. 45). Fry a patty to check the seasoning; never taste it raw (FB 1186, p. 41). - Headcheese: simmer head (eyes, eardrums, teeth and nasal passages out), tongue, heart and clean skin until the meat slips off the bone; chop, add broth, boil again, season and chill in pans. Scrapple: 4 parts ground cooked meat, 3 broth, 1 cereal (7 cornmeal to 3 flour) (FB 2138, pp. 46-48). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 2138 - the whole job in photos; AWI-68 - hoists, scald vats, smokehouses; Oregon custom-exempt FAQ, p. 2 - in normal times custom-killed meat "cannot be sold, traded, bartered or given away," so trade live pigs or shares of a live pig.

🫙 Rendering lard and cracklings Lard is 9-13% of the live weight of a meat-type hog and 14-18% of a fat one (FB 2138, p. 6); a 225-lb hog gave 27 lb of fat for the kettle (p. 22). 1. Sort it. Leaf fat (from around the kidneys) makes the best lard; render it apart for baking. Back fat and trimmings make the rest; caul and ruffle fat from the guts give darker lard, so render them separately (FB 2138, p. 40); strong intestinal fat is for soap (Minnesota, p. 2). 2. Keep it cold and render soon: at 32-35 °F no more than 5-7 days (same page). 3. Cut it small; take off the skin for whiter lard and pick out every bit of lean, which browns and darkens it (same page; FB 2138, p. 23). 4. Kettle: iron, steel or aluminum, never copper. A little water in the bottom, a small batch on a low fire, the rest added as it melts; don't fill it, or it boils over (Minnesota, p. 3; FB 2138, p. 40). 5. Heat: it sits near 212 °F while the water cooks off, then climbs; hold 235-245 °F (Minnesota, p. 3), never above 255 °F (FB 2138, p. 42). Stir often so nothing scorches. 6. Done when the bubbling stops and the cracklings float, chestnut-brown and easily crushed; fully rendered they sink. Full
rendering-lard-and-cracklings

255 °F (FB 2138, p. 42). Stir often so nothing scorches. 6. Done when the bubbling stops and the cracklings float, chestnut-brown and easily crushed; fully rendered they sink. Full rendering drives out the water so the lard keeps (same pages). 7. Strain through two or three layers of cheesecloth, press the cracklings, and pour into clean, scalded, dry crocks or tins of 5-10 lb, filled to the top; cool fast and store dark and cool, below 50 °F (FB 2138, p. 42; Minnesota, pp. 3-4). Yields: leaf fat 90-93% lard; mixed leaf, back and cutting fat 80-85%; gut fat 55-65%; pressed cracklings 4-6% of the fat (FB 2138, p. 42): the 27 lb of fat makes roughly 22 lb of lard (arithmetic). Air, light, water left in, and warm storage make lard rancid; 10% beef fat firms soft lard; slightly rancid lard is rescued by heating it with sliced potatoes until they brown, then straining (Minnesota, p. 4). ⚠ Hot fat burns badly: keep children back, keep a lid at hand to smother a fire, and never put water on burning fat (rule of thumb). Eat the cracklings as they are or in cornbread (rule of thumb). More in "Salt, sweeteners and fat" in Food From Scratch; soap in "Soap from fat and ashes" in the Make-Do Household guide.

🦠 Keeping pigs and people safe Trichinosis is a worm in the muscle of pigs, rats, bears and other meat-eaters, caught from raw or undercooked meat, most often pork. 8-15 days later come sudden muscle pain and swollen upper eyelids, then eye pain, sweats and fever to 104 °F; heart and nerve damage can kill in weeks 3-8 (Zoonoses, pp. 120-121). If that follows a meal of pork or bear, see the Medical guide. - Keep it out of the pigs: boil garbage with meat in it, feed no raw meat or carcasses (FB 1437, p. 5; Zoonoses, p. 113), and keep rats out of feed and pens (rule of thumb). - Cook pork until it changes from pink to gray all through, at least 170 °F (77 °C) inside (Zoonoses, p. 121; FB 2138, p. 46). FB 2138 says heating it through to 137 °F kills the worms (same page); cook well past that, since thick cuts fool you (rule of thumb). - Freezing works only in a deep freezer: 5 °F for 20-30 days or -10 °F for 10-20 days (FB 2138, p. 46). Wild trichinella in bear meat survives freezing (Hunting guide). With no freezer, cook it. - Home-cured and smoked pork is raw. People caught trichinosis from "imperfectly cooked fresh pork, and sausage, smoked hams, bacon, and shoulders," and from tasting sausage while seasoning it (FB
keeping-pigs-and-people-safe

- Home-cured and smoked pork is raw. People caught trichinosis from "imperfectly cooked fresh pork, and sausage, smoked hams, bacon, and shoulders," and from tasting sausage while seasoning it (FB 1186, p. 41). Cook country ham and bacon. Pork tapeworm (Taenia solium): pigs get the cysts by eating human feces; people get the tapeworm from undercooked pork, and its eggs can grow cysts in another person's brain, "the major cause of seizures" in many poor countries (Zoonoses, pp. 109-110). Pigs must never reach a latrine, outhouse pit or human waste, raw sewage must not fertilize their ground, and all pork must be cooked well (pp. 112-113); salting and pickling don't kill the cysts (p. 113). Latrines are in the Sanitation guide. Also from pigs: erysipelas from handling infected meat, brucellosis, and TB through raw milk and garbage (FB 1437, pp. 39-40). Wear gloves to butcher and to help a farrowing, cover cuts, wash well, and keep pregnant women away from abortions and afterbirths (rule of thumb). Bites, kicks and knife cuts: Field Care guide.

🚫 Never let pigs go feral A pig that gets loose for good does not stay a farm pig (rule of thumb). Free-ranging pigs spread diseases and parasites to people, lose more to predators, and breed with no control (Peace Corps, p. 285); free-range village pigs are "not-too-distant offspring" of wild ones (p. 283). A gilt can come in heat at about 5 months and farrow 114 days later (pp. 228, 231), and a good sow raises 8 or more (FB 1437, p. 7): one loose pair can be dozens within two years (arithmetic). Feral pigs root up meadows, camas beds and creek banks, raid gardens and grain, carry brucellosis and trichinella, and a wild sow is dangerous (rule of thumb). - Never release pigs: not to "fend for themselves," not when feed runs short, not to fatten on acorns in the woods. Sell, trade or butcher them. Releasing pigs is against the law in Oregon in normal times; the drive has no copy of the rule (rule of thumb). - Count the pigs every day, walk the fence weekly, fix holes at once, chain the gates, and castrate every boar you won't breed (rule of thumb; No Animal Doctor, p. 192). - A pig gets out: go after it the same day with a feed bucket while it still comes to you. 🧬 Keeping the line going - Records: breeding date, boar, farrowing date, pigs born and weaned, sicknesses; a big calendar will do (Peace Corps, p. 237). - Keep gilts from big litters that grew well and from calm sows that milked to 10-12 weeks; choose at 5-6 months, when faults show, and grow them on pasture with only ¼-⅓ of their feed as corn (FB 1437, pp. 6-7, 34-35). - Keep a good sow 6-8 years (p. 22); cull cross sows, pig-eaters, poor milkers and any that won't settle (pp. 6, 32). - Boars: "the boar is half the herd"; pick one to correct the sows' faults, and when his daughters join the herd trade him for an unrelated boar as good (FB 1437, p. 7). A neighborhood should keep at least two unrelated boars and swap them every few years (rule of thumb). There is no artificial insemination without liquid nitrogen to store semen (No Animal Doctor, p. 193). - Crossbreed for vigor: a crossbred sow to a boar of a third breed, then to a fourth (Peace Corps, p. 282), so keep several breeds in the valley (rule of thumb). Save seed of rape, kale, mangels, peas, barley and squash: they are the feed (Seed Bank guide). Ear notches last for life where tags tear out. 🐄 Cattle: a Family Milk Cow, Beef and Oxen How to keep cattle with no feed store, no vet and no freezer: whether your ground can carry a cow, dairy, beef and dual-purpose breeds, fences, water and sheds for our wet winters, pasture, hay and roots, the plants that kill cattle here, a family milk cow's daily routine and drying her off, breeding with a bull, calving and when to help, calves, castration, sickness with no vet, training and working oxen, butchering a beef and keeping 400 lb of meat without a freezer, hides and tallow, predators, fire season, and a year's work in the valley. What to do with the milk is in the Milk, Butter & Cheese guide. The cattle books are in Animals\Cattle-Horses-Pigs, no-vet medicine in Animals\Veterinary, yokes in Horses-Draft-Animals\Draft-Harness, predators and fire in Animals\Planning-Predators-Toxic-Plants, poisonous plants in Wild-Plants, and tanning in Trapping. ### The short version - A cow needs real land. Even farmed hard, 2 acres is "the least possible area" for one cow (Keeping One Cow, p. 15). On unwatered valley ground plan 3-5 acres and about 3 tons of hay a year (rule of thumb); on brush or serpentine, keep goats. - Cold rain is the enemy. Give a mud-free, three-sided shed (OSU EC1514, p. 7), and never work oxen in cold, wet weather: a wet yoke rubs necks raw (Animal Management, p.

rain is the enemy. Give a mud-free, three-sided shed (OSU EC1514, p. 7), and never work oxen in cold, wet weather: a wet yoke rubs necks raw (Animal Management, p. 312). - Change feed slowly, over a week or more. Lush clover or alfalfa causes bloat: the left side swells drum-tight (EC1514, pp. 13-14). - Keep pregnant cows away from ponderosa pine needles, never feed yew or hedge trimmings, and keep bracken and tansy ragwort out of pasture and hay (AIB 415, pp. 84, 113, 24, 105). - Calving: the calf should come within about 2 hours of the water bag; pull only while she strains; a backward calf must come out fast (Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 53, 56). - Colostrum: about 10% of the calf's weight within 4 hours; after 24 hours it can't absorb it (EC1514, p. 5; Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 67). - Brucellosis and TB reach people through raw milk and birth fluids: gloves at calvings; boil or pasteurize milk from untested cows (Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 114, 117-118). - A beef is about 400 lb of carcass. Butcher in cold weather, share it, and corn, salt, dry or pressure-can what can't be eaten in days (USDA FB 2209, pp. 19, 31-33).

🐄 Is a cow right for your land? Land. An Ottawa writer found "two acres of land is the least possible area that will provide cow-food for the entire year": an acre of clover and timothy for hay, an acre of green fodder and mangels, well manured (Keeping One Cow, p. 15). One family fed a cow from half an acre of clover cut three times plus an acre of garden crops (pp. 20-21); a good cow lived on about 1 acre of pasture until late July (p. 46). On rough range one cow needs from 1¼ acres in wet country to 25 acres in dry country, and cattle over a year eat twice what younger ones do (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 37). Our valley-floor soils are "used mainly for irrigated pasture and hay" (Soil Survey, p. 9); serpentine grows poor, low-calcium forage and holds no stock pond (p. 49). Pasture browns from June to the October rains, so without irrigation plan 3-5 acres of decent grass per cow and calf, plus hay (rule of thumb). Cow or goats? "From 6 to 8 goats can be kept upon the feed required for 1 cow," and a goat "can be kept where it would be impossible to keep a cow" (USDA FB 920, pp. 3, 25): brush and steep ground suit the Goats guide; grass, water and hay ground suit a
is-a-cow-right-for-your-land

where it would be impossible to keep a cow" (USDA FB 920, pp. 3, 25): brush and steep ground suit the Goats guide; grass, water and hay ground suit a cow. "Two to five families ... can readily unite in having one cow kept, dividing the milk and expenses" (Keeping One Cow, p. 11). Which kind (OSU EC1514, pp. 3-6): a family milk cow bred every year, her heifers replacing her and her steers becoming beef or oxen (rule of thumb); beef cows with calves, which need the most land and year-round feed but little daily work; or weaned calves bought at about 7 months, grazed one season and butchered when the grass ends, the least land and commitment. Buying. Beginners should buy "good, young, bred cows that have calved at least once," all from one reputable herd (EC1514, pp. 3-4). Pick a gentle cow not over 5 years old, with a large barrel, a big well-formed udder and teats set well apart (Keeping One Cow, p. 84); one with her second calf "you can keep her profitably for five years" (p. 17). Age by the front teeth: the first pair of big permanent incisors at 1½-2 years, the second at 2-2½, the third at 3-3½, the fourth at 4-5 (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 78). Pass over an animal that stays thin on a good appetite (Johne's disease; EC1514, p.
is-a-cow-right-for-your-land

at 2-2½, the third at 3-3½, the fourth at 4-5 (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 78). Pass over an animal that stays thin on a good appetite (Johne's disease; EC1514, p. 13). Keep new cattle apart 3 weeks (p. 6), and test for TB and brucellosis if anyone still can (USDA FB 1470, p. 30).

🏠 Fences, water and shelter Fences (Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 17-18): a board fence is the strongest, for corrals and handling pens; split rail lasts, "except that it generally cannot be built tall enough to be cattle proof"; a sapling fence (2-3-in saplings 6-8 ft long, crossed every 8-16 ft) takes moderate pressure; thorn brush is a stopgap; 3-6 strands of wire is "very cattle proof." Brace the corners of the outside fence and use electric wire for inside paddocks (EC1514, p. 8); electric fences "can be run off of solar charged batteries" (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 131). In closed range you pay for damage if your cattle get out (EC1514, p. 8). Barbed wire, staples and roofing nails cause "hardware disease" (UNH, p. 15): pick up wire scraps, and cut baling wire with pliers in one cut, never a hatchet (USDA FB 1470, pp. 35-36). Handling. A corral with a narrow alley and a squeeze chute or head catch makes every job safer; no electric prods (EC1514, p. 7). By hand, lift the tail near its base from one side, or pinch the nose between thumb and finger (Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 19-25). Strap a kicker's hind legs above the hocks, and never strike a cow for kicking (FB 1470, p. 38). Shelter. "Under most weather conditions, cattle do very well outside." In the Northwest they need "a mud-free
fences-water-and-shelter

the hocks, and never strike a cow for kicking (FB 1470, p. 38). Shelter. "Under most weather conditions, cattle do very well outside." In the Northwest they need "a mud-free area with protection from wind and rain" such as a three-sided shed, gutters on the roofs, and manure runoff kept out of creeks (EC1514, p. 7). Dry, draft-free, airy and sunny matters; temperature hardly does, and cows do best in the coldest weather and worst in summer heat (FB 1470, p. 17). In a shared open shed timid cows get pushed off the feed, so tie them at feeding and dehorn loose cows (p. 19). A tie stall can be 5 ft wide and 5 ft long with a 2-ft manger (Keeping One Cow, p. 21); a tied cow uses about 4 lb of straw bedding a day, 8 lb to soak up all the urine, 14 lb in a box stall (FB 1470, p. 24). Store hay apart from the animals: wet hay heats and can catch fire (EC1514, p. 7; PNW783, p. 8). Water. Cattle drink 4-20 gallons a day, much more in heat (EC1514, p. 9); cows drank 80% more in hot summer than in cold winter, and cows watered at will milked better than cows watered once a day (FB 1470, pp. 26-27). Barrels, tires and tubs make troughs, never ones that held chemicals (EC1514, p.

and cows watered at will milked better than cows watered once a day (FB 1470, pp. 26-27). Barrels, tires and tubs make troughs, never ones that held chemicals (EC1514, p. 7). Rats spread leptospirosis through water, and liver flukes live in snails on wet ground: fence off marshy spots (Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 118, 164). Plan water for a power failure (PNW783, p. 7).

🌾 Pasture, hay and winter feed How much: 2-2.5% of body weight in dry feed a day, up to 3% for calves under 500 lb (UNH, p. 11); on poor, mature grass hay intake falls to 1.5% and the animal goes short (EC1514, p. 9). A 1,000-lb cow eats about 25 lb of hay a day (arithmetic). Change feed slowly, over a week or more, or the rumen sours and bloats (EC1514, p. 13). Turn cattle onto spring grass a little at a time (UNH, p. 15) and give hungry stock dry hay before green feed (Animal Management, p. 316); young clover or alfalfa, "especially with the dew on," causes bloat (FB 1470, pp. 34-35). Don't graze below 3 inches, where the worms are (EC1514, p. 14). Making hay (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 37): cut just before the plants flower, after the dew is off; dry it on the ground 1-3 days, out of rain; stack it on dry ground near where you feed, peaked or covered so rain runs off, fenced from the cattle. Good hay is leafy with few seed heads; refuse moldy, dusty or hot bales (UNH, p. 12). Sun-bleached hay causes vitamin A shortage: watery eyes, rough coat, night blindness (EC1514, p. 8). Roots and fodder with no feed store (Keeping One Cow): peas and oats sown early and cut green from about 6 weeks (p.
pasture-hay-and-winter-feed

rough coat, night blindness (EC1514, p. 8). Roots and fodder with no feed store (Keeping One Cow): peas and oats sown early and cut green from about 6 weeks (p. 15); mangels, which keep until April if handled gently (p. 16); sugar beets, which don't flavor milk, while turnips do, so feed turnips only to a dry cow (pp. 18, 20); winter rye for spring (p. 21); and Jerusalem artichokes, a bushel a day in winter plus 8-10 lb of hay, about 1 ton of hay for 8 months (pp. 73-74). Cut up roots and apples: whole ones cause choke (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 166). Feed at the same hours daily; cows mind a change in feeding more than in milking times (FB 1470, p. 9). Mature oxen and dry cows do well on hay or pasture alone (UNH, p. 12). Salt and minerals. Salt always, about 1 ounce a day for a cow in milk, kept out of the rain (FB 1470, p. 27); trace-mineral salt where you can, and calcium to phosphorus near 1-2 to 1 (bone meal supplies both) (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 30). Oregon is short of selenium: it causes white muscle disease in calves and retained afterbirths, mastitis and poor fertility in cows (OSU EM 9094, pp. 1, 3). Feed a selenium mineral in a covered feeder (p. 5), but too much is toxic (EC1514,
pasture-hay-and-winter-feed

retained afterbirths, mastitis and poor fertility in cows (OSU EM 9094, pp. 1, 3). Feed a selenium mineral in a covered feeder (p. 5), but too much is toxic (EC1514, p. 11); stock a year or more now (rule of thumb). Lush spring grass can bring grass tetany: add magnesium to the mineral (No Animal Doctor, p. 329). Without irrigation, put up hay for the dry summer as well as the wet winter (rule of thumb).

Then check that name against this list. Most poisonings happen when cattle are hungry, thirsty, moved or stressed, or turned out in early spring when poisonous plants are the only green ones; for most there is no treatment (AIB 415, p. 11). 🥛 The family milk cow: daily routine, milk and drying off How much milk. Over 14,000 grade (mixed-breed) cows averaged 6,261 lb of milk a year (USDA FB 1470, p. 5): about 2,900 quarts, or 9-10 a day over a 10-month lactation (arithmetic). Family cows gave 10-20 quarts a day in full flow (Keeping One Cow, p. 19); one "fills a twelve-quart pail each night and morning," butter for six people (p. 20). Don't expect 30 quarts: "be quite satisfied if your cow gives half that" (p. 18). Fall-calving cows gave the most milk in a year; spring calvers slump in summer heat, flies and short pasture (FB 1470, p. 8). Milking three times a day gave about 12% more over 40 days and 18% over a year (p. 10). Every milking: 1. Twice a day, same times. Grain before milking; hay, and anything strong-smelling such as turnips, after it, so dust and taints stay out of the milk (FB 1470, p. 26). 2. Wipe each teat with a clean damp cloth, one per cow, and dry it; never wash teats in the milk pail (Keeping One Cow, p. 17). Strip the first squirts into a strip cup and look for clots (Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 82, 89). 3. Milk with dry hands, short nails and a steady grip; rough, slow milking makes cows kick. Near the end, press up
the-family-milk-cow-daily-routine-milk-and-drying-off

for clots (Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 82, 89). 3. Milk with dry hands, short nails and a steady grip; rough, slow milking makes cows kick. Near the end, press up on each quarter to bring the last milk down (FB 1470, pp. 10-11), and milk until the udder is slack (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 82): about 10 minutes a cow (Keeping One Cow, p. 17). 4. Dip the teats after (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 89), and dry them before she goes out in the cold, or they chap; oil cracked teats (FB 1470, pp. 37-38). 5. Weigh the milk now and then: a drop is often the first sign of sickness (FB 1470, p. 12). Strain and cool it at once, then see "Clean milking" and "Raw milk dangers" in the Milk, Butter & Cheese guide. Sharing with the calf. For the most milk, take the calf off after 2-3 days (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 82); a calf left with the cow is "the way in which nature adjusts the supply to meet the demand" (FB 1470, p. 11). If you can't milk twice a day, let the calf run with her by day, pen it at night, and milk once in the morning: less milk, far less work (rule of thumb). Drying off. The dry spell rests the udder, feeds the unborn calf and rebuilds the cow (FB 1470,
the-family-milk-cow-daily-routine-milk-and-drying-off

once in the morning: less milk, far less work (rule of thumb). Drying off. The dry spell rests the udder, feeds the unborn calf and rebuilds the cow (FB 1470, p. 5): a month to six weeks for an ordinary cow in good flesh, two months or more for a heavy milker or a thin cow (p. 6). Sources differ: Keeping One Cow says 4-6 weeks (p. 91), "some eight weeks" (p. 108), and no more than 6 for a one-cow family (p. 49); plan on 6-8 weeks (our reading). How: skip one milking, then two, then three; when she is down to 6-8 lb (3-4 quarts) a day, stop, leave the udder alone, and cut her grain (FB 1470, p. 6). Watch for a hot, hard quarter (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 87). July is a good time to dry her off, with pasture short and milk hard to keep (Keeping One Cow, p. 49); she should calve neither fat nor thin (EC1514, p. 3).

🐂 Breeding without AI Heat comes every 21 days and lasts 12-18 hours (EC1514, p. 21): bellowing, restlessness, riding other cows or standing to be ridden, clear mucus. The egg comes about 11 hours after heat ends, so put her with the bull toward the end of heat, while she is gaining weight (Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 42-43). Keep a cow in heat away from heavily pregnant cows, which get ridden and hurt (FB 1470, p. 6). Breed heifers at 18 months or more and growing; give a cow 2 months' rest after calving (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 43), but rebreed within 3 months for a calf every 12 months (EC1514, p. 5). Pregnancy lasts 283 days, give or take 19 (p. 4). Due date: count back 3 months from breeding and add 10 days, so bred March 10 is due December 20 (FB 1470, p. 15). Write every breeding down. A short season of 45-60 days gives calves of one age (EC1514, p. 4). The bull. One bull serves about 25 cows: own one, share one, or lease one tested free of the venereal diseases trich and vibrio; a shared bull brings disease, and "bulls also pose a safety risk" (EC1514, p. 4). One family gave its calf to the bull's owner for three seasons of service (Keeping One Cow, p. 46). Pick sound feet and legs, big testicles
breeding-without-ai

risk" (EC1514, p. 4). One family gave its calf to the bull's owner for three seasons of service (Keeping One Cow, p. 46). Pick sound feet and legs, big testicles and a good mother. A bull is half of every calf and over the years up to 80% of the herd's blood, so avoid inbreeding, which brings dwarf and deformed calves (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 41); swap bulls between neighborhoods every few years (rule of thumb). Many cows coming back into heat points to vibriosis (p. 118). Horned bulls are "decidedly more dangerous" (FB 1470, p. 38): never turn your back on a bull or handle one alone (rule of thumb). A skilled hand can feel a calf through the rectum at 60 days (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 44); otherwise watch for the next heat 3 weeks after breeding (rule of thumb).

🍼 Calving: when and how to help When to calve here. In western Oregon, late fall and winter calving brings mud, scours and pneumonia; spring calving puts cows on growing grass (EC1514, p. 4). Beef cows: March-April. The family cow: September-October, dry through the hot, smoky end of summer and milking all winter (FB 1470, p. 8; rule of thumb). Signs and setting. 24-72 hours ahead the ligaments beside the tailhead loosen, the vulva swells, mucus shows and the udder fills (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 53); close to it she may wander off, stop eating, and get up and down (Mississippi P2675, p. 2). Give a clean, dry, well-bedded pen in wet weather, keep children and dogs away (FB 1470, pp. 7, 32), and check at least every 3 hours (Mississippi, p. 2). Have lubricant, shoulder-length sleeves, soap, warm water, towels, and obstetric (OB) chains or soft ropes with handles (p. 5). Wear gloves: brucellosis and other birth infections reach people (Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 54, 118). Stages: getting ready, 2-6 hours, contractions 15 minutes apart, then the water bag; delivery, 30-60 minutes, heifers longer; afterbirth, 2-12 hours (Nebraska EC1907, pp. 2-3; Mississippi, p. 2). Help when there is no calf 2 hours after the water bag (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 53), after 30 minutes of straining with no progress (Mississippi, p. 5), or sooner if the legs look wrong

calf 2 hours after the water bag (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 53), after 30 minutes of straining with no progress (Mississippi, p. 5), or sooner if the legs look wrong or she is worn out; Nebraska allows heifers 2-3 hours and cows 1-2 (p. 3). Helping (Nebraska, pp. 3-4; Mississippi, pp. 6-7; FB 1470, p. 32): 1. Scrub her vulva and your arms; sleeve and lubricate. Feel which legs are coming (the picture). 2. Size check: pulling the front legs, the whole head should enter her pelvis and each fetlock come a hand's width past the vulva. If not, the calf may be too big: get the most skilled person you can. 3. Chains: two loops on each leg (the picture); never a chain on the jaw. 4. Pull only while she strains, a few inches on one leg, then the other ("walking out" the shoulders); once head and shoulders are out, pull down at about 45°. Hips stuck: push back a little and turn the calf a quarter turn. 5. Never pull with a vehicle; a calf jack pulls like seven men and kills in unskilled hands (Mississippi, p. 6; Nebraska, p. 4). Front or hind? Feel the soles and the two joints; then two loops of chain on each leg (Mississippi, pp. 6-7; Nebraska, p. 3) (a diagram drawn for this guide). Wrong positions, about 5% of calves

and the two joints; then two loops of chain on each leg (Mississippi, pp. 6-7; Nebraska, p. 3) (a diagram drawn for this guide). Wrong positions, about 5% of calves (Nebraska, p. 2; Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 55-58; Mississippi, pp. 4-5). Push the calf back between contractions, and cup each hoof in your hand as you bring it up, so it can't tear the womb. - A leg back: push the calf back, lift the knee, then bring the foot forward. Head back or down: push the legs back, bring the head (gently by the jaw or a nostril) onto them, then the legs. - Hind feet first: pull it quickly; the cord is pinched and the calf drowns if you wait (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 56). Only the tail (breech): push the rump forward, bring each hock up, then each foot; check for a twin (p. 58). - Upside down: maybe a twisted womb; skilled help only (same page). Wrong positions: 1 one leg back, 2 knees bent, 3 leg over the neck, 4 head down, 5 head back, 6 upside down (Diseases of Cattle, pp. 237, 239). The first hours: 1. Breathing: clear nose and mouth by hand, rub the calf hard or tickle a nostril with a straw. Still not breathing? Put a short hose in one nostril, hold the mouth and other nostril shut, and blow

rub the calf hard or tickle a nostril with a straw. Still not breathing? Put a short hose in one nostril, hold the mouth and other nostril shut, and blow every 5-7 seconds (Nebraska, p. 4). 2. Navel: soak it in 7% iodine; tie a bleeding cord with iodined string (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 67). 3. Colostrum: nursing within an hour (Nebraska, p. 5); 10% of its weight within 4 hours, 20% within 24 (EC1514, p. 5), about 8 lb (4 quarts) in 4 hours for an 80-lb calf (arithmetic). None is absorbed after 24 hours; spare colostrum can be "allowed to sour" and kept (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 67). 4. The cow: warm water to drink, and don't milk her out for a day or two, against milk fever (FB 1470, p. 7). 5. Afterbirth: never pull it. If she eats well, let it drop by itself, even 10 days (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 62; Mississippi, p. 3); fever or a stinking discharge needs skilled help. Bury afterbirths: they draw predators (Mississippi, p. 5). 6. Womb pushed out (prolapse): keep her lying still, the womb clean and wet in a clean sheet (rule of thumb), and get the most skilled hands you can (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 61). 📚 Go deeper: Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 52-65 - positions with drawings, prolapse, milk fever; Nebraska EC1907 and Mississippi P2675 -

🐮 Raising calves On the cow, beef calves nurse until 7-8 months (EC1514, p. 5); wean across a fence with a couple of hot wires, so cow and calf still see and hear each other (p. 6). By bucket: take the calf off after colostrum and feed whole milk at 4-5% of its weight twice a day (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 68), 2-4 quarts at 101-105 °F (OSU EM 9280, p. 2). Teach it to drink by letting it suck your fingers as you lower its nose into the pail (Keeping One Cow, pp. 16-17). Offer a little grain from 2-4 weeks and hay from 4-5 weeks; wean when it eats 1 lb of grain a day, at 6-8 weeks (Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 68, 71), or 8-14 weeks (UNH, p. 11). Always clean water, scalded buckets, and a mineral block from 3 months. House each calf in 18 sq ft, or a 4×8-ft hutch facing the sun with a small yard (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 70), on deep dry straw with fresh air but no drafts; ammonia smell at calf height means new bedding (EM 9280, p. 2). Don't let calves suck each other: it brings mastitis later (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 88). Scours (diarrhea) kill more calves than anything else (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 68). Mix 2 liters (about 2 quarts) of water, 1 teaspoon of salt and

Healthy Cattle, p. 88). Scours (diarrhea) kill more calves than anything else (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 68). Mix 2 liters (about 2 quarts) of water, 1 teaspoon of salt and 2 teaspoons of baking soda; give 1-2 liters 2-3 times a day, by tube if the calf is too weak (p. 69). Keep feeding milk and give the electrolyte between feeds, never mixed in (EM 9280, p. 2); Raising Healthy Cattle says stop milk 24-48 hours, but follow OSU's newer advice. A calf that won't drink, can't stand or runs over 104 °F needs skilled help (same page). Prevent scours with colostrum, dry pens and sick calves kept apart (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 70). Most Northwest calves need a selenium shot at birth, label dose only; while vaccines last, give a 7- or 8-way clostridial vaccine with tetanus at 2-3 months, a booster 3-6 weeks later and again at 6 months (EC1514, p. 11). One-cow families once sold the calf at 4 weeks (Keeping One Cow, p. 17); now keep heifers to replace the cow and raise steers for beef or a team (rule of thumb).

✂ Castration, dehorning and marking Steers are safer, easier to handle and gain faster than bulls (No Animal Doctor, p. 187). When: beef calves as young as you can, from a few days to 3 months (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 73), or 2-3 months (No Animal Doctor, p. 187); future oxen at 6 months to 1 year, so they grow a wider head and stronger horns first (UNH, p. 20). Very young castration brings more urinary stones later (No Animal Doctor, p. 187). Pick cool weather out of fly season, after a clostridial and tetanus shot if you have one (UNH, p. 20; Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 73). The knife (No Animal Doctor, pp. 188-189; Raising Healthy Cattle, pp. 73-74): 1. Tie the calf; wash your hands and the scrotum with soap, clean water and disinfectant; local anesthetic if you have it. 2. Pull the scrotum tight and cut off its lower third. Pull each testicle out steadily until the cord breaks (or scrape the cord through); trim hanging tissue. Over about 6 months, tie each cord tightly twice with clean string and cut below the tie. 3. Fly ointment on the wound, and walk the calf daily for 1-2 weeks so it drains. Bleeding steadily over 15 minutes: pack the scrotum with clean cotton and close it with clothespins for 12-24 hours (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 74). Burdizzo (crushing

Burdizzo (crushing clamp): no wound. Crush each cord separately, twice, at different heights, never across both at one level, or the scrotum dies (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 74; No Animal Doctor, pp. 187-188). Rubber ring: only young calves with small testicles, at 1-2 months (UNH, p. 20); "less preferable" where tetanus is about (No Animal Doctor, p. 189). Pain relief such as meloxicam needs a vet's prescription (EM 9280, p. 2). Dehorning: a hot iron before 4 months (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 75); caustic paste works only in the first 10 days and runs into eyes in rain (p. 76), so use the iron in our wet winters. On older cattle saw the horn off close, taking a ring of skin or it regrows, dress with pine tar, stop bleeding with a string twisted around the stubs for about 12 hours, and do it late fall to early spring, when there are no flies (FB 1470, p. 39). Leave horns on oxen (UNH, p. 7) and on cows that must guard calves: some "let the horns grow so the animals will be able to protect themselves" (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 75).
