🐃 Oxen: choosing and training a team An ox is a castrated bull trained to pull (Peace Corps Animal Traction, p. 17): slower than a horse, but it lives on rough feed, needs little harness and ends as beef (rule of thumb). Harness, carts and hauling are in the Horses guide. Choosing (UNH Working Steer Manual, pp. 5-7): two young bull calves of the same size and bone (half-brothers from one dairy match well; a fine-boned calf won't keep up with a heavy-boned one). Look for an alert calf that stretches when it gets up, a straight back, square feet, strong pasterns, a wide chest, no navel hernia, two testicles, and clean coat, eyes and nose. They must have horns: horns hold a cart back downhill, and hornless cattle "do not make a desirable team" (p. 45). For breeds, see the table above. Training (UNH, pp. 22-27; Peace Corps, p. 59): 1. Bond first: feed them yourself daily. Give short names that don't rhyme with each other or a command ("Bow" and "Whoa"). 2. Halter-train one calf at a time, walking at its shoulder, not in front. Every day, same place and hours; early morning and late afternoon are best. Peace Corps trainers ran two sessions of about 1½ hours a day. 3. One command at a time, at least a week each: Whoa (stop, and you stop too), Giddup,
oxen-choosing-and-training-a-team

Peace Corps trainers ran two sessions of about 1½ hours a day. 3. One command at a time, at least a week each: Whoa (stop, and you stop too), Giddup, Gee (turn right), Haw (turn left), and Back last. Say the steer's name with the command. 4. Then yoke them and teach it all again as a pair, without halters and without pushing on the yoke. Put the slower steer next to you (the "nigh" steer; the far one is the "off" steer). 5. The goad is a light stick no longer than 4 ft, for light taps only: the rump for Giddup, both briskets for Whoa, the outside flank or ear to turn. "Never use this tool to hurt your animals" (p. 25). Reward with a chin scratch and a kind word. 6. Cart and drag only after all five commands. Start the drag on a pole, not a chain, so they can't step over it; later a chain must clear the stone-boat by 6 in when the longest steer stretches out (pp. 28, 31). A team learns in 2 weeks to 2 months (Peace Corps, p. 59); an old teamster said of his eight-year-old team, "They're still learning" (UNH, p. 27). Simple yokes. A bow yoke is a carved hardwood beam with a U-shaped bow under each neck; it pushes against the front of the withers (Peace Corps,

(UNH, p. 27). Simple yokes. A bow yoke is a carved hardwood beam with a U-shaped bow under each neck; it pushes against the front of the withers (Peace Corps, p. 83). A head yoke is strapped behind the horns and makes a tight pair, good for carts that must back and brake (p. 85). Making a bow yoke (UNH, pp. 39-43): its size is the space between one bow's two holes, and calves start in a 4-in yoke, moving up as their necks grow. Use basswood or poplar for small yokes and maple, birch or oak for big ones, straight-grained, knots cut out, weak heartwood out of the neck seats; round the seats smooth "like the curve of your thumb"; drill the holes dead straight, about ⅛ in bigger than the bows. Bows are split from straight hickory, white oak or ash, shaved, steamed about 20 minutes (small ones), bent, tied until dry, and left in the yoke when not in use. Fit: an open hand slips between bow and neck; pulling, the yoke pushes on the neck just above the shoulders; head tossing or balking usually means a bad fit. A 6-inch yoke: 6 in between each bow's holes, 20 in between the inside holes, 1½-in bows (UNH, pp. 39-42) (a diagram drawn for this guide). Work limits (Animal Management, pp. 311-316): - Age: no heavy transport work

holes, 20 in between the inside holes, 1½-in bows (UNH, pp. 39-42) (a diagram drawn for this guide). Work limits (Animal Management, pp. 311-316): - Age: no heavy transport work before 4-5 years; oxen work to 16-17 years on good grass, 11-12 on poor. - Hours: 7-8 a day at 2-2½ mph, never more than 4 at a stretch, with 6 hours' grazing and time to chew the cud; graze an hour before starting. "Ruminants cannot stand being hurried." - Water 3 times a day in summer, twice in winter. Heat: work early morning and evening, not in hot sun. - Cold rain: "Bovine tolerance of wet with cold weather is small ... it is advisable to knock off work altogether." If you must work in rain, grease the yoke and the necks: a wet yoke makes "sore necks" (p. 312). - Condition: thin oxen pull only half as much; ease off while they shed their coats. Uphill they pull well but may lose heart and lie down; carts need a brake downhill (pp. 311-312, 316). How much: about one-tenth of body weight in steady pull all day; a 660-lb (300-kg) bull holds a 66-lb pull all day but tires in 3-4 hours at 286 lb (Peace Corps, p. 20). A 4-H team drags half its combined weight on a stone-boat for a short pull, resting between turns (UNH, pp.

🔪 Slaughter and butchering When. Only healthy animals past any drug withdrawal (UF VM114, p. 4); a moderately finished yearling or 2-year-old is tenderest (USDA FB 2209, p. 5). Pick cold weather: the carcass must chill below 40 °F inside within 24 hours without freezing (p. 19), which here means November to February on a cold night (rule of thumb). Pen the animal alone the day before, off feed 24 hours with water, and don't excite it: a fevered animal bleeds poorly and bruises (p. 6). Gear (same page): a rifle, a block and tackle, a spreader (a doubletree will do), a 6-in skinning knife, a steak knife, steel and whetstone, a cleaver, a 28-in meat saw, a prop pole, buckets, plenty of cold water and clean cloths. Killing (UF VM114, pp. 5, 7): 1. Aim where lines from each eye to the base of the opposite horn (or just above the opposite ear) cross: mid-forehead, above the eyes, not between them. Hold the muzzle a few inches from the head, square to the skull; watch for ricochet. 2. Caliber: a .22 long rifle for a calf or young animal; bulls and some grown cows need a 9 mm or .357 or larger. 3. Bleed at once: hoist by the hind legs, head 18-24 in off the floor; open the hide down the middle of the dewlap, slip the knife

.357 or larger. 3. Bleed at once: hoist by the hind legs, head 18-24 in off the floor; open the hide down the middle of the dewlap, slip the knife in under the point of the breastbone and cut the big vessels where they fork. Don't stick the heart; let it pump (FB 2209, p. 7). Where to aim: where lines from each horn (or poll) to the opposite eye cross, above the eyes (USDA FB 2209, p. 6). Skinning and gutting (FB 2209, pp. 7-17; Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, pp. 54-59): take the head off at the first joint and the feet at their joints; skin belly and sides with the carcass propped on its back, keeping hair off the meat; tie off the gullet and the rear gut (bung) with string; open the belly with the edge facing out, guarded by your hand, and don't cut the paunch or guts; cut the gall bladder off the liver; lift out heart and lungs together; saw down the middle of the backbone, wash in cold water, and hang the sides apart to chill. Look at the organs: single abscesses and bruises can be trimmed, but inflamed lungs or guts, or yellowish pearl-like growths scattered through the organs, are serious (FB 2209, p. 17). No freezer: what to do with 400 lb of beef Fresh beef keeps only at 34-36 °F (FB 2209, p. 31); hung in a cool, airy place without that, no more than 3 days (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 89). 1. Make it smaller: a veal calf of 1-3 months (160-200 lb) (FB 2209, p. 34), or share the beef. Under Oregon rules, neighbors splitting a beef should each own a share of the live animal; custom-cut meat can't be sold, traded or given away (OSU EM 9345, pp. 2-3). 2. Eat fresh first: in cold weather hang the sides about a week, then cut (FB 2209, p. 31). Bone it hot for ground meat and sausage the same day (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, p. 131). 3. Corned beef from the plate, rump and chuck (FB 2209, p. 32): per 100 lb of boned meat, rub with 8-10 lb of coarse salt and pack in a clean barrel or crock; after 24 hours cover with 4 lb sugar, 4 oz saltpeter and 2 oz baking soda in 4 gallons of water; weight it and cure 30-40 days, below about 38 °F. Weigh the saltpeter; never add extra. Ropy brine: wash the meat, fresh brine. 4. Dried beef: cure the round the same way (a pound more sugar), dry 24 hours, and smoke at 130-140 °F for 70-80 hours
no-freezer-what-to-do-with-400-lb-of-beef

brine: wash the meat, fresh brine. 4. Dried beef: cure the round the same way (a pound more sugar), dry 24 hours, and smoke at 130-140 °F for 70-80 hours until quite dry; store it dry, dark and fly-free (same page). 5. Plain salt: 1 part salt to 3 parts meat, strips under 1 in thick, layered in salt and kept under the brine at least 28 days; throw it out if the brine turns sour, thick or ropy (Slaughter and Preservation of Meat, pp. 90-93). 6. Can it in a pressure canner only: a water bath doesn't get hot enough (FB 2209, p. 33). Jerky from lean strips. ♻ Hides and tallow The hide: let it cool, spread it hair side down, scrape off flesh and blood, and rub in about 1 lb of clean salt per pound of hide, well into edges, head, legs and folds (USDA FB 2209, p. 34); it keeps 3-5 months if it never freezes or heats (USDA FB 1334, p. 8). A cow or steer hide of 40-70 lb makes sole, harness and belting leather; a 20-40-lb hide makes lace leather (same page). Split a big hide down the backbone into two sides. Warble holes spoil hides (FB 1470, p. 36), and a beginner shouldn't try a hair-on cattle robe or rug (FB 1334, p. 23). Bark tanning and rawhide: "Tanning hides" in the Clothing, Leather & Shoes guide. Tallow: save the caul and ruffle fat around the paunch and guts "as tallow for soap" (FB 2209, p. 17) and the kidney fat (p. 25). Render it within a week, slowly, never in copper ("Salt, sweeteners and fat" in the Food From Scratch guide); then make candles (Light Without the Grid), soap ("Soap from fat and ashes" in the Make-Do Household guide), pemmican, or dubbin for boots and harness: about equal parts tallow and neatsfoot or cod oil (FB 1334, p. 23). Manure: spread it soon, but not on snow or soggy ground; store the rest packed and moist under cover (FB

🐺 Predators and loose dogs Calves are what predators take: in California, predators caused about 1% of grown cattle deaths but 6% of calf deaths (UC ANR 8598, p. 3). Calve in a shed or pen near the house, rated highly effective against dogs, coyotes, lions, bears, wolves, foxes and bobcats (p. 5). Remove dead stock, gut piles and afterbirths, which draw predators (p. 9); they go for cows struggling to calve and calves slow to stand (Mississippi, p. 5). See "Dead animals and gut piles" in the Sanitation guide. Cougars: "Fence and shelter livestock. Move them to sheds or barns at night"; Oregon law lets a landowner kill a cougar that is damaging livestock; call ODFW (ODFW, p. 2). Bears: "Store livestock food in a secure place" (ODFW bears, p. 2). Guardian dogs bonded to cattle cut coyote and wolf visits (UC ANR, p. 6); see the Dogs guide. Cattle grazed with sheep or goats give the small stock some cover (p. 5), and a horned cow can defend her calf (Raising Healthy Cattle, p. 75).

🔥 Fire season and smoke Grazing is fire prevention: grazing 40-50% of the growing grass breaks up fuel, and ungrazed bunchgrass was 200% more likely to burn than grass grazed in spring (PNW783, p. 3); graze hard along roads and around buildings each spring (rule of thumb). Plan before July: which animals leave, where to (two or three places), who moves them, and water if the power fails (p. 7). Evacuate early, calmly, in daylight (same page). Cattle that stay go in a heavily grazed pasture, gates open, with feed and water for 7-10 days; store hay apart; with milk cows, sheltering in place may be best, but move calves, heifers and dry cows (p. 8). In smoke: less work (no oxen), no weaning, vaccinating or moving, clean water always, shade, wet down dust; heat makes smoke harm worse in cattle (p. 10). After: keep cattle off ash-fouled feed and water, check burned animals daily, and give smoke-hurt lungs several weeks (ODA, p. 1). No open burning June-October: bury afterbirths and carcasses in summer (rule of thumb). See "Animals and livestock" in the Wildfire guide.

🐴 Horses, Mules and Draft Animals How to keep, feed, handle, ride, shoe and pack horses, mules and donkeys, and how to put them to work in harness - written for a time when there may be no feed store, vet or farrier. The manuals are in Horses-Draft-Animals\ (Care-Feeding, Riding-Training, Hoof-Care-Shoeing, Packing-Travel, Draft-Harness). Horse health, vital signs, colic and first aid are in Animals\ and the Animals and vet care section of the Illinois Valley page. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - A horse can kill you without meaning to. Stay where it can see you, speak before you touch it, keep a hand on it as you move around the hindquarters, and never stand directly behind or in front of it. - Never wrap a lead rope or reins around your hand or body, and never tie a horse with a knot you can't pull loose. Never tie with a chain lead. (4-H Horse Project PNW 587, p. 51; Basic Horse Safety) - Wear a helmet and boots with a heel when riding. - The old books here (1867-1940s) teach good handling and shoeing but also harsh "breaking" methods and dangerous old medicines (purges, firing, chloroform). Use them for skills, not for doctoring.

🐎 Choosing an animal - For a first horse, pick an older, calm, well-trained one over a young or green horse - the 4-H manual says 6 to 18 years suits most purposes, and "a young horse and an inexperienced rider do not learn together" (PNW 587, p. 24). For hard work, not much under 5; with good care many stay useful past 20 (USDA FB 779, p. 8). Check it sound before you take it: walk and trot it on hard ground, look for limping, swellings, bad feet and bad habits. (USDA How to Select a Sound Horse; 🖼 points of the horse; 🖼 where unsoundness shows; conformation) - Age by the teeth: after about 12 years the front teeth turn triangular and slant forward. (USDA AIB 353, p. 18; PNW 587, p. 48; 🖼 mouths from 4 to 8 years; 🖼 14- and 22-year-old mouths) - Mules are tough, sure-footed, eat less and handle heat and rough country better; they tend to stand and fight rather than bolt. A well-trained mule is very steady; a badly trained one is hard work. Donkeys need shelter always - their coats aren't waterproof, which matters in our wet winters. (Donkey Care Handbook, p. 44) - Who's who: a mule is a mare bred to a jack (male donkey); a hinny is a jenny bred to a stallion and is smaller and

Mules are hardy but can still founder, and they fret if stabled long or kept alone. Donkeys live just over 30 years and should be kept with a companion. 🌾 Feeding and water - Total feed: 1.5-2.5% of body weight a day, most of it hay or pasture. Never less than 8-10 lb of hay a day for a 1,000-lb horse; an idle horse holds weight on about 18 lb of good hay. (Nebraska G1781, pp. 1-2; FM 25-5, p. 101) - Weigh a horse with a string: weight (lb) = heart girth (in) × heart girth (in) × body length (in) ÷ 330. Body length is point of shoulder to point of buttock. (G1781, p. 1; 🖼 where to measure) - Working horses: about 1.1 lb grain + 1.25 lb hay per 100 lb of body weight a day, grain split into 3 feeds. Keep each grain meal under about 5 lb for a 1,000-lb horse. Feed by weight: a quart of oats ≈ 1 lb, a quart of corn ≈ 1.7 lb. (USDA FB1419, p. 9; G1781, p. 3; UGA B1356) - Water: 5-15 gallons a day, double in heat or hard work (an idle horse drinks about 10-12 - G1781, p. 4). Give an exhausted horse small drinks every 5-10 minutes until it recovers. In cold weather, take the chill off the water or salt the feed (1-2 oz) so it keeps drinking (prevents impaction colic). (UGA B1356, p. 2; FM 25-5) - Salt: horses eat about 1½-3 oz a day of loose salt-mineral, which beats
feeding-and-water

feed (1-2 oz) so it keeps drinking (prevents impaction colic). (UGA B1356, p. 2; FM 25-5) - Salt: horses eat about 1½-3 oz a day of loose salt-mineral, which beats a block. Western Oregon soils are low in selenium - use a mineral that contains it. (Rule of thumb) (AIB 353; UGA B1356, p. 3) - Army feeding rules that prevent colic: water before feeding (or wait an hour after); never grain a hot horse (hay is fine); a little hay before grain; change feeds gradually over 1-2 weeks; never feed moldy or dusty hay. (FM 25-5, p. 103) - Body condition: keep them at 5-7 on the 1-9 scale - feel ribs, back and tailhead with your hands; a winter coat hides thinness. (G1781, p. 2; 🖼 where to feel) For the weight string: heart girth is 27, body length runs from the point of the shoulder (16) to the buttock (38) (FB 779, p. 5). Add a margin for waste and a late spring. - Donkeys are different: they do best on good barley straw (high fiber, low sugar), not rich horse hay (Donkey Care Handbook, p. 16; 🖼 a homemade straw feeder). Pasture in our wet climate (OSU EC1558): 1. Keep horses off pasture through the wet months. Wet soil compacts, the grass dies, and you buy more hay next year. Hold them in a sacrifice area (a dry lot) instead (pp. 4-5; 🖼 photo). 2. Graze only when the grass is over

🦷 Teeth and worms - Teeth: check at least yearly (twice for older horses). Sharp edges form on the outside of the upper molars and inside of the lowers - float (rasp) them (🖼 how to hold the float) or the horse drops feed and loses weight. (PNW 587, p. 46; Merillat Animal Dentistry) - Signs of tooth trouble: dropping grain while chewing, holding the head sideways, eating slowly, whole grain in the manure, losing condition (G1781, p. 4). - Worms: don't deworm blindly every 8 weeks. Adults need 1-2 treatments a year (one in fall for bots and tapeworms); youngsters 3-4. When dewormers run out: pick up manure, don't overgraze, rotate pastures and graze with cattle or sheep. (Penn State/SARE, pp. 1-2) - Know your high shedders: most horses carry few worms; a few shed most of the eggs. Penn State's line: deworm a horse whose fecal egg count is over about 300 eggs per gram; over 500 is a "high shedder" (Penn State, pp. 1-2). Foals need a special schedule - ask the books, not guesswork. - Kill eggs without drugs: a manure pile that heats to 130-150 °F kills most parasites, flies and weed seeds (OSU EC1558, p. 16; 🖼 covered piles); dragging or harrowing pastures in dry weather spreads droppings so eggs dry out (p. 15). - Donkeys can carry lungworm with no signs and pass

p. 16; 🖼 covered piles); dragging or harrowing pastures in dry weather spreads droppings so eggs dry out (p. 15). - Donkeys can carry lungworm with no signs and pass it to horses - worm them together (Donkey Care Handbook, p. 16). 📚 Go deeper: Penn State Managing Equine Parasites - the egg-count method and when to treat; 4-H PNW 587 - teeth and aging; Merillat Animal Dentistry - floating and dental work by hand (old book: skills only).

🦶 Hoof care and shoeing - Pick out the feet every day (🖼 how). A healthy frog feels like firm rubber (🖼 parts of the hoof). Thrush) (black, stinking rot in the frog) comes from wet, dirty footing - trim away dead tissue, apply an antiseptic, and get the horse onto dry ground. In our wet winters, give horses a dry gravel or wood-chip standing area. (TM 2-220, p. 97; PNW 587; OSU EC1558, p. 2) - Hooves grow about ⅜ inch a month. Trim barefoot horses every 6-12 weeks, donkeys and mules every 6-10; the Army reset shoes every 3-6 weeks (🖼 untrimmed vs. trimmed). (NMSU B-707, p. 2; Donkey Care Handbook, p. 14; TM 2-220) - Going barefoot (when shoes and nails run out): leave the sole, balance the wall, round off the outer edge so it doesn't chip (🖼 using the rasp), and check weekly. Most horses do fine barefoot on soft ground; hard rocky work wears feet faster than they grow. (TM 2-220, p. 98) - Making and fitting shoes: TM 2-220 The Horseshoer teaches forging shoes from bar stock, fitting and nailing (🖼 nailing and clinching), and even shoeing in the field with a ground fire and a rail for an anvil. Lungwitz's Text-Book of Horseshoeing is the standard reference (🖼 the foot from the side; farrier). Pair with the Blacksmithing guide. The same front

fire and a rail for an anvil. Lungwitz's Text-Book of Horseshoeing is the standard reference (🖼 the foot from the side; farrier). Pair with the Blacksmithing guide. The same front foot before (left) and after (right) trimming: the long toe is cut back and the pastern angle changes (FB 1419, p. 20). Taking shoes off for good (TM 2-220, p. 97): 1. Pull the shoes, then trim to balance and round the edge of the wall. Leave the dead sole. 2. Expect the hoof to break away and the horse to go a bit tender for the first few weeks. It isn't serious and passes as new horn grows. 3. On rough, rocky pasture, leave the front shoes on for the first few days while the horse settles, then pull them. 4. Even shod horses do better with 2-3 months a year barefoot. Mud is the enemy here. Wet ground softens hooves and soles, leading to cracks, stone bruises, abscesses and thrush; mud also causes "mud fever" (scratches) - crusty scabs on the lower legs (OSU EC1558, p. 2). For the dry lot, lay down twice as much footing as you have mud: landscape fabric, 3 inches of ¾-1½-inch crushed rock, then 6 inches of gravel or sand or up to 12 inches of wood chips (p. 5; 🖼 photo). Field tips from the Army farrier: store horseshoe nails wrapped

rock, then 6 inches of gravel or sand or up to 12 inches of wood chips (p. 5; 🖼 photo). Field tips from the Army farrier: store horseshoe nails wrapped in an oiled cloth in a watertight can, and a worn rasp can be re-sharpened with a three-cornered file and re-hardened (TM 2-220, p. 99) - see the Blacksmithing guide. 📚 Go deeper: The Horseshoer TM 2-220 - care of shod and unshod feet, field expedients; Lungwitz Text-Book of Horseshoeing - hoof anatomy, trimming, forging and diseased hooves; NMSU B-707 - how to judge a good trim; USDA Farm Horseshoeing - shoeing with simple tools. 🤠 Handling, saddling and riding - Leading: from the left side, right hand near the halter, slack folded (never wrapped) in your left hand. If the horse rears, let go with the hand nearest the halter so you stay on the ground. (PNW 587, p. 51) - Tying: use a quick-release knot (🖼 drawing; 🖼 step by step), about 3 ft of rope, tied at or above withers height to something solid. Any rope around the neck gets a bowline (it can't tighten), never a slip knot. Untie before taking the halter off. (PNW 587, p. 51; Basic Horse Safety, p. 3) - Saddle fit: with pad and rider on, the gullet must clear the withers. After a sweaty ride, even sweat marks = good fit; dry spots = pressure. A sliding saddle needs a breast collar, not a tighter cinch. Dry spots with raised skin lead to saddle sores and white hair - fix the fit now (UF Saddle Fit, p. 3). - Cinching): snug it gradually until a flat hand just slips under, walk the horse a few steps, then recheck after a short ride - many horses puff up their bellies. On the trail, stop after 1-2 miles to retighten. (PNW 587; Animal Management) - Mounting and riding: mount from the left, reins short enough to stop the horse (🖼 holding the reins), sit deep with heels
handling-saddling-and-riding

miles to retighten. (PNW 587; Animal Management) - Mounting and riding: mount from the left, reins short enough to stop the horse (🖼 holding the reins), sit deep with heels down. The 4-H manual (PNW 587) and FM 25-5 walk through riding step by step. - Starting young horses: handle foals early and teach them to lead before weaning. Light harness or saddle work at 2-3 years; no heavy work until they're nearly mature. First tie with a neck rope through the halter ring, tied with a bowline. (USDA FB1368) - Holding a horse for treatment: have a helper hold up another foot while you work on a leg; a twitch on the upper lip works for short jobs - tighten it only enough to stay on and take it off as soon as you can (PNW 587, p. 30). - Tack repair: cutting leather, hand-stitching with waxed thread and riveting are in TM 10-430 The Saddler and Hasluck's Harness Making (🖼 sewing awls; 🖼 stitching clamp). 📚 Go deeper: 4-H PNW 587 - handling, safety knots, tack, saddling and riding; UF Saddle Fit - checking tree fit and sweat patterns; The Saddler TM 10-430 - hand-repairing saddles and tack; USDA Breaking and Training Colts - gentling and starting young horses.

🩺 Health checks and first aid Normal vital signs at rest - the sources differ a little, so learn your own horse's normal by taking it twice a day for a week (PNW 587, p. 28; 🖼 vital-signs chart): | | Temperature | Pulse (beats/min) | Breaths/min | | 4-H PNW 587 | 99-101 °F (102+ = sick) | 32-48 (over 50 = distress) | 8-20 | | Raising Healthy Horses | 99-101.5 °F | 40-48 | 10-14 | | UGA B1356 | 99.5-101.5 °F | 32-36 | 8-12 | Take the pulse under the jawbone for 15 seconds × 4. A pinched fold of neck skin should flatten in 1-2 seconds; gums should be pink and moist; a healthy horse passes several piles of manure a day (PNW 587, p. 28). Act fast (no vet coming? treat these as emergencies) - temperature 102 °F or more, signs of colic, a deep puncture, a wound near an eye, joint or tendon, severe lameness, choking, off feed 12-24 hours, worsening cough, persistent diarrhea, or a mare in trouble foaling (PNW 587, p. 29). Colic (belly pain) - looking at or kicking at the belly, pawing, rolling, getting up and down, sweating, little or no manure, pulse over 60 (PNW 587, p. 31; UF VM275, pp. 3-4; 🖼 a horse in colic): - Take away all feed. Let it stand or lie
health-checks-and-first-aid

little or no manure, pulse over 60 (PNW 587, p. 31; UF VM275, pp. 3-4; 🖼 a horse in colic): - Take away all feed. Let it stand or lie quietly; walk it only briefly if it's throwing itself around - don't walk it to exhaustion. - Don't syringe in oil or water, and never put a hose down its nose or throat - the fluid goes into the lungs. Don't repeat painkillers without advice. - Water: sources disagree - UF lets the horse drink; the 4-H manual says no food or water until the vet sees it. - If it recovers on its own, no feed for 12-24 hours, then small meals over 3-5 days, and watch for manure (8-12 piles a day is normal) (UF VM275, p. 4). Choke) (feed stuck in the gullet) - saliva and feed running from the nose (🖼 photo), retching, sometimes a lump you can see or feel in the neck. It can still breathe. Remove all feed and water, keep it on bare ground or muzzle it, gently massage a visible lump; many cases clear in a couple of hours. Watch for fever over 101.5 °F or coughing in the days after - food in the lungs causes pneumonia (UF VM275, pp. 4-5). Wounds: hose with cold water, pat dry, apply antiseptic. For heavy bleeding use a pressure bandage, not a tourniquet;

- food in the lungs causes pneumonia (UF VM275, pp. 4-5). Wounds: hose with cold water, pat dry, apply antiseptic. For heavy bleeding use a pressure bandage, not a tourniquet; a horse can lose up to 4 gallons of blood without severe stress. Watch for proud flesh (red, lumpy tissue) in wounds over joints (PNW 587, p. 30). Eyes: rinse gently with saline (1 teaspoon salt in a pint of boiled water - Raising Healthy Horses, p. 9) or weak-tea-colored dilute betadine. Never alcohol or chlorhexidine near the eye, and no steroid ointments. Put on a fly mask (UF VM275, pp. 5-6; 🖼 a painful eye). Swollen face, noisy breathing (snakebite, bee sting): horses can't breathe through the mouth. Cut two pieces of soft hose as long as from the inner corner of the eye to the nostril, lubricate them, slide one into each nostril and tape them in place (UF VM275, p. 6; 🖼 photo). Donkeys hide illness. A dull donkey off its feed is an emergency - it can fall into hyperlipaemia (fat flooding the blood) and die. Coax it to eat with fresh grass or favorite food and warm water. When a donkey loses its companion, let it stay with the body until it loses interest, and watch it closely for three weeks (Donkey Care Handbook, pp. 108-110). 🚜 Harness and draft work - What an animal can pull all day: about one-tenth of its body weight in steady draft (a big horse pulling 150 lb at 2½ mph ≈ 1 horsepower). Donkeys pull about a fifth of their weight for 3-4 hours. A cart donkey should pull no more than twice its weight, cart included, on the flat. (Peace Corps Animal Traction, p. 20; Donkey Care Handbook) Sources differ: Starkey quotes 15% of body weight as normal pulling power for horses (Starkey, p. 118). - Collar fit: a flat hand should just pass between the collar and the windpipe (🖼 drawing). A short collar chokes; a long one bruises the shoulders. Give each horse its own collar and wipe it after every use. Sore shoulders are the #1 harness problem. (USDA FB1419; FM 25-5; 🖼 where collar sores form) - Harness, hitching, driving pairs and teams, carts, plows and sledges: FM 25-5, Mounted Instruction for Field Artillery, the Peace Corps Animal Traction manual and Starkey's Harnessing and Implements (🖼 harnessing options). 🐝 Bees: Honey, Wax and Pollination How to keep honey bees with no bee-supply store, no bought queens and no mite strips: hives you can build from scrap, gear you can make, free bees from swarms and bee trees, the bee year in the Illinois Valley, queens, swarms, mites and foulbrood, feeding and wintering through wet winters, honey and wax, bears, stings, and how many hives a family needs for sweetener and pollination. The bee books are in Animals\Bees; the Oregon State backyard bulletin and the beneficial-insects bulletin are in Gardening-Food, honey processing is in Food-From-Scratch\Wild-and-Local-Staples, wax and candles in Homestead-Skills\Soap-Candles, and bears in Animals\Planning-Predators-Toxic-Plants. ### The short version - Never give honey to a baby under 1 year - infant botulism (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 108). - Anyone who has had a whole-body reaction to a sting (hives all over, wheezing, faintness) must not work bees without epinephrine at hand. Scrape stingers out at once; don't pinch them. - Swarms are your only new bees now. Catch them March-June, set bait hives, and keep at least 3 colonies so one dead queen or one bad winter doesn't end your beekeeping (rule of thumb). - Count mites every month from spring to fall and act at 1-2 mites per 100 bees. Unchecked, mites double monthly and kill a colony in 2-3 years. - Leave about 60 lb of honey

from spring to fall and act at 1-2 mites per 100 bees. Unchecked, mites double monthly and kill a colony in 2-3 years. - Leave about 60 lb of honey on each colony for winter here, and harvest only sealed comb. - Burn American foulbrood - combs, frames and honey - and never feed honey from hives you don't know. - Electric-fence the hives against black bears: wires at 8, 20 and 32 inches, 6,000+ volts. - Beeswax catches fire. Melt it only in or over water, never over a bare flame, and never throw water on burning wax.

🐝 How a colony works A colony is one queen (the only egg-layer), several to 60,000 workers and, in spring and summer, a few hundred drones (males) (USDA AH 335, p. 36). The colony, not the bee, is the animal you keep. | | Egg to adult | Lives | Job | | Worker | 21 days (AH 335, p. 34) | About 6 weeks in summer; months for fall-raised "winter bees" (p. 35) | Nurse and build comb (wax glands work at 12-15 days old), then forage the last ~3 weeks (pp. 33-34) | | Drone | About 24-25 days (Langstroth, p. 68; FAO Forest, p. 148) | 8 weeks or less; thrown out when nectar fails in fall (AH 335, pp. 35-36) | Mating only | | Queen | About 16 days (rule of thumb) | Lays 2-5 years (p. 35) | Lays every egg | Left to right: worker, queen, drone. The queen is longer, with a long tapering abdomen (AH 335, p. 36). - The egg stage is 3 days for all three (p. 33): eggs standing in cells mean a queen laid within the last 3 days. - A virgin queen flies to mate 5-6 days after emerging, mates with 8-12 drones, and lays 2-5 days later (p. 44). Delayed over 3 weeks, she will likely lay only drones (p. 35). - Bees forage mostly

Delayed over 3 weeks, she will likely lay only drones (p. 35). - Bees forage mostly within 2 km (1¼ miles), up to 7 km when they must (FAO Forest, p. 77) - about 12,500 acres (AH 335, p. 43). - Which bees: there are no Africanized bees in Oregon (OSU EM 9186, p. 14). Keep the gentle colonies that winter well with low mite counts and raise queens from them: local bees are better adapted than imported ones (FAO 2006, p. 36), and "some locally derived stocks" resist mites (HBHC, p. 41).

Building a top-bar hive from scrap wood 1. Wood: seasoned (green wood warps), durable, no cracks or chemical smells (FAO Forest, p. 44); no treated lumber (rule of thumb). 2. Top bars exactly 35 mm (1⅜ in) wide, all the same: too narrow crowds the combs, too wide gets extra "brace comb" between them (pp. 43-44). It matches Langstroth frame spacing, 1⅜ in (AH 335, p. 52). 3. Comb guide: a strip of beeswax down the centre of each bar's underside (FAO Forest, p. 44), or a saw groove filled with melted wax (rule of thumb). 4. Size (rule of thumb): inside 36-42 in long (26-30 bars), 10-12 in deep, about 15 in wide at the top; bars rest across the side walls. Sides sloping in toward the bottom keep comb off the walls; straight sides work if you cut the attachments (p. 45). 5. Entrance: two or three 1-inch holes at one end, with corks (AH 335, p. 73 uses 1-inch auger holes). A follower board cut to the hive's shape shrinks the space for a small colony (rule of thumb); match hive space to colony strength (FAO 2006, p. 38). 6. Roof overhanging, weighted with rocks (OSU EM 9186, p. 5), straw under it in winter (FAO Forest, p. 44). Legs to waist height (p. 47); at least 1 ft up stops skunks (OSU EM 9186, p. 10).

Building Langstroth boxes from scrap - The two numbers that matter: the bee space, about ⅜ in - smaller gaps get glued with propolis, bigger ones filled with comb (AH 335, p. 9) - and 10 frames 1⅜ in centre to centre (p. 52). - Copy the drawing (🖼 AH 335, p. 53) or a borrowed factory box. Standard US sizes (rule of thumb): deep box 19⅞ × 16¼ in outside, 9⅝ in tall (18⅜ × 14¾ inside); deep frame 19 in top bar, 9⅛ in tall. Make every box the same so they swap (p. 53). - No foundation? Give frames a wax starter strip like a top bar (FAO 2006, p. 12), or cast sheets in a plaster-of-Paris press (FAO Forest, p. 114).
building-langstroth-boxes-from-scrap

Where to put the hives - Morning sun, facing southeast, out of the wind (OSU EM 9186, p. 5), with afternoon shade in our hot summers: shaded colonies can make 50% more honey in strong sun; white paint helps (FAO Forest, p. 47). Comb softens above 35 °C (95 °F) in the hive (p. 107). - Water within half a mile (AH 335, p. 51); out of sight of paths and thieves; not under dripping branches (FAO Forest, pp. 46-47). - Space and colour the hives so you can work from the side and young bees don't drift (OSU EM 9186, p. 5; AH 335, p. 33). A 6-ft fence or hedge in front lifts the flight path over people's heads (OSU EM 9186, p. 6). - Start with no more than 10 colonies in one place (FAO Forest, p. 47).

🧰 Gear you can make - Veil: a broad-brimmed hat with netting to the shoulders, tucked in (FAO Forest, p. 46; Kephart, p. 367). Always wear one: a sting in the eye or mouth is dangerous (FAO Forest, p. 49). - Clothes: light-coloured, smooth; bees go for dark, rough or woolly cloth, suede and leather (AH 335, p. 148). Tie cuffs and trouser legs; wash off the sting smell after (FAO Forest, pp. 46, 49). Gloves: long gauntlets, or a plastic bag over each hand held with a band (p. 46). - Smoker: a fuel can with bellows, made by a smith; fuel is dry cow dung, burlap or cardboard (p. 46), or dry punky rotten wood, which smoulders for hours (Kephart, p. 368). Puff cool smoke, never close enough to scorch bees (FAO Forest, p. 48): at the entrance first, then gently under the lid (AH 335, p. 41). - Hive tool: flat steel with a scraper end; an old knife bends too easily (FAO Forest, p. 46). See the Blacksmithing guide. Bee brush: grass or a feather (p. 48). - Feeder: a lidded pail with nail holes, upside down over the bars or inner-cover hole (AH 335, p. 50). Entrance reducer and robbing screen (🖼 OSU, p. 10; HBHC, p. 42). Mite-wash jar: a quart jar, #8 screen in the lid, a ½-cup scoop (HBHC, p. 8). -

🎣 Getting bees: swarms, bait hives, bee trees and splits Package bees came from California every April-May (OSU EM 9186, p. 14). That's over: new bees come from swarms, wild colonies and your own splits.
getting-bees-swarms-bait-hives-bee-trees-and-splits

Catching a swarm A swarm) is the old queen and 30-70% of the workers (OSU EM 9186, p. 14). Swarms come mostly March-June and hang in a cluster for about an hour while scouts search (AH 335, p. 38; 🖼 resting swarm). They are full of honey and "in the most peaceable mood" (Langstroth, p. 41). 1. Set a box, ideally with a comb or two of old comb in it, right under the cluster (rule of thumb). 2. Shake the cluster in with one sharp jolt (🖼 hiving a swarm). 3. Queen in? Bees stand at the entrance fanning, tails raised, and the rest march in within minutes (AH 335, p. 41). If they stream back to the branch, shake again. 4. Close it at dusk and move it to its stand (rule of thumb). 5. With no flow, feed 2:1 syrup for 2-3 weeks while they build comb (AH 335, p. 51). Check mites even in a new swarm (HBHC, p. 13).
catching-a-swarm

Bait hives An empty hive "rubbed inside with some beeswax" catches passing swarms where wild colonies are common (FAO Forest, p. 47); old wax smell draws them (plate 3.5, p. 96). Rule of thumb: about 10 gallons (40 L) inside, one entrance about 1 in across, 8-15 ft up in shade, an old dark comb inside, up by early March. Check weekly; move a caught swarm at dusk.
bait-hives

Bee trees and cut-outs - Bee lining (Kephart, pp. 358-366): a mile or more from tame bees, set out thin syrup (sugar in 3 times its bulk of water, or honey thinned half and half) with a drop of anise. Note which way the loaded bees fly home, move 200-300 yards to one side and repeat; the lines cross near the tree. Bee trees are seldom far from water. In settled country the tree belongs to the landowner (p. 366) - ask. - Saving the colony: cut out the brood combs, tie them into frames or onto top bars, let the bees cluster on them and carry them home at dusk (FAO Forest, p. 47; Kephart, p. 368).
bee-trees-and-cut-outs

Splits A split (nuc) is 3-5 combs of bees and brood from a strong colony (AH 335, p. 65). With a laying queen it reaches full strength in about 9 weeks, against 12 weeks for a 2-lb package; take splits from your strongest overwintered colonies in spring (p. 66). Giving a split a queen is under "Queens" below.

🌼 Forage, water and planting for bees - A colony feeds on the countryside, not your garden. One colony needs "several acres of abundant flowers" and uses 50-100 lb of pollen a season (AH 335, p. 23) and the nectar of 300-500 lb of honey a year (p. 47). What you plant fills gaps and feeds pollinators. - Local forage: western beekeepers build colonies up on manzanita in spring; wild buckwheat, star thistle and fireweed give honey crops (p. 21); AH 335's bee-plant table includes blackberry, ceanothus, cascara and alder (p. 24). Manzanita, which grows even on serpentine, blooms February-April and bees visit it (NRCS, pp. 1-2). Fireweed comes up after a burn (rule of thumb). - Plant (PNW 550, pp. 18-23): single (not double), open-pollinated flowers, something in bloom spring to fall - clover and vetch, phacelia, buckwheat, mustard and radish left to flower, aster, goldenrod and yarrow, lavender, thyme and catmint, penstemon. Leave bare ground and hollow stems for native bees. Buckwheat sown in late spring blooms into the July-August dearth (rule of thumb). - Spray nothing on open flowers; systemic insecticides (neonicotinoids) stay in nectar and pollen for weeks to a year (PNW 550, p. 24). - Water: set it up early in spring, never let it go dry (or they adopt the neighbour's trough), and give floats or a rock to stand on (OSU EM 9186,
forage-water-and-planting-for-bees

Water: set it up early in spring, never let it go dry (or they adopt the neighbour's trough), and give floats or a rock to stand on (OSU EM 9186, p. 7). - Poison bloom: avoid sites thick with California buckeye, death camas, laurel or rhododendron in flower (AH 335, p. 23). Rhododendron and laurel honey can poison people - drunkenness, tingling, blurred sight, vomiting for 2-3 days (Kephart, pp. 369-370; Grayanotoxin). Our western azalea is a rhododendron: if a May-June honey tastes bitter or makes the mouth tingle, don't eat it (rule of thumb).

👑 Queens: finding her, queenless signs, raising your own Finding her: longer than a worker, with a long tapering abdomen (🖼 AH 335, p. 36), usually on combs with eggs. You don't need to see her: eggs mean she was there within 3 days. A good queen lays a solid, compact brood pattern; replace spotty layers; queens under a year old are usually best (AH 335, p. 70; 🖼 poor and good brood). A spotty brood pattern (A, open cells scattered among the capped ones) and a good, solid one (B) (AH 335, p. 71). Queenless signs (OSU EM 9186, p. 11): emergency queen cells on the face of brood combs within 1-2 days; no new eggs within 4 days; bees growing more defensive. Experienced keepers hear the difference (AH 335, p. 42). Only drone brood, in raised bullet-shaped caps, means an unmated queen or "fertile workers," which lay only drones (Langstroth, p. 53); several eggs to a cell means laying workers (rule of thumb). Fixing it: give a comb of eggs and young larvae from another colony so they can raise a queen (queens come from larvae 12-24 hours old: AH 335, p. 64), or unite with a queenright colony through a sheet of newspaper - by the time they chew through, their smells have mixed (p. 41). A long-queenless colony is hard to requeen (OSU EM 9186, p.
queens-finding-her-queenless-signs-raising-your-own

colony through a sheet of newspaper - by the time they chew through, their smells have mixed (p. 41). A long-queenless colony is hard to requeen (OSU EM 9186, p. 11); if it's weak, shake the bees out and give the combs to another colony (AH 335, p. 70). Swarm cells or supersedure? Swarm cells hang on the bottom edges of combs, a dozen or more; supersedure or emergency cells sit on the comb face, 1-3 of them (OSU EM 9186, pp. 10-11). Where the queen cells are tells you why the bees are making them (a diagram drawn for this guide). Raising your own queens without grafting tools: 1. Pick the mother: gentle, productive, not swarmy, winters well (AH 335, p. 76), low mite counts (HBHC, p. 41). 2. Wait for the season: strong colonies, plenty of nectar and pollen, drones flying - April-June (AH 335, p. 66). 3. Split her colony: the queenless half, given combs of eggs and young larvae, starts emergency cells in 1-2 days. 4. About 10 days later, cut out extra capped cells and give each, with a couple of combs of bees, to a small queenless split - the "mating nucs" queen breeders use (AH 335, p. 64). Keep cells upright and handle them gently (rule of thumb). 5. Look for eggs about 2 weeks after she emerges (p. 64). None after 3
queens-finding-her-queenless-signs-raising-your-own

use (AH 335, p. 64). Keep cells upright and handle them gently (rule of thumb). 5. Look for eggs about 2 weeks after she emerges (p. 64). None after 3 weeks: she likely won't mate (p. 35); unite the split back. Keep the line going: keep a card per hive - queen or eggs seen, brood, stores, queen cells, mites, temper, what you did (OSU EM 9186, p. 15 has a sample sheet) - and breed only from the best. A queen mates with drones from up to 5 miles away, and in inbred lines workers remove many larvae (AH 335, p. 57), leaving gappy brood (rule of thumb); so swap swarms and queen cells with other beekeepers in the valley, and don't bring bees or combs in from outside - that is how diseases travel (FAO Forest, p. 41).

🌀 Swarm prevention A colony swarms when more than 6 frames of bees, crowding and lots of young bees line up (OSU EM 9186, pp. 4-5). Warnings: a beard of bees at the entrance on warm afternoons (AH 335, p. 37) and foragers slacking off (p. 42). 1. Room early: add space before the main flow, and more before the last box is two-thirds full (OSU EM 9186, p. 10). 2. Langstroth: swap top and bottom brood boxes every 10 days to 2 weeks until the flow starts (AH 335, p. 75). Top-bar: move full honey combs back and put empty bars at the edge of the brood (rule of thumb). 3. Split strong colonies in spring (OSU EM 9186, p. 11). 4. Once swarm cells appear, cutting them out isn't enough - the bees build more where you can't see. Move at least half the sealed brood and bees into a split (same page), and use the cells to raise queens. 5. If a swarm leaves anyway, the old hive raises a new queen from its cells; leave it a cell or two and look for eggs about 3 weeks later (rule of thumb).

🕷 Varroa and other pests without store chemicals Varroa mites are the main killer. Unchecked they double every month (HBHC, p. 5; 🖼 mites on bees and larvae), and untreated colonies usually die in 2-3 years, spreading mites as they collapse; bees with crumpled wings mean the mites are already heavy (FAO 2006, p. 19). Here they peak in August-September, as the winter bees are raised (rule of thumb). Counting mites (HBHC, pp. 9-10): 1. Shake bees from 1-3 brood frames (not the one with the queen) into a tub. 2. Scoop ½ cup (about 300 bees) into a jar of rubbing alcohol or soapy water, shake, and count the mites. No alcohol: shake them with 2 tablespoons of powdered sugar instead - less reliable (p. 9). 3. Mites ÷ 300 × 100 = mites per 100 bees. Act at 1+ in winter and spring, 2+ in summer and fall. 4. Count monthly from spring buildup (p. 7); if one colony is over, treat them all (p. 10). Controls with nothing bought - none is enough alone; stack them (HBHC, pp. 37-42): - Cut out capped drone) brood 2-3 times in spring; mites prefer it. Feed it to the hens (p. 39). In a top-bar hive, cut the drone comb off the brood combs' lower edges (rule of thumb). - Brood break: a split without a laying queen, or the
varroa-and-other-pests-without-store-chemicals

(p. 39). In a top-bar hive, cut the drone comb off the brood combs' lower edges (rule of thumb). - Brood break: a split without a laying queen, or the queen caged 1-2 weeks, leaves mites nowhere to hide (p. 40). Spring splitting and queen rearing does this anyway. - Breed from survivors that keep counts low (p. 41). - Screened floor of #8 mesh (only 5-10% fewer mites), robbing screens, hives spaced and marked against drifting, dead colonies removed fast, brood combs replaced after 5 years (pp. 37-38, 42). Mites die within days without bees, so empty hives and combs carry none (p. 5). If you stockpiled oxalic acid (HBHC, p. 29): 35 g, weighed (about 2⅓ level tablespoons with no scale) in 1 liter of 1:1 syrup; 5 mL on the bees in each occupied gap between combs, 50 mL at most per colony, only with no capped brood (late fall, winter, end of a brood break). Repeating it harms bees (FAO 2006, p. 21). Corrosive: gloves, goggles and a mask when mixing crystals. Vaporizing it is extremely dangerous. If you can still get it, stockpile pure oxalic acid dihydrate now (rule of thumb). Other pests: - Wax moth can't kill a strong colony; it wrecks combs in weak hives and in dark, warm, airless storage (AH 335, p. 132). Keep colonies strong and hives sized to them;
varroa-and-other-pests-without-store-chemicals

moth can't kill a strong colony; it wrecks combs in weak hives and in dark, warm, airless storage (AH 335, p. 132). Keep colonies strong and hives sized to them; store spare comb cool, light, airy and bee-tight, or in winter cold; 118 °F (48 °C) for 3 hours kills all stages (FAO 2006, p. 29). Render old black comb. - Robbing and yellowjackets in the dearth: narrow entrances, never spill syrup or leave comb out, cover open combs with a damp cloth (OSU EM 9186, pp. 9-10). Kill the first few hornets at a hive before the attack builds (FAO 2006, p. 28). - Skunks scratch at entrances at night - mud, scratch marks, torn grass in front. Raise hives 1 ft+ or lay a nail-point board or chicken wire in front (OSU EM 9186, p. 10). - Mice move in for winter: use a reducer (AH 335, p. 132). Ants: hive legs in cans of water or oil; toads: stands 16-24 in high (FAO 2006, pp. 27, 32).

☣ Foulbrood and other brood diseases American foulbrood (AFB) means burning. Its spores live 50+ years, spread about 1 km by robbing and drifting, and often arrive in foreign honey (FAO 2006, p. 10). - Signs: spotty brood; sunken, darker, pierced cappings; foul smell (🖼 FAO 2006, p. 10; 🖼 dead larvae in cells). - Matchstick test: push a matchstick into a dead larva and draw it out slowly. About an inch of ropy brown goo means AFB (FAO Forest, p. 150; 🖼 photo). - Then: burn combs, frames, honey and dead bees in a pit about 3 ft deep and fill it in; scorch the boxes inside until slightly brown (FAO 2006, p. 11). In fire season (no open burning June-October), shut it all in a bee-tight box or a well-covered pit and burn it after the rains (rule of thumb). - Saving the bees (shook swarm): brush them into a clean, scorched hive with only bars and wax starter strips, a queen excluder over the entrance; 3 days later burn those first combs and give fresh bars (FAO 2006, p. 12). Telling them apart (AH 335, p. 124; FAO 2006, pp. 12-15): | | Dead brood looks like | Smell | What to do | | AFB | Older larvae in capped cells, coffee-brown, ropy; scale stuck tight | Foul | Burn (above) | | European foulbrood |

| Smell | What to do | | AFB | Older larvae in capped cells, coffee-brown, ropy; scale stuck tight | Foul | Burn (above) | | European foulbrood | Young, coiled larvae dying before capping; rubbery scale lifts out | Sour | Requeen, remove the worst combs, feed or move to good forage (FAO 2006, p. 13) | | Chalkbrood | Hard white to black "mummies" that rattle | - | Strong colony, dry, ventilated hive sized to the bees (pp. 13-14) | | Sacbrood | Larva on its back, head dark, a watery sac | None | Usually recovers; requeen if bad (p. 15) | | Chilled brood | Dead brood at the edges of the nest after a cold snap | - | Too few bees; clears itself (AH 335, p. 129) | Nosema, a gut disease of adult bees, shows as crawling, trembling bees and spring dwindling, worst after long spells with no flying weather. 🍬 Feeding: sugar if you have it, honey if you don't The best feed is their own honey: leave enough, and save full combs of capped honey from strong colonies to give to light ones (AH 335, p. 74). Never feed honey from unknown hives - it spreads foulbrood (FAO 2006, p. 10; AH 335, p. 49). If you have white sugar (AH 335, pp. 50-51): - Spring 1:1 sugar to water by volume, stirred into water at about 140 °F; fall and new colonies 2:1 (new swarms get it 2-3 weeks). - Late-winter emergency: 1-2 lb of dry sugar on the inner cover, or candy (sugar and water 1:1 by weight, boiled to soft-ball like fudge, set on waxed paper) laid over the cluster. - Cane or beet sugar only; bees can't use milk sugar and some others (p. 45); skip brown sugar and molasses (rule of thumb). - Feed inside the hive, late in the day, entrances narrowed; no open buckets (p. 51; OSU EM 9186, p. 9). If you have no sugar: set a comb of capped honey from your own healthy hive right against the cluster, or pour 2:1 syrup - or your own honey thinned with a little warm water (rule of thumb) - into empty comb cells (AH 335, p. 74). Combine a hopelessly light colony with a strong one rather than feed it
feeding-sugar-if-you-have-it-honey-if-you-don-t

with a little warm water (rule of thumb) - into empty comb cells (AH 335, p. 74). Combine a hopelessly light colony with a strong one rather than feed it all winter (p. 72). Pollen for spring brood: a cake of your own trapped pollen with syrup and soy flour; 1 lb of pollen makes about 12 lb (pp. 74-75; 🖼 pollen traps). Never use another beekeeper's pollen (p. 49).

🌧 Wintering through wet winters How much to leave: a colony with no brood eats about 4 lb of honey a month; an average one about 60 lb between the last fall flow and first spring food, a strong one 80+ lb (AH 335, p. 72). The book's 90 lb is for cold climates; here plan on about 60 lb - winters are mild but the long summer dearth eats stores too (rule of thumb). A full deep frame holds about 5 lb (p. 73), so 60 lb is about 12 full combs (arithmetic). Also leave 500 square inches of pollen comb and at least 10 lb of bees (p. 72). Damp kills more than cold. Moisture from the cluster condenses on a cold lid and drips on the bees - chill, dysentery, mouldy combs - while wild colonies in thick tree hollows stay dry (Langstroth, pp. 131-133). Chalkbrood and nosema thrive in damp hives too (FAO 2006, pp. 14, 16). 1. Upper vent: a 1-inch hole high in the hive lets wet air out and gives a door on warm days (AH 335, p. 73; 🖼 winter hive). 2. Insulate the lid (straw, or a box of dry leaves over a cloth) so the top stays warmer than the walls; tilt the hive slightly forward so water runs out the door (rule of thumb). 3. Don't wrap it heavily
wintering-through-wet-winters

over a cloth) so the top stays warmer than the walls; tilt the hive slightly forward so water runs out the door (rule of thumb). 3. Don't wrap it heavily - heavily packed bees don't fly on warm days (p. 73), and we get many. 4. Stores against the cluster: most honey in the top box of a Langstroth; in a top-bar hive, honey combs next to the cluster (rule of thumb). Bees starve inches from honey they can't reach (p. 37). 5. Reducer on against mice (p. 73), hive up off the wet ground. Combine colonies under about 10 lb of bees in fall (p. 72). 6. Heft hives monthly. Mild winters start brood early and burn stores fast (rule of thumb), and a cold, rainy spring can starve a colony (p. 48): in February-March move honey against the cluster or feed (p. 74).

🍯 Harvesting honey: crush, strain, store When: take only sealed comb with no brood or pollen, and leave winter stores (FAO Forest, p. 48). Bees cap honey once it is under 20% water; then it won't ferment (Practical Action, p. 1). Work mid-morning to mid-afternoon in good weather, keep the hive open briefly (OSU EM 9186, p. 8), and cover combs at once (p. 10). Crush and strain (FAO Forest, pp. 48, 91; Practical Action, pp. 1-2): 1. Brush bees off with grass or a feather; cut the comb from the bar, leaving a finger's width as a guide for the next. For Langstroth boxes, set a bee-escape board under them the day before (AH 335, p. 100; 🖼 bee escape). 2. Work in a bee-tight room, screened windows (AH 335, p. 99), with clean, bone-dry food-grade plastic or stainless buckets (Practical Action, p. 2). Honey over 19-20% water ferments (p. 3). 3. Keep some as cut-comb honey - the wax is edible and the flavour best (FAO Forest, p. 91). 4. Crush the rest; pour through a coarse strainer, then finer cloths; let it drain for hours; finally squeeze the comb in a cloth bag (p. 91). A warm room (75-100 °F) helps it run (AH 335, p. 100); don't heat the honey. Save the wax. Crush and strain, step by step, with no extractor (a diagram drawn for
harvesting-honey-crush-strain-store

room (75-100 °F) helps it run (AH 335, p. 100); don't heat the honey. Save the wax. Crush and strain, step by step, with no extractor (a diagram drawn for this guide). Storing it: - Tight lids: honey pulls water from the air, then ferments (FAO Forest, p. 91); above 60% humidity it absorbs water (AH 335, p. 95). Sealed, it stays good for years (FAO, p. 91). - Cool: below 50 °F stops fermentation; it granulates fastest at 55-60 °F; warmth darkens it (AH 335, p. 97). A root cellar works (rule of thumb). - Under 17% water it won't ferment in a year; over 19% it will (p. 95). Dry wet honey with moving air over a shallow pan, never by heating (Practical Action, p. 4). - Granulated (solid) honey is fine (p. 3). To liquefy, set the jar in hot water at about 140 °F for 30 minutes - never on a flame (AH 335, p. 94). - Fermenting honey foams and smells of wine; 150 °F stops it (AH 335, p. 95), or make it into mead or vinegar (FAO Forest, p. 90). - Cooking with honey: the Food From Scratch guide. Honey as a burn dressing: "Burns" in the Field Care guide.

🕯 Beeswax: rendering and uses Bees eat about 8 kg of honey to make 1 kg of wax (FAO Forest, p. 106), so 30 lb of top-bar honey comes with about 3 lb of wax (arithmetic, from the 10 : 1 ratio on p. 107). Cappings give the best wax. Rules (FAO Forest, p. 111): - Never heat wax with a direct flame - always in or over water. It melts at 62-64 °C (144-147 °F), darkens above 85 °C (185 °F), and boiling ruins it. - Soft rainwater - hard water turns wax soapy. Pots: enamel, stainless or plastic; no aluminium, copper, brass, zinc, tin or iron. - Never throw water on burning wax - it spreads the fire (Practical Action, p. 3; 🖼 double boiler). Rendering step by step (FAO Forest, p. 112): 1. Soak the drained comb in warm water to wash out honey and pollen, three times. 2. Break it up, cover with clean water, and heat gently, stirring - wax is highly flammable. 3. Pour into a sack or coarse cloth bag and squeeze it between two sticks into a bucket. 4. Cool it slowly (bucket in a box of sawdust): the wax floats and sets in a cake. Scrape the dirt off below. 5. Melt again in an equal volume of water, strain through finer cotton into a lightly soaped bowl, and leave it
beeswax-rendering-and-uses

sets in a cake. Scrape the dirt off below. 5. Melt again in an equal volume of water, strain through finer cotton into a lightly soaped bowl, and leave it 12 hours. Store blocks away from strong smells; wax moths don't eat solid blocks (p. 111). In fire season, use the sun. A solar melter - black, insulated box, double-glass lid, sloping metal sheet running into a pan - needs only 68-70 °C and works best tilted about 40° to the sun (FAO Forest, pp. 112-113). Old black brood comb won't give up wax in the sun: soak it a day, tie it in a sack and boil it in water (p. 113). The black leftover ("slum gum") makes fire starters; burn it after dark so it doesn't draw bees (p. 114). Uses: candles need a thicker wick in beeswax than in tallow (Practical Action, p. 2) - see the Lighting guide for wicks, dipping and moulds. Salve: 1 cup of wax to 3 cups of oil, melted in a pot floating in water (FAO Forest, p. 129). Also cheese coating (the Milk, Butter & Cheese guide), foundation sheets (p. 114), and waterproofing thread (rule of thumb). Pure wax doesn't stick to your teeth when chewed; paraffin-cut wax feels greasy (p. 108).

🐻 Bears and fire season Black bears come mainly for the brood, and come back once they've had it (UF ENY-2060, p. 1). Oregon has 25,000-30,000 of them, and ODFW says to electric-fence beehives (ODFW, pp. 1-2). Building the bear fence (UF ENY-2060, pp. 1-5): 1. Heavy T-posts every 8 ft, 1½ ft into the ground. No trees as posts - bears climb them and drop in. Fence at least 3 ft from the hives, clear of anything a bear could climb. 2. Three wires at 8, 20 and 32 inches, 12- or 14-gauge high-tensile, on insulators (🖼 step photos); a gate of spring handles (🖼 p. 4). 3. Charger inside the fence, solar panel facing south; a 6-ft ground rod. 4. Test for 6,000-8,000 volts (🖼 finished fence). BearWise asks at least 6,000 V and 0.5 joules, and says lights and noisemakers don't work for long (ODFW BearWise, pp. 1-2). 5. Cut plants back 2-3 ft - anything touching the wire drains it (UF ENY-2060, p. 5). 6. Bait the wire with foil smeared with bacon grease so a bear's nose gets the first shock (rule of thumb). The fence in the list above, from the side and from above (a diagram drawn for this guide). With no working charger: "bear platforms" (hives on a strong raised stand) have also worked (AH 335, p. 132), and hives close to

above (a diagram drawn for this guide). With no working charger: "bear platforms" (hives on a strong raised stand) have also worked (AH 335, p. 132), and hives close to where people live are safer (FAO 2006, p. 33). For bears and cougars, see the Home Defense guide. Fire season (June-October): a smoker is a fire. Beekeepers' torches have started forest fires (FAO Forest, pp. 42, 56). Light it on bare ground, carry water, snuff it in a lidded can, never knock embers into dry grass, and keep brush cut round the apiary (rule of thumb). To evacuate hives, close the entrances at dusk with screen and move them at least 2 km (1¼ miles), or foragers fly back to the old spot (FAO Forest, p. 76). See the Wildfire guide.

🩹 Stings and allergic reactions Avoiding them: work gently on warm days when foragers are out; smoke first; never stand in the flight path; no perfume or strong soap; don't crush bees (FAO Forest, p. 48). If a colony turns hot, close it and stop for the day (OSU EM 9186, p. 8). Bees are touchiest in a dearth, guarding big stores, or getting ready to swarm (FAO Forest, p. 49), and when queenless (OSU EM 9186, p. 11). Many "bee stings" are yellowjackets (AH 335, p. 149). A normal sting: pain, redness and swelling - sometimes big, peaking in 24-48 hours (OSU EM 9186, p. 8). Scrape the stinger out at once with a fingernail or knife edge; pinching squeezes in more venom (AH 335, p. 147). A cold cloth helps (FAO Forest, p. 49). A whole-body reaction (anaphylaxis) follows 0.3-7.5% of stings (OSU EM 9186, p. 4): hives over the body, throat swelling, wheezing, vomiting, faintness, collapse - usually within minutes, sometimes up to 24 hours later (AH 335, p. 148). About 2% of people grow more sensitive with each sting (same page). - Give epinephrine (adrenaline) into the thigh muscle: adults 50 kg+ 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000), repeated every 5 minutes as needed; children 0.15 mg (WHO, p. 235). - Lay a collapsed person on their side, airway clear, kept warm (FAO Forest, p. 49).

🍎 Pollination for the garden and orchard - Apples, pears, plums, cherries, berries, squash, cucumbers and melons need or gain from insect pollination (AH 335, p. 123). Many apples won't set with their own pollen: plant two varieties that bloom together (p. 114). - Well-pollinated fruit is bigger and better shaped: an apple fills all its seeds only after several bee visits; a full strawberry needs about 21 (FAO Forest, p. 75). Misshapen fruit, half-filled pods and gappy seed heads at harvest mean too few bees (p. 77). - Squash has separate male and female flowers and must have pollinators; one hive per acre is usually enough, set out when 5-10% of plants flower (McCormack, p. 8; 🖼 squash flowers). - Field figures: ½ to 5 colonies per acre (AH 335, p. 80); per hectare (2½ acres): apple 4, pear 4, peach 2, strawberry 8, blackberry 7, cucumber and melon 7, squash 4 (FAO Forest, p. 78). For a family garden and orchard, one or two hives within a mile do the job (rule of thumb). - Seed saving: bee-pollinated varieties need ½ mile between them for pure seed; honey bees stick to one crop at a time (McCormack, p. 5). See the Seed Bank guide. - Native bees help: bumblebees, squash bees and mason bees. Mason bees nest in 7-8 mm holes or bamboo tubes (FAO Forest, pp. 79-80);

5). See the Seed Bank guide. - Native bees help: bumblebees, squash bees and mason bees. Mason bees nest in 7-8 mm holes or bamboo tubes (FAO Forest, pp. 79-80); hang drilled blocks under the eaves facing morning sun (rule of thumb).

🧮 How many hives for a family's sweetener Need: BYU's one-year list allows 70 lb of sugar or honey per adult (BYU, p. 1); the bare emergency ration (15 g a day) is about 12 lb a year (Food Security guide). Yield: unmanaged colonies seldom give more than 25-30 lb of surplus, well-managed ones 100 lb+ (AH 335, p. 70); the West averaged 27 lb (p. 21); OSU says one colony "can produce more than 40 pounds" (OSU EM 9186, p. 1). 🐕 Dogs: Guarding Stock, Herding, Hunting and Care How to keep working dogs with no store, no vet and no kibble: livestock guardian dogs against coyotes, bears and cougars, herding dogs, bird dogs and the Oregon law on hunting with dogs, watchdogs, feeding on meat, grain and scraps, the fish and foods that kill dogs, kennels, breeding and puppies, vaccines, first aid, humane training and a humane end. The dog books are in Southern-Oregon\Animals\Dogs: the Army's War Dogs manual (TM 10-396, 1943) and Military Working Dogs (FM 3-19.17, 2005), Wickham's 1891 shepherd-dog manual, Miller's 1919 American Hunting Dog and a parvovirus sheet. The guardian-dog and predator books are in Animals\Planning-Predators-Toxic-Plants, no-vet medicine and euthanasia in Animals\Veterinary, and the hunting and trapping law in Hunting and Trapping. Old dog books are full of poisons and beatings; this guide keeps their good parts and lists the rest under "Old advice in the library to ignore". ### The short version - Never let a dog eat raw salmon, steelhead or trout. Salmon poisoning kills most dogs that aren't treated. Cook all fish, meat and offal before dogs get it - raw offal also spreads tapeworm cysts to people (ODFW, p. 34; FDA, p. 156; Zoonoses, p. 119). - Vaccinate now, while vets exist: parvo from 6-8 weeks, repeated every 3-4 weeks to 16 weeks, a booster at 1 year, then every 3 years;

🐑 Raising a guardian pup with the stock Bonding begins at about 3 weeks, peaks at 6-8 weeks and levels off by 12; after 12 weeks it "may never be satisfactorily achieved" (AIB 588, p. 13). Texas A&M sets the limit at 16 weeks: "Do not bring the puppy into your home to socialize it" (p. 3). 1. Bring the pup home at 7-8 weeks and put it straight into its pen with the stock, away from the house (AIB 588, pp. 12, 21). 2. The pen: about 150 sq ft with 3-6 sheep, lambs if you have them (orphans are ideal); a pup-only corner with food and shelter behind panels it can crawl through but sheep can't; water both must share. Check it several times a day at first, then daily; a pat is fine, but the bond you want is dog-to-sheep; take out any sheep that bullies it (AIB 588, p. 13). Texas A&M uses a bigger pen with 4-6 calm animals of every kind the dog will guard (p. 3). 3. Rough play - chewing ears, pulling wool - stops at once: a sharp "No", bigger lambs that won't stand for it, or a pen next door for days to weeks with supervised visits (AIB 588, p. 13). 4. At 16 weeks or older, move it with "its" lambs to a bigger field. It will explore and

for days to weeks with supervised visits (AIB 588, p. 13). 4. At 16 weeks or older, move it with "its" lambs to a bigger field. It will explore and slip through fences; take it back every time, and never let it hang around the house or children (AIB 588, p. 14). 5. Teach enough to handle it: "No", "Come" (always pleasant - never call it to punish it), the leash (AIB 588, p. 14), "Stay" as you leave the pen, and short, watched spells tied up. 15-20 minutes, 3-4 times a week, keeps it catchable (Texas A&M, pp. 4-5). 6. At lambing or kidding, a young dog waits in the next pen until the mothers and young have "mothered up" (AIB 588, p. 18). 7. It is not a pet. A guardian petted at the house guards the house (AIB 588, p. 15). Praise it when you find it with the stock; take it straight back, with no fuss, when you find it elsewhere (Texas A&M, p. 5). The pup can reach its own corner, the lambs can't, and the water makes them mix (AIB 588, p. 13; a diagram drawn for this guide). Keep guardian and herding dogs from playing together (AIB 588, p. 18); loose farm pets teach a guardian pup bad habits (p. 19). Some lessons take up to a year to show (p. 21).

🔢 How many guardian dogs per flock - USDA: where predators are few, one dog does for most pastures; brush, timber and ravines need more. First-timers should start with one pup and add a second once it is settled - the young one copies the old (AIB 588, pp. 10-11). Keep a backup (p. 26). - Texas A&M: 1-2 dogs per 100 ewes or does; with bears, mountain lions or wolves, 1-2 per 50. Two dogs beat one except for small flocks near the house; add young dogs over the years (pp. 5-6). - The books differ: the USDA tells of one young Komondor guarding 600 ewe lambs on 125 acres (AIB 588, p. 11), but in open, coyote-only country. For our brushy hills, use Texas A&M: two dogs for a flock of up to about 50, raised a year apart, plus a night pen (rule of thumb, from both books). Pairs often split the work, one patrolling wide and one staying close; extra dogs roam more, which neutering helps (AIB 588, p. 11).

🚧 Fences that keep guardians home Fence respect "is the most important lesson an LGD can learn" (Texas A&M, p. 4). 1. Teach it young: an electric wire inside the bonding pen; a triangular PVC yoke stops a pup squeezing through (Texas A&M, p. 4). 2. New pasture: put the dog's shelter and feeder in it; walk the dog round the edge on a leash daily; leave it alone a few hours, then longer; bring it back at once each time it leaves (AIB 588, p. 21). 3. Jumpers and crawlers: a tire on a chain about 10 ft long (AIB 588, p. 21). Older dogs jump fences as high as 6 ft (p. 22). Never chain a dog beside a fence - it can hang itself (p. 26). Near roads keep it inside; elsewhere a dog patrolling just outside makes a buffer (pp. 21-22). The fence (UC ANR 8598, p. 8): a coyote squeezes through a 4 × 6 in gap in woven wire and climbs or jumps fences under 66 in, so add an electric top wire and a "trip wire" low on the outside. Electric netting cut coyote entries from 47% to 6%; energizers can run on solar-charged batteries. Electric fences fail on dry soil, poor grounding and weeds on the wire - a summer problem here. Against bears: at least 3 wires (5-6 better), lowest 7-9

solar-charged batteries. Electric fences fail on dry soil, poor grounding and weeds on the wire - a summer problem here. Against bears: at least 3 wires (5-6 better), lowest 7-9 in, highest 36-42 in, 8-10 in apart, energizer at least 6,000 V and 0.5 J (ODFW bear country, p. 2). Neighbors: a collar tag saying it is a livestock guardian, signs by the road, and a word with the neighbors (Texas A&M, p. 2). 🐕‍🦺 Herding dogs: basic training Sheep learn to ignore a quiet guardian but "will bunch and run from a dog that chases them" (AIB 588, p. 19); a herding dog uses that. Get a pup from a working strain; color doesn't matter (Wickham, p. 115). Wickham's rules: kindness and patience; one thing at a time; one short word per order, always the same; show the dog what you want; never punish it for what it doesn't understand (pp. 76-77). Yard lessons in a quiet place (Wickham, pp. 77-81): 1. A short name, and a wide collar worn for days before any line goes on. 2. "Come in!" - every time you call it to eat; on walks a light cord 20-30 ft long brings it back. 3. "Lie down!" - ease it gently down, praise it, step a little farther away each time until it stays. 4. "Speak!" - meat held just out of reach, rewarded at the first bark; later "Quiet!" (p. 86). 5. A whistle - whistle while it dozes, holding meat; later a pat replaces the meat. 6. "Stop!", "Steady!", "Hie on!" - with a plate of food and a check cord: wait, creep, eat. 7. "Over!" - meat tossed over a low board, then a stick raised bit by bit, to teach jumping fences. Out with the sheep (Wickham, pp. 85-92): only once "Come in!" works
herding-dogs-basic-training

- meat tossed over a low board, then a stick raised bit by bit, to teach jumping fences. Out with the sheep (Wickham, pp. 85-92): only once "Come in!" works every time. For a week just drive the sheep to one place saying "Hie on!". Teach hand signals - at a distance and in wind it sees what it can't hear. Don't send it round the flock until it is fast enough to circle them - 7-8 months for some, a year for others; a slow dog runs straight at them. Over-eagerness "must be checked, but not by whipping". "If the shepherd treats the sheep with gentleness, and does not allow the dog to bite them, he will be a protector of the flock" (p. 85). Train on cattle first if it must work both (p. 91). A full course takes two years; half of it by one year is good progress (p. 92). Where the dog goes for each command; use the same word every time (Wickham, pp. 85-90; a diagram drawn for this guide).

🦆 Hunting dogs: bird dogs and Oregon law The law (check each year's rules): - It is unlawful to "hunt any game mammal with dogs, except western gray squirrel" (ODFW big game, p. 21); dogs may not hunt or pursue cougar (p. 67) or black bear (p. 68). - "Use of dogs is permitted to hunt or pursue bobcat, raccoon, fox, and unprotected mammals" under the furbearer rules (furbearer regs, p. 6). - Pets may not "harass (chase, molest, worry, disturb) wildlife" except when hunting or in a pursuit season - Sept. 1 to Jan. 31 for wild upland birds (ODFW game birds, p. 34). A guardian that chases deer breaks the law too (AIB 588, p. 8). So in Oregon a hunting dog is a bird dog: pointers and setters point, spaniels flush, retrievers fetch. Quail in the open want a wide-ranging dog; grouse in the woods "a close, careful dog", quiet and "cat-like" (Miller, p. 160; p. 166). For ducks in cold water, a Chesapeake or Irish water spaniel (p. 173); double-coated dogs like the griffon stand icy water and wet brush (p. 81). Training a bird dog (Miller's lessons, without his spiked "force collar"): 1. A pup of hunting stock points at about 3 months. From 3 to 8 months teach manners: not to chase, to come to a whistle, heel, swim, and link guns with good
hunting-dogs-bird-dogs-and-oregon-law

of hunting stock points at about 3 months. From 3 to 8 months teach manners: not to chase, to come to a whistle, heel, swim, and link guns with good times (Miller, pp. 121, 154). Yard lessons start at 6-12 months (pp. 121, 152), never over half an hour (p. 153). 2. "Sit down!" - ease it down, pet it, a bit of biscuit. "Fetch!" - a corn cob, "Hold it!", "Give up!", praise; then farther, dropped, tossed, and "Dead bird - seek!" (pp. 153-154). 3. Steady on point: "Steady!", then "Whoa!" (Miller: "To ho!") if it starts to break, with a 30-ft check cord (pp. 154-155) on a plain collar or harness (our change). 4. Quartering: a whistle and a wave each time you turn, walking the way you want (p. 155). 5. The gun: "only one gun and one barrel to the covey" at first; a nervous pup gets weeks of walking up birds with no shells (p. 155; pp. 186-187). In the field: in trapping season keep the dog close and carry wire cutters for snares; keep it close where there is wolf sign; keep it from stagnant water and fish carcasses (ODFW game birds, p. 34).

🔔 Watchdogs and warning - "A dog's presence is a close substitute for human occupancy, and most burglars avoid houses with dogs. Small dogs may bark and attract attention" (COPS Burglary, p. 20). Post signs (WSDA, p. 1). - A German Shepherd answered a sound at 24 m that a man lost beyond 6 m (TM 10-396, p. 12). - On a small place a dog kept indoors at night means the house "cannot be entered nor the dog poisoned" (Miller, p. 108); bed it "free from draughts and commanding the whole of downstairs" (p. 112). - Guardians alert you to predators near the flock (AIB 588, p. 27); old shepherds belled every few sheep, and a dog tied in the yard took up the alarm (Wickham, pp. 111-113). - Teach "Speak!" and "Quiet!" so a bark means something (Wickham, pp. 79, 86). - Bark, don't bite. Don't train a household dog to attack: even the Army says "the highly aggressive dog tactics of the 1960s and 1970s are long gone" (FM 3-19.17, p. 5). Protecting people from your dog is your job (AIB 588, p. 24). Geese and guineas make good alarms too (Home Defense guide).

🎓 Basic obedience the Army way, without the harsh parts The Army's 1943 manual rests training on knowing how a dog's mind works, "constant repetition", "suitable recognition of a dog's progress" and "patience" (TM 10-396, p. 58). Keep that, but use a wide flat collar or harness instead of its choke chain and throwing chain (p. 63), and guide with hands and voice, not jerks. Gear: a 6-ft leash and a 25-ft long line (same page). The rules (TM 10-396, pp. 59-61, 66): - Lessons of about half an hour, twice a day; start with something the dog knows and end with praise for something it does well. Don't drill one command too long. Tone, not loudness, carries the order. - "The trainer must never lose patience". "No" is the only word for wrong; correct at the moment or not at all, never for clumsiness, slowness or not understanding, and never with the dog's name. - "A dog never is slapped with the hand or struck with the leash. The hand is an instrument of praise and pleasure" (p. 60). With a pup, holding back praise usually does it (AIB 588, p. 15). Never call a dog to scold it - go to it (AIB 588, p. 14; Wickham, p. 84). - Rewards: kind words, a pat, a romp (TM 10-396, p. 60). The Army avoided food treats; Wickham used

🐓 Keeping dogs from chasing stock "Without strong fences losses from sheep-killing dogs can be heavy" (FB 2222, p. 7). 1. Never teach the taste. Shepherds who left dead sheep lying, butchered in front of the dog and tossed it pieces raised sheep-killers; "an ounce of prevention is better than a pound of cure" (Wickham, pp. 116-117). Bury or burn dead stock (Zoonoses, p. 119) and feed only cooked meat, from a bowl. 2. Raise pups around stock and poultry (Wickham, p. 77), on a leash at first (rule of thumb). Say "No" the instant it chases a sheep or a vehicle (AIB 588, p. 14). 3. Dogs of 6-18 months often chase: a dangle chain with a short piece of 2×4, tire or PVC pipe slows them; take away any weak animal the dog keeps picking on (Texas A&M, p. 4). 4. No loose, idle dogs: they teach young dogs bad habits (AIB 588, p. 19), and a guardian may join strays in a kill (p. 28). 5. A dog found away from its post goes straight back, no reward; if that fails, a day or two kenneled away from the flock (Texas A&M, p. 5). 6. A dog that keeps killing must be shut up for good or put down; the USDA destroyed some guardians as "untrustworthy" (AIB 588, p. 26).

🍖 Feeding without kibble: what and how much "To a great extent, the dog is able to digest and utilize the same foods as man"; the Army fed meat, grain and "good mess scraps" (TM 10-396, pp. 37, 40): - Meat - about half the ration, with eggs, milk, cheese or fish (p. 38). Offal - heart, liver, lungs, tripe, udder - is "more nourishing to the dog than cuts of muscle meat". Fresh beats salted; never fried; fatty horse meat is good, brought in slowly (p. 37). Cook it all (next section). - Grain - about 25%: corn bread (best in cold weather and for hard workers), rice and rolled oats cooked well, dried bread soaked in broth or milk; never moldy bread (p. 38). - Vegetables - about 12½%: mashed tomatoes are good; not much high-fiber stuff (p. 39). - Calcium comes from bone: the Army ground raw bone in with the meat and gave sick dogs bone meal (pp. 40-41). Cooked whole bones splinter (p. 39); bake bones dry and pound them to meal (rule of thumb). Feed fairly dry, not sloppy (p. 40). How much: "a dog's main meal should consist of 1½ pounds of meat to each 50 pounds of body weight, depending upon the size of the dog and the amount of work he is required to do" (TM 10-396, p. 41). Grown guardians
