🛢 Asphalt, tar and pitch: what you can and can't do What asphalt is: "a natural or man-made by-product of petroleum distillation"; natural asphalt comes from distant pits such as Trinidad's, and road tar from coal-gas and coke works (FM 5-436, p. 15). There's neither here. Paving asphalt is solid at room temperature and must be heated to 250-350 °F (p. 20); "cutbacks" are asphalt thinned with gasoline, kerosene or diesel and catch fire easily; emulsions are asphalt in soapy water and won't burn (pp. 16, 21). Wood tar and pine tar: a charcoal retort gives about 50 kg of thick tar per tonne of hardwood, "useful ... as a wood preservation agent and caulking compound"; from softwood it's Stockholm tar (FAO Charcoal, pp. 31-32). Use it to caulk seams and protect posts and handles. It isn't a road binder: no book here uses it for roads, it softens in summer sun, and a road would need far more than a household could make (rule of thumb). It "cannot be allowed to escape into streams" (same page). Pine-pitch glue is in the Make-Do Household guide. Using what's left: - Old asphalt becomes gravel. Alone it makes a weak, potholed surface; blend it with 30-60% new gravel and lay it at least 3 in deep on a firm base (FHWA, pp. 70-71). When a paved road breaks up, grade it into
asphalt-tar-and-pitch-what-you-can-and-can-t-do

blend it with 30-60% new gravel and lay it at least 3 in deep on a firm base (FHWA, pp. 70-71). When a paved road breaks up, grade it into a crowned gravel road (rule of thumb). - Patching a pothole with bagged cold patch or saved asphalt (FM 5-436, pp. 119-121; 🖼 steps): 1. Cut a rectangle with straight-down sides around the hole and the weak stuff near it. 2. Dig out loose, wet base; refill with ¾-in crushed stone in thin tamped layers up to the old surface's bottom. 3. Paint bottom and sides with a thin coat of liquid asphalt; let it get tacky. 4. Shovel the patch in (don't dump it), layers no more than 3 in, coarse stuff raked to the middle. 5. Tamp hard, leave it slightly high, and drive slowly over it. Wet sand on top stops it sticking to tires. - Your own cold patch: the stone must be dry (dry a little in a pan over a fire, stirring); use about 2 quarts of liquid asphalt per cubic foot of crushed stone, shovel-mixed until every piece is dull black and the heap slowly creeps (pp. 118-119). - Cracks over ⅛ in: pack sand lightly mixed with asphalt, tamp, seal and sand. Sticky, bleeding patches: spread sand (pp. 116-117). The pothole patch above, step by step (FM 5-436, p. 120). Hot asphalt
asphalt-tar-and-pitch-what-you-can-and-can-t-do

pack sand lightly mixed with asphalt, tamp, seal and sand. Sticky, bleeding patches: spread sand (pp. 116-117). The pothole patch above, step by step (FM 5-436, p. 120). Hot asphalt is a fire and burn job (FM 5-436, pp. 100-101): never heat it near buildings or anything that burns; keep a fire extinguisher by; stand upwind; no smoking within 50 ft; long sleeves, cuffless pants, heavy gloves, boots. A dense yellow vapour means it's overheated "to the extent that a spark could cause an explosion": put the fire out and get everyone away. Don't heat asphalt over 400 °F or coal-tar pitch over 375 °F (FM 5-426, pp. 128-129); hot bitumen brings "burns and smoke-poisoning" (Biogas Digest, p. 24). No kettles or open fires June to October (rule of thumb). Dusty road? Never spread used engine oil (FHWA, p. 89); water it, or work a little clay into the gravel.
asphalt-tar-and-pitch-what-you-can-and-can-t-do

🛣 Gravel roads and driveways "The three most important things ... are drainage, drainage, and drainage!" (FHWA, p. 56). Even pavement fails without base and drainage (p. 131); a drained gravel road is the plan.
gravel-roads-and-driveways

Crown, shoulder and ditch - Three parts: a crowned surface, a shoulder sloping away, and a ditch (FHWA, p. 12). Standing water anywhere in that shape "is one of the major reasons for distress and failure" (p. 13). - Crown: about ½ in of fall per foot (4%), never over 6% (p. 22), in straight lines like a roof, not rounded, or the middle stays flat and potholes (p. 24). On a 12-ft driveway the centre sits 3 in above the edges (arithmetic); check with a string and line level ("Slope, grade, pitch and stairs" in the Practical Math guide). - Shoulder level with the road's edge, with no ridge of gravel or sod holding water on the road (pp. 26, 28). - Ditch sides 1 down : 3 across or flatter, never steeper than 1 : 2, flat-bottomed where there's room (p. 117); a narrow V-ditch scours in loose soil (p. 59). Dig from the outlet upstream (WHO Vector Control, p. 127). The shape that sheds water, and the shape that holds it (a diagram drawn for this guide).
crown-shoulder-and-ditch

Culverts and water bars Culvert rules (FM 5-34, p. 270): inlet at or below the ditch bottom; pipe out at least 2 ft beyond the foot of the fill; bedded on a layer at least a tenth of the pipe's width deep; slope 2-4% (never under 0.5%); a headwall at the inlet and rock at the outlet so the water can't dig. Make it a little steeper than the ditch so silt flushes, with upright rods at the inlet to stop branches (WHO, p. 128; 🖼 right and wrong). Pipes can be "made cheaply from used oil drums by cutting out the bottoms" (WHO, p. 129), or a box of durable logs (USDA FB 1660, pp. 24-25; woods that last: Shelter guide). Size for the worst storm: Cave Junction once got 8.12 in of rain in a day (Soil Survey, p. 5); FM 5-34 sizes culverts for up to 100 acres of runoff (pp. 268-269). Inspect them after every heavy storm (FM 10-67-1, p. 212); plugged culverts "cause serious damage when water flows over roads" (FHWA, p. 61). Mark weight limits on bridges and culverts, and keep the driveway clear 20 ft wide and 13 ft 6 in high for fire engines (OSFM, p. 18). Lay a culvert on the grade of the stream, not too high, too low or too flat (WHO, p. 129). Water bars turn water off
culverts-and-water-bars

fire engines (OSFM, p. 18). Lay a culvert on the grade of the stream, not too high, too low or too flat (WHO, p. 129). Water bars turn water off a sloping road before it cuts gullies; the Soil Survey recommends them here (p. 93). No book on the drive gives spacing, so (rule of thumb): dig a shallow trench about 30° across the road and pile the soil on its downhill side as a firm, rounded hump vehicles can cross; let it empty onto rock, brush or firm ground, never loose fill; space them closer the steeper the road, every 50 ft or less on a steep pitch; walk the road in the first big storm and add one wherever water starts to cut. Water bars turn water off the road onto firm ground (a diagram drawn for this guide from the rule of thumb above).
culverts-and-water-bars

Potholes, ruts and washboard - Washboard comes from hard braking and accelerating, dry weather, poor gravel and no crown (FHWA, p. 40). Fix it while the gravel is moist: loosen it to 1 in below the bottoms of the dips, mix, reshape to the crown and pack it (p. 41). - Potholes: don't just throw gravel in; cut them out and reshape so the road sheds water (p. 82). By hand: loosen around the hole with a mattock to below its bottom, refill with the same damp gravel in 2-3-in layers, tamp each, and restore the crown (rule of thumb). Right moisture for packing: a squeezed golf ball of it breaks into a few even pieces (FM 5-34, p. 267). - Tools: tractor grading blades and road rakes (FHWA, p. 16); a drag of heavy planks behind a tractor or horse (rule of thumb). Go slow; even a grader does poor work above 3-5 mph (p. 17). - Soft, wet spots: dig out the wet soil and refill with clean material that drains (p. 49); where springs rise under the road, a perforated pipe in a gravel trench leads the water to the ditch (p. 65).
potholes-ruts-and-washboard

Good gravel, and where to find it - A blend of stone, sand and fines with some natural clay to bind it into a crust; crushed rock beats rounded (FHWA, p. 70). Surface gravel wants 4-15% fines and a little stickiness; base or fill gravel has bigger stone and almost no clay and stays loose (pp. 69, 74-75). But too much clay goes slick and rutted "in a prolonged wet period" (p. 88), which is every winter here. - Layers: at least 3 in of surface gravel (p. 117), spread no more than 4 in at a time, damp and packed, finished at a 4% crown (p. 119). Loose gravel shrinks 30% or more as it packs (p. 82). - Home test: the jar test above shows the fines; a pinch of damp fines should hold together a little (the ribbon test in the Shelter guide) (rule of thumb). - Where to dig: Table 12 of the Josephine County Soil Survey rates every soil as a source of roadfill, sand and gravel; a "probable" source has clean sand or gravel at least 3 ft thick (pp. 120-121; 🖼 the table). Camas soils, "very gravelly sand" on the flood plains, rate probable for both (text, p. 36; 🖼 table, p. 233). - Local warnings: over fractured bedrock "Roads for year-round use need heavy base rock" (p. 43); Copsey clay needs drainage
good-gravel-and-where-to-find-it

probable for both (text, p. 36; 🖼 table, p. 233). - Local warnings: over fractured bedrock "Roads for year-round use need heavy base rock" (p. 43); Copsey clay needs drainage under any road (p. 39). Landslides can close highways and "isolate some communities" (Josephine County NHMP, p. 50), so keep back roads passable. Digging gravel in a live stream can need a state permit and hurts fish (rule of thumb).
good-gravel-and-where-to-find-it

Corduroy, log roads and stone roads - Corduroy over mud (FM 5-34, p. 64): logs 6-8 in across and about 13 ft long side by side, butt to tip; 6-in curb logs pinned along the edges; gaps filled with brush, rubble and twigs, then gravel or dirt on top; ditches and culverts as for any road. Heavy loads: lay it on 10-12-in sleeper logs. Lighter: sapling mats wired side by side, or two plank "treads" for the wheels (pp. 63, 65). - Macadam (stone road): "large rocks as a foundation and smaller ones as the surface is approached", raised well above the ground in wet climates and "bound with clay" (Christian, p. 229). - Creosoted ties and poles reused for curbs or culverts: gloves and long sleeves, and never burn them (Wood Handbook, p. 329). Corduroy roads in cross-section (FM 5-34, p. 64).
corduroy-log-roads-and-stone-roads

⛑ Safety: burns, dust, lifting and failing forms - Cement burns: wet cement in boots or gloves causes burns and ulcers you may not feel for hours, and its chromium causes skin allergy. Eye protection, dust mask, gloves, sleeves over gloves, pants over boots; rings and watches off; wash skin under cold running water (CAWST, p. 38). Alkali burns are worse than acid: brush dry powder off with a dry cloth, then flush; keep rinsing an eye 20 minutes (ATP 4-02.11, pp. 118, 132). - Quicklime heats when damp and can start a fire: see "Making lime" in the Natural Building guide. - Silica dust from crushing rock, cutting concrete or raking joints causes silicosis and lung cancer and "can remain airborne for several hours" (CMWG, p. 55; NPS, p. 8). Wet the work, wear a mask, work upwind, and never crush serpentine (rule of thumb). - Lifting: a sack is 94 lb, concrete 144 lb a cubic foot; don't fill a wheelbarrow to the brim (FM 5-428, p. 116). Lift with your legs and get help (rule of thumb). - Forms: protruding nails cause most form injuries; cut tie wires carefully, they whip; only the people stripping stay near (FM 5-428, p. 101). Stay out from beside a wall form while it fills (rule of thumb).

🪵 Firewood: Cutting, Splitting, Seasoning & Burning How to keep a household warm and cooking with wood: which local trees give the most heat, how much you'll need, felling and bucking safely, splitting, drying wood in our wet winters, burning it cleanly, keeping the chimney from catching fire, handling ashes in fire country, and growing your own firewood from oak, madrone and tanoak stumps. The manuals are in Firewood\ (Cutting-Felling, Splitting-Seasoning, Burning-Stoves-Chimneys, Woodlot); saws, axes and sharpening are in Engines-Motors\Chainsaws-and-Saws and the Blacksmithing guide. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst injuries and fires - Felling kills more woodcutters than anything else. Leave snags and dead trees to someone experienced, never cut alone, and keep everyone two tree-lengths away (WorkSafeBC Part 1, p. 13). - Plan your escape before you cut, about 45° back and away from where the tree will fall (🖼 drawing). - Never use an axe as a wedge or to drive one; wear eye protection when striking steel wedges (U. of Minnesota, p. 12). - Ashes start wildfires. Lidded metal can, on bare ground, well away from the house, for days. - Carbon monoxide and chimney fires - a CO alarm near the bedrooms, and a clean chimney.

🔥 Which wood, and how much All dry wood gives about the same heat per pound (~9,000 BTU) - so heavier (denser) wood gives more heat per cord (PNW-GTR-810, p. 9). | Local tree | Heat per cord (million BTU, dry) | How it burns | | Oregon white oak | ~30 | Hard to light, long-lasting coals - best overnight wood | | Pacific madrone | ~30 | Same; dries slowly and checks | | Tanoak | ~24-27 (estimated from density) | Excellent coals | | California black oak | ~22-24 (estimated) | Good coals | | Douglas-fir | ~21-24 | Easy to light, hot, some sparks | | Bigleaf maple | ~20-24 (estimated) | Good all-round | | Red alder | ~17-18 | Fast, clean; spring and fall fires | | Ponderosa pine / sugar pine | ~15-22 | Lights easily, burns fast, poor coals | | Incense cedar | ~15-17 (estimated) | Kindling - lights instantly, sparks a lot | (Oak, madrone, fir, alder and pine from OSU EC1628, p. 4 and PNW-GTR-810; burn traits from U. of Minnesota, p. 14.) Use the right wood for the job: cedar and pine for kindling and quick spring or fall fires; oak, madrone and tanoak for cold nights and overnight burns (rule of thumb). Creosote comes mostly from wet wood and smoldering fires, more than from the kind of
which-wood-and-how-much

fall fires; oak, madrone and tanoak for cold nights and overnight burns (rule of thumb). Creosote comes mostly from wet wood and smoldering fires, more than from the kind of tree (E-1388, p. 2). How much: - A cord) is a stack 4 ft × 4 ft × 8 ft (128 cubic ft) (🖼 drawing). A face cord is 4 ft high by 8 ft long with shorter pieces - three face cords of 16-inch wood make one full cord (CMHC, pp. 62, 64). A cord of green wood weighs roughly 5,000 lb (Cornell). - A whole house heated only by wood: 2-4 cords a winter; a stove that helps out: 1-2 cords (CMHC, p. 64). Add a cord or two if you also cook with wood, and keep a year ahead so next winter's wood is drying now (rule of thumb). - Trees per cord (trunk width at chest height): 10-inch ≈ 0.15 cord; 14-inch ≈ ⅓ cord; 22-inch ≈ 1 cord (Cornell, p. 1). A full cord and a face cord: three face cords of 16-in wood make one cord (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: PNW-GTR-810 Fuelwood Characteristics - tables for every Northwest tree; CMHC Guide to Residential Wood Heating; OSU EC1628. 🌲 Felling trees safely (OSU EC 1124 Safe and Effective Use of Chain Saws, written for Oregon woodland owners; USFS sawyer course) 1. Size it up. Don't fell in gusty wind, fog, snow or ice. Check the lean from two sides (a weight on a string works), look up for dead limbs ("widow-makers") and vines tying it to other trees, and bore in once to check for rot (🖼 drawing). Alder and maple often have rotten hearts (EC 1124, pp. 3-4). 2. Dead trees and snags) are a different job. They can fail across a circle 1-1½ times their height, farther downhill (USFS FS-1273, p. 36). Tanoak killed by Sudden Oak Death rots fast and can snap before it's fully dead - treat it as very high risk, and don't move infected tanoak wood to new areas (FS-1273, p. 181). 3. Clear an escape path about 45° back and away from the fall direction, and clear brush around the trunk (EC 1124, p. 5). 4. Notch (undercut) on the side it will fall, about one-third of the way through the trunk. The two cuts must meet exactly - if they don't, the trunk can split up and kick back ("barber chair"). An open-face notch (about 90°) is the most controlled (EC 1124, pp. 6-7; 🖼 the three notches). 5. Back cut from the other side, level and about 1 inch
felling-trees-safely

chair"). An open-face notch (about 90°) is the most controlled (EC 1124, pp. 6-7; 🖼 the three notches). 5. Back cut from the other side, level and about 1 inch higher than the floor of the notch. Stop to leave a hinge of uncut wood 1-1½ in thick - the hinge steers the tree. Wedge the back cut early. When it goes, set the saw down and walk out your escape path (EC 1124, pp. 7-8; 🖼 back cut and hinge). 6. Hung up in another tree? Don't cut the tree it's leaning on and don't work under it - see the professional fallers' methods for hang-ups and leaners (WorkSafeBC Part 2). A dead tree can land anywhere within 1 to 1½ times its height, and farther downhill (FS-1273, p. 36). Clear two escape paths at 45° back and away from the line of fall (An Ax to Grind, p. 47). The notch, back cut, hinge and wedge in steps 4 and 5 (a diagram drawn for this guide). With hand tools: a sharp crosscut saw and axe still fell and buck trees when fuel runs out - the USFS Crosscut Saw Manual, Saws That Sing (🖼 how the teeth cut) and An Ax to Grind (🖼 felling with an axe) cover it, and the Engines guide covers chainsaw care. 📚 Go deeper: OSU EC 1124 - the whole felling
felling-trees-safely

cut) and An Ax to Grind (🖼 felling with an axe) cover it, and the Engines guide covers chainsaw care. 📚 Go deeper: OSU EC 1124 - the whole felling sequence with drawings; WorkSafeBC Faller Standard Part 1; USFS hazard-tree guide - reading snags and rot. Pictures: 🖼 how far a snag can reach, FS-1273 p. 36, 🖼 felling factors, U. of Minnesota p. 9, Tree felling.

🪚 Bucking and limbing - Stand uphill of the log. Cut the side that's being squeezed (compression) first with a shallow cut, then finish from the side that's being stretched (tension) - this keeps the saw from pinching (EC 1124, pp. 8-9; 🖼 uphill stance). - Log supported at both ends (it sags in the middle): cut down from the top first, then up from below. Supported at one end: cut up from below first (U. of Minnesota, p. 11). - Bent-over saplings ("springpoles") whip when cut. Stand to the side and shave the inside of the bend with shallow cuts (EC 1124, p. 10). - Cut length to fit your stove - usually 16 in, a little shorter than the firebox. - Fire season: saws start fires. Cut early in the morning, keep the spark arrester in place, carry a shovel and extinguisher, and stay a while after you stop (rule of thumb). Cut the squeezed side first so the saw isn't pinched (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: WorkSafeBC Part 2 - binds and safe bucking; U. of Minnesota - bucking without pinching, p. 11. Pictures: 🖼 chainsaw kickback, EC 1124 p. 11, 🖼 limbing with an axe, An Ax to Grind p. 48, 🖼 bucking with an axe, p. 50, Chainsaw.

🪓 Splitting (UW-Extension Harvesting Firewood, pp. 15-16; U. of Minnesota, pp. 11-12) - Tools: a 6-8 lb splitting maul handles nearly everything; two steel wedges and a sledge for tough rounds. Keep wedge heads ground smooth - mushroomed steel throws chips. - Set up: a big round as a chopping block, at a height where the maul handle is level when it hits. An old tire bolted on top holds pieces upright. - Technique: swing with your legs and body, all the way through - half swings stick the maul. Aim for existing cracks, put knots at the bottom, and work slabs off the edges of big rounds before trying the middle (🖼 safe and unsafe splitting). - Size: split everything to 6 inches or less so it dries - rounds of 6-10 in at least in half, 10-14 in at least in quarters. - Safety: goggles, boots and shin protection; bystanders 20 ft away. - Easiest when: green wood splits easier than dry for most species; frozen wood splits easier still (rule of thumb). Safe and unsafe ways to split: never with your foot in the swing, and never strike steel with an axe (An Ax to Grind, p. 51). 📚 Go deeper: UW-Extension Harvesting Firewood from Your Woods; An Ax to Grind - axes and mauls. ☀ Seasoning: drying wood in a wet climate Wet wood wastes heat - a ton of wood at 60% moisture gives about 5.6 million BTU; dried to 20% it gives about 10.7 million (U. of Minnesota, p. 14). It also makes creosote and smoke. - How long: softwoods about 6 months, hardwoods about 12 (EPA Wet Wood is a Waste, p. 2); big oak and madrone pieces up to 2 years (CMHC, p. 61). In western Oregon: cut and split by spring, stack through a dry summer, cover before the rains - two summers is better (OSU EC1628, p. 2). - Cut early. Wood split in August is only half dry by November, and wood that isn't dry by November won't dry outdoors over the winter - move it under cover (USFS 1943 test). - Stacking: single rows, off the ground on rails or pallets (4-6 in), bark side up, in sun and wind (🖼 stacked piles). Cover only the top - side tarps trap moisture. Wood dried inside a closed shed takes nearly twice as long as wood in sun and wind (UW-Extension, pp. 16-18; EPA, p. 2). - Keep the woodpile at least 30 ft from the house so it can't carry a wildfire to the walls (UW-Extension, p. 17). - Is it dry? Cracks in the ends, faded gray color, a hollow knock when two pieces are

so it can't carry a wildfire to the walls (UW-Extension, p. 17). - Is it dry? Cracks in the ends, faded gray color, a hollow knock when two pieces are struck together, lighter weight, no hissing in the fire - or a moisture meter reading 20% or less on a freshly split face (CMHC, p. 61; EPA, p. 2). - Woodsheds and racks: plans for a 1-cord shed and cheap pallet or block racks (EPA shed plans; EPA 4 simple racks; 🖼 rack drawings; 🖼 shed drawing). 📚 Go deeper: EPA Wet Wood is a Waste; UW-Extension - stacking and drying; CMHC - drying tests, p. 61. 🏠 Burning safely: stoves, chimneys, ashes Burn hot and dry. Smoldering fires and wet wood coat the chimney with creosote, which condenses below about 250 °F and turns to sticky tar below 150 °F (E-1388, p. 2). Flaky, dry creosote means you're burning well; black, shiny tar means you're not (CMHC, p. 46). Chimney cleaning: at least once a year; some say every 3 cords. After cleaning, check after 2 weeks, 1 month and 2 months to learn how fast yours builds up, and check the stovepipe every 2-3 months (E-1388, pp. 3, 5). A stiff brush on rods or a rope (🖼 chimney brushes), from the top down, with the stove sealed below (rule of thumb). Chimney fire - roaring sound, shaking pipes, sparks out the top (E-1388, p. 3): 1. Close every air inlet and the damper to starve it. 2. Get everyone out; have someone watch the roof for sparks and check the attic. 3. A dry-chemical (ABC) extinguisher or baking soda thrown into the firebox can knock it down. 4. Chimney fires reach 2,000-3,000 °F - inspect the chimney before using it again; metal chimneys can be ruined after 2-3 fires. Clearances: follow the stove's label. For an unlabeled stove: 36-48 in from anything that burns, 18 in for stovepipe, and a non-combustible floor pad reaching 18 in in front (CMHC, p. 31; U. of Minnesota,
burning-safely-stoves-chimneys-ashes

For an unlabeled stove: 36-48 in from anything that burns, 18 in for stovepipe, and a non-combustible floor pad reaching 18 in in front (CMHC, p. 31; U. of Minnesota, p. 24; 🖼 clearances and a wall shield). Keep wood, furniture and drying clothes 3 ft away (USFA card). Clearances for a stove with no label, seen from above (a diagram drawn for this guide). Ashes in fire country (Crystal Lakes fire district; USFA): - Leave ashes in the stove 4+ days if you can; then into a metal can with a tight metal lid, set on dirt or concrete at least 10 ft from anything that burns, for at least a week - or soak and stir them with water. - Never a plastic bucket, cardboard box, or the garden in fire season. Buried "dead" coals have started wildfires. - Cold, wet wood ash is useful: lye for soap, nixtamal for corn, and potash for the garden. Carbon monoxide: smoke and CO alarms near bedrooms; both wear out after about 10 years (Crystal Lakes, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: E-1388 The Creosote Problem; CMHC - stoves, chimneys and clearances; Aprovecho Capturing Heat - homemade stoves; Arkansas Basics of Heating with Firewood. 🌳 Growing your own: thinning and coppicing Our hardwoods regrow from the stump - cut once, harvest again and again ("coppicing") (USFS PSW-GTR-185): - Black oak, tanoak and madrone all resprout from the root crown (🖼 tanoak sprouts), and it's almost impossible to stop them. - Cut stumps low - under 8 inches. Sprouts from tall stumps attach weakly and rot early (p. 35). - Cut in winter or spring: black oaks cut December-May sprouted 92% of the time; cut June-November, only 45% (p. 36). - In full sun, black oak and tanoak sprout clumps reached about 20 ft tall in 10 years (p. 36). Thin clumps to 3-4 of the best stems after a few years. - Bigleaf maple resprouts strongly; red alder only from young stumps (rule of thumb). Thin for firewood and fire safety at the same time: remove small, crowded trees and lower limbs ("ladder fuels", 🖼 drawing) and space out the crowns - the cut becomes firewood, and the woods burn less hot in a wildfire (OSU EC 1573, p. 3; EC 1574). In oak woodland, removing the Douglas-fir crowding the oaks gives both firewood and healthier oaks (KBO/Lomakatsi oak guide). 📚 Go deeper: PSW-GTR-185 - sprouting of black oak, tanoak and madrone; OSU EC 1573 - thinning; Restoring Oak Habitats in Southern Oregon; Wikipedia: coppicing. ⛽ Fuel Guide How long gasoline, diesel, kerosene and propane keep, how to tell when fuel has gone bad, what can be rescued, how to store fuel for the long haul - and how to get fuel out of gas-station underground tanks, drums and vehicles when there's no grid power. The manuals are in Fuel\ (Fuel-Quality-Storage, Station-Tanks-Pumping, Military-Fuel-Handling, Other-Fuels). Wood gas, biodiesel and alcohol fuel are in Homestead-Skills\Fuels. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent fires and deaths - Gasoline vapor explodes. No flames, smoking or sparks within 50 feet of open fuel. Use only pumps made for gasoline - ordinary electric motors spark. (FM 10-67-1, p. 21) - Static sparks ignite fuel. Touch bare metal with your bare hand before opening any cap. Keep the nozzle touching the can or tank the whole time you pour. Fill portable cans on the ground, never in a truck bed or on carpet (rule of thumb). (FM 10-67-1, pp. 21-23) - Never climb into a tank sump, manway or tank. Fuel vapor pushes out oxygen and can kill without any smell or warning; the lids are heavy. Work from ground level. (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets, p. 5; DoD UFM 3-460-03, p. 24) - Never put gasoline in a kerosene heater or lamp, and never store fuel inside the house. - Propane sinks into basements and ditches. Smell gas: put out flames, get out,

Never put gasoline in a kerosene heater or lamp, and never store fuel inside the house. - Propane sinks into basements and ditches. Smell gas: put out flames, get out, close the tank valve if it's safe. (Texas RRC Propane Safety, p. 11) - Empty cans and drums are more dangerous than full ones - they are full of vapor. (FM 10-67-1, p. 14) - Fuel-soaked clothes can burst into flame from static when you pull them off. Wet them with water first, and never take off a jacket or sweater within 50 feet of open fuel. 🔍 Is this fuel still good? - Jar test: pour a sample from the bottom of the can or tank into a clean clear jar. Good fuel is clear and bright. Let it stand 15 minutes. Haze, droplets or a second layer at the bottom = water. Water fully settles out in about a day. (FM 10-67-2, p. 36; p. 97; 🖼 Army samplers that reach the bottom) - Bad signs: darker color, a sour or varnish smell, or a drop on glass that leaves a sticky film when it dries (gum). Gum sticks valves and clogs carburetors. - E10 with a bottom layer has phase-separated (E10 blends): the bottom is ethanol plus water, not just water. E10 at 60 °F holds only about 4 teaspoons of water per gallon (3.8, to be exact) before this happens - less in the cold. Humid air rarely causes it; rain and water sitting in tanks do. (EPA phase-separation memo, p. 2; pp. 4-5) What the jar tells you: | You see | It means | Do this | | Clear and bright | Good fuel | Use it | | Haze or tiny droplets | Water mixed in | Let it settle a day, take fuel off the top, filter | | A separate bottom layer | Free water - or, in E10, ethanol + water | Drain the bottom off; see

🔧 Rescuing old fuel (FM 10-67-2 Petroleum Testing, p. 97) - Water and dirt can be fixed: let the fuel settle a few hours to a day, then pour or siphon off the top (Siphon), leaving the bottom inch behind, and filter it. The Army lets gasoline and diesel settle at least 2 hours after a tank is filled; water drops out in about 24 hours. - Phase-separated E10: the layers won't remix. Drain off and discard the bottom layer. The top is weaker (lower-octane) gasoline - fine for lawn, farm and older carbureted engines. - Stale but clean gasoline: blend it with fresh. The Army mixes a small test batch ("pilot blend") first and tests it. In its worked example, gummy old gasoline needed about 6 parts fresh to 1 part old to come back within limits. (FM 10-67-2, p. 98; 🖼 blending-ratio graph) Rule of thumb: 1 part old to 4 or more parts fresh for mildly stale gas, and use it in simple engines (generators, mowers, older trucks) - not modern high-compression or turbo engines. The staler it is, the more fresh fuel it needs. Blending can't save fuel that's bad in many ways at once. (FM 10-67-2, p. 97) - Can't be fixed: heavy gum and varnish, and gasoline mixed into diesel. 🛢 Diesel care - Water is the enemy. Drain water from the bottom of tanks and drums regularly, and check for it every time you gauge - the Army checks with water-finding paste every time and drains water the day after new fuel comes in, before it rises high enough to be drawn into the outlet. Keep drum bungs tight and covered so rain can't seep in. (FM 10-67-1, p. 141; 🖼 gauging the water in a tank) - "Diesel bug": yeast, fungus and bacteria grow where fuel meets water - brown, black or gray slime that clogs filters and eats tanks. A puddle of water in the tank bottom is enough to feed big colonies, and it's worst in hot, humid weather. Prevent with zero water and a biocide; badly slimed tanks must be drained and scrubbed. Tanks left unused for a long time collect water at low points. (DoD UFM 3-460-03, pp. 29-30) - Expect old station diesel tanks to be corroded inside. EPA found moderate or severe corrosion in 83% of the diesel tanks it inspected, and ethanol had crept into 90% of the diesel samples. (EPA Corrosion in USTs with Diesel, p. 8; p. 10; 🖼 photos of badly corroded tank parts) Filter station diesel well. - Keep it moving. Diesel kept for a generator lasts better if the same tank also feeds something used every
diesel-care

photos of badly corroded tank parts) Filter station diesel well. - Keep it moving. Diesel kept for a generator lasts better if the same tank also feeds something used every day (a heater or tractor) so the fuel turns over. Keep spare filters. (FEMA P-1019, p. 91) - Cold gelling: thin diesel with No. 1 diesel or kerosene (the Army blends kerosene in for winter - FM 10-67-2, p. 98) or add a cold-flow additive - before it gets cold; additives won't un-gel it. Additives don't change the temperature at which wax first clouds the fuel; they only help it keep flowing through filters a few degrees colder. (NREL Biodiesel Handling Guide, p. 29) "Summer" diesel bought in July can gel on a frosty valley morning - buy diesel in the season you'll burn it. (Alberta, p. 12) - Substitutes: diesel engines can run on No. 2 heating oil, which is nearly the same fuel (FEMA P-1019, pp. 91, 106). Kerosene and Jet A are close to No. 1 diesel. Kerosene is "dry" (low lubricity) and harder on modern injection pumps; older mechanical-pump diesels tolerate substitutes best. (Rule of thumb) Pictures: Diesel fuel, Heating oil, Cloud point (the temperature where wax first clouds the fuel), Jet fuel. 📚 Go deeper: DoD UFM 3-460-03 Petroleum Fuel Systems Maintenance - water, microbes and tank cleaning; EPA Corrosion in Diesel USTs - what's

🏪 Getting fuel out of gas-station tanks Why this matters here: a 2016 emergency exercise in Portland on a Cascadia earthquake found it would have catastrophic impacts on Oregon's petroleum infrastructure and make resupply very hard. Once delivery trucks stop, the fuel already in local station tanks may be all there is. (NASEO Petroleum Shortage Planning, pp. 7-8) What's under the concrete (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets; North Dakota training; cutaway drawings: 🖼 station tank, pump and piping, 🖼 diesel tank equipment): - Each tank is usually 8,000-20,000 gallons, about 8-10 ft across, with its bottom roughly 10-14 ft below the pavement. (Rule of thumb) - Fill pipes sit inside small round spill buckets (5-25 gallons, lids 1-2 ft) (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets, p. 7; 🖼 photo of the lids; 🖼 spill-bucket photo). The cap colors usually tell you the fuel: white = regular, blue = mid-grade, red = premium, yellow = diesel; orange marks vapor-recovery pipes, not fuel. (Rule of thumb - check by gauging.) - A large manhole (3-4 ft lid) right over each tank covers the turbine-pump sump - the pump, piping and leak sensor (🖼 sump photos). Other small risers are the tank gauge, spare ports and vents. - Lifting lids: big steel lids are heavy - get help. Square or oval lids can fall through the hole and smash the pump or piping below.
getting-fuel-out-of-gas-station-tanks

ports and vents. - Lifting lids: big steel lids are heavy - get help. Square or oval lids can fall through the hole and smash the pump or piping below. Expect fuel vapor when you open them. (EPA, pp. 5, 8) - Bail out the spill bucket first. Rain and snowmelt fill them; if you open the fill cap under water, the water runs into the fuel. (Vermont Simple Suction manual, p. 4) What's under the concrete: the fill pipe and spill bucket, the pump sump, a gauge port, and a tank whose bottom is 10-14 ft down (a diagram drawn for this guide). Step 1 - measure what's there (EPA Doing Inventory Control Right): - Use a long wooden stick (won't spark), marked in inches (the EPA uses ⅛-inch marks), with zero at the very end. Varnish keeps fuel from creeping up the wood. (EPA, p. 6; 🖼 Army gauge-stick drawing; Dipstick) - Lower it slowly down the fill pipe or gauge port, let it touch bottom gently, then bring it up quickly, and read the wet line. Wipe it and do it twice. (EPA, p. 8) - Water-finding paste on the tip changes color where there's water in the bottom; fuel-finding paste smeared where you expect the fuel line makes the reading sharper. A tank chart (if you can find one in the station office) converts inches to
getting-fuel-out-of-gas-station-tanks

the bottom; fuel-finding paste smeared where you expect the fuel line makes the reading sharper. A tank chart (if you can find one in the station office) converts inches to gallons. (EPA, pp. 6-7) Step 2 - the easy way: power the station. - At "suction" stations the pump is inside the dispenser - power the dispenser and it pumps. A check valve just under that pump keeps the line full ("primed") between uses. (Vermont, p. 3; 🖼 suction-system diagram) - At most modern stations the pump is the submersible turbine in the sump, usually 240-volt, ¾-2 hp (rule of thumb), plus the dispenser's electronics. That takes a stout generator. Connect only through the station's transfer switch - never by backfeeding. (🖼 transfer-switch diagram; Transfer switch) Several states have paid to prewire stations with generator hookups or "quick connects" (Florida required some by law in 2006). (NASEO, pp. 71-73; Florida SB 528 analysis) If the owner is around, work with them: they know their tanks and may already have a generator hookup. Step 3 - no power: pump it up by hand. - A siphon won't work - the fuel is below you, and a siphon only flows downhill. - Hose down the fill pipe: there's a drop tube inside with a flapper valve (it slams shut when the tank is about 95% full). Hose down the fill pipe: there's a drop tube inside with a flapper valve (it slams shut when the tank is about 95% full). The drop tube ends close to the tank bottom - within 6 inches in Vermont's manual, within 1 foot in EPA's. A smooth hose usually slides past when the tank isn't full, but it can snag; the separate gauge port is another way in. (Vermont, p. 5; EPA Inventory Control, p. 7; 🖼 drop-tube valve photos) - Suction lift is the limit. Air pressure can push water up at most about 33 feet in a perfect vacuum at sea level, and real pumps do far worse; gasoline's own vapor pressure cuts the lift further, especially when it's hot. (FM 10-67-1, pp. 485, 487) Hand and 12-volt suction pumps typically lift gasoline 10 feet or less (less in hot weather - gasoline boils in the hose). They work while the tank is fairly full and fail as it drops. (Rule of thumb, from the physics in FM 10-67-1) - For a deep or low tank, use a pump that goes down into the tank - a 12-volt submersible fuel-transfer pump rated for gasoline on a long hose - or a hand pump on a long rigid pipe. (Submersible pump, Hand pump) - Keep the hose end a few inches off the bottom to avoid water and sludge,

- or a hand pump on a long rigid pipe. (Submersible pump, Hand pump) - Keep the hose end a few inches off the bottom to avoid water and sludge, pump into metal cans on the ground, keep everything bonded (metal-to-metal contact or a ground wire), and filter through a water-separating funnel. A pump at the top lifts gasoline 10 ft or less; a pump lowered into the tank pushes it up (a diagram drawn for this guide). Bonding and grounding, the Army way (FM 10-67-1, pp. 21-22; drawings: 🖼 bond wire and ground wire, 🖼 grounding a tank truck, 🖼 bonding a farm tank; Static electricity, Ground)): - Bond = connect the two metal things (nozzle to can, pump to tank) so no spark can jump between them. Make the bond before you open the cap and keep it until the cap is back on. - Ground = a wire from the equipment to a metal rod driven down to permanently damp soil, clamped to clean, bare, unpainted metal. Rod depth by soil: clean sand or gravel 6 ft, clay 4 ft, silt, silty sand, peat or muck 3 ft. - In dry or rocky ground, dig a hole about 1 ft deep and 3 ft across, pour in 5 lb of salt dissolved in 5 gallons of water, drive the rod there and keep it damp. 🚗 Drums and vehicles - Drums: a rotary or lever drum hand pump threads into the 2-inch bung; the Army's have a bonding wire and a strainer. Keep the drum grounded, and cover the pump's suction pipe when it's not in use. (FM 10-67-1, p. 353; 🖼 drum pumps in a 55-gallon drum) - Open bungs slowly on a drum that's sat in the sun or been bumped around - pressure can spray out fuel and vapor. (FM 10-67-1, p. 14; 🖼 drum bungs and chimes) - Cars and trucks: most modern fillers have an anti-siphon screen or rollover valve, so a hose won't reach the fuel. It's usually easier to disconnect the fuel line at the engine and let the car's own fuel pump push fuel into a can (key on, or power the pump relay) - or drain from the fuel-filter or tank fittings underneath. Older vehicles and many diesel trucks have no screen. (Rule of thumb) - Gas in old vehicles goes stale too - jar-test it before trusting it. Drum pump. 🔥 Kerosene and propane Kerosene heaters (CPSC Kerosene Heater Safety, pp. 1-2): - Only water-clear 1-K kerosene (Kerosene), never gasoline (even a little is dangerous). Store it in blue cans that have never held gasoline, away from other fuel cans. - Refuel outdoors with the heater off and cool, and don't fill above the "full" mark - that space lets the fuel expand. - Keep it at least 3 feet from furniture and clothes. - Unvented heaters make carbon monoxide: run it with the room's door open to the rest of the house, and crack a window about an inch if the door must be closed or the house is tight. - Keep the wick clean and set at the right height. - If it flares up, don't carry it and don't throw water on it. Use its shut-off switch; if that fails, get everyone out. Propane (Texas RRC Propane Safety Tips; Propane, Gas cylinder): - Store cylinders outdoors and upright, never in a closed building; vapor is heavier than air and pools low. (p. 4) - Never put your head over a tank's valves - the relief valve can pop. Liquid propane causes frostbite on skin and eyes. (p. 4) - Keep big tanks painted white or silver; a dark, rusty tank heats up and can vent through its relief valve. Cap every line not connected to an appliance.

🌲 When the stored fuel runs out These are big projects - read the books before you build anything. - Wood gas: in World War II, cars, trucks and stationary engines in Europe ran on gas made by burning wood in a sealed canister. FEMA's plans fit 4-stroke gasoline engines of 10-150 hp; a diesel can run mostly on wood gas with a little diesel to light it. (FEMA Simplified Wood Gas Generator, p. 19; drawings: 🖼 WWII Imbert gasifier, 🖼 FEMA's simple gasifier, 🖼 exploded view of the parts, 🖼 photo on a tractor) Wood gas is about 20% carbon monoxide (Carbon monoxide poisoning). Many people died of "generator gas poisoning" in WWII. The danger is greatest when refueling, idling, or after shutdown - the unit keeps making gas after the engine stops - so keep it away from closed or poorly aired spaces. (FEMA, pp. 8, 73-74) - Alcohol: a farm still makes about 190-proof ethanol - too wet to mix with gasoline, but it runs most spark-ignition engines after you advance the timing, enlarge the carburetor jets and add preheat for cold starts. A gallon replaces about ⅔ gallon of gasoline. It's a poor diesel fuel on its own. (USDA Small-Scale Fuel Alcohol Production, p. 23; 🖼 how a still concentrates alcohol, 🖼 column still diagram; Still, Ethanol fuel) - Biodiesel is made from vegetable oil with

The short version is in Illinois Valley - Start Here. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Batteries give off hydrogen, which explodes at just 4% in air (DOE-HDBK-1084, p. 22). Vent the top of the room, and never mount a controller, switch or relay in or above a battery box (IEA, p. 53). - A shorted battery can explode. One golf-cart battery can push about 8,000 amps (Sandia, p. 15). Fuse at the + terminal, connect the battery last, and if a tool shorts it, don't grab it: get away (IEA, p. 22). - Never plug a generator into a wall outlet. Backfeeding can kill line workers and neighbors. Generators run outdoors only (CPSC, p. 1). - Panels are live whenever light hits them. Cover them with an opaque tarp before touching wiring (fire FAQ, p. 3). - Lithium: never charge below 32 °F,

p. 1). - Panels are live whenever light hits them. Cover them with an opaque tarp before touching wiring (fire FAQ, p. 3). - Lithium: never charge below 32 °F, never "equalize" it, and never cover or pick up a burning pack; soak it with water from a distance (FAA SAFO 09013). - Battery acid blinds. Goggles and rubber gloves; flush skin or eyes with water at least 15 minutes (NEETS 1, p. 96).

📋 Start with a load list For each thing you'll run, multiply watts × hours a day = watt-hours (Wh) a day, and add them up (Sandia, p. 16). Take watts from the nameplate or a plug-in watt meter. An example (use your own numbers): | Item | Watts | Hours a day | Wh a day | | 4 LED bulbs | 40 | 5 | 200 | | Laptop | 50 | 4 | 200 | | Radio and phone charging | 20 | 5 | 100 | | Fridge or freezer (watt-meter reading) | - | - | 450 | | Inverter idling | 10 | 5 | 50 | | Total | | | 1,000 Wh = 1 kWh | - Kill hidden loads. Standby "phantom" loads can add up to 100 W around the clock (NRCan, p. 14): 2.4 kWh a day. An idling inverter uses 10-50 W; switch it off (rule of thumb). - Skip the inverter for 12 V lights, fans, pumps and USB chargers (Arizona, p. 5; 🖼 12 V loads pictured). - Motors need about 6 times their running current to start: a 1 hp motor may need 6 kW for a moment (DOE Microhydro, p. 67). - Store water, not electricity. A solar pump run from its panels through its own controller, filling a raised tank, needs no battery: the

🧮 A worked example Panels: panel kW = (kWh a day ÷ sun hours) × 1.2 for losses (Sandia, p. 20). For the 1 kWh load above: - December: 1 ÷ 1.9 × 1.2 ≈ 630 W of panels. - July: 1 ÷ 7.1 × 1.2 ≈ 170 W. Check: each rated panel watt gives about 0.85 Wh per sun hour (Practical Action, p. 4), and 630 × 0.85 × 1.9 ≈ 1,020 Wh. Batteries: only 40% of a lead-acid label is usable (IEA, p. 17), so label Wh needed = daily Wh × days of backup ÷ 0.4. Above 40° latitude the IEA suggests 7-9 days of backup for solar alone (same page): 17,500-22,500 Wh of label for 1 kWh a day. Four 6 V, 220 Ah golf-cart batteries in series (🖼 drawing) make 24 V × 220 Ah = 5,280 Wh, about 2 days at 40% (arithmetic). The cheaper fix: use less in winter, add panels (salvaged ones are plentiful), and fill the gap with creek hydro or a generator. When either more panels or more batteries would do, add panels; don't put a new battery into an aged bank (IEA, p. 38). Controller: at 24 V with an MPPT controller, 630 W ÷ 24 V × 1.25 ≈ 33 A, so a 40 A controller (Arizona, p. 4). 📚 Go deeper: Sandia, p. 20 - a full

an MPPT controller, 630 W ÷ 24 V × 1.25 ≈ 33 A, so a 40 A controller (Arizona, p. 4). 📚 Go deeper: Sandia, p. 20 - a full worked example; IEA Lead-Acid Battery Guide, p. 17 - battery sizing. Pictures: 🖼 2 V cells wired into a 24 V bank, Arizona p. 5.

🔍 Salvaging and testing panels Count the cells: 36 cells is a "12 V" panel; 60 cells give about 30 V, and 72 cells about 36 V (Arizona, p. 2; 🖼 reading a panel's label). House-roof panels are 60- or 72-cell; they charge a 12 or 24 V bank well only through an MPPT controller (rule of thumb). Rooftop grid-tie systems go dead when the grid does. A grid-tied inverter "cannot operate disconnected from the grid" (Navy NWC TP 6563, p. 23; 🖼 grid-tied system); modern string and micro-inverters shut down the same way, by design (rule of thumb). The panels are fine: rewire them through a charge controller to batteries. Testing a used panel (Navy, pp. 26, 50-51): 1. Look for cracked glass and peeling layers (delamination). 2. In clear sun, face the panel squarely at the sun. 3. Open-circuit voltage (nothing connected): within 10% of the label, allowing for heat (hot panels read lower) (🖼 drawing). 4. Short-circuit current (🖼 drawing): meter on its 10 A range across the leads, one panel at a time (rule of thumb): within 20% of the label. Open-circuit volts first, then short-circuit amps on the 10 A range, one panel at a time (a diagram drawn for this guide). A 20-year-old panel usually still makes 80-90% of its label (rule of thumb). Wash panels with plain water early in the morning, so

time (a diagram drawn for this guide). A 20-year-old panel usually still makes 80-90% of its label (rule of thumb). Wash panels with plain water early in the morning, so cold water can't crack hot glass (p. 26). Bypass diodes let current flow around a dead module; a blocking diode stops the battery draining back through the panels at night (p. 19). 📚 Go deeper: Navy Maintenance of Photovoltaic Power Systems - testing and troubleshooting with only a voltmeter. The IEA uses × 1.3, because sun off cloud edges can reach 1,300 W/m² (IEA, p. 41). A good controller has (IEA, p. 21): - an equalize mode and a charge display; - battery temperature compensation, about -5 mV per °C per cell (IEA, p. 26); - a low-voltage load disconnect, typically off at 12.0 V and back on at 13.2 V for a 12 V battery (p. 36); - a fuse and lightning protection. Inverters: use pure sine-wave for electronics and radios (Arizona, p. 7), and size for the motor-start surge. Keep a spare controller and inverter in a Faraday can (EMP guide). 📚 Go deeper: IEA Recommended Practices for Charge Controllers - set points and features; Arizona, p. 7 - inverter types. 🔋 Choosing batteries and reading their charge Batteries wear out. For storing energy without them (a high water tank, hot water, stone and ice), see Storing Energy Without Batteries. Best to worst for solar: solar batteries; then leisure, golf-cart and traction batteries; then truck starting batteries. Avoid car batteries (IEA, p. 13). A car battery survives about 20 deep discharges. A deep-cycle battery emptied 80% each time lasts about 800 cycles; emptied 20%, about 6,000 (Practical Action Batteries, p. 5). Count on 40% of the label: a battery is worn out at 80% of new capacity, and should give at most half of that a day: 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.4 (IEA, p. 17). Series adds volts; parallel adds amp-hours (🖼 drawing). No more than 3-4 strings in parallel, all the same age and size, with equal cables (p. 18). Series adds volts, parallel adds amp-hours; the main fuse goes right at the bank's + post (a diagram drawn for this guide). How full is it? - Voltage at rest: a 12 V lead-acid battery reads 12.0 V empty to 12.9 V full (IEA, p. 26). Half-full is about 12.2 V, and 12.4 V is about three-quarters (typical flooded-battery tables). - Under load, never below about 10.8 V (p. 15). - Hydrometer (🖼 how to read one): full is about 1.280; recharge below 1.250 (Navy CE, p. 68). In cycled

- Under load, never below about 10.8 V (p. 15). - Hydrometer (🖼 how to read one): full is about 1.280; recharge below 1.250 (Navy CE, p. 68). In cycled solar batteries it reads true only after an equalizing charge (IEA, p. 26). Draw acid in with the bulb and read the float at the acid's surface: 1.150 is run down, 1.270 nearly full (NEETS 1, p. 95). Heat and cold: at 14 °F a battery gives only 60% of its capacity, and every 18 °F above 68 °F doubles plate corrosion (IEA, pp. 18-19). A discharged battery can freeze and crack; protect it below about 19 °F (IEA controllers, p. 31). Here: shade batteries from 100 °F summer heat and insulate them for January cold snaps (the record low is -6 °F) (rule of thumb). Storage: recharge stored lead-acid batteries every 3-6 months (IEA, p. 23), sealed ones every 3 (Practical Action, p. 6). 📚 Go deeper: IEA Lead-Acid Battery Guide for Stand-Alone PV - choosing, sizing and care; Practical Action Batteries - plain-language basics. 💧 Keeping lead-acid alive Watering: use distilled water, added after charging, up to the fill line. In freezing weather add water only if a charge follows, or it may freeze before it mixes (DOE-HDBK-1084, p. 44). If the plates show, top up at once; clean rainwater will do now and then (IEA, p. 25). Adding acid doesn't recharge a battery (NEETS 1, p. 97). Equalizing is a deliberate overcharge that brings every cell up and stirs the acid (IEA, p. 27; 🖼 gassing vs. voltage chart): - Flooded: hold about 2.45-2.50 V per cell (14.7-15.0 V on 12 V) for about 5 hours. - AGM: only about 2.35 V per cell (14.1 V) for about 8 hours (p. 46). Gel or AGM higher only if the maker allows (p. 21). - Remove catalytic recombiner caps first (p. 27). - With a hydrometer: charge at about 5 A until specific gravity stays steady for 4 hours, easing off if the acid reaches 110 °F (Navy CE, p. 67). - How often: monthly, or when cells drift apart (rule of thumb). Never equalize lithium. "Desulfators": plate sulfate from sitting deeply discharged "can never be recovered" (IEA, p. 23); equalizing restores cells that were only undercharged (p. 20). Treat pulse gadgets as unproven: equalize, then time the battery under a known load before trusting it (rule of thumb). Cleaning: neutralize spilled acid with

were only undercharged (p. 20). Treat pulse gadgets as unproven: equalize, then time the battery under a known load before trusting it (rule of thumb). Cleaning: neutralize spilled acid with about 1 kg baking soda in 4 L water (2 lb per gallon), then rinse (DOE-HDBK-1084, pp. 44-45). Grease the terminals (IEA, p. 25). 📚 Go deeper: DOE Primer on Lead-Acid Storage Batteries - watering, charging and care; IEA controllers, p. 46 - charge set points. 💥 Battery safety Hydrogen (DOE-HDBK-1084, pp. 22, 46): - Overcharging makes about 0.42 L of hydrogen per amp-hour in each cell - about 2.5 L for a 6-cell 12 V battery, 5 L for a 12-cell 24 V bank (arithmetic) - and 4% in air can explode. - Many explosions follow long, unregulated charging of a battery out of its vehicle: moving it vents gas, and a spark sets it off. - Vent from the highest point of the room; hydrogen collects under the ceiling (IEA, p. 24). Put conduit openings below the battery tops (Sandia, p. 51). - Check water with a flashlight, never a flame (Practical Action, p. 6). Shorts: put the main fuse right at the battery's + terminal (🖼 fuse and disconnect), and connect the battery last, after all wiring is checked (IEA, p. 28). Take off rings and watches, and tape wrench handles (rule of thumb). Acid and gases: goggles and rubber gloves; flush for 15 minutes. Overcharged batteries can also give off toxic arsine and stibine; the venting that keeps hydrogen low keeps them low too (DOE-HDBK-1084, p. 46). Where batteries go: out of living areas and not under electrical panels. A lockable polyethylene tool box holds four L-16 batteries (Sandia, p. 52). Up to about 20 six-volt batteries in a large, drafty room may not need forced venting (p. 51). 📚 Go deeper:

🔥 Lithium, LiFePO4 and salvaged packs Types (Lighting Global, pp. 3, 10; 🖼 cylindrical, prismatic and pouch cells): - LiFePO4 (LFP), 3.2 V per cell: the safest and longest-lived (1,000+ full cycles), but bulkier. - Phone, laptop, tool and e-bike cells pack more energy but are less stable. - Every pack needs a battery management system (BMS). Charging rules (Lighting Global, pp. 6-8): - Overcharge tolerance can be 50 mV or less per cell, and cells in series must be balanced. - Never charge below 32 °F (0 °C) or above about 113 °F: cold charging grows metal "dendrites" that short the cell and start fires. NFPA says 32-105 °F (NFPA, p. 1). - Draining a cell below 2.5-3 V can ruin it. Store at 20-40% charge near room temperature. - A 12.8 V LiFePO4 bank charges at about 14.2-14.6 V and needs no equalizing; follow the maker's datasheet (rule of thumb). In our winters, keep it where it stays above freezing, or use a BMS with a cold-charge cutoff (rule of thumb). Salvaged e-bike and tool packs: stop using one that smells, changes color, heats, swells, leaks or makes odd noises. Charge it with its own charger, never on a bed or couch, and not after it's full (NFPA, p. 1). Discard swollen, dented or long-dead packs; never build packs from mixed salvaged cells without a balancing BMS; in
lithium-lifepo4-and-salvaged-packs

a bed or couch, and not after it's full (NFPA, p. 1). Discard swollen, dented or long-dead packs; never build packs from mixed salvaged cells without a balancing BMS; in fire season, charge in a detached shed, on stone (rule of thumb). If one burns (FAA SAFO 09013): one cell's thermal runaway sets off the next, and the fire flares again and again. 1. Put out the flames with water or any extinguisher. 2. Soak the pack with water to cool it. Don't cover it, use ice, or pick it up. 3. Get out of a room with a burning battery bank: the gas is toxic and flammable, and a pack can reignite hours or days later (fire FAQ, pp. 2-3). 📚 Go deeper: Lighting Global Lithium-ion Batteries - types, charging and storage; Home Lithium-Ion Battery Fire Safety FAQ - fire behavior. 🔌 Wiring, fuses and grounding Voltage drop: volts lost = 2 × one-way feet × amps × (ohms per 1,000 ft) ÷ 1,000. Aim for 3-5% loss between array and battery (IEA, p. 53). Longest one-way run for a 3% drop at 10 amps (copper; halve it for 20 A, double it for 5 A), from NEETS 4, p. 20 (arithmetic): | Wire | Ohms per 1,000 ft | 12 V | 24 V | 48 V | | 10 AWG | 1.02 | 18 ft | 35 ft | 71 ft | | 8 AWG | 0.641 | 28 ft | 56 ft | 112 ft | | 6 AWG | 0.403 | 45 ft | 89 ft | 179 ft | | 4 AWG | 0.253 | 71 ft | 142 ft | 285 ft | | 2 AWG | 0.159 | 113 ft | 226 ft | 453 ft | - Example: 240 W at 12 V (20 A) over 50 ft of 10 AWG loses 2 V, about 17%. At 24 V it loses 1 V, about 4% (arithmetic). - Hot wire loses more: Sandia figures 11.2 V lost in 400 ft of 8 AWG at 36 A (p. 102). Round up a size. - Minimum: 14 AWG on a 10 A fuse, 12 AWG on a 20 A fuse (IEA, p. 33). Fuses) must be
wiring-fuses-and-grounding

36 A (p. 102). Round up a size. - Minimum: 14 AWG on a 10 A fuse, 12 AWG on a 20 A fuse (IEA, p. 33). Fuses) must be DC-rated. Car blade and glass fuses are made for 32 V or less and can't safely stop the huge current of a battery short; keep them off battery and array circuits (Sandia, p. 42). Protect the battery cable with a current-limiting DC fuse (class T or RK5) close to the battery (p. 45). Use time-delay fuses where motors start (NEETS 3, p. 94). Every wire leaving the battery's + post gets its own DC-rated fuse right at the post; connect the battery last (a diagram drawn for this guide). Grounding): bond the DC negative to ground at one point only (Sandia, p. 31; 🖼 example grounding system). Drive ground rods 8 ft deep with #6 copper (FM 5-424, p. 49), about 6 ft apart if you use several (p. 117). For lightning, use one ground electrode, bond all metal frames, and run + and - wires side by side so they don't form loops (IEA Lightning, pp. 7, 13; 🖼 bad and good module wiring). A ground rod driven 8 ft deep into moist soil, with #6 copper wire to it (FM 5-424, p. 49). 📚 Go deeper: Sandia PV Systems and the NEC - fuses, disconnects, grounding; Army FM

⛽ Generators, cars and backfeed - Never backfeed. A generator plugged into a wall outlet sends power out onto the lines and can electrocute line workers and neighbors on the same transformer (CPSC, p. 1). Use a transfer switch (🖼 diagram), or plug appliances straight into the generator. Outdoors only: carbon monoxide. - Run a generator under full load: charge batteries while it does other work (IEA, p. 46; 🖼 solar-plus-generator layout). Violent gassing means the charge rate is too high (Navy CE, p. 67). - A generator's small "12 V DC" outlet is a weak, unregulated charger; a proper multi-stage charger on its AC is better (rule of thumb). - From a car: connect + to +, - to - (Alternator and Regulator Servicing, p. 48). Disconnect a car's battery before putting a fast charger on it, or you can burn out the car's diodes (p. 47). A car alternator) rarely fills a deep-cycle bank, and idling for hours wastes fuel and makes CO (rule of thumb). A generator in a wall outlet sends power out onto the lines; a transfer switch connects the house to the grid or the generator, never both (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: CPSC Portable Generator Hazards - CO and backfeed; Alternator and Regulator Servicing - charging and testing. 🌊 Creek hydro, and why not wind While Oregon's water laws are enforced, most Illinois Valley creeks are closed to hydro by state rule (see Start Here). Measure the drop (head) (🖼 what head means): run a hose full of water downhill with a pressure gauge at the bottom; psi × 2.31 = feet of head (NCAT, p. 6). Measure the flow: time how long the creek takes to fill a container: a 55-gal drum in 40 seconds is 82.5 gallons a minute (gpm) (NCAT, p. 3). For a bigger creek: width × average depth (sq ft) × float speed (ft per second) × 0.25 for a shallow rocky bed, up to 0.75 for a smooth one, gives cubic feet per second (cfs); 1 cfs = 449 gpm (p. 4; 🖼 measuring a stream's cross-section). Power from a creek ≈ gpm × feet of head ÷ 10 watts (NCAT, pp. 8-9). A real case: 100 gpm with 35 ft of head left at the turbine (15 psi) gives about 200 W around the clock, nearly 5 kWh a day, to a 24 V bank (NRCan, p. 29). The rule predicts 350 W: small systems often fall short. Head from a hose and a pressure gauge, flow from a drum and a watch (a diagram drawn for this guide). Pipe size matters. ⚠ Old advice in the library to ignore - MPPT called "less important" and a risk to reliability (IEA, p. 21), worth only 5-10% (IEA controllers, p. 39). It is now standard and reliable, and essential for salvaged house panels on a 12 or 24 V bank. - Equalizing weekly at 2.5-2.6 V per cell (IEA, p. 20) or every 2 weeks (IEA controllers, p. 26). Modern makers say monthly, or when cells drift (rule of thumb); never past the limit on AGM or gel; never on lithium. - LEDs at 25-50 lumens per watt (Practical Action Rural Lighting, p. 3). Modern LEDs give about 80-150, so a 9-10 W LED replaces a 60 W bulb. - The 1983 appliance table of 300 W fridges and tube radios (DOE Microhydro, p. 66). Measure your own. - "Waking up" NiCd cells by fully discharging them (Practical Action Batteries, p. 4). Only for old sealed NiCd, never NiMH or lithium. (Its warning that a flat series pack can reverse-charge its weakest cell still holds.) - Car batteries for lighting (Rural Lighting, p. 5). About 20 deep cycles: a stopgap only. - Sandia's NEC section numbers (Sandia) are from the 1999 code; the principles still hold. - 1930s-70s wind and generator books (Homemade Six-Volt Wind-Electric Plants, Wind Power for Farms) predate modern charge control. Add a dump-load controller and a fused battery. -

It won't stop the chemistry, but it is the best way to cool the cells and stop the spread (FAA; Lighting Global, p. 8). 🧱 Storing Energy Without Batteries How to keep the energy from a sunny afternoon, a hot fire, a cold night or a running creek for later, when batteries are worn out or gone. It covers gravity batteries (lifting water, sand or weights) and why they hold so little; heat stored in water, stone and masonry; cold stored as ice and cold water; compressed air and flywheels; and the simplest store of all, doing the work while the power is there. The numbers come from the books on this drive. Where this guide works one out, it says (arithmetic), and you can check it with the Practical Math guide or the Calculator. The two DOE books added for this guide are in Off-Grid-Power\Energy-Storage. ### The short version - Lifting things stores almost nothing. 1,000 gallons of water raised 30 ft holds about 94 watt-hours: a light and a phone for one evening (arithmetic). The DOE's example: hoist a car 100 ft and you get back "only about 800 watts for ten minutes" (Wind Power for Farms, p. 129). - Heat stores about a thousand times more. The same 1,000 gallons warmed 50 °F holds about 122,000 watt-hours (arithmetic). Store energy as heat (water, stone, masonry) and cold (ice, cold water), not as height. - Spare electricity goes into hot water. An electric water heater stores it at close to 100%; batteries

heat (water, stone, masonry) and cold (ice, cold water), not as height. - Spare electricity goes into hot water. An electric water heater stores it at close to 100%; batteries manage 60 to 80% (Wind Power for Farms, p. 130). - Pump the water you need anyway into a high tank while the sun shines. The tank is the battery (NRCS Tech Note 1, p. 27). - Insulation decides how long any store lasts: hot, cold or ice. - Skip compressed air and homemade flywheels. Compressed air is 10 to 15% efficient, and fast wheels can burst. - A woodpile is a battery too. One pound of dry wood holds about twice what a 12-volt, 100 amp-hour battery holds (arithmetic).

💧 Gravity that works: store the water, not the electricity A tank of water up the hill doesn't store much energy, but it stores something better: water you can use with no power at all. Pump it when the sun shines, the wind blows or the creek runs, and let gravity deliver it later. - The tank is the cheapest battery for a solar pump: "The most effective and typically least expensive means of utilizing excess incoming solar energy is to incorporate a water storage tank" (NRCS Tech Note 1, p. 27). North Dakota's NRCS requires 3 days of storage on solar systems (same page). - Put it high enough. The tank must sit above every faucet. Each foot of height gives 0.43 psi (USDA FB 1448, p. 27), so a tank 40 ft up gives about 17 psi, a weak but usable house pressure (see the Practical Math guide). - Where: "an underground concrete tank on a hill is very desirable, avoiding trouble with frost"; attic, loft and trestle tanks are "unsatisfactory". Hold "more than one day's supply", a week or more for a windmill, and cover it tightly against heat, cold, dust, vermin and sunlight (FB 1448, p. 35; 🖼 underground concrete tank). - Steadier power needs less tank. "The more constant the power, the more reliable the equipment ... the less is the need of large water
gravity-that-works-store-the-water-not-the-electricity

35; 🖼 underground concrete tank). - Steadier power needs less tank. "The more constant the power, the more reliable the equipment ... the less is the need of large water storage" (FB 1448, p. 37). A ram pump that runs day and night (see the Water Wells guide) needs a smaller tank than a solar pump that only runs at midday. - Pressure tanks hold little. Only about one-fifth of a pressure tank's size is usable water, and it must be "absolutely air-tight"; never use a thin-walled tank (FB 1448, pp. 35-36). Pump while the sun shines; gravity delivers the water later, 0.43 psi for each foot the tank sits above the faucet (a diagram drawn for this guide). Pumped-storage hydro (pump water up to a pond, run it back through a turbine later) works for power companies because their lakes are huge (Wind Power for Farms, p. 127; 🖼 the hill-pond scheme). At home scale: a pond 1 acre across and 1 ft deep (326,000 gallons), 100 ft above the turbine, holds about 100 kWh before losses, perhaps 50 kWh back after pumping and turbine losses (arithmetic). That's a lot of digging and, in Oregon, a water right. Hot water does it with a tank.

⚖ Gravity batteries from sand, rocks or weights How it works: raise a heavy weight with spare power; later let it fall slowly, turning a generator. The energy is exactly weight × height: raising a 550-lb rock one foot takes 550 foot-pounds, and 550 foot-pounds a second is one horsepower (746 watts) (Wind Power for Farms, p. 27; foot-pounds × 0.0000003766 = kWh, NEETS 19, p. 87). Why it disappoints: a person cranking steadily makes about 50 watts. One hour of cranking equals lifting 1,000 gallons just 16 ft, or a ton of sand about 70 ft (arithmetic). The DOE puts it plainly: a few 55-gallon drums in the attic "would not produce much power" (p. 127). Every winch, gear and generator also loses some, so expect half back at best (rule of thumb). If you build one anyway (a night light, a teaching model): 1. A weight you can raise by hand or with a winch: a bucket of sand or a bag of rocks, 50-100 lb. 2. A rope over a drum or pulley that turns slowly as the weight falls. 3. Gearing up a lot, 100 to 1 or more (bicycle sprockets and chain, or belts and pulleys), so the slow drop spins a small permanent-magnet DC motor fast enough to make power (see "Motors as generators" in the Engines guide). 4. One LED of a watt
gravity-batteries-from-sand-rocks-or-weights

pulleys), so the slow drop spins a small permanent-magnet DC motor fast enough to make power (see "Motors as generators" in the Engines guide). 4. One LED of a watt or less, and a way to slow the fall: the load itself does that. 5. What to expect: 50 lb dropping 8 ft holds 0.15 Wh, a 1-watt LED for about 9 minutes with no losses, more like 4-5 minutes in practice (arithmetic). Keep people and animals out from under a raised weight, and check the rope every time (rule of thumb). Weights are good at slow, steady mechanical jobs, like turning a clock or a spit, not at making electricity (rule of thumb).

Getting heat into stone or water "Just piling mass near a stove will result in poor heat transfer to the mass. Only a small percentage of the heat will end up in the mass" (Aprovecho, p. 16). The fire's hot gases have to pass through the mass (a masonry heater), through water (a water jacket or tank), or warm the room air directly (p. 6). And seal the drafts first: a tight house needs far less stored heat (see "One warm room" in the Shelter guide).

Masonry heaters (big stone stoves) - How: "Masonry heaters use tonnes of mass in the form of bricks or stone"; you burn "one or two fires per day", fast and hot, and the masonry "continues to radiate warmth for many hours" (CMHC Residential Wood Heating, p. 20; 🖼 a masonry heater; Masonry heater). - How much: 1,000 lb of stone heated to about 200 °F holds 40,000 BTU, about two hours for a house losing 20,000 BTU an hour; five tons carries about ten hours (Aprovecho, p. 16). A good one holds about half a day (p. 17). - Good: stored heat keeps the house warm overnight, the radiant heat feels good, and the big hot fire burns clean (p. 7). - Bad: it heats whether you need it or not, so a warm day can overheat the room; it must weigh many tons; and it can't warm a cold house fast (p. 8). - Building one: "The mason must be experienced ... simple errors can result in the failure of the heater", and clearances to anything that burns must meet fireplace codes (CMHC, p. 39). Several tons on a floor is also an earthquake load: see the quake rules in the Natural Building guide. - Rocket mass heaters and cob benches are a homemade version. The library has no tested plans (Aprovecho only sketches a "Hot Cob" bench, p.

in the Natural Building guide. - Rocket mass heaters and cob benches are a homemade version. The library has no tested plans (Aprovecho only sketches a "Hot Cob" bench, p. 17); treat them like any stove: a working chimney and a carbon monoxide alarm (Rocket mass heater).

Stone and water that warm in the sun - Thermal mass evens out the day. Water in drums or a thick cob wall "tends to stay at the average 24 hour temperature"; a very thick wall averages several days (Aprovecho, p. 35). - Passive solar: south-facing windows let the winter sun warm masonry floors or walls, which give the heat back at night (HUD In the Bank, p. 73). A Trombe wall is a thick masonry wall behind glass on the south side; a sunspace is a glassed room with a masonry floor or water containers that you close off from the house at night (Trombe wall; Sunroom). Drums of water painted dark, in the sun, inside the glass, do the same job (rule of thumb). - Rock bins: an active solar system can blow warm air from a collector through a bin of rocks, which "carries enough heat to get through a few overcast days and nights" (HUD, same page). It needs a fan, so it needs power.

Hot water: where spare electricity should go - The best way to store surplus power: "Where batteries are 60 to 80 percent efficient, electric heaters approach 100 percent"; the only losses are a poorly insulated tank and the wiring. One kWh warms 30 gallons by about 13.5 °F (Wind Power for Farms, p. 130; 🖼 a simple electric heating system). - How: a water-heater element as the dump load on a hydro or wind controller (see the Off-Grid Power and Engines guides), or a solar panel wired straight to a DC element. The thermal mass of the water, or of concrete floors and brick walls, does the storing (same page). - Use an old electric water heater as the tank, insulated well. A tank that sits still keeps its hottest water at the top (rule of thumb). - Safety: a heated, closed tank needs a pressure-and-temperature relief valve - boiling water makes pressure, and even Aprovecho's carefully built wood-fired showers "occasionally leaked or even exploded!" (Aprovecho, p. 9). Water at 140 °F burns skin badly in about 5 seconds, at 158 °F in 1 (Ciochetti & Metcalf, p. 5).

Solar water heaters you can build Thermosiphon heater (no pump): a flat black panel of two seamed metal sheets, with an insulated tank mounted above it. Hot water rises into the tank and cool water sinks back to the panel. A panel about 3 × 6 ft heated 70 liters (74 quarts) to 140 °F by noon on a clear summer day. Raise the tank about 18 in off the ground "so that the coolest water will be in the heater", keep the water level above the tank's upper hose connection so it can circulate, insulate the tank with sawdust, straw or mud, and draw hot water from the top (VITA Village Technology Handbook, pp. 317-318; 🖼 the heater on its stand). The tank sits above the panel, raised at least 45 cm (18 in), with its water level above the upper hose (VITA, p. 317). Breadbox (batch) heater: water tanks sit right inside a glazed, insulated box in the sun. - Box: insulated to at least R-10 on the sides and bottom, one layer of glazing on top, on a stand of pressure-treated lumber set on footings (DOE Breadbox Solar Water Heaters, p. 18). - Tanks: the cheapest are old glass-lined electric water heaters with the outer jacket stripped. Don't use galvanized tanks, which rust; test a used tank for leaks with a garden hose. Tilt the tanks upright

old glass-lined electric water heaters with the outer jacket stripped. Don't use galvanized tanks, which rust; test a used tank for leaks with a garden hose. Tilt the tanks upright so the hot water collects at the top (pp. 18-19). - Weight: about 300 lb per full tank; a two-tank system weighs about 850 lb, so check a roof before putting one on it (p. 19). - Plumbing: inlet, outlet, drain lines and pressure-and-temperature relief valves (p. 28; materials list p. 32). - Freezing: "Draining the breadbox is the safest option" (p. 21). Our valley freezes most winters, so drain it from the first hard frost to spring (rule of thumb). Tilt the tank so hot water collects at its high end; fit a relief valve and a drain (a diagram drawn for this guide).

Hot stones and hay-boxes for cooking A hay-box (fireless cooker) is a heat store for the cooking pot. Measured: a 6-quart kettle of boiling water in a newspaper-packed box was still 172 °F after 4 hours and 155 °F after 8. Fill empty space with boiling water, which "will take up and hold the heat better than air would" (USDA FB 771, p. 11). For higher heat, add a hot soapstone, brick or stove lid under the pot in a metal-lined nest, kept away from anything that burns (pp. 4-6). Heavy pots of clay or iron hold heat best, and a good cooker holds cooking heat at least 8 hours (Peace Corps T-17, pp. 123-124). How to build one is in the "Hay-box cooking" section of the Make-Do Household guide. The kettle (D) sits on a hot soapstone (E) in a metal-lined nest (C), packed all round with insulation (B) (USDA FB 771, p. 9).

❄ Cold: storing winter for summer Melting ice soaks up 144 BTU per pound; that's why a block of ice is such a good "cold battery" (Fire Weather, p. 13). The springhouse, zeer pot, ice house and cellar details are in the Root Cellar guide ("Cooling without power"); here are the storage numbers. Ice: - Our valley rarely makes pond ice thick enough to cut (rule of thumb); even eastern Virginia only counts on 4-6 in (USDA FB 475, p. 5). Make it in cans on the coldest nights instead: galvanized cans 22 in square at the top; tip out the 1½-2 in shell, refill a few quarts at a time until solid (p. 10). - How it keeps depends on "the shape of the mass, its insulation, its drainage, and its solidity" (p. 6). Stack it as near a cube as you can (p. 5). - Packing: on a bed of sawdust or shavings at least 15 in deep, and at least 15-18 in from the walls (p. 13). - Drain it. A 50-lb block on slats at 80 °F lasts more than a day; sitting in its own meltwater it is gone in six or seven hours (Household Discoveries, p. 109). - How much: 1 ton of ice takes about 35 cu ft (FB 475, p. 12). A 14 × 20 ft ice house filled eight or ten

A 14 × 20 ft ice house filled eight or ten layers high lasts two or three families a year (Household Discoveries, p. 110), but a walk-in farm refrigerator burns through about 100 tons a year (FB 475, p. 17). Cool a small box, not a room. At least 15 in of sawdust under the ice, 15-18 in between the ice and the walls, and a floor that drains (a diagram drawn for this guide). Cold water and insulation: - Water holds the cold: a 10-gallon can of milk at 85 °F set in 30 gallons of 37 °F water ends at about 50 °F; with 60 gallons, about 45 °F (USDA FB 976, p. 6; 🖼 insulated cooling tank). - Cover and insulate it: an open metal tank in the sun lost more than ten times as much ice as a covered, cork-insulated wooden tank (p. 12). Night air and night sky: - A shaded draft box on the north side uses cold night air; in the Willamette Valley's 30s-at-night, 50s-by-day seasons it averages around 40 °F (Aprovecho, p. 34). - A buried box stays at 52-58 °F: cool, but not cold enough to stop bacteria (p. 36). - Night-sky trays: shallow trays of water under a clear sky lose about 20 BTU per square foot per hour, and froze below about 45 °F; they don't work on cloudy or windy nights (p. 38). - Don't build a homemade ammonia "Icy Ball" refrigerator: Aprovecho stopped theirs over "the potential for explosion" (p. 37).

🌬 Compressed air and flywheels: why not Compressed air: - Most of the energy turns into heat in the compressor: "When air is compressed, heat is generated" (Navy Construction Mechanic, p. 344). Then the air chills and freezes up the tool as it expands (p. 345). - Overall: "Typical overall efficiency is 10 to 15 percent" (DOE Compressed Air Sourcebook, p. 32), and it is "probably the most expensive form of energy" in a shop (p. 29). An 80-gallon tank gives back a few dozen watt-hours (table above). - Tanks burst. A receiver tank must be welded steel with a drain and a safety valve (Navy, p. 345). Never use a rusty, dented or homemade tank (rule of thumb). - Where air does make sense: running air tools directly from a compressor driven by a water wheel or windmill, not as storage (rule of thumb). Flywheels: - Energy rises with the square of the speed: twice as fast holds four times as much (Wind Power for Farms, p. 28). So a useful flywheel spins very fast, and modern ones need a housing that contains the wheel "should the wheel fracture or fail" (p. 132; 🖼 old and modern flywheels). - A wheel spun too fast "may fly apart." Stand to one side when it starts, and never run a cracked or unbalanced wheel (Navy Steelworker, p. 22). - Good use:

A wheel spun too fast "may fly apart." Stand to one side when it starts, and never run a cracked or unbalanced wheel (Navy Steelworker, p. 22). - Good use: smoothing out a pedal, treadle or water-wheel drive over a few seconds, not storing power for later (rule of thumb).

🗓 The best store of all: work while the power is there Most of what a battery does can be done by timing the work (rule of thumb): - Sunny midday: pump water up to the tank, run the grain mill and power tools, heat water, wash clothes, charge radios, lights and phones. - Rainy months (strongest creek): the heavy jobs move to hydro power; hot water from the dump load. - Hot fire: cook, heat water and bake in one firing; a masonry heater or hay-box holds the heat. - Cold nights: freeze ice in cans; cool the cellar with night air (see the Root Cellar guide). - Store the product, not the power: a full water tank, ground flour, dried food, split firewood and charged rechargeable batteries for small lights are all stored energy. - The woodpile is the biggest store most households have: 8,600 BTU in a pound of dry wood (Aprovecho, p. 18). See the Firewood guide.
