♨ Heat into Work and Power Can a fire do more than keep you warm? Yes: it can pump water, turn a saw, charge a phone and even make ice. This guide gives the honest numbers first, then covers stove-top thermoelectric generators, small steam engines and boiler safety, hot-air (Stirling) engines, refrigerators that run on a flame, and other ways to put heat to work. The books added for this guide are in Southern-Oregon\Off-Grid-Power\Heat-Engines (download list: local/library-files.txt). Wood gas, the best way to run a generator on wood, is in the Fuel guide and the Engines guide; storing heat in water and stone is in the Storing Energy guide. Where this guide works a number out, it says (arithmetic); check it with the Practical Math guide or the Calculator. ### The short version - Use heat as heat first. A stove gets about half of the wood's heat into the room, the pot or the water tank; the heat engines in this guide turn only 1 to 10% of it into work or electricity (Aprovecho, p. 18; table below). - For real electricity from wood, run an engine on wood gas. About 3 lb of wood per kWh at best, against 10-25 lb for a small steam plant (arithmetic, below). - A stove-top thermoelectric generator is worth having for phones, LED lights and radios while you heat or cook anyway.

against 10-25 lb for a small steam plant (arithmetic, below). - A stove-top thermoelectric generator is worth having for phones, LED lights and radios while you heat or cook anyway. Real stoves in a DOE contest made 14 to 268 watts (DOE stove report, p. 17). - Boilers explode. Never make one from a tank, a pipe, a water heater or a gas cylinder (rule of thumb). Test a boiler with water at 1½ times its working pressure, never with steam or air, and try the safety valve every morning (Maxims, p. 29, p. 121, p. 285). - If the water drops out of sight in the glass, kill the fire and never pump in water (Navy Boilerman, p. 324). - Hot-air (Stirling) engines are safe but weak: an antique one made about 50 watts (NASA Stirling Manual, p. 8). Use one to pump water slowly. - A gas or kerosene absorption refrigerator is the best heat-driven machine you can own. Keep it level: one stopped cooling when tipped just 1 to 2 degrees (NBS report, p. 33). - Every flame makes carbon monoxide (MSU Portable Kerosene Heaters, p. 3). Vent burners outdoors and keep a CO alarm with batteries (rule of thumb).

🧮 The honest numbers: what a pound of wood can do A pound of dry wood holds about 8,600 BTU of heat, and a stove gets roughly 50% of it into the house (Aprovecho Capturing Heat Three, p. 18). That is about 2.5 kWh of heat in the wood and 1.25 kWh delivered (1 kWh = 3,412 BTU) (arithmetic). How a thermoelectric generator works Heat one end of a joint between two different metals and a small voltage appears across it: the Seebeck effect (Kuphaldt Lessons in Electric Circuits vol. 1, p. 320). Many junctions in series make a thermopile: heat goes into one set and the other set is "bonded to a heat sink of some sort (air- or water-cooled)" (p. 323). A modern module (TEG, thermoelectric generator) is a flat square tile packed with such junctions. Power comes from the difference in temperature between its two faces, so a hot stove with a warm cold side makes almost nothing (rule of thumb). You can see the effect with a copper wire, an iron wire, a candle and a voltmeter (Kuphaldt vol. 6, p. 117).
how-a-thermoelectric-generator-works

What to expect in watts - Measured on real wood stoves: in a 2½-hour DOE-funded contest, five stoves fitted with thermoelectric generators peaked at 268, 139, 85, 32 and 14 watts and made 276, 235, 118, 47 and 28 watt-hours (DOE stove report, p. 17). The two that reached the market "were larger units closer to boilers" (p. 4). - What that runs: such stoves "can generate enough power to charge cell phones and light a home" in an outage (p. 2). A phone charge is roughly 10-15 Wh and an LED bulb 3-5 W (rule of thumb), so 28 Wh is two phone charges, and 276 Wh is a lit house for an evening plus every phone. - A single small module on a stove top makes a few watts; Wikipedia notes they are "put on top of a wood or coal burning stove" and "generate enough electricity to power an LED light or charge a mobile device" (Thermoelectric generator). - Stove fans (the little fans that sit on a stove and spin by themselves) run on the same modules (same article). They push warm air into the room with no wiring at all.
what-to-expect-in-watts

Choosing modules: TEG or salvaged Peltier - Modules sold as TEGs (generator modules) are built to take a hot side. Peltier modules from 12-volt camping coolers, wine coolers and computer coolers are built for cooling, but they also generate when heated on one face, usually less than a true TEG (rule of thumb). - Heat limits: most modules are bismuth telluride, which Wikipedia lists among the low-temperature materials, "up to around 450 K" (about 350 °F, 177 °C) (Thermoelectric generator). Cooling modules are often soldered for less. Never set a module straight on a stove top running at full heat; put a steel or aluminum plate between them, check it with a stove thermometer, and stay under the seller's rating, or about 250 °F (120 °C) for a salvaged Peltier you know nothing about (rule of thumb). - Testing a salvaged module: hold one face on a cup of hot water and the other in the air, and read the voltage on a meter; no voltage means a broken module (rule of thumb).
choosing-modules-teg-or-salvaged-peltier

Keeping the cold side cold The cold side is half the machine. Wikipedia: "The cold side must be cooled by air or water" (Thermoelectric generator). 1. Clamp the module firmly between the hot plate and a heat sink (a finned block from an old computer or amplifier) with a thin smear of heat-sink paste on both faces (rule of thumb). 2. Water cooling works best: a flat-bottomed pot or a closed metal box of water on top of the module. The water warms, so top it up or swap it; never let it boil dry (rule of thumb). 3. Air cooling: a big finned heat sink, ideally with a small fan run from the module's own output (rule of thumb). 4. A module whose two faces reach the same temperature makes nothing; if the output sags after an hour, the cold side has warmed up (rule of thumb).
keeping-the-cold-side-cold

Getting usable 5 V and 12 V out of it A single module gives a few volts that rise and fall with the fire, so it needs a regulator between it and anything you care about (rule of thumb): - Phones and USB lights: wire two to four modules in series (plus of one to minus of the next) and feed a small DC-DC converter with a USB socket: a buck converter steps a higher voltage down to 5 V, a boost converter steps a lower voltage up (Buck converter; Boost converter). Never plug a phone straight into a module (rule of thumb). - A 12-volt battery: use a converter set to about 14 V, or a small charge controller, plus a blocking diode so the battery can't push current back through the modules at night (rule of thumb). Charging limits and controllers are in "Charge controllers and inverters" in the Off-Grid Power guide; diodes are in "Motors as generators" in the Engines guide. - Good loads: phones, LED lights, a radio receiver (see the Radio guide), a fan. Bad loads: anything that heats (kettles, heaters, hair dryers); use the stove for heat. 📚 Go deeper: DOE Wood Stove Design Challenge report - the measured stoves and how they were tested (p. 21); Kuphaldt vol. 1, pp. 320-324 - thermocouples, thermopiles and the Peltier effect.
getting-usable-5-v-and-12-v-out-of-it

🚂 Steam: what a small engine can do What steam is good at: steady, heavy mechanical work from any fuel that burns. Farm steam engines were belted to threshing machines, and a steam engine copes with a load that changes a lot: Maggard's farm engine might "do eight horse work one day and sixteen horse work the next day" (Maggard Rough and Tumble, p. 11). What a small one needs: - Water: about 7½ gallons an hour for each horsepower (Maggard, p. 53). A 1-hp engine running an 8-hour day boils off 60 gallons unless you condense it (arithmetic). - Wood: at 2-4%, one horsepower-hour (746 watt-hours of work) takes about 7-15 lb of dry wood (arithmetic, from the table above). Someone has to cut, split and feed it. - A real boiler: a factory boiler for a ½-horsepower engine was "tested at 160 pounds cold water pressure" and rated "safe to run it at a steam pressure of 75 to 100 pounds" (Collins Boys' Book of Engine-Building, p. 267). Watson's book gives dimensioned drawings for engines and boilers "from five horse power down to model sizes" (Watson Small Engines and Boilers, p. 13), but a pressure boiler is skilled shop work in seamless or brazed tube (p. 118); a soldered tin boiler "is merely a makeshift" (p. 115). - A trained operator who stays with it the whole time
steam-what-a-small-engine-can-do

shop work in seamless or brazed tube (p. 118); a soldered tin boiler "is merely a makeshift" (p. 115). - A trained operator who stays with it the whole time it is under pressure. Hawkins: "Don't let any one talk to you when firing" (Maxims, p. 48).
steam-what-a-small-engine-can-do

Turning a pump, saw or generator - Belts carry the power from the engine's flywheel to the machine; a belt "ought to sag slightly as it hugs the pulley closer, and will last much longer" (Maggard, p. 138). - A pump or a saw suits steam best: both take steady power, and a saw can wait while the pressure comes back up (rule of thumb). - A generator: belt the flywheel up to a car alternator or a permanent-magnet DC motor and charge batteries; the speeds and wiring are in "Motors as generators" in the Engines guide. Steam engines slow down under load, so a governor or a charge controller is needed to keep the voltage steady (rule of thumb).
turning-a-pump-saw-or-generator

Condensing and reusing the water - Exhaust steam still holds most of its heat. At 212 °F each pound of exhaust steam "contains 1,146 heat units" (BTU) (Maxims, p. 202). Pass it through a feed-water heater to warm the water going into the boiler: "All the heat imparted to the feed water, before it enters the boiler, is so much saved" (p. 201). - Heat buildings with it: in most works "the exhaust steam produced will very nearly, if not quite supply sufficient exhaust steam to furnish all the heat required for" warming (p. 271). - Condensing it turns the steam back into water: the Navy's condensers "recover feed water by condensing exhaust steam" (Navy Boilerman, p. 245). Condensed steam is soft water and lays down little scale (rule of thumb). It takes a lot of cooling water: about seventy gallons an hour for each horsepower (Hawkins New Catechism, p. 361). A coil in a creek or a big tank is the homestead version (rule of thumb). - Use soft water. Hawkins wants "soft or rain water" even in a gas engine's water jacket, because hard water fills it with lime (New Catechism, p. 296); a boiler needs it more (rule of thumb). Scale on boiler plates is "a more or less perfect non-conductor of heat" (Maxims, p. 154), and the plate under it can be "heated to redness" (p.
condensing-and-reusing-the-water
(rule of thumb). Scale on boiler plates is "a more or less perfect non-conductor of heat" (Maxims, p. 154), and the plate under it can be "heated to redness" (p. 152).
condensing-and-reusing-the-water

Why boilers explode "The one great cause of boiler explosion is the inability of the boiler to withstand the pressure to which it is subjected at the time" (Hawkins Maxims, p. 284). Hawkins lists the reasons (pp. 284-285): 1. Bad design (not enough stays and braces). 2. Bad workmanship. 3. Bad material: blisters and flaws in the plate. 4. Too much pressure: a reckless operator, a wrong gauge or a stuck safety valve. 5. Overheated plates from low water. 6. Scale and mud that keep the water off the iron. The farm engineer's version: "A properly constructed boiler never explodes, except from low water or high pressure" (Maggard, p. 20). The damage comes from the hot water flashing into steam all at once when the shell lets go (Maxims, p. 284; Boiler explosion).
why-boilers-explode

What never to use as a boiler (Rule of thumb, from the failures in the books) - No propane or air tanks, fire extinguishers, pipe with caps on, kegs, milk cans or old water heaters as a steam boiler. They were never built or tested for fire on one side and steam on the other, and you can't see the corrosion inside. - No soft-soldered or tin boilers: a soldered tin boiler is good for about 10 pounds and "is merely a makeshift" (Watson, p. 115). - Even water heaters go bang: Aprovecho's "most carefully built wood fired showers ... occasionally leaked or even exploded!" (Aprovecho, p. 9). Any closed tank over a fire needs a working relief valve (see "Hot water" in the Storing Energy guide). - Never repair pressure parts yourself: no welding, brazing, patching or plugging of a cracked, bulged, thinned or leaking shell, tube or firebox. Retire it from pressure use.
what-never-to-use-as-a-boiler

The safety valve - Try it every morning before lighting the fire, by lifting the lever or rod by hand (Maxims, p. 29). A valve that sticks can stick "even though tried every day", if it is only lifted and dropped back (p. 198). - Nothing between the valve and the boiler: any shut-off valve there "should be taken out at once" (p. 131). - Never add weight, wedge it or screw it down to hold more steam. Maggard warns that a weak gauge tempts you to screw the valve down, when you may already have 110 pounds or more on a boiler set for 100 (Maggard, p. 79). - Test the gauge against a known-good gauge before you set the safety valve by it (same page). - If the pressure is already far too high, don't suddenly lift the valve wide open: the rush can hit the shell like a water hammer (Maxims, p. 198). Pull or smother the fire and let it cool (rule of thumb). - How a lever safety valve is built: 🖼 sectional view; Safety valve.
the-safety-valve

Water level: the gauge glass and the try-cocks - Keep the water in the glass, at the same height all day (Maxims, p. 48). Above the top of the glass, water carried into a hard-working engine can "knock out a cylinder head"; below the lower gauge "you may get your own head knocked off" (Maggard, p. 19). - Don't trust the glass alone. Open the try-cocks (gauge cocks): the lower one should give water and the upper one steam. Use them every day or they lime up and become useless (Maggard, p. 20). - An empty glass looks like a full one. "The glass looks much the same when empty as it does when full" (Navy Boilerman, p. 323). Blow the glass through to be sure (p. 324; 🖼 water gage column). - Blow down (open the blow-off cock to flush out mud) once or twice a day, more with dirty water, and close it again "when the water in the boiler has sunk to one and a half inches" (Maxims, p. 48): watch the glass the whole time (rule of thumb). - Check the water before lighting up each morning: "very many boilers have been ruined by neglecting this first simple precaution" (p. 29).
water-level-the-gauge-glass-and-the-try-cocks

The fusible plug A brass plug filled with soft metal sits in the crown sheet over the fire. If the water drops below it, the metal melts and steam blows into the fire to put it out (Maggard, p. 81; 🖼 fusible plugs; Fusible plug). Some states required one by law (Maxims, p. 175); Maggard thought it made operators careless (p. 81). Keep the plug, but never count on it: it is a last warning, not a water gauge (rule of thumb).
the-fusible-plug

If the water is low The Navy's rule, for when the water goes below the bottom of the glass or you don't know whether it is high or low (Boilerman, p. 324): 1. Stop the fire. On a wood fire, smother it with dirt or ashes (Maggard, p. 162); never throw water into the firebox, which can crack the sheets (same page). 2. Shut the feed. "You must never feed water to a boiler in an attempt to restore the water level after a low-water casualty!" (Boilerman, p. 324). Hawkins agrees: "Don't pump cold water into a hot boiler" (Maxims, p. 48). 3. Shut off the steam to the engine and get people away from the boiler (rule of thumb). 4. Let it cool slowly, then look inside for bulged or scorched plates before you use it again (rule of thumb).
if-the-water-is-low

Testing with water, never with steam or air - "Testing new boilers under steam pressure is both dangerous and unwise"; a water test does the same job safely (Maxims, p. 285). Water barely compresses, so a leak just drips; air or steam stores energy and a failure flies apart (rule of thumb). - Test pressure: 150 pounds of water pressure for every 100 pounds of working pressure (1½ times) (p. 121). - How: fill the boiler "with water to safety-valve" (Maxims, p. 134), pump it up with a hand force pump, and look for leaks, weeping seams and bulges (Maggard, p. 87; Collins, p. 123). - Even water tests hurt people: a blown rivet in one test scalded five men (Maxims, p. 285). Stand to the side.
testing-with-water-never-with-steam-or-air

Low-pressure and no-pressure choices - Don't need shaft power? Don't make steam. Hot water and space heat need no pressure at all; an open, vented tank can't build pressure (rule of thumb). - A hot-air engine uses the fire's heat directly with no boiler, and is "by all odds the safest to use" (Collins, p. 215). See the next section. - A thermoelectric module has no moving parts and no pressure (above). - Model engines: a copper boiler 4 inches across and 12 inches long will run an engine with a 1-inch cylinder "all day long at 1,000 revolutions per minute" at 50 pounds (Watson, pp. 115-117); even a model needs a safety valve, a water gauge and a water test (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Hawkins Maxims and Instructions for the Boiler Room - firing, the morning checks, explosions (pp. 284-285); Maggard Rough and Tumble Engineering - running a farm engine and boiler, with questions and answers (pp. 140-162); Navy Boilerman 3 & 2 - water-level emergencies, gauge glasses and safety valves.
low-pressure-and-no-pressure-choices

How they work A hot-air engine (today called a Stirling engine) keeps the same air shut inside. One end is heated by a fire and the other is kept cool. A loose piston called the displacer (or transfer piston) shuffles the air between the hot end, where it expands and pushes the power piston, and the cold end, where it shrinks again; a heavy flywheel carries it round (Collins, pp. 215-216; 🖼 how it works; Stirling engine). Better engines add a regenerator, a mesh or plates between the hot and cold ends that soaks up heat from the air going one way and gives it back on the way back (Hawkins New Catechism, p. 324). Why bother: they can "use any source of heat", run quietly and last a long time (NASA Stirling Manual, p. 7); there is no boiler to burst. Why they lost out: the old air engines had "high reliability and safety, but low specific power" (same page): big and heavy for the work they do.
how-they-work

What they really deliver - Antique hot-air engines: about 50 watts for an old machine; a modern air engine of the same kind made 850 W (NASA, p. 8). - The best small factory engines: a Philips air engine in a generator set built for 200 watts (p. 55) made at most about 0.48 kW, at 7.75 to 10% efficiency (p. 57). Factory Stirling generators of the early 1980s made 25 to 70 watts, and one cost $5,000 (p. 405). - Homemade engines from cans and pipe fittings are teaching models: they spin themselves and little more (rule of thumb). Getting the fire's heat into the hot end and out of the cold end is the hard part, and the books' factory numbers came from engineers with test rigs.
what-they-really-deliver

Best uses: pumping water and slow work - "The old hot air engines were used almost entirely for pumping water" (NASA, p. 406). A modern fluid-piston engine pumped water 10 feet high at 7% efficiency on propane (same page). - The pumped water cools the engine. In the Ericsson hot-air pumping engine "all the water passes" through a jacket around the cool end on its way from the well to the tank, while the bottom sits in the fire (New Catechism, p. 319; 🖼 the pumping engine; 🖼 in section). Heat the bottom "a very few minutes", then start it with a turn or two of the flywheel by hand (p. 321). - Other slow jobs: turning a grindstone, a churn or a fan, where a few dozen watts all day is enough (rule of thumb). For electricity, a thermoelectric module is simpler for the same few watts.
best-uses-pumping-water-and-slow-work

A simple build from pipe fittings Collins's model hot-air engine is made from plumbing parts (Boys' Book of Engine-Building, pp. 215-226; 🖼 cross-section; 🖼 the finished engine): 1. Hot cylinder: a 4-inch length of iron pipe a little over 2 inches across, a threaded cap on each end, the top cap drilled for the displacer rod (p. 216). (The old scan blurs the fractions; check the drawing.) 2. Displacer: a smaller capped pipe with a hardwood plug, deliberately loose so air can pass around it, on a rod through the top cap (pp. 217-218). 3. Power cylinder: "half as large as the expansion cylinder", with a piston of the same metal that fits "pretty accurately, as it is not packed" (pp. 219-220). 4. Connecting pipe from the top of the hot cylinder to the power cylinder, and a crankshaft with two cranks, one for each piston (pp. 221-223). 5. A heavy 5- or 6-inch flywheel and a firebox with air holes at top and bottom (pp. 224-226). 6. To run it: a flame centered under the bottom of the hot cylinder, then "Give the flywheel a couple of turns" (p. 226). The same layout scaled up, with a water-cooled top and a regenerator, is the old pumping engine (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Hawkins New Catechism, pp. 319-324 - the Ericsson and Rider pumping engines, with sectional drawings; NASA
a-simple-build-from-pipe-fittings

and a regenerator, is the old pumping engine (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Hawkins New Catechism, pp. 319-324 - the Ericsson and Rider pumping engines, with sectional drawings; NASA Stirling Engine Design Manual - the engineering, for anyone designing a serious engine.
a-simple-build-from-pipe-fittings

How a flame makes cold Gas and kerosene refrigerators use the absorption system: a small flame drives ammonia out of water under pressure until it condenses to a liquid, and the liquid boils off again in the cold box, soaking up heat. There are no moving parts; "The Servel is used in RV's now. Modern kerosene and propane refrigerators use this system" (Aprovecho, p. 37; Absorption refrigerator). The sealed system is under real pressure: the tested unit held 1.52 lb of ammonia and was pressure-tested to 717 psi (NBS report, p. 9). Never drill, cut, bend or heat its tubing (rule of thumb).
how-a-flame-makes-cold

Keeping an absorption refrigerator running From the National Bureau of Standards tests, for the Army, of a propane-fired household-type absorption refrigerator: - Level it carefully. It failed when tipped just 1 degree forward or to the left, and 2 degrees backward or to the right (NBS report, p. 33). One degree is under ½ inch across a 2-foot-wide fridge (arithmetic); use a spirit level on the freezer floor, and re-level after moving it (rule of thumb). - Keep it out of the heat. It worked at about 103 °F, slipped at 110 °F, and failed at 118 °F (p. 23). Once it failed it did not recover until the room was cooled well below that (p. 24). Its limit was about 105 °F (p. 33). In summer give it the coolest, shadiest spot and free air around the back (rule of thumb); the testers set it about 6 inches from the wall (p. 15; 🖼 the back, with condenser and heater box). - Right gas pressure: it ran best at 11 inches of water column, the maker's figure (p. 23, p. 33). That needs a proper low-pressure propane regulator, never a hose straight from the tank (rule of thumb). - Reset the thermostat with the seasons: no single setting was right for both a 70 °F and a 90 °F room (p. 33). - Choosing one: a freezer compartment "will
keeping-an-absorption-refrigerator-running

Reset the thermostat with the seasons: no single setting was right for both a 70 °F and a 90 °F room (p. 33). - Choosing one: a freezer compartment "will use much more fuel"; top-opening boxes are more efficient; units that run on both gas and electricity are "of especial value" (WHO field manual, pp. 271-272).
keeping-an-absorption-refrigerator-running

Fuel: how long a tank lasts The tested fridge was rated for 1,300-1,600 BTU an hour (NBS report, p. 9). With the burner on all day that is 31,000-38,000 BTU, or about ⅓ to ⅖ of a gallon of propane a day at 91,000 BTU a gallon (Univ. of Minnesota EB 436, p. 16) (arithmetic). The thermostat turns the flame down much of the time, so real use is less. A kerosene model burning the same heat would use about ¼ gallon a day (kerosene: 135,000 BTU a gallon, same page) (arithmetic).
fuel-how-long-a-tank-lasts

Burner care and carbon monoxide (Rule of thumb unless cited) - Clean flame: a steady blue gas flame, or a kerosene flame with no smoke. Soot in the flue or a yellow, smoky flame means a dirty burner, a wrong wick height or a blocked flue: fix it before you use the fridge again. - Clean the flue (the tube above the burner, with a baffle hanging inside) with a long brush, and keep spiders and wasps out of the burner's air holes. - Kerosene models: only clean 1-K kerosene, never gasoline (CPSC Kerosene Heater Safety, p. 1). Trim and clean the wick like a lamp wick (see "Kerosene lamps while the kerosene lasts" in the Lighting guide), and don't let the tank run dry. - Carbon monoxide: "Any heating system that burns fuel, and does not have a chimney, will give off some gases into the room" (MSU Portable Kerosene Heaters, p. 3). Vent the fridge's flue outdoors as RV fridges are, and keep a CO alarm in the room.
burner-care-and-carbon-monoxide

Solar and fire-driven ice makers - How they work: a heated vessel drives ammonia over to a condenser by day; at night one valve is turned and the liquid boils off in coils in an insulated box, making ice. The DOE-funded ISAAC ice maker had a solar collector, two pressure vessels, a condenser and piping, with "no moving parts or electrical components" (ISAAC report, pp. 3-4). On cloudy days a "burner coil, fueled by kerosene, propane or biomass" heats it instead (p. 5). - Hard to build well: the first two prototypes fell short, and the third worked well but "reliability was marginal and it was too expensive" (same page). - The Icy Ball was a 1930s fire-charged version; more than 100,000 were sold (Aprovecho, p. 37; Icyball). Aprovecho rebuilt one from small propane cylinders, then stopped because of "the potential for explosion" when its soldered safety plug proved unreliable (same page). Don't build one: use an absorption fridge you can buy or salvage, or store winter ice (see "Cold: storing winter for summer" in the Storing Energy guide).
solar-and-fire-driven-ice-makers

What a 12-volt "thermoelectric cooler" can do The plug-in camping coolers use Peltier modules run backwards. They cool only about 20 °C (36 °F) below the room and are much less efficient than a compressor fridge (Thermoelectric heat pump). Fine for a drive, poor for living off a battery (rule of thumb). Their modules are worth saving for stove-top power (above).
what-a-12-volt-thermoelectric-cooler-can-do

🔧 Other ways to put heat to work - Engine waste heat: only about 25% of an engine's fuel turns into work; "What happens to the remaining 75 percent of the heat? It is largely absorbed by the engine parts or passes out with the exhaust gases." An ordinary six-cylinder engine "generates sufficient heat to warm a six-room house in freezing weather" (Navy Construction Mechanic, p. 133). When a liquid-cooled engine runs (a tractor, a truck, a wood-gas generator), its hot coolant can warm a tank of wash water through a coil; never bring the exhaust indoors (rule of thumb). - Exhaust steam for heating and hot water (above, "Condensing and reusing the water"). - Stove fans that run on a thermoelectric module (above). - Hot water by thermosiphon with no pump, and heat stored in water and stone: see the Storing Energy guide. - Charcoal and wood gas for engines: see the Fuel guide.
other-ways-to-put-heat-to-work

🧯 Safety: burns, steam, carbon monoxide and fire - Scalds: water at 140 °F (60 °C) takes about 5 seconds to cause a severe burn, at 158 °F (70 °C) about 1 second (Ciochetti & Metcalf, p. 5). Steam and boiler water are far hotter. - Steam leaks: a hissing joint on a boiler means shut down and let it cool; never tighten a fitting under pressure (rule of thumb). A blown rivet during one water test "struck a man in the face, and ... parboiled him from head to foot" (Maxims, p. 285). - Carbon monoxide from every burner, firebox and engine: "you cannot see or smell CO", and a generator in a closed space can make dangerous levels "within minutes" (CPSC Portable Generator Hazards, p. 1). It takes 10 to 24 hours to clear it from the blood (MSU Portable Kerosene Heaters, p. 3; Carbon monoxide poisoning). - Boiler explosions: stay out of line with the ends and the firebox door of a boiler under pressure, and keep children and visitors away entirely (rule of thumb). - Fire: an unshielded single-wall stovepipe needs 18 inches of clearance to anything that burns (CMHC, p. 15). Boilers, engines and fridge burners are hot too: kerosene heater surfaces run 320 °F to more than 500 °F (MSU, p. 3). - Gasoline burners under a boiler: Watson calls gasoline "treacherous stuff" (Watson,
safety-burns-steam-carbon-monoxide-and-fire

burners are hot too: kerosene heater surfaces run 320 °F to more than 500 °F (MSU, p. 3). - Gasoline burners under a boiler: Watson calls gasoline "treacherous stuff" (Watson, p. 115); use wood, charcoal or a proper kerosene or alcohol burner (rule of thumb). - Ammonia from a cracked refrigerator: it smells strongly and burns the eyes and lungs; get out, air the room, and take the unit outside (rule of thumb).
safety-burns-steam-carbon-monoxide-and-fire

🕯 Light Without the Grid: Candles, Lamps & Lamp Oil How to make your own light when the power is off for good and the kerosene runs out: tallow and beeswax candles, wicks, rushlights, which oils and fats burn in a lamp, lamps made from a jar or a can, kerosene lamps while the kerosene lasts, more light from a small flame, and staying safe from fire, fumes and poisoning. It goes deeper than "Fire and light without stores" in the Make-Do Household guide. The books are in Homestead-Skills\Soap-Candles (Practical Action's Candlemaking, Gilbert White's rushlight letter), Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do (Household Discoveries, Shifts and Expedients, Seton, Rural Lighting) and Nuclear-Radiation\Shelter-and-Protection (Kearny's tested jar lamps). Household Discoveries ("HD" below) is cited by the PDF's page number; the number printed on the page is 10 higher. ### The short version - Cooking oil or fat in a jar is the safest light you can make. A cotton wick slightly less than ⅛ in thick, the flame just above the oil, burns about 1 oz of fat in 8 hours (Kearny, p. 104). Never kerosene, diesel or gasoline in an open lamp (ORNL-4941, p. 309). - Never water on burning wax, fat or oil: heat off, then a metal lid, damp cloth, wool rug, sand or earth. Melt wax in a pot standing in water, never dry over a flame; above about 150 °C (300 °F)

then a metal lid, damp cloth, wool rug, sand or earth. Melt wax in a pot standing in water, never dry over a flame; above about 150 °C (300 °F) it can catch fire by itself (Practical Action, p. 3). - Dip candles at about 70 °C (158 °F): 3-4 seconds in, 1-4 minutes to cool. A wick too thick drips; too thin drowns (Practical Action, pp. 2-5). - Rushlights stretch fat furthest: about 6 lb of grease dips 1 lb of rushes (over 1,600 lights), and 1½ lb of rushes lit a working family for a year (White, pp. 206-207). - Kerosene kills small children. Dark, marked, closed cans out of reach, never a drink bottle; if swallowed, don't make them vomit (Where There Is No Doctor, p. 29). - Every flame makes carbon monoxide and soot. Let air through; put lamps out before sleep (FM 21-76, p. 182). No flame in a damaged house until you know there is no gas leak (FEMA, p. 183). - Hang lamps from an overhead wire, clear of walls, curtains and beds (rule of thumb).

🧭 Which light for which job Flames "produce more heat than light" (Rural Lighting, p. 2); a candle gives about 1 lumen (table in the Make-Do guide). Use LEDs first, while batteries and panels last (Off-Grid Power guide): a modern 1-watt LED matches 80 or more candles (arithmetic). Then kerosene for close work while it lasts, fat jar lamps for all-night light, candles to carry and read by, rushlights for everyday (rule of thumb), and daylight: White's working families burned no candles in summer "because they rise and go to bed by daylight" (White, p. 207). Per pound of fat, a tiny jar lamp runs about 128 hours and White's rushlights about 130 hours (1,600 rushes at half an hour each from 6 lb of grease) (arithmetic); a small store candle in a drafty room lasted "not much more than two hours" (White, p. 207).

🐖 Fat and wax: where it comes from and how much Lard: 9-13% of a meat-type hog's live weight, 14-18% of a fat hog's; one meat-type hog "produces as much pork and lard as a family of two consumes in a year" (USDA FB 2138, p. 6). A 250-lb meat-type hog gives about 22-32 lb (arithmetic). Lard is soft: burn it in lamps, or harden it. Tallow (beef, mutton, deer, elk): "the hard fat and tallow of any animal that may be killed should be preserved" for candles, if it can be spared from greasing axles (Shifts, p. 93). Deer and elk fat is "highly saturated" (it sets hard) and usually trimmed off the meat (NDSU, p. 5): save it. The library has no figure for tallow per steer or sheep. Render it first (chill, render within a week, slow heat, no copper, strain into jars): "Salt, sweeteners and fat" in the Food From Scratch guide. Beeswax (rendering: "Beeswax: rendering and uses" in the Bees guide): bees eat about 8 kg of honey to make 1 kg of wax (FAO, p. 106). Frame hives give about 75 parts honey to 1 of wax, top-bar hives about 10 to 1 (p. 107). Unmanaged colonies seldom give over 25-30 lb of surplus honey, well-managed ones over 100 lb (USDA AH 335, p. 70). Estimate (arithmetic): a top-bar hive giving 30-100 lb of

Estimate (arithmetic): a top-bar hive giving 30-100 lb of honey yields about 3-10 lb of wax a year; a frame hive giving 100 lb, only about 1⅓ lb. Bayberry wax: boil the autumn berries in water and skim off the wax that floats; it sets into "a cloudy green mass" for candles, "either pure or mixed with some common tallow" (Saunders, p. 276). Those are eastern shrubs; our coast's Pacific wax myrtle (Myrica californica) isn't in the library, so try a small batch the same way (rule of thumb). A year's needs (arithmetic): one jar lamp 4 hours a night burns about 11 lb of fat a year; White's family's rushes took about 9 lb of grease.

🧈 Cleaning and hardening tallow Candle tallow "must be clear-grained fat" (HD p. 97). Simple cleaning (HD p. 179): render beef suet, mutton tallow or pork scraps, strain through coarse linen, and boil the fat in water with a little salt or alum. Cool it, lift off the cake of clean fat, scrape off the soft, dirty underside (p. 97), and dry the cake well, "or it will not keep sweet". Salty bacon-pot skimmings: set them "in a warm oven" so the salt sinks (White, p. 206). Stronger cleaning (HD p. 97): boil 2-3 hours in weak potash or soda lye (wood-ash lye: "Soap from fat and ashes" in the Make-Do guide), skimming; next day scrape the soft part off the cake; repeat two or three days, the last day in water with 1 lb alum and 1 lb saltpeter per 30 lb of tallow. Lye burns: gloves, goggles. Hardening. Even 3 parts mutton to 1 part beef tallow is "likely to be soft and often turn yellow, especially in summer time" (HD p. 97). So: - Stir 1 lb of alum, dissolved in hot water, into each 5 lb of tallow as it melts (p. 97); or melt 1¼ lb mutton tallow, 8 oz beeswax and 4 oz alum together, "as hard and durable as wax" (p. 97; leave out the camphor the book adds, see the old-advice table).

Pots and heat (Practical Action, pp. 3-4): aluminium or stainless steel; iron except for beeswax; no copper or brass; a jam or sugar thermometer; a double boiler whose water must not "boil away". Use an open fire only when nothing else will do; lid within reach. Melt wax in a pot standing in hot water, never dry over a flame (Practical Action, p. 3).

🧵 Wicks: making, pickling and sizing Cotton only: braided cotton strands, "not cotton thread", and no lead-core wicks (Practical Action, p. 2). Cotton string or cloth strips work, but "Nylon cannot be used" (FAO, p. 130). Use "as many strands ... as the size of the candle requires" (HD p. 97); unravelled cotton yarn and old cotton knits are the usual source (rule of thumb). - Twisted: strands twice the length you need, twisted slightly and doubled so the halves twist together (Shifts, p. 93). Braided: three even bundles, braided firmly (rule of thumb). - Self-trimming: braid in one strand a little shorter than the rest, pulled tight, so the wick bends out and burns off its own tip (HD p. 97), curling "into the hottest (outer) part of the flame" (Practical Action, p. 2). Pickling (soaking) wicks makes them burn cleaner (HD p. 97). The safe recipes from that page: - Lime and saltpeter: ½ lb lime and 2 oz saltpeter in 1 gallon of water. Soak 15-20 minutes, then hang in the sun until thoroughly dry. Lime burns skin: wear gloves. - Turpentine: soak, dry thoroughly (outdoors, away from flame (rule of thumb)), and use a wick "smaller than ordinary". - Or skip it: plain cotton primed in hot wax (Dipping, step 3) works (rule of thumb). Don't use the book's third recipe: chloride of lime (bleach) with

Don't use the book's third recipe: chloride of lime (bleach) with an ammonia salt gives off poison gas (Make-Do guide). Matching the wick to the candle (Practical Action, p. 2): "the larger diameter the candle, the thicker the wick". Too thick: the flame melts wax too fast and it drips. Too thin: it will "'drown' in its own wax pool". Beeswax needs a thicker wick than tallow. "Some trial and error testing is usually necessary": burn a test candle an hour out of drafts. You want a steady flame, the tip curling and glowing, and a pool that nearly reaches the rim without spilling. Spills: fewer strands. Shrinking flame: more. Write down what works (rule of thumb). Burn a test candle: fewer strands if it drips, more if the flame drowns (a diagram drawn for this guide).

🫕 Dipping candles step by step You need: a pot of wax or tallow deeper than the candles are long, standing in a pot of hot water; a thermometer; a rod; cotton wicks; a smooth board; a cool place to hang them. 1. Hang the wicks. Cut each twice the candle length plus a few inches and hang it over the rod to make a pair (Practical Action, p. 6), half a dozen to a rod (Shifts, p. 93), "a little more than twice the thickness of a candle" apart (HD p. 98). 2. Heat to about 70 °C (158 °F), "a good starting point" (Practical Action, p. 4), "over a slow fire, but do not let it burn" (HD p. 98). 3. Prime. First dip only: leave the wicks in about 2 minutes to drive out air and moisture. Draw each through your fingers to strip lumps, pull straight, and let harden (Practical Action, p. 4; HD p. 98). 4. Dip for 3-4 seconds and lift out smoothly (Practical Action, p. 5). Touch the bottoms gently on a smooth board to take off the drip (HD p. 98). 5. Cool 1-4 minutes, depending on the room (Practical Action, p. 5), in cool moving air if you can (HD p. 98). 6. Repeat until thick enough. With several rods, dip "in rotation" so each cools in turn (Shifts, p. 93).

5), in cool moving air if you can (HD p. 98). 6. Repeat until thick enough. With several rods, dip "in rotation" so each cools in turn (Shifts, p. 93). 7. Watch the wax. Too hot "will melt off more wax from the candles than it adds"; too cool, "a fine skin will form" and they go lumpy (Practical Action, p. 5). 8. 🫙 Moulds, pouring and rolled beeswax candles Tin moulds came "in frames of 6 or 13 tubes" (HD p. 96). Candles are moulded upside down: the tip forms at the bottom, where a small hole takes the wick. 1. Prime the wick (Practical Action, p. 7). Loop one end over a stick across the top; thread the other down through the hole with a large darning needle (HD p. 98). 2. Knot it under the hole (HD p. 98), or seal the hole with clay and tie the top to a pencil so the wick is tight and centred (Practical Action, p. 7). 3. Pour at about 90 °C (194 °F) into the centre, and tap the mould to free air bubbles (p. 7). 4. Fill the hollow that forms round the wick as it cools, but "Do not fill beyond the original wax level" (p. 8). 5. When quite cold, pull them out by the wick loops (HD p. 98). If one sticks, cool the mould in cold water (p. 8). Thread and tie the wick, seal the hole, pour, fill the hollow, then pull the candle out (Practical Action, p. 8). Pipe mould: Shifts used an 8-10 in piece of gun barrel; any straight, smooth metal pipe works. A stick through the wick loop across the top, the wick centred through a cork disc at the bottom, the

piece of gun barrel; any straight, smooth metal pipe works. A stick through the wick loop across the top, the wick centred through a cork disc at the bottom, the end stopped; pour, and when cool "warm the mould slightly and the candle will draw out" (Shifts, p. 93). Split-tube mould: bamboo or a plant stem split lengthwise and tied shut, the wick centred by "small sticks"; open it when the wax is solid (FAO, p. 130). Beeswax is "soft and sticky ... difficult to mould in rigid moulds" (Practical Action, p. 2). Instead: - Pour: ladle wax at about 70 °C down each hanging wick, turning it slowly; drips fall back into the pot (Practical Action, p. 6). Roll it tight round a primed wick. Beeswax is pliable at 35-40 °C (95-104 °F) and brittle below 18 °C (64 °F) (FAO, p. 108): roll it warm, by the stove in winter (rule of thumb). - Containers: tins and pottery are ideal, glass may crack, and "beeswax is perfect" (Practical Action, p. 9). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Candlemaking, pp. 4-9 - dipping, pouring, moulding and container candles,

🛠 Why candles drip, smoke or drown The flame melts a pool of wax, the wick soaks it up, and the heat turns it to vapour; a well-made candle burns down evenly "and dripping will not occur" (Practical Action, p. 1). | Trouble | Likely cause | Fix | | Drips, runs down one side | Wick too thick (Practical Action, p. 2); a draft; soft fat | Thinner wick; screen it, since candles "waste rapidly unless screened from the wind" (Shifts, p. 94); harden the tallow | | Drips and sputters | Warm, soft candle | Chill on ice 2-3 hours (wick off the ice); rub a pinch of salt into the wick (HD p. 99) | | Flame shrinks and drowns | Wick too thin | More strands; pour off the pool and relight (rule of thumb) | | Smoke and soot | Long, charred wick; dirty fat | Trim the wick; clean the tallow; beeswax candles "do not smoke as most other candles do" (FAO, p. 130) | | Wick smoulders when put out | Blown out downward | Hold it above your mouth and blow upward (HD p. 99) | | Hard to light | Match held to the top | Light the side of the wick (HD p. 99) | | Holes or a sunken top | Air bubbles, shrinking | Tap the mould; fill

Tallow softens and yellows in summer (HD p. 97): keep candles cool and dark, in the root cellar through our hot, dry summers (rule of thumb); bleach yellowed ones in "dew, air, and sunshine" (HD p. 99). Keep tallow, candles and fat in lidded tins: mice eat them and grease draws bears (rule of thumb). Keep wicks and matches dry in a closed jar (Kearny, p. 104).

🌾 Rushlights: Gilbert White's measured method A rushlight is the white pith of a rush, held up by one strip of its skin, dipped in fat and burned like a thin candle (Rushlight). Gilbert White weighed, counted and timed them in Letter 26 of The Natural History of Selborne (1775). He used "the common soft rush", found "in most moist pastures, by the sides of streams, and under hedges", best "in the height of summer", and "the largest and longest are best" (White, p. 205). Soft rush (Juncus effusus) grows in wet pastures and ditches around the valley (rule of thumb). Making them (White, p. 206): 1. Cut the longest rushes and put them in water at once, "for otherwise they will dry and shrink, and the peel will not run". 2. Peel off the green skin, leaving "one regular, narrow, even rib from top to bottom" to hold up the pith. 3. Bleach and dry: lay them on the grass to "take the dew for some nights", then dry them in the sun. 4. Dip them in "scalding" fat (a knack learned by practice): bacon-pot skimmings, salt settled out in a warm oven. "A little wax" makes them cleaner and burn longer; "mutton-suet would have the same effect". White's numbers: "about six pounds of grease will dip a pound of rushes" (p. 206). A pound of dry rushes held

and burn longer; "mutton-suet would have the same effect". White's numbers: "about six pounds of grease will dip a pound of rushes" (p. 206). A pound of dry rushes held "upwards of one thousand six hundred" (p. 207). A rush 2 ft 4½ in long burned "three minutes short of an hour", a longer one an hour and a quarter (p. 206), with "a good clear light" (p. 207). "One pound and a-half of rushes completely supplies his family the year round", since working people went to bed by daylight in summer (p. 207). (Arithmetic:) that is about 2,400 rushlights and 9 lb of grease a year; at White's cautious half hour each, 1,200 hours, over 3 hours a night on average. Burning them (rule of thumb): hold the rush slanting in a clip or split stick on a heavy base, over a tin or a dish of sand to catch drips; move it up as it burns; never leave one alight in an empty room. Leave two ribs of skin on and it burns slower and dimmer, like the old "watch-lights" (White, p. 207): a night light. Leave one rib of skin to hold up the pith, and burn the rush slanting over sand (a diagram drawn for this guide).

🫒 Lamp oils: what burns and what doesn't Good: kitchen fats, "lard, bacon grease, vegetable shortening, or vegetable oil" (ORNL-4941, p. 44), and non-drying oils like olive oil, which "become rancid and thicken ... but do not dry up" (HD p. 366). HD names lard oil, neat's-foot oil (boiled from cattle feet), olive, colza and rape-seed oil together (p. 367). Animal and fish oils are "very similar to the nondrying vegetable oils", though fish oil can smell "very offensive" (pp. 366-367); Northwest peoples burned the eulachon, or candlefish, for light (Shifts, p. 94). Hard fats like tallow need a soft-fat lamp whose flame warms the dish (below). Not good: drying oils like linseed (flax) "oxidize ... into a hard, resinous varnish" (HD p. 366): expect a gummed, crusted wick. The book doesn't test this in a lamp; it follows from the varnish (rule of thumb). The catch with vegetable oil: it is safe, "but their disadvantage is that they do not rise in the wick-carrier" (WHO, p. 106). So keep the wick short, the flame just above the oil (ORNL-4941, p. 309), or float it. As the oil drops, top it up or lower the wick holder (rule of thumb). Clarifying and storing: let oil settle a few days and pour off the top; to dry it, boil gently, stand, filter through cloth and heat briefly to 100 °C (212 °F) (Oil Extraction, pp. 5-6). Wet oil sputters (rule of thumb). For rancid or smelly animal oil, filter it through a burlap bag lined with flannel with charcoal quilted between, or stir clean charcoal lumps into it over a slow fire and strain (HD p. 367). Store it "in lightproof, airtight and moisture-proof containers in a cool place", never copper (Oil Extraction, p. 6), and don't leave lamps filled for months (Kearny, p. 104). Burn the old oil, eat the fresh (rule of thumb). Pressing oil: rape seed is 40-45% oil, mustard 25-45%, sunflower and sesame 25-50%, safflower 30% (Oil Extraction, p. 1). Dry and clean the seed, throw out mouldy ones, dehull sunflower (p. 1); soft seeds and nuts can be hand-pressed, hard ones need a ram press (p. 2). A cage press (a perforated metal cage under a plunger) can be driven by a screw or a car jack: raise the pressure slowly, and beware a leaking hydraulic jack's "poisonous hydraulic fluid" (p. 3). Nut meats: boil, add salt, skim (p. 2). Every pint burned is a pint not eaten: press for food first (rule of thumb).

Never gasoline or mixed fuels in an open lamp - The jar lamps are safe only with kitchen fats: "DO NOT USE KEROSENE, DIESEL FUEL, OR GASOLINE - USE ONLY FATS OR OILS OF THE KINDS FOUND IN THE KITCHEN" (ORNL-4941, p. 309). Knocked onto dry paper, the flame goes out by itself when the fuel is "a cooking oil or fat" and the wick is small (Kearny, p. 104). - Good kerosene gives off no burnable vapour below 110 °F (HD p. 91). Gasoline does even in freezing weather, so a little of it makes kerosene far more dangerous, and fuel mixed into cooking oil spills and burns like fuel (rule of thumb). Never use a can that ever held gasoline (WHO, p. 106). - Test doubtful kerosene outdoors (HD p. 92): a tablespoon of it on a cup of water heated to 110 °F, and a lit match. "If the oil takes fire it is unsafe."

🪔 Lamps you can make Fuel use: with the smallest practical wick, about 1 oz of oil or fat in 8 hours (Kearny, p. 104), or "about 3 ounces ... in 24 hr" (ORNL-4941, p. 308). 1 lb of fat lasts about 128 hours, five days and nights (arithmetic). Wicks: cotton string, cloth or rag; in the bush, plant fibres, beaten bark or peeled rush (Shifts, p. 91). Flat kerosene wicks: "Save old felt hats", or hem a strip of cotton stocking or flannel about three times the burner's width (HD pp. 139-140).

Wire-stiffened jar lamp From Oak Ridge's tested drawing (🖼 ORNL-4941, p. 309): 1. Base: two bent nails, about ½ in shorter than the jar is wide, tied one across the other so it won't rock. 2. Wick: cotton string "slightly less than ⅛-in. in diameter". Tie a fine wire (window-screen wire) round the nails at its middle, and wind its ends in opposite directions up the string so it stands stiff. 3. Oil: fill the jar no more than half full of cooking oil or fat, with the "flame from end of wick ... just above oil surface". 4. Reflector: foil ⅔ of the way around the jar and under its bottom. Hang it on light wire by a loop "large enough for finger". 5. Light it with a match tied to a stick. To put it out, drip oil on the wick. Keep spare wire and string. Oak Ridge's tested lamp: kitchen fat only, the jar no more than half full, the flame just above the oil (ORNL-4941, p. 309).
wire-stiffened-jar-lamp

Floating-wick lamp From the drawing (🖼 ORNL-4941, p. 310): 1. A block of soft pine ½ in narrower than the inside of the jar (2½ in for a 3-in jar), about ¾ in high. 2. A V-notch across the top: 5 even saw cuts, then whittle it out, leaving about 3/16 in under it. Bore a snug wick hole through the bottom of the notch with a knife point, from both sides. 3. A wick 1/16-3/32 in thick (thin cotton string or twisted threads). Float it on oil in a half-full jar with the same reflector. When not in use for days, take the wood out of the oil. A notched pine block floats the wick; take the wood out of the oil when the lamp sits unused for days (ORNL-4941, p. 310). Shifts floats a wick on "bottle wire and three bits of cork": "half an inch of wick is enough to last all night"; but rats can upset a lamp and carry off the burning wick (p. 93).

Hunter's lamp and soft-fat lamps - Hunter's lamp (slut lamp; Seton's names are "slot-lamp, grease-jet, hunter's lamp"): cotton cloth or twisted rag in a clam shell of oil or melted grease. Better, push the wick through a hole in a thin, flat stone in the grease to hold it up; better still, use a tin for "a steadier lamp, as well as a much larger light" (Seton, p. 239). - Soft fat (too stiff to climb a wick, too soft to mould): lay the wick so it rests on and overhangs the edge of the dish; "the flame soon heats the side sufficiently to melt a portion of the fat" (Shifts, p. 91). - Open flames: stand them in a tin tray on something that can't burn, away from drafts and children (rule of thumb).
hunters-lamp-and-soft-fat-lamps

Can lanterns and candle holders - Tomato-can lantern: a big hole in the bottom for the candle, the sides punched full of small holes from inside; it "will not go out in the wind" (Seton, p. 239). A candle pushed up through a hole in the side of a can makes "a boxed light, shining ahead like a searchlight" (Seton, p. 240). - Jar lantern: "a candle, a glass jar, and light wire to hang the lantern" (FEMA H-4, p. 76). To carry a candle, stick a short one in a tumbler with its own drips (HD p. 99). A tin candlestick's socket seam must be folded, not just soldered, or it will "melt apart" (Thatcher, p. 117). A hunter's lamp with its flat stone, a can lit through a side hole, and a punched tomato-can lantern (Seton, p. 240).

🛢 Kerosene lamps while the kerosene lasts Storage and heaters: "Kerosene and propane" in the Fuel guide. Keep it in a metal can marked KEROSENE, not red, never an old gasoline can, outside the house away from where children play (MSU E-1669, p. 4). Good kerosene is "clear and nearly colorless, like water" (HD p. 92). 1. Each morning, by daylight: clean, fill, trim (HD p. 138). Never fill a lamp while it is burning (p. 93) or hot. Fill to within about ½ in of the top, since "the oil expands with heat and runs over"; wipe it dry (p. 139; p. 92). 2. Trim by rubbing the char off with a finger or burnt match: "Don't cut it; you can't cut it even" (p. 92). The wick must reach the bottom (p. 138); renew it "every month or two, no matter how fresh it looks" (p. 92). 3. Keep the burner's air holes clear; once a month, boil the burner in washing soda or lye water (p. 92). 4. Light it low and turn it up slowly; if steam fogs a cold chimney, keep it low till that clears (p. 139). Too high or too low, it smokes; set the screw back a touch so the wick won't creep up (p. 94). 5. Turn it low before blowing it out and when carrying it. Use lamps with "a

set the screw back a touch so the wick won't creep up (p. 94). 5. Turn it low before blowing it out and when carrying it. Use lamps with "a broad, solid base", and don't light one that has stood part-empty a long time (p. 93). Chimneys and spares: the right chimney gives "perhaps twice as much" light; a cold draft or the flame touching a hot chimney cracks it (p. 93). Toughen new ones by boiling 10-15 minutes in strong salt water, wrapped in cheesecloth, and cooling them in the water (p. 139). Keep "two or three extra chimneys and burners, and a yard or two of wicking", with lamps all alike so parts swap (p. 138). For a night light, don't turn a lamp low (it throws off unburned carbon); use a small lamp turned up (p. 94). Kerosene-soaked rags in a heap can catch fire on their own (p. 138). Pressure lanterns are brighter but "noisy", "hot" and "troublesome to start" (Rural Lighting, pp. 3-4), and burn about 5 litres a week at six hours a night (pp. 6-7). No kerosene lamps in a small closed room: "They produce gases that can cause headaches or even death" (Kearny, p. 104).

🔆 Getting more light from a little flame - Reflect it: "Use reflective material such as aluminum foil, mirrors, or white boards to concentrate a weak light where it is needed" (Kearny, p. 104). A mirror also throws light "down a well or other deep, dark recess" (HD p. 96). - Light, clean walls: "dirt absorbs and masks light", and washing gets back 5-10% more light than dry wiping (TM 5-683, p. 131). Ceilings should be the lightest, off-white, not shiny; dirt can halve the light in a year (Navy CE, p. 181). Wash lamp soot off walls, chimneys and reflectors (rule of thumb); a clean, right-sized chimney can double a kerosene lamp's light (HD p. 93). - Task lighting: one small light close to the work and everyone at one table, not a lit room (rule of thumb). 🧯 Fire, fumes, burns and children Putting out a fire: - Burning wax or fat in the pot: heat off, then a metal lid or damp cloth. "On no account try to extinguish burning wax with water as it will intensify the fire" (Practical Action, p. 3). - A burning lamp: wrap it tightly in "a heavy woolen rug" to smother it. Burning oil on the floor: sand or earth, never water, "as it will only spread it". Clothes on fire: don't let the person run; wrap them in wool (HD p. 95). - Don't throw a burning lamp out of the window, though that page says to: you'd carry an open fire across the room, spill burning oil on yourself and the floor, and the window may be shut. Smother it where it stands (rule of thumb). - Keep a bucket of sand or earth by the lamps and the candle pot (FEMA H-4, p. 76). Where lamps go: a safe lamp is "short and heavy", with "two flat sides" so it won't roll, a screw-on metal lid and thick glass, and never at a table's edge; light bottle lamps "could easily topple, igniting the clothes of a child" (WHO, p. 106). "Keep lamps and matches out of reach of children" (Where There Is No Doctor, p. 22). Hanging lamps: the books disagree. FEMA says hanging helps "prevent lamps

(CPSC Portable Generator Hazards, p. 1) - Never refuel a hot or running engine. Keep the can touching the tank while pouring (stops static sparks). (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 60) - Never plug a generator into a wall outlet ("backfeeding") - use a transfer switch or interlock. It can kill someone working on the lines. (🖼 how a transfer switch is wired; Transfer switch) - Capacitors bite. Motor capacitors (and microwave ovens) can hold a deadly charge after unplugging. Discharge across the terminals with an insulated screwdriver or a resistor before touching. - Pull the spark plug wire before working on a mower blade, saw chain or anything the engine turns. - Keep away from diesel injection lines while the engine turns. The injection pump pushes fuel at 4,000-10,000 psi (Practical Action Diesel Engine Repair, p. 13). Never hold a hand or face near a cracked line or a nozzle that is spraying. ⛽ Small gas engines: why it won't start Every engine needs three things: compression, spark and fuel. Find which one is missing. (MAVCC Small Engine Repair, p. 590; how it works: 🖼 the four strokes drawn, Four-stroke engine, Two-stroke engine) Intake, compression, power, exhaust: fuel, compression and a spark at the right moment (Navy Construction Mechanic, p. 23). 1. Fuel: pull the plug, cover the hole with a finger and pull the starter 2-3 times. A wet finger means fuel is arriving. If dry, check: fuel in the tank, shutoff valve open, cap vent not blocked, carburetor bowl (drain it - water or gum?), fuel filter and line. (MAVCC, pp. 595-598; 🖼 drawings) 2. Spark: put a spare plug on the plug wire, rest it against the metal head and crank. A bright blue spark is good. Yellow, weak or none = clean or replace the plug, check the kill-switch wire, then the coil/magneto. (MAVCC, pp. 599-600; 🖼 spark-tester drawing) 3. Compression: spin the flywheel backward against compression - a sharp rebound is good. Weak = loose plug or head, stuck valve, worn rings. With a compression gauge, crank at least six times before you read it. (MAVCC, pp. 602-603; 🖼 flywheel check and gauge drawings) A tester plug on the plug wire, grounded to the cylinder head: crank and look for a bright blue spark (MAVCC, p. 599). Quick

🖼 flywheel check and gauge drawings) A tester plug on the plug wire, grounded to the cylinder head: crank and look for a bright blue spark (MAVCC, p. 599). Quick troubleshooting chart (MAVCC, p. 592): | What it does | Look at these first | | Won't start, plug dry | Empty tank, fuel valve shut, plugged tank vent, stuck or clogged float valve, blocked filter or line, choke not closing | | Won't start, plug wet | Choke stuck or overused, stale fuel, water in fuel, flooded (mixture too rich), too much oil in 2-stroke mix, fuel-soaked air filter | | Won't start, no spark | Kill button or wire grounded, bad plug, bad plug wire, dirty or wrongly gapped points (older engines), bad coil | | Won't start, weak compression | Loose plug or head bolts, blown head gasket, valve stuck open, worn rings or bore | | Starts but lacks power | Dirty air filter, carburetor out of adjustment, clogged muffler or exhaust port, low compression, governor fault | | Overheats | Cooling fins or blower blocked, engine overloaded, clogged muffler, late ignition timing | | Smokes or uses oil | Wrong oil, oil diluted by a rich mixture, worn rings, clogged crankcase breather, wrong 2-stroke mix | | Kicks back when you pull it | Ignition timing off, sheared flywheel key (🖼 drawing), loose blade |

Gas goes stale in about 60 days without stabilizer (sooner with ethanol). For longer storage, drain the tank and run the carburetor dry, or add stabilizer and run it a few minutes so it reaches the carburetor. Keep cans sealed - water in ethanol gas separates and ruins engines. (Oklahoma Extension BAE-1746, p. 2) - Ethanol is a solvent. In an old, neglected engine it can loosen years of deposits that then clog the filter and tiny carburetor passages - the main reason for "ethanol trouble." Older engines (before about 1995) may also have rubber or cork parts that suffer. (BAE-1746, pp. 1-2) Cleaning a carburetor (AAVIM Small Engines Vol 2; 🖼 float-type carburetors, 🖼 floats, needle valve and float settings): - Take a photo before you take it apart. Soak metal parts several hours in carb cleaner, then blow out every passage with air. (AAVIM, p. 97) - Plastic or nylon parts no more than 30 minutes; never soak cork or coated floats. (AAVIM, p. 95; p. 93) - Don't poke jets with wire - it enlarges them. Use a bristle, fishing line or air. - Always fit new gaskets. Float too high

Don't mix mineral and synthetic 2-stroke oils. 🚜 Diesel engines Diesels have no spark plugs - squeezing the air makes it hot enough to light the fuel. So a diesel needs compression and clean fuel with no air in the lines. (Practical Action Diesel Engine Repair, p. 5; 🖼 gasoline and diesel strokes side by side; Diesel engine) Diesels usually need less maintenance than gasoline engines because they have no ignition system. (FM 5-424, p. 114) Won't start or keeps dying: suspect air in the fuel lines (an "air lock"), an empty tank or a clogged filter. (Practical Action, p. 12) Bleed the air out (p. 16): 1. Fill the tank with clean diesel and open the tank valve. 2. Loosen the bleed screw on the fuel filter (and on the injection pump) until fuel runs out in a steady stream with no bubbles. Tighten it. 3. Loosen the injection line nut at the injector and crank the engine until fuel comes out without foam. 4. Tighten the nut and check every joint for leaks. Bleed in order, from the tank toward the injector (a diagram drawn for this guide). What the smoke and symptoms tell you (Practical Action, pp. 11-14): | Symptom | Common causes | | Lots of black smoke | Faulty injector (p. 14) | | Overheating | Low coolant, loose or torn fan belt, blocked water jacket, bad water pump, low oil, overload,

| Lots of black smoke | Faulty injector (p. 14) | | Overheating | Low coolant, loose or torn fan belt, blocked water jacket, bad water pump, low oil, overload, long running at high speed | | Burns too much fuel | Leaks in tank or lines, clogged air cleaner, wrong valve timing, overload, lots of stopping and starting, idling when not needed | | Burns oil | Worn or wrongly fitted piston rings, worn cylinder, damaged seals or head gasket | | Knocking or noise | Poor-quality fuel, loose connecting rod, worn or badly adjusted parts | Cleaning an injector nozzle: soak the nozzle valve and body in clean diesel, scrub the soot off with a copper (not steel) wire brush, and check the needle slides freely. (Practical Action, p. 15; 🖼 injector valve, taken apart; 🖼 cleaning the spray holes; Fuel injection) Don't run a diesel generator lightly loaded for long. It runs too cool, soot builds up in the engine and exhaust ("wet stacking"), and over time this can permanently damage it. (FEMA P-1019, p. 150) Give it a real load when you run it. Diesel fuel catches fire less easily than gasoline, but once burning a diesel fire is fierce (Practical Action, p. 6). 🪚 Chainsaws, crosscut saws and axes - A sharp chain throws chips; a dull one makes dust - and dust clogs the filter and raises kickback risk. (USFS Chain Saw and Crosscut Saw Training Course, p. 25) - The four chain rules: sharp, depth gauges set right, correctly tensioned (more bar and chain trouble comes from wrong tension than anything else), and well oiled. The chain should not hang below the bar but should still turn freely by hand. (USFS, p. 31; 🖼 parts of the chain; 🖼 right and wrong tension; Saw chain) - Filing: use the file size for your chain, with a guide. Hold the file level with about one-fifth of it above the cutter's top plate, guide mark parallel to the chain. File from the inside of each cutter outward, all of one side, then turn the saw around. Keep all cutters the same length. If the chrome is chipped, file until the chip is gone. (USFS, pp. 33-34; 🖼 filing angles; 🖼 file height and direction) - Depth gauges (the little humps in front of each cutter): check with a gauge tool every few sharpenings, file down only to the tool, and round off the front. Never file one lower than the tool. (USFS, p. 34; 🖼 what the depth gauge does; 🖼 gauge tool and rounding off) - After several hand filings, the angles

🔋 Generators Where to put it (CPSC, p. 1): - Outdoors, far from doors, windows and vents, exhaust pointed away from buildings. Put a battery-powered CO alarm in the house. (Engine-generator, Carbon monoxide poisoning) - In rain, run it under an open, canopy-like roof on dry ground where water can't puddle under it. Dry your hands before touching it. - Use heavy outdoor extension cords rated for more than the total watts on them, with all three prongs and no cuts. Don't pinch them in doors or windows. - Turn it off and let it cool before refueling. Keep its fuel outside living areas. - Set it nearly level - the Army 3 kW set allows no more than 15° of tilt - on planks or timbers if the ground is soft. (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 60) Maintenance (rule of thumb - the generator's own manual comes first): oil change every 50-100 hours (sooner when new), clean air filter, fresh or stabilized fuel, run it under load for 20-30 minutes once a month. Machines that sit idle for long periods should be "exercised" on a schedule to keep oil moving and moisture out. (TM 5-683, p. 41) Load: add up the running watts of what you'll plug in, plus the start surge of motors (fridges, pumps, power tools can need 2-3× their running watts for a second - rule of thumb).

⚙ Electric motors: testing and repair When a motor won't run, check the simple things first, in this order (Illinois Electric Motors for Farm Use, pp. 24-25; know the parts first: 🖼 cutaway of an induction motor, 🖼 main parts laid out, Induction motor): 1. Power: is the right voltage reaching the motor terminals? Check fuses, breakers and the switch. 2. Load: take the belt off. If the motor now runs, the machine it drives is stuck. 3. Bearings: power off, turn the shaft by hand. If it won't turn freely, a bearing is dry, worn or stuck. 4. Thermal protector: many motors have a red reset button; others reset themselves once cool. A tripped protector means something else is wrong - find it. 5. Starting switch: a motor that hums but won't start, yet runs if you spin the shaft by hand, has a fault in its starting circuit (see below). 6. Windings: a burned winding has a strong burned smell, and you may see charred insulation. Single-phase motor hums but won't start (pumps, compressors, shop tools): suspect the start capacitor or the centrifugal start switch, which should click open at about ¾ speed (Illinois, p. 28; 🖼 capacitor-start motor; 🖼 the two parts of a centrifugal switch; Motor capacitor). Discharge the capacitor and check it; if it's open or shorted, replace it (TM 5-683, p. 56). A bulged
electric-motors-testing-and-repair

motor; 🖼 the two parts of a centrifugal switch; Motor capacitor). Discharge the capacitor and check it; if it's open or shorted, replace it (TM 5-683, p. 56). A bulged or leaking one is dead; a meter with a capacitance setting tells for sure. Replace with the same microfarads and same or higher voltage (rule of thumb). Switch contacts can be dirty, burned or pitted, or a wire can burn in two. (Illinois, p. 24) Basic winding checks with a meter (Navy Electrician's Mate): - Windings must have no opens (infinite ohms through a winding), no shorts (much lower reading than its twin), and no grounds (any reading from a winding to the frame). - The three windings of a 3-phase motor should read nearly the same resistance; a high reading between any two leads means an open winding. (Navy Electrician's Mate, p. 237) - Insulation test (megger): right after shutdown while warm and dry, with capacitors disconnected. At least 0.5 megohm for motors 250 V and under, 1 megohm up to 1000 V. Write readings down - a steady fall over months warns of trouble even above the minimum. (TM 5-683, p. 54) - Armatures (brushed motors): test bar-to-bar on the commutator with a low-ohm meter; a "growler" finds shorted coils (a hacksaw blade buzzes over the bad coil). 🔁 Motors as generators What works best, easiest first: 1. Permanent-magnet DC motors (treadmill motors, wheelchair, scooter, some cordless tool motors): spin them and they make DC directly. Output voltage rises with speed, so choose one that makes at least 14-15 V at the speed you can actually turn it to charge a 12 V battery. Add a blocking diode so the battery can't run it as a motor. (Rule of thumb) (Brushed DC motor, Diode) 2. Car alternators: built-in rectifier and regulator, but they need high speed (rule of thumb: about 1,500+ rpm - step-up pulleys or belts for wind, water or pedals) and a battery connected to power their field - they are not self-starting. The field draws about 3 A, which wastes a lot at low power. (Alternator and Regulator Servicing, p. 11; 🖼 how an alternator makes current; 🖼 testing the rotor) 3. Induction motors (ordinary AC motors) as generators: drive it about 1-5% faster than its synchronous speed - e.g. a motor rated 1725 rpm (1800 synchronous) is driven at about 1820-1890 rpm. Output rises with the extra speed. (DOE Microhydropower Handbook Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 54) On its own (not tied to the grid) it needs capacitors across the windings to excite it. Sources disagree here: the DOE handbook (same page) and the European hydro guide say an induction generator can't run cut

grid) it needs capacitors across the windings to excite it. Sources disagree here: the DOE handbook (same page) and the European hydro guide say an induction generator can't run cut off from the grid (ESHA Layman's Guidebook Pt 2, p. 30), while village hydro schemes run them off-grid with a capacitor bank and controller (Practical Action Micro-Hydro O&M, p. 23). Expect some trial and error. - Rule of thumb: start with run capacitors whose current at rated voltage roughly matches the motor's no-load current, then trim until voltage and frequency are right. Use AC motor-run (film) capacitors, never electrolytic start capacitors. - Expect about 70-80% of the motor's rating as output (rule of thumb). Needs a ballast (dump) load or controller so voltage doesn't swing as loads switch. Aging capacitors make frequency creep up; a capacitor running hotter than the others is failing - feel them once a month. Too many capacitors overheat the generator. (Practical Action, pp. 23-26) 4. Build a permanent-magnet alternator from magnets and magnet wire for a wind turbine or slow water wheel - full plans in Hugh Piggott's Axial Flux Alternator and PMG Construction Manual. 🛠 Reusing a generator for water or wind power When the gasoline and diesel are gone, a portable generator still holds two valuable machines: an engine and a generator head (the part that makes electricity). There are two ways to keep using them. 1. Keep the whole set and change the fuel. FEMA's wood-gas plans say stationary engines on wood gas "run electric generators, pumps, and industrial equipment" (FEMA Wood Gas Generator, p. 19). A generator sits still, so it needs a gas cooler and a second filter that a moving vehicle wouldn't, and hot gas costs power: about 1% for every 10 °F above 70 °F (p. 28). Most portable generators have engines of 15 hp or less; for those FEMA says to use a 6-inch fire tube with a narrowed throat (p. 67). The rest (building it, and the carbon monoxide danger) is in the Fuel guide. 2. Take the generator head off and turn it with water or wind. The rest of this section is about that.
reusing-a-generator-for-water-or-wind-power

What's inside: two kinds of portable generator Standard generators (the open-frame kind) have a generator head bolted to the engine: - A spinning rotor makes the magnetic field and a still stator around it makes the power, so the output comes straight off the stator wires (NEETS 5, pp. 64-66; 🖼 rotating-field alternator with exciter). - The rotor's field is fed through brushes and slip rings, or with no brushes at all: a small exciter and diodes spinning on the shaft feed it (ESHA Small Hydro Pt 2, p. 31; 🖼 brushless alternator). The Army's 3 kW set is the brushless kind; its book gives the normal winding resistances (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 26). - A voltage regulator (AVR) holds the voltage steady by changing the field's strength, because the speed has to stay fixed for the frequency (NEETS 5, p. 78). Many cheap heads instead use a capacitor on an extra winding to make their field (rule of thumb). - Speed sets the frequency: a 2-pole head must turn 3,600 rpm for 60 Hz, a 4-pole head 1,800 rpm (NEETS 5, p. 76; 🖼 2-pole vs 8-pole). Almost all portable sets are 2-pole, 3,600 rpm (rule of thumb). - Most heads have only one bearing. The other end of the rotor is bolted onto the engine's crankshaft, so a head taken off the engine needs a new shaft end and
whats-inside-two-kinds-of-portable-generator

heads have only one bearing. The other end of the rotor is bolted onto the engine's crankshaft, so a head taken off the engine needs a new shaft end and bearing before a belt can drive it (rule of thumb; the hydro handbook notes horizontal generators "usually have a single bearing", DOE Microhydropower Handbook Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 57). Inverter generators (the quiet, closed-case kind). There is no manual for one in the library; this is how they are generally built (rule of thumb): - The engine's flywheel is the rotor: a ring of magnets spinning around a stator with many poles. It makes three-phase AC whose voltage and frequency both rise with speed, and there may be several separate sets of windings (for the inverter's own power, for battery charging). - A rectifier turns that into DC, and the inverter board turns the DC into steady 120-volt, 60 Hz power. The board usually also works the throttle and needs signals from the engine, so it rarely works without its engine. - The magnet-and-stator part is the same family as the flywheel alternator on small engines (MAVCC Small Engine Repair, p. 370; 🖼 flywheel alternator parts), and it behaves like any permanent-magnet alternator: voltage rises in step with speed (Piggott Axial Flux Alternator, p. 15).
whats-inside-two-kinds-of-portable-generator

Which parts are worth saving | Part | Best use | Watch out for | | Magnet alternator (from an inverter generator) | Charging batteries from a slow water wheel or wind rotor: rectify it to DC, then a diversion controller | Test it first (below). Keep its magnets away from iron and don't drop it | | Wound-field generator head (standard generator) | A fast turbine, like a Pelton wheel on a good drop, belted up to its speed | Wants 3,600 rpm; voltage holds but frequency swings with the load | | Engine | Wood gas (above), or turning a pump, mill or saw directly | Same care as any engine (top of this guide) | | Voltage regulator, capacitors | Stay with the generator head | Discharge capacitors before touching | | Inverter board | Rarely reusable without its engine; keep for parts | Can hold a deadly charge | | Bearings, pulleys, frame, outlets, breaker, wire | Your hydro or wind build | Check bearings (below) |

Taking it apart safely 1. Drain the fuel, unplug the spark plug wire, and work outdoors or with the doors open (rule of thumb). 2. Discharge every capacitor (inverter board, voltage regulator, capacitor-excited heads): the charge left in capacitors "is, in many cases, sufficient to cause a lethal shock." Use a shorting probe with its ground clip on first, touch each terminal several times, and keep your hands off the metal (NEETS 21, pp. 32-33; 🖼 shorting probe). Short a stored capacitor's terminals with a wire; "CHARGED CAPACITORS CAN KILL" (p. 34). 3. Photograph and tag every wire, and punch-mark the frame and end bells so they go back the same way (Navy Construction Electrician, p. 255; 🖼 punch marks). 4. Turn the shaft by hand before opening anything: binding means a bent shaft, bad bearings or debris (same page). 5. Taking a magnet flywheel off: hold it with a holding tool (the nut's thread direction depends on which way the engine turns), then use a puller, not a hammer: "Too much hammering will jar the magnetism out" (AAVIM Small Engines Vol 2, pp. 58-59; 🖼 flywheel pullers). Don't drop it, store it away from iron, and pick metal chips off the magnets (p. 60; MAVCC, p. 374). 6. Pulling a rotor out of a stator: lift the brushes first, support the rotor only by its shaft, and slide thin
taking-it-apart-safely

off the magnets (p. 60; MAVCC, p. 374). 6. Pulling a rotor out of a stator: lift the brushes first, support the rotor only by its shaft, and slide thin cardboard into the gap to protect the windings (Navy Construction Electrician, p. 256; Kuphaldt Vol 6, p. 174). 7. Bearings: leave good ones on the shaft; pull with the puller on the inner race (see "Electric motors: testing and repair" above; Navy Electrician's Mate, p. 224).
