Testing what you salvaged - Spin it and measure. Turn the shaft with a drill, a lathe or a rope at a speed you can count, and read the AC volts across the output wires. On a magnet alternator the voltage goes up in proportion to speed, so one reading tells you what it makes at any rpm (Piggott, p. 36). - Speed from frequency: Hz = rpm × number of poles ÷ 120, so a multimeter that reads Hz is a tachometer (same page). - DC after the rectifier ≈ 1.4 × the AC reading, minus about 1.5 V (same page). To charge a 12 V battery you need about 14 V DC. - Short two output wires and turn it: a good one becomes stiff but smooth; "If it trembles as you turn it then there is a fault" (Piggott PMG Manual, p. 42). No meter? A 3-volt flashlight bulb across two wires will glow when you turn it (p. 40). - A wound-field head makes little or nothing until its field is fed: spin it with the field wires on a 6-volt battery (Kuphaldt Vol 6, pp. 174-175), or flash the field as described in "Motors as generators" above. - With an ohmmeter: slip ring to shaft should read open (otherwise the rotor is grounded); ring to ring should match the spec (open = broken winding, low
testing-what-you-salvaged

generators" above. - With an ohmmeter: slip ring to shaft should read open (otherwise the rotor is grounded); ring to ring should match the spec (open = broken winding, low = shorted); each diode reads low one way and high the other. Never test diodes with a 110-volt test lamp (Alternator Servicing, pp. 17-19). The Army's brushless set: flash the field; if the voltage holds under load the stator and rotor are good; if not, test the diodes on the exciter rotor (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 95). - Megger the windings to the frame (minimums under "Electric motors" above). A head rated for standby use "may not hold up under continuous operation at full load", so run it well below its rating (DOE Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 59).

Matching it to a water wheel or wind rotor - The 3,600-rpm head is the hard part. "The 2-pole generator with a speed of 3600 rpm is too high for practical use with a microhydropower system"; 1,800-rpm heads are the usual choice (NRCan Micro-Hydropower Systems, p. 24). - Water: a Pelton wheel turns fastest on a high drop. Its buckets work best at about half the speed of the jet (ESHA Pt 2, p. 20), so an 8-inch Pelton on 100 ft of drop turns about 1,060 rpm, and needs about 3.4 to 1 to drive a 3,600-rpm head (arithmetic). Many small turbines run under 400 rpm and need a speed increaser (p. 28). Water wheels are slower still (NRCan, p. 23). - Wind: an 8-ft rotor in a 7 mph wind turns about 167 rpm (Piggott, p. 9); a 3,600-rpm head would need about 22 to 1 (arithmetic), which isn't practical. "Almost every small wind generator on the market uses a directly driven permanent magnet generator" (DFID-ITDG Small Wind Systems, p. 12): use the magnet alternator, or build Piggott's (above). - Belts: the speed ratio is generator rpm ÷ turbine rpm (DOE Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 81); pulley diameter × rpm is the same on both shafts (Illinois Electric Motors for Farm Use, p. 17). V-belts are the best choice and slip instead of breaking things if the
matching-it-to-a-water-wheel-or-wind-rotor

diameter × rpm is the same on both shafts (Illinois Electric Motors for Farm Use, p. 17). V-belts are the best choice and slip instead of breaking things if the turbine jams (DOE, p. 85). Don't go below the smallest pulley for the belt size, about 3 in for an A belt and 5.4 in for a B (p. 86; 🖼 table). Size the belts for 1.4-1.5 times the turbine's power (p. 89), make the distance between shafts adjustable because belts stretch, and expect to lose 3-6%, up to 10% if loose (pp. 95-96). Don't mix old and new belts, and mark the generator and its base so it goes back in line (Practical Action Micro-Hydro O&M, pp. 19-20). - Mounting: a car wheel-bearing hub makes a good bearing for a homemade alternator (Piggott, p. 15; 🖼 mounting it). Driving the shaft directly needs careful alignment and a coupling that flexes a little (Illinois, p. 17). - Runaway: with no load, a turbine and generator can reach two to three times normal speed (DOE Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 61), and a disconnected magnet alternator's voltage "may become dangerously high" (Piggott, p. 37). Always keep the dump load on (rules above). Pulley diameter × rpm is the same on both shafts (a diagram drawn for this guide).
matching-it-to-a-water-wheel-or-wind-rotor

Hooking it up - To charge batteries: a three-phase rectifier (six diodes, one pair per wire) turns the output into DC (Kuphaldt Vol 3, p. 122; 🖼 three-phase bridge), then a diversion controller and the battery. For a long wire run, rectify to a high voltage and step it down at the battery (NCAT Micro-Hydro, p. 18). - For heat and lights only, use the AC as it comes: heating doesn't care about frequency (DOE Vol 1 Pt 1, p. 153); hot water is the best place for the spare power (see Storing Energy Without Batteries). - Not for motors or electronics unless something holds the frequency steady: "Fluctuating frequency will destroy small motors and solid state equipment" (DOE Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 56). - A three-phase head on one phase gives only about a third of its rating (same page). - What to expect: magnet generators are over 80% efficient (NRCan, p. 25); the whole system is the turbine × the belt × the generator (ESHA Pt 2, p. 26). The water sets the limit: watts ≈ gallons per minute × feet of drop ÷ 10 (see the creek hydro section of the Off-Grid Power guide), and Oregon's water law applies (above). Rectify, fuse the battery at its + post, and let a diversion controller send spare power to a dump load (a diagram drawn for this guide).

📐 Practical Math, Measuring & Geometry Homestead math with no stores: measuring with your body and a string, mixing by ratio, squaring a foundation, areas, tanks, woodpiles and loads, slopes and heights you can't reach, and the numbers behind water, power and medicine - each with a worked Illinois Valley example. The books are in Math-Measuring\Arithmetic-Geometry (Navy Mathematics courses), Math-Measuring\Measuring-Surveying (USDA surveying, quantities, timber measuring) and Math-Measuring\Units-Tables (NIST unit tables, Army Engineer Field Data); Ray's arithmetic is in Children-Learning\Arithmetic, and FM 5-426 Carpentry and FM 5-125 Rigging in Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals. The interactive 🔢 Unit converter & calculators page (Unit converter) does the arithmetic, the 🧮 Calculator (basic and scientific) handles any other sum, and this guide shows how to do it with a pencil. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst mistakes - Same units before you multiply. Turn everything into feet (or inches) first. Mixing inches and feet is the commonest error - off by 12, 144 or 1,728 times. - A British or Canadian "gallon" is about 20% bigger than a US gallon (NIST HB 44, p. 8). Check where a recipe or manual came from. - Medicine: only doses printed in the medical books, in mg and mL, never drops. A second person redoes the arithmetic before anyone swallows it. - Loads are heavier than they look. A cubic yard of damp packed earth weighs about 2,600 lb

never drops. A second person redoes the arithmetic before anyone swallows it. - Loads are heavier than they look. A cubic yard of damp packed earth weighs about 2,600 lb (FM 5-34, p. 292). Never stand under a lift. - Measure twice, check a second way, and round the safe way: more posts, a bigger pipe, a smaller dose.

📏 Measuring with no tools Your body is a ruler - measure yours once (rule of thumb): | Measure | What it is | Typical adult | | Thumb width | Across the knuckle | about 1 in | | Span | Thumb tip to little-finger tip, spread | 8-9 in | | Cubit | Elbow to fingertip | 17-19 in | | Arm spread | Fingertip to fingertip | about your height | | Pace | One step | 2-2½ ft | Pace count (NRCS Surveying, p. 33): walk a measured 500 ft until the count varies by no more than 2-3 paces. 📐 Right angles and layout The 3-4-5 triangle (Pythagorean theorem): from the corner, mark 3 ft along one string and 4 ft along the other; when the marks are exactly 5 ft apart, the corner is square (🖼 Navy Vol. 1, p. 199). Multiples work - 6-8-10, 9-12-15, 12-16-20 - and bigger is more accurate: never start under 6 ft; use 12-16-20 for a 50 × 100 ft layout (FM 5-426, p. 48). Marks 3 ft and 4 ft out from the corner stake, exactly 5 ft apart: the corner is square (a diagram drawn for this guide). Check the diagonals: a rectangle is square only when both diagonals are equal (same page). For a 20 × 30 ft shed, √(400 + 900) = 36.06 ft (36 ft ⅝ in) each. Hang the lines on batter boards set back from the corners so they survive digging (FM 5-426, p. 46). The 20 × 30 ft shed: both diagonals 36 ft ⅝ in, and the strings hung on batter boards clear of the digging (a diagram drawn for this guide). With a string and stakes (a rope compass): - Bisect a line: swing equal arcs from each end; the line through the crossings halves it at a right angle (🖼 Navy Vol. 1, p. 198). Bisect an angle the same way from its arms (🖼 p. 199). - Center of a

the crossings halves it at a right angle (🖼 Navy Vol. 1, p. 198). Bisect an angle the same way from its arms (🖼 p. 199). - Center of a round thing (tank, millstone): bisect two chords; the lines cross at the center (🖼 p. 200). - Circle: string on a center stake; 10 ft of string gives 62.8 ft around (C = 2πr). - Oval (ellipse) bed or pond, 20 × 12 ft (geometry): two stakes 16 ft apart on the long center line (√(10² - 6²) = 8 ft each side of center), a loop of string 36 ft around (20 + 16) over both, pulled taut with a marking stick and walked around. A straightedge method is on 🖼 p. 200. Stakes 16 ft apart, a 36-ft loop of string and a stick kept tight inside the loop draw the 20 × 12 ft oval (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: Navy Vol. 1, ch. 18 - constructions; FM 5-426, pp. 44-48 - layout tools, batter boards, squaring; Steel square.

🌲 Heights and distances you can't reach Shadows (similar triangles)): height = your height × tree's shadow ÷ your shadow, at the same moment (🖼 Navy Vol. 1, p. 207). You: 6 ft, 4½-ft shadow; the fir's shadow 48 ft → 6 × 48 ÷ 4.5 = 64 ft. Stick (45°) method (similar triangles): hold a stick upright at arm's length with as much above your fist as from your eye to your fist. Back up until the fist lines up with the base and the stick top with the treetop: your distance from the trunk ≈ the height. A cruiser's stick does the same with printed marks (🖼 FB 1210, p. 14; Biltmore stick). Stick above the fist as long as eye to fist: where both ends line up, your distance from the trunk is about the tree's height (a diagram drawn for this guide). Abney or clinometer (percent): height = level distance × (top % - base %) ÷ 100, base negative if below your eye. At 66 ft, top +110%, base -8%: 66 × 1.18 = 78 ft. Felling: see the Firewood guide. Width of a river: - Compass: at A, opposite tree B, read B's bearing; walk along the bank until it has changed by 45°. The distance walked = the width (🖼 FM 5-34, p. 162). - No compass (geometry): from A pace 50 steps

walk along the bank until it has changed by 45°. The distance walked = the width (🖼 FM 5-34, p. 162). - No compass (geometry): from A pace 50 steps along the bank and plant a stick (C), 50 more to D; from D walk straight away from the river until C lines up with B. Those paces = the width. Triangles A-B-C and D-E-C are the same shape and size, so D to E equals the river's width (a diagram drawn for this guide). Thumb jump (rule of thumb): thumb at arm's length, close one eye then the other; it "jumps" along the far hillside. Judge the jump from a known width (a 60-ft barn) and multiply by 10 - arm's length is about ten times the space between your eyes. Check yours on a paced distance. Maps: ground distance = map distance × the scale's bottom number (FM 3-25.26, p. 44): on a 1:24,000 map, 1 in = 2,000 ft. The contour interval is in the margin (p. 17): with a 40-ft interval, lines ¼ in apart = 40 ÷ 500 = 8% (p. 113). 🏋 Levers, pulleys and loads Lever: push × your side of the pivot = load × load side. The mechanical advantage is how many times it multiplies your push - 10 lb lifting 100 lb is 10 (FM 5-125, p. 105). A 6-ft bar with the pivot 6 in from the load: 5½ ÷ ½ = 11, so a 100-lb push lifts about 1,100 lb. Block and tackle: count the rope lines holding the moving block - that's the advantage (FM 5-125, p. 110; 🖼 p. 112). Each sheave adds friction of about 10% of the load (p. 114); pull = (load + friction) ÷ advantage (p. 115). A 600-lb engine on 4 lines over 4 sheaves: (600 + 240) ÷ 4 = 210 lb. A person pulls about 100 lb straight down, 60 lb along the ground (same page): put three on it. Ramps (physics; friction adds more): push ≈ weight × height ÷ ramp length: a 500-lb log up a 12-ft skid onto a 3-ft wagon bed takes 125 lb plus friction (Bicycles & Carts guide). Rope: safe load = breaking strength ÷ at least 4; knots, sharp bends and age cut strength up to 50%. Fiber rope rule: safe tons = diameter in inches squared - ½-in rope = ¼ ton (FM 5-125, p. 20). ⚡ Electricity by the numbers - Watts = volts × amps (NEETS 1, p. 120): a 12-V pump drawing 5 A uses 60 W. - Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms - cover the one you want on the circle (🖼 NEETS 1, p. 116). A 12-ohm heater on 120 V draws 10 A = 1,200 W. - Watt-hours = watts × hours; 1,000 Wh = 1 kWh (p. 126). The pump 2 hours a day = 120 Wh. - Battery energy = volts × amp-hours. A 12-V, 100-Ah battery is 1,200 Wh on the label, but size a lead-acid bank on only 40% of that (IEA, p. 17): 480 Wh → the pump for 4 days. - Long wires waste power: volts lost = 2 × one-way feet × amps × ohms per 1,000 ft ÷ 1,000. Use the Off-Grid guide's wire table (Voltage drop). - 1 horsepower = 746 W (NIST SP 811, p. 62). 📚 Go deeper: NEETS Module 1, ch. 3 - Ohm's law, power and energy with practice questions; Off-Grid Power guide - load lists and battery sizing.

💧 Water flow and pressure - Flow by bucket and stopwatch: a 5-gallon bucket in 20 seconds = 5 ÷ 20 × 60 = 15 gpm; a 55-gallon drum in 40 seconds = 82.5 gpm (NCAT, p. 3). - Pressure from height (head): each foot of water = 0.433 psi (DOE, p. 113); each psi = 2.31 ft (NRCan, p. 41). A tank 40 ft above the house gives 17 psi before pipe friction; 60 psi on a gauge at the bottom of a full hose = 139 ft of drop (🖼 DOE, p. 114). - Suction lift has a hard limit: 21.2 ft at 1,000 ft elevation, 20.4 ft at 2,000 ft (USDA FB 1448, p. 28). At our ~1,300 ft keep a suction pump within about 20 ft of the water; deeper, the pump goes down the well. A siphon has the same limit. - Creek power: watts ≈ gpm × feet of head ÷ 10, about what NCAT's table of typical outputs shows (NCAT, p. 9): 30 gpm falling 50 ft ≈ 150 W, day and night. Pipes, summer flow, water law: Off-Grid guide. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1448, pp. 27-28 - pressure and suction tables; NRCan, pp. 41-44 - measuring head and flow; Micro hydro.

💊 Food, medicine and time math A year's food: people × calories a day × days, at 2,100 kcal per person a day and about 1,500 kcal per pound of dry grain (Food Security guide): 4 × 2,100 × 365 = 3,066,000 kcal ≈ 2,000 lb of grain-equivalent for a family of 4. Days of supply = stock ÷ daily use: 50 lb of flour at 1½ lb a day = 33 days. ### ⚠ Medicine arithmetic - read this first - Use only doses printed in the medical books (Medical guide; WTND green pages). This is arithmetic only. - Write the unit on every number - mg, mL, kg. Mixing mg and mL, or lb and kg, kills. - A second person redoes it without seeing yours. If the answers differ, stop. - Never measure medicine in drops or with unchecked kitchen spoons. Dose by weight (mg/kg): kg = lb ÷ 2.2 (WTND ch. 8, p. 4); mg = mg per kg × kg. Made-up numbers, not a real dose for any medicine: 10 mg/kg for a 44-lb child: 44 ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg; 20 × 10 = 200 mg; from a liquid with 100 mg in 5 mL: 200 ÷ 100 × 5 = 10 mL. Dosing an overweight child by actual weight can give far too much (WHO Formulary, p. 15). Spoons: 1 tsp = 5

mL: 200 ÷ 100 × 5 = 10 mL. Dosing an overweight child by actual weight can give far too much (WHO Formulary, p. 15). Spoons: 1 tsp = 5 mL, 1 Tbsp = 15 mL. Household spoons vary - mark one at exactly 5 mL of water from a syringe (🖼 WTND ch. 8, p. 3). Drops are unreliable: two books here put 64 (USU, p. 20) and 75 (Henley's, p. 706) drops in a teaspoon, before the dropper or liquid changes. ⚠ Old advice in the library to ignore - A child's aspirin dose by formula (Hospital Corpsman, p. 240): no aspirin for children with fever, flu or chickenpox (Reye's syndrome, WHO children's formulary, p. 39); use the books' weight-based doses, not formulas. - White-lead and red-lead paint and their spreading rates (Household Discoveries, p. 344; Wood-Frame House, p. 194): lead is poison. 🧰 Make-Do Household Guide How to make or replace everyday necessities when the store is gone - from basic supplies, things you can scavenge, and what grows around the Illinois Valley. Each section points to the detailed manuals in Homestead-Skills\ (especially Household-Make-Do\, Soap-Candles\ and Sanitation-Water\) and Electronics-Repair\. The links open each book on the drive at the right page. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - Never mix cleaning chemicals. Bleach + ammonia (or urine) makes toxic chloramine gas; bleach + vinegar or any acid makes chlorine gas. Use one product, rinse, then the next. - Lye (from ashes or the store) burns skin and blinds. Gloves and eye protection; flush any splash with plenty of water for at least 20 minutes (longer for an eye that still stings). Never use aluminum pots with lye. - Label every container. Never store chemicals or fuel in food or drink bottles, and never reuse a container that held chemicals or fuel for food or water. - Never put gasoline in a lamp, stove or heater, and never burn charcoal, a camp stove or a generator indoors (carbon monoxide). - Never throw water on burning wax or fat - it spreads the fire. Cut the heat and smother it with a metal lid or damp cloth.

🧽 Cleaning and disinfecting - Most cleaning is just soap, hot water and scrubbing - it removes most germs along with the dirt. Homemade lye soap works fine (see the soap section below). - Scouring powder: baking soda, fine wood ash, or fine sand on a damp rag. - Glass and hard-water film: white vinegar mixed half and half with water (not on marble or stone, and never together with bleach). - Disinfecting with bleach (for kitchen surfaces, sickrooms, after flooding): plain unscented household bleach, 5 tablespoons (⅓ cup) per gallon of water, or 4 teaspoons per quart. Clean first, leave it wet for at least a minute, and mix it fresh every day - diluted bleach loses strength. Drinking water needs a much weaker dose - use the table in Water\EPA - Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water (p. 2). - No bleach? Boiling water, scrubbing with soap, and drying things in full sun all kill germs. - Wash hands with soap (🖼 how-to drawing; Hand washing) before handling food or eating, after the toilet, after cleaning up a child or caring for a sick person, and after touching animals or garbage. Hand sanitizer (at least 60% alcohol) only works on hands that aren't visibly dirty. (OSU Twin-Bucket Toilet, p. 4) 📚 Go deeper: WHO/WEDC Technical Notes on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Emergencies - chlorine, latrines and hygiene after

🧼 Soap from fat and ashes 1. Make lye from ashes. Use hardwood ashes (they make the best lye); ashes of paper, cloth or garbage won't work (VITA, p. 342). Fill a bucket with ashes (🖼 VITA's leaching drawing; Lye), pour on boiling water and stir, top up with ashes and water, then let it stand 12-24 hours and carefully pour off the clear liquid (Practical Action Soapmaking, p. 2). A leaching barrel: crossed twigs and straw hold the ashes back while the brown lye drips out into a jar (VITA, p. 343). 2. Check the strength. Lye that floats a fresh egg or a potato is right. Too weak? Run it through fresh ashes again, or boil it down. (VITA, p. 343) 3. Make soft soap. Boil ½ cup of ash lye for every cup of clean fat until it is thick, rubbery and foamy. Age the brown jelly at least a month before use. (VITA, p. 344) Ash lye is potash, which only makes soft soap; hard bars need store lye (caustic soda), or boiled soap "salted out" with salt water (USDA 1940, p. 3; Practical Action, p. 4). Hard soap with store lye (USDA): weigh 2½ lb clean fat, melt it and let it cool to lukewarm. Dissolve 5½ oz lye in 11 oz cold water (lye into water, never water onto lye), pour it into the
soap-from-fat-and-ashes

clean fat, melt it and let it cool to lukewarm. Dissolve 5½ oz lye in 11 oz cold water (lye into water, never water onto lye), pour it into the fat and stir, heat and stir until smooth, stir in another 5½ oz water, and pour into a box. Cut into cakes after 24 hours; let them harden a week or more out of the sun. (USDA 1940, p. 3) - Clean kitchen grease first: melt it with about an equal amount of hot water, stir, let it cool, and lift the clean fat off the top (USDA 1940, p. 3). - Is it done? Cool a drop on a plate. Clear = ready. Weak and grey = needs more lye. A grey skin that slides on the plate = too much lye - add more fat (Practical Action, p. 3). - New ("green") soap is still caustic. Wear gloves to handle it and let bars cure at least 3 weeks (Practical Action, p. 4). - Keep children away and don't breathe the fumes. 👕 Laundry - Laundry soap: grate one bar of soap and mix with 1 cup washing soda (add 1 cup borax if you have it). Use 1-2 tablespoons per load, dissolved in hot water first. - Make washing soda from baking soda: spread baking soda in a pan and bake at 400 °F (200 °C) for about an hour, stirring now and then, until it turns dull and grainy. It's stronger than baking soda - wear gloves. - Ash water (old-time "lye wash"): soak hardwood ashes in water, let it settle, and use only the clear liquid for greasy or very dirty clothes. It's caustic - gloves, and never on wool or silk. - Washing by hand: soak overnight, agitate with a clean plunger in a bucket (or a washboard)), rinse twice, wring hard, and dry in the sun - sunlight helps disinfect. Stains (USDA Stain Removal from Fabrics): - Treat it while fresh, and try cold water first - hot water and soap set many stains. Test any remover on a hidden seam. (pp. 4, 6) - Blood: soak in cold water until the stain turns light brown, then wash in warm soapy water. Strong salt water (about 2 cups salt per gallon) loosens old stains. Never hot water. (p. 15) - Grease: rub in cornstarch, chalk or talc, let it soak up the grease, brush off (p. 8).

🪥 Personal care - Teeth: how you brush matters more than the paste. Brush twice a day with water, a little baking soda, or salt (or a 50-50 mix of the two). No brush? Chew the end of a fresh green twig until it frays into bristles (chew stick), or wrap rough towel around a finger. Use thread as floss. (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 17, p. 2; Medical\Manuals-PDF\Where There Is No Dentist, p. 63) - Deodorant: wash daily; dust on baking soda or cornstarch (baking soda can irritate some skin). - Salve: melt 1 part beeswax with 4 parts oil or clean tallow (by weight) over low heat and pour into small tins. Lip balm is firmer: about 1 part wax to 2 parts oil. - Hair: wash with soap, then rinse with a cup of water with a spoonful of vinegar in it to remove soap film. 📚 Go deeper: Where There Is No Dentist, p. 63 - gum care and keeping teeth without a dentist; Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 17 - teeth, gums and mouth.

🩲 Menstrual pads and diapers - Reusable pads (photos): several layers of absorbent cotton (old flannel or towel) sewn or folded into a pad, held in underwear. Rinse in cold water first, wash with soap, and dry in the sun. See Where Women Have No Doctor (Medical\). Change pads several times a day; a homemade tampon must be changed at least 3 times a day or it can cause a serious infection (Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 5, p. 4). - A pad that buttons on: a sleeve of heavy cotton about 4½ × 9½ inches with two button wings, plus removable folded towel liners about 6 × 8 inches. Wash and add bleach if you have it; dry in the sun, never under the bed - damp pads mold and cause itching. (WASHplus pattern - 🖼 step-by-step drawings) - Cloth diapers: absorbent cotton folded in layers, with a wool or plastic cover. Rinse, soak in a lidded bucket, wash hot with soap, dry in the sun. 📚 Go deeper: WASHplus Making Reusable Menstrual Pads - sewing pattern with drawings; Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 5 - periods and staying clean.

🧻 Toilet paper alternatives More detail (water washing, washing cloth wipes safely, which plants to avoid) is in Paper, Ink & Toilet Paper. - Water: a squeeze bottle of water, then wash your hands with soap - the cleanest option. - "Family cloth": cotton squares, used once, kept in a lidded bucket and washed hot, separately from other laundry. - Leaves: big soft thimbleberry leaves (common along roads and forest edges here in summer) or first-year mullein leaves. - ⚠ Learn poison oak first - it's everywhere in the Illinois Valley. Leaves in threes, lobed like small oak leaves, shiny or dull, red in fall. The bare stems in winter still cause the rash. (🖼 drawing) It grows as a shrub or a climbing vine, and the roots and stems carry the oil too (OSU EM 9184, p. 24). Also avoid stinging nettle. 📚 Go deeper: OSU EM 9184, p. 24 - poison oak photos and control; FM 3-05.70 Survival, p. 514 - poison oak and other plants to avoid.

🚽 Toilets when the water is off - Don't flush if the sewer lines might be broken, even if your pipes look fine. A septic system can keep working if nothing leaks or backs up. (OSU Twin-Bucket Toilet, pp. 4-5) - Twin-bucket toilet (Bucket toilet): two 5-gallon buckets marked "pee" and "poo". The poo bucket is lined with a heavy (3 mil or thicker) black bag; after each use, cover it with about ½ cup of sawdust, wood shavings, shredded paper or peat. Keeping urine out of the poo bucket is what stops the smell. (OSU, pp. 2-3) - Emptying: dilute urine with wash water and pour it on the ground, a different spot each time. Fill the poo bucket no more than half, then double-bag it with gloves on and store it sealed, away from food and water. In the country you can bury it - never within 100 feet of a well, spring or creek. (OSU, p. 3) - Hand-washing station: a jug of clean water with a spigot, a catch bucket, and soap in the toe of a sock tied to the jug - one by the toilet, one by the kitchen (OSU, p. 3). - Trench latrine (🖼 drawing; Pit latrine) for longer outages: about 1 foot wide, 5 feet deep and 13 feet long, well away from and downhill of any well or creek. 🔥 Fire and light without stores For candles, wicks, lamp oils and homemade lamps in detail, see Light Without the Grid. - Fire starters: cotton balls rubbed with petroleum jelly; fatwood (resin-soaked heartwood from old pine or fir stumps - smells like turpentine and lights even when damp); dry bark and pine pitch. - Char cloth (catches a spark): put squares of 100% cotton cloth in a metal tin with a small nail hole in the lid, set it in a fire until smoke stops coming out, then let it cool before opening. - No matches: a ferro rod or flint-and-steel onto char cloth (🖼 drawing) (steel struck on flint, quartz or pyrite throws sparks); a magnifying glass in sun (🖼 drawing); touching a 9-volt battery (or two AAs) to fine steel wool (🖼 drawing); or a bow drill (🖼 drawing) - drill about ⅝ in thick and a foot long, of dry cedar, fir, cottonwood or basswood, on a board of the same wood with a notch cut to the center of the pit; tinder of dry grass with shredded cedar bark (Seton's Book of Woodcraft, pp. 192-194, and the Army survival manuals - FM 21-76, ch. 7). - Oil lamp: a glass jar or tin, a wick of twisted cotton string or a cotton strip held up by a bent wire or a tin-lid holder, and any vegetable

🪵 Glue, patching and waterproofing - Pine pitch glue: gently melt pine resin (🖼 pine drawing) (it's flammable - heat beside the fire, not in it), stir in powdered charcoal (about 1 part to 3-4 parts resin) plus a pinch of fine plant fiber, and use while warm. Sets hard - for hafting tools, patching containers and seams. Plain heated resin works as glue too (FM 3-05.70, p. 455). - Flour paste: cook flour and water to a thick paste - for paper and labels. - Casein (milk) glue - skim-milk curd mixed with slaked lime and two other chemicals - makes wood joints as strong as the wood - water-resistant but not waterproof. Full recipe: VITA, p. 313. - Waterproof cloth or leather: rub in beeswax, tallow or a beeswax-oil mix, then warm it so it soaks in. - Waterproof boots (USDA): melt together 1 lb petroleum jelly + 2 oz beeswax, or 12 oz tallow + 4 oz cod oil. Apply warm (never hotter than your hand can bear), working it into the welt and sole edge, where shoes leak most. (USDA Care of Leather, pp. 12-13) 📚 Go deeper: Henley's Twentieth Century Formulas (1916) - hundreds of glues, pastes and cements; VITA Village Technology Handbook, p. 313 - casein glue; USDA Care of Leather, p. 10 - oiling and waterproofing shoes and harness.

👟 Clothing and footwear - Mending: running stitch for seams (🖼 drawing), backstitch where it must be strong (🖼 drawing), whipstitch for edges (🖼 drawing), and darning for holes (weave thread back and forth across the hole, then across the other way - 🖼 drawing). Patch from the inside for strength. Needles from stiff wire; thread from unraveled fabric, dental floss or fishing line. - Mend early - a few stitches on a weak seam or loose button save a big patch later. Shrink new patch cloth first and cut it on the straight of the weave. Darn with yarn raveled from a seam allowance, and don't pull it tight (it puckers). (USDA ABCs of Mending, pp. 4-8) - Sandals from old tires: trace your foot on tire tread, cut with a very sharp knife wetted with soapy water (steel belts make it slow - choose worn tread with no wire showing), sand the edges, and tie on with straps cut from an inner tube or with cord through slots. - Shoe care: work grease in well where the sole meets the upper, and let shoes dry somewhere warm, not hot. Re-sole before the welt and insole wear through - after that they're rarely worth fixing. (USDA Care of Leather, pp. 10-11) - Stay warm: wool keeps you warm even when wet; wet cotton pulls heat away - avoid it

🔧 Simple plumbing - Dripping faucet): shut the water off first, then replace the washer (🖼 cut-away drawing). A temporary washer can be cut from leather (cold taps) or rubber (hot taps). If the washer screw is stuck, put on a drop of kerosene and tap it; if the head splits, deepen the slot with a hacksaw. (USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs, pp. 4-5) - Toilet tank keeps running: usually a leaky, waterlogged float or a worn flapper/ball (🖼 ball cock drawing; Ballcock). A tank should empty in about 10 seconds. (pp. 9-11) - Clogged drain: put a little water in the sink and plunge hard; if that fails, open the trap) under the sink (🖼 drawing) and dig out the grease and hair with a bent wire (p. 12). - When you shut off the water for repairs, open the highest faucet so a vacuum can't suck dirty water back into the pipes from a tub or toilet (p. 12). - Frozen pipe: open the faucet and thaw from the faucet end back toward the supply - never from the middle, where trapped water can burst the pipe (🖼 drawing). Thaw drains from the low end upward. 🔌 Electronics: repair and salvage Manuals are in Electronics-Repair\ (and device-by-device guides in the iFixit archive in Kiwix). Start with the Navy safety manual and the Kuphaldt multimeter and soldering guides. To protect spare radios and parts from an EMP or solar storm, see the EMP Guide. Capacitors hold a charge after unplugging. Discharge them with an insulated tool or shorting probe (🖼 drawing) across the terminals and to the metal chassis, and recheck. (NEETS 16, p. 31; NEETS 21, p. 33) - Microwave ovens can kill: the capacitor holds about 2,000 volts. Short it out before touching anything inside, never run the oven with

16, p. 31; NEETS 21, p. 33) - Microwave ovens can kill: the capacitor holds about 2,000 volts. Short it out before touching anything inside, never run the oven with the cover off, and don't break the magnetron's ceramic parts (toxic). Old tube TVs and monitors (CRTs) hold high voltage and can implode - leave them alone unless you know how. - Household 120 V can kill - especially with wet hands. Work with one hand when anything might be live. With a typical body resistance of about 1,500 ohms, 120 V pushes about 80 milliamps through the body - more than enough to stop a heart; wet skin lets far more through. Take off rings and watches first. (Navy ET Safety, pp. 32-34) - If someone is being shocked, don't touch them. Cut the power, or push them free with a dry rope, belt or wooden stick, then start CPR if needed (p. 33). - Lithium batteries (laptops, phones, tools): throw out any that are swollen, dented, hot, or below about 2.5 volts. Charge only with a proper lithium charger, on a non-flammable surface, never unattended. Heat, overcharging and age can set off a fire that spreads fast with toxic fumes - get out (Lithium battery FAQ, pp. 2-3). Finding the fault - check the simple things first: power cord and plug, fuse, switch, batteries and their contacts, loose

toxic fumes - get out (Lithium battery FAQ, pp. 2-3). Finding the fault - check the simple things first: power cord and plug, fuse, switch, batteries and their contacts, loose wires. Then measure voltages, then test parts. Test a part in the circuit before you desolder it. Bulging or leaking capacitors (photos) are the most common failure in power supplies and chargers. - Look before you plug in - about 2 minutes finds most visible faults: loose or corroded connections, stray solder or wire bits (shake it and listen), charred resistors, and a white crust at an electrolytic capacitor's seal (🖼 how one is built). A discolored or leaking transformer means a short somewhere. If anything smokes or sizzles when powered, pull the plug at once. (NEETS 6, pp. 210-211) - The simplest explanation that fits all the symptoms is usually right (Kuphaldt, p. 37). Multimeter quick tests (touch the probes together first - the meter should read near zero ohms - Kuphaldt Multimeters, p. 30) - Continuity (beep): fuses, switches, cords, broken wires. - Diode (🖼 test drawing): conducts one way only - about 0.5-0.7 V on the diode setting forward, nothing backward. Both ways = shorted; neither = open. On an ohmmeter, a power rectifier should read at least 10 times higher backward than forward (NEETS 7, pp. 56-57). - Transistor (🖼 ohmmeter test): test it like two
electronics-repair-and-salvage

open. On an ohmmeter, a power rectifier should read at least 10 times higher backward than forward (NEETS 7, pp. 56-57). - Transistor (🖼 ohmmeter test): test it like two diodes back to back (base-emitter, base-collector), and check collector-emitter reads high both ways. Avoid the lowest ohms range (R×1), which can damage small transistors. (NEETS 7, p. 111) - Capacitor (discharged first): on the ohms setting a good one shows a brief "kick" then rising resistance; no kick = open, steady low reading = shorted. (NEETS 6, p. 171) Resistor color code (🖼 chart): black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. Bands 1-2 are digits, band 3 is the number of zeros, the last band is tolerance (gold 5%, silver 10%). Example: yellow-violet-orange-gold = 47,000 Ω ±5%. (Kuphaldt vol. 5, pp. 26-27) The example above, band by band: two digits, the number of zeros, then the tolerance (a diagram drawn for this guide). Soldering: use rosin-core solder (never acid-core plumbing solder); a 25-watt iron for circuit boards. Make the wires hold mechanically first, heat the joint, not the solder, and don't move it while it cools (🖼 a good joint; 🖼 a joint moved while cooling). Remove old solder with copper wick or a solder sucker. - Put the iron's tip on the bigger piece of metal

a good joint; 🖼 a joint moved while cooling). Remove old solder with copper wick or a solder sucker. - Put the iron's tip on the bigger piece of metal (the pad or lug), not the thin wire; a little fresh solder on the tip helps the heat flow. (Kuphaldt Soldering, pp. 24-26) - 63/37 tin-lead solder is best for electronics; zinc-chloride (acid) fluxes corrode circuit boards (NEETS 14, p. 80; Navy 2M, p. 195). Batteries (Practical Action Batteries): - Run dry cells in a radio until it quits, then finish them in a flashlight. Don't mix old and new cells (pp. 3-4). - A car battery is ruined after only about 20 deep discharges. Any lead-acid battery lasts far longer if you only use about half its charge before recharging. (p. 5; Rural Lighting, p. 5) - Top up vented lead-acid batteries with distilled water or clean rainwater - never acid (Rural Lighting, p. 5). 🍲 Hay-box cooking (saves fuel) Bring the pot to a full boil, then nest it tightly in hay, wool, newspaper or blankets in a box with a padded lid; it keeps cooking for hours on its own heat. Bring food back to a boil before eating if it has cooled below hot (food is safest kept above 140 °F). - Building one (Haybox; 🖼 cut-away drawing): a wooden box, old trunk or bucket with at least 4 inches of packing all round the pot, below it and in a thick cushion on top. Crumpled newspaper, packed hard, is the best cheap packing. Use a pot with straight sides and a tight lid, sized to the food - a big half-empty pot cools fast. (USDA FB 771, pp. 6-9) (The 1919 bulletin suggests asbestos - never use it.) - Times: boil beans or meat 20-25 minutes first, then 2-2½ hours in the box; soft foods need only a few minutes' boil and about 25 minutes in the box. It cuts fuel use by about 40%. (Practical Action Fireless Cookers, pp. 2, 5) - Meat and beans are the riskiest - don't leave them in the box too long, and reboil before eating (p. 5). - A hot stone or brick under the pot cooks hotter, but then the nest must be metal-lined so it can't scorch the packing (FB 771, p.

eating (p. 5). - A hot stone or brick under the pot cooks hotter, but then the nest must be metal-lined so it can't scorch the packing (FB 771, p. 6). 🫙 Containers and storage - Food-grade buckets (recycling number 1 or 2 on the bottom, from bakeries and restaurants), glass jars and metal cans with lids. Wash with soap, then rinse with the bleach solution above. Never store food in trash bags, paint cans or chemical drums. Containers of 20-30 lb are easy to lift and get used up before bugs move in. (USU Food Storage in the Home, pp. 11-12) - Keep mice out: metal cans or glass; hang sacks from wire. Set snap traps along walls. Seal cracks, keep food off the floor, and keep the store room between freezing and 70 °F - cooler keeps longer (USU, p. 9). - Clay-pot cooler (zeer): a small clay pot inside a bigger one with wet coarse sand between, and a wet cloth on top (🖼 how it works). Evaporation keeps vegetables cool - it works best in hot, dry weather, which suits our summers. Keep it in shade with a breeze and wet the sand three times a day. 💧 Clean water from plastic bottles (SODIS) Fill clear plastic (PET) bottles of 2 liters or less with clear water, lay them on a roof or shiny surface in full sun for 6 hours (🖼 drawing; SODIS) (two full days if it's more than half cloudy). Doesn't work with cloudy water - let it settle or filter it first. Details: Sanitation-Water\ and Water\. - Clear enough? Stand the full, open bottle on a page of large print (letters about ½ inch high) and look down through it. If you can read it, the water is clear enough. - Fill ¾, shake 20 seconds, then top up - the air helps kill germs. Lay bottles flat, on metal roofing if you have it. Drink straight from the bottle so it isn't re-contaminated. - Not green or brown bottles; replace scratched, cloudy ones (about yearly). SODIS does nothing for chemical pollution. (Eawag SODIS Manual, pp. 26, 86-87) - In long rainy spells, boil or use stored or rainwater instead (p. 27). 📚 Go deeper: Eawag SODIS Manual, p. 26 - step by step, with a question-and-answer section from p. 85; OSU Survival Basics: Water, p. 3 - boiling and bleach; CAWST Biosand Filter Manual - build a filter for cloudy water.

🐜 Pests - Roaches and ants (🖼 common roaches; German cockroach): powdered borax mixed with sugar or flour, dusted into cracks (roaches), or a sponge soaked in borax-and-sugar syrup in their trail (ants). Keep borax away from children and pets. - Mosquitoes: screens, netting over beds (🖼 drawing), and smoke; homemade repellents are weak. Cover water barrels and screen their vents so they don't breed there (Practical Action Household Water Treatment, p. 2). - Lice (🖼 drawing; head louse, body louse): comb wet hair with a fine-tooth (nit) comb (🖼 drawing) every day for two weeks; wash bedding hot. Body lice live in clothing seams - wash clothes and bedding at least weekly (FM 21-10, p. 96). - Ticks (🖼 western blacklegged tick photo; Ixodes pacificus): check every evening, especially after brush; pull straight out with tweezers. Grip close to the skin and pull with gentle, steady force without crushing it, and protect your fingers with cloth or gloves (FM 21-10, p. 98). 📚 Go deeper: Army FM 21-10 Field Hygiene and Sanitation, p. 96 - lice, ticks, mites and other pests; USU Food Storage in the Home, p. 13 - pantry pests.For hundreds more recipes - cleaners, polishes, glues, inks, waterproofing, pest control and home remedies - see the classic formula books in Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do\. ⚒ Blacksmithing and Hand Tools How to set up a simple forge, pick the right scrap steel, forge and heat-treat it, and make or repair basic hand tools - chisels, punches, tongs, knives, axes - plus how to sharpen and re-handle the tools you already have. The full books are in Blacksmithing-Tools\ (Blacksmithing, Heat-Treating-Steel, Hand-Tools); axe and crosscut-saw manuals are in Engines-Motors\Chainsaws-and-Saws. Farm blacksmithing (plow shares) and a short Practical Action brief are in Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst injuries - Hot steel looks exactly like cold steel. Assume everything near the forge is hot; pick things up with tongs, and set hot pieces down where no one will grab them. - Eye protection at the anvil, grinder and when quenching. Never use a cracked grinding wheel, never wear gloves at the wheel, stand aside when you switch it on. (Navy Steelworker, p. 22) - Never heat galvanized (zinc-coated) metal indoors - the fumes cause "metal fume fever." Strip the zinc first (rule of thumb: soak overnight in vinegar) and work outdoors. Drinking milk does not help, despite old advice (TM 10-440, p. 60 still recommends it - ignore that). - Quench oil can catch fire. Use a metal container with a close-fitting metal lid next to it, enough oil to fully cover the piece, and plunge it in quickly and completely. Never put water on an

a metal container with a close-fitting metal lid next to it, enough oil to fully cover the piece, and plunge it in quickly and completely. Never put water on an oil fire - smother it with the lid. (Rule of thumb) Oil fires usually start when there's too little oil for the piece. (Practical Action Blacksmithing, p. 3) - A coal or charcoal forge makes carbon monoxide - work outdoors or under an open-sided roof. - Fire season: Illinois Valley summers are dry. Keep a full water bucket or trough by the forge for embers as well as quenching (Practical Action, pp. 1-2), clear dry grass and leaves well back from the forge, and never leave a fire unattended. (Rule of thumb) - Oily rags can catch fire by themselves. Throw them out or keep them in a bucket of water. (USFS An Ax to Grind, p. 34)

🔥 A simple forge and anvil Rule-of-thumb setups; the books have full plans. - Forge: anything that holds a fist-sized pile of burning fuel with air blown up into the middle - a brake drum or steel tub lined with clay, or a brick or stone hearth with a pipe coming in at the bottom (the "tuyere"). The ICS Shop Equipment book and the Peace Corps manual show how to build forges and bellows. (ICS, p. 21; drawings: 🖼 brick forge, 🖼 tuyere, 🖼 village forges, 🖼 how a bellows works; Forge) - Air: a hand-crank blower, homemade bellows, a hair dryer or a small fan with a valve or gate to control it. Too much air wastes fuel and burns steel. (🖼 hand-built fan and pump designs; 🖼 a blower) - Fuel: charcoal (easy to make - see Homestead-Skills\Fuels), or coal turned to coke in the fire. Keep the fire clean: rake out clinker (glassy lumps), and work in the hot center. Screen coke to get rid of dust before you use it. (Practical Action, p. 2; Charcoal, Coke), Clinker)) - Anvil: a real anvil is best, but a chunk of railroad rail, a big block of steel, or a sledgehammer head set in a stump works. 🧪 Hardening and tempering 1. Anneal (soften) old steel before reshaping it cold or filing it: heat slowly to red, then bury it in dry wood ashes, lime or powdered charcoal and leave it until cold. (Selvidge, p. 56; Annealing)) 2. Harden: heat evenly to cherry red - rule of thumb: just past the point where a magnet stops sticking to it - and quench. - Plain carbon steel (springs, files, most scrap): water or brine (about ¾ lb salt per gallon) cools fastest and most evenly. Thin or very high-carbon pieces (files, knives) can crack in water - warm oil (80-150 °F; vegetable oil works) is gentler. (Steelworker, pp. 35-36) - Alloy steels: oil only. - Keep the piece moving in the quench. Steam and gas bubbles otherwise cling to it and leave soft spots, which can later crack or warp. (Selvidge, p. 57; Steelworker, p. 35; 🖼 a quench tank; Quenching) - The steel is now glass-hard and brittle - temper it right away, before it's fully cold. The Navy Steelworker manual takes parts out of the quench at about 200 °F - still too hot to touch - rather than letting them cool through the "cracking range" below that. (Steelworker, p. 31) 3. Temper: polish a spot bright with sandpaper or a stone, then reheat gently (over the fire, on a hot plate, or in an oven)

below that. (Steelworker, p. 31) 3. Temper: polish a spot bright with sandpaper or a stone, then reheat gently (over the fire, on a hot plate, or in an oven) and watch the colors run. 🧵 Clothing, Textiles, Leather & Shoes How to keep a household clothed and shod for years with no stores: dressing for our cold-wet winters, heavy mending, sewing machines, wool from sheep to yarn, linen, natural dyes, weaving, knitting, tanning, and boots and moccasins. Simple stitches, darning, tire sandals and boot-grease recipes are in the Make-Do Household guide; this guide goes further. The books are in Clothing-Leather\ (Sewing-Mending, Knitting-Hats-Gloves, Spinning-Weaving-Dyeing, Tanning-Hides, Shoes-Boots, Cold-Weather-Clothing), Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do, Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools and Trapping\Hides-Tanning. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Wet, not cold, is what kills here. Wear wool under a waterproof shell, no cotton in the winter rain, and change to dry socks at least twice a day (TC 21-3, p. 12). - Fleece and nylon melt onto skin. Wear wool or cotton at the stove, at the forge and near any fire (rule of thumb). - Never use the old poisons in tanning, fur and dye recipes: arsenic, mercury chloride, chrome, sulfuric or oxalic acid, gasoline, burning sulfur. Brains, bark, salt, alum, soap and smoke are enough. - Wear gloves with brains (deer and elk can carry chronic wasting disease) and lime (rule of thumb), and never put cut or cracked hands in alum liquor (USDA FB1334, p. 22). - Dye pots, tanning barrels and mordants never go back to food use, and stay away from children (rule of thumb). - Wet leather

alum liquor (USDA FB1334, p. 22). - Dye pots, tanning barrels and mordants never go back to food use, and stay away from children (rule of thumb). - Wet leather burns easily. Dry boots slowly; leather hotter than your hand can bear is almost sure to burn (USDA FB1183, p. 9).

🌧 Dressing for our cold-wet winters Our winters are "cold-wet" - near freezing, freeze-thaw, rain, wet snow, slush and mud - the hardest weather to dress for. You need a waterproof or water-repellent, windproof outer layer over insulation, and waterproof footwear. "Cold-dry" weather (below 14 °F) is colder but easier (TC 21-3, p. 6; 🖼 cold-wet vs cold-dry). On the valley floor most winter nights are in the 20s-30s °F, with weeks of rain from November to March (rule of thumb). The COLD rule (TC 21-3, p. 10; 🖼 drawing; FM 21-76, p. 176): | | Rule | Why | | C | Keep clothes clean | Dirt and grease clog the air spaces | | O | Avoid overheating | Better a little cool than sweaty; shed a layer before you work | | L | Wear it loose and in layers | Trapped air insulates; a tight outer layer crushes it (🖼 drawing) | | D | Keep it dry | Wet clothing carries heat away far faster than dry | Wool, not cotton. Cotton underwear, T-shirts, jeans and flannel lose what little warmth they have when wet and pull heat from the body. Wool keeps you warm when wet (hunter manual, p. 77). The Army's fallback is all-wool clothing, except perhaps a windbreaker (FM 21-76, p. 176). Cover the head and neck too - their blood vessels
dressing-for-our-cold-wet-winters

when wet (hunter manual, p. 77). The Army's fallback is all-wool clothing, except perhaps a windbreaker (FM 21-76, p. 176). Cover the head and neck too - their blood vessels don't narrow in the cold the way the hands' do (rule of thumb). Feet (TC 21-3, pp. 12, 41-42): trench foot (🖼 photo) comes from days of cold, wet feet, not from freezing; in bad cases the skin dies and amputation follows. 1. Change to dry socks at least twice a day. 2. Dry and massage your feet. 3. Dry leather boots whenever you can. 4. Wear socks that aren't tight, and only one pair of cushion socks at a time. Drying clothes (TC 21-3, p. 14; FM 21-76, p. 177): - Hang items separately, high in the shelter, away from the stove and steaming pots. Nylon melts if dried too close. - Pin damp socks inside your outer layer as you walk. Never put damp clothes in a sleeping bag. - Dry leather slowly; boots can dry between the sleeping-bag shell and liner. Bedding: wet down loses much of its warmth. No bag? Sew two layers of cloth and stuff them with dry leaves, pine needles or moss (FM 21-76, p. 177). Wool blankets beat heavy cotton quilts (Household Discoveries, p. 53). 📚 Go deeper: TC 21-3 Cold-Weather Soldier's Handbook - layers, feet, drying clothes, cold injuries; FM 21-76

🪡 Mending and hand sewing Hand-sewing basics (TM 4-42.21, pp. 17-22): - Cut thread about 36 inches, never more than a yard (it tangles). Cut it; never bite or break it. - Basting (🖼 drawing) holds work in place for a while. Backstitch (🖼 drawing) is the strong seam. Catch (cross) stitch (🖼 drawing) holds hems invisibly. Whipstitch (🖼 drawing) binds raw edges. - Darns are for holes under 1 inch; patches for bigger ones (pp. 39, 43; 🖼 four darns; 🖼 top patch). Cut a top patch 2½ inches bigger than the hole all round, with ½ inch turned under, its grain matching the garment's. Mend early (ABCs of Mending, pp. 5-6): overcast fraying seams, tape-stay pocket corners, rework raveled buttonholes with buttonhole stitch (🖼 drawing), and sew buttons on with a thread "shank" so the cloth isn't strained. Canvas, packs, tarps and leather (TM 4-42.21, pp. 71-74): - Use a triangular sailmaker's needle (🖼 drawing), pushed with a sewing palm (a leather strap with a metal pad - 🖼 putting one on). - Pull the thread across a cake of beeswax, and rewax it as you go (🖼 drawing). - Cut 2-strand thread 6 times the seam length, 4-strand 12 times. The lockstitch with a saddler's sewing awl - the same stitch a machine makes (TM 4-42.21, p. 79; 🖼 threading the awl; 🖼 the finished stitch; Lockstitch):
mending-and-hand-sewing

4-strand 12 times. The lockstitch with a saddler's sewing awl - the same stitch a machine makes (TM 4-42.21, p. 79; 🖼 threading the awl; 🖼 the finished stitch; Lockstitch): 1. Thread the awl, leaving ½ inch out of the needle. Pull out enough thread to reach the end of the seam. 2. Push the needle through; pull all that slack through to the underside; hold it and withdraw the needle. 3. Push the needle in a stitch-length away and pull it halfway back, forming a loop underneath. 4. Pass the slack thread through the loop. Pull the needle out, then pull handle and thread equally hard to lock the stitch in the middle of the cloth. Repeat. Pull out slack; push the needle through; pass the slack through the loop underneath; pull handle and thread equally to lock the stitch (TM 4-42.21, p. 80). Waxed thread for leather (The Saddler, p. 15; Hasluck, p. 36): twist 3-6 strands of flax (linen) thread. Taper each end first by untwisting it on your thigh and pulling it apart. Saddler's wax works best near 75 °F; cold wax is brittle. For shoes use waxed flax, never cotton - it is stronger, and the wax seals the stitch holes (FB1183, p. 9). 📚 Go deeper: TM 4-42.21 General Fabric Repair - every hand stitch, four darns, patches, canvas and webbing; USDA ABCs of

✂ Fibers, first garments and sewing machines Tell the fiber before you trust a salvaged garment (Turner, p. 95): | Burn a few threads | Fiber | | Burns fast, little ash, no smell | Cotton | | Burns slowly, black ball of ash, smells like burning feathers | Wool | | Melts and drips into a hard bead | Synthetic - keep it away from fire (rule of thumb) | Boiling a sample in weak lye (in an enamel pot) destroys wool but leaves cotton - so never wash wool with lye or chlorine bleach (rule of thumb). A first garment with no pattern (Turner, pp. 122-123): a kimono nightgown takes cloth twice the shoulder-to-floor length, plus a hem. Fold it crosswise, lay the drafted pattern on the fold, and cut the neck with the garment on the wearer. Its long straight seams (French or felled) are good machine practice. To remake old clothes, rip, wash and press first, and check the cloth is worth the work (Make-overs from Coats and Suits, p. 4). Lice live in seams: hang infested clothes in the cold, then beat and brush them. This does not kill the eggs (FM 21-76, p. 177). Rescuing a gummed-up treadle or electric machine (USDA FB1944, pp. 4-12; 🖼 two views of the machine; Sewing machine): 1. Pick out the oil holes. Run the machine while squirting

Rescuing a gummed-up treadle or electric machine (USDA FB1944, pp. 4-12; 🖼 two views of the machine; Sewing machine): 1. Pick out the oil holes. Run the machine while squirting kerosene or cleaning fluid into every hole and bearing, then oil each one freely. Never oil the tension discs. Never use gasoline indoors. 2. A stuck screw: soak it with cleaning fluid. "Left is loose, right is tight" (p. 5). 3. Replace a dirty wool wad in a long-bobbin oil well with raw wool (p. 8). 4. Then one drop per hole after each day's work, and now and then when idle (p. 10). 5. Skipped stitches: usually a needle of the wrong length or set wrong - the short groove faces the shuttle point. Sharpen a dull needle on a fine emery stone; scratch marks on the machine to record the needle length (pp. 11-12). Many electric heads from about 1900-1960 fit a treadle cabinet, run by a 3/16-inch leather round belt if the hand wheel has a belt groove. Stock spare needles, bobbins and belts now (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Turner Sewing and Textiles - seams, measuring and simple garments; USDA FB1944 - cleaning and adjusting machines.

🐑 Wool: from sheep to yarn Shearing (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 81-82; 🖼 handling the fleece; Sheep shearing): once a year when spring warms. If cold, wet weather follows, house the sheep 10-14 days or leave some wool on. Shear white sheep first, keep colored wool apart, and never throw hay over sheep's backs - it ruins the fleece. Here, shear in late April-May as the rains ease (rule of thumb). Washing without felting: - Raw fleece: soak a few ounces at a time in warm water with mild soap for about 30 minutes. Don't stir it or it felts. Rinse in water of the same temperature (CSU 4-H Spinning, p. 17). - Finished woolens: lukewarm suds (about 95 °F), rinses the same temperature. Never boil, rub, wring or twist; squeeze, pull to shape and dry away from the fire (USDA, p. 9; Household Discoveries, p. 206). - Local soap: the bulb of soaproot lathers "like ordinary soap" and has no alkali, which suits wool better than lye soap (Chesnut, p. 332). It grows on dry, rocky slopes here (rule of thumb). Carding and combing (CSU, p. 17; Hooper, p. 43): carding (🖼 hand cards) gives soft, fuzzy yarn; combing gives smooth yarn. Spread wool on one hand card, draw the other across it a few times, and roll the fibers off into a soft roll. No cards? A metal
wool-from-sheep-to-yarn

gives smooth yarn. Spread wool on one hand card, draw the other across it a few times, and roll the fibers off into a soft roll. No cards? A metal dog comb, or your fingers. Make a drop spindle) (CSU, p. 16; 🖼 spinning with distaff and spindle): 1. Sand a 12-inch, ½-inch dowel to a point at one end. Cut a ⅛-inch notch 1 inch from the blunt end as a hook. 2. Glue a 2-3-inch wooden disk (the whorl) 1½ inches from the point. Spin it like a top; if it wobbles, re-center the whorl. The spindle from the steps above, with the yarn leader tied on, wound round and hitched at the hook (a diagram drawn for this guide). Spin and finish (CSU, pp. 18-19): 1. Tie on an 18-inch leader of yarn. Twist the spindle and draw the fibers out as the twist runs up. Too much twist makes drafting hard; too little and the yarn falls apart. 2. Wind a skein around a chair back and tie it in 4 places. Soak it 20 minutes and hang it to dry with a weight. A balanced skein hangs straight. Angora rabbits give wool from a hutch: shear every 10-12 weeks, leave ½ inch of wool in winter, and keep newly shorn rabbits warm (USDA Handbook 309, p. 61). 📚 Go deeper: CSU 4-H Spinning - spindle,

shear every 10-12 weeks, leave ½ inch of wool in winter, and keep newly shorn rabbits warm (USDA Handbook 309, p. 61). 📚 Go deeper: CSU 4-H Spinning - spindle, washing, carding, skeins; Hooper Hand-loom Weaving - carding, distaff and spindle.

🌾 Linen, nettle and native fibers Fiber flax (USDA FB669; 🖼 the plant): 1. Climate: moderately cool, damp weather while growing and a dry spell at harvest. Heat and drought make it ripen early and short (p. 7). Here, sow very early on moisture-holding soil, or irrigate (rule of thumb). 2. Sow thickly - about 6 pecks an acre - so stalks grow tall and unbranched (p. 11). 3. Pull, don't cut, when the stalks yellow and the lower leaves drop (p. 12). 4. Ret to rot the gum that holds fiber to stalk: spread it on grass 2-8 weeks, turning once (dew retting), or weight bundles under soft water 6-15 days and watch closely - "a few hours' delay often causes loss" (pp. 16-17). 5. Dry the straw, break it (🖼 a flax brake), then scutch (beat) out the woody bits (Hooper, p. 37). Native fibers: - Douglas iris: the leaf edges are "as fine and strong as silk" and made the strongest nets and snare rope (🖼 twisting fiber into cord) - about six weeks' work for a 12-foot rope (Chesnut, p. 343). - Hemp dogbane: good fiber, but poisonous to livestock (AIB 415, p. 50). - Stinging nettle: gather with long rubber gloves and sleeves (OSU EM 9373, p. 2). Cut tall creek-side stalks after they brown in late summer or fall, then ret, break and scutch

nettle: gather with long rubber gloves and sleeves (OSU EM 9373, p. 2). Cut tall creek-side stalks after they brown in late summer or fall, then ret, break and scutch like flax (rule of thumb; no book here covers nettle fiber). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB669 Fiber Flax - growing, retting, breaking and scutching; Chesnut (1902) - native fiber and soap plants of our region.

🎨 Natural dyes with safe mordants Mordant with alum (USDA, p. 10): for each pound of dry wool, dissolve 4 oz alum and 1 oz cream of tartar in 4-4½ gallons of soft water. Bring it slowly to the boil, simmer 1 hour, and leave it overnight. The Navajo used raw alum, or water from burned green juniper needles (Navajo Native Dyes, p. 19). Skip the "chrome" mordant on the same USDA page - it causes cancer (see the last section). | Color | Plant | How | | Dull greenish yellow | Oregon grape roots, stems and leaves | With raw alum (Navajo, p. 39; USDA, p. 24) | | Soft brown | Alder bark peeled in fall | No mordant needed (Navajo, p. 23; Worst, p. 207) | | Black | Tannin (oak or tanoak bark, sumac) plus "iron liquor" | Steep iron filings in vinegar for days; mop it onto tanned leather (FB1334, pp. 19-20) | - Use enamel pots - tin or aluminum changes the color (Navajo, p. 12). - Test fastness: sun a sample half-covered with cardboard (USDA, p. 6). - Dye pots are never used for food again (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Navajo Native Dyes - plant dyes with only alum or juniper ash; USDA Home Dyeing with Natural Dyes - mordanting and dye recipes. 🧶 Weaving and knitting The simplest loom (Hooper, pp. 60-61): the one part every loom needs is the cross in the warp (🖼 securing the crosses) - alternate threads cross between two rods so they can't tangle. A board with the warp wound around it and two rods holding the cross is a working loom. For 10-yard warps, build a warping board (🖼 drawing) at least 6 ft × 1 ft with smooth hardwood pegs 1 inch thick, and tie cords through both crosses before taking the warp off, or it "will be irretrievably spoiled" (pp. 64-68). The next step up is the foot-power loom (Worst, p. 11; 🖼 parts named). Picture: Warp and weft. The cross keeps alternate threads in order; cords tied through it before the warp comes off keep it from tangling (a diagram drawn for this guide). Knitting habits from the WWI sock drives (Nicoll, pp. 25-26): - Join yarn without a knot: ravel both ends 3 inches, remove half the strands of each, overlap them and rub between damp palms. - Cast on (🖼 drawing) and off loosely. Press with a damp cloth and a cool iron - wool scorches. - Tie a few needlefuls of the same yarn to each article for darning later (🖼 repairing knitting). Socks, hats and mittens (Nicoll): - Socks: measure your own rounds per inch and adjust the pattern

of the same yarn to each article for darning later (🖼 repairing knitting). Socks, hats and mittens (Nicoll): - Socks: measure your own rounds per inch and adjust the pattern (p. 133). Graft) the toe closed so no seam blisters the foot (🖼 heel, sole and toe) (p. 139); knit extra into the heel (p. 143). - Helmet: 100 stitches in knit 2, purl 2 ribbing, with a face opening (p. 28); balaclava) (p. 31); mittens (p. 71). - Fur caps: rip apart an old cloth cap for the pattern and line it with wool. Muskrat is "as warm as any fur" (Farnham, p. 246). - Leather or fur mittens: woodsmen make them unlined and wear a knit liner they can pull out and dry. Trace the hand, add ¼-½ inch for seams, test the pattern in old cloth, and leave a long cuff (Farnham, pp. 248-249). 📚 Go deeper: Nicoll Knitting and Sewing - seventy patterns for socks, caps and mittens; Dillmont Encyclopedia of Needlework - stocking proportions and every stitch.

🦌 Tanning hides Hold a hide until you can work it (USDA FB1334, p. 8): salt it with 1 lb of salt per lb of hide; it keeps 3-5 months. Never let it freeze or heat. Work in wooden barrels, never iron (🖼 tools). Lime takes off the hair in 6-16 days (🖼 unhairing); a gallon of vinegar removes the lime (pp. 10-14). Unhairing on a tanner's beam: push the loosened hair off with the dull edge of a two-handled fleshing knife (USDA FB1334, p. 11). Bark tanning) - sole and harness leather (pp. 14-16): 1. Per hide, steep 30-40 lb of oak or hemlock bark, ground no coarser than corn, in 20 gallons of boiling water. Use rain water, and keep it away from iron. 2. Strengthen the liquor every 5 days; then bury the hide in wet bark for 6 weeks, and again for about 2 months. 3. It is done when a cut edge shows no white streak. Sole leather needs 2 months more. 4. Finish with dubbin (equal parts tallow and neatsfoot or cod oil), slicking (🖼 drawing) and staking (🖼 drawing). Staking: while the leather dries, work it back and forth in every direction over a dull-edged stake to soften it (USDA FB1334, p. 21). Local bark: tanoak bark "has high tannin content" and was once used widely to cure leather (USDA NRCS, p. 2);
tanning-hides

a dull-edged stake to soften it (USDA FB1334, p. 21). Local bark: tanoak bark "has high tannin content" and was once used widely to cure leather (USDA NRCS, p. 2); Oregon white and black oak bark also work. Sudden oak death kills tanoak and is under quarantine in Curry County, next door: don't haul tanoak bark, wood or leaves out of infested areas (rule of thumb). Brain-tanned buckskin) (Farnham, pp. 73-74, 142-147; Brain tanning)): 1. Soak the skin in water, or water with wood ashes, until the hair and the grain (outer skin) slip. 2. Flesh it on a beam (🖼 a fleshed hide), then scrape off hair and grain. 3. Boil the brains about an hour in a gallon of water; cool until you can hold your hand in it. Work the skin in it and wring it out. 4. Pull and stretch it without stopping until it is dry. Repeat if it is still stiff. 5. Smoke it over a cool smudge of punky hardwood inside a little tepee of sticks. Unsmoked buckskin dries hard every time it gets wet. Soap or lard can replace brains. Wear gloves with brains - the prions of chronic wasting disease concentrate in brain and spinal cord; use soap or egg yolk if in doubt (rule of thumb). Furs: salt-alum (FB1334, p. 27): 1. in brain and spinal cord; use soap or egg yolk if in doubt (rule of thumb). Furs: salt-alum (FB1334, p. 27): 1. Dissolve 1 lb alum in 1 gallon of water. Dissolve 4 oz washing soda and 8 oz salt in ½ gallon of water, and pour it in very slowly. 2. Thicken with flour to a paste; spread 2-3 coats on the flesh side, a day apart. 3. 👢 Boots, shoes and moccasins Boot care (USDA FB1183, pp. 9-12): - Wet boots: wash off mud, grease work boots while damp, stuff with paper, dry slowly. - Harder grease in summer, more grease in winter (p. 12); recipes are in the Make-Do guide. - Soles: stand them 15 minutes in warm grease, no hotter than your hand can bear (FB1334, p. 16). A home repair kit (FB1183, p. 9): last holder, 3-4 iron lasts, hammer, pincers, knives, rasp, awls, sole and heel nails, flax thread, bristles and wax. Half-soling sewn shoes (Leno, p. 131; Bower, p. 29): 1. Wet the new leather. 2. Take off the old sole without cutting the welt. 3. Carry the new sole well back into the waist (the narrow middle). 4. Cut a channel deep enough to bury the stitches, and sew with stout, well-waxed thread. Pegged soles: one well-driven row of pegs usually holds; two rows make a stiff, tiring sole (Leno, p. 109). Fit: measure the foot's length seated, then trace it on paper standing - it lengthens under load, and the difference sets the allowance (p. 45; 🖼 measuring diagram). Leno also covers pumps (turnshoes) and leggings. Moccasins in a wet climate (Farnham, pp. 260-266): frontier moccasins were one piece of buckskin stuffed with deer hair or dry leaves. In wet weather wearing them was "a decent way of going barefooted,"
boots-shoes-and-moccasins

climate (Farnham, pp. 260-266): frontier moccasins were one piece of buckskin stuffed with deer hair or dry leaves. In wet weather wearing them was "a decent way of going barefooted," because the leather is spongy. Improve them: - Add a rawhide sole, or sew on a thick "tap" that runs up the sides (p. 266). - Shape them by wetting and wearing them until dry (p. 264). - For uppers, 10-12 oz cotton duck rubbed with paraffin and ironed is waterproof and wears well. A child's moccasins can be cut from an old leather handbag (MP614, p. 9). Here, keep moccasins for indoors and the dry season, and save real boots for winter mud (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Leno Boot and Shoemaking - lasts, uppers, welted and pegged boots, mending; Bower Practical Shoe Repairing - soles and heels; USDA FB1183 - care of shoes and harness.

⚠ Old advice in the library to ignore - Arsenic sprinkled on stored furs (Farnham, p. 64), as a hair remover (p. 120) and to "poison" fur robes (p. 224); arsenical soap and corrosive sublimate (mercury chloride) in Lee's, p. 225. Deadly; old mounts and furs may still carry it (ATSDR Arsenic). Instead: salt, dry, cold storage. - Chrome tanning - FB1334, p. 17; the bulletin itself says the spent liquor "probably would be fatal to farm animals" (p. 19). Also the chrome (dichromate) dye mordant - USDA dyes, p. 10. Chromium(VI) causes cancer (ATSDR Chromium). Instead: bark or alum. - Sulfuric acid "salt-acid" pickle - FB1334, pp. 27-28; Farnham, p. 113. Burns and fumes. Instead: salt-alum. - Oxalic acid tan liquors - Farnham, p. 116; Household Discoveries, p. 409. Poisonous. Instead: brains, bark or alum. - Gasoline baths for furs - FB1334, pp. 25-26; Farnham, p. 150. Fire and fumes. Instead: lukewarm soapy water (rule of thumb). - Burning sulfur to bleach sheepskins - Farnham, p. 151. Toxic fumes. Instead: keep the natural color. - Formaldehyde and borax-heavy "pickles" in old taxidermy recipes (rule of thumb). Instead: salt and alum. - "40 to 45 percent of body heat" lost from the head - FM 21-76, p. 176. The real figure is about 10%, in proportion to skin area (rule of thumb) - but still cover head and neck. -

📜 Paper, Ink & Toilet Paper How to make the paper, ink and toilet paper a household goes through once the stores are gone: paper by hand from rags, plants and scrap paper; iron-gall and soot inks; pens, pencils and slates; keeping paper and books from mold; and what to use instead of toilet paper, tissues and paper towels, and where each may go. The two papermaking and ink books are in Homestead-Skills\Paper-Ink: Watt's The Art of Paper-Making (1890), whose chapter "Making Paper by Hand" covers the vat, mould and sizing, and the Bureau of Standards' Inks (Circular 426, 1940). The old recipe books are in Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do and the toilet books in Sanitation-Hygiene\Latrines-Toilets. Where no book covers a step, this guide says (rule of thumb). ### The short version - Rags make the best paper. Linen and cotton, cooked soft in weak lye or lime and pounded to pulp; there is "no better material" than linen (Watt, p. 20). - Lye burns skin and can blind. Gloves, goggles, no aluminum pots, children away; flush splashes with lots of water (Practical Action Soapmaking, p. 1). - Scrap paper is the easy win: soak, pound, form again (Leland, p. 159). - Iron-gall ink is tannin + iron + a little gum: oak galls, tanoak bark or sumac leaves, with rusty nails in vinegar (Practical Action Natural Dyeing, p. 4). Keep tannin and

ink is tannin + iron + a little gum: oak galls, tanoak bark or sumac leaves, with rusty nails in vinegar (Practical Action Natural Dyeing, p. 4). Keep tannin and iron about equal by weight; too much iron eats paper (NBS Inks, p. 35). - Soot ink never fades and doesn't harm paper (NBS, p. 37): use it for records that must last. - Never add mercury ("corrosive sublimate") or chromates as old recipes do. A few cloves or a little alcohol stop mold (Household Discoveries, p. 422). - Washing with water is the cleanest toilet paper, 2 cups to 3 quarts a time (Compendium, p. 10). Cloth wipes belong to one person and are washed hot. Only toilet paper goes into a septic or flush toilet (EPA, p. 6). - Learn poison oak and stinging nettle before you wipe with any leaf. Wipe front to back and wash your hands (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 18, p. 10).

🧺 What paper is, and fibers that work Paper is "a composition of linen, cotton, or other vegetable fibre reduced to powder and then combined with size, which is a kind of glue" (Leland, p. 112). 🔥 Cooking fiber soft Boiling in alkali removes grease, dirt and the "cementing substances" around the fibers; linen rags lose a fifth to a third of their weight (Watt, p. 45). ⚠ Lye "can cause blindness if splashed into the eye" (Practical Action, p. 1): gloves, long sleeves, goggles, children away, no aluminum (CAWST, p. 2); flush splashes with plenty of water. Wet lime is caustic too (rule of thumb). 1. Liquor: wood-ash lye ("Soap from fat and ashes" in the Make-Do guide); potash "affects but slightly" the fiber itself (Watt, p. 19). Or slaked lime, gentler on fine rags (p. 50), which helps pulp "felt together better" (Lime circular, p. 25). 2. How much: mills used about 5 lb of lime and 3 lb of soda ash per 100 lb of rags (Watt, p. 49), under 1 oz of lime and ½ oz of washing soda per pound (arithmetic). For ash lye, thin egg-floating lye with about 4 parts water (rule of thumb). 3. Simmer until a fiber pulls apart easily in your fingers, the old test for "tender" rags (Watt, p. 147). Mills boiled 2-6 hours under steam pressure (p. 49); an open pot takes half a day or more (rule of thumb). 4. Rinse until the water runs clear and the fiber stops feeling slippery, "until free of soda" (Lime circular 337, p. 92). Gloves on until

or more (rule of thumb). 4. Rinse until the water runs clear and the fiber stops feeling slippery, "until free of soda" (Lime circular 337, p. 92). Gloves on until then. 5. No fuel? Old mills retted rags, piling them damp until tender, with "considerable loss of fibre" to rot (Watt, p. 147).

🔨 Beating fiber into pulp - It is slow. Stamping rods took "forty pairs of stamps for twenty-four hours to produce one hundredweight of paper" (Watt, pp. 147-148). Pound wet fiber with a wooden mallet on a hardwood block, or in a mortar as Leland does (p. 159); plan on an hour or more for a few dozen sheets (rule of thumb). - Don't chop fibers short: cut fiber makes paper that "will be tender" (weak). Long pulp makes strong paper, shorter pulp fine writing paper; grasses beat in half the time of rags (Watt, p. 129). - Ready when a pinch shaken in a jar of water makes an even cloud (rule of thumb): "a fine paste, not ... lumpy and stringy, but soft" (Leland, p. 113).

🪟 The mould, deckle and vat In Watt (pp. 147-149) the mould is a wooden frame "neatly joined at the corners", with ribs a little over an inch apart and fine wires along it, "about fifteen or twenty in an inch". The deckle, a loose frame on top, "must fit very neatly or the edges of the paper will be rough". The vat was a warmed tub "about 5 feet square and 4 feet deep"; felts of wool cloth go between wet sheets. Build a small one (rule of thumb, after Watt): 1. Make two identical frames of straight, dry 1×2 wood, a bit bigger inside than your sheet (about 9 × 12 in for letter paper), corners glued and pegged square. 2. On one (the mould), fit thin ribs about 1 inch apart, flush with the top, and tack fine window screen tight over them (fiberglass, brass or bronze; steel rusts and stains). 3. The other frame is the deckle; it must sit snugly on the screen. Oil or wax all the wood. 4. Vat: a washtub or tote longer than the mould. Felts: two dozen pieces of wool blanket or flannel. Two matching frames: the mould carries the ribs and tight screen; the deckle sits snugly on top and makes the sheet's edges (a diagram drawn for this guide).
the-mould-deckle-and-vat

📄 Forming, couching, pressing and drying 1. Charge the vat with clean water and pulp, and stir before every sheet to keep it "uniformly mixed" (Watt, p. 148). More pulp, thicker sheets (rule of thumb). 2. Dip the mould with its deckle and lift "as much of the pulp as will form a sheet of paper" (same page). 3. Hold it level as it drains, "otherwise ... the sheet of paper would be thicker on one part than another". Shake gently front to back, then side to side, "propelling the pulp in four directions" (p. 149). Lift off the deckle. 4. Couch (say "cooch"): turn the mould face down onto a damp felt, press, and lift it away. Lay another felt on top; keep stacking felt, sheet, felt (same page). 5. Press hard: the mill used "a very powerful press" (same page); at home, boards above and below and a car jack under a beam, a cider press or heavy stones (rule of thumb). Then take the sheets off the felts, press them gently to remove felt marks, and next day separate and press once more (same page). 6. Dry slowly, hung over lines; cow-hair ropes "do not stain the paper" (p. 150), and slow loft drying was thought best (p. 145). In wet winters, dry indoors away from direct stove heat (rule of thumb). 7. Smooth: mills "hot-pressed" sheets
forming-couching-pressing-and-drying

paper" (p. 150), and slow loft drying was thought best (p. 145). In wet winters, dry indoors away from direct stove heat (rule of thumb). 7. Smooth: mills "hot-pressed" sheets between pasteboards with hot iron plates (p. 150); a warm flatiron over a cloth does the same (rule of thumb). Dip, shake level, couch onto a damp felt, then stack felt, sheet, felt and press hard (a diagram drawn for this guide). | Problem | Likely cause | | Thick and thin patches | Mould not held level (Watt, p. 149) | | Rough, ragged edges | Deckle too loose (p. 148) | | Weak paper that tears | Fibers chopped too short (p. 129) | | Ink spreads like on a blotter | Not sized yet (p. 136) | | Sheet sticks to the screen | Pulp too thin, or mould not pressed firmly onto the felt (rule of thumb) | 📚 Go deeper: Watt, ch. 🧴 Sizing: making paper take ink On unsized paper a pen stroke "would spread in all directions" (Watt, p. 136). Starch stirred into the pulp won't fix it: blotting paper is made "with starch alone" (p. 199). Hand-made paper was dipped in gelatine size after drying (p. 150). - Size from hide scraps: cover clean skin clippings with water and hold at 180-190 °F, "very important that the liquid should not actually boil", for 12-16 hours (pp. 140-141). Skim, strain, and stir in dissolved alum, which "greatly improves its sizing property, besides preserving it" (p. 141); more in warm weather (p. 143). Hide scraps and alum: Clothing & Leather guide. - Quicker: boil "clean parchment cuttings until they form a clear solution" and strain through muslin (Henley's, p. 508), or use "1 ounce of good glue in 1 pint of hot water" (Household Discoveries, p. 271). - Sizing: warm the size to lukewarm (Watt, p. 143); lay dry sheets in one at a time, each evenly wet; press out the extra, separate, press again, dry slowly (p. 150). - Thin paper needs stronger size. Sizing is "one of the most difficult and uncertain" jobs, upset by heat and damp (p. 143): test a few sheets first. - Starch brushed on the surface helps: bond paper was surface-sized with starch, "an additional barrier against the penetration of the ink" (NBS Inks,

143): test a few sheets first. - Starch brushed on the surface helps: bond paper was surface-sized with starch, "an additional barrier against the penetration of the ink" (NBS Inks, p. 39). Brush thin cooked starch onto dry sheets (rule of thumb). - Size and starch feed silverfish (Leland, p. 144); a few drops of clove or other essential oil keep paste from molding (Household Discoveries, p. 59).
