♻ Recycling scrap paper, cardboard and mending Re-pulping: tear scraps small and soak them a long time, changing the water now and then; pound the soft mass in a mortar, boil it, and "to give it consistency, add flour-paste or gum" (Leland, p. 159). - Handwritten paper is easier than print: "a little soda-ash will discharge ordinary writing ink", but printer's ink is carbon and leaves grey pulp (Watt, p. 104), fine for wrapping, card and the outhouse. Mills used 10-20 lb of soda ash per 100 lb of paper, boiled 12-24 hours (p. 105). Washing soda: "Laundry" in the Make-Do guide. - Cardboard: paste sheets together with size, or lay several wet sheets on each other as you couch (Watt, p. 200). Leland's paste for it has "a little alum and glue and a few drops of oil of cloves" to stop souring (p. 151). Papier-mâché: newspaper strips in flour paste, several layers, dried in the sun (A Book for Midwives, ch. 25, p. 6). - Mending: fill holes with pulp worked to a fine paste (Leland, p. 113); patch tears with thin paper and a paste of ½ tsp each starch and flour cooked thick with boiling water, which "will not mold or discolor paper" (Lee's, p. 204). - Waxed paper: rub paper on a hot iron plate with beeswax (Henley's, pp. 507-508). Dirty pages: rub with stale

which "will not mold or discolor paper" (Lee's, p. 204). - Waxed paper: rub paper on a hot iron plate with beeswax (Henley's, pp. 507-508). Dirty pages: rub with stale bread (Household Discoveries, p. 60).

✒ Iron-gall ink Iron and tannin from galls make a pale ink that the air turns black (NBS Inks, p. 7); it "turned black on the paper" (Household Discoveries, p. 416), darkest in about a week (NBS, p. 26). - Tannin: oak galls (the old imported kind held 60-70% tannic acid); crush, steep "in hot, not boiling, water", and strain (Household Discoveries, p. 416). Also sumac leaves (Practical Action, p. 4), tanoak bark, "high tannin content" (Tanoak guide, p. 2), and walnut hulls or maple bark (Trapper manual, p. 46). Local tribes blackened basket material with fresh oak bark, water and rusty nails (Chesnut, p. 354). - Iron: "rusty nails and a cupful of vinegar" in a bucket of water for "a couple of weeks" (Practical Action, p. 4), or iron filings in ½ gallon of vinegar for several days, some always left undissolved (USDA FB 1334, p. 19). - Copperas (green vitriol) is iron sulfate and "contains no copper"; blue vitriol (bluestone) is copper sulfate. Don't mix them up (NBS, p. 36). Good copperas is pale green; rusty means air has spoiled it, so keep it tightly closed (p. 20). The balance matters. Government record ink has about 31 g of tannin (tannic plus gallic acid) to 30 g of iron sulfate per liter (NBS, p. 13), about 1 oz of each per quart (arithmetic). With too little tannin,
iron-gall-ink

g of tannin (tannic plus gallic acid) to 30 g of iron sulfate per liter (NBS, p. 13), about 1 oz of each per quart (arithmetic). With too little tannin, writing "may become rusty in a comparatively few years" (p. 26); iron sulfate "caused decided weakening of the paper", tannin did not (p. 35), and some old manuscripts have crumbled to their margins (p. 34). When unsure, use less iron. With galls and copperas (Household Discoveries, p. 417): 2 oz crushed galls, 1 oz gum arabic, 1 oz copperas, 16 oz soft water; stand 2 weeks, shaking often. That is about 1.3 oz tannin to 1 oz copperas, close to the government balance (arithmetic). Leave out the "5 grains of corrosive sublimate" the book adds: it is mercury. Use a few cloves. In a glass jar, add iron water a spoonful at a time, testing a stroke on paper after each; stop when the strokes dry dark and stop improving. 🖤 Soot ink and other inks Carbon ink is the oldest: lampblack (soot) or charcoal held in glue, gelatin or gum; India-ink cakes are that paste dried, then rubbed with water (NBS Inks, p. 7). Carbon "cannot be bleached by any amount of exposure to intense light" (p. 37) and is unlikely to harm paper (p. 38). Homemade India ink (Household Discoveries, p. 419): boil an old kid glove (or a clean hide scrap) "until it forms a thick size"; hold a cold plate in a candle flame and, while it is still warm, mix the soot with the size. Test: let lines dry bone dry and sponge them. "If the ink runs, it is of poor quality." - Grind it fine and stir before each dip; coarse carbon settles (NBS, pp. 37-38). Never mix it with iron-gall ink: acid makes the carbon settle (p. 38). - A tenth part glycerine keeps India ink liquid (Henley's, p. 409); it works better with a brush than a steel pen (p. 408). - Printing ink is carbon in boiled linseed or nut oil (Household Discoveries, p. 422). The Wintu and other tribes "used the soot from burnt oak galls to make tattoos" (Tanoak guide, p. 2). - Sumac ink: "The berries and leaves of red or staghorn sumac boiled together in water make a permanent black ink" (Seton, p. 334). The Navajo

(Tanoak guide, p. 2). - Sumac ink: "The berries and leaves of red or staghorn sumac boiled together in water make a permanent black ink" (Seton, p. 334). The Navajo dyed black with three-leaved sumac (Navajo Native Dyes, p. 67), but three leaflets is also poison oak: pick no three-leaflet shrub unless someone who knows both shows you (rule of thumb). - Berry juice fades: dyes "have the unfortunate habit of fading" (NBS, p. 7), fine for children's pictures. Invisible ink: fresh milk shows when gently heated (Household Discoveries, p. 420).

🧊 Keeping ink, and bringing back faded writing - Mold: "a little alcohol or a few drops of any essential oil or a few cloves will prevent mold"; thin thickened ink with water or strained strong coffee (Household Discoveries, p. 422). - Air spoils ink: keep bottles nearly full, corked and dark (NBS, pp. 23-24). Make small batches; a two-year supply may end up "too full of sediment" (p. 24). - Freezing: a little alcohol prevents it (Household Discoveries, p. 422). Inks frozen solid at about 0 °F came back when thawed and shaken, and no bottle broke; they were about ⅚ full (NBS, p. 25; arithmetic). Leave headroom and keep ink indoors in frost (rule of thumb). Restoring faded iron-gall writing. It leaves rust in the strokes, so it can be brought back (faded dye ink leaves "literally nothing behind", NBS, pp. 32-33). "A 2- or 3-percent solution of tannic acid", or gall tea, turns the rust black: "by far the best treatment" (p. 33; Household Discoveries, p. 422). 1. Brush it on softly, or trace the letters with a pen dipped in it; rinse briefly in clean water and dry, or the whole sheet darkens in time (p. 33). 2. Try a corner first. For a treasured paper, think twice: NBS advised against treating the Declaration of Independence (p. 34). 📚 Go deeper: NBS Circular 426 Inks -

33). 2. Try a corner first. 🪶 Pens: reed, quill and brush Reed or bamboo pen (VITA, p. 360): 1. Take dry bamboo or stiff reed about 6 in × ⅜ in. Whittle one end to width and shave it thin so it flexes, keeping the tip on the hard outer side. 2. Cut the tip straight across, then shape it "by gently writing on the sandpaper with the dry pen". 3. For an ink hole, rest the knife point at least ⅛ in up from the tip and twist to drill a hole about 3/32 in. 4. For a reservoir pen, bind a thin bamboo cover plate on with a rubber band or fine wire (p. 361). The reservoir pen: the tip cut from the hard outer side of the bamboo, and a thin notched cover plate bound on to hold more ink (VITA, p. 361). Quill pen (rule of thumb; no book here shows how): take a big goose or turkey wing feather; soak the barrel, harden it in hot sand for a minute, strip the lower barbs and scrape off the outer skin and inner pith. Cut a long scoop on the underside, a short slit up the point, and trim the tip square and thin. Recut it as it wears. Brush: India ink "applies well with a brush" (Henley's, p. 408). A gold nib "cannot be rusted" by any ink (NBS, p.

square and thin. Recut it as it wears. Brush: India ink "applies well with a brush" (Henley's, p. 408). A gold nib "cannot be rusted" by any ink (NBS, p. 18).

✏ Pencils, charcoal, chalk and slates - Hoard pencils. An 1871 traveler gave up ink (it dries, clogs and corrodes pens) and "trusted simply to the powers of a good HH. pencil" (Shifts and Expedients, pp. 31-32). Pencil "lead" is graphite and clay, "not lead (the metal)" (Kuphaldt, p. 97). - Don't make real lead pencils from melted lead in reeds, as an old book does (Shifts, p. 217). Lead fumes poison: never melt lead indoors, and keep children away (ODFW, p. 27). - Sharpener: a block with coarse sandpaper on one side and fine on the other (Household Discoveries, p. 62). - Charcoal: a burnt stick marks well enough to lay out a tepee (Seton, p. 467). For drawing sticks, char peeled willow twigs in a tin with a nail hole, like char cloth ("Fire and light without stores" in the Make-Do guide), in the stove during fire season (rule of thumb). - Soapstone, chalk and slate pencils mark iron (ICS, p. 55). Stop smudging with "a light wash of gum of any kind, diluted varnish, or even milk" (Leland, p. 259). Slates save paper. Children learned their tables "upon their slates or on the blackboard" (Ray's Primary, p. 11); a "stick or chalk board" is a toddler's toy (WHO/UNICEF, p. 2); a kitchen slate keeps the list of supplies running low (Household Discoveries, p. 69). - Blackboard paint:

11); a "stick or chalk board" is a toddler's toy (WHO/UNICEF, p. 2); a kitchen slate keeps the list of supplies running low (Household Discoveries, p. 69). - Blackboard paint: 1 lb shellac in 1 gal alcohol, with 4 oz each of fine lampblack, powdered emery and ultramarine (Henley's, p. 491). Lacking those, a smooth dark board or flat stone takes chalk or soapstone (rule of thumb). - Wax tablet: a shallow tray of beeswax, written on with a point and smoothed to erase (rule of thumb); beeswax takes "any sharp-pointed instrument" (Household Discoveries, p. 421). - Birch bark: no book here covers it, and paper birch is not a valley tree (rule of thumb). 📚 Keeping paper and books from mold - Damp breeds "molds and fungi". Keep books on "open, airy, well-lighted shelves"; after a wet spell wipe the covers and set them "in the sun or before a fire for a few hours"; camphor, wrapped in paper, in closed boxes (Henley's, p. 127). In our wet winters, check monthly (rule of thumb). - Light and damp age writing; mold destroys "both ink and paper" (NBS, p. 27). Store records dry and dark, off the floor and away from outside walls (rule of thumb). - Insects: oil of lavender or cedar on the shelves; silverfish "loves starch" (Household Discoveries, p. 59). - Records that must last: soot ink or balanced iron-gall ink on rag paper, never berry or dye ink (NBS, pp. 7, 37).

🧻 Toilet paper alternatives: water, cloth, leaves, cobs There are two ways: wash ("typically ... 0.5-3 litres", about 2 cups to 3 quarts) or wipe with "paper, leaves, corncobs, rags or stones" (Compendium, p. 10; arithmetic). Agree as a household what you'll use, and plan a supply that lasts (Sphere, p. 143). Water: pour from a squeeze bottle or jug with one hand and wash with the other, then wash your hands with soap (rule of thumb). The wash water carries feces: keep it out of the urine bucket; small amounts may soak into the soil (EcoSanRes, p. 38). Pour-flush toilets suit water-washers (Hesperian ch. 7, p. 35). Cloth wipes ("family cloth") belong to one person each: shared towels spread disease (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 153; pink eye, Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 16, p. 3). Cut soft cotton (flannel, old T-shirts) 6-8 inches square, a day's worth plus spares each; many families use cloth for urine only (rule of thumb). Used cloths go in a lidded bucket ("Toilet paper alternatives" in the Make-Do guide). Wash them like cloth diapers: 1. Rinse in cold water, then wash with soap ("Menstrual pads and diapers" in the Make-Do guide). 2. Wash above 140 °F, or soak in 0.05% bleach (about 2 Tbsp of 6% bleach per gallon): "Dishes, laundry and periods" and the bleach-strength table in the Sanitation guide. 3. A

above 140 °F, or soak in 0.05% bleach (about 2 Tbsp of 6% bleach per gallon): "Dishes, laundry and periods" and the bleach-strength table in the Sanitation guide. 3. A little vinegar in the last rinse, as for diapers (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 15, p. 23). Dry in full sun. 4. Wash water goes to the latrine or wastewater system, not the garden (Oregon DEQ, p. 12), and never into a creek. Wash a sick person's cloths separately, with bleach (rule of thumb). Leaves: no book in the library recommends any particular leaf for wiping. Leaves are a normal choice (Compendium, p. 29), but which leaf is up to you. Rub a new one on your inner arm and wait a day before trusting it (rule of thumb). - ⚠ Poison oak: "leaves of three, let it be"; vine or shrub, "all over low elevation in western Oregon"; "the roots and stems also contain the oil" (OSU EM 9184, p. 24). "All parts, at all times of the year" cause the rash, bare winter stems too (FM 3-05.70, p. 514). "for hours or cause blisters" (OSU EM 9373, p. 2). - Thimbleberry (rule of thumb): big soft leaves on "a thornless, wideleaved shrub, 3 to 8 feet high, with showy white flowers" (Chesnut, p. 369), in forest shade (OSU EC 1306, p. 4). - Mullein (rule of thumb): first-year rosettes of "wooly basal leaves" on roadsides and dry open ground (USFS PNW-GTR-513, p. 131); gentle enough to put on wounds (AFH 10-644, p. 90), but the hairs bother some people (rule of thumb). 🧼 Wiping, handwashing and children - Wipe from front to back: "Wiping forward can spread germs, amebas, or worms into the urinary opening and vagina" (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 18, p. 10; Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 10, p. 7). - Teach children "to wipe or wash carefully, and to wash their hands after using the toilet. Girls especially should be taught to wipe from front to back"; wash babies after they defecate (Hesperian ch. 7, p. 11). - Wash hands after the toilet and after cleaning up anyone else (OSU, p. 4), with soap "or an alternative such as ash" (Sphere, p. 143). Put a tippy tap by every toilet ("Handwashing and water for hygiene" in the Sanitation guide).
wiping-handwashing-and-children

🧣 Handkerchiefs, towels and reusing paper - Handkerchiefs, not tissues. Someone with a cold "should cover his nose and mouth when he coughs or sneezes, and wash his hands often", and should not blow but "just wipe" the nose (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 13, p. 13). Each person keeps their own, washed hot like cloth wipes (rule of thumb). - Flour sacks make dish towels and dishcloths (Household Discoveries, p. 68); hem old sheets into napkins (rule of thumb). - Paper bags wrap things, then wipe up milk or grease and go in the fire; waxed box liners wrap cheese and lunches (p. 67). Newspaper goes under carpets, wraps woolens against moths and covers plants on frosty nights (p. 68); damp, it polishes windows (p. 275). - Paper too far gone: shred it for the bucket toilet, or burn clean paper in the cooking fire, never in the open June to October ("Garbage, sickroom and birth waste" in the Sanitation guide).

🎒 On Foot: Backpacking and Travel When the Roads Are Empty With no fuel and no car, walking is how a household reaches Grants Pass, the coast, family or a trade. This guide covers planning, loads and packs, feet, water and food on the move, camp, wildlife, cold rivers, snowy passes and staying safe on the road. Miles, travel days and route files are in other guides, and this one links to them. Its new books are in Southern-Oregon\Travel-On-Foot: the Army's Military Mountaineering (TC 3-97.61, 2025) and Foot Marches (ATP 3-21.18, 2017), Horace Kephart's Camping and Woodcraft (1916, two volumes), ODF's fire-season rules, OSU's poison-oak bulletin and a National Park Service trip planner. The older Foot Marches (FM 21-18) and Knapik's Load Carriage are in Southern-Oregon\Bicycles-Carts\Trailers-Carts; the Air Force survival handbook (AFH 10-644, the whole book despite "Signaling" in its file name) is in Southern-Oregon\Comms-Signals\Visual-Sound-Signals. ### The short version - Cold rivers kill. Wade alone only where it is knee-deep or less and the current mild (TC 3-97.61, p. 345). Unbuckle hip and chest straps first (p. 344), never tie yourself to a rope, and "if in doubt, turn back or wait for help" (NPS North Cascades, p. 1). Oregon rivers stay "dangerously cold" in warm weather (OSMB, p. 17). - Feet first. Cover a hot spot the minute you feel it (Knapik, p. 49); change socks at noon and

rivers stay "dangerously cold" in warm weather (OSMB, p. 17). - Feet first. Cover a hot spot the minute you feel it (Knapik, p. 49); change socks at noon and never "walk them dry" (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 144-145). - Carry less: plan family loads on 10-20 kg (22-44 lb) (World Bank, p. 65). - Plan by time, not miles: about 15 miles a day on roads (what the walking-routes tool assumes), plus an hour per 1,000 ft of climb (FM 3-97.6, p. 72). Late December has only about 9 hours of daylight (arithmetic). - Water: 2-4 quarts a day when cool, 4-8 in the mountains, never over 1¼ quarts an hour (NY hunter manual, p. 81; FM 3-97.6, p. 17; FM 21-10, p. 56). Treat every drop. - No fires in fire season. ODF's 2026 rules ban "campfires, cooking fires and warming fires" from May 15 (ODF closure, p. 1). Eat cold, or use a stove in a cleared spot. - Leave a written plan; turn back early. Leaving "a safe shelter to travel in adverse weather conditions is foolhardy" (AFH, p. 427). And "Travelling alone is dangerous" (p. 426).

Distance, hills and daylight - Miles and days from Cave Junction are in "Travel times from Cave Junction" in the Bicycles & Carts guide and "Walking out" in the Start Here guide; print directions and maps from Walking-Routes\WALKING-ROUTES.html. All assume 15 miles a day with a pack. - Hills: the Bicycles guide has the Army rule (a third more distance, an hour per 1,000 ft up). Checks: 800 ft of climb an hour "is good work", and "If you cannot talk without catching your breath ... you are going too fast" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 146); distances are "reduced by half over average gradients of 10 percent" (🖼 FM 21-18, p. 66). - The first days are hardest: stiff legs on day two; poor sleep, constipation and sore feet by day three (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 142-143). Make the first days 8-10 miles (rule of thumb). - Daylight at Cave Junction (arithmetic, 42° N): about 9 hours on December 21, 10 in mid-November and late January, 12 at the equinoxes, 15¼ on June 21. A 15-mile day takes 7½-8 hours with rests, so plan 10-12 miles in midwinter. Start looking for camp "at least two hours before sunset" (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 212). - Season: snow can fall in any month above 5,000 ft, and flash floods run "many miles downstream" of the rain (FM 3-97.6, p. 15). Choosing a route Where there are no bridges, "keep away from streams and follow the ridges between them" (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 49-50), and "Travel on trails rather than taking shortcuts through the brush" (AFH, p. 446). The library's back-road routes climb high Forest Service roads, such as Grayback Road (FR 4611) toward Grants Pass and Medford and Sanger Peak Road (FR 4803) toward Crescent City; US-199 stays lower. The route files give no heights, so read each climb off a topo map (rule of thumb) ("Reading a topo map" in the Navigation guide). No book on the drive gives camping limits on public land; the Forest Service has long allowed about 14 days in one spot (rule of thumb).
choosing-a-route

The plan you leave behind, and when to turn back Leave a note "stating departure time, destination, route of travel, personal condition, and available supplies", and carry "sufficient water to reach the next probable water source" (AFH, p. 427). The NPS trip-plan form is in "Getting un-lost" in the Navigation guide. Turn-around rules to write on the plan (rule of thumb): 1. A turn-around time: if you aren't at the pass, ford or planned camp by then, go back. 2. A river above the knee, or rising: "Not every river or stream can be crossed safely" (TC 3-97.61, p. 351). 3. Snow above the knee on a pass and no snowshoes; smoke or a fire column ahead; a hot east wind in fire season. 4. Water down to half with no sure source ahead; someone hurt, sick or limping; a checkpoint that says no.

Caches "Bears will demolish any such pile [of stones] that one man could build." Hang the bundle from a peeled pole between two trees 15-20 ft up, trees "too slender for a bear to climb, yet too stout for him to shake" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 233). Hide damp-proof things under an old, half-buried log, away from camp so one raid or fire doesn't take both (p. 236). Dried food needs a "completely waterproof" container (AFH, p. 369).

To get fit, add load or distance, "but not at the same time" (FM 21-18, p. 80). Children, elders and the injured: - The slowest walker sets the pace (AFH, p. 428). For children, "avoid long distances" and keep "a good easy pace, say two or three miles an hour" (Boy Scouts 1911, p. 173). - No book on the drive gives loads for children or older people. Start a child at about a tenth of body weight and a frail adult at 10-15 lb, and adjust by day two (rule of thumb). Past frostbite or trench foot makes it likelier again (FM 21-18, p. 106). - Carrying someone: two poles through a blanket, jackets or sacks; with no poles, roll a blanket in from both sides and grip the rolls (FM 4-25.11, pp. 211-212). Use four carriers who swap often (rule of thumb). To fetch help, "Send two people if possible" (AFH, p. 426). - Animals, carts, sleds: "Travel and packing" in the Horse guide; donkeys of 100-110 kg "regularly carry loads of 25-50 kg over distances of up to 20 km" (Starkey, p. 82). 🚶 Pace, rests and walking technique The day's rhythm. On roads this guide follows FM 21-18; on steep trails and in cold, the newer books' shorter stops. 1. Start in fewer layers, a little chilly (AFH, p. 428); stop to fix laces, straps and layers in the first half hour (ATP 3-21.18, p. 25). 2. On roads: rest 15 minutes after the first 45, then 10 in every hour, feet up (FM 21-18, p. 48). 3. On steep trails and in cold: "shorter breaks taken more often are better ... especially in colder weather" (TC 3-97.61, p. 109); "Long halts eat up daylight; they stiffen the muscles; and they cause chills" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 142). Lean the pack on a tree or bank. 4. At any long stop, put on a layer: "It is much easier to keep a warm body warm" (ATP, p. 25). 5. Halfway: a 15-minute stop in which everyone changes socks (FM 21-18, p. 91). - Uphill: slow and steady, zigzagging rather than charging straight up (TC 3-97.61, p. 107). The rest step: pause on the straight rear leg, "so the bone, not muscle, supports the weight" (ATP, p. 25; 🖼 TC 3-97.61, p. 108). - Downhill: bend the knees; "Even one pole can be very helpful". Go straight down scree in short shuffling steps, heels dug in; never walk below someone on a loose

- Downhill: bend the knees; "Even one pole can be very helpful". Go straight down scree in short shuffling steps, heels dug in; never walk below someone on a loose slope (TC 3-97.61, p. 109). - Heat: don't march "at the hottest time of day" (FM 21-18, p. 61); 3½ mph with 40 lb or more is "hard work" (FM 21-10, p. 57). Heat illness: "Heat and cold in the Valley" in the Field Care guide. Drop no wrappers; they tell others who passed (FM 21-18, p. 84). The rest step: after each step, pause on the straight rear leg so bone, not muscle, holds the weight; lower row, the same with a stick or ice axe (TC 3-97.61, p. 108).

Fitting and loading a pack - The hips carry the load: "A waistband will support 80 to 90 percent of the weight" cinched "around the pelvic girdle" (AFH, p. 454); in one test a frame and wide hip belt cut shoulder pressure from 203 to 15 mm Hg (Knapik, p. 31). - Heavy things close to your back, balanced side to side; high on easy ground, lower on rough ground ("low or midway"); rain gear and first aid on top (AFH, p. 453; TC 3-97.61, p. 156). - Nothing dangling: "flip-flops" and "stick-outs" snag in brush and can throw you off a log bridge; the best pack is one roomy sack holding everything (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 126). - Adjust at every rest (AFH, p. 450). Numb, tingling arms ("rucksack palsy"): move the straps or use a frame and hip belt (Knapik, p. 47). Lift a heavy packboard by sitting against it and rolling to your knees; never drop it (Packboard, p. 1).
fitting-and-loading-a-pack

Boots and socks - Fit: a thumb's width past the big toe, and a finger under the unlaced tongue (🖼 FM 21-18, pp. 107-108). Pressure means too small, rubbing too big. Carry spare laces (p. 109). - Break boots in before the trip, alternating with an old pair and taping known hot spots (ATP 3-21.18, p. 110). Dry them slowly with a warm cloth inside; on freezing nights keep them in the sleeping bag (FM 21-18, p. 107). Resoling: "Boots, shoes and moccasins" in the Clothing guide. - Socks: "The wool cushion-sole sock is best"; dry damp ones inside your shirt (FM 21-18, p. 109). A thin nylon or polyester liner under the wool cuts blisters (Knapik, p. 48). - Wet feet: stop "and wring out the hose; do not 'walk them dry'" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 144). No dry socks left: grass insoles an inch thick, made fresh daily (AFH, p. 191).
boots-and-socks

Blisters Prevention: two socks, good insoles, a lighter load, distance built up slowly, and "Cover skin when hot spots appear" (Knapik, p. 47). A hot spot is "a localized warm or burning sensation"; cover it with moleskin or tape at once (p. 49). Draining: the books disagree. TC 3-97.61 says "Never drain blisters unless" infected (p. 49); FM 21-18 drains all of them (p. 102); Knapik leaves small ones and drains big ones on weight-bearing spots (p. 50). This guide follows Knapik: 1. Small (under 5 mm, about 3/16 in) and not painful: leave it whole, inside a doughnut of moleskin (Knapik, p. 52). 2. Big and tight on the sole or heel: wash around it, flame a needle, prick it at the edge, press the fluid out and leave the skin on; cover past the edges (🖼 FM 21-18, p. 102). 3. Torn open: take off the loose roof and treat it as a wound (Knapik, p. 51); see "Wounds and infection when there's no hospital" in Field Care. 4. Spreading redness or pus: infection, which can become cellulitis or blood poisoning (Knapik, p. 48). Rest the foot. For a big, tight blister on the sole or heel (step 2): clean it, flame the needle, prick it at the edge, and cover it with the skin left on (FM 21-18, p. 102).
blisters

Trench foot and frostbite - Trench foot comes from days in wet, cold boots at 32-50 °F, sitting or standing still, laced tight (FM 21-18, p. 106): an ordinary valley winter. Early on, feet are pale, numb and not painful, so check each other. Prevent it with dry socks and boots daily; in wet boots, wiggle the toes. Treat gently: feet "should not be rubbed or massaged"; clean, dry, raise, and carry the person (same page). Mild cases heal with about 24 hours of drying (TC 3-97.61, p. 54). - Frostbite (high passes in winter): warm small spots with body heat, hands in armpits, bare feet on a companion's chest; no massage, fire or snow (FM 21-18, p. 105). Don't thaw deep frostbite on the trail: "it is safer to walk on frozen feet" (p. 106).
trench-foot-and-frostbite

A daily foot routine | When | What | Source | | Before the trip | Toenails "short and square, and straight across"; boots broken in | 🖼 FM 21-18, p. 100 | | Each morning | Clean, dry, powdered feet; tape known hot spots | p. 101 | | At halts | One boot off at a time; rub, powder, dry socks; loosen laces over the arch | ATP, p. 110 | | Evening | Wash feet and dry them well; dry socks and boots; look for red, swollen spots | Kephart Vol. 2, p. 144; ATP, p. 110 | Rub healthy feet only. A stress fracture needs two or three weeks of rest (FM 21-18, p. 107).

🧥 Clothing, cold and heat What to wear is in "Dressing for our cold-wet winters" in the Clothing guide. On the trail: - Three layers: one next to the skin that moves sweat, an insulating one, and a wind-and-rain shell. Wool "provides warmth when wet"; soaked clothing loses heat "several hundred times faster" than dry; cotton is a poor choice (NY hunter manual, p. 77). - Start cool; "Do not sit around when overheated and damp ... But do not muffle up on the march" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 145). Dry underwear and socks at night "are as warm as an extra blanket" (p. 104). Carry spare socks, hat and gloves, and a poncho or "extra-large plastic trash bag" (TC 3-97.61, p. 73). - Hypothermia creeps up from wet brush, wind and "Resting against cold surfaces"; chocolate, peanuts or raisins help (NY hunter manual, p. 82). Heat: a hat and light clothing that covers the skin (p. 77). Treatment of both: Field Care. Smoke: the Wildfire guide.
clothing-cold-and-heat

too much plain water dilutes the blood's salt (Field Care). - Don't eat snow: it "will contribute to loss of body heat" (TC 3-97.61, p. 46). Running short? "physical activity must be reduced" (p. 75); walk in the cool hours (rule of thumb).

Finding, carrying and treating water - Finding: streams, springs, rain; a short tube fills a bottle from a trickle off rock; "Water is scarce above the timberline" (TC 3-97.61, p. 75). By a muddy pond, dig a hole "about 18 inches across and down about 6 inches below water-level, a few paces from the pond", bail it three times, then take the clearer water (Seton, p. 292). Still treat it. Summer ridges are dry: plan refills at creeks and springs on the topo map (rule of thumb). - Skip water below farms or mine tailings (TC 3-97.61, p. 75). "Never drink from the well of an abandoned farm" (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 214); "It is not true that running water purifies itself" (p. 213). - Carrying: wide-mouth bottles; bladders "can break and have freezing issues" (TC 3-97.61, p. 73). Sleep with your water on freezing nights (p. 75). - Treating: "Virtually all surface waters are microbiologically contaminated", and Giardia and Cryptosporidium "thrive in domestic and wild animals" (TC 3-97.61, p. 75). A 1-minute boil kills them; tablets miss Crypto and work slower in cold water; many filters don't stop viruses (p. 76). Methods: "Step 3 - Kill the germs" and "After a wildfire" in the Water Purification guide.
finding-carrying-and-treating-water

🍞 Food on the move - How much: a loaded march burns over 300 calories an hour (FM 21-18, p. 65); Kephart lists 3,400 a day for moderate work, 4,150 hard, 5,500 very hard (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 185), against everyday adult needs of 1,600-3,000 (Dietary Guidelines, p. 152). Plan 3,000-4,000 calories, about 2 lb of dry food, per person per walking day (arithmetic). - Calories per pound: fat about 4,080 and butter 3,410 (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 185); parched corn 1,915, cornmeal 1,655, bread 1,205 (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 159). Fresh food would be "five or six pounds a day" (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 182). - Carry one extra day's food (TC 3-97.61, p. 74). Eat little and often: 25-75 g of carbohydrate an hour in four bits (ATP, p. 106). Parched corn (pinole), the lightest trail food in the library: 1. Parch dry corn "in clean hot ashes until it bursts", sift it, and pound it to meal (Parker, p. 118). 2. Stir it into water, "one tablespoonful to a pint" (same page). Two heaping tablespoons with raisins or chocolate made Kephart "a square meal" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 158). 3. Go easy: it swells. A handful (2 or 3 oz) was "even considered dangerous unless cooked" (Parker, p. 119). Make at home before you leave: jerky and pemmican ("Jerky and pemmican" in Preserving Food), hardtack ("Staples" in
food-on-the-move

or 3 oz) was "even considered dangerous unless cooked" (Parker, p. 119). Make at home before you leave: jerky and pemmican ("Jerky and pemmican" in Preserving Food), hardtack ("Staples" in Food From Scratch) and dried fruit. A fist-size piece of pemmican "would make a meal for two men" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 160). Eat lean jerky with fat and grain, not alone (rule of thumb). Little fuel: in fire season, plan no-fire meals or a legal stove (rule of thumb). A broad, shallow pot "boils water much sooner"; skip foods that need long boiling (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 106-107). Use a lid: only 10-40% of a fire's heat reaches the pot (Aprovecho, p. 7). In the wet season, burn "dry, dead hardwood no larger than a pencil" for "less smoke" (AFH, p. 563).
food-on-the-move

Choosing a campsite A good site has water; wood if fires are allowed; a level spot "well above any chance overflow" ("Observe the previous flood marks"); "Security against the spread of fire"; morning sun; shelter from winter wind; and privacy (Kephart Vol. 1, p. 213). Move on if the site is: - in a creek bottom, dry streambed or drainage (flash floods), under dead trees or dead limbs, in poison oak, or in a slide path, which shows as a strip of young growth down the slope (AFH, p. 195); - on the valley floor, where cold air pools (AFH, p. 194); camp "up the hillside above the valley floor", clear of rockfall (TC 3-97.61, p. 77); - beside brush, tall grass or boulders where snakes live (FM 3-05.70, p. 530), or on an animal trail (ODFW bears, p. 2).
choosing-a-campsite

Tarp and debris shelters - Tarp or poncho lean-to: back to the wind, a stick or line under the middle so rain can't pool (FM 3-05.70, pp. 69-70). Kephart tied one long side of a 7 × 9-ft cloth to a pole 4 ft up and staked the other out at 45° (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 104-105). More in "Emergency tarp and plastic shelters" in the Shelter guide. - Debris hut, warm with no fire (FM 3-05.70, pp. 82-83): 1. Rest one end of a long ridgepole on a stump, rock or two short stakes, about waist high. 2. Lean sticks along both sides as ribs, wide enough for your body and steep enough to shed rain; lay brush across. 3. Pile dry leaves, needles and grass at least 3 ft thick, "the thicker the better", with branches on top. 4. Put a 1-ft layer inside to lie on, and pull a heap of debris into the doorway behind you. - Off the cold ground: "Don't bed down on the cold, hard earth" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 105). Fir boughs are best, spruce prickly, pine thin (AFH, p. 222). Kephart's 1-lb "bed tick" is a cloth bag stuffed with dry leaves: "A 3-pound blanket on top of such a mattress is warmer than a 5-pound one without it" (p. 106). On snow, use a foam pad (TC 3-97.61, p. 73).
tarp-and-debris-shelters

leaves: "A 3-pound blanket on top of such a mattress is warmer than a 5-pound one without it" (p. 106). On snow, use a foam pad (TC 3-97.61, p. 73). Debris hut: (1) the ridgepole on a stump with ribs along both sides; (2) piled at least 3 ft thick with leaves and brush (FM 3-05.70, p. 83).
tarp-and-debris-shelters

Fire and fire season The law in 2026 (ODF closure, pp. 1-2), on forest land protected by ODF's Southwest Oregon District: - "Open fires are prohibited, including campfires, cooking fires and warming fires", except on private land with the owner's permission at low (GREEN) danger and at designated campgrounds. "Smoking is prohibited while traveling." - Camp stoves on bottled fuel are allowed in areas cleared "for 50 feet in all directions". While traveling, except on state highways, county roads and driveways, carry "one shovel and one gallon of water or one 2½ pound or larger fire extinguisher" (p. 2): on foot, a small shovel and a gallon among your bottles (rule of thumb). - The 2026 closure began May 15; ODF reissues it yearly. Treat June through October as no-fire months whether or not anyone says so (rule of thumb). Illegal outdoor burning can cost $12,000 a day (DEQ, p. 1). Where a fire is allowed (wet season or a legal fire ring): keep it small and off slopes; drown it, stir, and feel the ashes until "all steaming and sizzling stops"; "Never just bury a fire" (ODFW hunter manual, p. 34). Never burn poison oak: the smoke can put people in "intensive care" (OSU PNW 108, p. 4).
fire-and-fire-season

A quiet, hidden camp Kephart's "masked camp" is "invisible from trails, and from opposite ridges", screened by evergreens so smoke and firelight don't show, near a trail but not on it, with dead wood about so there's no noise of chopping, and with the way in and out hidden (Kephart Vol. 2, pp. 237-238). Also BLISS: "Blend in", "Low silhouette", "Irregular shape", "Small", "Secluded location" (FM 3-05.70, p. 68). Toilet: a "cat hole" 6-8 inches deep, at least 200 ft from camp and water (NPS North Cascades, p. 1); more in the Sanitation guide.
a-quiet-hidden-camp

Food storage in bear country - Hang it: ODFW says "at least 10 feet high and 6 to 10 feet from a tree trunk" (ODFW bears, p. 2); BLM on the Rogue says twelve feet "between two trees and six feet from tree trunks" (BLM, p. 16). Use 10-12 ft up and 6 ft out, on a line between two trees, with food, pots, garbage and anything scented. Carry at least 50 ft of cord (NPS North Cascades, p. 1). - "Sleep at least 100 yards from cooking and eating areas"; no food, soap or lotion in the tent; "Do not bury garbage-bears will dig it up"; "Avoid berry patches"; "Don't hike after dark" (ODFW bears, p. 2). Hang food, pots, garbage and anything scented 10-12 ft up and at least 6 ft from the trunks, on a line between two trees (a diagram drawn for this guide).
food-storage-in-bear-country

Poison oak, ticks and rattlesnakes 📷 Is that poison oak? Photograph it with the plant identifier (🔧 Tools tab). Leaves of three, let them be, whatever it says. - Poison oak is common in western Oregon in brush, woods, clearcuts, stream banks and canyons, as a shrub or vine, usually with three leaflets, red in fall (OSU PNW 108, pp. 1-2; 🖼 photos, p. 3). The oil is in every part but the pollen, all year, bare winter stems too. It rides on clothes, packs, firewood and dogs: "Wash your skin with soap and water as soon as possible", wash clothes separately, wash the dog (p. 4). No water: wipe with dirt or sand, but not over blisters (FM 21-76, p. 132). - Ticks: check your whole body often (AFH, p. 70); pull a tick straight out with fine-tipped tweezers close to the skin, with no nail polish, petroleum jelly or heat (🖼 CDC, p. 50). More in "Disease and safety" in the Hunting guide. - Rattlesnakes: no hands into crevices, heavy brush or hollow logs; "Don't step over a fallen tree. Step on the log and look" (FM 3-05.70, p. 531). Bites: "Rattlesnakes, spiders and stings" in Field Care (no cutting, sucking, ice or tourniquet).

🌊 River and creek crossings "The force of flowing water may be extremely great and is most often underestimated." Treat every stream as a danger and avoid it if you can (TC 3-97.61, p. 343).
river-and-creek-crossings

When not to cross - Knee-deep is the limit for one person, in "mild to moderate" current only. Swift water runs over 5 ft a second, about walking speed (arithmetic) (TC 3-97.61, p. 345). "Six inches of fast-moving water can knock you off" your feet (Spotter guide, p. 12). - Our rivers are cold all year. A fall in brings "involuntary gasping", and cold water "drains body heat 25 times faster than cold air" (OSMB, p. 17). In very cold water, "Wade across if you can get only your feet wet"; otherwise find another way (FM 3-05.70, p. 296). - Never cross above rapids, falls or a logjam. Logjams and fallen trees ("strainers", "sweepers") let water through but trap people (OSMB, p. 14; AFH, p. 496). - Wait for the water to drop. Snow-fed streams run lowest in early morning (TC 3-97.61, p. 343). After heavy winter rain, wait a day or more; a bridge is worth a long detour (rule of thumb). "Not every river or stream can be crossed safely. If it is possible, cross at a different time or place, use a different technique, or choose another route" (p. 351).
when-not-to-cross

Picking the spot and getting ready Look from high ground first. Cross where the river widens, usually shallower; avoid bends (the outside is deep and fast) and narrows; choose low banks (TC 3-97.61, pp. 343-344). Below the crossing you want a shallow bar to wash up on, not rapids (FM 3-05.70, p. 295). Riffles in a line mean rocks; a hump and drop behind a rock is a "hole" that sucks at your feet (TC 3-97.61, p. 351). Then (TC 3-97.61, p. 344 unless noted): 1. Sleeping bag, dry clothes and food in waterproof bags (trash bags work), dry clothes on top. 2. Socks and insoles off and stowed; boots back on for grip. 3. Pack high and snug, then unbuckle the waist and chest straps so you can get out of it if swept off your feet. "Unbuckle your pack straps ... Never tie yourself in while you cross" (NPS North Cascades, p. 1). 4. The Army normally keeps clothes on, with dry ones packed. In our cold water, keep them on and change on the far bank (rule of thumb). 5. A stout pole about 3 in thick and 7-8 ft long (FM 3-05.70, p. 297). 6. A lookout 50-100 m upstream for floating logs, and someone downstream with a pole or rope to throw (TC 3-97.61, p. 351).
picking-the-spot-and-getting-ready

Crossing alone (TC 3-97.61, p. 345; 🖼 Fig. 13-1 on the same page.) 1. Face slightly across the current; in strong current, turn more side-on and lean upstream. 2. Plant the pole upstream of you as a third leg, and probe with it. 3. Aim slightly downstream; going straight across fights the current. 4. Lead with the downstream foot in small steps; never move one foot until the other is set, and never cross your legs. 5. Step on the upstream side of rocks; the downstream side is scoured and the rock may roll. 6. On the far bank, drain your boots and put on dry socks (p. 344). Crossing alone: the pole is planted upstream as a third leg; from above (right), the walker side-shuffles across with the current coming from the side (TC 3-97.61, p. 345).
crossing-alone

Crossing as a group - Know who can't swim before you start (TC 3-97.61, p. 351). - Chain: side by side facing the far bank, arms linked, the biggest person upstream leaning into the current. Conga line: all face upstream, each holding the clothes or pack behind the shoulders of the person upstream. Wedge: the biggest at the upstream point, small people and the injured in the middle (pp. 346-347). One person calls each step. If someone loses control, don't cling so hard that the whole line goes down (p. 346). - Rope handline: stretched across at 30-45° downstream; cross on its downstream side, one at a time (p. 348; 🖼 pp. 349-350). Taking the rope over first is the most dangerous job: the strongest swimmer, belayed, in a life jacket if you have one (pp. 347-348). Never tie directly into a rope in moving water; you must be able to let go (p. 348). - If you're swept away: shed the pack; face downstream, feet up in front to fend off rocks, and "work with the flow of water" toward the nearest bar; keep away from eddies. Get out and get warm fast: "Hypothermia will set in quickly in colder waters" (pp. 350-351). The chain: side by side, arms locked, facing the far bank, the biggest person on the upstream end (TC 3-97.61, p. 346).
crossing-as-a-group

❄ Snow and the passes - Stay off the passes in storms and deep snow: snow can fall any month above 5,000 ft (FM 3-97.6, p. 15), and the back-road routes climb into country that holds snow into spring ("high passes can get snow", Start Here). In winter take the lower highway route or wait for a clear spell (rule of thumb). - Walking on snow: best is snow that holds you, next best calf-deep; avoid thigh-deep. Go early after a cold night, while the crust holds (AFH, p. 467). - Snowshoes: bend a sapling about 1 in thick and 5 ft long into a loop about 12 in wide and lace it with cord; in a pinch, lash pine boughs together at the cut ends and tie them on (AFH, pp. 255-256; 🖼 TC 21-3, p. 52). Take them off when the snow holds you (AFH, p. 468). - Sunglasses against snow blindness (TC 3-97.61, p. 73). In fog or with snow over the trail, use the compass and pace count in the Navigation guide. Avalanche signs. Our danger is mostly on steep, open slopes and gullies high up after big storms (rule of thumb). - Most slides start on slopes of 30-45°; slab avalanches cause about 90% of deaths (AFH, p. 431). Watch winds of 15 mph or more, and the time during and just after storms (p.
snow-and-the-passes

on slopes of 30-45°; slab avalanches cause about 90% of deaths (AFH, p. 431). Watch winds of 15 mph or more, and the time during and just after storms (p. 433). - Slide paths: "Steep, open gullies and slopes, pushed over small trees, trees with limbs broken off, and tumbled rocks" (AFH, p. 434); "broken tree stumps at different heights" (TC 21-3, p. 46). - Danger now: "If the snow echoes or sounds hollow, conditions are dangerous. If the snow cracks and the cracks persist or run, the danger of a slab avalanche is imminent" (AFH, p. 434). - Crossing: one at a time, never tied together, each trailing a line about 100 ft long. If caught: drop the pack, "use swimming motions" toward the side, get an arm up, make a breathing space. Buried people have about a 50% chance after 30 minutes, so dig fast (p. 435).
snow-and-the-passes

🛡 Safety on the road This is about avoiding trouble, calming it, and turning back. Fighting and patrolling are outside these guides. - Together, by day: "Don't travel or hunt alone" (NY hunter manual, p. 80); "Don't hike after dark" (ODFW bears, p. 2). - Low profile: a pack with "nothing exposed to advertise your mission" (Kephart Vol. 2, p. 108); earth tones that "blend into your surroundings" (NPS North Cascades, p. 1). Don't show food, tools or weapons; spread valuables among the packs (rule of thumb). - Most people are like you: in American disasters looting has been "very rare", though massive in some catastrophes abroad (Quarantelli, p. 12). - Meeting strangers (AFH, pp. 168-169): if you can, "wait until only one person is near and, if possible, let that person make the initial approach". "Displaying fear, displaying weapons, and making sudden or threatening movements" can "prompt a hostile response". Smile; "Approach them slowly and don't rush matters." Keep any promise; don't enter a house uninvited. What to say: "Don't be a target" in Home & Property Protection.
safety-on-the-road

Checkpoints and roadblocks No book on the drive covers these from the traveler's side; these steps are (rule of thumb): 1. Stop well short, in daylight and plain view. Never approach at night or try to slip around. 2. One person walks forward slowly, hands empty and visible; the rest wait. 3. Say who you are, where you're going and why, and ask to pass. Offer road news. 4. Keep your voice low and give them space ("Someone at the gate, strangers, or a break-in" in Home & Property Protection; De-escalation, p. 15). 5. Don't argue or force it. If refused, thank them and turn back or go another way. Pass towns by day; camp well away. Share freely (rule of thumb): bridges out, safe fords, fire and smoke, water, sickness on the road, weather. Keep to yourself: how many live at home, what you carry, where your cache is, when you'll be back, and whether you are armed. Oregon law on force is in Home & Property Protection.
checkpoints-and-roadblocks

📡 Staying in touch and trail signs - Radios: section 5, "FRS / GMRS / MURS", of the Radio guide. No radio: the Signals guide covers whistles, mirrors and "Runners, relays and written messages"; no signal fires June-October. Agree on whistle signals before you leave (stop, come here, help), as the Army settles its sound signals in advance (FM 21-18, p. 47). - Signs for people behind you: one stone set on another, a twig broken and left hanging, or a tuft of grass tied in a knot all mean "this is the trail" (Seton, p. 267; 🖼 chart, p. 268). "All trails should be marked" (AFH, p. 429). - Notes at forks and camps: a dated note in a jar under a small cairn: names, date, which way, all well or not (rule of thumb). Write nothing you wouldn't want a stranger to read.
staying-in-touch-and-trail-signs

🆘 Getting lost Follow "Getting un-lost" in the Navigation guide: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. Before leaving each place, "study their backtrail carefully" (AFH, p. 429). "If you get lost, the best thing you can do is stay put and wait", using a whistle, bright clothing or a mirror (NPS North Cascades, p. 1), but that works only if someone has your trip plan and will come. If no one will, walk a bearing to a big handrail such as US-199 or the Illinois River ("Terrain association" in the Navigation guide).

🚲 Bicycles, Carts & Hauling Without Fuel When the gas runs out, everything you move goes on your back, on wheels you push, or on a bicycle. This guide covers how much one person can move and how fast, travel times from Cave Junction, loading a bike, building a trailer (welded steel or no-weld pallets), hitches and trailer brakes, wheelbarrows and handcarts, hills, keeping a bike running with few tools, spares to stock, and local hazards. The books are in Bicycles-Carts\ (Bicycle-Repair and Trailers-Carts). Pack animals, wagons and harness are in Horses-Draft-Animals\ and the Horse guide; brazing and forge work are in Blacksmithing-Tools\ and the Blacksmithing guide. Know the limits of the books. The repair manuals date from 1896 to 1978. Their methods for tubes, tyres, spokes, cup-and-cone hubs, chains and steel frames still work. But the library has little on modern parts: hydraulic disc brakes, tubeless tyres, indexed ("click") shifting, suspension and e-bikes. Stock their spares (pads, bleed kit and fluid, sealant, cables) now. A plain steel bike with rim brakes is the easiest to keep running (rule of thumb). ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - A loaded bike takes longer to stop (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 97), and wet rim brakes stop much worse. Start every descent slowly, test the brakes at the top, and remember that a trailer with no brake shoves the bike

p. 97), and wet rim brakes stop much worse. Start every descent slowly, test the brakes at the top, and remember that a trailer with no brake shoves the bike downhill (rule of thumb). - Don't wreck your body. A normal day load on your back is 10-20 kg (22-44 lb); 50 kg (110 lb) only for short distances (World Bank, p. 65). Put heavy loads on wheels. - Never ride a kinked frame tube or fork. A buckled tube is weakened and must be replaced (Burr, p. 73). Keep at least 2 in of seat post inside the frame (Henry, p. 54). - Never clean parts in gasoline. Use kerosene, diesel or degreaser, outdoors, away from flames. - Fire season (June-October): don't drag metal. A chain or trailer part scraping on rock can start a wildfire. Haul in the cool early morning and carry water (rule of thumb). - Braze outdoors, and only steel frames. Brass gives off zinc fumes. Aluminium and carbon frames cannot be brazed.

🏋 How much one person can move The biggest lesson in these books: get the load off your back and onto wheels. 🗺 Travel times from Cave Junction Walking pace with a load (FM 21-18, p. 89): on roads 4.0 km/h (2.5 mph) by day, 3.2 km/h at night; cross-country 2.4 km/h by day, 1.6 km/h at night. A normal day is 20-32 km (12-20 mi), or 5-8 hours on the move. - Rest 15 minutes after the first 45 minutes, then 10 minutes in every hour (FM 21-18, p. 48). - At halts, lie down with your feet up. Carry spare socks; tape known hot spots before they blister (FM 21-18, p. 101; 🖼 photo of friction blisters; Blister). In hills, plan by time, not miles. Add one-third to the map distance, then 1 hour for every 1,000 ft (300 m) of climb, or every 2,000 ft (600 m) of descent (FM 3-97.6, p. 72). 🎒 Loading a bicycle How to load it (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 97): - Touring cyclists usually carry 30-50 lb, on the bike - a backpack makes balance harder. (Bicycle touring) - Put heavy items low in the panniers and split the load front and rear. Too much weight in front spoils the steering. - A loaded bike needs lower gears, sways more and takes longer to stop. Practise with the load before a real trip. Making a bike carry more (Practical Action, Bicycles): - Panniers can be sacks or baskets hung from wood across the carrier, or a light steel frame. Keep the sides balanced, and strengthen the carrier (p. 2; 🖼 pannier frame drawing; Pannier). - The load is limited by the rear wheel and tyre; a stronger rear wheel helps (p. 3). - Longer carrier without cutting the frame: bolt on extra stays and move the rear wheel back about 250 mm (10 in). The chain and brake rods must be lengthened (p. 3; 🖼 extension drawings). - A small 20-inch rear wheel is stronger, keeps the load low and makes pedalling easier, but handles potholes worse (p. 4; 🖼 drawing). A pannier frame bolted to the carrier, sizes in mm (640 long, 500 tall, 320 wide); the carrier is strengthened with steel angle (Practical Action, p. 2). Pushing big loads: in Zambia, people pushed two 50

carrier, sizes in mm (640 long, 500 tall, 320 wide); the carrier is strengthened with steel angle (Practical Action, p. 2). Pushing big loads: in Zambia, people pushed two 50 kg sacks of maize on one bicycle up to 30 km (19 mi) to town (Bicycle Trailers in Zambia, p. 1). Before a loaded trip (rule of thumb): tyres firm, brakes grabbing hard, carrier bolts tight, nothing able to swing into the spokes, and patch kit, pump and water aboard. 🛒 Bicycle trailers: welded steel or no-weld pallets A trailer lets a rider move about three times the bike's own load, roughly 200 kg (450 lb) (Practical Action, Bicycle Trailers, p. 1). But not always. In northern Ghana, trailers promoted in the 1990s failed: heavy to pull loaded, poor on footpaths, and twice the cost of a bicycle. A plain bike with a strong carrier was more flexible (World Bank, p. 39). Welded steel trailer (Bicycle Trailers, pp. 3-4; frame drawings: 🖼 p. 2, 🖼 p. 3): - Frame: 19 mm (3/4 in) mild-steel square tube, or round tube at least 22 × 1.5 mm (25 × 1.5 mm is better). Reinforce each joint with a piece of tube or bar inside it. - Ordinary bike wheels are fine for light loads on good roads, but not for heavy loads on rough tracks. Use strengthened wheels (p. 4). - A local welder in Zambia built these from the drawings for about $100 each (Zambia report, p. 1). No-weld pallet trailer - about one day and about 20 euros (Low-tech Lab). You need 2 pallets, 2 bicycle wheels, wood screws and 1 old inner tube; a crowbar, hammer, saw and screwdriver. 1. Decide what it must carry. Keep it no wider than 1 m (39 in) (p. 3). 2. Take the pallets apart with the crowbar and hammer (p. 3). 3.

The side boards must be as thick as the wheel so they frame it (p. 4; 🖼 the numbered boards; Pallet). 4. Fix the wheels before the outer boards go on (p. 5). 5. Hitches (Bicycle Trailers, p. 4; 🖼 hitch design; 🖼 Poston's scrap-steel hitch): - Hitch above the rear wheel, to the carrier or the frame under the seat. It is simpler than an axle-level hitch, works on earth roads, and lets the trailer double as a handcart. - The recommended joint is a rubber ball in a steel socket. - Any hitch must hold the load, let the bike lean, come off easily, and take braking and pulling forces from every direction (Low-tech Lab, p. 6). Trailer brakes and carrying the injured (Bicycle Ambulance, pp. 2-3; 🖼 frame diagram): a stretcher trailer carries two people, with a shock absorber and a ball-joint hitch so the bike can turn. Its overrun brake works by itself: when the bike slows, the trailer pushes a rod into a sprung tube, which pulls a brake cable on the trailer wheel. No

turn. Its overrun brake works by itself: when the bike slows, the trailer pushes a rod into a sprung tube, which pulls a brake cable on the trailer wheel. No trailer brake? Slow down early, drag a foot, or walk it down steep hills (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Bicycle Trailers - parts list with tube sizes and frame drawings; Low-tech Lab pallet trailer - the no-weld build; Bicycle Ambulance - hitch and overrun-brake part sizes; Trailer Hitch (Poston) - a lathe-free hitch from scrap steel and rubber. 🛞 Wheelbarrows, handcarts, sledges and travois A better wheelbarrow (Wilson, The Wheelbarrow): - Use one large wheel with most of the load directly over it. Leave little weight on the handles, and take that with a shoulder strap. The traditional Chinese barrow built this way carried up to six people (p. 1). - A homemade barrow wheel can run on a standard bicycle axle and cone bearings, with a solid tyre of strips cut from old car tyres (p. 2; 🖼 wheel drawing). - Choose air-filled tyres (adjust pressure for rough ground), keep the load low, and make several light trips rather than one heavy one (USFS Handtools for Trail Work, p. 42, with 🖼 wheelbarrow drawings). Handcarts: - A balanced handcart, with most of the weight on the wheels, is easier than a one-wheel barrow (World Bank, p. 65). - A good load cart has a low centre of gravity, a wide wheelbase and big wheels. Pulled carts are easier to control on rough ground. A cart pulled from a hip belt finished a 3.2 km mixed course 54% faster than people carrying rucksacks. The carts were noisy in brush and rock, and gear caught in the wheels - so guard the wheels (Knapik, p. 37). - Cart bodies are often built on scrap car or pickup axles. Large wheels roll through ruts and holes better than small ones
wheelbarrows-handcarts-sledges-and-travois

so guard the wheels (Knapik, p. 37). - Cart bodies are often built on scrap car or pickup axles. Large wheels roll through ruts and holes better than small ones (Starkey, p. 85; 🖼 big wheel vs small wheel in a rut; 🖼 cart wheel, hub and bearing, labeled; Handcart). Sledges are cheap and narrow, and go where carts can't - too steep, muddy or narrow. But they pull harder, snag on stumps, and their ruts turn into gullies (Starkey, p. 83; 🖼 simple wooden sledge; Sled). Travois (behind a horse or mule): two straight poles 14-20 ft long with a platform 2-3 ft wide behind the animal, and three people to handle it at ditches and streams (FM 25-7, p. 166; 🖼 travois drawing). 📚 Go deeper: Wilson The Wheelbarrow - the big-wheel barrow and a homemade wheel; Wheelbarrow construction drawings - six dimensioned sheets for a steel barrow; Selvidge, p. 104 - replacing a wagon spoke, and p. 95 - shrinking on an iron tyre. ⛰ Hills and grades The extra push on a slope is roughly the total weight times the grade (rule of thumb, simple physics). A 10% grade rises 10 ft for every 100 ft along the road (Grade)). | Grade | Extra push for a 220 lb (100 kg) load | | 5% | about 11 lb | | 10% | about 22 lb | | 15% | about 33 lb | That is on top of the push needed on the flat. (Rules of thumb:) - Pushing much over 25-30 lb for long is very tiring. - On grades over about 10%, use two people (one pulling with a rope or hip belt), or split the load. - A loaded bike on a steep Forest Service road is often faster walked and pushed than ridden. - Going down: a trailer with no brake shoves the bike. Slow down at the top, not halfway. Drag a foot or add a brake. On a handcart, put someone behind holding back on a rope. 📚 Go deeper: Knapik Load Carriage - terrain factors and energy cost; FM 3-97.6 - moving in steep country.

🩹 Flat tyres: patching tubes and booting tyres Patching a tube (Henry, pp. 61-65): 1. Before you take the tyre off, mark where it sits against the valve, or count spokes from the valve, so you can find the thorn later (p. 63). 2. Lever one side of the tyre off and pull the tube out. Careless levering tears the tube (p. 64; Tire lever, Inner tube). 3. Find the leak: pump the tube up a little and listen or feel near your face, or dunk it in water and watch for bubbles (p. 64). 4. Find the cause: feel inside the tyre at the matching spot for the thorn (p. 64). 5. Roughen around the hole with sandpaper (p. 65). 6. Coat tube and patch with rubber cement. Wait about 10 minutes until it is tacky (p. 65). 7. Press the patch on hard, dust with talc ("French chalk") and refit the tube dry (p. 65). Tips: old inner tubes make good patch rubber (p. 61). A patch kit more than a year old may have gone bad (p. 62). If a tyre goes soft with no hole, check the valve first (p. 62). Tyres lose 10-20 psi within a week anyway, so check pressure often (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 72). Booting a cut or burst tyre: - Glue canvas inside the tyre over the damage, or a patch

a week anyway, so check pressure often (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 72). Booting a cut or burst tyre: - Glue canvas inside the tyre over the damage, or a patch cut from an old tyre (Henry, p. 70). - Fill small tread cuts with leather dust (rasped from scrap leather) mixed into rubber cement (Henry, p. 69). - A modern road kit: two denim boots about 1 × 2 in, 6 patches, 2 tyre levers, a spare tube, talc and a pressure gauge (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 34). 📚 Go deeper: Henry Cycle Building and Repairing - tyres, tubes, valves and repairs; Adult Cycling Manual - the tool and tyre kit. 🔩 Wheels, hub bearings and chains Truing a wobbly wheel (Henry, pp. 44-46; 🖼 truing a wheel in its own fork with chalk; Wheelbuilding): 1. Spin the wheel in the frame and hold chalk beside the rim so it marks the spots that stick out. 2. A spoke pulls the rim toward its own side of the hub. At each chalk mark, tighten the spokes that run to the other side of the hub, a little at a time, with a spoke (nipple) key. 3. Fix out-of-round the same way: tighten spokes at the high spots, loosen them at the low spots. 4. File off spoke ends that poke through the nipples, or they will puncture the tube. 5. Replace broken spokes one at a time, so you keep the lacing pattern (🖼 lacing drawing; Spoke). Rim rubbing the chalk on the left? Tighten the spokes that run to the right side of the hub, a little at a time (a diagram drawn for this guide). Hub bearings (Henry, pp. 46-47; 🖼 hub parts named; 🖼 cup, cone, balls and locknut, with how to hold the spanners): - A clicking wheel usually has a broken ball or worn cones. Open the hub; clean cups, cones and axle in kerosene. - Throw away chipped balls. Take a sample ball when you look for new ones. - Grease the cups, put the
wheels-hub-bearings-and-chains

the hub; clean cups, cones and axle in kerosene. - Throw away chipped balls. Take a sample ball when you look for new ones. - Grease the cups, put the balls back, screw the cone up tight, then back it off about half a turn. Twisted by its spokes, the wheel should spin freely with almost no side play. The parts of a cup-and-cone hub, and the two-wrench grip: hold the cone still while you turn the locknut against it (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 58). Chains: - Soak a filthy chain in kerosene for 2-3 days, hang it to drip, wipe it, then oil it (Henry, p. 52). - To shorten an old riveted chain, file off the burred pin heads and punch the pins out (Henry, p. 53; 🖼 chain links drawn; 🖼 putting a chain on). - Modern chains need a chain tool: push the pin almost out, leaving about 1/32 in in the side plate so it can go back in. A chain wears out in 1-2 years of average use, and a new chain may skip on a worn freewheel, so the two often need replacing together (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 104; Freewheel). 📚 Go deeper: Henry - lacing and truing wheels, hubs and chains; Adult Cycling Manual, p. 103 - chain cleaning, oiling and stiff links; Burr Bicycle Repairing - bearings, forks and shop-made tools.

🛑 Brakes, gears and field fixes Rim brakes (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 48; 🖼 center-pull and side-pull brakes): released, the pads should sit about 1/16 in from the rim, and they should hit the rim before the lever reaches the handlebar. New cables stretch - tighten them again after about a week. Derailleur gears (p. 81; 🖼 rear derailleur with its screws lettered): won't shift onto the largest cog? Back out its limit (stop) screw. Still short? Take up cable slack with the barrel adjuster. Shifts by itself? Tighten the thumbscrew holding the shift lever. Field fixes: - Bent crank: hold the bike steady and push the crank back with your foot - usually straight enough to finish the trip (Henry, p. 47). - Bent frame tube: a slight bend can be straightened, but a buckled (kinked) tube cannot. Replace it (Burr, p. 73; 🖼 truing a frame; Bicycle frame). - Broken steel frame tube - braze it over a sleeve (Rowe, pp. 60-61; 🖼 Burr's drawings of a tube mended over an inner sleeve; Lugged steel frame): 1. File the broken ends smooth and clean them bright, inside and out. 2. Fit a sleeve of light steel tube inside both ends; pin it if needed to hold the frame in line. 3. Coat the joint with borax mixed with water to a paste (the flux) (Borax). 4. Heat it
brakes-gears-and-field-fixes

both ends; pin it if needed to hold the frame in line. 3. Coat the joint with borax mixed with water to a paste (the flux) (Borax). 4. Heat it in a charcoal fire or a blacksmith's forge. At a low red heat, lay on brass spelter and let it flow into the joint. Don't overheat. 5. Work outdoors (zinc fumes). Steel only - aluminium frames (smooth welds, no lugs, often marked 6061 or 7005) and carbon frames cannot be brazed. The mend from steps 1-5, cut open: a sleeve inside both broken ends, brass flowed into the joint (a diagram drawn for this guide). Old words in the old books: paraffin = kerosene; French chalk = talc; spanner = wrench; cover = tyre; solution = rubber cement. 📚 Go deeper: Adult Cycling Manual - brake, derailleur, headset and bottom-bracket adjustment; Rowe Hard Soldering - brazing with blowpipe, charcoal or forge; Burr - frame tubes, lugs and forks. 📦 Spares to stockpile (Rule of thumb, building on the kit list in the Adult Cycling Manual, p. 34.) - A good floor pump - above all (Bicycle pump) - Tubes and patch kits for every tyre size you own; spare tyres - Chains with spare links; brake pads; inner cables and housing - Spokes in the right lengths for each wheel - Loose bearing balls (3/16 in and 1/4 in are common), grease, chain oil, rim tape, valve cores - Tools: tyre levers, chain tool, spoke key, pressure gauge (Bicycle tools) Match tyres by the ISO number on the sidewall, not by "26 inch." 🌲 Illinois Valley hazards (Rules of thumb for our area.) - Goatheads (puncturevine) grow in dry, disturbed ground - road edges, driveways, bare lots. Carry extra patches or thorn-resistant tubes. Learn the plant and pull it before it seeds (weed photo list, p. 53; Puncturevine). - Rocky and serpentine Forest Service roads cause pinch flats under load. Run tyres firmer when loaded, and walk the worst rock. (Serpentinite) - Fire season (June-October): keep chains and metal parts from dragging and throwing sparks. Haul in the early morning with plenty of water. - Wet winters wash the oil off chains and rust them. Wipe and re-oil after every rain ride. - Rim brakes stop much worse when wet. Brake earlier; drag them lightly first to wipe the rims. 📚 Go deeper: Adult Cycling Manual, p. 97 - riding a loaded bike safely; Knapik, p. 37 - carts on rough ground.

⚠ Old advice in the library to ignore - Homemade rubber cement from rubber dissolved in "benzine" (gasoline or naphtha) (Henry, p. 61). Very flammable, and benzene fumes are toxic. Use bought cement; if you must make it, mix it outdoors, far from any flame. - Boiling a chain in mutton tallow (Henry, p. 52). Hot fat is a fire hazard, and tallow holds grit. Soak in kerosene, wipe, and oil lightly. - Wrapping joints in asbestos cloth or wicking while brazing (Rowe, p. 61; p. 60). Asbestos causes cancer - use wet rags or a sheet-metal shield. Brass spelter gives off zinc fumes that cause "metal fume fever," so braze outdoors. - "Cleaning solvent from gasoline station" in the tool list (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 34). Never clean parts in gasoline. Use kerosene, diesel or degreaser, outdoors. - Obsolete parts: single-tube and beaded-edge tyres, cotter-pin cranks (Henry, p. 47) and 1890s frames. Skip those pages; the hub, wheel, patching, brazing and truing methods are still good. - Military load limits of 30-45% of body weight (Knapik, p. 20) are for fit young soldiers. Plan family loads on 10-20 kg. 📚 Go deeper: Henry, p. 46 - the sound old method: hubs cleaned in kerosene; Adult Cycling Manual, p. 103 - kerosene chain cleaning.

🧭 Navigation & Weather Without GPS or Forecasts How to find your way in the hills around the Illinois Valley with a paper map and compass - or with neither - and how to read the weather coming when there is no forecast: map reading, declination, pace count, terrain association, finding yourself when lost, the sun and stars, clouds and wind, our local weather from valley fog to east-wind fire days, lightning, and a home weather log. The books are in Navigation-Weather\Land-Navigation and Navigation-Weather\Weather; the local topo maps are in Maps\Topo-USGS and Maps\Forest-Service (see the Maps section of the Illinois Valley guide). ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Set your compass to 14° East. Older maps print bigger numbers; always use the newest. Ignoring declination puts you about a quarter mile off for every mile you walk. - Leave a written trip plan with someone who stays home. With no search and rescue, nobody comes unless someone knows your route and your return time (NPS Trip Plan). - When you hear thunder, move: off peaks and ridges, away from taller trees, and out of rock overhangs and cave mouths. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder (Backcountry Lightning, pp. 1-2). - Never cross fast water. Six inches can knock you off your feet; two feet carries away most vehicles (Spotter Guide, p. 12). - A dry east

Lightning, pp. 1-2). - Never cross fast water. Six inches can knock you off your feet; two feet carries away most vehicles (Spotter Guide, p. 12). - A dry east wind after a front in late summer or fall is extreme fire weather - the pattern behind the September 2020 fires. Be ready to leave. - Sun, watch, moon and moss methods are rough. Check any no-compass direction with a second method before you commit to a long walk.

🗺 Reading a topo map Scale. The library's local quads (US Topo and FSTopo) are 1:24,000: 1 inch = 2,000 ft (🖼 using the bar scale; Topographic map). On the 1:100,000 Forest Service sheet, 1 inch is about 1.6 miles. Map distance is "as the crow flies"; walking a steep slope is farther (USGS FS 035-01, p. 1; PMS 475, p. 133). Contour lines (FS 035-01, p. 1; PMS 475, pp. 41-42; Contour line; 🖼 a contour map beside the land it shows; 🖼 FM 3-25.26, p. 107): - Brown lines join points of equal height; the heavier, labeled ones are index contours. - Close together = steep. Far apart = gentle. Circles inside circles = a hilltop. - V-shaped bends point uphill and upstream - creeks and draws. - U-shaped bends point down a ridge - spurs and ridge ends. The same land as a picture (top) and as contour lines (bottom): the lines almost touch at the cliffs and spread far apart on level ground (PMS 475, p. 40). Name the land. Learn to spot these on the map and on the ground - it is the heart of navigating without GPS (FM 3-25.26, pp. 115-118): | Feature | On the map | On the ground | | Hill (🖼 drawing) | Closed rings | Ground falls away on all sides | | Saddle) (🖼 drawing) | Hourglass

🧭 Compass and declination Use 14° East for the Illinois Valley. NOAA's model gives 13.9° E for Cave Junction in November 2026, shrinking about 0.1° a year. The FSTopo Cave Junction sheet prints 14°8′ (2024) and the US Topo sheet 14°18′ (2023). Older maps print larger numbers - use the newest value. See Magnetic declination. Which way to correct (FS 035-01, p. 2; PMS 475, p. 86): - Here the magnetic north (MN) arrow sits to the right (east) of true north (🖼 north arrow on a quad; 🖼 declination diagrams). - Map → compass: subtract 14°. A map bearing of 90° becomes 76° on an unadjusted compass. - Compass → map: add 14°. - Memory aid: "declination east, compass least." - Easiest: set the compass's declination screw to 14° E once and forget it. Here the compass needle points 14° east of true north: subtract 14° going from map to compass, add 14° going back (a diagram drawn for this guide). Why it matters: 1° of error puts you about 920 ft off in 10 miles (PMS 475, p. 86). Ignoring all 14° puts you about 1,300 ft off for every mile (general practice: worked out from the angle). Grid north on the Cave Junction quad is only about half a degree from true north - ignore it on foot. That's why the margin shows three norths (FM 3-25.26,
compass-and-declination

Grid north on the Cave Junction quad is only about half a degree from true north - ignore it on foot. That's why the margin shows three norths (FM 3-25.26, p. 62; 🖼 three norths). The way back (back azimuth): add 180° if the bearing is 180° or less; subtract 180° if more. A slip here can be disastrous - check it twice (FM 3-25.26, p. 58; 🖼 direct and back bearing). Compass habits (PMS 475, p. 84; FM 3-25.26, p. 97; 🖼 parts of a compass): - Hold it level at waist height (🖼 centerhold), take every bearing twice, and walk where the direction-of-travel arrow points, not where your hunch says (🖼 following a bearing). - Keep away from metal: 55 m (180 ft) from high-voltage lines, 18 m (60 ft) from a truck, 10 m (33 ft) from barbed wire or phone lines, half a meter from a rifle. Belt buckles and clipboards throw it off too. 📚 Go deeper: USGS Finding Your Way - taking a bearing off a topo map; PMS 475, pp. 82-86 - parts of a compass and setting declination.

👣 Pace count: measuring distance on foot (FM 3-25.26, pp. 52-53; PMS 475, pp. 133-134) 1. Measure a 100 m (328 ft) course on ground like where you'll travel - a road shoulder with a tape or a measured fence line works (rule of thumb). 2. Walk it naturally and count your steps. The Army's example is about 120 steps per 100 m. Walk it several times and average. 3. Expect more steps (🖼 why the ground is longer than the map) uphill, into a headwind, in mud, sand, snow or brush, in rain, and in fog or darkness. 4. Keep a separate, shorter night count (p. 141). 5. Don't try to remember the count. Move a pebble from one pocket to the other, or tie a knot, every 100 m (pace count beads). ⚠ The Forest Service (NWCG) counts a "pace" as two steps - every time the same foot lands. The Army counts every step. Pick one and never mix them. 📚 Go deeper: PMS 475, p. 133 - pacing worksheet; FM 3-25.26, p. 52 - pace count and other ways to measure distance.

🏞 Terrain association: handrails, catching features, aiming off Match the map to the ground as you go (🖼 drawing). It is far more forgiving than walking a compass line, because you keep comparing what you expected to see with what you do see. Pure compass walking piles up errors with every detour (FM 3-25.26, pp. 131, 139). Keep the map turned so its north matches the land (p. 140; 🖼 by the land; 🖼 by compass). Plan a route this way (FM 3-25.26, p. 140): - Handrail: a line you follow without careful compass work - a road, stream, ridge or power line. Ours include Hwy 199, the Illinois River and its East and West Forks, the Caves Highway (OR 46), and numbered Forest Service roads on the FSTopo sheets (local: rule of thumb). - Catching feature: something across your path that tells you you've gone too far. - Attack point: a sure landmark no more than about 500 m from the goal. From there, walk an exact bearing and pace count. Aim off on purpose (FM 3-25.26, p. 100; 🖼 deliberate offset). Heading for a spot on a road or creek, aim about 10° to one side. When you hit the road, you know which way to turn. Each degree moves you about 18 m sideways per 1,000 m walked, so 10° is about 180 m. Aim to one
terrain-association-handrails-catching-features-aiming-off

hit the road, you know which way to turn. Each degree moves you about 18 m sideways per 1,000 m walked, so 10° is about 180 m. Aim to one side of the spot on purpose; when you reach the road you know which way to turn (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: FM 3-25.26, ch. 11 - terrain association in depth; MVUM Wild Rivers - which forest roads are real roads.

📍 Finding yourself on the map (resection) Resection (FM 3-25.26, p. 68; Position resection; 🖼 drawing; 🖼 PMS 475, p. 131): 1. Orient the map. 2. Take compass bearings to two or three landmarks you can name on the map. 3. Turn each into a map bearing (add 14°, unless your compass is already set), then into its back azimuth (±180°). 4. Draw each line back from its landmark. Where they cross is you. Three lines make a small triangle - you are inside it. Resection: back bearings drawn from two or three peaks you can name cross where you stand (a diagram drawn for this guide). Local candidates are peaks on the FSTopo sheets such as Grayback Mountain, Kerby Peak and Eight Dollar Mountain - check on the sheet which you can really see from where you stand (rule of thumb). Modified resection (p. 70; 🖼 drawing): if you know you're on a road, river or ridgeline, one bearing to one landmark is enough. You are where that line crosses your road or ridge. 📚 Go deeper: FM 3-25.26, pp. 68-70 - intersection, resection and modified resection with drawings; PMS 475, p. 131 - finding your own position by triangulation; AFH 10-644, p. 406 - azimuth, biangulation and triangulation.

🆘 Getting un-lost STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan (Today's Hunter, p. 80): 1. Stop. Admit you're turned around. Sit down. 2. Think. Retrace your route in your head: the last place you were sure of, and what you've passed since. 3. Observe. Look for the five terrain features, a peak you can name, the sound of a road or the river. Try a resection. 4. Plan. Pick the nearest big handrail on the map (a road or river) and walk a bearing to it, aiming off so you know which way to turn when you reach it. - If you can't get back before dark, stop early and spend the effort on shelter, warmth and a signal (p. 80; Signals guide). - Staying put only works if someone will come. That page assumes searchers in "a few days." Now it works only if someone at home has your trip plan. - Never shelter under a rock overhang in a thunderstorm - lightning arcs across the gap. Trip plan before every trip into the hills (NPS Trip Plan, pp. 1-2): who is going, the route, start and return times, a backup plan, the vehicle and the gear. Leave it with someone who isn't going, check in when you're back, and agree that they act at the deadline. 📚 Go deeper: NPS Trip Plan form - print a stack; Today's Hunter, pp.

A thunderstorm cell lives about 30 minutes (🖼 life cycle), but its gust front can set off new ones (AC 00-6B, pp. 167-168). Wind signs: - Roseburg (nearest station in the 1903 Weather Bureau study): in spring and summer, rain follows southwest winds and a falling barometer by 12-24 hours; in winter, southerly winds by about 12

(nearest station in the 1903 Weather Bureau study): in spring and summer, rain follows southwest winds and a falling barometer by 12-24 hours; in winter, southerly winds by about 12 hours (Garriott, p. 137). - Portland, Oregon: wind turning from northwest through northeast to southeast means rain; a shift to northwest means clearing (p. 131). - Cold front (🖼 cold and warm fronts): wind from the south or southwest before it, then an abrupt shift to west, northwest or north (AH 360, p. 101). - Back to the wind, low pressure is on your left and a little ahead (AH 360, p. 84). - ⚠ Valley winds are bent by the hills. Judge by cloud movement or ridgetop wind. Barometer: watch the trend, not the number. A drop of more than about 0.06 inch in 3 hours means change is coming; about 0.18 inch or more in 3 hours means a strong storm (general practice). The old Roseburg rule "rain after the barometer falls to 29.90" uses sea-level readings; at our ~1,300 ft an unadjusted barometer reads about 1.3-1.4 inches lower (general practice). Sayings that hold up (somewhat): "Evening red and morning gray..." (Red sky at morning; 🖼 photo) has a basis, because weather mostly moves west to east (Garriott, p. 18). Hard, greasy, ragged clouds mean wind (Shifts and Expedients, p. 183). Forecasts weeks ahead from the moon, almanacs

a basis, because weather mostly moves west to east (Garriott, p. 18). Hard, greasy, ragged clouds mean wind (Shifts and Expedients, p. 183).
