🌦 Illinois Valley weather through the year The baseline (NRCS soil survey, p. 5): winter averages 40°F at Cave Junction (record low -6°F, December 1972), with about 24 inches of snow a season in that older record (NOAA's 1991-2020 normal is only about 7 inches); summer averages 67°F, and Grants Pass has hit 108°F. Only about 15% of the rain falls April to September, and summer afternoon humidity runs 25-30%. It cools 3-5°F for every 1,000 ft you climb, and above about 4,500 ft it can freeze in any month. Most winters bring one or two damaging windstorms; every few years a continental air mass from the east brings days well below freezing in winter, or a sweltering week in summer. Valley fog and inversions (AH 360, p. 35; AC 00-6B, p. 146; EPA Smoke Guide, p. 26; Inversion)): - On clear, calm nights cold air drains off the slopes (🖼 drawing) and pools on the valley floor, deepening until about midnight. Fog forms if the air is moist (🖼 radiation fog). - Fog is common the morning after rain then clearing, and usually burns off by noon unless cloud moves in above it. - In winter an inversion can trap fog and woodstove smoke for days (🖼 smoke under an inversion). Burn hot and dry (Firewood guide). Frost (Garriott, p. 137; AH 360, p. 35): heavy frost follows a
illinois-valley-weather-through-the-year

trap fog and woodstove smoke for days (🖼 smoke under an inversion). Burn hot and dry (Firewood guide). Frost (Garriott, p. 137; AH 360, p. 35): heavy frost follows a high or rising barometer, evening temperature at 40°F or below, clearing sky and light wind. Frost hits low spots first. The mid-slope "thermal belt" stays warmest at night - the best spot for tender crops, and also where wildfires stay active all night. Winter storms off the Pacific (NRCS, p. 5; Spotter Guide, p. 12): warm storms carrying a long plume of subtropical moisture (an atmospheric river) bring several inches of rain a day, high snow levels and fast-rising rivers (general practice). Cave Junction got 8.12 inches in one day on 22 December 1964. Stay off low crossings and out of creeks when they rise. Summer thunderstorms are most frequent over the mountains (NRCS, p. 5). In fire season, watch the ridges for smoke for a day or two after lightning (rule of thumb). Heat: in a hot spell, take regular breaks in shade and drink often; do heavy work in the cool morning (rule of thumb). Heat exhaustion - heavy sweat, pale clammy skin, dizziness, nausea - means shade, rest, water and cool wet cloths. Confusion or collapse is heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency - cool them fast (ATP 4-02.11, pp. 188-189; Field care guide). East wind = fire
illinois-valley-weather-through-the-year

rest, water and cool wet cloths. Confusion or collapse is heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency - cool them fast (ATP 4-02.11, pp. 188-189; Field care guide). East wind = fire weather (AH 360, p. 211; NWS Medford, pp. 14-15; Foehn wind): in late summer and fall, after a cold front, high pressure inland can send strong, dry north-to-east winds downslope, warming and drying as they come. On 7-9 September 2020, Medford's humidity fell to about 7% and Slater Butte (4,600 ft, near where the Slater Fire started south of Takilma and O'Brien) recorded gusts of 55-60 mph. Warning signs: very clear air, warm dry nights, and east wind on the ridges after a front. Pack the car and watch for smoke. Another nearby east-wind fire: the Chetco Bar Fire. Smoke: inversions hold smoke in the valley at night. With no air-quality reports, judge smoke by how far you can see (EPA Smoke Guide, pp. 95-96) - in daylight, not at sunrise or sunset, only when humidity is under 65%, looking at dark landmarks at known distances: | Farthest dark landmark you can see | Healthy adults | Children, elders, pregnant, heart or lung disease | | More than 10 miles | Watch for changes | Watch; shorten activity if you feel it | | 5-10 miles | Shorten and ease outdoor work | Minimize or avoid outdoor activity | |

⚡ Lightning safety (Backcountry Lightning, pp. 1-2; NWS Lightning brochure, p. 2; Spotter Guide, p. 13) - If you can hear thunder, lightning is within about 10 miles. Start moving to shelter then. - Flash to bang: count the seconds and divide by 5 for miles. Don't stake your life on it. - Stay sheltered 30 minutes after the last thunder. People are struck going out too soon. - Ground current is the big danger, not a direct strike: about half of casualties come from current spreading through the ground; direct strikes cause only 3-5% of deaths. - Caught outside: get off peaks and ridges, away from taller trees, out of overhangs and cave mouths (🖼 safer and riskier terrain). Spread a group 20 ft apart, so one strike can't hurt everyone. Crouch with feet together (🖼 the lightning position). - A struck person carries no charge. Start CPR or rescue breathing right away (Field care guide). - The US averages about 300 people struck and about 30 killed a year. - At home: unplug radios and ground antennas (Radio guide). 📚 Go deeper: Backcountry Lightning - picking terrain, group spacing, the lightning position; NWS brochure - family rules and first aid.

Ham (Amateur), CB, Shortwave, GMRS/FRS & MURS - how they work and how to use them This guide explains, in plain language, how to communicate by radio when the internet and phones are down. It covers what each type of radio is, what it can do, which frequencies/channels matter in an emergency, and the basic procedures for calling for help. Legal note (normal times): Transmitting on ham (amateur) frequencies requires a license (easy to get - see below). GMRS requires a cheap license (no test). CB, FRS, MURS need no license. Shortwave listening needs no license (you're only receiving). In a genuine life-or-death emergency, calling for help on whatever radio you have is generally accepted (the ham rules, 47 CFR §97.405, say nothing in them stops a station in distress from using any means it has). Listening is always legal. Learn and practice before you need it.

2. In the Illinois Valley 🏔 The valley is ringed by mountains (Klamath Mountains): VHF/UHF needs a repeater on a peak (🖼 why: radio waves travel in straight lines), and NOAA warns that mountain valleys may get little or no weather radio even inside the usual 40-mile range (NOAA brochure, p. 3). Valley to valley, VHF/UHF gets through by way of a repeater on a peak that both radios can see (a diagram drawn for this guide). - Weather radio: try Medford 162.400, Mt. Ashland 162.475 and Brookings 162.550 MHz; SAME code 041033. - Ham: JCEC repeater 145.490 (-, tone 136.5), Eight Dollar Mtn; net Mondays 8:00 pm. - No license: Monday check-in on FRS channel 3 and MURS channel 3 after the 7:00 pm IVARC net. - HF: Oregon Emergency Net, nightly 6:00 pm, 3.980 MHz LSB. (Club websites, Nov 2026 - verify. Full lists: Illinois Valley guide.) 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 144 - radio in mountains; FM 24-18, p. 102 - picking a radio site; NOAA Weather Radio brochure, p. 3 - reception in valleys.

3. How radio actually works (the 60-second version) - A radio turns your voice into radio waves at a certain frequency (measured in kilohertz kHz or megahertz MHz). Another radio tuned to the same frequency turns the wave back into sound. - Both radios must be on the same frequency/channel AND the same mode (e.g. FM, AM, SSB) to hear each other. - Only one person talks at a time. You press PTT (push-to-talk) to transmit, release it to listen. You cannot hear others while you hold PTT. - Frequency bands behave very differently: - VHF/UHF (high frequency numbers, ~30 MHz-3 GHz): travel in roughly straight "line of sight." Great locally, blocked by hills/buildings. Used by FRS, GMRS, MURS, and ham 2m/70cm. Extended by repeaters (see below). - HF / shortwave (low numbers, ~3-30 MHz): can bounce off the ionosphere and travel hundreds or thousands of miles ("skip"). Used by ham HF, CB (27 MHz), and shortwave broadcasters. Range changes with time of day and the sun. (🖼 ground waves and sky waves; 🖼 layers of the ionosphere; Ionosphere, Skywave) - Skip zone: HF can leave a zone of silence - a nearby station unheard while a far one is loud (NEETS 10, p. 106; 🖼 skip-zone drawing). - Match the antenna: vertical talks best to vertical, horizontal to horizontal (FM 24-18, p. 45; 🖼 polarization drawing). Handhelds and car
3-how-radio-actually-works-the-60-second-version

loud (NEETS 10, p. 106; 🖼 skip-zone drawing). - Match the antenna: vertical talks best to vertical, horizontal to horizontal (FM 24-18, p. 45; 🖼 polarization drawing). Handhelds and car whips are vertical - hold the radio upright. 📚 Go deeper: NEETS Module 10, p. 100 - the ionosphere by day and night; NEETS Module 12 - AM, FM and SSB.

4. CB Radio (Citizens Band) - no license, simple, vehicle-friendly - What it is: 40 channels around 27 MHz (in the HF band). No license needed. Cheap, everywhere, popular with truckers and off-roaders. - Range: usually 1-15 miles (more in flat/open terrain; occasionally hundreds of miles when "skip" conditions bounce signals off the ionosphere). - Power limit: 4 watts AM / 12 watts SSB (SSB radios reach farther). - Key channels: - Channel 9 - traditional emergency / help channel. - Channel 19 - highway / trucker channel (road conditions, traffic, convoys). - Channel 1-40 - general use; pick an unused one for your group. - Modes: Most CB is AM. Higher-end radios add SSB (USB/LSB) for more range - but both radios must use the same mode (Single-sideband modulation). - Good for: vehicle-to-vehicle, convoys, short local coordination with zero setup (🖼 common whip antennas; Whip antenna). 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 55 - repairing a broken whip antenna (🖼 repair drawing); Citizens band radio - channels, history and photos.
4-cb-radio-citizens-band-no-license-simple-vehicle-friendly
5. FRS / GMRS / MURS - the walkie-talkie families These are the little handheld radios ("walkie-talkies"). Great for family/group.
5-frs-gmrs-murs-the-walkie-talkie-families

FRS (Family Radio Service) - no license - The blister-pack walkie-talkies (Family Radio Service). 22 channels in UHF (462/467 MHz). - Low power (0.5-2 W), fixed antenna. Range ~0.5-2 miles. - No license, no setup. Good for keeping a family/group in touch on foot.
frs-family-radio-service--no-license

GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service) - cheap license, no test - Shares channels with FRS but allows higher power (up to 50 W), detachable antennas, and repeaters - so range can reach 5-50+ miles via a repeater. - One GMRS license (~$35, no exam) covers your entire family for 10 years. - Best all-round family emergency radio: cheap, legal, powerful, easy (General Mobile Radio Service).
gmrs-general-mobile-radio-service--cheap-license-no-test

MURS (Multi-Use Radio Service) - no license - 5 channels in VHF (151/154 MHz), up to 2 W. No license (Multi-Use Radio Service). - VHF often works better outdoors/rural than FRS/GMRS UHF. Good for property/farm. In hill country: use high ground, get clear of buildings and leafy trees (they soak up more signal than evergreens), and keep away from power lines (🖼 good radio sites; 🖼 poor radio sites). 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 102 - choosing a good radio spot; Walkie-talkie - photos of handheld radios.

6. Ham (Amateur) Radio - the serious emergency option Ham radio is the backbone of emergency communications. When everything else fails, hams relay health-and-welfare traffic, weather, and coordination across towns, states, and continents (Amateur radio; Amateur radio emergency communications).
6-ham-amateur-radio-the-serious-emergency-option

Licensing (USA) - easier than you think Three license levels, each a multiple-choice test (questions are public - you can study the exact pool): 1. Technician - entry level. Grants VHF/UHF (local, repeaters) plus some HF. Enough for local/regional emergency comms. ~1 evening of study. 2. General - adds most HF privileges → long-distance / cross-country. 3. Amateur Extra - full privileges. Get at least a Technician license now while it's easy, and ideally General so you can use HF for long distance. In a true life-or-death emergency, calling for help without a license is generally accepted (see 47 CFR §97.405) - but you'll be far more effective if you've practiced.
licensing-usa--easier-than-you-think

The main ham bands and what they do - 2 meters (144-148 MHz, VHF) and 70 cm (420-450 MHz, UHF): local simplex + repeaters. Your everyday "talk around town" bands. - HF bands (e.g. 80m, 40m, 20m): long distance. - 40m (7 MHz): reliable regional (100s of miles), day and night - great for a state/region emergency net. - 20m (14 MHz): long-distance (cross-country / international) in daytime. - 80m (3.5 MHz): regional at night.
the-main-ham-bands-and-what-they-do

Repeaters - how hams get range from a handheld A repeater is a radio on a tower/hilltop that receives your weak signal and re-transmits it with a big antenna and power, massively extending range. To use one you set your radio to the repeater's output frequency, an offset (so it transmits on the input), and sometimes a CTCSS "tone." Local repeater lists (and emergency nets) are worth printing out for your area (Repeater).
repeaters--how-hams-get-range-from-a-handheld

Simplex (radio-to-radio, no repeater) If repeaters are down, you talk simplex - directly, radio to radio, line of sight. The national 2m simplex calling frequency is 146.520 MHz. Wilderness protocol: back-country hams listen and call on 146.52 for 5 minutes at the top of the hour, every 3 hours from 7 AM to 7 PM, so someone beyond a repeater can be relayed (ARRL manual, p. 84).
simplex-radio-to-radio-no-repeater

HF from a valley: "NVIS" A wire dipole hung low - 1/10 to 1/4 of a wavelength up (roughly 25-60 ft on 80m, worked from the formula in section 8) sends its signal almost straight up; it comes back down like a fountain over a few hundred miles with no skip zone, and the hills matter much less (FM 24-18, p. 279; 🖼 the "fountain" drawing; 🖼 Army NVIS antennas; Near vertical incidence skywave). NVIS: a low antenna sends HF almost straight up, and it falls back like a fountain on the stations around you, hills and all (FM 24-18, p. 283).
hf-from-a-valley-nvis

Nets A net is a scheduled on-air meeting. In a directed net a net control station says who talks next. Listen first, check in when invited, keep a log, and tell net control if you leave (ARRL manual, p. 7, 18).
nets

Ham digital & data (advanced, FYI) Hams can also send text/email/images with no internet via Winlink (email over radio), FT8 (weak-signal), and APRS (position/text). Useful but needs more gear and practice (Winlink, FT8, APRS). 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 14 - ARES, traffic nets and RACES; FM 24-18, p. 278 - NVIS in full.
ham-digital--data-advanced-fyi

7. Shortwave (SWL) - hearing the outside world - What it is: Using a shortwave receiver to listen to broadcasts on the HF bands (roughly 1.8-30 MHz). No license needed to listen. - Why it matters: When local media and internet are down, shortwave lets you hear international news, government/emergency broadcasts, and ham traffic from far away - because HF signals bounce worldwide. - What to listen for: - International broadcasters (news from outside the affected area). - NOAA Weather Radio (VHF 162.400-162.550 MHz) - continuous US weather & emergency alerts. Every emergency kit should have a NOAA weather radio. - Ham bands (40m/20m) - to hear emergency nets and relays. - AM/FM broadcast and Emergency Alert System (EAS) on a normal radio. - Modes: Broadcasts are usually AM; ham/utility voice is often SSB (USB/LSB). A radio with SSB hears far more. - Tip: A simple long wire antenna dramatically improves shortwave reception (🖼 long-wire antenna drawing). - NOAA Weather Radio: repeats every 4-6 minutes; a SAME radio set to your county code wakes up only for your county's alerts (NOAA brochure, p. 2; Specific Area Message Encoding). - No batteries at all: a crystal radio - wire, a homemade coil, a crystal detector and headphones - hears AM stations; in 1922 tests, high-power ones up to about 50 miles away (NBS Circular 120, p. 4; 🖼 wiring diagram and

8. Antennas, power & range (the practical stuff) - Antenna height beats power. Getting the antenna up high (roof, tree, mast) adds more range than buying a bigger amplifier. - Use the right antenna for the band. A proper resonant antenna (correct length for the frequency) works far better than a random wire. - Line of sight (VHF/UHF): range ≈ limited by the horizon and obstructions. Height = range. Repeaters overcome this. - HF skip: range changes with the time of day and solar conditions. Lower bands (80m) are better at night; higher bands (20m) are better in daytime. - Power: keep radios charged. Stock spare batteries, a 12V battery, a solar panel, and car-charging cables. A radio with a dead battery is a paperweight. - Grounding & safety: never put an antenna where it can touch power lines; ground equipment to reduce static/lightning risk. - EMP and solar storms: in government tests, most ham equipment wasn't damaged when its power cord was unplugged and the antenna coax disconnected (NCS TIB 85-10, p. 166) - more in the EMP Guide.

Build a wire antenna (half-wave dipole) Total length in feet = 468 ÷ MHz (3-50 MHz; FM 24-18, p. 47), cut in two equal halves with the coax at the center. 3.980 MHz (Oregon Emergency Net): 117.6 ft · 7.2 MHz: 65 ft · 14.3 MHz: 32.7 ft. Insulators at the ends and center - plastic or glass (plastic spoons, bottle necks) beat wood or rope. The wire must touch nothing else (FM 24-18, p. 55; 🖼 improvised insulators; Insulator)). 3. Tie one end through a spring or strip of inner tube so swaying trees don't snap it. 4. Batteries: a car battery survives only about 20 deep discharges; deep-cycle batteries take 1,000 or more, and shallow use lasts far longer (about 800 cycles at 80% discharge vs 6,000 at 20%). 9. How to call for help (procedure) 1. Listen first. Make sure you're not interrupting other emergency traffic. 2. Use the emergency call: - Voice distress: say "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY" (life-threatening) or "PAN-PAN" (urgent but not immediately life-threatening), then your info (Mayday, Pan-pan). - On CB, call on Channel 9. On ham, break into the local emergency net or call on a repeater / 146.520 simplex. 3. Give the essentials - slowly, clearly, repeat: - Who you are (name / call sign). - Where you are (address, cross-streets, GPS coords, landmarks). - What the emergency is (injury, fire, trapped, etc.). - What you need (medical, rescue, relay a message). 4. Spell hard words with the phonetic alphabet (below). 5. Stay on, don't wander off frequency. Keep the radio on so responders can call back. Repeat your message at intervals if no answer.

NATO phonetic alphabet Alpha Bravo Charlie Delta Echo Foxtrot Golf Hotel India Juliet Kilo Lima Mike November Oscar Papa Quebec Romeo Sierra Tango Uniform Victor Whiskey X-ray Yankee Zulu. Numbers: say digits individually ("one-two-zero"). (NATO phonetic alphabet)

Common "pro-words" - "Over" = I'm done talking, your turn. - "Out" = conversation finished (don't say "over and out"). - "Roger" / "Copy" = I received and understand. - "Say again" = repeat (don't say "repeat"). - "Affirmative / Negative" = yes / no. - "Break" = pause / someone with emergency traffic wants in. (Procedure word) 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 58 - procedure words, phonetic alphabet, signal reports; Pub 102, pp. 148-149 - the international voice distress procedure, with worked Mayday examples.

10. Passing messages for others Much of radio's work after a disaster is carrying short messages for people with no radio. Send in this order (ARRL manual, p. 36): EMERGENCY (life and death - when in doubt, don't) → PRIORITY (important, time-limited) → WELFARE ("Is my family OK?" / "All well here") → ROUTINE (last). - Write the message down first and count the words, so the receiver can check it (🖼 a filled-in radiogram, part by part). - Ready-made welfare texts include "Everyone safe here. Please don't worry." (🖼 blank welfare message form) - Log the time, station, frequency and message. 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 33-34 - welfare form, standard texts, how to write a radiogram; ICS 213 General Message form - the standard paper form emergency offices use.

11. When the radio can't reach: signals without one - Three of anything means distress: three fires in a triangle, three columns of smoke, three shots (FM 21-76, p. 238-243). In wildfire country keep signal fires small, cleared around and watched (rule of thumb). - A whistle is usually heard within about 200 yards (a few reports claim up to a mile - AFH 10-644, p. 509); a mirror is the best signal on a sunny day (🖼 aiming a signal mirror). SOS: three short, three long, three short (SOS). - Ground-to-air symbols in a clearing: V = need help · X = need medical help · N = no · Y = yes · arrow = going this way. Make them at least 6 m (20 ft) long (the two Army manuals differ on width) (FM 3-05.70, p. 329; 🖼 the symbols drawn). 📚 Go deeper: FM 3-05.70, p. 318 - signaling devices and how to use them; Signals and Morse guide - mirrors, ground symbols, Morse by light and sound; AFH 10-644, p. 509 - the Air Force signaling chapter, with pictures.

📡 Signals, Morse Code & Messages How to get a message across with no phones and no working radio: learning Morse by ear, sending it by lamp, whistle, flag or smoke, calling for help from the ground to an aircraft, mirrors and signal fires (and their danger in fire season), semaphore, alarm codes, runners, message forms, a neighborhood OK/HELP card plan, and what to listen to. The books are in Comms-Signals\Morse-Code, Comms-Signals\Visual-Sound-Signals and Comms-Signals\Messaging-Plans. Radios: the Radio guide and the Radio-Weather folder. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Three of anything means "help" - three fires, three blasts, three shots. Use threes for nothing else (FM 3-05.70, p. 318). - No signal fires or "tree torches" in fire season (roughly June-October). In our dry summers they can start a wildfire that kills the people signaling. Use a mirror, cloth panels, ground symbols and sound instead. - Learn only today's 5-symbol ground code: V = need help, X = need medical help (Pub 102, p. 144; 🖼 the five symbols drawn). An old Army code in the library uses X for "unable to proceed". - Never hold a mirror flash on a pilot's cockpit for more than a few seconds - it can blind them (FM 3-05.70, p. 324). - Learn Morse from the International table only. The 1911 Scout handbook prints old American Morse, different for many

few seconds - it can blind them (FM 3-05.70, p. 324). - Learn Morse from the International table only. The 1911 Scout handbook prints old American Morse, different for many letters. - Agree every alarm signal in advance, and use the alarm bell or horn for nothing else (FM 24-5, p. 129).

👂 Learning Morse by ear Morse is sounds, not dots on paper. Think of each letter as a sound ("di-dah" is A), never count dots and dashes, and practice by whistling or saying the sounds aloud (TM 11-459, pp. 3-5). Two proven methods (Pierpont, pp. 159-161; pp. 171-172): - Koch method: start with two letters sent fast (12 words per minute or more). Add one new letter at a time, and only when you copy 90% correctly. Don't look at a chart. - Farnsworth method: each letter is always sent at full speed (18-25 wpm), with wide gaps between letters that you close up as you improve. - Both avoid the "10 wpm plateau" of learning slowly (p. 161). - Short sessions work best: Koch recommended two half-hour sessions a day, spread apart; even 45 minutes gave less (p. 160). A 30-day plan (rule of thumb, built on Koch's rules). A partner sends from the table below by whistle or flashlight while you write what you hear. If you fall behind, stretch the plan - accuracy matters more than the calendar. | Days | What to do (two half-hour sessions a day) | | 1-2 | Two letters that sound very different, such as K and M, in random mixes, until you get 9 in 10. | | 3-20 | Add one letter each time you reach 90% on a
learning-morse-by-ear

very different, such as K and M, in random mixes, until you get 9 in 10. | | 3-20 | Add one letter each time you reach 90% on a 5-minute mix. A common Koch order: K M R S U A P T L O W I N J E F Y V G Q Z H B C D X (general practice). | | 21-25 | Numbers, then period, comma, question mark and slash. Keep mixing in all the letters. | | 26-28 | Procedure signals (AR, K, SK, BT, AS) and the calling routine below. Short real messages. | | 29-30 | Whole messages with your partner, by lamp and by whistle, across a field. | - Send each letter at full speed, even as a beginner - slow down only by leaving longer gaps between letters (TM 11-459, p. 4). - Look-alikes (S/H, U/V, and mirror pairs like B/V, D/U) cause most errors - give the ones you miss extra practice (Pierpont, p. 159). - Copy behind: at higher speeds, let a letter or two go by before writing (TM 11-459, p. 5). - After day 30, ten minutes a day keeps the skill (rule of thumb). 🔦 Morse without a radio: light, sound, flags and smoke - Light: flashlight, lantern or car headlights, with a hat or board as a shutter. Short flash = dot, longer flash = dash (Bluejackets, p. 442). Best at dusk and night. See Signal lamp; aiming a lamp's beam at a far station: 🖼 FM 24-5 drawing. - Sound: whistle, horn or bugle (Whistle, Bugle) - short blast = dot, long blast = dash. On a drum, one tap = dot, two quick taps = dash. Sound works in fog and at night (Signal Book 1916, p. 34) but is slow and easily confused - keep to short, pre-agreed messages (Pub 102, p. 17). - Flags or arms: call with "AA AA AA" and end with AR (Pub 102, pp. 19-20). The Army rule: flag swung to your left for a dash, to your right for a dot (FM 3-05.70, p. 328). - Smoke: spread a blanket over a smoky fire and lift it off to send short and long puffs (Seton, p. 270). Not in fire season - see the fire section below. See Smoke signal. - Knocking through a wall: Morse, or the 5×5-grid tap code (general practice). | If this goes wrong | Try this (rule of thumb) | | Dots and dashes blur together | Very short dots, long dashes, clear gaps | | They keep missing

🆘 Distress signals and talking to aircraft - Threes: three fires, three columns of smoke, three shots or three whistle blasts mean distress, because nature rarely makes things in threes (FM 3-05.70, p. 318; AFH 10-644, p. 509). - SOS by light, sound or flag: three short, three long, three short, sent as one sound and repeated (FM 3-05.70, p. 328). - A flag flown upside down signals distress (Signal Book 1916, p. 41). Body signals to aircraft - stand in the open, move slowly and repeat until understood (FM 21-60, p. 59; 🖼 the signals drawn): | Signal | Means | | Both arms straight up | "Pick us up" | | One arm up | "All OK, do not wait" - easy to confuse with the one above, so be deliberate | | Lying on your back, arms stretched overhead | "Need medical assistance" | | Arms waving, crossed overhead | "Do not land here" | | Cloth waved up and down / side to side | Yes / No | | Arms out to the sides, slowly raised and lowered again and again | Official distress signal (Pub 102, p. 140) | Body signals to a pilot, each with its meaning; face the aircraft in the open and move slowly (FM 3-05.70, p. 330). Not understood: it flies straight and level without rocking, or flashes RPT (🖼 aircraft replies drawn; Search and rescue). 📚 Go deeper: FM 21-60, p. 59 - body signals drawn; Pub 102, p. 140 - official distress signals; Distress signal.

The Army manuals disagree (4 m × 6 m in FM 3-05.70, p. 329; 1 m × 6 m in FM 21-76, p. 243) - bigger is always better. 2. Straight lines and square corners - nature has none. 3. High, open ground seen from every side - a field, a river gravel bar, a logged ridge (local examples: rule of thumb). 6. 🪞 Signal mirrors The best daytime signal. A mirror flash has been seen up to 100 miles away and it works even on hazy or overcast days (AFH 10-644, p. 509). See Signal mirror. Aiming without a sighting hole (AFH 10-644, pp. 510-511): 1. Hold one arm out and make a V with two fingers, with the plane or distant hill in the V (🖼 drawing; 🖼 FM 3-05.70 drawing). 2. Tilt the mirror so the bright spot of light lands on your fingers, then work it through the V onto the target. 3. Or line the target up with the top of a 4-5 ft stake, and sight along the mirror's top edge onto the stake top (🖼 drawing). 4. Keep sweeping the horizon even when nothing is in sight - a pilot may see you first. Aiming with a stake (step 3): line the stake top up with the aircraft, then tilt the mirror until the flash lands on the stake top (AFH 10-644, p. 511). - No mirror? A can lid, polished metal, foil or a shiny card will do (p. 510). The military mirror with a sighting hole, for comparison: 🖼 the MK-3 signal mirror. - Don't flash rapidly, and don't hold the beam on the cockpit for more than a few seconds - it can blind the pilot (FM 3-05.70, p. 324). - Talking with

🔥 Signal fires and smoke - and the wildfire danger What the manuals teach (AFH 10-644, pp. 511-512): - Three fires in a triangle or a line. AFH 10-644 says about 100 ft apart; FM 3-05.70 says 25 m (83 ft) (p. 318). Bright flames at night, lots of smoke by day. - Smoke works best on calm, clear days and has been seen up to 50 miles away. - White smoke (green leaves, moss, wet plants) shows against dark forest. Black smoke (rubber, oily rags, plastic) shows against snow or sky - stay upwind of it (general practice). - Lay the fires before aircraft come, ready to light in seconds. ⚠ Illinois Valley: June to October, do NOT build signal fires. - Only about 15% of our yearly rain falls April to September, and summer afternoon humidity runs 25-30% (NRCS soil survey, p. 5). A tree torch or a spark can start a wildfire that kills the people signaling (Wildfire). - Clearing to bare earth under a tree torch, as the manuals say, is not enough in our brush and grass (AFH 10-644, p. 513; FM 3-05.70, p. 319). - A gasoline smoke pot can explode when lit (AFH 10-644, p. 514). Pen flares and tracer rounds start fires too (FM 3-05.70, p. 321). - In fire season use: mirror, cloth panels and ground symbols, a banner on a
signal-fires-and-smoke-and-the-wildfire-danger

10-644, p. 514). Pen flares and tracer rounds start fires too (FM 3-05.70, p. 321). - In fire season use: mirror, cloth panels and ground symbols, a banner on a pole, whistles and horns. - If you must burn (wet season, or truly no choice): a small fire on a cleared, wetted patch, with water, a shovel and a person watching it, put dead out afterward (general practice). 📚 Go deeper: AFH 10-644, pp. 511-514 - fire and smoke signals; Firewood guide - ashes and fire-season burning rules.

🚩 Flags, semaphore and signal stations Simple flag colors (FM 21-60, p. 37; 🖼 Army flag signals drawn): red = danger; green = all clear / understood; yellow = disregard. At night use colored flashlights. Good for a gate or a lookout. Semaphore spells words with two flags (or bare arms) held at clock positions - by day and in sight only. Pictures: Bluejackets Manual, pp. 444-447 and Flag semaphore; full charts: 🖼 Bluejackets alphabet, 🖼 Signal Book 1916 hand-flag chart, 🖼 FM 24-5 semaphore code. - Letters A to G use one arm stepping around a circle (Scout Handbook 1911, p. 234). - After the numeral sign, A-I mean 1-9 and K means 0. - Always face the receiving station. The receiver stops the sender by holding both arms straight out sideways (Signal Book 1916, pp. 22-23). Siting a flag or lamp station (Signal Book 1916, pp. 43-44): - Stand where the background behind you, as the other station sees it, is one plain color. Use a white flag against green or dark hillsides. - Record the compass bearing to each partner station and drive two aiming stakes in line with it (Compass). - How far you can see to a ground-level object: eye 10 ft up, about 4 miles; 30 ft, about 7; 100 ft, about 13. Ridges around the valley make good relay points (Horizon). 📚 Go

📣 Whistles, bells and alarm codes - Range: most whistle or shout contacts happen within 200 yards, a few at about a mile. A pole banged on a hollow log also carries (AFH 10-644, p. 509). - Rapid strokes of a bell, horn or whistle = "general alarm - act now", no answer needed (Signal Book 1916, p. 38). - Every alarm must be agreed in advance, known to everyone, and used only with good cause (same page). A bell, siren or air horn kept for alarms is never used for anything else (FM 24-5, p. 129; Air horn, Siren)). Visual signals get misunderstood - standardize and practice them (FM 21-60, p. 5). - The 1911 Scout whistle code is a good start: one long blast = "attention, look out for my next signal"; two short = "all right"; a string of short, sharp blasts = "rally, danger, alarm" (Scout Handbook 1911, p. 236). Make a household/neighborhood signal card (rule of thumb - fill in your own and post it): | Signal | Means | Answer | | 3 blasts, repeated | I need help - come to me | 2 short blasts: "heard you, coming" | | String of short, sharp blasts / rapid bell | General alarm (fire, intruders) - act on the plan | None needed | | Red cloth on the gate | Danger, don't come

🏃 Runners, relays and written messages Briefing a runner (FM 24-5 (1939), pp. 68, 70) - tell them: - who the message is for and where to find them; - which route, and which danger spots to avoid; - how fast to go, and whether to wait for a reply; - where to report back, and what to do if it can't be delivered. Spoken messages must be short. The runner repeats it back to you and memorizes it (p. 70). Write it down whenever you can. Speeds and relays (FM 24-5, pp. 69, 71-72): a runner covers about 3 mph routine and 5 mph priority (urgent: as fast as they can and still arrive); a rider 6 and 8 mph. On dangerous routes send two runners in sight of each other, each with a copy, or use two routes. Mark routes with arrows at forks. For long, frequent runs, set up relay posts - say, a house halfway to O'Brien (rule of thumb). Use a standard form. The ICS 213 has To, From, Subject, Date, Time (24-hour clock), Message, Approved by, Reply and Replied by. The sender keeps a copy; the reply comes back on the bottom (ICS Forms Booklet, pp. 65-66; 🖼 the blank form; Incident Command System). Log every message and event with date and time on an ICS 214 activity log (p. 68). The ham "radiogram"

Booklet, pp. 65-66; 🖼 the blank form; Incident Command System). Log every message and event with date and time on an ICS 214 activity log (p. 68). The ham "radiogram" works on paper too (ARRL manual, p. 34): number and precedence, address, text of 25 words or fewer (X for a period), and signature. The "check" is the word count, so the receiver knows nothing was lost (🖼 a filled-in example, part by part). Precedence (ARRL, p. 36): EMERGENCY (life or death - when in doubt, don't) → PRIORITY → WELFARE → ROUTINE. Short codes save time: - "ARL ONE" = "Everyone safe here. Please don't worry." "ARL TWO" = "Coming home as soon as possible." (ARRL, p. 39). - One-letter signals you can flash or sound: V = I need assistance; W = I need medical assistance; K = I wish to communicate; N = no; C = yes (Pub 102, p. 26). Note: at sea W means medical help; on the ground the symbol is X. 🏘 The neighborhood OK/HELP plan From the rural edition of Map Your Neighborhood (MYN Rural, pp. 1-2): 1. Pick a Neighborhood Communication Site everyone knows: a mailbox cluster, a crossroads, or a central home or barn. 2. After a disaster, each household takes its OK/HELP card there with name, date and time, plus the kind of help needed, and tapes it up. 3. Anyone who can help writes on the card what they'll do and when, then reports back. 4. Someone checks every home. Who to check first (MYN Discussion Guide, p. 8): HELP homes, then homes with no card - people there may be hurt. Then recheck the OK homes. Print the HELP/OK window card now (🖼 what it looks like). Your household plan: a meeting place, a way to find each other if separated, and an out-of-area contact, posted at home (Oregon 2 Weeks Ready, p. 6; FEMA, p. 18). Add the neighborhood site, your signal card and a check-in time (rule of thumb). Locally: the county plan counts on door-to-door notice, broadcast stations and amateur radio, and the RVCOG Disaster Registry lists residents needing special help (County EOP, p. 71). Know who they are on your road. 📚 Go deeper: MYN Discussion Guide - the first meeting, 9 steps after a disaster, neighbor map; MYN Rural - rural sites, wells and propane.

📻 Listening when you can't transmit - NOAA Weather Radio repeats its message every 4-6 minutes; a SAME radio wakes up only for your county (NOAA brochure, p. 2; NOAA Weather Radio; Specific Area Message Encoding; Emergency Alert System). For Josephine County program SAME 041033 and try WXL85, 162.400 MHz (Medford). It officially covers eastern Josephine County, and mountain valleys may get poor reception - also try 162.475 and 162.550 and note which works at home (NOAA brochure, p. 3; Illinois Valley guide). - AM reaches farther at night: the layer of the sky that soaks up AM signals by day fades after dark (Navy Basic Electronics, p. 328; 🖼 layers of the ionosphere; Skywave). Listen for outside news after sunset. - Keep every battery radio in the shelter. Small AM sets with built-in antennas are the most likely to survive an EMP (Nuclear War Survival Skills, p. 35). - Log what you hear (time, station, message) and post news at the Neighborhood Communication Site, so one radio serves the whole road (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: NOAA Weather Radio brochure - how SAME alerts work; Radio guide - shortwave, crystal sets and local frequencies.

🤝 Community, Barter & Keeping Watch How neighbors look after each other when no government, police or stores are coming: forming a neighborhood group, running meetings and making fair decisions, knowing who has what skills and tools, sharing work, trading fairly and keeping records, keeping watch, calming angry people, settling disputes and theft without violence, and looking after people's minds through grief and long hard months. The books are in Southern-Oregon\Community-Barter\ (Organizing-Neighbors, Barter-Trade, Watch-Conflict, Wellbeing); the Map Your Neighborhood plan and its OK/HELP card are in Southern-Oregon\Comms-Signals\Messaging-Plans. ### ⚠ Rules that keep a group safe, fair and together - Rescuer safety comes first, and nobody goes alone - always teams of at least two. In the 1985 Mexico City earthquake untrained volunteers saved 700 lives, but about 100 of them died (CERT manual, pp. 2, 58). - Watchers watch and report. They don't confront, chase or carry weapons on patrol (Neighborhood Watch Manual, p. 20). - No punishment by force. Physical force is "never recommended" except to stop an injury (De-escalation slides, p. 4). Beatings and armed posses are crimes and start feuds that outlast the emergency (rule of thumb). - Help is voluntary. Pool work by agreement - never force people to work (a 1918 booklet on the drive says otherwise; see Old advice at the end). - Never announce who is away or what the group has stored

force people to work (a 1918 booklet on the drive says otherwise; see Old advice at the end). - Never announce who is away or what the group has stored (Watch Manual, p. 21). - Write it down - trades, stores and incidents (Braun, p. 19; De-escalation, p. 23).

🏘 Forming a neighborhood group Keep it small. Map Your Neighborhood (MYN) uses 15-25 homes, ideally ones within sight of each other - any more can't all be checked in the "golden 60 minutes" after a disaster. In the country, include as many homes as you can check in an hour or two (MYN, pp. 3, 19). Invite people in person (a flyer on the porch doesn't bring them out), ask one or two neighbors to help, and meet in someone's home - attendance drops at a school or church (p. 19). The 9 steps after a disaster (MYN, pp. 14-16; rural changes from MYN Rural, p. 3): | Step | At home first (1-6), then together (7-9) | | 1 | Care for your own family. | | 2 | Protect head, hands and feet: hard hat or bike helmet, sturdy shoes, leather gloves - kept under the bed (p. 6). | | 3 | Smell or hear gas? 🗳 Meetings and fair decisions Small group: "friendly, serious, courteous discussion is preferable to formal parliamentary procedure" (Braun 1933, p. 13). A bigger meeting (Robert's Rules, 1915, pp. 281-282, 291): - The organizers agree beforehand on the place, time, who calls the meeting to order and who will be nominated chair. - Elect the chair by majority voice vote, then a secretary to keep minutes. Simple rules of order (Robert's Rules, pp. 32, 286): 1. A member proposes something ("I move that..."). 2. Someone else seconds it - otherwise it isn't discussed. 3. The chair repeats it so everyone knows exactly what's being decided. 4. Discussion. One speaker at a time; everyone who wants to speak gets a turn before anyone speaks twice (rule of thumb). 5. The chair asks "Are you ready for the question?" and takes the vote. 6. The secretary writes down the decision. Before founding anything permanent, make sure a majority agrees with the plan - groups that skipped this "have found themselves in the minority" (p. 290). Choosing what to do first: list the problems and rank them, then rank again asking "Which can we do with our own resources?" and "Which will benefit the most people?" (Peace Corps PACA, p. 116). Robert's Rules of Order. 📚 Go deeper: Robert's Rules of Order (1915) - Part II: calling a mass meeting and founding a society;

🤲 Sharing the work - Give everyone a job. People are less frightened when they have responsible jobs. Set a daily routine, post the assignments, and rotate the unpleasant tasks (FEMA HS-4, p. 97). A useful job (sorting supplies) also calms a disruptive person (CERT, p. 152). - Pool teams and machines. Three small farms that work together can each finish haying in two or three days instead of the whole season, then help the big farm (USDA Circular 112, p. 7). Barn raising. - A labor committee lists everyone with farm (or other) experience who volunteers, and sends them where they're needed at rush times (p. 9). - People new to hard work should do light work, a few hours a day, for the first days (p. 10). - Credit the hours in the group's points ledger (next section), so work counts as much as goods. 📚 Go deeper: USDA The Farm Labor Problem (1918) - pooling crews for planting and haying (use its methods, not its 1918 coercion); FEMA HS-4 - daily routine and duty rosters in a shelter.

🔄 Barter and fair trade What trades well (Barter): a good that many people need, that lasts, is cheap to store, divides into small amounts and is easy to carry (Menger 1892, pp. 30-31). Such goods naturally become money (p. 36; Commodity money). Plain barter fails when A wants what B has, B wants what C has, and C wants what A has (p. 21). Coincidence of wants. - Likely trade goods here: salt, sugar, coffee, soap, matches and lighters, seeds, canning lids, batteries, fuel, firewood - and skills: sewing, repair, medical care (general practice). - Don't trade prescription drugs casually (general practice) - fakes and wrong doses kill (see the Medical guide). Setting up a barter group (Braun 1933, pp. 13-15): a few people first survey what the community needs and has to trade; present it at a meeting; elect a steering committee; choose a trading place; write a membership agreement. Start small, "with people you know." Members meet weekly on practical trading business only - don't leave everything to one manager. The trader should be trustworthy, "a natural trader but not a sharp, hard bargain driver," and should arrange three-way trades: A has potatoes and wants oranges, B has oranges and wants beans, C has beans and wants potatoes (p. 15). Braun's three-way trade: no two of them can swap directly, but passed round the ring each gets

has oranges and wants beans, C has beans and wants potatoes (p. 15). Braun's three-way trade: no two of them can swap directly, but passed round the ring each gets what they want (a diagram drawn for this guide). Fair exchange - the points ledger (p. 19): - 1 hour of work = 100 points; an 8-hour day = 800. Value goods in work: a cord) of wood = one day's work = 800 points (🖼 what a cord looks like). - Record every credit and debit in the member's passbook and in a central book, and balance them regularly like a bank account. Rules that kept barter groups healthy (pp. 17, 21): put off paper scrip as long as possible; refuse junk; admit new members fully only after they show they cooperate; and nobody can take more from the group than they put in. Shared credit and local notes (Cleveland Fed, pp. 1-3): Ithaca Hours were pegged to one hour of local labor. In

👀 Keeping watch Structure (Watch Manual, pp. 10-11): - One block captain per 10-15 houses. - A phone tree: call the next person, skip down if they're out, and the last person calls the captain to confirm. With phones down it becomes a runner chain (general practice). Practice it, and use it to stop rumors you've checked. - Daily check-in: OK/HELP cards at the communication site (MYN Rural, p. 2), or the radio check-ins on the Illinois Valley page. Each house calls the next, skips anyone who's out, and the last one calls the captain to confirm (a diagram drawn for this guide). Patrol rules (p. 20): watch members "do not possess police powers and they shall not carry weapons or pursue." They "should never confront suspicious persons." Carry flashlights and radios that report to a staffed base. Walk in pairs, observe, report - don't intervene (general practice). Describing what you saw (p. 24): note what can't be changed - height, build, skin and eye color, scars, tattoos. Clothes can change. Write it down at once, even on your hand. Never hesitate to say "I'm not sure." Night watch: keep watch-standers on a consistent schedule rather than switching shifts, and protect their daytime sleep - sentry duty is among the jobs most damaged by sleepiness (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 154). 🗣 Calming an angry person From the Kentucky de-escalation slides (pp. 15-24): - Distance: slightly more than a leg's length, at an angle and off to the side (p. 17) - far enough that you can't be hit or kicked. Hands visible. Never touch a hostile person (p. 15). No face-to-face, toe-to-toe or finger-pointing (p. 16). - Voice: slow and calm (p. 19). Listen - really listen (p. 21). - Move onlookers away - they become "cheerleaders" or victims. Send one for help. Two calm people with one angry person lowers the chance of violence (same page). - Never say "I know how you feel," get into power struggles, raise your voice, threaten, or give ultimatums (p. 24). - Afterwards, write down every threatening incident (p. 23). A bit more than a leg's length away, off to the side and at an angle, hands in view, with a second calm person nearby (a diagram drawn for this guide). 📚 Go deeper: Using Verbal De-Escalation - 25 plain slides on stance, voice and what not to say; CERT, p. 152 - giving a disruptive person a useful job; Conflict Resolution Education Guide, p. 31 - rules for fighting fair.

⚖ Settling disputes and dealing with theft Where conflict comes from: limited resources, unmet needs, or different values. Values don't have to change - first admit each side sees it differently (Conflict Resolution Guide, pp. 22-23). Giving in ("soft") or threats ("hard") don't last; only "principled" responses tend to make agreements that hold (pp. 23-24). Four principles: separate the people from the problem; focus on interests, not positions; invent options that help both; use fair, outside standards. Six steps: set the stage, hear each side, find the interests, list options, judge the options, agree (pp. 24, 26). Fight fair: attack the problem, not the person; no put-downs; don't drag up the past (p. 31). Mediation (FAO, p. 27): a mediator helps both sides design their own solution; an arbitrator decides for them. To find interests, keep asking "Why is this important for you?" (p. 128). Turn insults into problems: "You are selfish, the whole community suffers" becomes "consider a solution that meets your family's interests and the community's" (p. 129). Water, firewood and fence-line disputes fit this well (general practice). Mediation. Protecting shared stores (general practice): don't advertise what you have; keep common stores in locked, rodent-proof containers with a written in-and-out log; two people to open them; rotate who guards and who counts. When something goes missing - a fair process (rule of thumb): 1. Write down the facts
settling-disputes-and-dealing-with-theft

written in-and-out log; two people to open them; rotate who guards and who counts. When something goes missing - a fair process (rule of thumb): 1. Write down the facts - what, when, who saw what. Not guesses or rumors. 2. Two calm people talk to the person privately. Listen first. 3. If it's still disputed, use a mediator; if both sides agree to it, three neutral members decide (arbitration). 4. Repair the harm: return it, replace it, or work it off in ledger points. 5. Repeated or serious harm: the group can vote, under its written agreement, to remove someone from the barter group or shared stores. Report crimes to the sheriff while there is one. 6. Never beatings, public humiliation, locking people up, or taking a family's own food. Remember that hungry people steal - fair food sharing prevents a lot of theft (see the Food Security guide). 📚 Go deeper: Conflict Resolution Education Guide - principled negotiation and mediation in plain English; FAO Negotiation and Mediation Techniques - disputes over land, water and wood.

💛 Grief, stress and psychological first aid Look, listen, link (WHO Psychological First Aid, p. 25): look for safety, urgent needs and people in severe distress; listen and help them feel calm; link them to practical help, information and loved ones. - Don't pressure anyone to tell their story. Sit quietly, offer water, allow silence (p. 21). - Don't say "You should feel lucky you survived," don't make false promises, and don't take away their sense of being able to care for themselves (p. 22). - Someone who seems unreal or far away: feet on the floor, tap their hands on their lap, have them name what they see and hear, breathe slowly (p. 30). - Most people recover once basic needs are met and others support them. Don't leave a severely distressed person alone (p. 27). - Don't label normal reactions as disorders (PFA Field Guide, p. 12). Accept emotional injury as being as real as a sprained ankle (FM 4-25.11, p. 174). To the grieving, never say "It could be worse," "Everything happens for the best," or to a child, "You're the man of the house now" (PFA Field Guide, p. 41). Look after the helpers (🖼 self-care toolkit): work in pairs (WHO, p. 50); watch for helpers taking on survivors' feelings and burning out - time away helps (CERT, p. 144); sleep, exercise, eat, and balance work,
grief-stress-and-psychological-first-aid

toolkit): work in pairs (WHO, p. 50); watch for helpers taking on survivors' feelings and burning out - time away helps (CERT, p. 144); sleep, exercise, eat, and balance work, play and rest (p. 146). Over months: expect a "disillusionment" low in the second half of the first year and again around the anniversary (CERT, p. 151). Counter it with scheduled good activities, problem-solving and helpful thinking (Skills for Psychological Recovery, p. 49), deliberately rebuilding friendships (p. 65), and regular support-group meetings (Where Women Have No Doctor, p. 14). Psychological first aid. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Psychological First Aid - a short field guide; PFA Field Operations Guide - children, grief and handouts; Skills for Psychological Recovery - worksheets for the months after.

👵 Children, elders and neighbors who need help - About 1 in 6 people has a disability that affects daily life (Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 9). - Name one person to check on each older or disabled neighbor; keep wheelchairs and walkers in one fixed place; and ask neighbors now whether they're willing to help (Red Cross Seniors, pp. 8, 10, 15). - Older adults: speak clearly in a low pitch, and don't assume confusion is permanent (PFA Field Guide, p. 13). - Children: crouch to eye level and use simple feeling words - mad, sad, scared, not "terrified" (same page). Children cope the way their parents cope (FEMA Are You Ready?, p. 188). Schooling with no school: older children tutor younger ones (peer tutoring) (Peer Tutoring, pp. 17-21). Structured tutoring beats casual help; short focused stretches (up to 4 weeks) work best; math, then reading, show the biggest gains. Train tutors to be kind - untrained tutors drift into threats and put-downs (p. 21). The tutors gain skill and confidence too. For family talk and journaling, use the day-by-day prompts in the Oregon toolkit. One-room school. 📚 Go deeper: Red Cross Disaster Preparedness for Seniors by Seniors - written by elders after a two-week outage; NWREL Peer Tutoring - teaching mixed ages with few adults.

The Illinois Valley Fire District has run free CERT Basic classes in Cave Junction (local listings 2025-2026, not from a file - verify). - We're used to waiting. Sheriff patrols were cut back after public-safety levies failed from 2012 on (general knowledge) - one more reason to organize before anything happens. - Wells and propane: most Valley homes have both, so use the rural MYN steps (MYN Rural, p. 3). - Mailbox clusters on the side roads make natural communication sites (general practice). - Radios: cheap FRS/GMRS handhelds reach about 1-2 miles in our hills (general practice). Listen to the local nets now - see the Illinois Valley page and Signals guide. - Fire season (roughly June-October): the night watch doubles as a fire lookout. 📚 Go deeper: MYN Rural Settings - the rural plan; Red Cross Seniors - building a support network before you need it.

🛡 Home & Property Protection (Defensive Only) How to keep your family, home, food, tools and animals from being easy targets when no deputy is coming: looking like a poor choice to thieves, hearing trouble early, slowing people down, getting everyone to safety, calling the neighbors, and staying within Oregon law. This guide is strictly defensive. On purpose, it has nothing on fighting, patrolling or building traps. The books are in Southern-Oregon\Home-Security\ (Home-Hardening, Safe-Room, Neighborhood-Watch, Rural-Property, Law), with the watch and de-escalation books in Southern-Oregon\Community-Barter\ and guardian-dog books in Southern-Oregon\Animals\Planning-Predators-Toxic-Plants. ### ⚠ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Never booby-trap anything: no spring guns, tripwires, spikes or rigged doors. Traps can't tell a thief from a child, a firefighter or a neighbor coming to help. In 2018 a man in Williams (here in Josephine County) rigged a house with shotgun traps. One went off into an FBI bomb technician's leg, and in 2023 he got 150 months in federal prison (U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon, 2023). See the law. - Don't shoot at property, or at anyone who is not an immediate deadly threat to a person. Oregon never allows deadly force just to stop theft or vandalism (ORS 161.229). - Know who is on your land before you do anything. At night the "intruder" may be a neighbor, a lost child, a confused elder or someone running

(ORS 161.229). - Know who is on your land before you do anything. At night the "intruder" may be a neighbor, a lost child, a confused elder or someone running from a fire. - Keep firearms locked away from children and thieves. It's Oregon law (ORS 166.395). - A person's life is worth more than any property. Let things go. Physical force is "never recommended" except to stop an injury (De-escalation, p. 4). - Avoid confrontation and call the neighbors. Watchers "should never confront suspicious persons" (Watch Manual, p. 20).

🧅 Layers: deter, detect, delay, respond Think of protection as layers. Each one makes a thief more likely to give up or be seen, and buys your family time. The Watch Manual compares it to sports: "the more defenses a team has... the less likely the opponent will be to score" (Watch Manual, p. 32). | Layer | What it means | On a Valley lot (examples) | | Deter | Make your place look like a poor choice | Someone home, a dog, no supplies on show, a locked gate | | Detect | Know early that someone is coming | Dog, geese, gate bell, gravel, motion light, radio check-ins | | Delay | Slow them down | Strong doors and strike plates, locked outbuildings, pinned windows | | Respond | Protect people, not things | Safe room or escape, whistle alarm, neighbors on the radio | Why layers matter more out here: - Secluded houses are attractive targets: set back on large lots, they "reduce the chance that neighbors or passersby will see or hear a burglar" (COPS Burglary, p. 22; 🖼 photo). - Devices work best together. Burglars get in less often when a house has two or more (window locks, deadbolts, lights, alarms), and the devices "slow them down, making them more vulnerable to being seen" (p. 25). - Help is far away. Each layer must

🤫 Don't be a target Look lived-in. "Most burglars do not target occupied houses, taking great care to avoid them"; some ring the doorbell first to check (COPS Burglary, p. 20). So: - Someone home most of the time, no set times when everyone leaves, and be seen around the property often (WSDA Farm Security, p. 1). - Never announce who is away (Watch Manual, p. 21). - No spare key under the mat or in the car. Leave one with a trusted neighbor (Seattle Police, Outside the Home, p. 2). Don't advertise supplies. Burglars read a house's contents from what they can see outside (COPS Burglary, p. 25). After a collapse the "signs of wealth" change (rule of thumb): | Gives you away | Quieter way (rule of thumb) | | Bright windows when every other house is dark | Curtains or blankets over lit rooms (cover windows people can see into: Seattle Police) | | A generator roaring every evening | Run it in daylight, only as needed, outdoors and away from windows (carbon monoxide). See the Off-Grid Power guide | | Cooking smoke and smells at all hours | Cook at the same times as the neighbors | | Empty food boxes and fuel cans by the road | Burn, compost or bury packaging well back from the road | | Talking about your stores at trades

| | Empty food boxes and fuel cans by the road | Burn, compost or bury packaging well back from the road | | Talking about your stores at trades | Keep amounts private. Share through the group, not at the roadside | Quiet sharing. Hungry people steal, so fair sharing prevents theft (Community guide). Give through the group or a welcome point (below), so no one house becomes "the place with food" (rule of thumb). What to say to strangers (rule of thumb): friendly and short. "We're getting by like everyone. The table at the crossroads has water and news." Don't say how many live here, who is away, what you have, or that you're armed. 📚 Go deeper: COPS Burglary, p. 20 - occupancy and how burglars check; Seattle Police, Deterring Burglary From Outside the Home - looking at your home "through the eyes of a burglar".

🚪 Doors, frames, locks and windows Doors get kicked, not picked. "The most common way used to force entry through a door with a wooden jamb is to kick it open." The weak point is "almost always the strike plate," which is held only by short screws into thin trim (Seattle Police, Door Security; 🖼 how a strike plate sits in the jamb). The cheapest big fix (Seattle, Door Security): 1. Take out the short screws in every exterior door's strike plates and hinges. 2. Put in 3- to 4-inch wood screws that bite into the wall stud. "This one step alone will deter or prevent most through-the-door forced entries." 3. Better still, fit a four-screw heavy-duty strike plate, plus at least one long screw in each hinge. 4. Against pry bars, add a latch guard over the gap where the bolt meets the frame (🖼 photo). Long screws carry a kick into the wall framing instead of the thin jamb (a diagram drawn for this guide). Doors and locks (Watch Manual, pp. 32-33): - Exterior doors metal or solid wood. Hollow-core or poorly fitting doors "can mean trouble" (🖼 door types; 🖼 door and frame cross-section). - A deadbolt with a bolt that sticks out at least 1 inch, on every outside door and the door from the garage into the house. - Hinges on the inside, or pins

Exterior doors carry 3 hinges (USDA AH 73, p. 146; 🖼 hinge drawing). - Change the locks when a place changes hands. - Double-cylinder deadbolts (key both sides) only where a thief could break glass and reach the thumb-turn, and keep the key in the inside lock while anyone is home so you can get out in a fire (Seattle, Door Security). - A door viewer (peephole) lets you see and talk without opening (general practice). Windows have latches, not locks (Seattle, Window Security): - Double-hung windows (🖼 drawing; sash window): drill a hole down through the inner sash into the outer one and drop in a sash pin, a long nail or an Allen wrench (🖼 photos). A second hole 5 inches up lets you pin it open for air. - Sliding glass doors and sliding windows: a snug dowel or a hinged "Charlie bar" in the inside track, plus screws half-way into the top track so the panel can't be lifted out (🖼 p. 2). - Security window film makes glass shatterproof (p. 2). - Bars on bedroom windows must open from the inside. 🌳 Fences, gates, lighting and sightlines The three CPTED ideas (Crime prevention through environmental design; COPS CPTED, pp. 15, 17-19): 1. Control access. "Fences, tree lines, hedges, or berms define the boundaries"; drives and paths guide people; "gates and doors limit points of entry." 2. See and be seen. Lighting, windows that look out on the approaches, and plants chosen and trimmed so views are kept open (p. 18). 3. Show ownership. Gardens and upkeep "show that someone cares and is paying attention" (p. 19). Sightlines and brush, with fire safety first. Dense shrubs and privacy fences near doors and windows give a burglar cover (COPS Burglary, p. 21). Seattle Police use a 3/6 rule: shrubs under 3 ft, tree limbs above 6 ft (Outside the Home, p. 1; 🖼 pictures). Here the stricter fire rules win: - Limbs on mature trees at least 10 ft up, none over the roof (OSU EM 9184, p. 8). - Nothing that burns within 5 ft of the house (Ready Set Go, p. 4; 🖼 the zones). Seattle suggests thorny Oregon grape under windows; here, plant only beyond 5 ft, and pick fire-resistant shrubs (OSU PNW 590). - Clear brush that hides the driveway approach: 10 ft side clearance, 13.5 ft overhead, so a fire engine fits (OSU EM 9184, p. 8; wildfire section). Fences and gates: - The boundary "is the property

driveway approach: 10 ft side clearance, 13.5 ft overhead, so a fire engine fits (OSU EM 9184, p. 8; wildfire section). Fences and gates: - The boundary "is the property owner's primary line of defense." Make gates strong, mounted securely, and locked with heavy chain and padlock; use ditches, large rocks or locking posts to close side gaps (WSDA Farm Security, p. 1). - A solid privacy fence hides a burglar. See-through fencing such as chain-link keeps the view open (Seattle, Outside the Home, p. 2). - Make sure helpers can get in. Neighbors and the fire crew must be able to open or cut the gate fast (rule of thumb). Skip razor wire or spikes where children or firefighters might climb. Lighting (security lighting): enough to see about 100 ft at the entry, with motion lights on side and back yards (Seattle, p. 1). On a secluded lot a motion-activated light works as an alert, while steady light only helps if someone is there to see (COPS Burglary, p. 22). With no grid, aim solar lights along the approaches (Off-Grid Power guide). Signs and address: "No Trespassing" signs define the boundary (WSDA, p. 1), but signs "are only good if you can back them up" (Seattle, p. 2). Keep a reflective address sign visible from both directions, day and night, so neighbors and responders find you (OSU EM 9184,

🧱 Fortifying the property: barriers that delay without harming The aim is to make getting in, and carrying things out, slow, noisy and easy to see, so a thief gives up or gets noticed. Full-height fences with locked gates "hinder a burglar in carrying away stolen goods" (COPS Burglary, p. 47). Nothing here may hurt anyone who touches, climbs or runs into it in the dark, block a way out of the house, or keep out a fire engine (see the rules at the top and the limits at the end).

One way in: the driveway and vehicle barriers One entrance you can watch. The U.K. "Secured by Design" scheme cut burglary partly by "creating greater oversight around a single road entry" (COPS Burglary, p. 46). On a rural lot that means one driveway gate, with every other gap closed to vehicles by boulders, which don't burn (PNW 590, p. 8); posts or bollards of steel, concrete or heavy timber (Alberta Farm Fuel Storage, p. 22); or earth berms and ditches (COPS CPTED, p. 17; WSDA, p. 1). Keep every barrier easy to see by day and night (white paint, reflectors), and never dig a ditch or pit across a path or drive (rule of thumb). Keep it open to a fire engine (FEMA P-737, pp. 75-76; 🖼 drawings): - Set the gate about 50 ft back from the public road, so a fire engine or a visitor waiting at it is out of the traffic lane. - Driveway at least 12 ft wide, strong enough for 40,000 lb, no steeper than 16%, with gate openings "wide enough" (Ready Set Go, p. 7). A drive longer than 150 ft needs a turnaround (inside radius 30 ft, or a "T" 60 ft across). - 13.6 ft clear overhead. Other books say 13.5 ft (OSU EM 9184, p. 8) or 15 ft (Firewise, p. 2); use FEMA's figure as the least, and the

Stronger windows and glass doors - Stronger glass, ground-floor windows first (Seattle, Window Security, p. 1): "double-pane, storm or divided light windows, or laminated glass that is forced-entry resistant" (COPS Burglary, p. 40). For glass doors: double- or triple-pane laminated glass, or film and metal grilles (Seattle, p. 2). - In fire country (FEMA P-737, pp. 48-49): laminated glass comes apart when its plastic core gets hot, so shutter it or pair it with tempered glass in a double-pane unit, which lasts about 10 minutes in a wildfire, twice as long as single-pane. No plastic glazing (acrylic, polycarbonate): it "can melt during a wildfire". - Shutters: solid metal. They "are unlikely to ignite or melt and are therefore recommended over wooden or plastic shutters" (p. 49). Closed, they also stop a quick smash-and-grab (rule of thumb). - Bars and grilles only with an inside quick-release. They "may violate building codes and pose a safety threat by blocking fire exits" (COPS, p. 40). Use them on "particularly vulnerable" windows such as secluded basement ones, with interior release latches on any fire-exit window; in bedrooms they must come off "easily from the inside" (Seattle, p. 2). Never bar the only way out of a room. - Glass block meets Oregon's wildfire window rule (Oregon BCD, p. 8) but can't be opened: use it only where nobody needs to climb out, like a

of a room. - Glass block meets Oregon's wildfire window rule (Oregon BCD, p. 8) but can't be opened: use it only where nobody needs to climb out, like a bathroom (rule of thumb). - In an emergency: planks or small tree trunks across windows, clear sticky tape on the glass "to prevent flying glass", and heavy curtains (ICRC First Aid in Armed Conflicts, p. 256). Living fences: thorny hedges that don't feed a fire Thorny shrubs "deter perimeter access" where you can't keep a view (COPS Burglary, p. 47). Here are the thorny ones on OSU's fire-resistant hedge list for Jackson and Josephine counties (OSU Privacy Screens, p. 8), plus two natives: | Plant | Grows to | Notes | | Pyracantha | 12 ft tall, 12 ft wide | Evergreen; sun or part shade; little water (p. 11) | | Thorny silverberry (Elaeagnus ebbingei) | 12 ft tall, 12 ft wide | Evergreen; sun; little water. Not E. umbellata, which is invasive (p. 11) | | Flowering quince | 12-15 ft tall, 10-12 ft wide | Many trunks; sun; little water (p. 9) | | Black hawthorn, native | 15-20 ft tall, 10-15 ft wide | A small tree (PNW 590, p. 48) | | Native roses: Wood's, Nootka, bald-hip | Wood's rose 3-6 ft each way | Spreads. Skip sweetbriar and multiflora rose, both invasive (PNW 590, p. 40) | Don't plant English hawthorn, English holly or Himalayan blackberry: all three invade the local oak woods (KBO Restoring Oak Habitats, p. 41). Blackberry thickets are also "flammable" and burn "well in winter"; get rid of them (OSU EM 9184, p. 20). Fire spacing comes first: - Nothing within 5 ft of the house. From 5 to 30 ft, groups 10 ft or more

rid of them (OSU EM 9184, p. 20). Fire spacing comes first: - Nothing within 5 ft of the house. From 5 to 30 ft, groups 10 ft or more apart, and "avoid planting in rows" (PNW 590, p. 7). Farther out, shrubs at least 2-3 times their height apart (EM 9184, p. 16), or a dense screening clump with 5-10 ft cleared around it (p. 5). - A hedge touching a fence or shed is a wick that can carry fire to a wooden building, "possibly your home" (OSU Privacy Screens, p. 4). - So plant staggered clumps of mixed kinds, not a solid row (pp. 6-7), in the gaps where people would push through (rule of thumb). Prune out dead wood yearly: heavy shearing leaves dead, flammable twigs inside (p. 7). The books don't say how many years a hedge takes to stop anyone.

A wall against stray bullets: protecting people A thick wall keeps a stray shot from reaching the family: along a safe room's outside wall, or on the side of the house that faces the road. It is never a place to shoot from. "Protection from view (e.g. a bush) is not necessarily protection from fire" (ICRC, p. 254). Thickness that stops an ordinary rifle bullet (the Army's 7.62 mm; 🖼 FM 5-34, Table 4-1, p. 127): | Concrete | Gravel, small rocks, brick or rubble | Soil or sand | Solid timber | | 12 in | 20 in | 42 in (3½ ft) | 36 in (3 ft) | A sandbag wall (FM 5-34, p. 139, with a drawing): 1. Use fill that isn't serpentine (limits below). Build on the ground, clear of the house. 2. Fill bags three-quarters full (for a lasting wall, 1 part cement to 10 parts earth). Set the bottom row about 6 in below ground, then lay rows alternately end-on and side-on, like brickwork. Against a bank, lean the wall into it, about 1 ft in for every 4 ft up. 3. Earth-filled bags count as soil, so make the wall about 3½ ft thick (rule of thumb, from the table). Earth-filled boxes, baskets or oil drums work too (ICRC, p. 256). Lay bags alternately end-on (headers) and side-on (stretchers), joints broken, leaning into
a-wall-against-stray-bullets-protecting-people

thick (rule of thumb, from the table). Earth-filled boxes, baskets or oil drums work too (ICRC, p. 256). Lay bags alternately end-on (headers) and side-on (stretchers), joints broken, leaning into the bank (FM 5-34, p. 139). Earth is heavy: about 90 lb per sq ft for each foot of depth, so a sandbag wall 6 ft high presses about 540 lb on each square foot under it (arithmetic). To carry earth on a wooden floor, Kearny adds a beam of three 2x6s under the joists, on posts about 4½ ft apart (Nuclear War Survival Skills, p. 55). Keep soil off wood: "there should be no wood-soil contact of any kind". Use metal flashing or a covered 2-3 in air gap, and never bank earth against siding or sills (USDA FB 1993, p. 13). A FEMA safe room is tested against flying debris (a 15-lb 2x4 at 100 mph), not bullets (P-320, p. 26). With no wall, lie down away from windows, in the middle of the building, with "at least two walls between you and the direction from which the sound of shooting is coming" (ICRC, p. 255). After the firing stops, wait 10-20 minutes more (p. 254).

Outbuildings, fuel and the well - Fuel-theft checklist (Alberta Farm Fuel Storage, p. 14): tanks in a well-lit spot, out of sight of the road but in sight of the house; valves and caps locked; pump power off at a switch in a locked building; hoses with cam-lock (quick-coupler) fittings, taken off and locked away; and a log of fuel bought and used, so a loss shows. - Distances from a tank (p. 21): 3 ft from another fuel tank, 10 ft from any building, 20 ft from flames, propane, grass and weeds, 100 ft from forest or water, 165 ft from a well (Alberta's metric figures, rounded (arithmetic)). Ring the tank with boulders or posts against vehicles (p. 22). - Keep fuel, fertilizer and pesticides out of the well house: spills reach the water "through the top of the casing". Keep the well capped, its sanitary seal unbroken and vent screens in place (OSU EM 8651, p. 3). - Barn doors: an old fastening slides two bars into slots above and below double doors and "may be also worked from the inside"; a simple latch goes inside the door that closes first (Handy Farm Devices, p. 195; 🖼 p. 194). Any building with people or animals in it needs a door that opens from inside (rule of thumb). - Buried valuables: "During the Civil War, people buried their valuables

Any building with people or animals in it needs a door that opens from inside (rule of thumb). - Buried valuables: "During the Civil War, people buried their valuables to protect them" (FEMA H-S 4, p. 53). Gravel and noisy birds: sources for two old tricks - A gravel strip at least 5 ft wide around the house is a fire rule: a "noncombustible area" of "gravel, rock mulches, or hard surfaces" (OSU EM 9184, p. 5). The crunch underfoot is a bonus (rule of thumb). - Geese are "large, hardy, aggressive, noisy birds", sometimes kept to "act as watch dogs", and may live 30 years. Guinea fowl "are valued for watch dog services on some farms" (Raising Healthy Poultry, p. 124).

Fire and legal limits on any barrier 1. Two ways out of every room (Firewise, p. 2). Anything over an escape window opens from inside, without a key or tool. 2. Burnable fence parts at least 10 ft from the house (FEMA P-737, p. 64), and the first 5 ft of fence must not burn: use a metal gate or panel (OSFM, p. 11). A wooden gate on a garage "ignited and led the fire to the home" (🖼 FEMA P-737, p. 63). 3. Open the gate when you evacuate if the fence by the house can burn, "to break up the wick to your home" (OSFM, p. 11). Leave the driveway gate unlocked for the fire crew (rule of thumb). 4. Don't dig serpentine soil for berms or bags: common in the valley (Start Here), it can carry natural asbestos (UC ANR 8400, p. 1). Use boulders, or fill from other ground (rule of thumb). 5. Barriers stay on your own land: never block a public road (ORS 166.025). And no traps, spikes or hidden pits, ever (the law). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA P-737, Fact Sheets 10, 14 and 17 - windows and shutters, fences, and driveways in fire country; Alberta Farm Fuel Storage and Handling - theft, siting and barriers for fuel tanks; OSU Fire-Resistant Shrubs and Trees for Privacy - a screen that won't spread fire.

🔔 Early warning with no grid Dogs. "A dog's presence is a close substitute for human occupancy, and most burglars avoid houses with dogs." Small dogs bark and draw attention (COPS Burglary, pp. 20-21). "A good watch dog in the house and yard area is one of the best security measures" (WSDA, p. 1; Guard dog). Livestock guardian dogs guard stock, not people. Common breeds are the Great Pyrenees, Anatolian Shepherd, Maremma and Akbash (Texas A&M, p. 5; Livestock guardian dog; Great Pyrenees; Anatolian Shepherd; Maremma; 🖼 photo). Socialize them with people: unsocialized dogs may "harm employees" (same page). Known problems include dogs "overly aggressive to people" and dogs that roam onto neighbors' land (USDA AIB 588, p. 28). See the predator sections of the Chickens, Rabbits and Goats guides. Other alarm animals. "Donkeys, llamas and cattle will sometimes protect sheep that graze with them" (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 133; 🖼 guard llama). Geese honk loudly at strangers and are an old farm alarm (general practice). Simple noise alarms (rule of thumb): - A bell on every gate and door that rings when it opens. - Cans with pebbles tied to fence wire, where people don't walk. - Gravel on paths and under windows crunches underfoot. - Never string a line across a path, driveway or doorway. It trips children, elders and firefighters in the dark, and it's one step

🏠 A safe room and a household plan A safe room is a place to wait behind a strong door while help comes. It is not a place to fight from. FEMA's full version. Taking Shelter from the Storm (FEMA P-320) has plans for reinforced tornado rooms, which also make a strong hardened room: - Where: a basement, a bathroom, closet or laundry room, or a separate room within 150 ft (p. 41; 🖼 floor plans). - Size: at least 3 sq ft per person for a short stay, 7 for a long one, 10 for a wheelchair user (p. 37). - Door: ordinary steel house doors fail FEMA's tests; a real safe room needs a tested, labeled door (p. 53; 🖼 label). - Cost: about $9,400-$25,500 new, plus the door, and more in an existing house (p. 56; 🖼 construction drawings). Possible safe-room spots in an ordinary house: an inside bathroom or closet, a garage corner, or a room outside within 150 ft (FEMA P-320, p. 41). The everyday version (rule of thumb, built from the door advice above): - An inside room with a solid-wood or metal door, a deadbolt, and the strike plate and hinges screwed into the studs with 3-inch screws. - A second way out (a window that opens from inside), a smoke alarm and a fire extinguisher (🖼 how to use one). A locked

the studs with 3-inch screws. - A second way out (a window that opens from inside), a smoke alarm and a fire extinguisher (🖼 how to use one). A locked room in a burning house is a death trap. If there is smoke, get out. - Kept stocked (P-320, p. 69): 1 gallon of water per person per day, food, first-aid kit and medicines, a flashlight for every 4 people, a battery radio, a portable toilet, a crowbar to open a jammed door, plus a whistle or air horn and an FRS radio. The household plan (rule of thumb; fill it in on the Oregon My Pocket Plan): | Decide now | Example | | Who goes where | Kids and grandma to the back bedroom; one adult with the radio | | Who calls for help, and how | Air horn, then FRS channel 3 to the neighbors | | Two ways out | Front door; back bedroom window | | Outside meeting spot | The neighbor's barn | | Code words | "Safe room now," "all clear," and one that secretly means "I'm being forced, stay hidden" | Practice it, once at night too, until the children know it (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA P-320 - sizing, locations and full building plans; FEMA Are You Ready?, p. 62 - preparing a safe room.
