🥫 Protecting food, water, fuel, tools and livestock Food and water: - Shared stores go in locked, rodent-proof containers with a written in-and-out log, and it takes two people to open them (Community guide). - Don't keep everything in one place. Split stores between the house, the cellar and an outbuilding, so a thief or a fire takes only part (rule of thumb). - A hidden cache (rule of thumb): sealed, rodent-proof containers of foods that keep (Food Security guide). Tell one other adult where. - Lock the pump house (rule of thumb; Wells guide). Fuel (WSDA, pp. 1-2): - Lockable caps on fuel outlets; fuel tanks, pumps and electric-fence units secured and locked. - Place fuel tanks where they can be seen from the house. Keep stored fuel, chemicals and fertilizer "to a minimum" and locked up. Storage and safety: Fuel guide. Tools, machinery and valuables: - Mark everything in at least two places, one easy to see and one hidden (WSDA, p. 2). - Operation ID (Watch Manual, p. 34): engrave your Oregon driver's license number starting with "OR" and ending with "DL". Never your Social Security number. Marked items are hard to sell, so burglars avoid them. - Keep a property list with serial numbers and marks, plus photos, stored away from the things themselves (p. 34). - Machinery: take the keys out; remove the distributor cap,

👥 Neighborhood watch after the collapse How to set up a watch, block captains, the phone or runner tree, describing people and the night shift table are all in the Community guide: Keeping watch. The key rules: - Watchers watch and report. They "shall not carry weapons or pursue" and "should never confront suspicious persons" (Watch Manual, p. 20; Neighborhood watch). - What counts as suspicious (p. 24): someone peering into cars or windows, people at homes at unusual hours, tampering with gas, power or water, signs of forced entry, and "anything that feels uncomfortable or looks out of place." A roster that doesn't wear people out (rule of thumb, from the Community guide): - 2-hour shifts in pairs, the same nights each week, with a written handover. Protect watchers' daytime sleep (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 154). - Nobody stands watch two nights running. Spread it across every capable adult; give elders, parents of babies and the sick lighter daytime jobs. - In fire season the watch is also the fire lookout. Daily check-in: post OK/HELP cards at the communication site (MYN Rural, p. 2), or follow the Signals guide's OK/HELP plan. Checkpoints: a welcome point, not a roadblock (rule of thumb): - Never block a public road. Obstructing "vehicular or pedestrian traffic on a public way" is disorderly conduct under Oregon law (ORS 166.025). Gates on your own driveway

of thumb): - Never block a public road. Obstructing "vehicular or pedestrian traffic on a public way" is disorderly conduct under Oregon law (ORS 166.025). Gates on your own driveway are fine. - Put a table at a crossroads turnout, on private land with permission, with two calm, unarmed neighbors, a radio, water and a news board. - Everyone may pass. Nobody is stopped or searched. The table offers news and help, and quietly notes descriptions and vehicles (Watch Manual, p. 24). Helping people on the move (rule of thumb): meet them at the welcome point, not your house, and give through the group. Use look, listen, link: check urgent needs, listen, connect them to help (WHO Psychological First Aid, p. 25). Newcomers who stay join the group's work and barter rules (Community guide). 📚 Go deeper: Neighborhood Watch Manual, pp. 20-24 - patrol rules and what is suspicious; MYN Rural Settings - the rural check-in plan; COPS CPTED, p. 19 - showing a neighborhood is cared for.

🚧 Someone at the gate, strangers, or a break-in Before you open anything: 1. Find out who it is: through the viewer, a window, or by calling out. 2. Talk through the closed door or gate. Don't open it. Let them know someone is home; most burglars avoid occupied houses (COPS Burglary, p. 20). 3. Point them to help that isn't your house, such as the welcome point (rule of thumb). If they're upset, use the Community guide's Calming an angry person: a slow, calm voice, hands visible, never threats or ultimatums (De-escalation, pp. 15-24; De-escalation). If someone is trying to get in, or is already inside (rule of thumb): 1. Sound the alarm: air horn or whistle, a string of short blasts. 2. Everyone goes to the safe room, or out the escape route to the meeting spot. Take the kids and elders first. 3. Call the neighbors on the radio: who you are, where, what's happening. 4. Stay put. Don't go looking for the intruder. Let them take things. Property can be replaced. People can't. Remember what you saw (Watch Manual, p. 24): what can't be changed (height, build, skin and eye color, scars, tattoos) and the vehicle's make, type and plate. Write it down at once. "Never hesitate to say, 'I'm not sure.'" Afterwards (WSDA, p. 2): - Check everyone first, then give first aid (Injuries guide).

⚖ Oregon law on force in defense of people and property This is not legal advice. It quotes the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition, from oregonlegislature.gov) in plain words. Laws change, and courts decide each case on its facts. The key test in every section is what you "reasonably believe," and other people judge that afterwards. | Situation | What the law says | In plain words | | Defending yourself or another person (ORS 161.209) | You may use physical force against "what the person reasonably believes to be the use or imminent use of unlawful physical force," and only "a degree of force which the person reasonably believes to be necessary" | Only against a real, present attack, and only as much force as needed | | If you started it (ORS 161.215) | No justification if you provoked it or were "the initial aggressor," unless you withdraw and make that clear | Starting a fight takes away your defense | | Deadly force (ORS 161.219) | Only if you reasonably believe the other person is committing or attempting a felony that uses or threatens force against a person, or a burglary in a dwelling, or is using or about to use unlawful deadly force against a person | Reserved for a threat to people's lives and bodies | | Your land and buildings (ORS 161.225) | Physical
oregon-law-on-force-in-defense-of-people-and-property

or about to use unlawful deadly force against a person | Reserved for a threat to people's lives and bodies | | Your land and buildings (ORS 161.225) | Physical force to stop a criminal trespass when you reasonably believe it necessary. Deadly force only to defend a person (as above), or to prevent arson or "a felony by force and violence by the trespasser" | Trespassing alone never justifies deadly force | | Your things (ORS 161.229) | "Physical force, other than deadly physical force," to stop theft or criminal mischief | Never deadly force over property | | Pointing a gun (ORS 166.190) | Purposely pointing a loaded or empty firearm at someone "except in self-defense" is a crime | Don't wave guns at people at the gate | | Threatening (ORS 163.190) | Menacing: trying "to place another person in fear of imminent serious physical injury" by word or conduct | Threats are a crime too | "Deadly physical force" means force that "is readily capable of causing death or serious physical injury" (ORS 161.015). Booby traps and spring guns. No Oregon law allows them. A trap can't "reasonably believe" anything; it hits whoever comes: a child, a firefighter, a neighbor coming to help. Setting a loaded spring gun, set gun or any device rigged to fire when someone touches a wire or string is a crime
oregon-law-on-force-in-defense-of-people-and-property

a firefighter, a neighbor coming to help. Setting a loaded spring gun, set gun or any device rigged to fire when someone touches a wire or string is a crime in itself (ORS 166.320). Any trap also creates "a substantial risk of serious physical injury to another person," which is recklessly endangering (ORS 163.195), and if someone is hurt or killed the charges grow. Courts have long made trap-setters pay even when the person hurt was a trespasser (Katko v. Briney; Spring-gun; Booby trap). Then there's the Williams case in the warning box at the top. Firearm storage: the Cindy Yuille and Steve Forsyth Act (SB 554 as passed): - Whenever a firearm is not carried by or under the control of its owner or an authorized person, it must be secured with an engaged trigger or cable lock, in a locked container, or in a locked gun room (ORS 166.395; trigger locks, gun safe). - It is not secured if the key or combination is "readily available" to someone not authorized. - The fine is higher if a minor gets an unsecured gun. If an unsecured gun is used to hurt someone within two years, the owner is treated as negligent in a lawsuit (with narrow exceptions). - Report loss or theft within 72 hours (ORS 166.397). Directly supervise any minor you hand a firearm to, with some hunting

as negligent in a lawsuit (with narrow exceptions). - Report loss or theft within 72 hours (ORS 166.397). Directly supervise any minor you hand a firearm to, with some hunting and target-range exceptions (ORS 166.403). Training: if you keep firearms, get real training from a qualified instructor. This guide doesn't teach firearm use. Why it still matters when the courts are closed: courts reopen, and in Oregon a prosecution for murder or "any degree of manslaughter may be commenced at any time" (ORS 131.125). Neighbors remember, too: a shooting over a chainsaw can start a feud that outlasts the emergency (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Oregon SB 554 (2021), enrolled - the full storage, theft-reporting and transfer law, with the legislature's reasons; ORS chapter 161 (sections 161.195-161.275) is quoted above from oregonlegislature.gov.

🔥 Fire as a threat to your home A fire, whether set on purpose or blown in from the hills, can take everything at once. The defenses are those in the Illinois Valley wildfire section: - First 5 ft: nothing that burns. Firewood and lumber 30 ft away (OSFM, p. 13; Defensible space)). - Within 100 ft: grass short, trees spaced, and no ladder fuels (🖼 drawing). - Vents covered with 1/8-inch metal mesh (🖼 how embers get in). Water and tools ready (rule of thumb): full buckets or barrels, a charged hose if you have pressure, shovels and rakes by the door, and a fire extinguisher you know how to use (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep: 🖼 CERT, pp. 171-172). Pull the pin, aim at the base of the fire, squeeze, and sweep (CERT, p. 172). At night: the watch looks for smoke and glow as well as people (Community guide). If the house is on fire, everyone gets out. Never stay in a safe room in a burning building. 📚 Go deeper: OSFM Defensible Space Homeowner Guide - the zones, step by step; FEMA P-737 - hardening the house itself; OSU EM 9184 - year-round checklists. 🔥 No fire department coming? Clearing with hand tools, water with no power, deciding to stay or go, and riding out the fire front are in the Wildfire guide.

😴 Stress, fatigue and judgment The worst outcomes come from tired, frightened people deciding fast in the dark (rule of thumb). - Sleep is protection. Keep watch-standers on a consistent schedule (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 154). - Check rumors before acting. Use the phone or runner tree to confirm facts (Community guide). - Don't escalate. Two calm people with one angry person is safer than one (De-escalation, p. 21). Swap out anyone losing their temper (rule of thumb). - Look after the helpers. Watchers and helpers burn out; time away helps (CERT, pp. 144-146). - After a scare, use psychological first aid: look, listen, link (Community guide; Psychological first aid). - Despair and guns don't mix. Oregon's legislature found that "a proven barrier to the impulse to commit suicide is securing firearms with a lock or storing firearms in locked containers" (SB 554, p. 1). In hard months, let a trusted person hold the key for anyone who is struggling (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: WHO Psychological First Aid - a short field guide; CERT, p. 144 - stress in helpers.

⏳ What to Expect: Disaster Scenarios & Timelines What really happens, hour by hour and month by month, in the disasters most likely to hit the Illinois Valley, and what to do at each stage. The timelines come from official plans and after-action reports: the Oregon Resilience Plan, the Josephine County hazard plan, the state's review of the 2020 Labor Day fires, federal and state power-outage and fuel plans, and fifty years of disaster research. The books are in Disaster-Scenarios\ (Cascadia-Earthquake, Local-Hazards, Fire-Heat-Drought, Grid-Supply-Pandemic, How-People-Respond), with more in Wildfire\, Earthquake-Tsunami\, Nuclear-Radiation\ and EMP-Solar-Storms\. ### ⚠ Five rules that hold in every scenario 1. Plan to be on your own for at least two weeks. The state's own Cascadia exercise said so (Cascadia Rising, p. 12). At the end of one highway, plan longer. 2. Leave early. Alerts fail when cell towers burn or lose power (2020 fire review, p. 9). A Level 2 "Be Set" notice may be the only warning you get. 3. Check on people who live alone. Most who died in the 2021 heat dome lived alone (heat report, p. 10). 4. Generators, grills and camp stoves stay outdoors. Carbon monoxide kills in every outage (CPSC). 5. Expect neighbors to help, and be one. Panic and looting are rare; survivors do most of the rescuing (Quarantelli, p. 16).

❄ 2. Winter storm, ice, flood and landslides What it is and how likely here. The county rates winter storms #2 of all hazards: high probability, high vulnerability. Recent ones: in February 2019 fallen trees closed US-199 at the California line and 2,500 customers lost power around Grants Pass, Cave Junction and O'Brien; in January 2021 snow left 45,000 customers in the area without power (county plan, p. 64). The valley is "one way in, one way out": a storm on US-199 can strand Cave Junction and cut the whole valley's power "for an extended period" (p. 140). Floods are rated high probability, moderate damage. The benchmark is the Christmas flood of 1964: 10 inches of rain in six days, the Rogue and Illinois Valleys cut off and I-5 closed (p. 45). In 2015, water covered US-199 near Selma and closed roads near O'Brien (p. 46). 🌡 3. Extreme heat and drought What it is and how likely here. The county rates heat waves high probability, moderate damage. Days with a heat index over 90 °F are expected to rise from about 13 a year to about 40 by the 2050s (county plan, p. 57). In the June 2021 heat dome Josephine County saw 92-108 °F, with two more heat waves later that summer (p. 58). In Portland it killed 72 people; in a normal year, none. Most were 60 or older and lived alone, and half had only a fan (heat report, pp. 2, 8-12). Drought is also rated high probability: extreme drought years 1924, 1977 and 2001, severe ones as recently as 2014 and 2020 (p. 33). 🔌 4. Long power outage, including fire-season shutoffs What it is and how likely here. Storms knock out power almost every winter (scenario 2). 🦠 5. Pandemic What it is and how likely here. A new germ spreads around the world, usually "within several weeks or months." The last century had flu pandemics in 1918, 1957, 1968 and 2009 (WHO, pp. 51-52), and then COVID-19 - so expect one or two in a lifetime (estimate). A pandemic comes in waves of several weeks to a few months, and a later wave can be worse: the mild spring wave of 1918 came before the deadly autumn one (p. 52; Spanish flu). ⛽ 6. Economic crisis, fuel and supply-chain breakdown What it is and how likely here. Oregon has no refineries; more than 90% of its fuel comes from four refineries near Seattle, mostly through one pipeline to the Portland fuel hub (fuel plan, p. 9). Gas stations hold about two to three days of fuel (p. 11). Groceries hold more shelf-stable food than most people think; the real problem in a catastrophe is delivery, not supply (CNA, p. 9). In the 1970s oil shortages states used odd-even days to cut gas lines (NASEO, p. 45; 1973 oil crisis). In the Great Depression people formed barter associations to trade work and goods (Braun 1933, p. 5). 🌎 7. Cascadia M9 earthquake (and the coast tsunami) What it is and how likely here. The Cascadia subduction zone last broke on January 26, 1700 (1700 Cascadia earthquake). About half of past quakes were centered off the southern Oregon coast; the odds of one hitting southern Oregon in the next 50 years are about 37% (Resilience Plan, p. 31). The county puts it at 37-43% for any Cascadia quake and 7-12% for the full M9, and rates our vulnerability high (county plan, p. 39). 🚨 8. Riots and law and order breaking down What it is and how likely here. Fifty years of disaster research found panic flight so rare that fire researchers stopped using the idea, and looting "unusual in the typical natural and technological disasters" of countries like ours (Quarantelli, pp. 6-7, 11-12). Mass looting did happen after Hurricane Hugo on St. Croix and after Hurricane Katrina, where three things came together: many poor people living beside obvious wealth, organized youth gangs, and a police force that was ineffective or corrupt (pp. 13-14). Even there, help between people "swamped" the theft, and after the first emergency days reported crime usually drops (p. 14). The EMP Commission warns that disorder becomes more likely when shortages cause conflict and police are absent for a long time (EMP Commission 2008, p. 167). 🤝 What every scenario has in common The first 72 hours. No outside help, so neighbors are the first responders. In the first half hour after a disaster, about a third of survivors search for missing people and about one in ten actively rescue them (Quarantelli, p. 16). Your jobs: injuries, fires, water, a toilet, warmth or cooling, and checking the people next door. The 2-week mark. Oregon tells everyone to be ready for at least two weeks (Be 2 Weeks Ready, p. 2). The old 2004 FEMA book's "at least three days" (p. 33) is too short for here. Two weeks is also about when most big storm outages have ended, and the longest disruption most businesses can stand (Resilience Plan, p. 22). When things usually improve. Most storm, fire and heat emergencies ease within days to weeks. A Cascadia quake, EMP or national crisis takes months to years (see the tables). Plan for the long tail, not just the first days. Why most neighbors help. After disasters, help and sharing far outweigh theft, even in the worst cases (Quarantelli, p. 14); citizen groups spring up to clear debris, move supplies and pass messages (EMP Commission 2008, p. 167). Plan on cooperating, and organize early. Rumor control. Rumors make things worse. Pick one trusted source (a radio station, the ham net, a neighborhood runner) and write down news with

Pick one trusted source (a radio station, the ham net, a neighborhood runner) and write down news with the time and who said it (rule of thumb); help correct misinformation (Psychological First Aid, p. 35). Mental health. Feeling overwhelmed, confused, afraid or numb is a normal reaction (WHO Psychological First Aid, p. 9). Keep routines, give everyone a job, keep children close and talking, and watch for anyone who stops eating or caring for themselves (rule of thumb). 🔥 Wildfire: Defending Your Place With No Grid How a household in the Illinois Valley can get its people, house, animals and land through a wildfire when no engine, air tanker, alert or phone is coming: reading the danger, hardening and clearing with hand tools, water without the grid, hand line, deciding ahead whether to stay or go, the fire's arrival, and the years after. The basics (5-ft and 30-ft rules, vent mesh, evacuation levels, a cleaner-air room) are in the Illinois Valley guide ("Wildfire"), Home Defense ("Fire as a threat to your home") and the Shelter guide ("Earthquake and wildfire hardening"). Most books are in Southern-Oregon\Wildfire: the federal firefighters' Incident Response Pocket Guide (IRPG), fire-behavior guide (PMS 437) and tactics guide (PMS 465); the Australian Country Fire Authority's (CFA) plan for staying to defend a house, adapted here because it assumes phone apps and daily ratings; Cohen's Forest Service research on how homes ignite; the State Fire Marshal (OSFM); and OSU Extension. FEMA P-737 is in Southern-Oregon\Shelter-Building\Wildfire-Quake-Hardening, Fire Weather (AH 360) in Southern-Oregon\Navigation-Weather\Weather, and the thinning and slash bulletins in Southern-Oregon\Firewood\Woodlot. ### The short version - Leaving early beats staying late. Deaths "can occur because people wait too long to leave" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 2); leaving early "does not mean waiting to see or smell smoke" (CFA, p. 11). Decide before fire season, not on the day. -

East wind: the night is not safe "East wind in fire control means an exceptionally dry wind from an easterly quadrant that may blow continuously for 24 to 48 hours or longer. East wind often reaches maximum strength during night and early morning hours. Surface wind of 60 mph is not uncommon", with humidity "extremely low around the clock" (PMS 465, p. 227; Foehn wind). When fire turns wind-driven, "This change can occur quickly" (p. 262). The 2020 numbers and warning signs are in Navigation & Weather ("Illinois Valley weather through the year"). On an east-wind day (rule of thumb): a lookout awake all night; the car fueled, packed and facing out; tanks full; protective clothes laid out; no saw, mower, grinder or fire of any kind; a leaving time agreed with the neighbors.

Smoke columns, spotting and flame length - The column: smoke trapped under an inversion means calmer fire; when it "begins to boil through the inversion ... Expect lowering RH, possible wind shifts, and increasing flames, spread, and spotting" (IRPG, p. 54). "sudden calm, smoke at your feet" mean a wind change; torching trees and more spot fires mean a blow-up (p. 53). - Spotting (embers starting fires ahead) is usually 100 ft to ¼ mile, sometimes miles; the Cerro Grande Fire spotted 10 miles ahead (PMS 437, p. 153). 🏠 How houses catch fire Three ways: embers land on something that burns; a surface fire creeps to the walls or roof; or radiant heat from burning plants or buildings nearby. "Most commonly, homes are lost in wildfires when they come into contact with embers or low-intensity surface fires - not from a giant wall of flames" (OSU EM 9247, p. 2). - Embers cause up to 90% of house fires (OSFM, p. 5), get in "through vents, windows, and other openings" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 3), and pile up where snow drifts on the roof and deck (p. 5). - Flames have to be close. By Cohen's calculations even crown fires won't light wood walls more than 40 m (130 ft) away (Cohen, p. 2): there a wall needs over 10 minutes of heat, but crown-fire flames last about 1 minute in one spot (p. 3). Test walls 10 m (33 ft) from crown fires didn't ignite, and homes with nonflammable roofs and 10-18 m (33-60 ft) of clearance survived 95% of the time (pp. 3-4). - The house can be the fuel: homes with flammable roofs "ignite and burn without the surrounding vegetation also burning" (Cohen, p. 4). The roof "is the most vulnerable component" (EM 9247, p. 3). - Late burning comes from "residual spot fires or creeping ground fire" (IRPG, p. 31). Single-pane glass can fail

🔨 Hardening the house with what you have Vents, gutters and woodpiles are in the Shelter guide; windows, fences, gates and the driveway in Home Defense. The order: 1. Roof first. Clean it and the gutters spring and fall, and in summer under madrones, which drop leaves then (EM 9184, p. 9); debris gathers in valleys and where roof meets wall (P-737, p. 25). Untreated wood shakes are unrated and "not desirable" (BCD, p. 3): keep hand-split shakes for sheds, and salvage metal roofing from buildings you won't defend (rule of thumb). 2. Vents: 1/8-inch metal mesh over the old 1/4-1/2 in screen, which "may be plastic" (OSFM, p. 8). This follows current Oregon advice over FEMA's 2008 "maximum opening of 1/4 inch" (P-737, p. 40). 1/16 in clogs, and clogged debris can make embers; keep cardboard away from vents (BCD, p. 5). 3. Vent covers. Ready, Set, Go! says cover attic and ground vents with "pre-cut plywood" (p. 9); FEMA advises against it because people fall (P-737, p. 42). So cut and label covers now; always fit the ground and crawlspace vents; gable vents only from a tied-off ladder with time to spare (rule of thumb). 4. Gaps and gutters. Caulk gaps; open eaves trap heat (BCD, p. 6). Seal pipe and wire holes with mortar (P-737, p. 72; lime mortar: Masonry & Roads). Vinyl gutters "can fail under

🪓 Clearing around the house with hand tools Work from the house outward (rule of thumb). The books differ on trees; this guide uses: - Spacing: at least 10 ft between crowns within 100 ft (OSFM, p. 14), 15-20 ft within 30 ft of the house and more on slopes (EM 9247, p. 5); branches 15 ft from the house (PNW 590, p. 7), 10 ft from a chimney (OSFM, p. 15). - Limbing: 6 ft up, or a third of the height on trees under 18 ft (OSFM, p. 14); mature trees 10 ft, taking no more than a third of the live branches at once; conifers in fall and winter, hardwoods in spring (EM 9184, p. 7). - Keep some: deciduous trees "block embers" (OSFM, p. 15); mature ponderosa pine and bigleaf maple "catch and filter embers" (EM 9247, p. 5). Brush and ladder fuels. Small trees and brush under big ones are "ladder" fuels that carry a ground fire into the crowns (EC 1573, p. 2). Space shrubs 2-3 times their height apart (EM 9184, p. 16), none over one metre (about 3 ft) by a window (CFA, p. 4). Worst burners: Scotch broom, gorse, blackberry, juniper, many manzanitas and ceanothus (EM 9184, p. 15). - Oak, madrone and tanoak resprout, and the sprouts "can quickly become new ladder fuels"; sometimes don't cut (EM 9184, pp. 15-17).

Black oaks cut December-May sprouted 92%, June-November 45% (PSW-GTR-185, p. 36), but summer tool work starts fires: cut in late fall, after the first real rain (rule of thumb). - Blackberry: dig the crowns with a Pulaski or grub hoe (EM 9184, pp. 20-21). Scotch broom: cutting old plants in late summer may kill them, but don't graze it: it is "toxic to livestock in large quantities" (p. 20). Take out the brush and low limbs that let fire climb, and space the crowns (a diagram drawn for this guide). Grass under 4 in within 100 ft (OSFM, p. 16). Dry grass makes flames "three times the height of the grass": cut it green, before fire season; in season mow only early in the morning (EM 9184, p. 9). Slash with no chipper. Lop and scatter it 12-18 in deep at most; it only moves the fuel, dry slash takes "a decade or more" to rot, and never "within 100 feet of the home" (EC 1574, p. 2). Hand-pile pieces under 6 in across (p. 3) and burn them in winter (see "Burning on purpose"). Animals mow too. Cattle keep grass down; goats and sheep browse brush but need fencing,

⛏ Hand tools and firebreaks Pulaski): ax plus grub hoe, "about 5½ pounds"; short, shallow swings, the hoe landing on its corner; goggles; "Never sharpen the top of the hoe" (MTDC, p. 25). McLeod): rake plus hoe, "inefficient in rocky or unusually brushy areas" (p. 26). Fire shovel: scrapes "down to mineral soil" (p. 29). Carry tools "at your side and downhill, with blades forward"; "Never throw a tool" (p. 11). Saws in fire season: Firewood guide ("Bucking and limbing"). Grub with short, shallow strokes and let the hoe land on its corner (MTDC, p. 25).

Building a hand line A hand line (fireline) is a strip cleared of fuel and scraped to bare mineral soil (Firebreak). 1. Anchor it to something that won't burn: road, creek, rock, plowed field or burned ground (IRPG, p. 23). Building "without safe anchor point" is one of the 18 Watch Out Situations (p. 140). 2. Width: "one and one half times as wide as the dominate fuel is high", 1-3 ft of it scraped to mineral soil, on the side away from the fire; in timber, 20-30 ft cleared with a 3-4 ft scrape (PMS 465, p. 42). Brush 6 ft tall needs a 9-ft line (arithmetic). 3. Down to mineral soil, or fire creeps through roots; unburned material goes outside the line, burning material into the burn (p. 37). Limb the trees on both sides: heat crosses a narrow line without flames touching (pp. 40-41). 4. Below a fire on a slope, dig a "cup trench" to catch rolling logs and cones (p. 38); above it, the steeper the slope, the wider the line (p. 17). 5. Short and straight, tied to roads, rock and creeks; on a ridge, on top or just over (IRPG, p. 101). Never build line downhill toward a fire, mid-slope above it, or with unburned fuel between you and it (p. 20). Clear a strip, then scrape the side away from the fire

build line downhill toward a fire, mid-slope above it, or with unburned fuel between you and it (p. 20). Clear a strip, then scrape the side away from the fire down to bare soil (PMS 465, p. 42). A cup trench below a fire on a slope catches burning logs and cones (PMS 465, p. 38). The burning edge itself is the "Safest place to work; firefighters can usually escape into the burned area" (IRPG, p. 99). "Most firelines will be unsuccessful in stopping a crown fire" (PMS 465, p. 42).

Small fires, spot fires and wet sacks - "Don't overestimate your ability" (ODFW, p. 34). "Do not ever try to fight a fire alone"; "Always have two ways to exit"; "If you feel the heat, you are too close" (CERT, p. 173). - Dirt first: throw mineral soil, scrape a line around, stir hot embers into dirt (PMS 465, pp. 52, 91). - In grass: let it burn to a barrier, "cold-trail" the dead edge (feel along it, line any live spot), or use a "gunnysack or swatter" (PMS 465, pp. 30, 59; Fire flapper). Soak a burlap sack, work from the burned side, press or drag it on the base of the flames instead of flapping, and re-wet it often (rule of thumb). - "Getting frequent spot fires across line" is a Watch Out: time to go (IRPG, p. 140).

Burning out: mostly don't Burning out is "setting fire inside the fireline to consume fuel between the fireline and the edge of the fire", so crews "keep one foot in the black"; backfiring sets fire well ahead of the main fire, a riskier method (PMS 465, pp. 112-113). Firing needs lookouts, escape routes, anchor points and "Adequate resources ... for both firing and holding" (IRPG, p. 26). Household rule (rule of thumb): never backfire. Burn out only a narrow strip of grass or litter off a finished, anchored line, with the wind carrying it away from the line, someone holding the line with water and tools, and a lookout. If unsure, don't.

🚪 Stay or go: decide before fire season "Do not wait to be advised to leave" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 10). Alerts failed in 2020 (What to Expect guide); now there are none. Stay only if every answer is yes (CFA, p. 3): - [ ] At least two fit adults "physically and mentally prepared to work long and hard" - [ ] About 2,600 gal of water, and pumps and hoses that run with the power out, tested this season - [ ] Protective clothing for each, and the house hardened and cleared to 100 ft - [ ] A safety zone at the house: "Do not commit to stay and protect a structure unless a safety zone ... has been identified" (IRPG, p. 27) - [ ] Not a worst-weather day; children, elders and the sick already gone (CFA, p. 3), and the animals - [ ] Everyone knows "staying to defend may involve trauma, injury or possibly death" (CFA, p. 5) Places you can't defend: "narrow canyon bottoms, mid-slope with fire below, and narrow ridges near chimneys and saddles" (IRPG, p. 28). Worst-weather days: "Do not plan to defend on CATASTROPHIC days" (CFA, p. 3). With no ratings, call it catastrophic when an east wind breaks twigs from trees and humidity is under 15%, or leaves crumble to dust (rule of thumb, from CFA, p. 2 and

Triggers: write them down A trigger is something you can see that means "go now". Leaving early "does not mean waiting for a warning or a siren" (CFA, p. 11); firefighters "Set trigger point for safe retreat" (IRPG, p. 30). Examples (rule of thumb): a worst-weather day; a smoke column building over a named ridge upwind; ash or embers falling; fire crossing a named road or creek (time your escape against its spread, IRPG, p. 21); any one adult saying "go".

LCES for a household Firefighters' LCES "must be established and known to ALL firefighters BEFORE it is needed" (IRPG, p. 21): | | Firefighters' rule (same page) | At home (rule of thumb) | | Lookouts | "good vantage points"; "Knowledge of trigger points" | Someone on a high point with binoculars, day and night on east-wind days, taking turns | | Communications | "Sound alarm early, not late" | Whistle and bell codes (Signals guide); walkie-talkies (Radio guide) | | Escape routes | "More than one"; "Avoid steep, uphill escape routes"; "Timed considering slowest person"; "Marked for day or night" | Two roads out, driven at night; a printed map (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 8); car facing out (CFA, p. 7) | | Safety zones | "Back into clean burn"; rock, water, meadows, roads; bigger if upslope, downwind or near heavy fuel | A plowed or grazed-down field, irrigated pasture, gravel lot or big pond, sized below |
lces-for-a-household

Safety zones: how big "Separation distance between the firefighter and the flames should be at least four times the maximum continuous flame height" (IRPG, p. 22): | Flame height | Distance to the flames | Area | | 10 ft | 40 ft | 1/10 acre | | 20 ft | 80 ft | ½ acre | | 50 ft | 200 ft | 3 acres | | 100 ft | 400 ft | 12 acres | That counts radiant heat only, on flat ground with no wind, for a three-person crew, and is "Not intended for structure protection" (same page). With wind over 10 mph or slope over 20%, it may need "more than double" (p. 21). Measure from the flames to where you stand: at least four times the flame height (a diagram drawn for this guide).
safety-zones-how-big

Getting out and last resort - Keep "old shoes and a flashlight handy in case of a sudden evacuation at night" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 8). Lock up (CFA, p. 11); open any wood gate joined to the house to break the "wick" (OSFM, p. 11). Don't leave "the key in the ignition" (FEMA 2004, p. 127): keep it on a hook by the door (rule of thumb). - Caught outside (IRPG, p. 46): "Escape if you can." In light fuels "you may be able to move through the flames into the black"; on a flank, "try to get below the fire"; "Use bodies of water" and "heat barriers such as large rocks"; "Structures and vehicles may be an option for temporary refuge". Expect "Extremely heavy ember showers" and a "Superheated air blast" before the flames; lie face down, protect your airway, and "WHEN IN DOUBT, WAIT IT OUT" (p. 47). You have no fire shelter: a pond or plowed ground is your last refuge (rule of thumb).
getting-out-and-last-resort

Hours before the front 1. Protective clothing on: "always first thing to do" (CFA, p. 8). Anyone not defending leaves now. 2. Fill the bath, buckets and tanks; roll out hoses; set up and test pumps and backpack sprayers (CFA, p. 7). 3. Clear the walls: furniture, doormats and BBQ cylinders away; inside, furniture away from windows (same page); cloth curtains down unless the blinds are metal (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 9). 4. Close up: windows, doors, vent covers; gas off at the tank (same page); fans off so they can't draw embers in (P-737, pp. 42-43); wet wool blankets or cotton towels around the inside of windows and doors (CFA, p. 8); a ladder under the attic hatch and a flashlight in the attic (p. 7). 5. Wet the house: fill the gutters, "Hose down the side of the house facing the fire", sprinklers on when embers appear; "Patrol for embers ... You may need to do this for several hours"; "Drink lots of cool water" (CFA, p. 8).
hours-before-the-front

As the front passes: shelter inside "As the fire front approaches it will become extremely hot outside. You will be unable to survive out in the open" (CFA, p. 9). Bring plastic hoses and fittings in, and go inside when "The skin on your ears and hands will alert you" (same page). Then: - Stay where you can see the fire. "Most bathrooms are unsuitable to shelter in": one door. Every shelter room needs two ways out; a window counts. Check the roof space for embers; drink water. - If the house catches fire: shut the door on the burning room, close doors as you move to the far end, then go out to burned ground. "Do not return to the house for any reason if it's on fire." "If it's hot inside the house, it is four to five times hotter outside" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 9). The flames pass quickly: about a minute in one spot for a crown fire (Cohen, p. 3).
as-the-front-passes-shelter-inside

Right after: ember patrol "Exercise extreme caution before deciding to go outside", then "Actively patrol your property for embers for hours after the fire has passed" (CFA, p. 10): roof lines and gutters, garden beds and mulch, outdoor furniture, woodpiles, doormats, decks, sheds, window ledges and door sills, under the house, inside the roof and under the floorboards (same page), and the attic (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 9). "Water down the outside of the house, including the roof" (CFA, p. 10); stay clear of "the structural collapse zone" (IRPG, p. 31). Duff, stumps and log piles smolder for days: patrol day and night for at least 3 days, then daily for 2 weeks and after every dry, windy day (rule of thumb).
right-after-ember-patrol

😷 Smoke, heat and people Protective clothing (CFA, p. 7): a wide-brimmed hat, smoke goggles, a P2 (N95-type) mask, a long-sleeved collared shirt and long pants of cotton or another natural fibre, "Tough leather garden gloves - not rubber or synthetic", sturdy boots, wool or cotton socks. Many synthetics "can melt or catch fire" (AFH 10-644, p. 177). If your clothes catch fire, "do not run ... Lie down and roll" (Scout Handbook 1911, p. 284). A bandana is not a mask. "Cloth face coverings, bandanas (damp or dry), handkerchiefs ... should not be relied on" (EPA Smoke Guide, p. 78). CFA lists a cotton scarf as an option (p. 7); this guide follows the EPA: cotton shields skin from embers, not lungs. Use an N95 or P100 marked "NIOSH", two head straps, no ear loops; a beard breaks the seal; replace it when breathing gets hard; it raises heat-illness risk (EPA Protect Your Lungs, pp. 1-2). For ages 2 to 7 an N95 rarely fits (EPA Smoke Guide, p. 77): children leave early. Smoke and carbon monoxide bring "headaches and visual impairment, then impaired decision-making, and possible death"; rotate people out, and don't sleep where "smoke can concentrate at night" (IRPG, p. 44). With no power for a filter fan, open windows at night to cool off even if some smoke comes in, then close them and the curtains
smoke-heat-and-people

night" (IRPG, p. 44). With no power for a filter fan, open windows at night to cool off even if some smoke comes in, then close them and the curtains by day (EPA Smoke Guide, p. 49); night inversions can hold smoke here, so look first. Heat and burns. Drink "lots of cool water often even if you don't feel thirsty" (CFA, p. 9). Care: Field Care ("Heat and cold in the Valley"; "Burns"); exhaustion: Home Defense ("Stress, fatigue and judgment").
smoke-heat-and-people

🐐 Animals and livestock Leave early, in daylight, to places agreed ahead (PNW 783, pp. 7-8). "Never leave pets behind"; keep them "indoors or leashed" (ODA, p. 2). Horses: Horse guide ("Local dangers"); poultry and rabbits: Chickens and Rabbits; goats: Goats. If they must stay (PNW 783, p. 8): a pasture "light on fuel", such as one "heavily grazed", or a ploughed paddock (CFA, p. 4); "remove rugs and halters" (p. 7); "Leave gates open"; feed and water for "seven to 10 days"; irrigation on; electricity and propane off; "disked, plowed or scraped ground" around the barn; dry bedding wetted or removed. A burning barn (4-H Horse, p. 61): "Never lock stall doors". Blindfold a horse that won't lead with a wet cloth. "Do not turn a horse loose, because it might run back into the barn." "Do not risk your own life". After: burned animals may hide pain; badly burned ones may need to be put down (PNW 783, pp. 8-9). Burns "may worsen for up to six (6) weeks"; froth from nose or mouth means fluid in the lungs (ODA, pp. 1-2).
animals-and-livestock

Hot ground, stump holes and mop-up - Stump holes: roots burn underground under hot ash; "Minor burns are often experienced due to burning stump holes" (PMS 465, p. 262). Probe ash with a tool before stepping, and mark holes (rule of thumb). - Mop-up "is normally a slow, tedious job": "break up and scatter burning fuels, then cool them down with water. Dig, scrape, and scatter." Water alone "can actually insulate hot spots" (PMS 465, p. 85). "dig out burning roots" and stir embers into dirt (p. 52). Crews mop up a set distance, "100 feet, 500 feet" (p. 51); do at least 100 ft around buildings (rule of thumb). - Mix ash and dirt "until all steaming and sizzling stops"; "Never just bury a fire" (ODFW, p. 34). A smoldering log can "break out afresh with a rising wind" (Scout Handbook 1911, p. 186).
hot-ground-stump-holes-and-mop-up

Burned trees - Warning signs: "Trees burning for any period of time"; "Dead, broken, or burning tops"; "Absence of needles, bark, or limbs"; "Leaning or hung-up trees"; "Potential for trees to domino" (IRPG, p. 36). Mark "No Work Zones" (p. 37). - Fall zone: a circle as wide as the tree is tall, up to 1.5 times, and farther downhill on a slope (FS-1273, p. 36). Trees with recent fire damage fail more (p. 56); near the house, take dead trees down the year they die (p. 84). Felling: Firewood guide ("Felling trees safely"). Keep out of a dead tree's fall zone, and stay farther away below it on a slope (FS-1273, p. 36).
burned-trees

Ash, ruins and wells - Ash from burned buildings can hold arsenic, lead, asbestos and caustic chemicals; dust masks don't stop asbestos or carbon monoxide. A burned lithium battery that pops, hisses or smokes: move "upwind at least ... (330 feet)" (EPA Smoke Guide, p. 120). - Ash from CCA-treated decks and fences "may contain lethal amounts of arsenic". Mist, don't dry-sweep; wash garden produce; children, pregnant women and elders stay out of cleanup (p. 121). - Fence any new sinkhole, "as it may be a dug well" (OWRD, p. 1). Don't use a propane cylinder with "fire damage" (propane safety, p. 8). - Water: see Water Purification ("After a wildfire") and Water Wells ("Keeping well water clean").
ash-ruins-and-wells

Debris flows and erosion A debris flow is a fast mudflow of soil, rock, trees and ash. On burned land one can start "after only a few minutes of heavy rainfall-about half an inch an hour or more", "days to years after a fire", travel many miles, and hit places "that were neither burned nor received any rain" (USGS, p. 1; Debris flow). USGS (same page): "LEAVE BEFORE A STORM ARRIVES. IF YOU WAIT, YOU ARE TOO LATE"; if you can't, "GET TO HIGH GROUND" (upstairs, the roof, uphill, a tree); listen for "cracking, breaking, roaring, or a fast-moving freight train". With no forecast, people below a burned slope go when the first hard rain of the season starts (rule of thumb). Slowing erosion by hand. Severe heat can make the top few inches of soil shed water ("hydrophobic"); treat first where "streams, roads or buildings are directly downslope" (OSU EM 9562, p. 2). - Contour logs need no fuel: burned trees 6-10 in thick, 10-30 ft long, laid across the slope "in full contact" with the ground so soil settles behind them (EM 9562, p. 3). - Straw mulch at 1-2 tons an acre (p. 2); straw-bale check dams last only "the first few storm events" (p. 3). Don't sow non-native grass: it does little the first year and can "increase fire hazard as they cure" (p. 2).
debris-flows-and-erosion

Replanting - Grasses, shrubs and hardwoods return on their own. For conifers, "Most seed falls within one or two tree lengths" of a seed tree, and bare mineral soil is a good seedbed for most (OSU EM 9561, p. 1). Thick-barked black and Oregon white oaks resist heat; tanoak and canyon live oak "re-sprout after being top-killed" (KBO oak guide, p. 45). - Use seed from "parent trees adapted to local conditions"; plantings fail from poor site preparation, competing plants and animal damage (EM 9561, p. 3). With no nursery, gather cones and seedlings from surviving local trees (rule of thumb). Near the house, plant fire-resistant kinds (PNW 590, p. 7; OSU privacy plants).
replanting

🤝 Neighbors: lookouts, signals and shared breaks "In rural areas, your neighbor can be at your home faster than any emergency response" (EM 9247, p. 2); now they are the only response. "Your Home Ignition Zone overlaps onto adjacent properties" (p. 5), and "your trees may pose a greater risk to your neighbor's home than to your own" (Ready, Set, Go!, p. 4). - Lookouts on worst-weather days, in turns, day and night, who know the triggers and sound the alarm "early, not late" (IRPG, p. 21; the rota (rule of thumb)). - Signals: agree an alarm ahead (Signals guide: "Whistles, bells and alarm codes", "The neighborhood OK/HELP plan"; Radio guide). Give a fire's "exact location" (ODFW, p. 34). No signal fires in fire season. - A meeting place such as a mailbox cluster, crossroads or central barn (MYN Rural, p. 1), and a road map of water, gates, fuel breaks, hazards and livestock (PNW 783, p. 7). - A road crew clears brush along the shared road out and keeps shared water signed and clear (P-737, p. 77). Mow or slash a 3 m (10 ft) break around each property (CFA, p. 4), joined along the lines; small owners can pool work (EC 1575, p. 3). - A new smoke is the best chance to stop a fire and also where firefighters die (IRPG, p. 19): go with tools
neighbors-lookouts-signals-and-shared-breaks

can pool work (EC 1575, p. 3). - A new smoke is the best chance to stop a fire and also where firefighters die (IRPG, p. 19): go with tools and water, LCES first (rule of thumb). Organizing: Community & Barter ("Forming a neighborhood group"; "Keeping watch").
neighbors-lookouts-signals-and-shared-breaks

🍂 Burning on purpose: wet season only The books put the fire season at June through September (AH 360, p. 211), but east winds peak in September and fall can stay dry. This library's rule: no open burning June-October, until real rain (rule of thumb). Oregon allowed burning only outside fire season, on burn days, with fines "up to $12,000 per day" (DEQ, p. 1), a permit from ODF and the fire district (EC 1574, p. 4), and liability "if the fire escapes" (p. 3). What not to burn, and the burn barrel: Sanitation ("Burning trash and brush, and ash"). Slash piles (EC 1574, pp. 3-4): 1. In the open, 10 ft from trees, snags and brush, 100 ft from streams, away from buildings, propane and power lines. 2. Twigs under ½ in at the bottom, limbs parallel, at least 4 ft wide and 4 ft high; cover it when about 80% built so it will light in the rain. 3. Burn "during daylight, and when it's wet or rainy with little or no wind", with "a shovel and water nearby". 4. Check it after: piles "may smolder for days or even weeks, roaring back to life in windy, warm weather, even during dry winter conditions" (p. 3). Stir and drown the last of it; look again after the next dry, windy day (rule of thumb). "Many wildfires start from
burning-on-purpose-wet-season-only

weather, even during dry winter conditions" (p. 3). Stir and drown the last of it; look again after the next dry, windy day (rule of thumb). "Many wildfires start from escaped burn piles", and broadcast burning around homes is "very risky" (EM 9184, p. 14). Never burn poison oak (p. 25). Fire in the oak woods. The region's low-elevation oak woodlands are "fire adapted", kept by "Relatively frequent low- to mixed-severity fire"; prescribed burns there go "prior to leaf out in the spring or after leaf fall in the autumn" (KBO oak guide, p. 45). Cultural burning, the way the valley's first peoples tended the land with fire, is covered in "Tending the land with fire" in Skills of the Valley's First Peoples (Cultural burning).

☢ Nuclear Fallout Guide What to do if there is a nuclear detonation or a radiation release: how to shelter, how long, how to protect food, water and animals, how to clean up, and when potassium iodide (KI) helps. The full manuals - shelter plans, the homemade KFM fallout meter, farm and livestock guides - are in Nuclear-Radiation\. ### The three rules 1. Get inside. Stay inside. Stay tuned. Most deaths from fallout are avoidable just by being behind enough mass in the first day or two. 2. Fallout is dust. It hurts you from what lands on and near you, so put mass and distance between you and the roof, walls and ground outside. 3. Time is on your side. Radiation from fallout drops fast - 90% in the first 7 hours, 99% in 2 days.

⚡ The first minutes - If you see a flash: drop behind anything solid, face down, cover your head, and don't look at it - the flash can blind you even when you are too far away for the blast to hurt you (FEMA H-20, p. 14). The blast wave can arrive many seconds later - stay down until it passes. Being outdoors in the first minute can mean burns, cuts from flying glass and broken bones (FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 76). What happens in those seconds: 🖼 flash, heat and blast drawing; Effects of nuclear explosions, Flash blindness. - Fallout near a blast can start arriving in 15-30 minutes; 100-200 miles downwind, often 5-10 hours or more. Use the time before it arrives to put out small fires, bring people, pets and water inside, and move to the best shelter you can reach. (FEMA Protection in the Nuclear Age, H-20, p. 7; 🖼 how fallout comes down; Nuclear fallout) - Officials will tell everyone within about 50 miles to shelter until they know where the fallout is going. (FEMA Planning Guidance, 3rd ed., p. 54) - Know the sirens. A 3-5 minute steady blast means "turn on the radio." A 3-5 minute wavering tone (or short blasts repeated) is the attack warning - go to shelter now. (FEMA H-20, p. 12; what they look like: Civil defense siren) First-hour
the-first-minutes

A 3-5 minute wavering tone (or short blasts repeated) is the attack warning - go to shelter now. (FEMA H-20, p. 12; what they look like: Civil defense siren) First-hour checklist: get people and pets inside; close doors, windows and blinds; take a few minutes to check the house for fires - stamp out smoldering drapes, throw burning furniture outside (FEMA H-20, p. 26); fill containers and tubs while the taps run (rule of thumb); carry food, water, radio, medicines and the toilet bucket to the shelter spot. 📚 Go deeper: FEMA H-20 Protection in the Nuclear Age - warning signals, the flash, fallout timing, fires; FEMA Planning Guidance, 3rd ed. - today's official "Get Inside, Stay Inside, Stay Tuned" advice.
the-first-minutes

🏠 Where to shelter Best to worst: a basement (especially a corner below ground level) → the middle floors and center of a large concrete or brick building → a crawl space or interior room of a house → a vehicle (poor). See the 🖼 FEMA drawing of protection inside different buildings and Fallout shelter. Protection factors: 10 means a tenth of the outdoor dose. A 1-story wood house gives only 2-3 on its main floor and 10 in a basement; basements and the middle of big buildings give the most (FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 78). Most homes in the Illinois Valley are one-story wood frame with no basement. FEMA says these, and vehicles, are not adequate shelter on their own (Planning Guidance, p. 76). Plan now: a nearby building with a basement or thick masonry, a crawl-space shelter you can shield, or an outdoor trench shelter (plans in MP-79, In Time of Emergency, and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix A - see the 🖼 Door-Covered Trench Shelter and 🖼 Pole-Covered Trench Shelter drawings). Permanent backyard plans: 🖼 FEMA H-12-1 outside concrete shelter, 🖼 FEMA H-12-2 aboveground shelter. - Inside any building: get as far from the roof and outside walls as you can, away from windows and doors. Close and lock windows, turn off fans, A/C and forced-air heat, close fireplace dampers. (CDC Where to Go; 🖼 CDC picture:
where-to-shelter

walls as you can, away from windows and doors. Close and lock windows, turn off fans, A/C and forced-air heat, close fireplace dampers. (CDC Where to Go; 🖼 CDC picture: best places inside a building) - No need to tape windows or hang plastic sheeting - fallout shelters don't have to be airtight. A building with minor damage still works if it is structurally sound. (EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 31; Planning Guidance, p. 76) - Stuck in a poor shelter? If a good one is under 15 minutes away, move within about 30 minutes of the blast, before heavy fallout arrives. If you're already in a moderate shelter, stay 1-2 hours, then move. (FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 77) "Adequate" means it cuts your dose 10× or more. Concrete, brick, stone and earth stop a lot; wood, drywall and sheet metal stop little (Planning Guidance, p. 76; 🖼 EPA dose-reduction diagram by building type). Adding shielding - each of these stops about as much as 4 inches of concrete (FEMA H-20, p. 22): | Material | Thickness | | Brick | 5-6 in | | Sand or gravel | 6 in | | Packed earth | 7 in | | Hollow concrete block (sand-filled) | 8 in (6 in) | | Water | 10 in | | Books or magazines | 14 in | | Wood (firewood stack) | 18
where-to-shelter

Hollow concrete block (sand-filled) | 8 in (6 in) | | Water | 10 in | | Books or magazines | 14 in | | Wood (firewood stack) | 18 in | Pile it on the floor above you and around the walls of your shelter spot: earth-filled drawers and boxes, water jugs, firewood, books, heavy furniture. Every extra ~4 inches of packed earth roughly halves what gets through - about 3 feet of earth cuts it around 1,000× (Nuclear War Survival Skills, 1979, p. 23: one "halving thickness" of packed earth is 3.6 in; 🖼 halving-thickness drawing; Radiation protection). Crawl space: shelter under the center of the house, ring yourself with blocks or earth-filled containers, and pile mass on the floor above. Each 3.6 in of packed earth halves what gets through, so about 3 ft cuts it around 1,000 times (a diagram drawn for this guide). Quick shelters, step by step (FEMA H-20, pp. 23-25; HS-4, p. 67): 1. Table shelter: a sturdy table or workbench in the most-underground basement corner, loaded on top and walled around with shielding. Crawl in and block the opening. (🖼 drawing of a basement table shelter) 2. Door-roof shelter: walls of dressers or appliances, a roof of heavy doors propped and piled with shielding. Fill drawers and boxes with earth after they're in place - full ones are too heavy to carry.

or appliances, a roof of heavy doors propped and piled with shielding. Fill drawers and boxes with earth after they're in place - full ones are too heavy to carry. 3. Crawl-space shelter: cut an access now. Under the middle of the house, wall a spot with blocks or earth-filled containers up to the joists and pile mass on the floor above. Make sure no heavy appliance sits right above you. Dig down so you can sit up. 4. Last resort: dig a trench beside a slab house and tunnel no more than 4 feet under the slab; shore it and pile shielding on the slab inside. A table shelter (step 1): heavy material stacked on and around a sturdy table in a basement corner; dirt in the window wells adds more (OCD H-6, p. 26). Ventilation: a crowded, sealed shelter gets dangerously hot in warm weather. Kearny's homemade air pump (KAP) - plans in Nuclear War Survival Skills and the ORNL Expedient Shelter Handbook - moves air without bringing in fallout dust (🖼 KAP swinging in a doorway; 🖼 photos of homemade KAPs). In a heat wave, plan on about 4 quarts of water and 10 grams of salt per person a day and as few clothes as practical (NWSS 1979, p. 62). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA H-20 - shielding table and home expedient shelters; FEMA HS-4 Citizen's Guide

🧰 Stocking the shelter FEMA says to have at least two weeks of water, food and supplies ready to carry to the shelter (H-20, p. 13; 🖼 illustrated 1961 supply chart). | Item | How much / what kind (FEMA H-20, pp. 29-31) | | Water | H-20's bare minimum is 1 quart per person per day just to drink; today FEMA advises storing 1 gallon per person per day. Kearny says store 15 gallons per person for two weeks (NWSS 1979, p. 71; 🖼 storing water in lined bags and pits). | | Food | Canned or sealed, no cooking needed. Most adults do fine on half their usual amount - not children or pregnant women. | | Toilet | Bucket with a tight lid, liner bags, a second lidded can, bleach, toilet paper (🖼 hose-vented toilet-can; Bucket toilet). | | Radio and light | Battery radio, flashlight, spare batteries - the radio "may be your only link." | | Medicines, babies | Two weeks of regular medicines and a first-aid kit; formula or canned milk and diapers. | | Tools | Shovel, pick, saw, hammer, crowbar, broom, nails, wire (H-20, p. 18). | - Water hiding in your house: the water heater (20-60 gallons), toilet tanks (not bowls) and the pipes - shut the main valve, open the highest faucet, draw from the lowest (H-20, pp. 31-32). Don't

house: the water heater (20-60 gallons), toilet tanks (not bowls) and the pipes - shut the main valve, open the highest faucet, draw from the lowest (H-20, pp. 31-32). Don't ration drinking water below thirst - nothing is gained by it. - Never burn charcoal indoors; any stove used inside needs good ventilation. - Toilet routine: a little bleach after each use, lid back on; when you can step out briefly, bury the waste 1-2 feet deep (H-20, p. 33). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA H-20, Part 4 "Shelter Living" - supply lists, water, food and sanitation; Expedient Shelter Handbook Appendix C - emergency water storage, lights and sanitation; Shelter Management Handbook H-16 - running a shelter with a group.

⏳ How long to stay in The 7-10 rule: every 7× increase in time after the blast cuts the radiation 10× (once the fallout has finished falling). (FEMA H-20, p. 8; see the 🖼 seven-ten rule chart and the 🖼 decay curve for the first two days) | Time after blast | Radiation level (example) | | 1 hour | 1,000 R/hr | | 7 hours | 100 R/hr | | 2 days | 10 R/hr | | 2 weeks | 1 R/hr | - Stay sheltered at least 12-24 hours unless officials say otherwise or fire, collapse or a medical emergency forces you out (FEMA Planning Guidance, pp. 53, 76). In heavy fallout areas it can be several days to two weeks, with only short trips out once levels drop (H-20, p. 9). 🧼 Cleaning yourself up (decontamination) (CDC Decontamination; EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 32; pictures: 🖼 CDC step-by-step sheet, 🖼 FEMA self-decontamination steps, Radioactive contamination) - Taking off your outer layer of clothes removes up to 90% of the fallout on you. Do it before you enter the shelter if you can, and do it gently so dust doesn't shake loose. Bag the clothes and put them away from people and pets. - Shower with soap and shampoo - no conditioner (it glues particles to hair). Don't scrub hard or scratch the skin; keep cuts covered. Keep suds out of your mouth and don't swallow the water. - No shower? Wipe exposed skin, blow your nose, wipe eyelids, ears and face with a damp cloth. - Clothes from closed drawers and closets are fine to wear. No clean clothes? Take off the outer layer, shake or brush it off, put it back on, then rewash your hands and face. - A cut or wound with fallout in it: flush with plenty of clean water or saline, or keep it covered (EPA Q&A, p. 33). - Visitors: have them strip the outer layer, bag it, and wash before coming in - then they're no danger to you (EPA Q&A, p. 33). Radiation sickness is not contagious (H-20, p. 9). - Pets: bring them in. Wash with soap or shampoo and water, wearing

💊 Potassium iodide (KI) - KI only protects the thyroid, and only from radioactive iodine. It does nothing against other fallout. Take it only when health officials say to - or, with no officials, when you have reason to believe fresh fallout or a reactor plume is arriving. Table salt and iodine tincture are not substitutes (tincture is poisonous to swallow). Iodine dietary supplements aren't either - use only FDA-approved KI. (CDC How KI Works; FDA, p. 12; 🖼 CDC picture sheet: how KI fills the thyroid; where the gland is: Thyroid) - One dose protects about 24 hours. It works best just before or as the plume arrives and still helps 3-4 hours after. Avoid repeat doses for newborns and pregnant or breastfeeding women. 🥫 Food and water (EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 29; FDA; Nuclear War Survival Skills Ch. 8) - Food that was indoors is fine. Sealed cans, jars and bags that were outside are fine after wiping the outside - bag the wiping cloths. Stored grain and canned food have no radioactive-iodine risk. - Don't eat garden produce or anything left uncovered outdoors until levels have dropped and it's declared clear - then wash and peel it. Leafy vegetables: strip the outer leaves of cabbage and lettuce and wash the rest thoroughly. Roots and tubers: normal washing and peeling is enough. Fruit: wash before eating. (FB 2107, p. 14; PA-515, p. 7) - Don't drink fresh milk from animals grazing fallout-covered pasture for the first weeks (radioactive iodine concentrates in milk). Milk made into cheese and aged two months or more is fine - the radioactive iodine (Iodine-131) decays away (it loses half its strength every 8 days - USDA Ag Handbook 234, p. 9; USDA puts the wait at 30-60 days - PA-515, p. 8). If you have a baby, keep canned or dry milk in a protected place. - Water: bottled and sealed water is certain. Covered wells, tanks and cisterns are the best sources; deep wells are well protected. Tap water is fine for washing. - Boiling does not remove radioactivity. To clean doubtful water: stir in clay

To clean doubtful water: stir in clay soil, let it settle several hours, and pour off the clear water - or filter it through a bucket of packed earth. Both remove most fallout particles. (Rain barrel) Water sources, safest first (NWSS 1979, pp. 76-77): deep wells and covered tanks → covered shallow wells → deep lakes → shallow ponds → streams (worst after the first heavy rains) → roof runoff → melted snow. With the power off, a well can still be used with a homemade bail-can on a rope (🖼 bail-can drawing; Well). Settling method (NWSS 1979, pp. 78-79): 1. Fill a bucket three-quarters full of the doubtful water. 2. Dig clay or clayey soil from at least 4 inches below the surface (fallout stays near the top). 3. Stir in about 1 inch of dry clay for every 4 inches of water until it's all suspended. 4. Let it settle at least 6 hours. The clay carries the fallout down. 5. Earth filter (NWSS 1979, pp. 77-78; 🖼 cut-away drawing of the filter can): 1. Punch about a dozen nail holes, from the bottom upward, within 2 inches of the center of the bottom of a 5-gallon can or bucket. 2. Put in 1½ inches of washed pebbles, then one layer of towel or burlap cut a bit bigger than the can. 3. Add 6-7 inches of crumbled soil with some clay in it, dug from 4+ inches deep, pressed down in layers. Not pure clay (too tight) or sand (too loose). 4. Cover with one layer of towel held by a few stones. Set the can on sticks over a pan. 5. Pour in (settled) water. Expect about 6 quarts an hour at first, 2 quarts an hour later. If it runs faster than a quart in 10 minutes, repack the soil. Replace the soil after about 50 quarts. Disinfect the filtered water. 🐄 Livestock and gardens (USDA FB 2107, pp. 8-14, PA-516; Oregon ODOE, p. 2) - Shelter animals if you can (a barn helps), and take them off pasture. Feed protected feed - hay from inside the stack, covered silage, grain from closed bins (🖼 USDA plan: dairy barn with a built-in family fallout shelter; Silage). - Water from a covered well, tank or flowing spring is best; open pond water clears more slowly but improves quickly. - Hold off on slaughter, fresh milk and eggs until levels drop. - Gardens: stop harvesting; after levels drop, wash and peel produce. 📟 Measuring radiation - A meter turns guessing into decisions - when to leave the shelter, which room is safest, whether the water is clear. - KFM (Kearny Fallout Meter): a homemade meter from a can, foil and paper. Build it before you need it. The patterns must print exactly to scale - check against a ruler; OISM warns online copies of the templates aren't fully reliable and recommends the printed book. Full patterns and tables: ORNL-5040 and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix C. See it first: 🖼 photos of a finished KFM, 🖼 full-scale cut-away drawing. It is a kind of electroscope. - Old civil-defense meters turn up at sales: the yellow CD V-715 reads high levels (fallout); the CD V-700 is a low-range Geiger counter for checking food, water and people (Geiger counter). Manuals and a home-study course are in Nuclear-Radiation\Measuring-Radiation. What a KFM is made of (ORNL-5040, pp. 33, 39): an 8-ounce can (or a cut-down soup can), 2 square feet of aluminum foil, clean thread, clear plastic, doorbell wire. A drying agent goes in the bottom - gypsum from heated drywall, or silica gel, not calcium chloride or salt. Charge it by rubbing a plastic ruler on dry paper (🖼 the other way: charging with unrolled tape). Using it (ORNL-5040, pp. 69-73): 1. Charge it and read the gap between the two foil leaves on the

on dry paper (🖼 the other way: charging with unrolled tape). Using it (ORNL-5040, pp. 69-73): 1. Charge it and read the gap between the two foil leaves on the paper scale. 2. Hold it on a stick about 3 feet above the ground for a set time - 1 minute if you have no idea of the level - then read again. The table on the meter turns the drop into a dose rate. 3. ⚡ EMP, Solar Storms & Faraday Cages What a nuclear electromagnetic pulse (EMP) or a severe solar storm would really do, how to protect radios, solar gear and this library, how to build and test a Faraday container, what to do when a solar-storm warning comes, and how to check and repair equipment afterward. It's based on what government tests actually measured, not internet stories. The reports are in EMP-Solar-Storms\ (Effects-and-Threat, Protection-Shielding, Grounding-Surge, Recovery). ### The short version - The danger comes in through long wires - power lines, antennas, long cables. Small gear that isn't plugged into anything mostly survives. - Unplugged, switched-off cars and trucks were not affected in tests; a few running ones stalled and restarted. - A solar storm threatens the power grid, not your phone. You'd likely get 18-72 hours' warning. - The real long-term problem is the grid going down for months. Plan for that (see the off-grid power section of the Illinois Valley guide). - Keep spares and a second copy of this library in a metal container, sealed at the seams.

🔌 Rule one: unplug and disconnect Wires are the antennas. Even a few feet of cable can pick up thousands of volts from E1; long power and antenna lines pick up far more (Low Cost EMP Protection (Navy 1982)). (CISA guidelines, p. 44; 🖼 drawing: E1 reaches a radio the way a broadcast or lightning does) - Unplug at the device - power, data and antenna cables - not just at the wall. Coil any cable you can't remove. - Pull battery packs from small electronics in storage; turn phones and radios off and take them off chargers. - Disconnect outdoor antennas and coax (Coaxial cable) from radios when not in use. - Unplug everything or nothing: pulling only a TV's power cord while it stays on cable or phone lines removes its ground path (NIST Surges Happen, p. 11; 🖼 NIST drawing of a surge crossing between two connections). - Backup generators: don't leave one connected to the grid through an automatic transfer switch without strong surge protection - the utility line can carry the pulse in (CISA, p. 45; Transfer switch). A generator stored disconnected is far better off. - Surge protectors still help with lightning and the surge when power comes back - just don't count on them for E1. Keep spare protectors and fuses (Surge protector). Long power and antenna wires collect the pulse; unplug at

surge when power comes back - just don't count on them for E1. Keep spare protectors and fuses (Surge protector). 🗑 Faraday containers: building one that works How it works: a closed metal shell keeps the pulse on the outside. It only works if the shell is continuous - the leaks are at seams, lid edges and holes, and a long narrow slot leaks far more than a round hole. Seams must be bare metal touching bare metal (no paint) (MIL-HDBK-419A Vol 1, p. 275; 🖼 how fields leak through an opening; 🖼 a badly joined seam, warped between rivets; Electromagnetic shielding). A plain metal box is not automatically a Faraday cage - ordinary cabinets gave little protection until their seams were taped and gasketed (Navy 1982). Options, best to simplest (CISA, pp. 45, 86): 1. Metal can with a tight metal lid (galvanized trash can, paint can, cookie tin, steel ammo can - Waste container, Ammunition box): - Wrap each item in a plastic or paper bag or cardboard so it doesn't touch the metal. - Seal the lid seam with conductive tape (aluminum or copper foil tape - the kind with conductive glue) all the way around. Trash cans leak at the lid, handles and base unless sealed. - Ammo cans: the rubber gasket breaks metal contact - scrape a strip of bare metal at the rim and add conductive tape over the closed lid seam (rule of thumb). - No wires passing through. Don't drill holes (🖼

scrape a strip of bare metal at the rim and add conductive tape over the closed lid seam (rule of thumb). - No wires passing through. Don't drill holes (🖼 right and wrong ways through a shield). 2. Foil wrap: item in a plastic bag, then 2 or more layers of heavy-duty foil, every seam folded and overlapped, any cables inside the wrap (Aluminium foil; folded-over joint: 🖼 overlap seam). 3. Nesting adds protection: a foil-wrapped item inside a sealed metal can is better than either alone. 4. Microwave oven (unplugged, never switched on; Microwave oven): an expedient shield for small items - test it first. Wrap each item, tape the lid seam all the way round with conductive tape, and leave no holes or wires through (a diagram drawn for this guide). Bag, then two or more layers of foil with folded seams, then, best of all, a sealed can (a diagram drawn for this guide). Weak or useless: Mylar food bags (little protection); refrigerators (plastic liner and rubber gasket); many cheap "Faraday bags" (the closure leaks). Does it need a ground wire? No - a closed storage container doesn't need to be grounded (rule of thumb). How good is good enough? For stored spare electronics, CISA considers 20 dB of shielding adequate (CISA appendix, p. 126); critical military gear uses 80 dB (DHS 2022). See the difference: 🖼

Testing yours (and what it doesn't prove): - Put a phone inside and call it, and a battery AM/FM radio tuned to a station. If the call won't ring and the radio goes silent, the shell has no big leaks at those frequencies. - This is a rough check, not a measurement - silence just means the signal dropped below what the radio can hear. NOAA rates geomagnetic storms G1 to G5 (NOAA Space Weather Scales): | Level | How often (per 11-year cycle) | What happens | | G3 strong | ~200 | Grid voltage corrections; GPS and HF radio come and go; auroras as far south as Oregon (Aurora) | | G4 severe | ~100 | Widespread grid voltage problems; some protection systems trip; GPS degraded for hours | | G5 extreme | ~4 | Grid collapse and transformer damage possible; HF radio out 1-2 days; GPS degraded for days | For a G4-G5 warning (rule of thumb): 1. Charge batteries, power banks, radios and laptops; fill water containers; get fuel. 2. Unplug sensitive electronics from the wall - the risk is outages and surges when power returns. 3. Disconnect long outdoor antennas and feedlines. 4. Expect GPS and HF radio to be unreliable; have paper maps (Maps\) and use VHF/UHF locally. 5. Solar panels don't need protecting from a solar storm - their wiring is far too short. (S5 "solar panel damage" on NOAA's scale means satellites.) 6. Have the generator ready, connected only through a transfer switch or interlock - never backfeed. 📚 Go deeper: NOAA scales, p. 1; LANL

🔧 After an event: check and repair 1. Power-cycle anything that's locked up - in tests most "upsets" cleared this way (Harry Diamond Labs, p. 44). 2. Vehicles: restart. If one won't run, disconnect the battery for several minutes to reset the electronics, then check fuses (EMP Commission 2008, p. 131). 3. Fuses and breakers (Circuit breaker): a surge protector firing can blow the equipment's fuse - check and replace. Breakers are likely fine; reset them (ORNL radio study; Sandia breakers). 4. Surge protectors fail one of two ways: no power, or power with no protection left. Replace any that took a hit (NIST Surges Happen, p. 7). 5. Look and sniff: burnt smell, scorch marks, swollen or leaking capacitors. Discharge big capacitors before touching (inverters, microwaves, power supplies). What to look for: 🖼 scorch marks where a capacitor blew off a board; 🖼 a resistor exploding under a test pulse; swollen capacitors: Capacitor plague. 6. Radios: if dead, suspect the antenna input stage and power supply first - those took the damage in tests (ORNL radio study). 7. Solar: panels are probably fine; test the charge controller and inverter; swap in shielded spares. 8. Generators: check the output breaker, brushes and voltage regulator - see the Engines guide. 9. 📖 Stories, Games and Fun for Long Evenings How to keep spirits up and children learning when the power is gone and the winter evenings are long: why stories, play and a steady routine matter so much in hard times, how to open the library's books and e-books, what to read aloud at each age, teaching reading and numbers at the kitchen table, telling stories with no book, games that need no power (cards, board games you can scratch on a plank, group and outdoor games, string figures, pencil-and-paper and word games), toys to make, songs, home-made books and plays, safe light to read by, and a simple evening routine. The activity books are in Stories\Games-and-Things-to-Make; the classic stories are in Stories\Picture-Books-and-Rhymes, Stories\Read-Aloud-and-Early-Readers, Stories\Ages-9-to-13 and Stories\Teens-and-Adults; the McGuffey readers and Ray's arithmetic are in Children-Learning; the books on stress and children are in Community-Barter\Wellbeing (all under Southern-Oregon\; the download list is local/library-files.txt). Page numbers are the PDF page numbers, so they match the links. ### The short version - Give every day the same shape: meals, chores, play, a story, bed at the same time. "Children feel safest when there is order and predictability" (SPR, p. 101; FEMA, p. 189). - Read aloud every evening, teens included. A flame "smaller than that of a birthday candle" is enough to read by with foil behind it (Kearny, p. 104). - Play

- Read aloud every evening, teens included. A flame "smaller than that of a birthday candle" is enough to read by with foil behind it (Kearny, p. 104). - Play is how children tell you what scared them. Disaster or violent play is normal; name the feelings with them. The same upsetting scene over and over means they need more help (PFA, p. 140). - Fun needs almost nothing: one deck of cards, a 6-ft string tied into a loop (Jayne, p. 36), stones on a board scratched into a plank, beans, corn husks, a handkerchief. - Plan one thing to do alone and one with others each day, and don't let anyone sit alone doing nothing for long (SPR, pp. 99, 101). Grown-ups too. - Older children can teach and mind younger ones, but not near water: many child drownings happen "in the company of other children" (WHO, p. 90). - Lamps and matches out of reach of children (Where There Is No Doctor, p. 22); never fall asleep with a lamp burning (FM 21-76, p. 182). - Skip the old books' fire balloons, fireworks, gunpowder, melted lead, arsenic and acids. See "Old advice in the library to ignore".

🧠 Why stories, play and routine matter - Children copy the grown-ups. They "look to adults for cues about safety" (PFA, p. 35), and their reactions "are influenced by the behavior, thoughts, and feelings of adults" (FEMA, p. 189). A calm evening of cards and a story tells them more than any speech. - Routine gives back a sense of control. Disasters "disrupt normal routines and activities that provide a sense of purpose, control, and pleasure"; planning pleasant activities helps mood and control come back (SPR, p. 31). FEMA's list: hug and touch your children, spend extra time with them "such as at bedtime", "re-establish your daily routine for work, school, play, meals, and rest", and give them real chores so they feel they are helping (FEMA, p. 189). - What helps, according to the disaster workers' handbook: toys, playing cards, board games, balls, paper, crayons and books; building blocks, play dough, cut-outs and team games are calming; older children reading to younger ones; and for teens, music, games, "making up and telling stories, or making a scrapbook" (PFA, p. 36). For children it also recommends "reading out loud, doing a joint art activity, and playing cards, board games, or sports" (p. 35). - Singing pulls a group together. "A short time devoted to singing will do more to unify the people and bring them into a neighborly and co-operative

"A short time devoted to singing will do more to unify the people and bring them into a neighborly and co-operative spirit than anything else possible" (Golden Book, p. 122). - Join in. "Nothing can more quickly gain the respect and affection of a child" than a grown-up who plays (Bancroft, p. 40). - Babies and toddlers learn by play and talk. From age 2: "Teach your child stories, songs and games. Talk about pictures or books" (WHO/UNICEF cards, p. 2). With no toys: "Use any household objects that are clean and safe. Make simple toys. Play with the child" (p. 3). The age-by-age table is in "Keeping children learning at home" in the Childbirth & Children guide. - Grown-ups need it too. 📚 Reading aloud by age How to read aloud (rule of thumb unless cited): - Same time and place every evening, one lamp, everyone close. Little ones on a lap or beside you. - Read a little slower than you talk, and do the voices. Stop at an exciting moment so they beg for tomorrow. - Let them hear favorites again. Children love "some degree of repetition", along with "action, in close sequence" and familiar things "tinged with mystery" (Bryant, p. 76). - Ask "what do you think happens next?" and let a child who can read take a page or a part. - Don't stop reading aloud when they can read alone: a chapter a night of a long book holds a family together, and teens will listen to books that are too hard for them to read yet. - Old books, old attitudes. About 50 of the classics are marked "Some words and attitudes are of its time" in their library description. That is a good thing to talk about while reading aloud: how people saw things then, and why we see them differently now. With little ones, change a word or skip a page.
